osce.title: Requesting a diagnostic wax-up
osce.text:
OSCE 1 — Requesting a diagnostic wax-up
Blueprint: Diagnostic wax-ups (W + OS-P + SCE). This is RCSEd’s own published sample station (Appendix D) — expect a version of it.
Station purpose: to test understanding of the practical steps needed for a diagnostic wax-up when plan-
ning an implant-retained prosthesis. Equipment: pre-operative photographs of the patient with and
without the denture. No interaction with the examiner.
CANDIDATE INSTRUCTIONS
Venue: clinic. You are about to request a diagnostic wax-up to ascertain the most appropriate implant-retained tooth
replacement option. The patient is a middle-aged edentulous patient. They are unhappy with the complete denture they
have worn for 15 years and would like something fixed, but do not want to change or compromise the facial appearance,
which they like. You have pre-operative photographs with and without the denture. Describe the practical steps you would
take for requesting the diagnostic wax-up, including the request to the laboratory. You are not expected to go into details of
the site of implant placement or the risks or benefits of implant treatment.
DIRECTION OF THOUGHT
The key clinical fact is “does not want to change the facial appearance which they like.” The denture flange is providing
lip support. A fixed prosthesis without a flange may not reproduce it. So the wax-up here is not decoration —
it is the diagnostic test of whether a fixed prosthesis is possible at all. Structure: records →mounting →
prescription →verification. End with what you would do with the result.
MODEL ANSWER
“I would start by explaining the purpose to the patient and taking consent, including consent for
clinical photographs, which I already have. I would record the existing denture in detail because it
is my reference for the appearance the patient likes.
Records: primary impressions in stock trays, or an intraoral scan, and cast a study model of both
arches. I would then make special trays and take definitive impressions in an elastomeric material —
addition silicone or polyether — and also duplicate the existing denture so the laboratory has the
current tooth position and flange contour to work from.
I would take an interocclusal record at the patient’s existing occlusal vertical dimension, having
first checked the freeway space, and a facebow record, and mount the casts on a semi-adjustable
articulator.
Clinically I would record: the midline, the incisal level at rest and on smiling, the smile line, the
occlusal plane, the amount of lip support currently provided by the flange, the shade and the tooth
mould.
My written laboratory prescription would identify the patient and me, give the date required, and
ask specifically for a diagnostic wax-up of the planned teeth set to reproduce the tooth positions
and lip support of the existing denture, at the recorded vertical dimension, and would ask the
technician to indicate whether that tooth position can be achieved without a labial flange. I would
ask for a duplicate in clear acrylic to serve as a radiographic guide, with radiopaque markers, and a
vacuum-formed matrix or putty index for a chairside mock-up. I would state the materials and ask
for the work to be returned disinfected, and I would keep the custom-made device statement in the
notes.
When it returns, I would try the wax-up in the mouth as a trial denture or mock-up, check it with the
patient in a mirror, assess lip support, speech and appearance, photograph it, and only then decide
whether a fixed prosthesis is realistic. If the wax-up shows the appearance depends on the flange, I
would discuss an implant-retained overdenture instead. I would record all of this in the notes.”

EXAMINER CHECKLIST
1. Explains purpose/consent
2. Photographs and duplicate of existing denture
3. Primary then definitive impressions in an appropriate material (or scan)
4. Interocclusal record at recorded OVD
5. Facebow and articulator mounting
6. Records aesthetic parameters (midline, incisal level, smile line, lip support, shade)
7. Written laboratory prescription with specific instructions
8. Requests duplicate for radiographic guide ± matrix
9. Verification/try-in in the mouth with the patient
10. States the decision the wax-up will inform (flange vs no flange) and records it
Pitfalls. Reciting a generic impression sequence without engaging with the lip-support problem; forget-
ting the written prescription; forgetting to try the wax-up in the mouth.
Running this station to time
Time check. The model answer is 717 words, 5 minutes 7 seconds at 140 words per minute — and because
this station carries no interaction with the examiner, there is no question to break the delivery and no
prompt to rescue an omission: whatever is not said is simply not marked. About 250 words must go,
by naming each record in a clause and spending the recovered time on the prescription and the flange
decision.

The compressed answer — what a strong candidate says in five minutes
“This patient likes their face, and it is the flange of the present denture that is producing that lip support
— so this wax-up is not decoration, it is the test of whether a fixed prosthesis is possible at all.
Consent and the reference. I explain the purpose and take consent, including for the clinical photographs
I already have. The existing denture is my record of the appearance they like, so I describe it in the notes
and duplicate it for the laboratory.
Records. Primary impressions in stock trays or an intraoral scan, study casts of both arches; special trays;
definitive impressions in addition silicone or polyether. An interocclusal record at the existing occlusal
vertical dimension, having first checked the freeway space, a facebow record, and both casts mounted on
a semi-adjustable articulator.
Clinical measurements, recorded before the patient leaves: the midline, the incisal level at rest and on
smiling, the smile line, the occlusal plane, the lip support the flange is currently giving, the shade and
the mould.
The prescription is written, not spoken. It identifies the patient and me, gives the date required, and
asks for a diagnostic wax-up set to reproduce the tooth position and lip support of the existing denture
at the recorded vertical dimension, working from the duplicate. Then the instruction that matters: I ask
the technician to state whether that tooth position can be achieved without a labial flange. I also ask
for a duplicate of the wax-up in clear acrylic with radiopaque markers as a radiographic guide, and a
vacuum-formed matrix or putty index for a chairside mock-up. I state the materials, ask for the work back
disinfected, and keep the custom-made device statement in the notes.
When it returns, I try it in the mouth — as a trial denture or mock-up, not judged on the articulator. I
look at it with the patient in a mirror, assess lip support, speech and appearance, and photograph it in the
same views as the pre-operative photographs so the two compare directly.
Then the decision the whole exercise exists to make. If the tooth position and lip support can be repro-
duced without a flange, a fixed implant-retained prosthesis is realistic and I plan from that wax-up. If the
appearance depends on the flange — and after fifteen years of resorption it often does — a fixed bridge
will not give this patient the face they want, and I would discuss an implant-retained overdenture, which
keeps the flange, before any implant is planned.
And I record all of it: the consent, the records taken, a copy of the written prescription, the try-in findings
and the photographs, what I told the patient about the flange, and the review at which we agree which
option to proceed with.”
Marking priority when the clock beats the candidate
Ask for these first (the six that carry the station): 7 written prescription with specific instructions ·
10 the flange-versus-no-flange decision, stated and recorded · 9 try-in in the mouth with the patient ·
2 photographs and duplicate of the existing denture · 6 aesthetic parameters, above all lip support · 4
interocclusal record at the recorded OVD.
Accept these late or on prompting: 1 purpose and consent · 3 primary then definitive impressions in an
appropriate material · 5 facebow and articulator mounting · 8 duplicate for the radiographic guide, plus
matrix.
The commonest way five minutes is wasted here: reciting a generic complete-denture impression se-
quence — stock trays, border moulding, wash impression, tray adhesive — for two minutes, as though
the station were about impressions. The prescription then arrives at four minutes and the try-in, the flange
decision and the records never arrive at all. The photographs were put on the table because the answer is
about lip support, and with a silent examiner nobody will steer the candidate back.

osce.title: Selecting a guide and transferring the plan to surgery
osce.text:
OSCE 2 — Selecting a guide and transferring the plan to surgery
Blueprint: “Request the appropriate radiographic and surgical guides”; “Demonstrate an ability to select guides to optimize the planning and
execute treatment”; “Explain transfer of planning information into the surgical procedure using appropriate guides” (W + OS-P + SCE).
EQUIPMENT
study casts with a wax-up of a missing UR2 and LR6, a clear acrylic radiographic guide, examples of non-limiting, partially
limiting and fully limiting guides, a CBCT printout.
CANDIDATE INSTRUCTIONS
Two implant sites are planned: the UR2 and the LR6. Using the models and guides provided, describe the type of guide
you would select for each and explain how the information from your planning is transferred into the surgical procedure.
DIRECTION OF THOUGHT
Two different sites, two different answers. Anterior = aesthetic, high precision of angulation and depth, tooth-
supported partially limiting or fully guided. Posterior = anatomical risk (canal), fully guided or partially
limiting plus direction indicator and radiograph. Always: guide derived from the wax-up, radiopaque markers,
safety margin retained.
MODEL ANSWER
“The starting point for both is the diagnostic wax-up, because the guide is how I make the surgery
restoratively driven.
I would duplicate the wax-up in clear acrylic and place radiopaque markers — gutta-percha or
barium sulphate — in the planned tooth positions to make a radiographic guide. The patient wears
this for the CBCT, which lets me relate the planned tooth position to the available bone.
For the UR2 I would use a tooth-supported guide, which is the most accurate support. Because the
aesthetic tolerance is small, I would use at least a partially limiting guide indicating the entry point
and angle, or a fully limiting sleeve guide if I have merged the CBCT with an intraoral scan. My
planning target is the shoulder about 3 mm apical to the planned mid-facial gingival margin and
1–2 mm palatal to the emergence of the adjacent teeth, angled through the cingulum so the screw
channel emerges palatally.
For the LR6 the critical constraint is the inferior alveolar canal. I would plan a length that leaves at
least 2 mm of clearance, and use a tooth-supported guide with a drill stop, or a fully guided protocol.
Even with a guide, I would keep the 2 mm safety margin because static guided surgery has a mean
angular deviation of about 2 to 4 degrees and apical deviation of about 1.3 to 1.6 mm.
Transfer into surgery: the guide is seated and its fit verified on the teeth before the flap is raised; I
check it is fully seated and stable, that the patient can open far enough for the drill and sleeve assem-
bly, and that irrigation can reach the osteotomy. After the pilot drill I place a direction indicator
and take a periapical radiograph at the LR6 to confirm angulation and depth before continuing. I
record the guide type used and the final implant position.
Limitations I would state: a guide does not compensate for a poorly fitting guide or for lack of
anatomical knowledge, sleeves restrict irrigation, and posterior access may be inadequate.”
EXAMINER CHECKLIST
1. Guide derived from the wax-up
2. Radiographic guide with radiopaque markers
3. Tooth-supported preferred
4. Correct 3-D targets for the anterior site
5. 2 mm canal safety margin posteriorly
6. Names the levels of guidance (non-limiting/partially/fully limiting)
7. Verifies guide seating and access before drilling
8. Direction indicator + radiograph
9. States guided-surgery accuracy limits
10. Records what was used

Running this station to time
Time check. The model answer is 575 words, 4 minutes 6 seconds at 140 words per minute — but there
are two sites needing two different answers, three guides to pick up and compare and a CBCT printout to
refer to, which pushes honest delivery past six minutes. The fix is a fixed 90 seconds per site on one frame
— support, level of guidance, the single controlling constraint — with the shared wax-up and radiographic-
guide preamble compressed to two sentences.

Checklist 10 — records: guide type and
level of guidance used, the verification
radiograph, the final implant position,
system, diameter and length; what the
patient is told (the guide is worn for the
scan, and it assists but does not replace
judgement); and review, with the guide
retained until the case is restored.
The compressed answer — what a strong candidate says in five minutes
“Both guides start from the diagnostic wax-up, because the guide is how I make the surgery restoratively
driven rather than driven by the shape of the bone.

osce.title: Flap design and atraumatic elevation
osce.text:
OSCE 3 — Flap design and atraumatic elevation
Blueprint: “Evaluate the different flap designs and design the appropriate flap”; “importance of raising the flap atraumatically” (W + OS-P + SCE).
EQUIPMENT
a typodont/pig jaw model with an edentulous UL1 site showing a buccal concavity; scalpel handle, blades, periosteal eleva-
tors, retractors.
CANDIDATE INSTRUCTIONS

An implant is to be placed at the UL1 with simultaneous guided bone regeneration for a buccal dehiscence. Using the model
and instruments provided, describe and, where possible, demonstrate your flap design and how you would raise the flap
atraumatically.
DIRECTION OF THOUGHT
Aesthetic zone + GBR = need access, need to preserve papillae, need coronal advancement for tension-free
closure, need incisions on sound bone away from the membrane.
MODEL ANSWER
“Design principles first: adequate access for the implant, the graft and the membrane; a base wider
than the apex to preserve blood supply; incisions over sound bone and not over the graft or the
membrane edge; preservation of the papillae because this is the aesthetic zone; and a design that
allows tension-free primary closure.
I would use a slightly palatally displaced crestal incision across the edentulous UL1 site, extended
intrasulcularly to the UL2 and UR1 with papilla-sparing incisions, and a single vertical relieving
incision at the mesial line angle of the UL3 — placed at the line angle, not through a papilla, and
away from where the membrane will sit. A second relieving incision distal to the UR1 only if I need
more advancement.
I would incise firmly to bone in one stroke, then elevate a full-thickness mucoperiosteal flap using
a sharp periosteal elevator, starting at the vertical incision and working against the bone rather than
against the tissue, so the periosteum lifts cleanly. I would retract with a broad retractor resting on
bone, never crushing the flap margin, handle the flap only at its base with tissue forceps, and keep
it moist with saline-soaked gauze.
For tension-free closure over the membrane I would make a periosteal releasing incision at the
base of the buccal flap, scoring the periosteum with the blade almost parallel to the flap and then
blunt-dissecting, taking care not to perforate the flap. I would test with tissue forceps that the flap
passively reaches 3–4 mm beyond the closure line without tension.
Closure: horizontal mattress sutures to evert and take the tension, with interrupted sutures between
them for accurate margin adaptation, using 5/0 monofilament or ePTFE, with the suture line lying
over sound bone rather than over the membrane.”
EXAMINER CHECKLIST
1. States access/blood supply/sound-bone/tension-free principles
2. Palatally displaced crestal incision
3. Papilla preservation
4. Vertical relief at a line angle, away from the graft
5. Firm incision to bone
6. Sharp elevator working against bone
7. Broad retractor on bone; flap handled at the base; kept moist
8. Periosteal releasing incision described safely
9. Tests for passive closure
10. Appropriate suture material and technique
Running this station to time
Time check. The model answer is 484 words, 3 minutes 27 seconds at 140 words per minute — but the
verb is describe and, where possible, demonstrate, so the words are spoken while the hands pick up a blade,
elevate on a model and test a flap, which runs at perhaps two-thirds of reading speed. Realistically that
is the whole five minutes with nothing spare, and the compression is to state each design principle in a
single clause before the blade is picked up, then narrate continuously while working.

wider than the apex so the blood supply is preserved; incisions over sound bone and never over the graft

lost papilla; and a design that will allow tension-free primary closure over a membrane.

UL3 — at the line angle, not through the papilla, and deliberately away from where the membrane will

osce.title: Suturing (practical)
osce.text:
OSCE 4 — Suturing (practical)
Blueprint: “Consider and justify the choice of suture material and technique used for wound closure” (W + OS-P + SCE).
EQUIPMENT
suturing pad or pig jaw with a raised flap over a simulated graft site; needle holders, tissue forceps, scissors; a selection of
sutures (3/0 silk, 4/0 Vicryl, 5/0 ePTFE, 5/0 monofilament nylon).
CANDIDATE INSTRUCTIONS
A buccal flap has been raised and a bone graft placed with a collagen membrane. Select an appropriate suture and demon-
strate closure. Explain your choice of material and technique as you work.
DIRECTION OF THOUGHT
Over a membrane →monofilament/ePTFE, not silk. Technique →horizontal or vertical mattress to take tension
and evert, plus interrupted. Say the removal time.

MODEL ANSWER
“I would choose a 5/0 ePTFE or monofilament suture on a reverse-cutting 3/8 circle needle. I would
avoid braided silk here because it is multifilament and wicks bacteria into a grafted site, which risks
membrane contamination.
I will place horizontal mattress sutures first to evert the wound edges and carry the tension, then
simple interrupted sutures between them to adapt the margins precisely.
Technique: I pass from the mobile buccal flap to the fixed palatal tissue, entering perpendicular
to the surface about 3 mm from the margin, taking equal bites of each side and equal depth, so the
edges meet passively. I position the knot to one side of the incision line, and I tie so that the tissue is
approximated but not blanched — tension causes ischaemia, necrosis and membrane exposure.
I would remove these sutures at 10 to 14 days because the site is grafted, rather than the usual 7 to
10 days, and I would review the closure at one week for any sign of dehiscence.”
EXAMINER CHECKLIST
1. Selects monofilament/ePTFE and justifies avoiding silk
2. Appropriate size (4/0–5/0)
3. Correct needle handling in the needle holder (2/3 from the tip)
4. Mobile to fixed
5. Perpendicular entry ~3 mm from the margin, equal bites
6. Mattress suture placed and named correctly
7. Interrupted sutures for adaptation
8. Knot placed off the incision line, secure throws
9. Approximation without blanching
10. States removal time and review
Running this station to time
Time check. The model answer is only 365 words, 2 minutes 36 seconds at 140 words per minute — which
looks generous and is not. This is a performance station: the marks are in the hands, and threading
a needle, placing a horizontal mattress and two interrupted sutures and tying them takes three to four
minutes on a pad even when the fingers are practised, with speech running at perhaps half rate while
the hands work. The rule here is not to cut words but to front-load every justification into the first 45
seconds, then let the hands run.
The five-minute run sheet

The examiner does
What earns the mark

because the site is grafted, not the usual
7 to 10; then records (material, size,
number and type of sutures), what the

mid-suture: it is the row candidates most
often reach after the bell.
The compressed answer — what a strong candidate says in five minutes
“Choosing first, while I open the pack. I would use a 5/0 ePTFE or monofilament nylon on a reverse-
cutting three-eighths circle needle. I would not use the braided silk here: it is multifilament, it wicks
bacteria along its length into a grafted site, and contamination of that membrane is what causes the graft
to fail. Five-oh in the aesthetic zone gives me accurate adaptation with the least tissue trauma; four-oh
would be acceptable posteriorly.
Loading the needle. I hold it in the needle holder about two-thirds of the way back from the tip, on the
tips of the beaks rather than in the joint, so I do not bend or blunt it.
Direction of the pass. Always from the mobile buccal flap to the fixed palatal tissue — I move the side
that moves, and the fixed tissue anchors it.
The bite. I enter perpendicular to the surface, about 3 millimetres from the margin, and take equal
bites and equal depth on each side, so that the edges rise to meet each other passively rather than being
dragged together.
The technique, and why. I place horizontal mattress sutures first. They evert the wound edges and, more
importantly, they carry the tension away from the margin itself — over a graft and a membrane, the
margin is the last place I want load. Then I place simple interrupted sutures between them for accurate
adaptation of the edges, because the mattresses alone leave the margin slightly open.
Tying. Secure throws, and I lay the knot to one side of the incision line, not on it, so it does not sit in the
wound and act as a plaque trap.
And the judgement that matters. I tie so the tissue is approximated but not blanched. If the edges
blanch I have made them ischaemic; ischaemia becomes necrosis, and necrosis over a membrane becomes
membrane exposure and a failed graft. If I cannot close it without blanching, the answer is not a tighter
suture — it is to go back and release the flap further with a periosteal releasing incision.
Afterwards. I would remove these at 10 to 14 days rather than the usual 7 to 10, because the site is
grafted and I want the closure supported for longer. I record the material, the size, and the number and
type of sutures placed. I tell the patient not to disturb them with their tongue, not to brush over them, to
keep the rest of the mouth clean, and to ring me if anything opens or if they can see the membrane. And
I review at one week to check for dehiscence, which is when it declares itself.”
Marking priority when the clock beats the candidate
Ask for these first (the six that carry the station): 1 monofilament or ePTFE selected and silk rejected
with the reason · 6 mattress suture placed and correctly named · 9 approximated without blanching, with
the consequence · 10 removal at 10–14 days over a graft, plus review · 4 mobile flap to fixed tissue · 7
interrupted sutures for margin adaptation.
Accept these late or on prompting: 2 size 4/0–5/0 stated · 3 needle held two-thirds from the tip in the
needle holder · 5 perpendicular entry about 3 mm from the margin with equal bites · 8 knot laid off the
incision line.

osce.title: Implant site preparation
osce.text:
OSCE 5 — Implant site preparation
Blueprint: “Demonstrate understanding of the principles of site preparation for the placement of dental implants” (W + OS-P + SCE).
EQUIPMENT
bone-analogue block or model, surgical motor (may be non-functional), a drill sequence, direction indicators, depth gauge,
torque ratchet, irrigation.
CANDIDATE INSTRUCTIONS
Describe and demonstrate the preparation of an osteotomy for a 4.1 mm diameter, 10 mm long implant at the LR5 in D3
bone. Explain each step.
DIRECTION OF THOUGHT
Order:
position from the guide →sequential drilling →temperature control →verification →under-
preparation for D3 →insertion torque. Mention heat threshold and the 2 mm canal margin.
MODEL ANSWER
“I confirm the position from the surgical guide, not from the shape of the bone, and confirm the
planned length allows at least 2 mm of clearance from the inferior alveolar canal.
I mark the entry point with a round bur or a precision drill through the guide. I then drill se-
quentially, from the pilot drill upwards in diameter, at the manufacturer’s recommended speed
— around 800 to 1500 rpm — with copious sterile saline irrigation and intermittent, pumping
pressure so that irrigant reaches the cutting flutes and debris is cleared. I use sharp drills within
their recommended number of uses. The reason is that bone necroses at 47 degrees for one minute,
and blunt drills, continuous pressure and inadequate irrigation are the main causes of overheating.
After the pilot drill I insert a direction indicator, check angulation mesiodistally and buccolingually
and parallelism with the adjacent teeth, and take a periapical radiograph with the indicator in place
because the canal is close.
I check the osteotomy with a depth gauge and probe the walls to confirm no perforation, particularly
lingually where there may be a concavity.
Because this is D3 bone, I would under-prepare — stopping one drill short of the final diameter, or
using an osteotome or densifying protocol — to improve primary stability.
I insert the implant at low speed, around 15 to 30 rpm, then finish by hand with a ratchet, mon-
itoring insertion torque, aiming for 25 to 45 Ncm and avoiding torque above 50 Ncm which risks
compression necrosis. I then record the system, diameter, length, site, lot number and insertion
torque.”
EXAMINER CHECKLIST
1. Position from the guide
2. Confirms safety margin from the canal
3. Sequential graded drilling
4. Correct speed
5. Copious sterile saline, intermittent pressure, sharp drills
6. States the 47 °C threshold

7. Direction indicator + radiograph
8. Checks walls/depth for perforation
9. Under-preparation for D3 justified
10. Insertion torque range and recording
Running this station to time
Time check. The model answer is 434 words, 3 minutes 6 seconds at 140 words per minute — but describe
and demonstrate means the drill sequence is physically worked through on a block while the words are
spoken, and hands changing drills, seating a direction indicator and fitting a ratchet run well below
reading speed; the honest cost is over six minutes. The compression is a fixed order narrated without
pause — position, drill, cool, verify, under-prepare, insert, record — with every number attached to the
action rather than explained after it.

osce.title: Bone defects: identification and management
osce.text:
OSCE 6 — Bone defects: identification and management
Blueprint: “Describe the different types of bone defects and suggest appropriate means to manage these” (W + OS-P + SCE).
EQUIPMENT
four models showing (a) a buccal dehiscence around a placed implant, (b) a fenestration, (c) a knife-edge ridge 3 mm wide,
(d) a vertical deficiency of 6 mm in the posterior mandible.
CANDIDATE INSTRUCTIONS

Identify the bone defect present on each model and state how you would manage it, including whether it is within the scope
of a general dentist with a special interest in implant dentistry.
MODEL ANSWER
“Model A — dehiscence. Bone is missing from the crest apically along the implant face, communi-
cating with the crest. If the implant is in the correct prosthetic position with good primary stability, I
would treat this with simultaneous guided bone regeneration: decorticate the buccal plate to open
marrow spaces, apply a composite graft of autogenous bone chips collected from the osteotomy with
a slowly resorbing xenograft for volume stability, cover with a native collagen membrane extending
2–3 mm beyond the defect, and achieve tension-free primary closure with a periosteal releasing
incision. I would use a two-stage submerged protocol and allow 4 to 6 months.
Model B — fenestration. A window of exposed implant with intact crestal bone. Same GBR ap-
proach; generally more predictable than a dehiscence because the crestal bone is intact.
Model C — knife-edge ridge, 3 mm. A horizontal deficiency. Options: a narrow-diameter implant if
the prosthetic space allows; a ridge split and expansion with simultaneous placement and grafting,
which is more predictable in the maxilla than the mandible; or staged horizontal GBR followed by
placement at 6 to 9 months. I would judge which is within my competence — a straightforward
simultaneous GBR is, an extensive staged augmentation may not be.
Model D — 6 mm vertical deficiency, posterior mandible. This is a vertical deficiency. Vertical
augmentation is significantly less predictable than horizontal and has a higher complication rate.
My GDP-level alternatives are a short implant, which the evidence shows performs comparably
to a longer implant with augmentation over the medium term with fewer complications, or a non-
implant option. If vertical augmentation is genuinely required, this is a Complex case on the SAC
classification and I would refer.”
EXAMINER CHECKLIST
1. 1–4 Names each defect correctly
2. GBR principles (decortication, graft, membrane, closure)
3. Composite graft rationale
4. Simultaneous vs staged decision criteria
5. Ridge split indications and maxilla/mandible difference
6. Short implants as an evidence-based alternative to vertical augmentation
7. Identifies the referral threshold explicitly
Running this station to time
Time check. The model answer is 425 words, 3 minutes 2 seconds at 140 words per minute — deceptively
short, because there are four models, each needing a name, a management plan and a competence judge-
ment, and the candidate must physically pick each one up and orientate it. That is a fixed 60 seconds per
model with 60 seconds left for the referral decision; anything over a minute on the dehiscence is taken
directly from the vertical defect, where the discriminating marks sit.

Q: Model A? “A buccal dehiscence — bone missing from the crest apically along the face of the implant,
communicating with the crest. If the implant is in the correct prosthetic position with good primary
stability, I would treat it with simultaneous guided bone regeneration: decorticate the buccal plate to
open the marrow spaces and bring in blood supply; a composite graft of autogenous chips collected from
the osteotomy against the implant surface, layered with a slowly resorbing xenograft outside it for volume
stability; a native collagen membrane extending 2 to 3 millimetres beyond the defect margins; and
tension-free primary closure after a periosteal releasing incision. Two-stage, submerged, 4 to 6 months
before uncovering.”
Q: Why the two materials rather than one? “The autogenous chips are the only osteogenic component —
living cells — so they go against the implant surface where regeneration matters. The xenograft resorbs
very slowly, so it is what still holds the buccal contour in two years’ time. One provides the biology, the
other the volume.”
Q: Model B? “A fenestration — a window of exposed implant with the crestal bone intact. Same GBR
approach, and generally more predictable than a dehiscence precisely because the crest is intact: the
defect is contained and the closure is not sitting over the defect margin.”
Q: When simultaneous and when staged? “Simultaneous when the implant can be placed in the correct
prosthetic position with good primary stability and the defect walls will contain the graft. Staged when
I would have to place the implant in the wrong position to get stability, when there is not enough bone

osce.title: Guided bone regeneration: materials and barriers
osce.text:
OSCE 7 — Guided bone regeneration: materials and barriers
Blueprint: “Differentiate between the different types of soft and hard tissue augmentation materials”; “role of barriers in bone augmentation and
their application during surgery along with their limitations” (W + OS-P + SCE).
EQUIPMENT
samples/packaging of autogenous bone collector, DBBM xenograft, FDBA allograft, 𝛽-TCP alloplast, native collagen mem-
brane, dPTFE membrane, titanium-reinforced membrane, tacks.
CANDIDATE INSTRUCTIONS
Identify the materials on the table. Explain how you would select between them for a buccal dehiscence around an implant
at the UL1, and describe the role and limitations of the barrier membrane.
MODEL ANSWER
“These are, in turn, an autogenous bone collector, a deproteinised bovine bone mineral xenograft,
a freeze-dried bone allograft, a beta-tricalcium phosphate alloplast, a native collagen membrane, a
dense PTFE membrane, a titanium-reinforced membrane and fixation tacks.

The three mechanisms are osteogenesis — only autogenous bone, which contains living cells; os-
teoinduction — mediated by BMPs, principally autogenous and demineralised allograft; and osteo-
conduction, which all of them provide as a scaffold.
For a buccal dehiscence at the UL1 I would use a composite graft: autogenous chips collected
from the osteotomy, placed against the implant surface for their osteogenic potential, layered with
a deproteinised bovine bone mineral on the outside for its very slow resorption, which maintains
buccal contour in the aesthetic zone. I would cover this with a native collagen membrane extending
2 to 3 mm beyond the defect margins, stabilised under the flap or with tacks.
The membrane’s role is to exclude fast-migrating epithelial and connective tissue cells so that
slower osteoprogenitor cells can populate the space. Its limitations are that a collagen membrane has
poor space maintenance and will collapse into a non-space-maintaining defect, and that its resorp-
tion time is unpredictable — anywhere from about four weeks to six months. A dense PTFE mem-
brane maintains space better and tolerates exposure, but must be removed. A titanium-reinforced
membrane maintains space best, but that level of defect is a complex case which I would refer.
The commonest complication is membrane exposure, which follows tension at closure, a suture line
over the membrane, denture pressure or smoking. If a collagen membrane exposes without infection
I would manage it with chlorhexidine, no brushing and close review; an exposed PTFE membrane I
would remove early.
Consent: I must tell the patient that the xenograft is bovine in origin and the collagen membrane
porcine, and offer synthetic or autogenous alternatives if that is unacceptable to them.”
EXAMINER CHECKLIST
1. Identifies all materials
2. Osteogenesis/induction/conduction defined
3. Composite graft rationale
4. DBBM chosen for volume stability
5. Membrane function stated correctly
6. Membrane extended beyond defect and stabilised
7. Collagen limitations (space maintenance, resorption)
8. Exposure management differs by membrane type
9. Recognises titanium-reinforced = refer
10. Consent to material origin
Running this station to time
Time check. The model answer is 464 words, 3 minutes 19 seconds at 140 words per minute — but there
are eight items to pick up and name before a word of the actual question is answered, and the instruction
then has three separate parts: identify, select, and the role and limitations of the barrier. Naming the
materials must be done as a single 40-second sweep along the table, not one considered sentence per
packet, or the membrane limitations and the consent mark are never reached.

“In order: an autogenous bone collector, a deproteinised bovine bone mineral

the graft — is autogenous bone alone, because only it contains living cells. Osteoinduction — recruiting
host cells through BMPs — is principally autogenous bone and demineralised allograft. Osteoconduction
— acting as a scaffold for ingrowth — is provided by all of them, and it is all a xenograft or an alloplast
provides.”

osce.title: Local anaesthesia and a drug interaction
osce.text:
OSCE 8 — Local anaesthesia and a drug interaction
Blueprint: “Apply an understanding of the range of local anaesthetics available, their side effects and the methods of using”; “Suggest appropriate
management for drug interactions” — both marked W + OS-P + SCE.
EQUIPMENT
a selection of cartridges (lidocaine 2% with adrenaline 1:80,000; articaine 4% with adrenaline 1:100,000; prilocaine 3% with
felypressin; mepivacaine 3% plain), a syringe, needles, and a medical history card.
CANDIDATE INSTRUCTIONS

You are to place a single implant at the LR5. The medical history card shows: 68-year-old male; propranolol 80 mg twice
daily for essential tremor; warfarin (INR yesterday 2.4); simvastatin 40 mg. Select an appropriate local anaesthetic, justify
your choice, and describe any modifications you would make to your management.
DIRECTION OF THOUGHT
Two traps: adrenaline + non-selective beta-blocker, and warfarin. Plus the LR5 site raises the mental fora-
men/anterior loop. Say maximum doses.
MODEL ANSWER
“Three issues arise.
First, propranolol is a non-selective beta-blocker. Adrenaline in the presence of unopposed al-
pha stimulation can produce a hypertensive response with reflex bradycardia. I would not regard
adrenaline as absolutely contraindicated, but I would limit the dose, aspirate carefully to avoid
intravascular injection, and inject slowly. A reasonable choice is lidocaine 2% with adrenaline
1:80,000, limited to two cartridges, or prilocaine 3% with felypressin if I want to avoid adrenaline
entirely. Each 2.2 mL lidocaine cartridge contains 44 mg of lidocaine; the maximum is 4.4 mg per
kilogram to 300 mg. Articaine 4% at 88 mg per cartridge has a maximum of 7 mg per kilogram.
Second, warfarin with an INR of 2.4 measured within 24 hours. SDCEP guidance is to treat with-
out interrupting the warfarin when the INR is below 4.0, using local haemostatic measures: an
atraumatic technique, sutures, oxidised cellulose or collagen in the site, pressure with gauze, and
tranexamic acid mouthwash if bleeding is troublesome. I would treat early in the day and early in
the week, and give clear written post-operative bleeding instructions with an emergency number.
Third, simvastatin: if an antibiotic were indicated, I would avoid clarithromycin and erythromycin
because of the risk of rhabdomyolysis, and avoid azole antifungals. If prophylaxis is indicated I
would use a single 3 g dose of amoxicillin. I would also avoid NSAIDs for analgesia because of the
warfarin, and use paracetamol.
Technique for the LR5: I would use buccal and lingual infiltration rather than an inferior alveolar
nerve block. This limits the dose of adrenaline, avoids a block in an anticoagulated patient where a
haematoma in the pterygomandibular space is undesirable, and leaves the patient able to report a
sharp sensation if the drill approaches the mental or inferior alveolar nerve. I would also plan the
implant at least 5 mm anterior to the radiographic mental foramen, or measure the anterior loop on
CBCT.
I would record the agent, the number of cartridges, the batch number, the technique used and the
patient’s response.”
EXAMINER CHECKLIST
1. Identifies the beta-blocker/adrenaline interaction
2. Practical management (limit dose, aspirate, slow injection, or alternative agent)
3. Quotes cartridge content and maximum dose
4. Applies SDCEP warfarin guidance (INR <4.0, treat)
5. Local haemostatic measures listed
6. Avoids NSAIDs
7. Statin–macrolide interaction identified
8. Chooses infiltration and justifies it
9. Mental foramen/anterior loop precaution
10. Records agent, dose, batch and response
Running this station to time
Time check. The model answer is 549 words, 3 minutes 55 seconds at 140 words per minute — which
leaves barely a minute once the medical history card has been read aloud, a cartridge selected from four
and the syringe assembled. There are three drugs and a site-specific technique to cover, so the shape is
a fixed 60 seconds per drug problem with the last minute for the injection technique and the records; the
numbers must be stated, not derived.

take for pain and what not to, when to
ring); and review, with a same-day
telephone call and the sutures checked at
one week.
The compressed answer — what a strong candidate says in five minutes
Q: What do you notice on this card? “Three things: propranolol, a non-selective beta-blocker; warfarin
with an INR of 2.4 taken yesterday; and simvastatin. And the site itself — the LR5 sits near the mental
foramen.”
Q: Deal with the propranolol. “Adrenaline in a patient on a non-selective beta-blocker acts on unop-
posed alpha receptors, which can produce a hypertensive response with reflex bradycardia. I would
not call adrenaline absolutely contraindicated, but I would limit the dose, aspirate carefully to avoid an

osce.title: Infection control and aseptic technique
osce.text:
OSCE 9 — Infection control and aseptic technique
Blueprint: “Show an awareness of the importance of infection control and aseptic technique”; “Discuss maintenance of infection control and the
aseptic technique” (W + OS-P + SCE).
EQUIPMENT
a surgical trolley with a mix of appropriate and inappropriate items (sterile drapes, gown, gloves, sterile saline, an air-turbine
handpiece, a non-sterile bur block, an implant in a damaged sterile pouch with a past expiry date, chlorhexidine mouthwash,
steel curettes).

CANDIDATE INSTRUCTIONS
Prepare the trolley for implant surgery. Identify any items that are inappropriate and explain why. Describe your aseptic
technique.
MODEL ANSWER
“Working through the trolley: I would remove the air-turbine handpiece — an air-driven hand-
piece risks driving air into the tissues and causing surgical emphysema and contamination; implant
surgery requires an electric surgical motor with sterile tubing. I would remove the non-sterile
bur block. I would discard the implant — the pouch is damaged and the expiry date has passed,
so sterility cannot be assumed, and I would record that. I would remove the steel curettes from
the implant tray, because steel scratches the titanium oxide layer; titanium, PEEK or carbon-fibre
instruments are used on implant surfaces.
Environment: a designated clean surgery, surfaces cleaned and disinfected, doors closed, minimal
traﬀic, only the equipment I need on the field.
Instruments: decontaminated and sterilised in line with HTM 01-05 — cleaning in a washer-
disinfector or ultrasonic bath, inspection, packaging, a vacuum type B autoclave for hollow and
lumened instruments, correct storage, and retained cycle records.
Team: surgical scrub, sterile gown, sterile gloves, mask, cap and eye protection for the operator and
assistant.
Patient: chlorhexidine 0.2% mouthrinse for one minute, perioral skin disinfection and sterile
drapes.
Field: sterile saline irrigation, single-use or use-limited drills, the implant handled only with its
sterile carrier and never with gloved fingers or non-titanium instruments.
Finally: sharps handled with a re-sheathing device, an instrument and swab count, correct waste
segregation, and recording of implant and graft batch numbers for traceability.”
EXAMINER CHECKLIST
1. Rejects air-turbine and states why
2. Rejects non-sterile items
3. Rejects the damaged/expired implant and records it
4. Rejects steel instruments for the implant surface
5. Environment control
6. HTM 01-05 / vacuum autoclave and cycle records
7. Scrub, gown, gloves, mask, eye protection
8. Patient chlorhexidine rinse and draping
9. Sterile saline and implant handling
10. Sharps, waste, counts and batch traceability
Running this station to time
Time check. The model answer is 398 words — 2 minutes 51 seconds at 140 words a minute — which
looks generous until you remember that your hands are on the trolley: lifting four wrong items off it and
giving a reason for each takes far longer than reading the same sentence aloud. Budget 90 seconds for the
four rejections, one clause of reason each, and keep the remaining three minutes for the aseptic chain,
from the room to the batch numbers.

“And the patient, and the field itself?”
Checklists 8 and 9. Chlorhexidine 0.2%

the implant handled only by its sterile

“Anything to finish with?”

The compressed answer — what a strong candidate says in five minutes
“Four things come off this trolley before anything else.
The air-turbine handpiece. An air-driven handpiece exhausts into the surgical field and can drive air into
the tissues — surgical emphysema — so it is never used for a bone cut. I would use an electric surgical
motor with a reduction handpiece and sterile irrigation tubing, torque and speed set at the console.
The bur block. Not sterile, so it does not belong on a sterile field.
This implant. The pouch is damaged and the expiry date has passed, so sterility cannot be assumed. It
is discarded, a replacement opened, and I record the batch number and the reason for the discard and
report it to the manufacturer as a device incident. I would not use it and I would not re-sterilise it.
The steel curettes. Steel scratches the titanium oxide layer and leaves metal debris at the interface. Any-
thing that touches an implant surface is titanium, PEEK or carbon fibre.
What stays — the sterile drapes, gown, gloves, saline and the chlorhexidine — I will use.
The technique starts with the room. A designated clean surgery, surfaces cleaned and disinfected before
the list, doors closed, traﬀic limited to operator, assistant and patient, and only the equipment I actually
need laid out.
Instruments are decontaminated and sterilised to HTM 01-05 — washer-disinfector or ultrasonic bath,
inspection under magnification, packaging, then a vacuum type B autoclave, which is what hollow and
lumened items such as the surgical handpiece and the irrigation line require. Sterile storage, pouch in-
tegrity and expiry checked at the point of use, and cycle records retained.

osce.title: Post-operative care and advice
osce.text:
OSCE 10 — Post-operative care and advice
Blueprint: “Suggest appropriate and adequate postoperative care and advice including the use of post-operative painkillers and antibiotics” (OS-P
+ SCE).
EQUIPMENT
a simulated patient or the examiner acting as a patient; a blank post-operative instruction sheet.
CANDIDATE INSTRUCTIONS
You have just placed an implant at the UL1 with a bone graft and a collagen membrane. Give the patient their post-operative
instructions.
DIRECTION OF THOUGHT
This is a spoken station: plain language, no jargon, structured, ending with warning signs and a contact number.
Cover: bleeding, swelling, pain, medication, hygiene, diet, denture, activity, what is normal, what is not, review.
MODEL ANSWER
As spoken to the patient
“Everything went as planned. Here is what to expect and what I need you to do — I’ll also give you
this in writing.
Bleeding: some oozing today is normal. If it bleeds, bite firmly on the gauze I’ve given you for 20
minutes without checking it. Don’t rinse today.

Swelling and bruising: these are normal and are usually worst around two to three days, then settle.
Use a cold pack on the outside of the lip, 20 minutes on and 20 minutes off, for the first day, and
sleep with an extra pillow.
Pain: take ibuprofen 400 mg with food, up to four times a day, and paracetamol 1 gram up to four
times a day — you can take them together. Take the first dose now, before the numbness wears off.
Avoid aspirin.
Antibiotics/mouthwash: [if prescribed] finish the whole course. Start the chlorhexidine mouth-
wash tomorrow, twice a day for two weeks — hold it in your mouth, don’t swill vigorously.
Cleaning: brush all your other teeth normally, but do not brush over the wound until I tell you.
Diet: soft food, nothing hot today, and chew on the other side. Keep well hydrated.
Denture: leave your denture out for the next 48 hours; then bring it in and I’ll adjust and reline it so
it does not press on the graft.
Activity: no smoking at all — smoking is the biggest single thing that will make this graft fail. No
alcohol and no strenuous exercise for two to three days.
What’s not normal — contact me if: the bleeding doesn’t stop with pressure; the pain gets worse
after day three rather than better; you get a temperature or the swelling spreads; you feel something
rough or a piece of material coming through the gum; or you have any numbness that hasn’t gone
by tomorrow. If you have diﬀiculty swallowing or breathing, that’s an emergency — call 999.
Here is my number and the out-of-hours number. I’ll see you in a week to take the stitches out.”
EXAMINER CHECKLIST
1. Bleeding advice
2. Swelling/cold pack/head elevation
3. Specific analgesia with doses and pre-emptive timing
4. Antibiotic/chlorhexidine instructions
5. Hygiene — no brushing over the wound
6. Diet
7. Denture management for a grafted site
8. Smoking, alcohol, exercise
9. Warning signs including the airway emergency
10. Written instructions, contact number and review appointment
Running this station to time
Time check. The model answer is 509 words — 3 minutes 38 seconds of pure speech at 140 words a minute
— but this is spoken to a patient who interrupts, and a candidate who greets, hands over the sheet, checks
understanding and answers one question will pass five minutes comfortably. Nothing can be dropped,
because every heading is an instruction the patient needs; the compression is one sentence per heading
and no physiology at all.

The compressed answer — what a strong candidate says in five minutes
“That all went to plan — the implant is in, with a graft and a small membrane over it. Let me tell you what
to expect and what I need you to do, and you will have all of it in writing as well.
Bleeding. Some oozing today is normal, and it looks worse than it is because it mixes with saliva. If it
bleeds, bite firmly on the gauze for twenty minutes without checking it. Do not rinse at all today.
Swelling and bruising. Both are normal, usually worst at two to three days, then they settle. Hold a cold
pack against the outside of your lip, twenty minutes on and twenty minutes off, for the first day, and
sleep with an extra pillow tonight.
Pain. Take ibuprofen four hundred milligrams with food, up to four times a day, and paracetamol one
gram, up to four times a day. You can take them together, and together they work better than either alone.
Take your first dose now, before the numbness wears off — do not wait for it to start hurting. Please
avoid aspirin.
Your medicines. Finish the whole course of antibiotics. Start the mouthwash tomorrow, twice a day for
two weeks — hold it in your mouth gently, do not swill it hard.
Cleaning. Brush all your other teeth normally, but do not brush over the wound until I tell you it is safe.
Keeping the rest of your mouth clean matters more than usual just now.
Eating. Soft food, nothing hot today, and chew on the other side. Drink plenty, but no straws.
Your denture. Leave it out completely for the next forty-eight hours. Then bring it to me and I will ease
it and put a soft lining in it. Please do not wear it until I have done that — pressure on a graft is one of
the main reasons it fails. Leave it out at night from now on.
Smoking, alcohol and exercise. No smoking at all — smoking is the single biggest thing that will make
this graft fail. No alcohol, and no hard exercise or heavy lifting for two to three days, because that can
restart the bleeding.
Ring me if the bleeding does not stop after twenty minutes of firm pressure; if the pain gets worse after
day three instead of better; if you get a temperature or the swelling starts spreading; if you feel something
rough or gritty coming through the gum, because that can be the graft or the membrane showing and I
need to see it; or if any numbness in your lip is still there tomorrow morning.
And this one is an emergency — call 999 if you get diﬀiculty swallowing or any diﬀiculty breathing.

osce.title: The surgical record
osce.text:
OSCE 11 — The surgical record
Blueprint: “Demonstrate understanding of the role of clear, accurate, contemporaneous record keeping” (OS-P + SCE).
EQUIPMENT
a blank clinical record proforma, an implant packaging label with lot number, a graft box, a membrane packet.
CANDIDATE INSTRUCTIONS
Complete the clinical record for the implant placement you have just performed. Say aloud what you are writing and why.
MODEL ANSWER
“I would record, contemporaneously: date and time; the operator and assistant; that the medical
history was checked and unchanged; that consent was confirmed and the risks re-stated on the day;
the local anaesthetic — agent, concentration, vasoconstrictor, number of cartridges, technique, batch
number; that aseptic technique was used; the flap design; the site; the drilling sequence; the implant
system, diameter, length and lot number, with the label stuck into the notes; the insertion torque
and, if measured, the ISQ; whether a cover screw or healing abutment was placed; any augmentation
— graft material, brand and lot number, membrane type and lot number; suture material and
technique and the number of sutures; any complication and how it was managed; the post-operative
instructions given, and that they were given in writing; medication prescribed with doses; the
review arrangements; and my signature.
I would also give the patient an implant record card with the system, diameter, length and lot
number so that any future clinician can identify and service the implant. That is both good practice
and a medical device traceability requirement.
Records must be contemporaneous — if I have to add anything later I would date and sign the
addition rather than alter the original entry.”
EXAMINER CHECKLIST
1. Date/operator/assistant
2. MH checked, consent confirmed on the day
3. LA details including batch
4. Flap and site
5. Implant system, diameter, length, lot number
6. Insertion torque ± ISQ
7. Graft and membrane with lot numbers
8. Sutures and closure

9. Post-operative instructions given in writing, medication, review
10. Patient implant card and the principle of contemporaneous, unaltered records
Running this station to time
Time check. The model answer is 335 words — 2 minutes 24 seconds at 140 words a minute, the shortest
in this part, and the only station where the clock is not the enemy. The enemy is silence: the instruction is
say aloud what you are writing, and an entry made quietly scores nothing. Spend the whole five minutes at
dictation pace, reading the lot numbers off the label, the box and the packet in front of you rather than
from memory.

osce.title: Abutment selection
osce.text:
OSCE 12 — Abutment selection
Blueprint: “Select the appropriate abutment to restore the implant” (W + OS-P + SCE).
EQUIPMENT
models of (a) an ideally placed UR1 implant with 3 mm of soft tissue, (b) a buccally inclined UL2 implant, (c) an LR6 implant
with 2 mm of soft tissue; a tray of abutments — stock straight titanium, angled titanium, Ti-base, custom CAD-CAM, zirconia,
multi-unit; and an angulated screw channel abutment.

CANDIDATE INSTRUCTIONS
For each of the three implants, select an appropriate abutment and justify your choice.
MODEL ANSWER
“I decide in a fixed order: retention type, level, angulation, height and margin position, material,
and stock versus custom.
(a) UR1, ideally placed, 3 mm of soft tissue. I would restore this screw-retained at implant level,
using a custom CAD-CAM abutment or a Ti-base with a milled ceramic superstructure. My rea-
sons: the emergence profile through 3 mm of tissue needs to be customised to support the papillae
and the mid-facial margin; screw retention removes any cement risk at that depth; and a Ti-base
gives a titanium-to-titanium connection at the implant with an aesthetic ceramic above. If the tissue
were thin I would avoid a plain titanium abutment because of grey show-through.
(b) UL2, buccally inclined. The screw channel would emerge through the labial surface. My op-
tions are an angulated screw channel abutment, which lets me keep screw retention with the access
hole moved palatally — my preferred solution — or a cement-retained restoration on an angled
abutment, in which case I would keep the margin at or no more than 1 mm below the mucosal
margin, use a minimal volume of radiopaque cement, and take a radiograph to check for excess.
(c) LR6, 2 mm of soft tissue, posterior. A stock or custom straight titanium abutment, screw-
retained, is appropriate. Aesthetics are not critical; titanium gives maximum strength for posterior
loading; screw retention gives retrievability, which matters most in the site with the highest mechan-
ical complication rate.
In all three I would confirm that the abutment gives adequate restorative space — about 5 to 6
mm for a screw-retained crown and 7 to 8 mm for cement retention — and I would torque to the
manufacturer’s value and re-torque after ten minutes.”
EXAMINER CHECKLIST
1. States a systematic decision order
2. Screw retention preferred where angulation allows
3. Custom abutment for emergence profile in the aesthetic zone
4. Ti-base rationale/avoids zirconia-on-titanium interface
5. Grey show-through with thin tissue considered
6. ASC abutment identified for the inclined implant
7. If cementing — margin position, radiopaque cement, minimal volume, radiograph
8. Titanium chosen for posterior strength
9. Restorative space requirements quoted
10. Torque and re-torque at 10 minutes
Running this station to time
Time check. The model answer is 449 words — 3 minutes 12 seconds at 140 words a minute — but there
are three models to pick up, an abutment tray to choose from three times, and a “why?” after each, so the
honest delivery is nearer seven minutes. The fix is a fixed 60 seconds per model — abutment named, one
sentence of justification, one caveat — after 30 seconds spent stating the decision order, leaving the last
minute for restorative space and torque.

Q: How do you approach a choice like this? “In a fixed order, every time: retention type, level, angu-
lation, height and margin position, material, then stock against custom. And a governing preference —
screw retention wherever the angulation allows it, and always where the margin would sit more than

superstructure. The emergence profile through 3 mm of tissue has to be customised to support the papillae
and the mid-facial margin — a stock abutment cannot do that. And screw retention removes the cement
risk entirely at that depth, where excess would be undetectable.”
Q: Why a Ti-base rather than full zirconia onto the implant? “Because it gives a titanium-to-titanium
connection at the implant interface. Zirconia bearing directly on a titanium platform is a harder material
against a softer one, with wear of the platform and microgap concerns; the Ti-base keeps the metal-to-
metal joint and puts the ceramic above it.”
Q: Anything about the tissue itself? “Yes — if the tissue were thin, I would avoid a plain titanium
abutment because of grey show-through at the margin. That is an argument for a ceramic superstructure
on the Ti-base, or for a zirconia abutment above a titanium base.”
Q: The UL2 is buccally inclined. “Then the screw channel emerges through the labial surface, which
is unrestorable as a screw-retained crown. My preferred answer is this — the angulated screw channel

osce.title: Screw- versus cement-retained: decision and steps
osce.text:
OSCE 13 — Screw- versus cement-retained: decision and steps
Blueprint: “Show an understanding of the different steps involved in the provision of a screw retained prosthesis”; “difference between screw and
cement retained restoration and their application” (W + OS-P + SCE).
CANDIDATE INSTRUCTIONS
Explain the differences between screw- and cement-retained implant restorations and describe the clinical and laboratory
steps for providing a screw-retained crown on an LR5 implant.
MODEL ANSWER
“The essential difference is retrievability. A screw-retained crown can be removed and replaced
without damage, which matters because implant restorations require maintenance — screws loosen,
ceramic chips, and biological problems need access. A cement-retained crown is diﬀicult or destruc-
tive to remove.
The second key difference is cement. Residual submucosal cement is a well-documented cause of
peri-implant disease, and screw retention eliminates that risk entirely.
Screw retention also needs less restorative space — about 5 to 6 mm compared with 7 to 8 mm —
and demands a passive framework, because there is no cement layer to absorb misfit.
Cement retention has two advantages: it can compensate for unfavourable implant angulation where
the screw channel would emerge through an aesthetic or occlusal surface, and it gives an unin-

terrupted occlusal surface. Angulated screw channel abutments have reduced the first advantage
considerably.
My preference is screw retention wherever angulation allows, and always where the margin would
sit more than about 1 mm below the mucosa.
Steps for the screw-retained crown at LR5: 1. Confirm osseointegration clinically and radiograph-
ically, and check the peri-implant tissues. 2. Remove the healing abutment; assess the emergence
profile and soft tissue. 3. Take an implant-level impression — a closed-tray coping is acceptable
for a single unit, an open tray if access allows — in polyether or addition silicone in a custom tray;
verify the coping is fully seated, radiographically if it is deep. 4. Record the opposing arch, the inte-
rocclusal relationship and the shade; take photographs. 5. Written laboratory prescription: implant
system, platform, connection, screw-retained crown, material, shade, contact points, emergence
and occlusal scheme. 6. At try-in: verify complete seating clinically and radiographically, check
proximal contacts with floss, check emergence and cleansability, check the occlusion. 7. Fit: clean
the internal connection, seat the crown, hand-tighten, radiograph to confirm seating, then torque
to the manufacturer’s value, check the occlusion is light in intercuspation and free in excursions, re-
torque after 10 minutes. 8. Seal the screw access with PTFE tape over the screw head and composite
over that, so the screw can be retrieved. 9. Give hygiene instruction specific to the site, take a baseline
periapical radiograph, record everything, and arrange review and maintenance.”
EXAMINER CHECKLIST
1. Retrievability
2. Cement risk
3. Space requirement difference
4. Passive fit requirement
5. Angulation/aesthetics advantage of cement, and ASC as the alternative
6. States a preference with justification
7. Correct impression sequence and verification
8. Laboratory prescription content
9. Torque, radiographic verification, re-torque at 10 min, light occlusion
10. PTFE + composite seal, baseline radiograph, hygiene and review
Running this station to time
Time check. The model answer is 495 words — 3 minutes 32 seconds at 140 words a minute — but it
carries a five-part comparison and a nine-step clinical sequence, and every one of those steps invites a
“why?”, so the honest delivery is past six and a half minutes. The compression is a 90-second cap on
the comparison — four differences, one clause each, then the stated preference — with the steps run at
roughly ten seconds apiece, grouped into impression, prescription, try-in and fit.

The compressed answer — what a strong candidate says in five minutes
Q: What is the essential difference? “Retrievability. A screw-retained crown comes off and goes back on
without damage. That matters because implant restorations require maintenance over a lifetime — screws
loosen, ceramic chips, and biological problems need access to the platform. A cement-retained crown is
diﬀicult or destructive to remove, so a small problem becomes a remake.”
Q: And the second difference? “Cement. Residual submucosal cement is a well-documented cause of
peri-implant mucositis and peri-implantitis, and it is hard to detect and harder to remove once the margin
sits deep. Screw retention eliminates that risk entirely.”
Q: Any technical differences? “Two. Screw retention needs less restorative space — about 5 to 6 mm
against 7 to 8 mm — because it does not need abutment height for retention. And it demands a passive
framework, because there is no cement layer to absorb a misfit; the stress goes straight into the components
and the bone.”
Q: What does cement retention offer? “It compensates for unfavourable angulation where the screw
channel would emerge through an aesthetic or occlusal surface, and it gives an uninterrupted occlusal
surface. But angulated screw channel abutments have largely removed the first advantage, which is
why the balance has shifted.”
Q: Your preference? “Screw retention wherever the angulation allows, and always where the margin
would sit more than about a millimetre below the mucosa. I would accept cement only with a supragingi-
val or just-subgingival margin, radiopaque cement, minimal volume, and a radiograph.”

osce.title: Implant impression (practical)
osce.text:
OSCE 14 — Implant impression (practical)
Blueprint: “Apply knowledge of the different impression techniques used when restoring implants”; “Justify the choice of impression material and
technique” (W + OS-P + SCE).
EQUIPMENT
a model with three implant analogues in the lower left quadrant (one divergent); open- and closed-tray copings, guide screws,
a custom tray with windows, stock trays, impression materials, pattern resin, dental floss.
CANDIDATE INSTRUCTIONS
Take, or describe taking, a definitive impression of these three implants. Justify your choice of technique and material.
MODEL ANSWER
“With three implants, one of which is divergent, I would use an open-tray (pick-up) technique
with splinted copings, because the closed-tray technique relies on re-seating the copings into the
impression, and with divergent implants that re-seating is unreliable.

Steps: remove the healing abutments and clean the connections. Seat the open-tray impression
copings, confirm each is fully seated by feel and, because these are deep, with a periapical radio-
graph. Splint the copings with pattern resin — I would section the resin once set and re-join it, to
compensate for polymerisation shrinkage — or use floss and light-cured composite.
Check the custom tray for fit and that the guide screws project freely through the windows without
contacting the tray. Apply the correct tray adhesive and allow it to dry.
Material: polyether, because it is rigid, hydrophilic and dimensionally stable, which suits splinted
copings. Addition silicone of heavy and light body is an acceptable alternative — but I would not
use latex gloves with addition silicone, because sulphur inhibits the set.
Load the tray, syringe material around each coping, seat, and hold still until fully set. Then unscrew
the guide screws completely before removing the impression, remove the impression, attach the
analogues, and check that each coping is fully embedded and undistorted.
Also record: the opposing arch, an interocclusal record on rigid bases, the shade with photographs,
and a facebow if the occlusal scheme is being altered. Disinfect the impression and send it with a
written prescription.”
EXAMINER CHECKLIST
1. Chooses open tray and justifies it
2. Splinting with sectioned/re-joined resin
3. Verifies coping seating radiographically
4. Custom tray with windows, checks screw clearance
5. Adhesive applied and dried
6. Selects polyether/PVS with justification
7. Latex/PVS incompatibility noted
8. Unscrews guide screws before removal
9. Attaches analogues and inspects
10. Opposing arch, records, disinfection, prescription
Running this station to time
Time check. The model answer is 392 words — 2 minutes 48 seconds at 140 words a minute — but that
figure is misleading, because this is a practical station and narrating while the hands work is far slower
than reading aloud: seating three copings, checking each is home, splinting with pattern resin, sectioning
and re-joining it, and painting and drying tray adhesive cannot be done at speaking speed. Budget six
minutes of real work into five by justifying once at the start, then giving each step a single clause while
the hands keep moving.

impression, an interocclusal record on

The compressed answer — what a strong candidate says in five minutes
“Before I touch anything, the choice and the reason. Three implants, one of them divergent, so I would
take an open-tray pick-up impression with the copings splinted. A closed-tray impression relies on
unscrewing the copings, removing the impression, and re-seating each coping back into its own space
— and with a divergent implant that re-seating is unreliable, so the cast reproduces the wrong angulation.
In an open-tray technique the copings come out in the impression and never move.
So — healing abutments out, connections irrigated and inspected for tissue or debris.
Copings on. These are the open-tray copings with the long guide screws. I seat each one, tighten by hand,
and confirm it is fully home. These sit deep, so I do not accept feel alone — I take a periapical radiograph
of each. A coping that is a fraction unseated makes an impression that is accurate to nothing.
Tray next. The custom tray with windows: I try it in and confirm that all three guide screws project freely
through the windows without contacting the tray, because a screw touching the tray lifts the impression
and distorts it. I adjust the windows if needed.
Splinting. I connect the copings with floss and then pattern resin, applied in small increments to limit the
shrinkage. Once set I section the resin between each pair and re-join the sections with a small amount
of fresh resin, which compensates for polymerisation shrinkage. Floss and light-cured composite does
the same job.
Adhesive. Correct adhesive for the material, painted onto the tray, and allowed to dry fully before I load
it.
Material — polyether. It is rigid, so it holds the splinted copings without flexing on removal; it is hy-
drophilic, so it copes with a moist sulcus; and it is dimensionally stable. Addition silicone in heavy and
light body is an acceptable alternative — but I would not handle it in latex gloves, because sulphur
inhibits the set and you get an unset layer exactly where the detail matters.
Taking it. Syringe material around each coping and into the sulcus, load and seat the tray, and hold it
absolutely still until it is fully set — not just until it feels firm.

osce.title: Assessing restorative space and freeway space
osce.text:
OSCE 15 — Assessing restorative space and freeway space
Blueprint: “Demonstrate an understanding of the importance of interocclusal and intra-occlusal space in relation to the planning of tooth
replacement” (SCE, with practical assessment).
EQUIPMENT
a patient/manikin, Willis gauge, dividers, ruler, indelible pencil, articulated study casts of an edentulous patient.
CANDIDATE INSTRUCTIONS
Demonstrate how you would measure the freeway space and determine whether there is adequate restorative space for a
mandibular implant overdenture with stud attachments.
MODEL ANSWER
“Freeway space is the rest vertical dimension minus the occlusal vertical dimension, and is nor-
mally 2 to 4 mm.
To measure it: I seat the patient upright with the head unsupported and the lips relaxed. I mark two
points, one on the tip of the nose and one on the chin, with an indelible pencil.
I record the occlusal vertical dimension with the patient in maximum intercuspation, or with the
dentures in occlusion, measuring between the marks with a Willis gauge or dividers.
I then establish the rest position: I ask the patient to relax, moisten the lips, swallow and let the
jaw drop naturally; or I use phonetics — asking them to repeat ‘Emma’ or count from fifty to sixty
and stop, then measure. I repeat the measurement three times and take the mean, because the rest
position is variable.
The difference between the two is the freeway space. If it is less than about 2 mm, there is little room;
if it is greater than 4 mm, the vertical dimension may have collapsed and there may be more space
available than the current denture suggests.

For a stud-retained mandibular overdenture I need approximately 8 to 10 mm of restorative space
measured from the implant platform to the opposing occlusal plane — that accommodates the
attachment housing, the acrylic thickness around it and the denture tooth. A bar would need 12
to 15 mm.
I would confirm this on articulated study casts, measuring from the planned platform level to the
opposing occlusal plane, and I would check whether alveoloplasty at the time of surgery is needed to
create space, or whether the vertical dimension can be increased within the freeway space. I would
record the measurements and the method used.”
EXAMINER CHECKLIST
1. Defines freeway space correctly
2. Correct patient positioning
3. Two marks and a measuring device
4. Measures OVD
5. Establishes rest position by relaxation/swallowing and/or phonetics
6. Repeats and averages
7. States normal range 2–4 mm
8. Quotes stud (8–10 mm) and bar (12–15 mm) space requirements
9. Confirms on articulated casts
10. States remedies for inadequate space (alveoloplasty, altering OVD within the freeway space) and records findings
Running this station to time
Time check. The model answer is 440 words — 3 minutes 9 seconds at 140 words a minute — but this
station is measured, not merely described: the patient has to be seated and relaxed, the rest position
established three separate times and averaged, and the casts measured afterwards, which is well over six
minutes at a comfortable pace. The compression is to say every figure out loud the moment the gauge
reads it, and to describe each manoeuvre in one clause, because the marks here are in the spoken numbers
rather than in the account of the technique.
