The compressed answer — what a strong candidate says in five minutes
“Freeway space is the difference between the rest vertical dimension and the occlusal vertical dimen-
sion, and it is normally 2 to 4 millimetres. I will measure both and say the numbers as I get them.
Position first. I sit the patient upright, head unsupported against nothing, Frankfort plane horizontal, lips
together and relaxed. If the head is supported the mandible postures differently and every figure after this
is wrong.
Two marks. One on the tip of the nose, one on the point of the chin, in indelible pencil — and the same two
marks for every measurement, because moving them by a millimetre changes the answer by a millimetre.
The occlusal vertical dimension. I ask the patient to close fully into maximum intercuspation — or, with
dentures, into occlusion — and measure between the marks with the Willis gauge. That reads sixty-two
millimetres. OVD, sixty-two.
Now the rest position, which is the harder half. I ask the patient to relax, moisten the lips, swallow, and
let the jaw drop naturally, and I measure without them knowing exactly when. I also check it phonetically
— asking them to repeat ‘Emma’, or to count from fifty to sixty and stop — and measure at the point they
stop, because the mandible returns to rest.
And I do it three times, because the rest position is variable. Sixty-five. Sixty-five. Sixty-six. Mean,
sixty-five point three.
So the freeway space is sixty-five point three minus sixty-two — three point three millimetres, which
sits within the normal range. If it were under 2 millimetres I would have almost no room to work in; if it
were over 4 I would suspect the vertical dimension had collapsed, and there is then more space available
than the present denture suggests.
Now the restorative space, which is a different measurement. For a stud-retained mandibular over-
denture I need approximately 8 to 10 millimetres, measured from the implant platform to the opposing
occlusal plane — that has to accommodate the attachment housing, an adequate thickness of acrylic all
around it, and the denture tooth. Anything less and the acrylic fractures over the housing. A bar-retained
overdenture needs 12 to 15 millimetres, because the bar, the clip and its housing sit above the platform.
I confirm that on the articulated casts, with dividers, from the planned platform level — which is the
crest less the intended sink depth — to the opposing occlusal plane. On these casts that measures nine
millimetres, so a stud attachment is feasible and a bar is not.
If there were not enough space, I have three options. Alveoloplasty at the time of placement, to lower
the platform and gain the millimetres surgically. A lower-profile attachment system. Or increasing the
occlusal vertical dimension, but only within the freeway space and never reducing it below about 2
millimetres, because a patient closing onto no freeway space gets soreness, muscle pain and a denture
they cannot tolerate.

osce.title: Fitting the prosthesis
osce.text:
OSCE 16 — Fitting the prosthesis
Blueprint: “Demonstrate the fitting of a prosthesis” (OS-P); “Deliver a satisfactory restoration to the patient” (OS-P + SCE).
EQUIPMENT
a model with an implant analogue, a completed screw-retained crown, torque wrench, articulating paper of two thicknesses,
shimstock, floss, PTFE tape, composite.
CANDIDATE INSTRUCTIONS
Fit this screw-retained crown. Describe and demonstrate each check you make.
MODEL ANSWER
“Before I start: confirm the patient’s identity and the work returned matches the prescription, and
check the peri-implant tissues are healthy.
1. Remove the healing abutment, irrigate and inspect the internal connection.
2. Seat the crown by hand and confirm it is fully seated — visually, by probing the margin, and
radiographically with a paralleling periapical, because a wedge-shaped gap on the radiograph
is the sign of a misfit. I would never force a non-seating restoration with the torque wrench —
that causes screw fracture, bone loss and pain.
3. Check proximal contacts with floss — they should offer resistance but allow the floss to pass,
and I check the contact is cleansable.
4. Check emergence and contour — the restoration must be cleansable with an interdental brush;
an over-contoured or ridge-lap emergence is a future peri-implantitis risk.
5. Check the occlusion: in intercuspation the implant crown should hold shimstock only under
heavy clenching and not under light tapping — that is, about 25 to 30 micrometres lighter than
the adjacent teeth. In excursions there should be no contact on the implant where the natural
canine can guide. I check working and non-working sides.
6. Check aesthetics with the patient using a mirror, in daylight if possible, and confirm they are
happy before final torquing.
7. Torque to the manufacturer’s value with a calibrated torque wrench, and re-torque after ten
minutes to compensate for embedment relaxation.
8. Seal the access: PTFE tape over the screw head so it can be retrieved, then composite, then re-
check the occlusion because the composite adds height.
9. Give site-specific hygiene instruction — interdental brush of the correct size, single-tufted brush,
superfloss.

10. Take a baseline periapical radiograph, photograph, record the abutment, torque value, batch
numbers and occlusal scheme, give the patient their implant card, and arrange the maintenance
recall.”
EXAMINER CHECKLIST
1. Checks work against prescription; assesses tissues
2. Verifies complete seating clinically and radiographically
3. States never to force with torque
4. Proximal contacts
5. Contour/cleansability
6. Light occlusion in ICP, none in excursion
7. Patient approval of aesthetics before torquing
8. Torque + re-torque at 10 min
9. PTFE + composite, re-check occlusion
10. Baseline radiograph, hygiene, records, recall
Running this station to time
Time check. The model answer is 433 words — 3 minutes 5 seconds at 140 words a minute — but the
instruction is describe and demonstrate, so the hands are working: a radiograph taken before torquing, floss
through two contacts, two thicknesses of articulating paper, shimstock in three positions, a torque wrench,
then PTFE and composite. That is well over six minutes of real chairside time, and it fits into five only by
giving each of the ten checks a single narrated clause, with the justification kept for three places — the
refusal to force, the shimstock figure, and the PTFE.

Checklist 10 — baseline periapical
radiograph and photographs; records
(abutment, torque value, batch numbers,
occlusal scheme); what the patient is
told — site-specific hygiene with an
interdental brush of a named size,
single-tufted brush and superfloss, the
implant card handed over, and that the
crown can be unscrewed if it ever needs
attention; then the maintenance recall
interval.
The compressed answer — what a strong candidate says in five minutes
“Before the healing abutment comes off, I confirm this is the right patient, check the work against my
written prescription — correct system and platform, correct shade, screw-retained as I asked — and assess
the peri-implant tissues: no bleeding on probing, no suppuration, healthy keratinised cuff.
Healing abutment out, connection irrigated and inspected for tissue tags or debris.
I seat the crown by hand only. I check it visually, run a fine probe right round the margin, and then take
a paralleling periapical, because at this depth the eye and the probe are not enough — the sign of a misfit
is a wedge-shaped radiolucent gap between crown and platform. If it is not fully seated, I do not force it
home with the torque wrench. Torquing a non-seated restoration fractures screws, causes marginal bone
loss and hurts; I would find the cause instead — soft tissue over the platform, a proximal contact that is
too tight, or a laboratory error.
Contacts. Floss through each contact: it should meet resistance but pass and not shred. If it shreds, the
contact or the finish is wrong. And I check the contact is cleansable, not just present.
Contour and emergence. I check an interdental brush of the correct size passes on both sides. An over-
contoured or ridge-lap emergence looks fine on the day and is a peri-implantitis risk for the next twenty
years.
Occlusion, and it is deliberately light. In intercuspation the implant crown should hold shimstock only
under heavy clenching, and let it pull through under light tapping — about 25 to 30 micrometres lighter
than the adjacent teeth. That is because there is no periodontal ligament: the natural teeth intrude under
load and the implant does not, so an implant crown built to the same height takes a rising share of the
force. In excursions there should be no contact on the implant at all where the natural canine can guide
— I check working side, non-working side and protrusion, not just tapping.
Then the patient. I give them a mirror, in daylight if I can, and I get their approval of the appearance
before I torque it, because after torquing and sealing, a change is a remake.
Torque. To the manufacturer’s value with a calibrated wrench — I would not guess it by hand — and
I re-torque after ten minutes, which compensates for embedment relaxation as the microscopic surface
irregularities flatten and the preload drops.

osce.title: The mis-fitting framework
osce.text:
OSCE 17 — The mis-fitting framework
Blueprint: “Describe how to manage a mis-fitting prosthesis or framework” (OS-P).
EQUIPMENT
a model with four implant analogues and a cast framework that does not seat passively; a periapical radiograph showing a
wedge-shaped gap; probes, screws.
CANDIDATE INSTRUCTIONS
This framework does not seat. Demonstrate how you would confirm and manage the misfit.
MODEL ANSWER
“First I confirm the misfit objectively rather than assuming it.
• Visual and tactile: inspect each interface and run a fine probe around the margin.
• The one-screw or Sheﬀield test: tighten only the most distal screw and examine the fit at the
opposite end; a visible gap or rocking confirms the framework is not passive. I repeat this from
the other end.
• Radiographic: a paralleling periapical at the affected abutment — a wedge-shaped radiolucent
gap between framework and implant confirms it.
• Patient symptoms: pressure or pain as the screws are tightened is a warning sign.
Then I identify the cause: soft tissue or bone interference over the platform; a component not fully
seated; an incorrectly oriented analogue; impression distortion; an inaccurate cast; laboratory dis-
tortion during firing; or simply the wrong component.
I do not force it. Torquing a non-seating framework causes screw fracture, marginal bone loss and
pain.
Management according to cause: remove any tissue or bone interference and re-try; if the framework
itself is distorted, section it at the point of misfit and re-join it by soldering or laser welding, then

re-verify; if the error is in the impression or the cast, take a new impression with splinted open-tray
copings, or make a verification jig, and have the framework remade.
I would explain the position to the patient honestly, apologise for the delay, provide or adjust a pro-
visional in the meantime, and record everything — and I would discuss the case with the technician
to find out where the error arose so it doesn’t recur. I would not criticise the laboratory in front of
the patient.”
EXAMINER CHECKLIST
1. Visual and tactile check
2. One-screw/Sheﬀield test named and performed
3. Radiographic confirmation and the wedge-shaped gap
4. Patient symptoms considered
5. Lists possible causes
6. States explicitly that the framework must not be forced, with the consequences
7. Removes interference and re-tries
8. Section and re-join as a remedy
9. New splinted impression/verification jig and remake
10. Communication with patient and technician, provisional, records
Running this station to time
Time check. The model answer is 402 words, 2 minutes 52 seconds at 140 words per minute — comfortable
on paper, but the verb is demonstrate: screws have to be turned, a fine probe run round four interfaces, the
test repeated from the other end, and the periapical read. Handling doubles the honest running time, so
the causes and the remedies must each be delivered in a single clause, not a paragraph.
The five-minute run sheet
Time
The examiner does
What earns the mark

the framework, screws, probes and the
periapical: “This framework does not
seat. Demonstrate how you would
confirm and manage the misfit.”
Nothing is marked yet, but the candidate
must state the organising principle in
one sentence — “I confirm the misfit
objectively before I assume it, and
whatever I find I do not force it” — then
seat the framework by hand and
hand-tighten one screw only. Saying “I
do not force it” this early protects
checklist 6 if the clock beats them later.
0:30–2:00
Silence. Slides the periapical across
halfway through.
Checklists 1, 2, 3 and 4, performed and
narrated together. Fine probe run round
every interface with the eye at the level of
the joint; the one-screw or Sheﬀield test
named aloud, the most distal screw
tightened, the far end examined, then
repeated from the other end, because a
framework can fit from one direction and
not the other; the periapical described as
a wedge-shaped radiolucent gap;
pressure or pain on tightening named as
a warning that stops the candidate.
2:00–3:00
“So it does not fit. What now?”
Checklists 6 then 5, in that order. “I do
not force it” with the consequences —
screw loosening and fracture, marginal
bone loss, pain — then the causes in one
sweep: soft tissue or bone over a
platform, a component not fully seated, a
rotated or wrong analogue, impression
distortion, an inaccurate cast, laboratory
distortion during casting or firing.

Time
The examiner does
What earns the mark
3:00–4:15
“And what do you actually do about
each of those?”
Checklists 7, 8 and 9, escalating. Remove
the interference and re-try; section at the
point of misfit, lute the sections
intra-orally, return for soldering or laser
welding, and re-verify with the same
tests; and if the error lies in the
impression or the cast, a verification jig,
a new splinted open-tray impression
and a remade framework. Explicitly
refuses to grind the intaglio.
4:15–5:00
“Anything else?”
Checklist 10 — what the patient is told
(an honest explanation of the delay, an
apology, the provisional adjusted or
replaced so they are not inconvenienced),
the discussion with the technician to
find where the error arose, without
criticising the laboratory in front of the
patient, and the record: which tests, from
which end, the radiographic finding, the
cause identified, the decision taken and
the re-try appointment.
The compressed answer — what a strong candidate says in five minutes
“I will confirm this objectively before I assume anything — and whatever I find, I will not force it.
Seating it. I hand-tighten one screw only, and I look first. Visually and tactilely, with my eye down at
the level of the joint and a fine probe run right round each of the four interfaces — a probe that catches at
one margin and not the others tells me where the problem is.
The one-screw test. I tighten only the most distal screw and examine the fit at the opposite end. A visible
gap, or rocking under finger pressure, means the framework is not passive. Then I repeat the test from the
other end, because a distorted framework can appear to seat from one direction and not from the other.
Radiographically. A paralleling periapical at each abutment. On this film there is the classic sign — a
wedge-shaped radiolucent gap between the framework and the implant platform, widening away from
the tightened screw.
And by the patient. Pressure, tightness or pain as I tighten is a warning sign, not something to work
through. I stop.
So it is confirmed, and I do not force it. Torquing a non-passive framework transmits static stress into the
implants and components: screw loosening, screw or abutment fracture, marginal bone loss, and pain.
The causes, quickly. Soft tissue or bone lying over a platform; a component not fully seated; the wrong
analogue, or one rotated in the cast; impression distortion from unsplinted copings, a coping that moved,
or a flexible tray; an inaccurate or damaged cast; or laboratory distortion during casting, soldering or
ceramic firing — a framework can be passive before firing and not afterwards.
The remedies, in escalating order. First, remove any tissue or bone interference and re-try; that costs
nothing and solves a proportion of them. Second, if the framework is accurate in its parts but distorted
overall, section it at the point of misfit, lute the sections together intra-orally with pattern resin, and
return it for soldering or laser welding — then re-verify with exactly the same tests, from both ends.
Third, if the error is in the impression or the cast, I make a verification jig, take a new splinted open-tray
impression, and have the framework remade. What I do not do is grind the intaglio until it drops in; that
produces a framework that looks seated and is not.
Then the professional part. I explain the position to the patient honestly and apologise for the delay, and
I adjust or replace the provisional so they leave comfortable and are not inconvenienced. I discuss the
case with the technician to establish where the error arose so it does not recur — but I would not criticise
the laboratory in front of the patient.
And I record it: which tests I performed and from which end, the radiographic finding, the cause I iden-
tified, the decision taken, what I told the patient, and the appointment for the re-try and re-verification.”
Marking priority when the clock beats the candidate
Ask for these first (the six that carry the station): 2 one-screw/Sheﬀield test performed and repeated
from both ends · 6 states explicitly that it must not be forced, with the consequences · 3 radiographic

osce.title: Writing the laboratory prescription
osce.text:
OSCE 18 — Writing the laboratory prescription
Blueprint: “Prescribe an appropriate type of restoration from the laboratory”; “Evaluate the laboratory techniques involved in implant reconstruction”
(W + OS-P + SCE).
EQUIPMENT
a blank laboratory prescription form, a working cast with an implant analogue at the UR1, photographs, a shade tab.
CANDIDATE INSTRUCTIONS
Complete the laboratory prescription for a definitive restoration of the UR1 implant. Explain your entries.
MODEL ANSWER
“Header: patient identifier, my name, practice address and GDC number, the date sent and the date
required.
Work required: ‘UR1 — definitive implant crown, screw-retained’ — then the implant details:
system, platform diameter, connection type, and the analogue supplied.
Abutment: ‘custom CAD-CAM titanium base with a milled lithium disilicate superstructure’ — or
‘custom titanium abutment’, with the margin to follow the gingival scallop and lie no more than
1 mm subgingival, and the emergence profile to be copied from the provisional restoration/cus-
tomised impression coping supplied.
Materials: framework and veneering material specified; for a bruxist I would specify monolithic
zirconia.
Aesthetics: shade — with the shade tab photographed in the mouth alongside the adjacent teeth —
plus stump shade, characterisation, translucency, surface texture and any notes on the incisal edge
and mamelons; photographs attached.
Form and function: contact points to be light and cleansable; contour to permit an interdental brush;
occlusion — light contact in intercuspation and no contact in excursions; and whether a bisque
try-in is required.
Administration: state that the impression and cast are disinfected; request that the work be returned
disinfected; request the custom-made device statement for my records; give my contact number
in case the technician has questions; and record the laboratory’s details and, on return, the batch
numbers.
I would keep a copy of the prescription in the notes.”
EXAMINER CHECKLIST
1. Patient and clinician identifiers, dates
2. Precise description of the work and tooth notation
3. Implant system, platform, connection
4. Abutment type, material and margin position
5. Emergence profile instruction

6. Materials specified
7. Shade and aesthetic detail with photographs
8. Occlusal instruction
9. Try-in requirement
10. Disinfection statement, custom-made device statement, copy retained
Running this station to time
Time check. The model answer is 352 words, 2 minutes 31 seconds at 140 words per minute — the shortest
in this part, and the trap is that the candidate has to write as well as speak, and writing is far slower than
talking. Ten headed entries filled in legibly will not fit in five minutes at conversational pace; the fix is
note form in the box, one clause of justification aloud, with full explanation reserved for three entries
only.
The five-minute run sheet
Time
The examiner does
What earns the mark
0:00–0:45
Puts the blank prescription form, the
working cast with the UR1 analogue, the
photographs and the shade tab in front of
the candidate: “Complete the laboratory
prescription for a definitive restoration of
the UR1 implant. Explain your entries.”
Checklist 1, written while speaking.
Patient identifier, clinician name,
practice address, GDC number, date
sent and date required — filled in, not
discussed. The candidate should state
the organising principle once: the
prescription is a written instruction the
technician must be able to work from without
telephoning me, which frames everything
that follows.
0:45–1:45
Silence. Lets the candidate work down
the form.
Checklists 2 and 3. The work described
precisely and in FDI notation — “UR1,
definitive implant crown,
screw-retained” — not “crown please”;
then the implant system, platform
diameter, connection type and
confirmation that the correct analogue is
supplied with the cast.
1:45–3:00
“Tell me about the abutment entry.”
Checklists 4, 5 and 6, and the first of the
three entries worth explaining. Custom
CAD-CAM titanium base with a milled
lithium disilicate superstructure, or a
custom titanium abutment; the margin
to follow the gingival scallop and lie no
more than 1 mm subgingival, with the
reason — cement retrievability and
cleansability; the emergence profile to
be copied from the customised
impression coping or the provisional
supplied; and framework and veneering
materials named, monolithic zirconia
for a bruxist.
3:00–4:00
“And the aesthetic and functional
instructions?”
Checklists 7, 8 and 9. Shade recorded
with the tab photographed in the
mouth beside the adjacent teeth, plus
stump shade, characterisation,
translucency, surface texture and incisal
notes, photographs attached; contacts
light and cleansable, contour to admit an
interdental brush; occlusion — light
contact in intercuspation, no contact in
excursions; and whether a bisque try-in
is required stated explicitly, one way or
the other.

Time
The examiner does
What earns the mark
4:00–5:00
“Anything left on the form?”
Checklist 10 — the administrative block
candidates skip: the impression and cast
are disinfected and the work is to be
returned disinfected, the custom-made
device statement requested for the
records, a contact number for queries,
the laboratory’s details, and the batch
and lot numbers recorded on return.
Then a copy of the prescription kept in
the notes, the patient told the return date
and what the try-in appointment
involves, and the work checked against
the prescription on receipt before the
patient is seated.
The compressed answer — what a strong candidate says in five minutes
“I will fill this in as I talk. The test of a prescription is whether the technician can work from it without
ringing me.
Header. Patient’s name and identifier, my name, the practice address, my GDC number, the date sent and
the date required — the date required matters because a bisque try-in has to be built into the timetable.
Work required. ‘UR1 — definitive implant crown, screw-retained’, in FDI notation. Then the implant
details: the system, the platform diameter and the connection type, and I confirm the correct analogue
is in the cast I am sending.
Abutment. ‘Custom CAD-CAM titanium base with a milled lithium disilicate superstructure’ — or a
custom titanium abutment if the tissue is thin. The instruction that matters here is the margin: to follow
the gingival scallop and to lie no more than 1 millimetre subgingival. That is not aesthetics, it is so that
any cement can be reached and removed, and so the margin can be cleaned.
Emergence profile. ‘Copy the emergence profile from the customised impression coping supplied’ —
the provisional has been shaping that tissue for weeks, and the definitive crown must reproduce it, not
invent a new one.
Materials. Framework and veneering material specified. If this patient were a bruxist I would prescribe
monolithic zirconia and say so on the form, with the reason.
Aesthetics. The shade, with the tab photographed in the mouth alongside the adjacent teeth so the
technician sees my lighting, not just my letter. Then stump shade, characterisation, translucency, surface
texture, and a note on the incisal edge and mamelons. Photographs attached and referenced by number.
Form and function. Contact points light and cleansable; contour to allow an interdental brush to pass;
and the occlusion written out — light contact in intercuspation and no contact in any excursion, so that
the implant is not the guiding unit. And I state whether I want a bisque try-in: on a single upper central
with a demanding shade, yes.
Administration. I state that the impression and cast have been disinfected, and ask for the work to be
returned disinfected. I request the statement of manufacture for the custom-made device for my records.
I give my direct number for queries, record the laboratory’s name and address, and on return I record the
batch and lot numbers of the materials used.
And finally, records. A copy of the prescription goes in the notes — it is a legal instruction and my
evidence of what I asked for. I tell the patient the date the work is due, that there may be a try-in before
the crown is finished, and what that appointment involves. When the work comes back I check it against
my own prescription on the cast before the patient is in the chair, because that is the point at which an
error is still cheap to correct.”
Marking priority when the clock beats the candidate
Ask for these first (the six that carry the station): 2 precise work description in FDI notation · 3 implant
system, platform and connection · 4 abutment type, material and margin position with the reason · 5
emergence profile copied from the coping or provisional · 8 occlusal instruction written out · 10 disinfection
both ways, custom-made device statement and copy retained.
Accept these late or on prompting: 1 identifiers and dates · 6 materials specified, monolithic zirconia for
a bruxist · 7 shade and aesthetic detail with photographs · 9 bisque try-in stated one way or the other.

osce.title: Digital workflow and guided surgery
osce.text:
OSCE 19 — Digital workflow and guided surgery
Blueprint: “Demonstrate understanding of the role of digital techniques in restoring implants” (W + OS-P + SCE).
EQUIPMENT
an intraoral scanner (or images of scans), scan bodies, a printed surgical guide, a CBCT/STL merge on screen.
CANDIDATE INSTRUCTIONS
Explain the digital workflow from planning through to the definitive restoration for a single implant, and state the limitations
of each stage.
MODEL ANSWER
“The chain is: intraoral scan →digital wax-up →CBCT →merge of the DICOM and STL data →
virtual implant planning →guide design and manufacture →guided placement →scan body
impression →CAD design →milled or printed restoration.
Stage by stage:
Scan and digital wax-up. I scan both arches and the bite, and design the planned tooth position
digitally — the digital equivalent of the diagnostic wax-up. This keeps the plan restoratively driven.
Limitation: accuracy falls across long edentulous spans, and deep subgingival margins scan poorly.
CBCT and merge. The CBCT is justified individually and I report the whole volume. The merge
relies on matching common reference points — usually teeth. Limitation: metal artefact degrades
the merge, and in a fully edentulous patient there are no teeth to match, so a radiographic guide
with markers is needed.
Virtual planning. I place the implant virtually with correct 3-D position, respecting 1.5 mm to teeth,
3 mm to implants, 2 mm of buccal bone and 2 mm from the canal.
Guide manufacture and surgery. Tooth-supported guides are most accurate. Limitations: mean
angular deviation of about 2 to 4 degrees, so the 2 mm safety margin is retained; sleeves restrict
irrigation, so heat control needs attention; and posterior access may be inadequate for the drill-and-
sleeve assembly.
Restorative digital stage. A scan body is screwed to the implant and scanned, transferring the
implant position digitally, and the abutment and crown are designed and milled. Limitation: scan
body wear or incomplete seating introduces error, and for multiple implants across a long span a
conventional splinted impression may still be more accurate.
Overall advantages: patient comfort, immediate re-scanning, archiving, communication, restora-
tively driven planning. Overall limitations: cost, learning curve, and the fact that a guide replaces
neither anatomical knowledge nor surgical judgement.”
EXAMINER CHECKLIST
1. States the full workflow in order
2. Digital wax-up as the restorative driver
3. CBCT justification and full-volume reporting
4. DICOM/STL merge and its reference points
5. Metal artefact and edentulous merging limitation
6. Correct 3-D planning parameters
7. Guide support types and accuracy figures

8. Retains the 2 mm safety margin despite guidance
9. Scan body use and its error sources
10. Balanced statement of advantages and limitations
Running this station to time
Time check. The model answer is 443 words, 3 minutes 10 seconds at 140 words per minute — but the
instruction asks for a workflow and a limitation at every stage, which is effectively eighteen items, and a
candidate who separates them into two passes will deliver the limitations after the bell. The fix is a fixed
45 seconds per stage, with the limitation named in the same breath as the stage, and the whole chain
stated once at the start as a spine.
The five-minute run sheet
Time
The examiner does
What earns the mark
0:00–0:40
Indicates the scanner, the scan bodies,
the printed guide and the merged
CBCT/STL on screen: “Explain the
digital workflow from planning through
to the definitive restoration for a single
implant, and state the limitations of each
stage.”
Checklist 1 — the whole chain named in
order, in one breath, before any stage is
expanded: intraoral scan, digital wax-up,
CBCT, DICOM/STL merge, virtual
planning, guide design and manufacture,
guided placement, scan body impression,
CAD design, milled or printed
restoration. Thirty seconds spent here
buys permission to be brief afterwards.
0:40–1:50
Silence, then: “And the limitations of
those first steps?”
Checklists 2, 3, 4 and 5. Digital wax-up
as the restorative driver — the plan is
prosthetically led, not bone-led; CBCT
justified individually and the whole
volume reported; the merge matched on
common reference points, usually teeth;
and the two limitations that matter —
accuracy falls across long edentulous
spans and deep subgingival margins,
and metal artefact degrades the merge,
with a radiographic guide carrying
markers needed in the fully edentulous
patient.
1:50–3:10
“How do you place it virtually, and how
accurate is the guide?”
Checklists 6, 7 and 8. The 3-D parameters
as numbers — 1.5 mm to a tooth, 3 mm
between implants, 2 mm of buccal
bone, 2 mm from the canal;
tooth-supported guides most accurate,
then mucosa-supported, then
bone-supported; mean angular
deviation of about 2 to 4 degrees; and
the decisive statement that the 2 mm
safety margin is retained despite the
guide, not consumed by it. Sleeves
restrict irrigation, and posterior access
may not admit the drill-and-sleeve
assembly.
3:10–4:10
“And the restorative stage?”
Checklist 9. The scan body screwed to
the implant and scanned to transfer the
position digitally, then abutment and
crown designed and milled or printed.
Error sources named specifically: wear
or damage to the scan body, and
incomplete seating; and the honest
concession that for multiple implants
across a long span a conventional
splinted open-tray impression may still
be more accurate.

Time
The examiner does
What earns the mark
4:10–5:00
“So overall — is it better?”
Checklist 10 and the close. A balanced
answer: comfort, immediate re-scanning,
archiving, communication and
restoratively driven planning against cost,
learning curve and the fact that a guide
replaces neither anatomical knowledge
nor surgical judgement. Then records
(the CBCT report written in the notes
with the justification, the plan and the
STL files archived, the guide’s fit and
sterilisation checked and recorded),
what the patient is told (the dose, and
that the plan may be converted to a flap
intra-operatively), and review at the
planned surgical and restorative stages.
The compressed answer — what a strong candidate says in five minutes
Q: Take me through the workflow. “Intraoral scan, digital wax-up, CBCT, merge of the DICOM and
STL data, virtual implant planning, guide design and manufacture, guided placement, scan body im-
pression, CAD design, milled or printed restoration. I will take each stage with its limitation attached.”
Q: The scan and the wax-up. “I scan both arches and the bite, and design the planned tooth position
digitally — the digital equivalent of the diagnostic wax-up, and the reason the whole plan stays restora-
tively driven rather than driven by where the bone happens to be. Its limitation is accuracy: scanning
drifts across long edentulous spans, because there are no landmarks for the software to stitch to, and
deep subgingival margins scan poorly because the scanner only records what it can see.”
Q: The CBCT and the merge. “The CBCT is justified individually, and I report the whole volume, not
only the site — that report goes in the notes. The merge works by matching common reference points, in
a dentate patient the teeth. Its limitation is metal artefact: a heavily restored arch degrades the surfaces
the software matches on. And in a fully edentulous patient there are no teeth to match at all, so I need a
radiographic guide with fiducial markers, or a dual-scan protocol.”
Q: The virtual plan. “I position the implant in three dimensions to the restorative plan: at least 1.5 mm
from an adjacent tooth, 3 mm from an adjacent implant, 2 mm of buccal bone, and 2 mm clear of the
inferior alveolar canal, with the emergence under the planned tooth.”
Q: The guide. “Tooth-supported guides are the most accurate; mucosa-supported guides depend on the
tissue and need fixation pins; bone-supported guides need a flap. The published mean angular deviation
is about 2 to 4 degrees, with linear deviation of a millimetre or more at the apex — which is why the
2 mm safety margin is retained and not spent. A guide narrows the distribution; it does not abolish it.
Practically: the sleeve restricts irrigation, so I use copious external irrigation and intermittent drilling for
heat control, and I check mouth opening and posterior access for the drill-and-sleeve assembly before I
order it.”
Q: The restorative stage. “A scan body is screwed to the implant and scanned; that transfers the im-
plant’s three-dimensional position and rotation into the design software, and the abutment and crown
are designed and milled or printed. Its errors are mechanical: a worn, damaged or autoclaved-out-of-
shape scan body, or one not fully seated — which I confirm radiographically if I am in any doubt. And
I would say honestly that for multiple implants across a long span a conventional splinted open-tray
impression is still at least as accurate.”
Q: Overall? “Advantages: patient comfort, immediate re-scanning if something fails, archiving and com-
munication, and a genuinely restoratively driven plan. Limitations: cost, a real learning curve, and the
important one — a guide replaces neither anatomical knowledge nor surgical judgement. I plan every
case so that I could complete it freehand if the guide did not seat.
Records and follow-up: the CBCT report and its justification written in the notes, the plan and the STL
and DICOM files archived, the guide checked for fit on the cast and sterilised before use, and that recorded.
I tell the patient what the scan dose is and why it is justified, and that if the guide does not seat accurately
on the day I will raise a flap and place freehand rather than proceed blind.”
Marking priority when the clock beats the candidate
Ask for these first (the six that carry the station): 1 the full workflow stated in order · 2 digital wax-up
as the restorative driver · 6 the 3-D planning parameters as numbers · 8 the 2 mm safety margin retained

osce.title: Peri-implant assessment and maintenance
osce.text:
OSCE 20 — Peri-implant assessment and maintenance
Blueprint: “Identify appropriate maintenance care regimes”; “Assess treatment outcomes and demonstrate understanding of the parameters used
to monitor outcomes” (W + SCE, assessed practically).
EQUIPMENT
a manikin with an implant-supported crown at the LR6, a plastic/titanium probe, a steel probe (distractor), interdental
brushes of various sizes, single-tufted brush, superfloss, a periapical radiograph.
CANDIDATE INSTRUCTIONS
Carry out a peri-implant assessment on this implant and give the patient appropriate maintenance advice.
MODEL ANSWER
“I would first update the medical history, ask about smoking and about any symptoms — soreness,
bleeding, bad taste, discharge, or a feeling of movement.
Assessment: - Plaque and bleeding scores for the whole mouth, because peri-implant health de-
pends on overall plaque control. - Peri-implant probing at six sites with a light force of about 0.2 to
0.25 newtons — the force at which the probe tip just blanches my fingernail. I would use a plastic or
titanium probe. (Selecting the plastic probe over the steel one is a checklist item.) Probing implants is safe
and essential; the old advice not to probe is obsolete. - Record bleeding on probing and suppuration,
probing depths, mucosal recession and the width of keratinised mucosa. - Assess mobility —
and if there is any doubt, I would remove the restoration to distinguish a loose prosthesis from a
mobile implant, because a mobile implant means loss of osseointegration. - Assess the prosthesis:
fit, contour, cleansability, screw integrity, wear, chipping, occlusion, and check for residual cement. -
Compare a standardised periapical radiograph with the baseline taken at fitting. I would only take a
new radiograph if there were a clinical indication — increased probing depth, bleeding, suppuration
or symptoms — because the exposure must be justified.
Diagnosis using the 2017 criteria: health, mucositis if there is bleeding on gentle probing without
bone loss, and peri-implantitis if there is bleeding or suppuration with increased probing depth and
bone loss beyond initial remodelling.
Maintenance advice: professional biofilm removal with titanium or plastic instruments and glycine
air-polishing, then site-specific hygiene instruction — I would size an interdental brush to fit the
embrasure and demonstrate it in the mirror, add a single-tufted brush around the emergence and
superfloss under the pontic area if there is one, and recommend a powered brush.
Recall interval: risk-based — three to four months for this patient if there is a history of periodontitis
or smoking, otherwise three to six months. I would record the findings, the advice given, and the
next review.”
EXAMINER CHECKLIST
1. Medical history and symptoms updated

2. Whole-mouth plaque and bleeding scores
3. Selects the plastic/titanium probe
4. Probes 6 sites with gentle force, states the force
5. Records BOP, suppuration, recession, keratinised mucosa
6. Assesses implant vs prosthesis mobility
7. Assesses prosthesis fit, contour, cleansability, cement
8. Compares with baseline radiograph; justifies any new exposure
9. Applies the 2017 diagnostic criteria
10. Individualised hygiene demonstration and risk-based recall, recorded
Running this station to time
Time check. The model answer is 492 words, 3 minutes 31 seconds at 140 words per minute — but the
verb is carry out: six sites have to be probed, the prosthesis examined, the radiograph compared and an
interdental brush sized and demonstrated, and hands are always slower than speech. Roughly 150 words
must go, and they go by naming each finding as it is recorded rather than explaining why it is recorded,
keeping justification for the probe, the force and the radiograph.

“Before I touch her I update the history — any change in health or medication, whether she still smokes,
and whether she has had soreness, bleeding, a bad taste, discharge or any feeling that it has moved.
Then the probe, and this matters. I take the plastic or titanium probe, not the steel one — a steel tip
scratches the machined titanium surface, and a scratched surface is a plaque trap. Probing an implant is
safe and necessary; the old advice never to probe is obsolete.
Whole mouth first. Plaque and bleeding scores for the whole dentition, because peri-implant health
depends on her overall plaque control, and an implant is not assessed in isolation from the teeth beside it.

light force of 0.2 to 0.25 newtons, which I calibrate against my thumbnail until the nail bed just blanches.
The seal round an implant is weaker than a periodontal attachment, so the same force penetrates further,
and heavy probing produces a falsely deep reading and a bleeding point I have created myself.
As I go I record: the six probing depths, bleeding on probing, any suppuration, mucosal recession, and
the width of keratinised mucosa on the buccal.
Mobility. Any mobility is significant. If there is doubt I would remove the restoration and test the

that is loss of osseointegration and the implant comes out.

wear, chipping, the occlusion, and I look and probe specifically for residual cement, which is a common
and correctable cause of inflammation.

today tells me nothing without that comparison. I would only take a new exposure if there is a clinical
indication: increased probing depth, bleeding, suppuration or symptoms. The exposure has to be justified.

bleeding or suppuration, increased probing depth against baseline, and radiographic bone loss beyond
initial remodelling.
Maintenance.

polishing. Then the part that actually changes the outcome: site-specific hygiene, individualised, and
demonstrated. I size an interdental brush to this embrasure — the right size is the one that meets slight
resistance, not the one in the cupboard — and I put it in her hand and have her use it in front of the
mirror. A single-tufted brush round the emergence, superfloss under any pontic, and a powered brush
for the rest.
Records and review. I record the six depths, bleeding, suppuration, recession, keratinised width, the
prosthesis findings, the radiographic comparison and the diagnosis; that I demonstrated the brushes and
she performed them back to me; and I set a risk-based recall — three to four months, because of the
smoking and the periodontal history — otherwise three to six.”

osce.title: Atraumatic extraction and ridge preservation
osce.text:
OSCE 21 — Atraumatic extraction and ridge preservation
Blueprint: minor augmentation; bone defects; graft and barrier materials (W + OS-P + SCE).
EQUIPMENT
model or pig jaw with a restorable-looking upper premolar; periotomes, luxators, forceps, curettes; xenograft, collagen plug,
collagen membrane, sutures.
CANDIDATE INSTRUCTIONS
This upper first premolar is unrestorable. An implant is planned in 4 months. Extract the tooth and perform ridge
preservation, describing each step.
DIRECTION OF THOUGHT
The whole point is preserving the buccal plate. Sequence: atraumatic extraction →debride →confirm walls
→graft →seal →suture →instructions.
MODEL ANSWER
“I would confirm the tooth, the medical history and consent, including consent to the graft material
and its bovine origin, then anaesthetise with buccal and palatal infiltration.
I would extract atraumatically and flaplessly: sever the periodontal ligament circumferentially with
a periotome, then luxate with fine luxators applied to the ligament space rather than levering off the
buccal plate, and deliver with forceps using rotational movements. This is a two-rooted premolar,
so if it resists I would section it and remove the roots individually rather than force it.
I would then debride the socket thoroughly with curettes, remove all granulation tissue, irrigate
with saline, and probe the walls circumferentially to confirm the buccal plate is intact — that
determines whether this is an Elian Type 1, 2 or 3 socket and therefore what I do next.
Assuming an intact socket, I would place a slowly resorbing deproteinised bovine bone mineral
into the socket, filling it to just below the crest without over-packing, because volume stability is
what I need over four months.
I would seal it with either a collagen plug or membrane tucked under the buccal and palatal soft
tissue margins, or a free epithelialised punch graft from the palate as a socket seal. I would not
attempt full primary closure by advancing the buccal flap here, because that pulls keratinised tissue
coronally and reduces vestibular depth.
Closure: a figure-of-eight or crossed mattress suture in 4/0 monofilament to retain the graft. If I
had used a dense PTFE membrane I would deliberately leave it exposed and remove it at three to
four weeks.
Post-operatively: written instructions, analgesia, chlorhexidine from day one, no brushing over the
site, soft diet, no smoking, an interim bonded pontic rather than a denture if possible, review at one

week, and reassessment for implant placement at four months. I would record the graft material, its
lot number and the socket classification.”
EXAMINER CHECKLIST
1. Consent including graft origin
2. Periotome/luxator technique, no buccal levering
3. Sectioning if resistant
4. Debridement and irrigation
5. Probes and classifies the socket
6. Selects a slowly resorbing xenograft with justification
7. Barrier or socket seal
8. Appropriate suture technique
9. Interim prosthesis avoiding pressure
10. Instructions, review and records including lot number
Running this station to time
Time check. The model answer is 470 words, 3 minutes 21 seconds at 140 words per minute — but the
instruction is extract the tooth and perform ridge preservation, describing each step, so the periotome, the luxators,
the curettes, the graft and the suture all have to be handled while the commentary runs. About 120 words
must go, and they go by stating each step in a clause as the hand performs it, with justification kept for
three places only: why nothing levers off the buccal plate, why the socket walls are probed, and why the
flap is not advanced.
The five-minute run sheet

chosen for volume stability over four
months rather than rapid turnover, filled
to just below the crest and not
over-packed. Sealed with a collagen
plug or membrane tucked under the

epithelialised punch graft from the
palate. Explicitly refuses to advance the
buccal flap for primary closure, because
it drags keratinised tissue coronally and
loses vestibular depth.
3:50–5:00
“Finish off.”
Checklists 8, 9 and 10. A figure-of-eight
or crossed mattress suture in 4/0
monofilament to retain the graft, not to
close it; a dense PTFE membrane left
deliberately exposed and removed at
three to four weeks if that was the
choice. Then what the patient is told
and given — written instructions,
analgesia, chlorhexidine from day one,
no brushing over the site, soft diet, no
smoking, and an interim bonded pontic
rather than a denture so nothing presses
on the graft. Then review at one week
and reassessment at four months, and
the record: graft material, lot number
and socket classification.
The compressed answer — what a strong candidate says in five minutes
“Everything I do here is aimed at one thing — preserving the buccal plate.
Consent first. I confirm the tooth, check the medical history, and take consent that includes the graft: I
would tell her plainly that the material is deproteinised bovine bone mineral — of bovine origin — and
offer a synthetic or allogeneic alternative if she would rather not have it. That conversation happens before
I anaesthetise, not after.
Anaesthesia. Buccal and palatal infiltration.
The extraction — atraumatic and flapless. No flap, because raising one strips the periosteum from a thin
buccal plate and accelerates the resorption I am trying to prevent. I pass a periotome circumferentially to
sever the periodontal ligament, working apically in small increments. Then fine luxators in the ligament
space, rotated gently — at no point do I lever off the buccal plate, which is the single commonest way this
operation is ruined in the first thirty seconds. Forceps last, with rotational movements rather than buccal
pressure. This is a two-rooted premolar: if it resists, I section it and deliver the two roots individually,
which is quicker and far safer than forcing it.
Then the socket. I debride it completely with curettes — all granulation tissue out, because residual soft
tissue will not be replaced by bone — and irrigate with saline. Then I probe every wall circumferentially
to confirm the buccal plate is intact. That is a decision point, not a formality: an intact plate with intact soft
tissue is an Elian Type 1 socket and I proceed. If the buccal plate is missing or the soft tissue is deficient
— Type 2 or Type 3 — this becomes a staged augmentation with a flap and a fixed membrane, which is
beyond what I would do myself, and I would refer.
The graft. Assuming Type 1, I place a slowly resorbing deproteinised bovine bone mineral, in incre-
ments, filled to just below the crest and not over-packed. I choose it deliberately for volume stability —
I need this ridge to hold its dimension for four months, so I want a material that resorbs slowly, not one
that turns over quickly.
The seal. A collagen plug or a collagen membrane tucked under the buccal and palatal soft tissue
margins, or a free epithelialised punch graft taken from the palate as a socket seal. What I would not
do is advance the buccal flap to get primary closure — that pulls keratinised tissue coronally, reduces
vestibular depth, and leaves me a worse soft tissue bed for the implant than I started with.
Sutures. A figure-of-eight or crossed mattress suture in 4/0 monofilament across the socket, to retain the
graft rather than to close the wound. If I had used a dense PTFE membrane, I would leave it deliberately
exposed and remove it at three to four weeks.

osce.title: Transcrestal sinus floor elevation
osce.text:
OSCE 22 — Transcrestal sinus floor elevation
Blueprint: minor augmentation; limitations and timing (W + OS-P + SCE).
EQUIPMENT
maxillary model with 7 mm residual height at the 26; osteotomes, mallet, drills, graft material, CBCT printout.
CANDIDATE INSTRUCTIONS
This patient has 7 mm of residual bone height beneath a flat sinus floor at the UL6. Describe and, where possible, demon-
strate a transcrestal sinus floor elevation with simultaneous implant placement, including how you would confirm the
membrane is intact.
MODEL ANSWER
“First, indications. The ITI decision tree indicates a transcrestal approach with simultaneous place-
ment where residual height exceeds 6 mm and the sinus floor is horizontal. Here I have 7 mm and
a flat floor, so the criteria are met. Below 6 mm, or with an oblique floor or septa, a lateral window
is indicated, and that is outside my scope. I would also confirm on the CBCT that the membrane is
under 2 mm thick, there are no septa, no sinus pathology and the ostium is patent.
Technique: aseptic preparation, chlorhexidine rinse, buccal and palatal infiltration. Mid-crestal
incision with a full-thickness flap for direct vision.
I prepare the osteotomy conventionally but stop 1 to 2 mm short of the sinus floor, confirming depth
with a depth gauge and, if needed, a periapical radiograph.
I then use concave-tipped osteotomes of increasing diameter with gentle malleting to green-stick
fracture the floor. I place a small increment of graft material into the osteotomy and use the os-
teotome to push it upward — the graft, not the metal tip, elevates the membrane, which reduces the
risk of tearing. I repeat this in small increments to gain the 3 to 4 mm I need.
I confirm the membrane is intact with the Valsalva manoeuvre — the patient pinches the nose and
blows gently; I look for air bubbling in the osteotomy and for movement of the membrane. There
should be neither. I also check by gentle probing with a blunt instrument.

I then place the implant, which needs to engage the residual 7 mm for primary stability. Because
this is D3 or D4 bone, I would under-prepare the osteotomy and use a tapered implant. I would aim
for at least 25 Ncm.
Closure with 4/0 monofilament interrupted sutures. Prosthetic loading at approximately 3 months.
Post-operatively: sinus precautions — no nose-blowing, sneeze with the mouth open, no straws,
no smoking, no diving or flying if advised — plus antibiotics and consideration of a decongestant,
analgesia and review at one week.
Complications I would warn about and be prepared for: membrane perforation, which is the com-
monest; benign paroxysmal positional vertigo from malleting; graft migration into the sinus; si-
nusitis; and, rarely, displacement of the implant into the sinus. If I perforated the membrane sub-
stantially, I would abandon the elevation, close, and re-plan at 3 to 6 months.”
EXAMINER CHECKLIST
1. States the >6 mm / flat floor indication
2. Excludes sinus pathology and septa on CBCT
3. Osteotomy stopped 1–2 mm short
4. Osteotome technique with graft-mediated elevation
5. Valsalva to confirm integrity
6. Under-preparation for D3/D4
7. Primary stability target
8. Loading at ~3 months
9. Sinus precautions and medication
10. Names complications and the fallback plan
Running this station to time
Time check. The model answer is 533 words, 3 minutes 49 seconds at 140 words per minute — the longest
of this group, and the instruction adds demonstrate where possible, so the osteotomes and mallet must be
handled as well. Around 170 words have to go. They go by compressing the complication list and the
post-operative instructions to one clause each, and by putting the indication and the competence limit
in the first 45 seconds, where they cannot be lost.

number, elevation achieved, Valsalva
