“The indication first, because it decides whether I do this at all. The ITI decision tree indicates a tran-
screstal elevation with simultaneous placement where the residual height is above 6 mm and the sinus
floor is horizontal. Here I have 7 mm and a flat floor, so the criteria are met and this is within the scope
of a general dentist with an interest in implants. Below 6 mm, with an oblique floor, or with septa, the
indication is a lateral window — and a lateral window is not within my competence. I would refer that
patient to a specialist colleague. On the CBCT I also confirm the membrane is under 2 millimetres thick,
there are no septa, no sinus pathology and the ostium is patent; a blocked ostium or an active sinusitis
is a contraindication until it is treated.
Preparation. Aseptic technique, chlorhexidine rinse, buccal and palatal infiltration, a mid-crestal incision
and a full-thickness flap — I want direct vision of the crest for this, not a flapless approach.
The osteotomy. I prepare conventionally but stop 1 to 2 millimetres short of the sinus floor, checking
with a depth gauge and, if I am not certain, a periapical radiograph.

osce.title: Interpreting a cone beam CT for implant planning
osce.text:
OSCE 23 — Interpreting a cone beam CT for implant planning
Blueprint: interpret radiographic findings; assess need for investigations (W + SCE, practical interpretation).
EQUIPMENT
printed or on-screen CBCT cross-sections of a posterior mandible and an anterior maxilla, with a measuring tool.
CANDIDATE INSTRUCTIONS
Report these cone beam CT images and state how they affect your implant plan.

MODEL ANSWER
“I would report in a fixed order.
Preliminaries: type of image, date, patient identifiers, field of view, and whether the image quality
is diagnostic. I note that the whole volume must be examined and reported, not just the region of
interest, and that a written report goes in the notes.
Systematic review of the volume: dentition and restorations, periapical status, bone levels, the
maxillary sinuses including membrane thickness, septa and ostia, the mandibular canals and mental
foramina, the temporomandibular joints, the airway, and any incidental finding. If I found, for
instance, an unexplained radiolucency or a calcified carotid atheroma, I would report it and act on
it.
Region of interest, posterior mandible: I measure the vertical height from the crest to the superior
border of the canal, the buccolingual width at the crest and at 5 mm apically, the ridge inclination,
and I look specifically for a lingual concavity — the submandibular fossa — which is the classic
cause of lingual plate perforation. I identify the mental foramen and any anterior loop. I plan an
implant length that leaves at least 2 mm of clearance from the canal.
Region of interest, anterior maxilla: I measure ridge width, look for a buccal concavity, assess the
position of the incisive canal, assess the nasal floor, and assess the buccal plate thickness and the
bone level on the adjacent teeth.
Bone quality: I make an approximate assessment from the trabecular pattern and grey values, recog-
nising that CBCT grey values are not standardised Hounsfield units and are approximations only.
Effect on the plan: the CBCT tells me implant length, diameter, angulation and position; whether
augmentation is needed and of what kind; whether the case is Straightforward, Advanced or Com-
plex; and therefore whether it is within my competence. If the measurements showed, for example,
5 mm above the canal with a marked lingual concavity, I would use a shorter implant, or reconsider
the option entirely, rather than proceed.”
EXAMINER CHECKLIST
1. Image identification and quality
2. States whole-volume reporting requirement
3. Systematic review of the volume
4. Measures vertical height to the canal
5. Measures ridge width at two levels
6. Identifies lingual/buccal concavity
7. Identifies mental foramen and anterior loop
8. States the 2 mm safety margin
9. Caveats on CBCT grey values
10. Translates findings into an implant plan and a complexity judgement
Running this station to time
Time check. The model answer is 449 words, 3 minutes 13 seconds at 140 words per minute — but there
are two regions of interest to measure with the tool in hand, and every measurement has to be spoken as
a number while it is taken. Roughly 120 words must go, and they go by giving the systematic review of
the whole volume one line per structure so that the two minutes it would otherwise consume are spent
on the measurements and the plan, which is where the marks specific to implant planning sit.
The five-minute run sheet
Time
The examiner does
What earns the mark
0:00–0:30
Displays the cross-sections of the
posterior mandible and the anterior
maxilla with the measuring tool: “Report
these cone beam CT images and state
how they affect your implant plan.”
Checklists 1 and 2. Image type, date,
patient identifiers, field of view and
whether the quality is diagnostic — in
three sentences — followed immediately
by the statement that must not be left out:
the whole volume must be examined
and reported, not only the region of
interest, and a written report goes in the
notes. Candidates who go straight to the
site lose both marks in the first ten
seconds.

Time
The examiner does
What earns the mark
0:30–1:30
Silence. Lets the candidate run the
survey.
Checklist 3, one line per structure,
delivered fast. Dentition and
restorations, periapical status, bone
levels; the maxillary sinuses including
membrane thickness, septa and ostia;
the mandibular canals and mental
foramina; the temporomandibular joints;
the airway; and any incidental finding —
with the explicit undertaking that an
unexplained radiolucency or a calcified
carotid atheroma would be reported
and acted on, not merely noticed. Speed
is the mark here, not detail.
1:30–3:00
“Now the posterior mandible. Show me
your measurements.”
Checklists 4, 5, 6, 7 and 8, with the tool
actually on the image and each figure
spoken as a number. Vertical height
from the crest to the superior border of
the canal; buccolingual width at the
crest and again 5 mm apically; ridge
inclination; and the specific search for a
lingual concavity — the submandibular
fossa — the classic cause of lingual
plate perforation. The mental foramen
identified and the anterior loop
measured. Then the rule: an implant
length that leaves at least 2 mm of
clearance from the canal.
3:00–4:00
“And the anterior maxilla?” Then: “How
reliable is the bone density on this?”
Checklists 5 and 6 again in the second
region, then checklist 9. Ridge width, a
buccal concavity, the position of the
incisive canal, the nasal floor, buccal
plate thickness and the bone level on the
adjacent teeth. Then the caveat, stated
plainly: bone quality is judged
approximately from the trabecular
pattern and grey values, and CBCT grey
values are not standardised Hounsfield
units — they vary with the machine, the
field of view and the patient’s position,
and are approximations only.
4:00–5:00
“So what does all that mean for your
plan?”
Checklist 10 and the close. The findings
translated into decisions — implant
length, diameter, angulation and
position; whether augmentation is
needed and of what kind; and the
complexity judgement:
Straightforward, Advanced or Complex,
and therefore whether it is within my
competence or referred. A worked
instance — 5 mm above the canal with a
marked lingual concavity means a
shorter implant, or reconsidering the site,
not proceeding. Then records (the
written report dated and signed in the
notes, with the justification for the scan),
what the patient is told (the findings,
any incidental finding and any medical
referral), and review — the planning
appointment deferred until the report
and any referral are complete.
The compressed answer — what a strong candidate says in five minutes
“I report in a fixed order.
Preliminaries. This is a cone beam CT, taken on the date shown, of the named patient, with the field of
view indicated, and I would state whether the image quality is diagnostic for the purpose for which it was
justified. Two things follow from that: the whole volume must be examined and reported, not just the
site I am interested in, and a written report goes in the notes over my signature.
Survey of the volume, one line each. Dentition and restorations, periapical status, alveolar bone lev-
els. The maxillary sinuses — aeration, membrane thickness, any septum, the patency of the ostia. The

mandibular canals and mental foramina — course, symmetry, any bifid canal. The temporomandibular
joints, the airway, and the cervical spine where it is in the volume. Any incidental finding — an unex-
plained radiolucency, or a calcified carotid atheroma — I would report, and act on by written referral,
and record that I had done so.
Region of interest, posterior mandible. I measure the vertical height from the crest to the superior
border of the canal, and I read that number off the scale rather than estimate it. I measure the buccolingual
width at the crest and again 5 millimetres apically, because a ridge that is adequate at the crest can be
knife-edged below it. I note the ridge inclination, which decides whether the implant can be restored
where the tooth was. And I look specifically for a lingual concavity — the submandibular fossa — which
is the classic cause of lingual plate perforation and of the floor-of-mouth haematoma that follows it; the
cross-section is the only image that shows it. I identify the mental foramen and measure any anterior
loop, which extends the danger zone mesially. Then I plan a length that leaves at least 2 millimetres of
clearance from the canal.
Region of interest, anterior maxilla. Ridge width, and specifically a buccal concavity at the site, which
will decide whether I need augmentation or an angulated approach. The position of the incisive canal,
which can occupy the planned site at a central incisor. The nasal floor. And the buccal plate thickness
and the bone level on the adjacent teeth, because the papillae depend on the neighbours’ bone, not on
the implant.
Bone quality. I make an approximate assessment from the trabecular pattern and the grey values — but I
would qualify it: CBCT grey values are not standardised Hounsfield units. They vary with the machine,
the field of view, the reconstruction algorithm and the patient’s position, so they are an approximation
and not a density measurement.
The effect on the plan. The scan gives me implant length, diameter, angulation and three-dimensional
position; whether augmentation is needed and of what type; and the complexity of the case — Straight-
forward, Advanced or Complex — and therefore whether it is within my competence or should be
referred. As an example: if this section showed 5 millimetres above the canal with a marked lingual
concavity, I would use a shorter implant, or reconsider the option entirely, rather than proceed on the
height alone.
Records and follow-up. The full report written, dated and signed in the notes, with the justification for
the exposure. I explain the findings to the patient, including any incidental finding and why I am writing
to their doctor. And I defer the planning appointment until the report and any referral are complete.”
Marking priority when the clock beats the candidate
Ask for these first (the six that carry the station): 2 whole-volume reporting stated explicitly · 4 vertical
height measured to the canal · 6 lingual or buccal concavity identified · 8 the 2 mm safety margin · 9 grey
values are not Hounsfield units · 10 findings translated into a plan and a complexity judgement.
Accept these late or on prompting: 1 image identification and quality · 3 the systematic review of the
volume · 5 ridge width measured at two levels · 7 mental foramen and anterior loop.
The commonest way five minutes is wasted here: describing the images instead of measuring them. A
candidate who narrates the trabecular pattern and the cortices for two minutes has produced a radiology
essay and no numbers, and the four marks that belong to implant planning — the height, the two widths,
the concavity and the 2 mm margin — are never spoken. The second loss is reporting only the site: the
whole-volume statement takes four seconds and is worth a mark, and it is left out more often than any
other item on the checklist.

osce.title: Reporting a panoramic radiograph
osce.text:
OSCE 24 — Reporting a panoramic radiograph
A panoramic radiograph of the kind used at this station — simulated illustration, not a clinical image
Blueprint: interpret radiographic findings (W + SCE).
EQUIPMENT
a panoramic radiograph of a partially dentate patient with several incidental findings.
CANDIDATE INSTRUCTIONS
Provide a full radiographic report of this panoramic radiograph.
MODEL ANSWER
“Image type, date, and an assessment of quality — positioning, presence of the tongue against the
palate, any ghost shadows or artefacts, and whether it is diagnostically acceptable.
Dentition: teeth present and absent, unerupted or impacted teeth, restorations, caries, periapical
status, root morphology, retained roots.
Periodontal: generalised or localised bone loss, its pattern and severity, furcation involvement where
visible, calculus.
Bone: trabecular pattern, any radiolucent or radiopaque lesion, cortical outlines.
Maxillary antra: floor outline, opacity, mucosal thickening, septa, any lesion.
Mandibular canals and mental foramina: course, symmetry, relationship to the crest, any bifid
appearance.
Condyles and rami: outline, symmetry, flattening or erosion.
Other structures: hyoid, styloid processes, cervical spine, soft tissue calcifications including carotid
atheroma, and the airway.
Then the region of interest for implant planning: apparent vertical bone height at the proposed
sites, remembering the magnification of approximately 20 to 30%, which is not uniform, and that
this image gives no buccolingual information.
Conclusion: a summary of the findings, the diagnoses they support, what I cannot determine from
this image, and what further investigation I would justify — for example a small field-of-view CBCT
if the canal position is critical, or periapicals for the periodontal or periapical assessment.
Finally, I would record the report in the notes with the date and my signature, and act on any inci-
dental finding — for instance referring a patient with a calcified carotid atheroma to their general
medical practitioner.”
EXAMINER CHECKLIST
1. Image type, date, quality
2. Dentition
3. Periodontal
4. Bone and lesions

5. Antra
6. Canals and foramina
7. Condyles and other structures
8. Incidental findings identified and acted on
9. States magnification and lack of buccolingual data
10. Conclusion, further investigation, and written report in the notes
Running this station to time
Time check. The model answer in this part is only 241 words, 1 minute 43 seconds at 140 words per minute
— but it is a skeleton of headings, not a spoken report, and a candidate who inflates each heading into a
paragraph will spend all five minutes on the dentition and never reach the antra; the compression here is
the reverse of the other stations — one line per structure, delivered fast, so that two full minutes remain
for the incidental findings and the implant-planning conclusion.
The five-minute run sheet
Time
The examiner does
What earns the mark
0:00–0:30
Mounts the panoramic and says: “Give
me a full radiographic report of this
film.”
Checklist 1. Image type, date and
quality in three sentences — positioning,
tongue against the palate, ghost shadows
and artefacts, and an explicit statement
of whether it is diagnostically
acceptable. Never start with the teeth.
0:30–2:00
Silence. Lets the candidate run the
sequence.
Checklists 2, 3 and 4, one line each.
Dentition — teeth present and absent,
unerupted or impacted, restorations,
caries, periapical status, retained roots.
Periodontal — pattern and severity of
bone loss, furcations, calculus. Bone —
trabecular pattern, any radiolucency or
radiopacity, cortical outlines. Speed here
is the mark, not detail.
2:00–3:00
Silence, or “keep going.”
Checklists 5, 6 and 7, again one line each.
Antra — floor outline, opacity, mucosal
thickening, septa. Mandibular canals
and mental foramina — course,
symmetry, relation to the crest, any bifid
appearance. Condyles and rami —
outline, symmetry, flattening or erosion.
3:00–4:00
“Anything else on the film?” — the
prompt that separates candidates.
Checklist 8. The structures outside the
jaws: hyoid, styloid processes, cervical
spine, the airway, and soft tissue
calcifications, above all a calcified
carotid atheroma, with the statement
that it would be acted on by referral to
the general medical practitioner.
Checklist 9 follows — magnification of
roughly 20 to 30% and not uniform, and
no buccolingual information.
4:00–5:00
“So what does this mean for the implant
plan?”
Checklist 10 — the conclusion: summary,
diagnoses supported, what cannot be
determined from this image, and the
justified further investigation (small
field-of-view CBCT if the canal position
is critical; periapicals for the periodontal
and periapical assessment). Then
records (report written, dated and
signed), what the patient is told, and
review.
The compressed answer — what a strong candidate says in five minutes
“This is a panoramic radiograph, taken on the date shown, of a partially dentate adult. Before I report
it I will comment on quality: the patient is positioned symmetrically with the occlusal plane correctly
angled, there is no evidence of slumping or rotation, the tongue is against the palate so there is no air
shadow over the apices, and I can identify the usual ghost shadows of the contralateral ramus and hard
palate. I would state whether it is diagnostically acceptable for the purpose it was taken.

osce.title: Obtaining consent for implant surgery
osce.text:
OSCE 25 — Obtaining consent for implant surgery
Blueprint: principles of valid consent; issues and complexity of informed consent; ensuring understanding (W + SCE, examined practically).
EQUIPMENT
a simulated patient (or examiner), a written information leaflet, a consent form.

CANDIDATE INSTRUCTIONS
This patient has agreed in principle to a single implant at the LR6. Obtain consent for the surgical phase.
MODEL ANSWER
As spoken
“Before we book the surgery I want to go through exactly what’s involved, so you can decide with
all the facts. Please stop me at any point.
What we’re doing and why: you’ve lost the lower right first molar and we agreed an implant is
the option that suits you because it doesn’t involve preparing your other teeth. We also discussed
a bridge, a denture, and leaving the gap — and you can still change your mind about any of those
today.
The procedure: it’s done under local anaesthetic in about an hour. I make a small incision in the
gum, prepare a channel in the bone with cooled drills, place the implant, and close with stitches.
There’s a healing period of about three months before we make the crown, and you’ll have stitches
out in a week.
What to expect afterwards: swelling and discomfort for a few days, some bruising, and a soft diet.
The risks I need you to know about. Common and usually temporary: pain, swelling, bruising,
bleeding, and infection which we treat with antibiotics. Less common: the implant not attaching
to the bone — that happens in around two to five in a hundred, and if it does we remove it, let
it heal and try again. Because this is the lower jaw, there is a nerve running below, and there’s a
small risk of bruising or damage to it, which can cause numbness or tingling in your lip and chin —
usually temporary, occasionally permanent. I’ve planned the implant to leave a safety margin of at
least two millimetres from that nerve, and I’ll check the position with an X-ray during the procedure.
Other risks are damage to the neighbouring tooth, and later problems — gum infection around the
implant, which we call peri-implantitis, and mechanical problems like the screw loosening or the
crown chipping.
What you have to commit to: cleaning around it every day with the brushes I’ll show you, and
coming for maintenance appointments every six months. Implants don’t decay, but they can get
gum disease, and without maintenance they can be lost.
Costs: here’s the written estimate for the surgery and the crown, and here’s what maintenance and
any future component replacement is likely to cost.
Alternatives if it fails: we’d discuss a bridge or a denture, and I’d tell you honestly what the site
can take.
Here’s a written information sheet. I’d like you to take it home and come back — I don’t want you to
sign today. Before you go, can I ask you to tell me in your own words what we’ve agreed and what
the main risks are, so I can be sure I’ve explained it clearly?
I’ll record all of this in your notes, and we’ll confirm your consent again on the day.”
EXAMINER CHECKLIST
1. Restates diagnosis and why treatment is proposed
2. Restates alternatives including no treatment
3. Describes the procedure and timeline
4. General surgical risks
5. Site-specific risk — nerve injury — with mitigation
6. Failure rate quoted honestly
7. Late biological and mechanical risks, and the maintenance commitment
8. Written costs
9. Written information plus cooling-off period
10. Checks understanding by asking the patient to summarise, and states what will be recorded
Running this station to time
Time check. The model answer is 608 words, 4 minutes 20 seconds of uninterrupted speech at 140 words
per minute — and a patient interrupts, asks about the nerve, and asks what it costs. Add the greeting,
the leaflet, the estimate and the teach-back and the honest delivery is past seven minutes. Nothing can be

dropped, because each item is a limb of valid consent, so the compression is in phrasing: one sentence
per risk with the figure attached, and the last minute reserved for the close.
The five-minute run sheet
Time
The examiner does
What earns the mark
0:00–1:30
Sits as the patient who has agreed in
principle to a single implant at the LR6:
“So — are we going ahead with this,
then?” May add: “How long does it
take?”
Checklists 1, 2 and 3. Why treatment is
proposed — the LR6 is missing, and an
implant suits her because it does not
involve preparing the adjacent teeth —
and, in the same breath, the alternatives
including no treatment: a bridge, a
denture, and leaving the gap, with the
explicit statement that she can still
change her mind today. Both must be
restated even though she has “already
agreed”; consent is not inherited from a
previous appointment. Then the
procedure and the timeline in plain
words and no jargon: local anaesthetic,
about an hour, a small incision, a channel
prepared in the bone with cooled drills,
the implant placed, stitches; stitches out
at a week, about three months of
healing before the crown; then swelling,
discomfort, bruising and soft diet in one
sentence.
1:30–2:45
May ask: “Is it risky?”
Checklists 4, 5 and 6 — the highest-value
stretch on the station. Common and
temporary: pain, swelling, bruising,
bleeding, infection treated with
antibiotics. Then the site-specific risk
named as such: this is the lower jaw, a
nerve runs below the site, and injury
can cause numbness or tingling of the lip
and chin, usually temporary,
occasionally permanent — immediately
followed by the mitigation: the implant
is planned to leave at least 2 mm of
clearance and the position is checked
radiographically during the procedure.
Then the failure rate given honestly as a
number: around two to five in a
hundred do not integrate, and if that
happens the implant is removed, the site
heals, and it can usually be replaced.
2:45–3:40
May ask: “And once it’s in, that’s it?”
Checklist 7. The late risks and the
commitment together: peri-implantitis
explained as gum disease around the
implant; mechanical problems — screw
loosening, crown chipping or wear;
then the obligation stated as a condition
rather than a suggestion — daily
cleaning with the brushes she will be
shown, and maintenance appointments
every six months. The line that earns the
mark: implants do not decay, but they can
get gum disease, and without maintenance
they can be lost.
3:40–4:20
May ask: “What’s it going to cost?”
Checklist 8. A written estimate handed
over — the surgery and the crown
itemised separately — plus the ongoing
cost: maintenance appointments and the
likely cost of replacing components in
future. Verbal figures alone do not score;
the estimate has to be in her hand and a
copy in the notes.

Time
The examiner does
What earns the mark
4:20–5:00
“So shall I sign?” — the closing test.
Checklists 9 and 10. Declines the
signature today: the written
information leaflet is handed over and
she is asked to take it home and come
back, a cooling-off period. Then the
teach-back — “tell me in your own
words what we have agreed and what
the main risks are” — which is the mark,
not the offer to answer questions. Then
what is recorded: the discussion, the
alternatives offered, the risks named
individually including the nerve, the
estimate and leaflet given, that she was
not asked to sign on the day, and that
consent will be confirmed again on the
day of surgery.
The compressed answer — what a strong candidate says in five minutes
“Before we book anything I want to go through exactly what is involved, so that you decide with all the
facts. Please stop me at any point.
Why we are doing this. You have lost the lower right first molar. We agreed an implant because it replaces
that tooth on its own and does not involve cutting down the teeth either side. We also talked about a
bridge, a denture, and simply leaving the gap — a perfectly reasonable choice — and you can still change
your mind today.
What the procedure involves. It is done under local anaesthetic, and takes about an hour. I make a small
incision in the gum, prepare a channel in the bone with cooled drills, place the implant, and close it with
stitches. Stitches come out in a week, and there is a healing period of about three months before we make
the crown. Afterwards, expect swelling and discomfort for a few days, some bruising, and a soft diet.
The risks, and I want to be specific. Common and usually temporary: pain, swelling, bruising, bleeding,
and infection, which we treat with antibiotics.
One risk is specific to this site. Because this is the lower jaw, there is a nerve running below the implant.
There is a small risk of bruising it or damaging it, which would cause numbness or tingling in your lip
and chin — usually temporary, occasionally permanent. What I do about it: I have planned the implant
from the scan to leave at least two millimetres of clearance from that nerve, and I will check the position
with an X-ray during the procedure before I finish.
Failure. In around two to five in every hundred, the implant does not attach to the bone. If that happens
we remove it, let the site heal, and in most cases we can place another.
Then the longer-term risks. The gum around an implant can become infected — peri-implantitis — and
it can lose bone. And mechanically, the screw can loosen and the crown can chip or wear, and components
sometimes need replacing.
Which brings me to what you have to commit to. Cleaning around it every day with the brushes I will
show you, and coming for maintenance appointments every six months. Implants do not decay, but
they can get gum disease — and without that maintenance they can be lost. If that is not something you
can commit to, a bridge or a denture may suit you better, and I would rather we said so now.
Costs. Here is the written estimate — the surgery and the crown are itemised separately. And here is
what the maintenance appointments and any future component replacement are likely to cost — the
part people are usually not told. If it ever failed, we would look again at a bridge or a denture.
Now, I am not going to ask you to sign today. Here is the written information sheet with everything we
have covered. Take it home, read it, and come back — with any questions.
Before you go, could I ask you to tell me in your own words what we have agreed and what the main
risks are? Not to test you — so that I can be sure I have explained it clearly.
And I will write all of this in your notes: what we discussed, the alternatives, the risks I have named
including the nerve, that I gave you the estimate and the leaflet, and that you have taken them away to
think about. We will confirm your consent again on the day of the surgery.”

osce.title: Consent for grafting materials
osce.text:
OSCE 26 — Consent for grafting materials
Blueprint: “importance of consent in the context of undertaking surgical procedures and the use of grafting materials and barriers” (W + SCE).
EQUIPMENT
samples of xenograft, allograft, alloplast, collagen membrane; a simulated patient.
CANDIDATE INSTRUCTIONS
Explain to this patient the graft materials you propose to use and obtain their consent.
MODEL ANSWER
“There isn’t quite enough bone on the outer side of where the implant needs to go, so I plan to add
some bone graft material and cover it with a membrane while it heals. I want to explain exactly what
those materials are, because some people have strong views about them.
There are four kinds:
Your own bone, which I can collect from the site as I drill. It’s the best biologically because it contains
living cells, but there’s only a small amount and it tends to shrink.
Human donor bone, from a regulated tissue bank, processed so there are no living cells. It works
well, but some people are uncomfortable with human donor material.
Animal-derived bone, which is the one I’d normally recommend here. It’s usually from cattle,
sometimes from pigs. It’s processed at high temperature so that only the mineral scaffold remains
— no proteins and no cells. The reason I favour it is that it barely resorbs, so it holds the shape of
the ridge for years. The theoretical risk of disease transmission is regarded as essentially eliminated
by the processing, and there are no reported cases from these products, but I want you to know the
origin.
Synthetic material, made in a laboratory. No animal or human origin at all, so it avoids those
concerns; the trade-off is that it’s less well documented in this particular application.
The membrane I’d use is also usually collagen of porcine — that is, pig — origin, though there are
synthetic ones.
So: is there any religious, cultural, dietary or personal reason that would make animal-derived or
human-derived material unacceptable to you? If so, we use your own bone with a synthetic material
and a synthetic membrane, and I’d explain what that means for the predictability.
Whichever we choose, I’ll record the material, the manufacturer and the batch number in your notes,
and you’ll get that on your implant card.”

EXAMINER CHECKLIST
1. Explains why a graft is needed
2. Names all four categories
3. States bovine/porcine origin explicitly
4. States human donor origin explicitly
5. Explains processing and residual risk honestly
6. Explains the membrane and its origin
7. Asks directly about religious, cultural, dietary or personal objections
8. Offers an acceptable alternative pathway
9. Explains the consequence of choosing the alternative
10. States that material and lot number will be recorded and given to the patient
Running this station to time
Time check. The model answer is 460 words, 3 minutes 17 seconds at 140 words per minute — but four
sample pots have to be picked up and shown, the patient interrupts, and checklist 7 is a question, which
means the patient’s answer and your response to it also have to fit inside the five minutes. Roughly 120
words must go, and they go by naming each material in a single sentence with its origin attached instead
of explaining the biology of each one.
The five-minute run sheet
Time
The examiner does
What earns the mark
0:00–0:40
Sits as the patient, at a planning
appointment, not on the day of surgery:
“You mentioned something about
needing extra bone?”
Checklist 1. Why a graft is needed, in
plain words — there is not enough bone
on the outer side of where the implant
has to sit, so material is added and
covered with a membrane while it heals.
Then the framing sentence that buys the
rest of the station: some of these materials
come from animals and some from human
donors, people have strong views about that,
and I would rather you knew now than on the
day. Raising origin before the day of
surgery is itself the mark; a candidate
who does this on the morning of the
operation has given the patient no real
choice.
0:40–2:10
Slides the four sample pots forward.
Silence.
Checklists 2, 3 and 4 — the densest
stretch. All four categories named, one
sentence each, each with its origin said
out loud in the patient’s language: your
own bone, collected from the site as I
drill; human donor bone from a
regulated tissue bank — the word donor
must be used; animal bone, from cattle,
sometimes from pigs — cow and pig,
not “xenograft”; and synthetic, made in
a laboratory with no animal or human
origin at all. Naming the categories
without naming those origins scores 2
and forfeits 3 and 4.
2:10–3:00
May ask: “Is it safe, though?”
Checklists 5 and 6. Processing and
residual risk, honestly: the animal
material is treated at high temperature so
only the mineral scaffold remains — no
cells, no proteins — the theoretical risk of
disease transmission is regarded as
essentially eliminated, there are no
reported cases, and I am telling you the
origin anyway. Then the membrane,
which candidates forget: it too is usually
collagen of porcine — pig — origin,
though synthetic ones exist.

Time
The examiner does
What earns the mark
3:00–4:05
Waits. If the question is not asked,
prompts: “Does it matter what it’s made
of?”
Checklists 7 and 8 — the two that carry
the station. The question asked directly
and in full: is there any religious,
cultural, dietary or personal reason that
animal-derived or human-derived material
would be unacceptable to you? All four
grounds should be offered, and
vegetarian or vegan diet named among
them, because a patient who would
never raise religion will raise diet. Then
the alternative pathway offered without
being asked twice: your own bone with
a synthetic substitute and a synthetic
membrane.
4:05–5:00
“And if I did want the synthetic?”
Checklists 9 and 10. The consequence of
the alternative stated honestly —
synthetic material is less well
documented in this application,
autogenous bone is limited in volume
and resorbs, so the result may be less
predictable and I may need to stage it —
said as information, not as pressure.
Then records: the material, the
manufacturer and the batch number in
the notes, that the origin was discussed
and which option was chosen, and the
batch details given to the patient on an
implant card they keep. Consent
confirmed again on the day.
The compressed answer — what a strong candidate says in five minutes
“Before we fix a date, there is something I want to go through. There is not quite enough bone on the
outer side of where your implant has to sit, so I plan to add some graft material and cover it with a thin
membrane while it heals. I am raising it now rather than on the day, because some of these materials
come from animals or from human donors, and people have strong views about that. You should decide
with time, not in the chair.
There are four kinds.
Your own bone. I can collect a small amount from the site as I drill. Biologically it is the best, because it
contains living cells — but there is only a little of it, and it tends to shrink.
Human donor bone. It comes from a regulated tissue bank and is processed so that no living cells remain.
It works well. Some people are uncomfortable with the idea of donor material, and that is a perfectly
reasonable thing to feel.
Animal-derived bone — and this is the one I would normally recommend here. It is usually from cattle,
sometimes from pigs. It is processed at high temperature so that only the mineral scaffold is left: no cells,
no proteins. The reason I favour it is that it barely resorbs, so it holds the shape of the ridge for years.
Synthetic material, made in a laboratory. No animal or human origin at all, so it avoids all of that. The
trade-off is that it is less well documented in this particular situation.
And the membrane over the top — which people often do not think to ask about — is also usually
collagen of porcine, that is pig, origin. There are synthetic membranes too.
On safety, honestly. The processing means the theoretical risk of disease transmission is regarded as
essentially eliminated, and there are no reported cases from these products. I am not raising the origin
because I think it is dangerous — I am raising it because it is your decision what goes into your body.
So let me ask you directly. Is there any religious, cultural or dietary reason — including if you are
vegetarian or vegan — or any personal reason at all, that would make animal-derived or human-derived
material unacceptable to you?
(waits, and takes the answer at face value — no persuading)
If the answer is yes, we have a route. We use your own bone, collected from the site, together with a
synthetic substitute and a synthetic membrane. Nothing of animal or human origin at all.
And I owe you the consequence of that. The synthetic materials are less well documented for this job, and
your own bone is limited in amount and shrinks a little as it heals, so the result may be less predictable

osce.title: Medical history interpretation and risk stratification
osce.text:
OSCE 27 — Medical history interpretation and risk stratification
Blueprint: consider local and systemic risk factors; drug interactions (W + SCE).
EQUIPMENT
three medical history cards.
CANDIDATE INSTRUCTIONS
For each of these three patients, state the implant-relevant risks, what further information you need, and how you would
modify your management.
Card 1:
64-year-old female; metastatic breast cancer; denosumab 120 mg monthly; tamoxifen; on
chemotherapy. Card 2: 52-year-old male; type 2 diabetes, HbA1c 71 mmol/mol; smokes 15/day; treated
periodontitis.
Card 3:
40-year-old female; rheumatoid arthritis; methotrexate; prednisolone 5 mg;
ibuprofen self-prescribed.
MODEL ANSWER
“Card 1. The critical fact is denosumab 120 mg monthly — that is the oncology dose, not the os-
teoporosis dose, in a patient with malignant bone disease. That places her in the high MRONJ risk
group and elective implant placement is contraindicated. Chemotherapy adds immunosuppres-
sion. I would liaise in writing with her oncology team, avoid elective surgery, provide a prosthetic
alternative, and manage any necessary extractions under the SDCEP high-risk pathway with spe-
cialist input.
Card 2. Three additive risk factors: HbA1c of 71 mmol/mol is poorly controlled diabetes; smoking
15 a day roughly doubles failure risk; and a history of periodontitis is the strongest risk factor
for peri-implantitis. Together this is a high-risk profile. I would not place implants now. I would
liaise with the diabetes team, deliver very brief smoking cessation intervention with referral, confirm
periodontal stability against the EFP criteria, and re-assess. If the picture improves, I would reduce
the scope, use screw-retained cleansable designs, consent explicitly to the elevated risk, and commit
to three-monthly maintenance.

Card 3. Methotrexate means immunosuppression — meticulous asepsis, a lower threshold for an-
tibiotic cover, and critically NSAIDs must be avoided because they increase methotrexate toxicity.
She is self-prescribing ibuprofen, which is a genuine safety issue I would address and communicate
to her rheumatologist. Prednisolone 5 mg long term impairs healing; steroid cover is generally
unnecessary for minor oral surgery but I would confirm with her physician. Her rheumatoid disease
may affect hand function and cervical spine positioning, so I would assess her dexterity directly and
plan short, comfortable appointments. Analgesia would be paracetamol with codeine if needed.”
EXAMINER CHECKLIST
1. Identifies oncology-dose denosumab as high risk
2. States elective implants contraindicated in Card 1
3. Identifies poor glycaemic control with a number
4. Quantifies smoking risk
5. Identifies periodontitis history as the peri-implantitis risk factor
6. States the plan to modify risk before treating
7. Identifies the methotrexate–NSAID interaction
8. Identifies the self-prescribing safety issue and acts on it
9. Addresses steroids and immunosuppression practically
10. Addresses dexterity and positioning
Running this station to time
Time check. The model answer is 431 words, 3 minutes 5 seconds at 140 words per minute — comfortable
in the abstract, and almost always lost in practice, because the marks are not spread evenly across the
three cards. Card 1 carries two checklist points; cards 2 and 3 carry eight between them. Nothing needs
cutting so much as rationing: a fixed 90 seconds per card, timed, and no card opened until the one before
it has been closed with a management decision.

The compressed answer — what a strong candidate says in five minutes
Q: Card 1. “The critical fact is denosumab 120 milligrams monthly. That is the oncology dose — the
osteoporosis dose is 60 milligrams every six months — in a patient with malignant bone disease, and she
is on chemotherapy as well. That puts her in the high-risk group for medication-related osteonecrosis of
the jaw, and elective implant placement is contraindicated. I would not place implants and I would not
defer the decision. I would liaise in writing with her oncology team, offer her a prosthetic alternative, and
if an extraction becomes unavoidable manage it through the SDCEP high-risk pathway with specialist
input. I would also want her dentition made as stable as possible and kept under close preventive review.”
Q: Card 2. “Three risk factors, and they are additive. First, an HbA1c of 71 mmol/mol — the target is
under 58, so this is poorly controlled diabetes, with impaired healing and increased infection risk. Second,
15 cigarettes a day, which roughly doubles implant failure risk and worsens every peri-implant outcome.
Third, and most important for the long term, a history of periodontitis — the strongest known risk factor
for peri-implantitis. Together that is a high-risk profile, and my answer is that I would not place implants
now.”

osce.title: A medical emergency during implant surgery
osce.text:
OSCE 28 — A medical emergency during implant surgery
Blueprint: recognise clinical situations which are unsafe or could lead to an adverse event; patient safety (W + SCE).
EQUIPMENT
a manikin, emergency drugs box, oxygen, AED.
CANDIDATE INSTRUCTIONS
Ten minutes into implant surgery your patient becomes flushed, develops a widespread rash and wheeze, and their blood
pressure falls. Manage this emergency.
MODEL ANSWER
“This is anaphylaxis until proved otherwise. I would work through the standard approach.

Stop treatment. Remove any potential trigger — in dentistry the commonest are chlorhexidine,
latex, antibiotics and, rarely, local anaesthetic. Note what has been given and when.
Call for help immediately — dial 999, state anaphylaxis, and send a team member for the emergency
drugs, oxygen and the AED.
Position: lay the patient flat with the legs raised, unless breathing is diﬀicult, in which case sit them
up; if pregnant, tilt to the left.
Adrenaline: 500 micrograms — 0.5 mL of 1:1000 — intramuscularly into the anterolateral thigh.
Repeat after 5 minutes if there is no improvement.
Airway and breathing: high-flow oxygen through a non-rebreathe mask at 15 litres per minute.
Monitor pulse, blood pressure, oxygen saturation and level of consciousness continuously; be pre-
pared for cardiac arrest and start CPR if there is no output.
Hand over to the paramedics with a clear account of what happened, what was given and at what
time.
Afterwards: document the whole event contemporaneously with timings, ensure the patient is
referred for allergy investigation, report the reaction through the Yellow Card scheme, inform the
patient’s general medical practitioner, replace the used emergency drugs, and hold a significant
event analysis with the team.
I would also note that this is why the whole team must have annual medical emergency and im-
mediate life support training, and why the emergency drugs and oxygen must be checked and in
date.”
EXAMINER CHECKLIST
1. Recognises anaphylaxis
2. Stops treatment and removes the trigger, naming likely dental triggers
3. Calls 999 and summons the team
4. Correct positioning
5. Adrenaline 500 𝜇g IM 1:1000, anterolateral thigh
6. Repeat at 5 minutes
7. High-flow oxygen
8. Monitoring and readiness for CPR
9. Handover and documentation with timings
10. Yellow Card, allergy referral, drug replacement, significant event analysis
Running this station to time
Time check. The model answer is 372 words, 2 minutes 39 seconds at 140 words per minute — the shortest
in this group, and the one candidates most often fail. The reason is that the clock that matters here is not
the OSCE clock but the patient’s: an examiner watching an anaphylaxis station is timing how many
seconds elapse before adrenaline is drawn and given, and a beautifully ordered answer that reaches it at
two minutes has let a simulated patient deteriorate. Speak it in real time, in the order you would do it,
and hold the governance for the last ninety seconds.
The five-minute run sheet

The examiner does
What earns the mark

Checklists 6, 7 and 8. Repeat adrenaline
at 5 minutes if there is no improvement
— the station will end before the patient’s

per minute through a non-rebreathe

Airway obstruction and cardiac arrest are

2:15–3:30
“The paramedics arrive.”
Checklist 9. A structured handover —
what happened, when it started, what
has been given and at what time, the

suspected trigger. Then
contemporaneous documentation with
timings, which is the half of checklist 9
candidates drop: the exact times of onset,
of the 999 call, of each adrenaline dose,
of oxygen, and the observations at each
point. The times are the record; a
narrative without them is worth little.
3:30–5:00
“The patient is in hospital. What now?”
Checklist 10 — the aftermath, and the
last row that everyone runs out of time
for. Referral for allergy investigation so
the trigger is identified, Yellow Card
report of the reaction, the general
medical practitioner informed, used
emergency drugs replaced and the box
re-checked and dated, and a significant
event analysis with the whole team.
Then what the patient is told and
recorded, an allergy alert on the records
and a warning card, and the standing
requirement: annual medical
emergency and immediate life support
training for the whole team, with drugs
and oxygen checked in date.
The compressed answer — what a strong candidate says in five minutes
“This is anaphylaxis until proved otherwise. Flushing, a widespread rash, wheeze and a falling blood
pressure — I am not going to work through a differential; I am going to treat it.
Stop. Treatment stops, and I remove any potential trigger. In dentistry the likely ones are chlorhexidine,
latex, antibiotics and, rarely, local anaesthetic — so the chlorhexidine goes, gloves and rubber items go,
and I note what has been given and at what time.
Help, now. (to the team) ‘Dial 999, say anaphylaxis. You — bring the emergency drugs, the oxygen and
the AED.’ I do not leave the patient.
Position. Flat, with the legs raised, to support the circulation. If breathing is the dominant problem I sit
them up; if she were pregnant, I would tilt her to the left.

osce.title: Managing altered sensation after implant placement
osce.text:
OSCE 29 — Managing altered sensation after implant placement
Blueprint: strategies for managing complications; risk and adverse events (W + SCE).
EQUIPMENT
a diagram of the lower lip and chin, a probe, cotton wool, a periapical radiograph showing an implant close to the canal.
CANDIDATE INSTRUCTIONS
A patient telephones the day after placement of an LR5 implant reporting numbness of the lip. Describe your management.
MODEL ANSWER

“I would see the patient today, not at a routine review.
History: exact distribution; whether it is complete numbness (anaesthesia), reduced sensation (hy-
poaesthesia), tingling (paraesthesia) or unpleasant/painful sensation (dysaesthesia); the time of
onset; and whether it has changed.
Examination and documentation: I would map the affected area onto a diagram of the lip and chin
with measurements, photograph it, and perform objective tests — light touch with cotton wool,
sharp/blunt discrimination, two-point discrimination and thermal testing — comparing with the
contralateral side. I would record all of this and the date. This mapping repeated at each visit is
how I will judge recovery.
Imaging: a periapical, and if inconclusive a small field-of-view CBCT, to determine whether the
implant is impinging on or within the canal.
Action: - If the implant is impinging, remove it or back it out immediately. The evidence favours
decompression within 24 to 36 hours; delay reduces the chance of recovery. - If the implant is clear
of the canal and the injury is likely from indirect trauma or haematoma, I would consider a short
course of a corticosteroid with an NSAID — recognising the evidence is limited — and monitor.
Communication: explain honestly what has happened, apologise under duty of candour, describe
what I am doing and the likely course, and give realistic information — many such injuries improve
over weeks to months, but some are permanent.
Follow-up and referral: review at 1 week and 1 month with repeat mapping. If there is no mean-
ingful improvement, refer to oral and maxillofacial surgery early — within weeks, not months —
because the window for any surgical intervention is limited.
Governance: inform my indemnity provider, record everything contemporaneously, and undertake
a significant event analysis reviewing my planning, my safety margin and whether CBCT was used.”
EXAMINER CHECKLIST
1. Sees the patient the same day
2. Characterises the sensory disturbance correctly
3. Maps and documents with diagram and measurements
4. Objective sensory testing
5. Imaging to determine implant position
6. Removes/backs out an impinging implant within 24–36 h
7. Considers steroid/NSAID with appropriate caveat
8. Duty of candour and honest prognosis
9. Structured review and early referral if not improving
10. Indemnity notification, records, significant event analysis
Running this station to time
Time check. The model answer is 436 words, 3 minutes 7 seconds at 140 words per minute — but the
diagram, the probe and the cotton wool are on the bench, and the examiner expects the mapping to be
shown, not described, which costs a minute that the word count does not contain. Roughly 130 words
must go, and they go from the sensory vocabulary: name the four terms in one clause each rather than
defining them, and protect the two things this station is really about — the 24-to-36-hour window and the
duty of candour.
The five-minute run sheet

Time
The examiner does
What earns the mark

Checklists 1 and 2. The first sentence

checklist 1 and it must be unconditional

Then the telephone history in one breath:

Checklists 3 and 4 — the highest-value

Map the affected area onto the diagram

Checklists 5 and 6 — the decision the
station turns on. A periapical, and if

CBCT, to establish whether the implant
is impinging on or within the canal.
Then the action, with the number
attached: if it is impinging, remove it or
back it out immediately — the evidence
favours decompression within 24 to 36
hours, and delay reduces the chance of
recovery. This is a same-day surgical
decision and must be stated as one. If the
implant is clear of the canal, the injury is
more likely indirect — retraction, a drill

2:50–3:45
“And medically?”
Checklist 7, with its caveat, and the
beginning of the honest conversation. A
