NSAID may be considered where the
implant is clear of the canal — and the
candidate must say that the evidence
for this is limited, because the mark is
for the caveat as much as the drug. Then
the prognosis given honestly and
without false comfort: many such
injuries improve over weeks to months,
some do not, and some are permanent.

Time
The examiner does
What earns the mark
3:45–5:00
“How do you follow her up, and what
do you tell her?”
Checklists 8, 9 and 10 — follow-up and
candour, the rows candidates run out of
clock for. Duty of candour discharged
explicitly: tell her honestly what has
happened, apologise, say what is being
done and what to expect — and record
that the apology was given. Then the
structured review: one week and one
month, with the mapping repeated onto
a fresh diagram each time, so recovery is
measured rather than remembered. And
the referral window: if there is no
meaningful improvement, refer to oral
and maxillofacial surgery early —
within weeks, not months, because the
window for surgical intervention closes.
Finally: indemnity provider informed,
contemporaneous records, significant
event analysis on the planning, the
safety margin and whether a CBCT
should have been taken.
The compressed answer — what a strong candidate says in five minutes
“I would see her today. Not at her one-week review — today. Altered sensation the day after a lower
implant is time-critical, and the single thing that most changes the outcome is how quickly it is assessed.
On the telephone I establish the essentials: exactly where she is numb; whether it is complete numbness
— anaesthesia, reduced sensation — hypoaesthesia, tingling — paraesthesia, or unpleasant or painful
sensation — dysaesthesia, which is the most troublesome; when it started, and in particular whether she
was ever normal after the local anaesthetic wore off; and whether it has changed since.
When she arrives, I map it. I draw the affected area onto a diagram of the lip and chin with measure-
ments, photograph it, and date and sign it. That map is the baseline — without it I will have no way of
telling in six weeks whether she is better, and ‘it seems a bit smaller’ is not a record.
Then objective testing, each side compared: light touch with cotton wool, sharp–blunt discrimination,
two-point discrimination, and thermal testing, always against the contralateral side. I record every result.
Imaging. A periapical, and if that is inconclusive a small field-of-view CBCT, for one purpose: to estab-
lish whether the implant is impinging on, or within, the inferior alveolar canal.
And then the decision, which is today’s decision. If the implant is impinging, I remove it or back it
out immediately. The evidence favours decompression within 24 to 36 hours, and every hour of delay
reduces the chance of recovery. I would not wait to see whether it settles, and I would not wait for an
opinion.
If the implant is clear of the canal, the injury is more likely from indirect trauma — retraction, a drill
overrun, the injection itself, or a haematoma in the canal. There I would consider a short course of a
corticosteroid with an NSAID, while being clear that the evidence for this is limited, and monitor closely.
Now what I tell her, and I would not delegate this. I explain honestly what has happened and why. I
apologise — this is the duty of candour, and it is a professional obligation, not an admission that ends
my career. I tell her what I am doing about it today. And I give her a realistic prognosis: many of these
injuries improve over weeks to months; some improve only partly; and some are permanent. I would
rather she heard that from me now than discovered it herself in three months.
Follow-up is structured, not ‘come back if it’s no better’. I review at one week and at one month, and
at each visit I repeat the mapping onto a fresh diagram and repeat the objective tests, so recovery is
measured. If there is no meaningful improvement, I refer to oral and maxillofacial surgery early —
within weeks, not months — because the window in which surgical intervention can help is limited, and
a late referral closes it.
And the governance. I inform my indemnity provider at the outset, and record everything contempo-
raneously — the maps, the test results, the imaging, the decision I made and why, the apology given and
what she was told. Then a significant event analysis: was my planning adequate, did I leave a genuine 2
mm safety margin, and should I have had a CBCT before I drilled.”

osce.title: Harvesting particulate autogenous bone
osce.text:
OSCE 30 — Harvesting particulate autogenous bone
Blueprint: use autogenous bone harvested from the oral cavity for minor augmentation (FGDP skill 7; W + OS-P + SCE).
EQUIPMENT
model of a posterior mandible; bone scraper, bone collector/trap, rongeur, chisel.
CANDIDATE INSTRUCTIONS
You require autogenous bone for a small buccal dehiscence. Demonstrate and describe how you would harvest it.
MODEL ANSWER
“I need only a small volume, so I would use intraoral particulate sources rather than a block — block
harvesting from the ramus or symphysis is an advanced procedure with recognised morbidity and
is outside my scope.
Sources, in order of preference here: 1. Bone collected during the osteotomy into a sterile bone
trap in the suction line. This is free bone I am producing anyway. I would use a dedicated sterile
trap, collect during the first drills before significant blood and saliva contamination, and use clinical
judgement about its quality. 2. A bone scraper used on the external oblique ridge or the buccal
cortex adjacent to the site. I extend the existing flap slightly, identify a flat cortical area away from
the mental nerve and the canal, and draw the scraper in firm, controlled strokes away from vital
structures, collecting the shavings in the scraper chamber. I take only cortical shavings, not a full-
thickness block. 3. A rongeur on any sharp bony crest I am reducing anyway during alveoloplasty.
I would keep the harvested bone moist in sterile saline and use it promptly, placing it directly
against the implant surface where its osteogenic cells are most valuable, then layering a depro-
teinised bovine bone mineral over it for volume stability.
Precautions: identify and avoid the mental nerve and the inferior alveolar canal; avoid perforating
into the marrow space or the lingual plate; use irrigation with the scraper to avoid heat; and warn
the patient about additional post-operative discomfort at the harvest site.
I would record the source, the approximate volume and the composite ratio used.”
EXAMINER CHECKLIST
1. States that block harvesting is out of scope
2. Bone trap technique and its limitations
3. Bone scraper technique with direction of stroke
4. Correct donor site selection

5. Avoids mental nerve and canal
6. Keeps bone moist in saline
7. Places autogenous bone against the implant surface
8. Layers xenograft for volume stability
9. Warns patient about donor-site morbidity
10. Records source and materials
Running this station to time
Time check. The model answer is 396 words, 2 minutes 50 seconds at 140 words per minute — and the
verb is demonstrate and describe, so three instruments have to be picked up, one has to be put back down,
and the scraper has to be drawn across the model in the right direction while you talk. Budget 40 seconds
for the scope statement and the instrument choice, 90 seconds for the harvest itself, and keep the last
minute for handling, layering and the record — the four marks that sit after the bone is out.
The five-minute run sheet
Time
The examiner does
What earns the mark
0:00–0:40
Presents the posterior mandible model
and a bench carrying a bone scraper, a
bone collector, a rongeur and a chisel:
“You require autogenous bone for a small
buccal dehiscence. Demonstrate and
describe how you would harvest it.”
Checklist 1, and it must come first, with
the hands. The chisel is put down and
named as the block-harvesting
instrument: I need a small volume, so I
would use intraoral particulate sources —
block harvesting from the ramus or
symphysis is an advanced procedure
with recognised morbidity and is outside
my scope. Naming the limit and
declining the instrument is a mark, not a
hedge, and it is lost by silence: a
candidate who simply never touches the
chisel has not scored checklist 1. Then
the sources listed in order of preference,
one clause each.
0:40–1:40
Watches the hands.
Checklist 2. Bone collected during the
osteotomy into a sterile trap in the
suction line — free bone that is being
produced anyway. The mark includes
the limitations, which candidates omit:
a dedicated sterile trap, collection
during the early drills before significant
blood and saliva contamination, a small
and unpredictable yield, and clinical
judgement about whether what is in the
trap is worth using.
1:40–2:50
May ask: “Show me on the model.”
Checklists 3, 4 and 5 — the practical core.
The scraper on the external oblique
ridge or the buccal cortex adjacent to the
site, reached by extending the existing
flap slightly rather than opening a
second site. A flat cortical area is
identified and named, away from the
mental foramen and the canal. Then the
stroke itself, demonstrated: firm,
controlled strokes drawn away from
vital structures, cortical shavings only,
not a full-thickness block, shavings
collected in the scraper chamber, and
irrigation to avoid heat. Checklist 5
must be said as the hand moves — the
mental nerve and the inferior alveolar
canal identified and avoided, and no
perforation into the marrow space or
through the lingual plate.

Time
The examiner does
What earns the mark
2:50–3:50
“You have your bone. What now?”
Checklists 6, 7 and 8, and these are worth
as much as the harvest. The bone is kept
moist in sterile saline and used
promptly — never allowed to dry on the
drape. It is placed directly against the
exposed implant surface, because that is
where its living osteogenic cells are
worth having and there is not enough of
it to waste anywhere else. Then
deproteinised bovine bone mineral
layered outside it for volume stability,
because autogenous bone alone resorbs
and will not hold the buccal contour. The
composite is the answer; autogenous
alone is not.
3:50–5:00
“Anything else before you close?”
Checklists 9 and 10 — what the patient is
told and what is written. Warn the
patient in advance about donor-site
morbidity: additional soreness and
swelling at the harvest site, which is a
second surgical site even though it is
through the same incision. Consent must
have covered the bovine origin of the
layered xenograft and the porcine
membrane. Then record the source of
the autogenous bone, the approximate
volume, the composite ratio, and the
brand and lot numbers of the xenograft
and membrane, the lot numbers going
onto the implant card. Review at one
week for both the graft and the donor
site.
The compressed answer — what a strong candidate says in five minutes
“First, what I am not going to do. (putting the chisel back) This is a small buccal dehiscence and I need
only a small volume, so I would use intraoral particulate sources. Block harvesting from the ramus or
symphysis is an advanced procedure with recognised morbidity — donor-site pain, altered sensation,
and in the symphysis pulpal damage — and it is outside my scope. If I needed a block, I would refer.
My sources, in order of preference.
First, bone from the osteotomy itself. I collect into a sterile bone trap in the suction line — this is free
bone I am producing anyway. I use a dedicated sterile trap, and I collect during the first drills, before
the field is heavily contaminated with blood and saliva. The limitation is honest: the yield is small and
unpredictable, and I use clinical judgement about whether what is in the trap is clean enough to place.
Second, and here for the volume I actually need, a bone scraper. I extend the existing flap slightly rather
than opening a second site, and I work on the external oblique ridge or the buccal cortex just adjacent. I
identify a flat cortical area, and — critically — I locate the mental foramen and know where the inferior
alveolar canal runs before I start.
The stroke matters. (demonstrating) Firm, controlled strokes, always drawn away from the vital struc-
tures, never towards them, so that if the instrument runs on it runs into safe bone. I take cortical shavings
only — not a full-thickness block — I do not perforate into the marrow space or through the lingual plate,
and I irrigate as I go so the shavings are not heated. The shavings collect in the scraper chamber.
Third, a rongeur on any sharp bony crest I am reducing anyway during alveoloplasty — again, bone I
would otherwise discard.
Handling. The harvested bone goes straight into sterile saline and is kept moist, and I use it promptly.
Dried autogenous bone is dead autogenous bone, and its only advantage over a substitute is that it contains
living cells.
Placement, and this is where the small volume earns its keep. The autogenous chips go directly against
the exposed implant surface — that is where I want osteogenic and osteoinductive potential, and I have
too little of it to spread thinly. Over that I layer a deproteinised bovine bone mineral, chosen for its
very slow resorption, to hold the buccal volume — because autogenous bone alone would shrink and the
contour would be lost. Then a collagen membrane, extended onto sound bone, and tension-free closure.

osce.title: Membrane selection and placement
osce.text:
OSCE 31 — Membrane selection and placement
Blueprint: role of barriers in bone augmentation and their application during surgery, with limitations (W + SCE).
EQUIPMENT
a model with a grafted buccal dehiscence; collagen membrane, dPTFE membrane, titanium-reinforced membrane, tacks,
scissors, tweezers.
CANDIDATE INSTRUCTIONS
Select and place an appropriate membrane over this graft, explaining your choice and the limitations of the material.
MODEL ANSWER
“This is a contained buccal dehiscence with the graft supported by the implant and the residual
bone walls, so it is a space-maintaining situation. I would select a native collagen membrane.
Preparation: I trim the membrane so it extends 2 to 3 mm beyond the defect margins onto sound
bone in every direction. I would use dry tweezers and handle it minimally, because a collagen
membrane becomes adherent and diﬀicult to reposition once wet.
Placement: I tuck the palatal or lingual edge under the palatal flap and stabilise it, then drape it
over the graft and tuck the buccal edge apically under the buccal flap. If the membrane were mobile
I would fix it with titanium tacks or by trapping it under the cover screw.
Stability is essential — this is the second “S” of the PASS principles: primary closure, angiogene-
sis, space maintenance, stability. A mobile membrane allows soft tissue ingrowth and defeats the
purpose.
Then closure: a periosteal releasing incision to advance the buccal flap for tension-free primary clo-
sure, with the suture line lying over sound bone rather than over the membrane edge, and horizontal
mattress plus interrupted sutures in a monofilament or ePTFE.
Limitations I would state. A collagen membrane has poor space-maintaining capacity — it col-
lapses into any non-supported defect, which is why it must be used with a supporting graft. Its

resorption is unpredictable, anywhere from about four weeks to six months. It is of porcine or
bovine origin, so consent must cover that. A dense PTFE membrane maintains space better and
tolerates exposure but must be removed; a titanium-reinforced membrane is best for large or vertical
defects but that level of augmentation is Complex and I would refer.
Exposure, the commonest complication, follows tension at closure, a suture line over the membrane,
denture pressure or smoking. If a collagen membrane exposes without infection, I manage with
chlorhexidine, no brushing and close review; an exposed PTFE membrane I would remove early.”
EXAMINER CHECKLIST
1. Correct membrane choice with justification
2. Trims to overlap 2–3 mm onto sound bone
3. Handles minimally and appropriately
4. Tucks and stabilises both edges
5. States fixation options
6. Cites PASS principles
7. Periosteal release and tension-free closure
8. Suture line off the membrane
9. States collagen limitations (space maintenance, resorption, origin/consent)
10. Exposure management differing by membrane type
Running this station to time
Time check. The model answer is 454 words, 3 minutes 15 seconds at 140 words per minute — but
three membranes are laid out, one has to be chosen and trimmed with scissors, and it has to be tucked
under two flaps on a model while you keep talking. Roughly 130 words must go, and they go by stating
each limitation as a clause with its consequence attached rather than as a paragraph — “resorption is
unpredictable, four weeks to six months, so I cannot rely on a fixed barrier period” is the whole of that
mark.
The five-minute run sheet
Time
The examiner does
What earns the mark
0:00–0:40
Presents the model with the grafted
buccal dehiscence and three membranes
— collagen, dPTFE and
titanium-reinforced — with tacks and
scissors: “Select and place an appropriate
membrane, explaining your choice and
the limitations of the material.”
Checklist 1, and it needs the defect read
out loud before the hand moves. This is
a contained buccal dehiscence,
supported by the implant and the
residual bone walls — a
space-maintaining situation —
therefore a native collagen membrane.
The other two are picked up and put
down with a reason each: dPTFE
maintains space better and tolerates
exposure but is non-resorbable and must
be removed; titanium-reinforced is for
large or vertical defects, and that level of
augmentation is Complex and I would
refer. Naming that limit is a mark, and it
is only available here, at the moment the
membrane is rejected.
0:40–1:40
Hands over the scissors and tweezers.
Checklists 2 and 3. The membrane
trimmed so that it extends 2 to 3 mm
beyond the defect margins onto sound
bone in every direction — the figure
said, and the overlap shown on the
model. Then handling: dry tweezers,
handled minimally, positioned once,
because a native collagen membrane
becomes adherent and effectively
unrepositionable as soon as it is wet.
Candidates who wet it “to make it drape”
and then wrestle it into place have
demonstrated the error the checklist is
testing.

Time
The examiner does
What earns the mark
1:40–2:40
Silence. Watches the placement.
Checklists 4, 5 and 6. Both edges tucked:
the palatal edge slid under the palatal
flap first and stabilised, then the
membrane draped over the graft and the
buccal edge tucked apically under the
buccal flap. Then fixation options
named — titanium tacks, trapping it
under the cover screw, or a periosteal
suture — if the membrane is mobile.
And the principle: PASS — primary
closure, angiogenesis, space
maintenance, stability — with its
consequence, that a mobile membrane
permits soft tissue ingrowth and
defeats the whole purpose.
2:40–3:40
“Close it.”
Checklists 7 and 8. A periosteal
releasing incision to advance the buccal
flap for tension-free primary closure —
tension is the origin of the commonest
complication here. Then the detail that
separates candidates: the suture line
must lie over sound bone, not over the
membrane edge, because a suture line
over the barrier is where dehiscence
begins. Horizontal mattress to evert and
take the tension, plus interrupted
sutures to appose, in a monofilament or
ePTFE.
3:40–5:00
“What are the limitations, and what if it
exposes?”
Checklists 9 and 10, plus the record.
Collagen limitations, three, each with
its consequence: poor space
maintenance — it collapses into any
unsupported defect, hence the graft
beneath it; unpredictable resorption,
roughly four weeks to six months;
porcine or bovine origin, so consent
must cover it. Then exposure managed
by membrane type: collagen exposed
without infection — chlorhexidine, no
brushing, no denture pressure, close
review, accepting some graft loss; an
exposed PTFE membrane removed
early. Finally: brand and lot numbers
recorded and given on the implant card,
the patient told to avoid pressure on the
site, not to smoke, and to report
anything showing through, and review
at one week, then before uncovering at
four to six months.
The compressed answer — what a strong candidate says in five minutes
“Reading the defect first. This is a contained buccal dehiscence, and the graft is supported by the implant
body and the residual bone walls — so this is already a space-maintaining situation and I do not need
the membrane to hold space for me. That decides the choice.
I would use a native collagen membrane. (putting the others down) Not the dense PTFE — it maintains
space better and tolerates exposure without infection, but it is non-resorbable and would require a second
procedure to remove it, which this defect does not justify. And not the titanium-reinforced membrane:
that is the right material for a large or vertical defect, and a defect that needs one is Complex augmenta-
tion, which I would refer rather than attempt.
Trimming. I trim it so that it extends 2 to 3 millimetres beyond the defect margins onto sound bone
in every direction. Under-extension is the commonest error — the barrier has to sit on bone all the way
round, or soft tissue simply enters at the edge.
Handling. Dry tweezers, minimal handling, and I place it once. Once a collagen membrane is wet it
becomes adherent and cannot realistically be repositioned, so I decide where it is going before it goes
there.

osce.title: Post-operative wound review and suture removal
osce.text:
OSCE 32 — Post-operative wound review and suture removal
Blueprint: postoperative care and advice; recognise unsafe situations (OS-P + SCE).
EQUIPMENT
a model or simulated patient with a healing implant/graft site; suture scissors, tweezers, mirror, probe.
CANDIDATE INSTRUCTIONS
This patient is attending one week after implant placement with simultaneous guided bone regeneration. Review the wound
and remove the sutures.

MODEL ANSWER
“I would start with the patient rather than the wound: how have the last seven days been — pain,
swelling, bleeding, any medication taken, any problems with the instructions, and are they smoking?
Examination: extra-orally for swelling, bruising, lymphadenopathy or any sign of spreading infec-
tion, and I would check sensation of the lip and chin against the baseline if this was a mandibular
case. Intra-orally I look for: wound edge apposition, colour, any dehiscence, any membrane expo-
sure, suppuration, granulation tissue, mobility of the healing abutment if one is present, and plaque
accumulation. I would not probe the implant at this stage.
Suture removal: clean the area with chlorhexidine on a cotton pledget, lift each suture gently with
tweezers, cut the strand below the knot and close to the tissue so that no external, contaminated
portion is drawn through the wound, and withdraw it towards the wound rather than away from it.
Count the sutures removed against the number recorded as placed.
Because this is a grafted site, I would consider leaving the sutures a further few days — to 10 to 14
days — if healing is not yet secure.
Advice: may now brush gently around but not directly over the site with a soft brush; continue
chlorhexidine for another week; continue soft diet; continue not smoking; and I would re-emphasise
the warning signs.
Documentation: healing assessment, sutures removed and count, sensation check, advice given,
and the next review — typically at 2 to 3 weeks then at 3 months for a grafted case.
If I found membrane exposure, I would manage it according to membrane type; if I found suppu-
ration or spreading infection, I would drain, irrigate, consider antibiotics and review at 48 hours.”
EXAMINER CHECKLIST
1. History of the week, including medication and smoking
2. Extra-oral examination
3. Sensation check against baseline
4. Systematic intra-oral wound assessment
5. Does not probe the implant at 1 week
6. Antiseptic before removal
7. Correct cutting technique below the knot
8. Counts sutures against the record
9. Considers delaying removal in a grafted site
10. Advice, documentation, next review, and a plan for exposure or infection
Running this station to time
Time check. The model answer is 417 words, 2 minutes 59 seconds at 140 words per minute — which is
why this station looks easy and why full marks are expected on it. The time is not lost to length; it is lost
to silence. Four of the ten points — not probing, the antiseptic wipe, where the cut is made, the count —
are things the hands do in a second and the mouth must take five seconds to say. The rule here is narrate
every action as it happens, including the actions you decide not to take.
The five-minute run sheet
Time
The examiner does
What earns the mark
0:00–0:45
Presents the healing site: “This patient is
attending one week after implant
placement with simultaneous guided
bone regeneration. Review the wound
and remove the sutures.”
Checklist 1, and it comes before the
mirror goes in. Start with the patient,
not the wound: pain and its trend,
swelling, bleeding, what analgesia was
actually taken and whether it worked,
whether the antibiotics or
chlorhexidine were completed, whether
the post-operative instructions caused
any diﬀiculty — and whether they have
smoked. Smoking must be asked about
by name; it is the single behaviour that
most threatens a grafted site at one week,
and “any problems?” does not elicit it.

Time
The examiner does
What earns the mark
0:45–1:45
Watches. Offers nothing.
Checklists 2 and 3. Extra-oral first —
swelling, its character and whether it is
still increasing, bruising,
lymphadenopathy, trismus, and any
sign of spreading infection. Then
checklist 3, which candidates simply
forget in the rush to the sutures:
sensation of the lip and chin tested and
compared against the baseline recorded
at placement, because this was a
mandibular case. Said aloud as it is done.
A sensory deficit found at one week and
not recorded against a baseline is a
deficit nobody can date.
1:45–2:45
Silence.
Checklists 4 and 5. A systematic
intra-oral assessment, named item by
item: wound edge apposition, tissue
colour, dehiscence, membrane exposure,
suppuration, granulation tissue, mobility
of the healing abutment if present,
plaque accumulation, and any temporary
prosthesis pressing on the site. Then the
negative that scores: “I would not probe
the implant at this stage” — said out
loud, with the reason, that the seal at one
week is immature and probing disrupts
healing and tells me nothing useful.
Leaving the probe on the tray silently
does not score checklist 5.
2:45–3:50
Hands over tweezers and suture scissors.
Checklists 6, 7 and 8 — three marks in
sixty seconds of hands, all of them
narrated. Clean the area with
chlorhexidine on a cotton pledget first.
Then the technique, described as it is
performed: lift the suture gently with
tweezers, cut the strand below the knot
and close to the tissue, so that no
external, contaminated portion of the
suture is drawn through the wound, and
withdraw it towards the wound rather
than away from it so the healing edges
are not pulled apart. Then checklist 8:
count the sutures removed against the
number recorded as placed, and say the
numbers. A suture left buried is a suture
that will present as an abscess.
3:50–5:00
“Anything else?”
Checklists 9 and 10, including the closing
decision. Because this is a grafted site,
state the judgement explicitly: if healing
is not yet secure I would leave some or
all of the sutures to 10 to 14 days rather
than remove them on schedule. Then
advice: gentle brushing around but not
directly over the site; chlorhexidine for a
further week; soft diet continued; not
smoking; warning signs restated. Then
documentation — the healing
assessment, the sensation check against
baseline, the number of sutures
removed, the advice given — and the
next review: 2 to 3 weeks, then 3
months for a grafted case. Finally the
two contingencies: membrane exposure
managed by membrane type;
suppuration or spreading infection
drained and irrigated, antibiotics
considered, reviewed at 48 hours.
The compressed answer — what a strong candidate says in five minutes
“I start with her, not with the wound. How have the last seven days been — how much pain, and is it
settling or increasing? How much swelling, and has it peaked? Any bleeding? What painkillers did you

actually take, and did they work? Did you finish the chlorhexidine? Were the instructions manageable?
And have you smoked at all this week? I ask that directly, because it is the thing most likely to lose this
graft and nobody volunteers it.
Extra-orally, I look for swelling and whether it is still increasing, bruising, lymphadenopathy, trismus,
and any sign of spreading infection. And because this was a lower case, I test the sensation of the lip
and chin and compare it with the baseline I recorded at placement — light touch and sharp–blunt, both
sides — and I record the result whether or not it has changed.
Intra-orally, systematically: wound edge apposition; the colour of the tissue; any dehiscence; any mem-
brane exposure; suppuration; granulation tissue; mobility of the healing abutment if there is one; plaque
accumulation; and whether any temporary denture is pressing on the site.
And one thing I deliberately do not do: I will not probe the implant at one week. The seal is immature,
probing at this stage disturbs healing, and a reading now would tell me nothing I could use.
Suture removal. First I clean the area with chlorhexidine on a cotton pledget — the sutures have been
sitting in plaque for seven days and I do not want to drag that into the wound.
Then, one at a time: I lift the suture gently with tweezers, and I cut the strand below the knot, close to
the tissue, so that the portion that has been exposed to the mouth never passes through the wound. Then
I withdraw it towards the wound, not away from it, so I am not pulling the healing edges apart.
And I count. Six were placed — I have removed six. If the count is short I look for a buried suture rather
than assume, because a retained suture presents as an abscess in a fortnight.
Because this is a grafted site, I make a judgement rather than follow a rule. If the wound edges are not
yet securely healed I would leave some or all of the sutures a further few days — to 10 to 14 days — and
see her again, rather than remove them on the calendar.
Advice. She may now brush gently around the site with a soft brush, but not directly over it. Continue
chlorhexidine for another week. Continue the soft diet. Do not smoke. And the warning signs again:
increasing pain or swelling after this point, a bad taste, discharge, anything showing through the gum, or
any change in the feeling of the lip — telephone, do not wait.
Documentation: the healing assessment item by item, the sensation check against baseline, the number
of sutures removed against the number placed, the advice given, and the next review — 2 to 3 weeks,
and then at 3 months because this site is grafted.
And if I found something. Membrane exposure I manage by type — a collagen membrane exposed
without infection conservatively, with chlorhexidine and no brushing; a PTFE membrane removed early.
Suppuration or spreading infection I drain and irrigate, consider systemic antibiotics, and review at 48
hours, not at the next routine appointment.”
Marking priority when the clock beats the candidate
Ask for these first (the six that carry the station): 7 cut below the knot, withdrawn towards the wound,
with the reason · 5 states out loud that the implant will not be probed at one week · 3 sensation checked
against the placement baseline · 4 systematic wound assessment naming dehiscence and membrane ex-
posure · 8 sutures counted against the record · 10 advice, documentation, review interval and the expo-
sure/infection contingencies.
Accept these late or on prompting: 1 the week’s history including analgesia and smoking · 2 extra-oral
examination · 6 chlorhexidine before removal · 9 removal delayed to 10–14 days in a grafted site.
The commonest way five minutes is wasted here: working in silence. This is a full-marks station that
candidates routinely score six on, because they clean the site, cut the sutures correctly and count them —
and say none of it. The examiner marks what is said; a perfectly executed cut below the knot is invisible
unless the candidate narrates where the blade is going and why. The second loss is the sensation check:
fifteen seconds, checklist 3, and forgotten by almost everyone who heads straight for the scissors — as is
checklist 9, where the mark is for deciding to leave a grafted site to 10 to 14 days rather than following the
standard interval.

osce.title: Second-stage (uncovering) surgery
osce.text:
OSCE 33 — Second-stage (uncovering) surgery
Blueprint: one or two stage procedures; soft tissue management (W + OS-P + SCE).
EQUIPMENT
a model with two submerged implants — one with abundant keratinised tissue, one with 1 mm; blades, tissue punch, eleva-
tors, healing abutments.
CANDIDATE INSTRUCTIONS
Uncover these two implants. For each, select and justify your technique.
MODEL ANSWER
“Before I start: confirm the healing period is complete, check the site clinically, and take a periapical
to confirm bone levels and to locate the cover screw.
Implant A, abundant keratinised tissue. I can afford to remove a small amount of tissue, so a
tissue punch or a small crestal incision is appropriate. It is quick, needs no flap, and heals rapidly. I
would locate the cover screw precisely — with a probe through the mucosa or from the radiograph
— punch or incise, remove the tissue plug, expose and unscrew the cover screw, clean the internal
connection, and place a healing abutment of appropriate height so it emerges through the mucosa
without being over-contoured.
Implant B, 1 mm of keratinised tissue. A tissue punch is contraindicated here, because it excises
the very tissue I need. I would use an apically positioned flap: a crestal incision displaced palatally
so that the band of keratinised tissue is carried buccally, with two short vertical relieving incisions, a
partial-thickness dissection buccally, and the flap sutured apically at the new position with periosteal
sutures. That both uncovers the implant and increases the width of keratinised mucosa buccally.
If the tissue were also thin, I would consider a connective tissue graft at the same time — second
stage is one of the two best moments to modify the phenotype, the other being placement.
In both cases: select a healing abutment of correct diameter and height to begin shaping the emer-
gence, check it is fully seated radiographically if in doubt, hand-tighten, give hygiene instructions
specific to a healing abutment, and record what was placed. I would allow 2 to 4 weeks of soft
tissue maturation before impressions.”
EXAMINER CHECKLIST
1. Confirms healing period and takes a radiograph
2. Locates the cover screw before incising
3. Punch justified where KM is abundant
4. Rejects punch where KM is scarce, with reason
5. Palatally displaced crestal incision described
6. Apically positioned flap technique
7. Considers CTG for a thin phenotype and states the timing rationale
8. Cleans the connection and selects an appropriate healing abutment
9. Verifies seating
10. Hygiene advice, soft tissue maturation period, records
Running this station to time
Time check. The model answer is 420 words, 3 minutes exactly at 140 words per minute — but two
implants have to be uncovered and the marks are not shared between them. Implant A carries one
checklist point; implant B carries four. So the ration is deliberate: 50 seconds for the punch, a full 100
seconds for the apically positioned flap, and the punch described in the past tense — chosen, justified,
done — rather than performed slowly on a model where nothing is at stake.
The five-minute run sheet

Time
The examiner does
What earns the mark
0:00–0:35
Presents the model with two submerged
implants — one with abundant
keratinised tissue, one with 1 mm —
and blades, a tissue punch, elevators and
healing abutments: “Uncover these two.
For each, select and justify your
technique.”
Checklists 1 and 2, before any blade is
picked up. Confirm the healing period
is complete and the site is clinically quiet,
and take a periapical — for bone levels
and, specifically, to locate the cover
screw. Then checklist 2 as an action:
locate the cover screw precisely before
incising, by probing through the mucosa
and by reference to the radiograph.
Cutting first and hunting afterwards is
how keratinised tissue is wasted.
0:35–1:25
Indicates implant A.
Checklist 3, and briskly — this is one
mark and it is not worth 90 seconds.
Keratinised tissue is abundant here, so
I can afford to remove a small amount: a
tissue punch, or a small crestal incision,
justified on exactly that ground — quick,
no flap, rapid healing. Punch centred
over the located cover screw, tissue plug
removed, cover screw unscrewed,
connection inspected. The justification is
the mark; the technique is not.
1:25–3:10
Indicates implant B: “And this one?”
Checklists 4, 5, 6 and 7 — the stretch that
decides the station. First the rejection,
said explicitly: “A tissue punch is
contraindicated here, because with 1
mm of keratinised mucosa it excises the
very tissue I need.” Then the alternative,
described so the examiner can see it: an
apically positioned flap — a crestal
incision displaced palatally, so the
existing band of keratinised tissue is
carried buccally rather than split down
the middle; two short vertical relieving
incisions; a partial-thickness dissection
buccally, leaving periosteum on the
bone; the flap sutured apically at its new
position with periosteal sutures. Then
what that achieves: it uncovers the
implant and widens the buccal band in
one procedure. Then checklist 7: if the
tissue is also thin, a connective tissue
graft at the same visit — because
second stage is one of the two best
moments to modify the phenotype, the
other being placement.
3:10–4:05
“Now finish both.”
Checklists 8 and 9, which apply to both
implants and are commonly dropped.
Clean the internal connection of
granulation tissue and debris before
anything is seated. Select a healing
abutment of appropriate diameter and
height — tall enough to emerge through
the mucosa, not so wide or so contoured
that it blanches the tissue, the diameter
chosen to begin shaping the emergence
profile. Then checklist 9: verify
complete seating, radiographically if in
doubt, and hand-tighten only — a

I take a periapical — to check the bone levels and, just as importantly, to locate the cover screws. Then I
find each cover screw through the mucosa with a probe before I incise. I do not want to be searching for
it after I have cut.
Implant A — abundant keratinised tissue. Here I can afford to lose a little tissue, so a tissue punch is
appropriate, or a small crestal incision. It is quick, it needs no flap, and it heals in days. I centre the punch
over the cover screw I have located, remove the tissue plug, unscrew the cover screw, and inspect the
connection.
Implant B — one millimetre of keratinised tissue. Here a tissue punch is contraindicated, and this is
the whole point of the second implant: a punch would excise the only keratinised tissue this implant
has, and I would be creating a problem in order to save five minutes.
Instead, an apically positioned flap. I make a crestal incision displaced palatally, so that the existing
band of keratinised tissue is carried buccally on the flap rather than divided. I add two short vertical
relieving incisions, raise a partial-thickness dissection buccally — leaving periosteum on the bone for
the flap to be sewn to — and suture the flap apically in its new position with periosteal sutures. That
does two jobs at once: it uncovers the implant and it increases the width of keratinised mucosa on the
buccal, which is where I want it for long-term maintenance.
And if the tissue were thin as well as narrow, I would place a connective tissue graft at the same visit.
Second stage is one of the two best moments to modify the soft tissue phenotype — the other is at
placement — and once the restoration is on, doing it becomes much harder and less predictable.
Then, at both implants. I clean the internal connection thoroughly — granulation tissue, debris, any
bone that has grown over the screw — because anything left in there will compromise the fit of everything
that follows.

the mucosa so the tissue heals around it rather than over it, and of a diameter that begins to shape the
emergence profile without over-contouring and blanching the tissue. I verify that it is fully seated —
radiographically if there is any doubt — and I hand-tighten it; a healing abutment is not torqued.

brush over it and a single-tufted brush around the emergence, demonstrated in her hand at the chair, not
described. Chlorhexidine for the flap site for a week. And telephone if a healing abutment feels loose or
comes out.
Timing. I allow 2 to 4 weeks of soft tissue maturation before impressions, and longer at implant B,
where the flap has been repositioned and must stabilise before I record anything.
And I record: the technique used at each implant and the reason, the make, diameter and height of each
healing abutment, that seating was verified, the graft if placed, the hygiene instruction given, and the
review.”

osce.title: Selecting implant dimensions from the planning data
osce.text:
OSCE 34 — Selecting implant dimensions from the planning data
Blueprint: plan in detail and select the techniques for implant placement; bone quality and quantity (W + OS-P + SCE).
EQUIPMENT
CBCT cross-sections and a wax-up for three sites: an upper lateral incisor (5.8 mm space), a lower first molar (9 mm above
the canal, 9 mm wide), and an upper second premolar (6 mm below the sinus, 7 mm wide).
CANDIDATE INSTRUCTIONS
Select an implant diameter and length for each site and justify your choices.
MODEL ANSWER
“Upper lateral incisor, 5.8 mm mesiodistal space. I need 1.5 mm to each adjacent root, so the
maximum diameter is about 2.8 mm at the crest — which is tight. I would select a 3.3 mm narrow-
diameter implant in a titanium-zirconium alloy for strength, and accept slightly under 1.5 mm on
one side only if the CBCT shows the roots diverge apically; otherwise I would discuss orthodontic
space adjustment or an alternative prosthesis. Length around 10 to 12 mm depending on the nasal
floor and the incisive canal. Position: shoulder 3 mm apical to the planned mid-facial margin, 1 to 2
mm palatal to the emergence of the adjacent teeth.
Lower first molar, 9 mm above the canal, 9 mm wide. I must leave 2 mm clearance from the canal, so
the maximum length is about 7 mm — I would choose a short implant of 6 to 7 mm, and compensate
with a wide diameter of 5.0 mm, since diameter increases surface area and resistance to bending far
more eﬀiciently than length. Ridge width of 9 mm allows 5.0 mm with 2 mm of bone each side. Bone
is likely D2, so I would drill conventionally and consider counter-sinking to avoid excessive torque.
Upper second premolar, 6 mm below the sinus, 7 mm wide. With only 6 mm and a flat floor, this
sits exactly at the boundary of the ITI decision tree. My options are: a short implant of 6 mm with
no sinus procedure; or a transcrestal elevation to gain 3 to 4 mm allowing an 8 to 10 mm implant
— but the tree indicates a lateral window at 6 mm or less, so I would be cautious. Diameter 4.1 mm
with 7 mm of width leaves about 1.5 mm each side. Bone will be D3 or D4, so I would under-prepare,
use a tapered implant, and load conventionally at 3 to 6 months.
In every case, the position comes from the wax-up, not from where the bone happens to be.”
EXAMINER CHECKLIST
1. Applies the 1.5 mm rule to the incisor space
2. Selects a narrow implant with a strength-appropriate material
3. Offers orthodontic/alternative option where space is marginal
4. Applies the 2 mm canal margin
5. Chooses a short, wide implant with a biomechanical justification
6. Checks ridge width against diameter plus 1.5–2 mm each side

7. Recognises the 6 mm sinus decision boundary
8. Modifies technique for D3/D4
9. Correct 3-D position for the anterior site
10. States that the wax-up drives position
Running this station to time
Time check. The model answer is 508 words, 3 minutes 38 seconds at 140 words per minute — the longest
in this group, across three sites, and every mark on it is a number. That means the compression cannot
come from the figures; it has to come from the reasoning around them. Eighty seconds per site, and at
each one the shape is fixed: the limiting anatomy, the subtraction, the implant I choose, the technique I modify —
four sentences, with the arithmetic said out loud rather than implied.

“One principle before the numbers: the position comes from the wax-up, not from where the bone
happens to be. If the two conflict, I graft or I change the prosthesis.
Upper lateral incisor, 5.8 mm of space. I need 1.5 mm to each adjacent root, so 5.8 minus 3 leaves 2.8
mm at the crest — narrower than any implant I can place. So a 3.3 mm narrow-diameter implant in a
titanium–zirconium alloy, because 3.3 mm in commercially pure titanium is mechanically marginal here
and the alloy gives the strength back. I would accept slightly under 1.5 mm on one side only, and only
if the CBCT shows the roots diverge apically so the tight point is at the crest alone. If not, I would not
force it — I would discuss orthodontic space opening or a resin-bonded bridge. Length 10 to 12 mm,
depending on the nasal floor and incisive canal.
And the three-dimensional position, which matters more here than the dimensions: the shoulder 3
mm apical to the planned mid-facial gingival margin, and 1 to 2 mm palatal to the emergence of the
adjacent teeth — deep enough for an emergence profile, palatal enough to keep the buccal plate.
Lower first molar, 9 mm above the canal, 9 mm wide. The canal is the limit. I must leave 2 mm of
clearance, so 9 minus 2 gives me 7 mm — that is my maximum length, and I would choose a short
implant of 6 to 7 mm. I am not apologising for that: I compensate with diameter, 5.0 mm, because
diameter increases surface area and resistance to bending far more eﬀiciently than length does.
Checking the width: 9 mm of ridge minus a 5.0 mm implant leaves 2 mm each side. Bone here will be
D2, so I drill conventionally and consider counter-sinking to avoid excessive insertion torque and crestal
pressure necrosis.
Upper second premolar, 6 mm below the sinus, 7 mm wide. Six millimetres is exactly the ITI decision
boundary, and I would say so: with a flat floor at 6 mm or less, the tree points to a lateral window —
and that is Complex; I would refer for it, not attempt it.
Within my scope, two options. A short 6 mm implant with no sinus procedure; or a transcrestal eleva-
tion to gain 3 to 4 mm, allowing 8 to 10 mm — but at exactly 6 mm with a flat floor I would be cautious,
because that is where the tree stops recommending it. Diameter 4.1 mm in a 7 mm ridge leaves about 1.5
mm each side.
Bone here will be D3 or D4, so I change the technique: under-prepare the osteotomy, use a tapered
implant for primary stability by compression, omit the countersink, and load conventionally at 3 to 6
months.
To finish. I record the diameter and length for each site, make sure a back-up size either side is on the
shelf on the day, and use a depth stop at the molar. Each patient is consented to the issue at their own
site — the space compromise and orthodontic alternative at the incisor, the nerve and the 2 mm margin at
the molar, the sinus and possible referral at the premolar. And on the day I re-confirm every one of these
against the guide and the radiograph before I drill.”
Marking priority when the clock beats the candidate
Ask for these first (the six that carry the station): 4 2 mm canal clearance, 9 −2 = 7 mm said as arithmetic
· 5 short 6–7 mm implant at 5.0 mm with the bending-resistance reason · 1 the 1.5 mm rule giving 2.8 mm
· 7 6 mm named as the sinus boundary, lateral window referred · 2 3.3 mm titanium–zirconium with the
strength reason · 10 the wax-up drives position.

osce.title: Preparing the surgical tray
osce.text:
OSCE 35 — Preparing the surgical tray
Blueprint: infection control and aseptic technique; range of surgical components required (W + OS-P + SCE).
EQUIPMENT
a bench of instruments, some appropriate and some not; a surgical kit; implant packaging.
CANDIDATE INSTRUCTIONS
Lay out a surgical tray for a single implant placement with possible simultaneous guided bone regeneration. Name each
item and its purpose. Identify anything missing.
MODEL ANSWER
“Working in the order of the operation.
Anaesthesia: syringe, needles, cartridges, topical. Incision and reflection: scalpel handle and
blades — a 15 or 15c for the crestal incision — periosteal elevator, tissue forceps, retractors of ap-
propriate width, and a Mitchell’s trimmer or curette. Osteotomy: the implant system’s surgical
kit — round or precision drill, sequential twist drills with depth marks, direction indicators, depth
gauge, countersink and tap if required, drill extensions; the electric surgical motor with a ster-
ile handpiece and sterile irrigation tubing; and sterile saline. Placement: implant carrier/driver,
ratchet and torque wrench, cover screws and healing abutments in a range of heights, and screw-
drivers. Augmentation: bone scraper or trap, graft material, membrane, tacks and a tack driver, and
rongeur. Closure: needle holder, suture scissors, tissue forceps, and sutures — I would have both
a monofilament or ePTFE for the grafted site and a resorbable alternative. General: high-volume
suction and a fine surgical sucker, gauze, a throat screen, saline-soaked gauze to keep the flap moist,
and a sterile marker.
Missing or wrong items I would look for: an air-driven handpiece — remove it; steel curettes on
the implant tray — remove them; an implant with a damaged pouch or past expiry — discard and
record; non-sterile bur block; missing torque wrench; and no drill stop where the canal is close.
Before starting: confirm the correct patient, site and implant with a surgical safety check — patient
identity, medical history, consent confirmed, site marked, implant system, diameter and length avail-
able with a back-up size, allergies, and radiographs displayed. I would also confirm the instrument
and swab count with my assistant, and record the batch numbers.”
EXAMINER CHECKLIST
1. Anaesthesia items
2. Incision and reflection instruments named with purpose
3. Correct drilling kit including direction indicators and depth gauge
4. Electric motor with sterile tubing and saline
5. Torque wrench and ratchet
6. Augmentation instruments and materials
7. Closure instruments and appropriate sutures
8. Identifies inappropriate items (air-turbine, steel instruments, expired implant)
9. Surgical safety check including back-up implant sizes

10. Counts and batch number recording
Running this station to time
Time check. The model answer is 414 words, 2 minutes 57 seconds at 140 words per minute — and this
is a full-marks station that candidates routinely score seven on. The clock is not the enemy; itemising
is. There are more than forty objects on that bench and only ten marks, so the discipline is one clause of
purpose per group of instruments, not per instrument — “retractors of appropriate width, to protect the
flap and give me vision” covers the group — and the last ninety seconds are reserved for what is wrong,
what is missing, and the safety check.

“I will work in the order of the operation.
Anaesthesia: syringe, needles, cartridges, topical.

to raise the flap cleanly off bone in one plane; tissue forceps, so I handle the flap by its edge and do not
crush it; retractors of appropriate width for vision and to protect the flap from the drill; a Mitchell’s
trimmer to clear the crest.

teeth and the guide before going deeper, a depth gauge, a countersink and tap if the bone is dense, drill
extensions. The drive is an electric surgical motor with a sterile handpiece and sterile irrigation tubing,
torque and speed set at the console — and sterile saline, never tap water.
Placement: the implant carrier and driver, the ratchet, and the torque wrench; cover screws and healing
abutments in a range of heights, and the screwdrivers for them.

chips, the graft material, the membrane, tacks and a tack driver, a rongeur.

ePTFE suture for the grafted site, because braided material wicks plaque along a line that has to hold for
ten to fourteen days. A resorbable alternative available.
General: high-volume and fine surgical suction, gauze, a throat screen, saline-soaked gauze to keep the
flap moist while I drill, a sterile marker.
Now, what is wrong on this bench. The air-driven handpiece comes off — it exhausts into the surgical
field and can drive air into the tissues, causing surgical emphysema; that is what the electric motor is for.
The steel curettes come off the implant tray — steel scratches the titanium oxide layer; anything touching
an implant is titanium, PEEK or carbon fibre. The non-sterile bur block comes off. And this implant,
with a damaged pouch and a passed expiry date, is discarded — I open a replacement and record the
batch number and the reason for the discard, and report it as a device incident.
And what is missing. There is no torque wrench — I cannot seat an abutment or verify insertion torque
without one. And there is no drill stop, which I want here because the canal is close and a stop is the
difference between a controlled depth and a nerve injury.

osce.title: Torque, preload and the torque wrench
osce.text:
OSCE 36 — Torque, preload and the torque wrench
Blueprint: prosthetic components; fitting a prosthesis (OS-P).
EQUIPMENT
a torque wrench, abutment screws, a model with an implant analogue, an abutment.
CANDIDATE INSTRUCTIONS
Torque this abutment correctly, explaining the underlying mechanics and how you look after the instrument.
MODEL ANSWER
“First I confirm the manufacturer’s specified torque value for this component — it is not a universal
figure, and using another system’s value is an error.
Mechanics. Tightening a screw generates preload — the tensile clamping force in the screw shank
that holds the joint together and resists separation under load. Most of the torque I apply is con-
sumed by friction at the threads and under the screw head; only a fraction becomes preload. That
is why the manufacturer specifies a torque value calibrated for their component, screw material and
surface coating — gold-coated screws, for instance, have lower friction and achieve higher preload
for the same torque.
Settling, or embedment relaxation: the microscopic roughness of the mating surfaces flattens under
the initial clamping load, so preload falls by roughly 2 to 10% within the first minutes. That is why
I re-torque after approximately ten minutes.
Technique. Ensure the connection is clean and dry and the components fully seated — verified ra-
diographically if deep. Engage the driver fully to avoid rounding the screw head. Apply the wrench
slowly and smoothly, in a controlled arc, supporting the implant/abutment against rotational force,
until the wrench signals the set value. Do not use a jerking motion and do not exceed the value ‘for
good measure’. Then re-torque at ten minutes.

Care of the instrument. Torque wrenches are precision devices: they must be dismantled, cleaned
and sterilised according to the manufacturer’s instructions, inspected for damage, wear and con-
tamination, and checked or calibrated at the recommended intervals — many require annual cali-
bration or replacement of the spring mechanism. A wrench dropped on the floor should be checked
before reuse. I would keep a record of calibration as part of clinical governance.
Never use a torque wrench to force a non-seating component — that causes screw fracture, bone
loss and pain.”
EXAMINER CHECKLIST
1. Uses the manufacturer’s value
2. Defines preload correctly
3. Explains friction consumption of torque
4. Explains settling and the 10-minute re-torque
5. Cleans and verifies seating first
6. Correct driver engagement and controlled application
7. Supports against rotational force
8. Does not exceed the specified value
9. Cleaning, sterilisation and calibration record
10. States never to force a non-seating component
Running this station to time
Time check. The model answer is 418 words, 2 minutes 59 seconds at 140 words per minute — but the
wrench has to be picked up, engaged and turned while the mechanics are explained, and the mechanics
are where candidates spend three minutes on physics that earns two marks. This is a numbers station:
quote the figures — the torque value, the fraction of it that becomes preload, the 2 to 10% settling loss,
the ten minutes, the annual calibration — and let the numbers carry the explanation instead of explaining
around them.

before reuse. The mark includes the
calibration record kept as part of
clinical governance. Then checklist 10 as
an absolute: never use a torque wrench
to force a non-seating component —
forcing an interference causes screw
fracture, crestal bone loss and pain.
Finally: record the component, the
screw, the torque applied and the
ten-minute re-torque, tell the patient to
report looseness or clicking immediately,
and check the screw at review.
The compressed answer — what a strong candidate says in five minutes
“First, the value. I confirm the manufacturer’s specified torque for this exact component — I look it up
rather than remember it, because it is not a universal figure. In practice it is somewhere between 15 and
35 newton centimetres: 35 Ncm is common for a definitive abutment screw, 15 Ncm for some prosthetic
and temporary screws, and a healing abutment is hand-tightened only. Using another system’s number
is an error, not a shortcut.
Before I turn anything, I make sure the connection is clean and dry and the components are fully seated
— and if the margin is deep I verify seating radiographically, because a component that is not down will
not be made to go down by torque.
Now the mechanics. Tightening a screw generates preload — the tensile clamping force in the screw
shank that holds the joint together and resists separation under function. Preload is what stops the screw
loosening; loosening is a preload problem, not a screw problem.
But most of the torque I apply never becomes preload. The great majority — of the order of ninety per
cent — is consumed by friction, under the head and along the threads, and only around a tenth ends
up as clamping force. That is exactly why the value is calibrated for their component, screw alloy and

osce.title: Retrieving a fractured abutment screw
osce.text:
OSCE 37 — Retrieving a fractured abutment screw
Blueprint: managing complications relating to implant restorations (W + SCE).
EQUIPMENT
a model with an implant analogue containing a fractured screw fragment; ultrasonic scaler, explorer, screw removal kit,
magnification.
CANDIDATE INSTRUCTIONS
This abutment screw has fractured within the implant. Describe and demonstrate your retrieval.

MODEL ANSWER
“First, why did it fracture? Almost always fatigue from repeated loosening, or overload from an
eccentric occlusal contact, a cantilever or a non-passive fit. I must correct that, or I will simply repeat
the problem.
Assessment: magnification and good illumination; assess how much of the fragment is exposed,
whether it is loose or tight, and take a periapical to check the implant body for fracture and the bone
levels.
Retrieval, escalating from least to most invasive: 1. Ultrasonic scaler tip applied to the fragment
in a counter-clockwise direction at low power with light pressure. Vibration frequently walks a
loose fragment out without any instrument entering the threads. 2. A fine explorer or a sharp
probe engaged in the fragment’s flute and rotated anticlockwise. 3. A proprietary screw removal
kit — these have a guide that seats in the implant connection to keep the instrument centred, and a
reverse-thread extractor or a small trephine that engages the fragment. Follow the kit instructions
precisely. 4. If the internal threads are damaged, a thread-repair tap for that system may salvage
the implant.
Throughout: protect the airway with a gauze screen and high-volume suction; irrigate to keep the
site cool; and never allow a rotary instrument to touch the internal threads, because destroying
them usually means losing the implant.
Afterwards: clean the connection, place a new screw — never reuse one — and torque to the manu-
facturer’s value, re-torquing at ten minutes. Then correct the cause: adjust the occlusion, eliminate
excursive contacts, reconsider a cantilever, verify passive fit, and provide a night guard if there is
parafunction.
If retrieval fails, the options are to refer, or to accept that the implant is not restorable and plan
removal — which I would explain honestly, along with the cost implications. I would record the
whole episode and treat it as a significant event.”
EXAMINER CHECKLIST
1. Asks why it fractured before retrieving
2. Magnification and radiographic assessment
3. Ultrasonic counter-clockwise as first line
4. Explorer technique
5. Proprietary kit with centring guide
6. Thread repair option
7. Airway protection and irrigation
8. Protects internal threads
9. New screw, correct torque, re-torque
10. Corrects the underlying cause; states the fallback and records it
Running this station to time
Time check. The model answer is 422 words, 3 minutes 1 second at 140 words per minute — but there
are four escalating retrieval methods to describe and demonstrate, and candidates give each a paragraph.
They do not need one. The shape here is a ladder: one sentence per rung, in order, least invasive first,
with the reason for the order said once — and the ninety seconds saved goes on the two marks that bracket
the retrieval, which are why it broke and what stops it breaking again.
The five-minute run sheet

“You have the fragment out. Now

Checklists 9 and 10 — the part

The compressed answer — what a strong candidate says in five minutes
“Before I touch it — why did it break? An abutment screw does not fracture spontaneously. It is almost
always fatigue from repeated loosening, or overload: an eccentric occlusal contact, an excursive interfer-
ence, a cantilever, parafunction, or a framework that never fitted passively. I have to find that and correct
it, or I will be doing this again next year with a smaller fragment.
Assessment. Magnification and good illumination — I am not attempting this by naked eye. I look at
how much of the fragment is exposed, and whether it is loose or still tight, because a fragment that has
unwound comes out with vibration alone and a tight one will not. And a periapical, to check the implant
body itself is not fractured and to see the bone levels — if the implant is fractured, I am planning removal,
not retrieval.
Then I escalate from least invasive to most, and I do not skip rungs.
First, an ultrasonic scaler tip on the fragment, applied in a counter-clockwise direction, at low power
and with light pressure. Vibration alone walks a great many fragments out, and nothing has entered the
threads.
Second, a fine explorer or sharp probe, engaged in the flute of the fragment and rotated anticlockwise.
Third, a proprietary screw removal kit for this system. These have a guide that seats into the implant
connection and keeps the instrument centred — that centring is the whole value of the kit, because it is
what stops the extractor wandering into the threads. Then a reverse-thread extractor or a small trephine
engages the fragment. I follow the kit instructions exactly rather than improvise.
Fourth, if the internal threads are damaged, a thread-repair tap for that system may still salvage the
implant.
Throughout, two things I am protecting. The airway — a gauze screen and high-volume suction,
because a small titanium fragment released under vibration is an inhalation or ingestion risk. And the
internal threads: I never let a rotary instrument touch them. Destroying the threads turns a repairable
screw fracture into a lost implant.
Once it is out. I clean the connection, and I place a new screw — never a reused one, because the old
screw has already been through the loading that broke its partner. Torqued to the manufacturer’s value,
and re-torqued at ten minutes, because settling costs preload in the first few minutes and low preload is
what caused this in the first place.
Then I correct the cause, which is the actual treatment. Adjust the occlusion — check the static contacts
and eliminate excursive interferences on the implant. Reconsider the cantilever if there is one. Verify the
framework seats passively. Provide a night guard if there is parafunction. If I do not do this, everything
above is a repair, not a solution.
And if retrieval fails, I say so honestly. The options are to refer to someone with the equipment and
experience to try again, or to accept the implant is not restorable and plan its removal and the rebuild
that follows — and I would explain that plainly to the patient, including what it costs, rather than keep
going until I have wrecked the threads.

osce.title: Removing a cemented crown and residual cement
osce.text:
OSCE 38 — Removing a cemented crown and residual cement
Blueprint: managing complications; peri-implant disease (W + SCE).
EQUIPMENT
a model with a cemented implant crown; crown removal instruments, ultrasonic, burs, titanium curettes, floss, air-polisher,
periapical radiograph showing residual cement.
CANDIDATE INSTRUCTIONS
This radiograph shows residual cement around an implant with peri-implantitis. Explain and demonstrate how you would
remove the crown and the cement.
MODEL ANSWER
“Consent first, and this is the crucial preliminary. I would tell the patient: ‘To treat this properly I
need to get underneath the crown, because I believe there is cement left behind driving the infection.
The crown is cemented, so there is a real chance I will damage or destroy it and it will need remaking,
with the cost that involves. If we don’t do this, the infection continues and the implant may be lost.’
I would record that discussion.
Crown removal, least destructive first: 1. Ultrasonic vibration applied to the crown margins, which
frequently breaks a weak temporary cement seal. 2. A crown removal instrument — a sliding-
hammer type or a Wamkey-style device — used cautiously, protecting the implant from excessive
lateral force. 3. If those fail, section the crown with a fine diamond or carbide bur, cutting from
occlusal to buccal, and expand it off the abutment. I would protect the implant shoulder and the
soft tissue, use copious water and high-volume suction, and accept that the crown is being sacrificed.
Cement removal: - Irrigate and inspect under magnification and good illumination. - Titanium or
PEEK curettes and scalers — never steel — worked circumferentially. - Dental floss knotted and
drawn around the abutment in a see-saw motion is particularly effective at engaging cement in the
sulcus. - Glycine or erythritol air-polishing delivered subgingivally to reach thread surfaces and
residual particles. - If access is inadequate, a small flap may be needed for direct vision.
Verification: a periapical radiograph to confirm no radiopaque cement remains — while noting
that a non-radiopaque cement will not show, which is why cement selection matters in the first
place.
Then prevent recurrence: replace the restoration with a screw-retained, cleansable design; if ce-
mentation is unavoidable, keep the margin at or within 1 mm of the mucosal margin, use minimal

radiopaque cement and an extra-oral replica technique. Proceed with peri-implantitis therapy, and
record everything.”
EXAMINER CHECKLIST
1. Consent to possible destruction of the crown, with cost
2. Ultrasonic first
3. Crown removal instrument
4. Sectioning technique with implant and tissue protection
5. Magnification and illumination
6. Titanium/PEEK instruments only
7. Knotted floss technique
8. Glycine air-polishing
9. Radiographic verification with the non-radiopaque caveat
10. Converts to a screw-retained cleansable design and records
Running this station to time
Time check. The model answer is 444 words, 3 minutes 10 seconds at 140 words per minute — but the
first mark on the sheet is a conversation, not a technique, and it cannot be rushed: the patient has to be
told the crown may be destroyed and what that will cost, before a single instrument touches it. Budget 50
seconds for consent, then run the two removals as ladders — one sentence per rung — and keep the last
minute for verification, the non-radiopaque caveat and the redesign.

stability will be judged.
The compressed answer — what a strong candidate says in five minutes
“Consent first, and this is the crucial preliminary. I would say to her: ‘To treat this properly I need to
get underneath the crown, because I believe there is cement left behind that is driving the infection. The crown is
cemented on, so there is a real chance I will damage or destroy it getting it off, and it would need remaking — with
the cost that involves. If we don’t do this, the infection continues and you may lose the implant.’ And I record that
conversation before I start, because I am about to destroy something she paid for.
Crown removal, least destructive first.
One: ultrasonic vibration applied to the crown margins. A weak or temporary cement seal frequently
breaks with vibration alone, and nothing is damaged.
Two: a crown removal instrument — a sliding-hammer or a Wamkey-style device — used cautiously,
protecting the implant from excessive lateral force. I am mindful that I am applying force to an implant
that already has bone loss around it.
Three: if those fail, I section it. A fine diamond or carbide bur, cutting from occlusal to buccal, then
expanding the crown off the abutment. I protect the implant shoulder and the soft tissue, use copious
water and high-volume suction, and I accept that the crown is being sacrificed. Getting to the cement
matters more than saving the restoration.
Then the cement itself.

osce.title: Surgical management of peri-implantitis
osce.text:
OSCE 39 — Surgical management of peri-implantitis
Blueprint: appropriate management of common complications; problem solving of clinical outcomes (W + SCE).
EQUIPMENT
a model with a peri-implantitis defect around a posterior implant; flap instruments, titanium brush, curettes, saline, graft,
membrane, burs.
CANDIDATE INSTRUCTIONS
Non-surgical therapy has failed at this posterior implant, which has a 5 mm circumferential intrabony defect. Describe the
surgical management.

MODEL ANSWER
“First, confirm that the criteria for surgery are met — the ITI decision tree specifies persistent sup-
puration and/or bleeding on probing with probing depths of 6 mm or more after non-surgical
therapy and re-assessment at about a month. I would also confirm that cause-related therapy has
been done: risk factors modified, the prosthesis assessed and modified or replaced for cleansability,
and any residual cement removed.
Consent must include the likely soft tissue recession and possible exposure of metal, the cost, the
possibility that treatment does not arrest the disease, and that the implant may still need removal.
Surgery: 1. Local anaesthesia and antiseptic preparation. 2. Full-thickness mucoperiosteal flap
with intrasulcular incisions and relieving incisions as needed for access, preserving as much kera-
tinised tissue as possible. 3. Complete removal of the inflamed granulation tissue from the defect
with curettes, so the defect morphology can be seen clearly. 4. Decontamination of the exposed
implant surface — mechanically with a titanium brush or ultrasonic tips, chemically with saline,
chlorhexidine or hydrogen peroxide, and/or with Er:YAG laser irradiation. No single method is
clearly superior; the aim is thorough biofilm and calculus removal without damaging the surface
excessively. 5. Defect-specific decision. This is a circumferential intrabony defect — Type 1 CID in
the ITI classification, and the tree indicates that defects with an intrabony component are suitable for
reconstructive therapy: a bone graft or substitute, with or without a membrane, and with or without
a soft tissue graft. Had this been a supracrestal or combined semicircular defect in a non-aesthetic
site, resective therapy with bone recontouring, implantoplasty and an apically positioned flap
would be indicated instead. 6. Adequate flap adaptation and tension-free closure. 7. Post-operative
care: antiseptics, analgesia, and peri-operative systemic antimicrobials where indicated; no brushing
over the site; review at one week.
Then supportive therapy every 3 to 5 months, with professional biofilm removal and reinforcement
of hygiene, and a new baseline radiograph against which to judge stability.
I would add that surgical management of peri-implantitis, particularly reconstructive therapy, is
Complex, and unless I had specific training and experience I would refer for this phase having done
the diagnosis and cause-related therapy myself.”
EXAMINER CHECKLIST
1. Confirms surgical criteria from the decision tree
2. Confirms cause-related therapy completed first
3. Consents for recession and possible failure
4. Flap design preserving keratinised tissue
5. Complete granulation tissue removal
6. Names mechanical, chemical and laser decontamination
7. Correctly classifies the defect
8. Selects reconstructive therapy with justification, and states the resective alternative
9. Post-operative regimen
10. 3–5 monthly supportive therapy and a referral judgement
Running this station to time
Time check. The model answer is 496 words, 3 minutes 32 seconds at 140 words per minute — and the
surgery itself, which is the part candidates enjoy, carries three of the ten marks. The other seven sit before
it (criteria, cause-related therapy, consent) and after it (post-operative regimen, supportive therapy, the
referral judgement). Roughly 150 words must go, and they go from the surgical narrative: one clause
per step of the operation, so that the entry criteria at the start and the referral judgement at the end both
survive.
