“First, do the criteria for surgery actually exist? The ITI decision tree specifies persistent suppuration
and/or bleeding on probing with probing depths of 6 millimetres or more, after non-surgical therapy
and re-assessment at about a month. If that is the case here, surgery is indicated.
And second, has cause-related therapy really been done? I would check rather than assume: risk factors
modified — smoking, glycaemic control, periodontal disease treated in the rest of the mouth; the prosthe-
sis assessed and modified or replaced so it can actually be cleaned; and any residual cement removed.
If the crown is over-contoured and I cannot get a brush under it, no amount of surgery on the bone will
hold.
Consent, and it has to be specific. She must be told to expect soft tissue recession, and that metal or
threads may become visible afterwards; what it costs; that treatment may not arrest the disease; and
that the implant may still have to be removed in the end. That conversation is recorded.
The surgery. Local anaesthesia and antiseptic preparation. A full-thickness mucoperiosteal flap with
intrasulcular incisions, relieving incisions where I need access, preserving as much keratinised tissue
as I possibly can — I will want it at closure. Then complete removal of the inflamed granulation tissue
with curettes, right down into the defect, because until it is out I cannot see the defect morphology and I
cannot make the next decision.
Decontamination of the exposed implant surface. Mechanically with a titanium brush or ultrasonic
tips; chemically with saline, chlorhexidine or hydrogen peroxide; and/or Er:YAG laser irradiation. I
would say honestly that no single method has been shown to be clearly superior — the aim is thorough
removal of biofilm and calculus without unnecessary damage to the surface.
Now the defect decides the treatment. This is a circumferential intrabony defect — a Type 1 CID
in the ITI classification. The tree indicates that defects with an intrabony component are suitable for
reconstructive therapy: a bone graft or substitute, with or without a membrane, and with or without a
soft tissue graft. Had it instead been a supracrestal or combined semicircular defect in a non-aesthetic
site, the indication would be resective — bone recontouring, implantoplasty and an apically positioned
flap — and I would not attempt to reconstruct a defect that has no walls to hold the graft.
Then adequate flap adaptation and tension-free closure.
Post-operatively: chlorhexidine, analgesia, peri-operative systemic antimicrobials where indicated, no
brushing over the site, and review at one week.
And then the part that determines whether any of this lasts: supportive therapy every 3 to 5 months,
with professional biofilm removal and reinforcement of hygiene, and a new baseline radiograph taken at
healing against which I judge stability from then on.
One thing I would say plainly. Surgical management of peri-implantitis — and reconstructive therapy
especially — is Complex. Unless I had specific training and experience in it, I would refer for this surgical
phase, having done the diagnosis, the risk factor control, the prosthesis assessment and the cause-related

osce.title: Implantoplasty
osce.text:
OSCE 40 — Implantoplasty
Blueprint: management of compromised outcomes (W + SCE).
EQUIPMENT
a model with an implant with exposed threads; diamond and tungsten carbide burs, polishers, high-volume suction, rubber
dam.
CANDIDATE INSTRUCTIONS
Describe and demonstrate implantoplasty on this exposed implant surface.
MODEL ANSWER
“Indication: exposed, roughened implant threads in a non-aesthetic site with a supracrestal or com-
bined defect that cannot be reconstructed, where the aim is to render the exposed surface smooth
and less plaque-retentive so that the patient can maintain it.
Contraindications: the aesthetic zone, where the metal will show; a narrow implant, where re-
moving surface material risks weakening it to the point of fracture; and defects with an intrabony
component that could be reconstructed instead.
Technique: 1. Flap access with granulation tissue removed and the defect visualised. 2. Protect the
surrounding tissues — this is the critical step. I would use a rubber dam sheet or gauze packed
around the site to catch titanium particles, and high-volume suction held immediately at the bur,
with copious water coolant. 3. Reduce the exposed threads with a fine-grit diamond or a tungsten
carbide bur under copious irrigation, working with light pressure, following the contour of the
implant and avoiding notching. 4. Progressively polish with silicone polishers and polishing paste
until the surface is smooth to a probe — the smoother the better, since surface roughness is exactly
what I am trying to eliminate. 5. Irrigate copiously, remove the protective packing carefully with
the particles it has caught, and inspect. 6. Apically position the flap so the smoothed surface is
accessible for cleaning, and close.
Cautions to state: loss of implant diameter reduces fracture resistance, particularly in narrow im-
plants; titanium particles disseminated into the tissues are a recognised concern; and heat generation
must be controlled with irrigation. Implantoplasty does not regenerate bone — it is a resective,
maintenance-enabling procedure.

Afterwards: hygiene instruction with an interdental brush that can reach the newly accessible sur-
face, and 3- to 5-monthly supportive care.”
EXAMINER CHECKLIST
1. States indication (non-aesthetic, non-reconstructable)
2. States contraindications including narrow implants and aesthetic sites
3. Flap access and granulation removal
4. Tissue protection against titanium particles
5. High-volume suction at the bur
6. Appropriate burs with copious irrigation
7. Progressive polishing to a smooth finish
8. Irrigation and removal of debris
9. Apically positioned flap for access
10. States the limitations, and the maintenance regime
Running this station to time
Time check. The model answer is 401 words, 2 minutes 52 seconds at 140 words per minute — but the
verb is describe and demonstrate, and the demonstration alone (packing the site, holding the suction at
the bur, reducing, then the whole polishing sequence) needs two of the five minutes. Roughly 120 words
must go, and they go by stating the indication and each contraindication in a single clause so that the
tissue-protection step gets the time the checklist gives it.

“The indication first. Implantoplasty is for exposed, roughened threads in a non-aesthetic site, where
the defect is supracrestal or combined and cannot be reconstructed. I am not growing bone back — I am
turning a plaque-retentive surface into one the patient can actually clean.
And where I would not do it. Not in the aesthetic zone, because I will expose grey metal under thin
mucosa. Not on a narrow implant, because I am removing diameter from something already slender
and I risk fracturing it. And not where there is a contained intrabony component that would respond
to regeneration — I would reconstruct that rather than grind it away. I should be clear about the limit:
resective peri-implantitis surgery is Advanced on the SAC classification. I would do this in a posterior
site in a patient whose disease I had already controlled, and I would refer an aesthetic-zone case, or a
combined defect needing regeneration, rather than start it.

every scrap of granulation tissue removed first. Grinding on top of granulation tissue achieves nothing
and drives particles into it.
Now the step that matters most — protection. Before any bur turns I pack the site with a rubber dam
sheet or gauze, right round the implant and into the flap, so the titanium swarf is caught rather than
scattered. I have high-volume suction held at the bur tip, not resting in the cheek, and copious water
coolant running throughout.

ing the contour of the implant so I do not notch it and create a stress riser. Water the whole time: I am
cutting titanium, and the heat goes straight into bone.
Then polishing, which is not the optional bit. Progressively finer silicone polishers and polishing paste,
until the surface is smooth to a probe drawn over it. A half-polished surface is rougher than the machined
implant I started with, so a rushed finish makes the problem worse rather than better.
Clearing up. Copious irrigation, then I lift the packing out carefully with the particles it has trapped,
irrigate again, and inspect the field under suction before I close.
Closure. The flap is apically positioned, not replaced coronally — the entire point is that the smoothed
surface is reachable with an interdental brush. Burying it defeats the procedure.
The honest limitations. I have reduced the diameter, and therefore the fracture resistance, of the im-
plant. Titanium particles disseminated into the tissues are a recognised concern — which is exactly why
I packed and suctioned. Heat generation must be controlled by irrigation. And implantoplasty does not
regenerate bone: it is resective and maintenance-enabling, nothing more.

osce.title: Explantation
osce.text:
OSCE 41 — Explantation
Blueprint: recognise compromised outcomes and suggest appropriate management (W + SCE).
EQUIPMENT
a model with an integrated implant; counter-torque device, piezo tips, trephines of various diameters.
CANDIDATE INSTRUCTIONS
This implant must be removed. Describe the techniques available and select one, explaining your reasoning.
MODEL ANSWER
“First, confirm the decision. Removal is indicated for mobility, implant fracture, progressive bone
loss unresponsive to treatment, uncontrollable infection, bone loss beyond roughly half to two-thirds
of the implant length, or a malposition that makes a cleansable, restorable prosthesis impossible. In
the ITI framework, this is the point at which it becomes ‘irrational to keep’ the implant.
Techniques, from least to most destructive:
1. Counter-torque (reverse-torque) device. A driver engages the internal connection and applies
increasing anticlockwise torque — many devices generate 200 Ncm or more — until the implant
unscrews. This is my first choice because it removes the implant with almost no bone loss, which
is everything if the site is to be reconstructed. It works best where there is some bone loss already;
a fully integrated implant in dense bone may resist it, and there is a risk of fracturing the implant
or stripping the connection.
2. Piezo-surgery with fine tips used circumferentially in the interface, which is bone-sparing and
avoids damage to adjacent roots and soft tissue, though it is slower.
3. Trephine of the smallest diameter that will pass around the implant, used with copious irrigation.
This is the most destructive, since it sacrifices a cylinder of surrounding bone, and it also generates
significant heat.
4. Sectioning and elevation where a fractured implant cannot be engaged.
Selection here: I would attempt counter-torque first, escalating to piezo and only then to a trephine.

Afterwards: thorough debridement of all granulation tissue, irrigation, and assessment of the resid-
ual defect. Then either allow 6 to 8 weeks of soft tissue healing before staged grafting, or graft
immediately if the defect is contained. Provide an interim prosthesis — ideally a bonded pontic
rather than a denture, so nothing presses on the site.
Consent must cover: possible fracture of the implant during removal; the extent of bone loss and the
likely need for grafting; the time to reconstruction; the possibility that a new implant is not possible;
and the costs. In the aesthetic zone, explantation with ridge reconstruction is Complex, and I would
refer.”
EXAMINER CHECKLIST
1. Confirms the indication and uses the “irrational to keep” framing
2. Counter-torque as first choice with reasoning
3. States its limitations
4. Piezo-surgery as second line
5. Trephine described with its cost in bone and heat
6. Sectioning for fractured implants
7. Debridement and defect assessment
8. Healing/grafting timeline
9. Interim prosthesis avoiding pressure
10. Consent points and a referral judgement
Running this station to time
Time check. The model answer is 462 words, 3 minutes 18 seconds at 140 words per minute — so the
words fit, and that is precisely the trap. The verb is describe and select, and the marks do not stop when
the implant comes out: checklists 7 to 10 are debridement, timing, the interim prosthesis, consent and the
referral judgement. Give each technique one sentence and its cost in bone, and spend the spare ninety
seconds on what happens afterwards.

“Before I remove anything, I confirm it should come out. Removal is indicated for mobility, implant
fracture, progressive bone loss that has not responded to treatment, uncontrollable infection, bone
loss beyond roughly half to two-thirds of the implant length, or a malposition that makes a cleansable,
restorable prosthesis impossible. In the ITI framework, this is the point at which the implant becomes
‘irrational to keep’ — the treatment has stopped being worth its own morbidity.
Then I choose the least destructive technique that will work, because the bone I leave behind is the
bone I have to rebuild in.
My first choice is a counter-torque device. A driver engages the internal connection and applies increas-
ing anticlockwise torque — many devices generate 200 Ncm or more — until the implant unscrews. I
choose it because it removes the implant with almost no bone loss at all, and if this site is going to be
reconstructed, that is the whole game.
Its limitations, and I would state them before the examiner asks. It works best where there is already
some bone loss to reduce the integrated surface area. A fully integrated implant in dense bone may
simply resist it, and the forces involved risk fracturing the implant or stripping the internal connection
— at which point I have lost my engagement and my options narrow.
If counter-torque fails, I escalate — piezo-surgery second. Fine tips used circumferentially in the bone–
implant interface, which is bone-sparing and avoids damaging adjacent roots and soft tissue. It is slower,
and I accept that.
A trephine is third and last, and I say why. The smallest diameter that will pass around the implant,
under copious irrigation — because it sacrifices a cylinder of surrounding bone and generates signifi-
cant heat, and heat necrosis compounds the defect I am about to graft. It is the technique I use when the
others have failed, not the one I reach for first.
And where the implant is fractured and cannot be engaged at all, sectioning and elevation.

osce.title: Free gingival graft
osce.text:
OSCE 42 — Free gingival graft
Blueprint: soft tissue augmentation materials and techniques (W + SCE).
EQUIPMENT
a model with an implant site lacking keratinised mucosa; blades, template material, sutures, palatal stent.
CANDIDATE INSTRUCTIONS
This implant site has 1 mm of keratinised mucosa. Describe how you would perform a free gingival graft.
MODEL ANSWER
“Indication: to increase the width of keratinised mucosa to at least 2 mm, which is associated with
less plaque, less inflammation, less recession and greater comfort during brushing. It is the most
predictable procedure for that purpose — a connective tissue graft is for thickness and aesthetics,
not primarily for width.
Recipient site preparation: 1. Anaesthetise. Make a horizontal incision at the mucogingival junc-
tion, then a partial-thickness (split-thickness) dissection apically, leaving the periosteum intact

on the bone — the periosteum is the vascular bed on which the graft will survive. 2. Remove or
apically suture any mobile muscle fibres and loose tissue so the bed is immobile. 3. Make a template
of the recipient bed in sterile foil or paper.
Donor site: 4. From the palate, between the distal of the canine and the mesial of the first molar,
staying at least 2 mm from the gingival margin and superficial enough to avoid the greater palatine
bundle — a shallow vault reduces the safe zone. 5. Outline with the template and harvest a graft
of uniform thickness, typically 1 to 1.5 mm, epithelialised. 6. Remove any fatty or glandular tissue
from the deep surface.
Placement: 7.
Transfer immediately, keep it moist in saline, and adapt it precisely to the bed.
8. Suture with fine (5/0 or 6/0) sutures at the coronal margin, plus peripheral and cross-over
(compressive) sutures to hold the graft immobile against the periosteum. Immobility is what
determines survival, since the graft initially survives by plasmatic circulation before revascularising
at around 3 to 5 days.
Donor site care: 9. Haemostatic dressing and a pre-made palatal stent or vacuum-formed plate,
since the donor site heals by secondary intention and is the most uncomfortable part of the procedure
for most patients.
Post-operative: no brushing over the graft, chlorhexidine, soft diet, no denture over the site, analge-
sia, warning about donor-site bleeding, and review at one week.
Limitations to state: poor colour and texture match producing a visible ‘patch’, which is why it
is generally avoided in the aesthetic zone; primary contraction of about 25 to 45%; and donor-site
morbidity.”
EXAMINER CHECKLIST
1. States the indication is KM width
2. Distinguishes from CTG
3. Split-thickness bed leaving periosteum
4. Immobilises the bed
5. Template used
6. Correct donor site and avoidance of the greater palatine bundle
7. Appropriate graft thickness and de-fatting
8. Immobilisation sutures and the plasmatic circulation rationale
9. Palatal stent and donor care
10. States limitations including colour mismatch and contraction
Running this station to time
Time check. The model answer is 470 words, 3 minutes 21 seconds at 140 words per minute — but it is
built as nine numbered steps across three sites, and a candidate who narrates every step at equal weight
will run to six minutes and finish somewhere in the palate. Around 120 words have to go, and they go
by giving each step a clause and reserving whole sentences for the three that carry the biology — the
intact periosteal bed, the immobilisation sutures, and the greater palatine bundle.

osce.title: Subepithelial connective tissue graft
osce.text:
OSCE 43 — Subepithelial connective tissue graft
Blueprint: soft tissue augmentation; gingival biotype influence (W + SCE).

EQUIPMENT
model, blades, sutures, palatal model.
CANDIDATE INSTRUCTIONS
Describe how you would harvest and place a subepithelial connective tissue graft to thicken the buccal tissue at an implant
site.
MODEL ANSWER
“Indication: to increase soft tissue thickness and improve contour, colour stability and the position
of the mucosal margin — phenotype modification. Best performed at implant placement or at
second stage, rather than after the definitive crown is fitted.
Recipient site: a split-thickness envelope or pouch created from an intrasulcular or a small crestal
incision, extended beyond the defect in all directions, with no vertical releasing incisions if possible
so that blood supply is maximal. If coverage is also required, a coronally advanced flap with de-
epithelialised papillae.
Donor site — two common techniques: - Single-incision technique: one horizontal incision about
2 mm apical to the gingival margin, parallel to the long axes of the teeth; a split-thickness dissection
creates a pouch; the connective tissue is then dissected free from within and delivered through the
single incision. Primary closure of the donor site is achieved, which gives less pain and better healing.
- Trapdoor technique: parallel horizontal incisions with a flap raised, the graft harvested beneath,
and the flap replaced.
Boundaries: between the distal of the canine and the mesial of the first molar; stay superficial to the
greater palatine bundle; take a graft of 1 to 2 mm thickness; avoid the rugae anteriorly, which are
thin and irregular.
Placement: transfer immediately, keep moist, position over the defect, and secure with sling sutures
around the implant or the adjacent teeth, plus peripheral sutures, so it is immobile. Advance the
overlying flap coronally without tension.
Prosthetic support: modify the provisional to a concave subgingival contour so it does not push
the tissue apically during healing.
Donor care: haemostatic dressing, palatal stent, and warning about discomfort and bleeding.
Post-operative: no brushing, chlorhexidine, soft diet, no trauma to the site, and review at 1 and 2
weeks with sutures removed at 10 to 14 days.
Honest limitations: around implants, coverage procedures are considerably less predictable than
around teeth; complete coverage of a buccally positioned implant is unlikely, though thickening the
tissue and arresting further recession is achievable.”
EXAMINER CHECKLIST
1. States the indication is thickness/phenotype
2. States optimal timing
3. Split-thickness envelope preferred, minimal releasing incisions
4. Describes single-incision or trapdoor harvest
5. Correct donor boundaries and bundle avoidance
6. Appropriate graft thickness
7. Immediate transfer, kept moist
8. Sling and peripheral sutures for immobility
9. Concave provisional contour
10. Donor care and honest statement of predictability around implants
Running this station to time
Time check. The model answer is 445 words, 3 minutes 11 seconds at 140 words per minute — but two
harvest techniques are described in full, and candidates who narrate both blade by blade arrive at the
sutures with a minute left. Around 100 words have to go: describe the single-incision harvest properly
and reduce the trapdoor to a single contrasting clause, then spend what is saved on checklists 8, 9 and
10 — immobility, the provisional contour, and the honest statement about predictability round implants.

— the prosthetic step candidates forget
entirely. Donor care: haemostatic
dressing, palatal stent, warning about
discomfort and bleeding. Post-operative:
no brushing, chlorhexidine, soft diet,
review at 1 and 2 weeks, sutures out at
10 to 14 days. Then the honesty mark:
coverage procedures around implants
are considerably less predictable than
around teeth; complete coverage of a
buccally positioned implant is unlikely
— thickening the tissue and arresting
further recession is achievable. And the
scope clause: in the aesthetic zone this
is Advanced to Complex, and I would
refer.
The compressed answer — what a strong candidate says in five minutes
“The indication is thickness, not width. I am modifying the phenotype — increasing soft tissue thickness
to improve contour, colour stability and the position and long-term stability of the mucosal margin. If
I wanted width of keratinised mucosa, I would be describing a free gingival graft instead.
Timing matters as much as technique. This is best done at implant placement or at second stage, while
the site is still open and the tissue can be positioned. Doing it after the definitive crown is fitted is the
least favourable moment — the architecture is set, access is poor and the result is unpredictable.
Recipient site. I raise a split-thickness envelope or pouch from an intrasulcular or small crestal incision,
extended beyond the defect in all directions so the graft is fully enclosed by vascular tissue. I avoid
vertical releasing incisions if I possibly can, because they cut across the blood supply to the very flap
that has to nourish the graft. If I also need coverage, then a coronally advanced flap with de-epithelialised
papillae.
Harvest — I would use the single-incision technique. One horizontal incision about 2 mm apical to
the gingival margin, parallel to the long axes of the teeth; a split-thickness dissection creating a pouch;
then the connective tissue is dissected free from within and delivered out through that single incision.
The advantage is that the donor site closes primarily, which means less pain and better healing — and
palatal pain is what patients remember. The alternative is the trapdoor technique — parallel horizontal
incisions, a flap raised, the graft harvested beneath and the flap replaced.
Boundaries, and I would state them before I cut. Between the distal of the canine and the mesial of the
first molar. Superficial enough to stay clear of the greater palatine bundle — and a shallow vault brings
it closer. A graft 1 to 2 mm thick. And anteriorly I avoid the rugae, where the tissue is thin, irregular and
of poor quality.
Placement. Transfer immediately, keep it moist, and position it over the defect so it is completely covered.
Then sling sutures around the implant or the adjacent teeth, plus peripheral sutures, so the graft is
immobile — it has no blood supply of its own for the first days and any movement destroys the vessels
that are forming. And I advance the overlying flap coronally without tension; a flap under tension will
dehisce and expose the graft.
Then the prosthetic step that is routinely forgotten. I modify the provisional to a concave subgingival
contour. An over-contoured, convex provisional will press the tissue I have just thickened straight back
apically during healing, and I will have done the operation for nothing.
Donor care: haemostatic dressing, a palatal stent, and an honest warning about discomfort and bleeding.
Post-operatively: no brushing over the site, chlorhexidine, soft diet, no trauma, review at one and two
weeks, sutures removed at 10 to 14 days.
And I would be honest about what this achieves, because the consent depends on it. Around teeth, root
coverage with a connective tissue graft is highly predictable. Around implants it is considerably less so —
the tissue attaches differently, there is no cementum or periodontal ligament to support coronal migration,
and complete coverage of a buccally positioned implant is unlikely. What I can realistically offer is
thicker tissue, better contour and colour, and arrest of further recession. If the implant is malpositioned,

osce.title: Chairside pick-up of overdenture attachments
osce.text:
OSCE 44 — Chairside pick-up of overdenture attachments
Blueprint: fitting a prosthesis; laboratory techniques; deliver a satisfactory restoration (OS-P).
EQUIPMENT
an edentulous mandibular model with two implant analogues and stud abutments; a denture, autopolymerising acrylic,
block-out spacers, handpiece and burs, articulating paper.
CANDIDATE INSTRUCTIONS
Pick up these two stud attachment housings into this denture chairside. Describe each step.
MODEL ANSWER
“First I check the prerequisites: the implants are osseointegrated and the peri-implant tissues are
healthy; the abutments are the correct height so the housing sits at the level of the mucosa without
impinging; and the denture is otherwise satisfactory — extension, occlusion, vertical dimension
and fit. If the denture is not satisfactory, I would remake it rather than commit attachments to a
poor prosthesis.
Steps: 1. Torque the stud abutments to the manufacturer’s value. 2. Place the black processing
inserts (or equivalent) in the metal housings and seat the housings on the abutments. 3. Place
block-out spacers — the white rubber washers or equivalent — around the base of each abutment,
so acrylic cannot flow into the undercut beneath the housing. This is the step most often omitted,
and omitting it locks the denture on. 4. Relieve the fit surface of the denture generously over
each housing until it seats fully with clearance all round, verified with pressure-indicating paste.
Also create a small vent hole through the lingual flange for each housing so excess acrylic and air
can escape. 5. Check the denture seats fully and the occlusion is correct with the housings in
place, before adding any acrylic. 6. Apply a little petroleum jelly to the mucosa and to the patient’s
lips. 7. Mix autopolymerising acrylic to a flowable consistency, place a small amount into each
recess in the denture — not onto the housings — seat the denture, and have the patient close into
their normal occlusion and hold, gently, without biting hard, until set. The occlusion, not finger

pressure, positions the denture. 8. Remove the denture with the housings captured, and inspect.
9. Remove the block-out spacers, trim and polish the excess acrylic, ensure no sharp edges and no
acrylic inside the housing. 10. Replace the processing inserts with the definitive retention inserts
of the appropriate strength — I would start with the lowest retention and increase only if the patient
wants more. 11. Re-seat, re-check the occlusion and the extension, and confirm the patient can
insert and remove the denture themselves — and have them demonstrate it. 12. Instructions: how
to clean around the abutments with a single-tufted brush, how to clean the housings, that inserts
wear and will need replacing, and that the denture will need relining as the ridge resorbs. Record
the abutment heights, insert type and torque values.”
EXAMINER CHECKLIST
1. Confirms prerequisites and denture quality
2. Torques abutments correctly
3. Processing inserts in housings
4. Block-out spacers placed
5. Denture relieved and vented, verified with pressure paste
6. Occlusion checked before acrylic
7. Patient closes into occlusion to seat
8. Trims, polishes, removes spacers
9. Definitive inserts selected, starting with lowest retention
10. Patient demonstrates insertion/removal; hygiene and maintenance instructions; records
Running this station to time
Time check. The model answer is 521 words, 3 minutes 43 seconds at 140 words per minute — and the
verb is pick up, so twelve steps have to be performed while they are described, and hands are slower than
speech. Roughly 170 words must go, and they go by narrating each step in a clause as the hands do
it, keeping whole sentences for the two omissions that ruin the denture: the block-out spacers and the
generous relief.
The five-minute run sheet

The examiner does
What earns the mark

Checklists 1 and 2, before any component

Then the judgement that earns the mark:

Silence. Watches the hands.
Checklists 3 and 4 — the pass/fail pair.
Black processing inserts placed in the
metal housings, housings seated on the

block-out spacers — the rubber washers
— around the base of each abutment, so

beneath the housing. The candidate

in the undercut locks the denture onto

“Carry on.”
Checklists 5 and 6. Relieve the fit surface
generously over each housing with an
acrylic bur until the denture seats fully
with clearance all round, and verify
with pressure-indicating paste — not by
eye. Cut a small vent hole through the
lingual flange over each housing so
excess acrylic and air escape rather than
lifting the denture. Then, before any
acrylic is mixed: seat the denture and
check the occlusion with the housings
in place. Acrylic added to a denture that
is not seating, or that is now propped
open, sets the error permanently.
2:45–3:45
Hands over the acrylic.
Checklist 7, and the technique detail is
the mark. Petroleum jelly to the mucosa
and the patient’s lips.
Autopolymerising acrylic mixed to a
flowable consistency, a small amount
placed into each recess in the denture
— not onto the housings. Seat the
denture and have the patient close into
their normal occlusion and hold gently,
without biting hard, until set. Said
explicitly: the occlusion positions the
denture, not finger pressure — finger
pressure seats it crooked and locks in a
rocking base.
3:45–5:00
“It has set. Finish the job and tell the
patient what they need to know.”
Checklists 8, 9 and 10. Remove the
denture with the housings captured;
inspect; remove the block-out spacers;
trim and polish the excess; no sharp
edges and no acrylic inside the housing.
Then replace the processing inserts
with the definitive retention inserts —
starting with the lowest retention and
increasing only if the patient wants
more. Re-seat, re-check the occlusion
and the extension, and have the patient
insert and remove the denture
themselves in front of you. Then
instructions and records: single-tufted
brush around each abutment, cleaning
the housings, inserts wear and need
replacing, the denture will need
relining as the ridge resorbs; record
abutment heights, insert type and
torque values, and set a review.
The compressed answer — what a strong candidate says in five minutes
“Before I commit anything to this denture I check three things. That the implants are integrated and
the peri-implant tissues are healthy; that the abutments are the correct height, so each housing sits at
the level of the mucosa without impinging on it; and that the denture itself is satisfactory — extension,
fit, occlusion and vertical dimension. If the denture is not good, I remake it. There is no point building
retention into a prosthesis that is already wrong; I will simply have made the patient’s problem harder to
take out.
First I torque the stud abutments to the manufacturer’s value for this system, which I confirm rather
than remember.
Then the housings. I place the black processing inserts in the metal housings and seat the housings on
the abutments. The processing insert is a working part, not the final one.
Then the step this station is really about. I place block-out spacers — the rubber washers — around
the base of each abutment, so that acrylic cannot run into the undercut beneath the housing. This is
the step most commonly omitted, and omitting it locks the denture onto the abutments. If that happens
I am cutting a patient’s new overdenture off their implants at the fit appointment.
Now the denture. I relieve the fit surface generously over each housing with an acrylic bur — consid-
erably more than looks necessary — until the denture seats fully with clearance all round, and I verify

that with pressure-indicating paste rather than trusting my eye. I also cut a small vent hole through
the lingual flange over each housing, so excess acrylic and trapped air can escape instead of lifting the
denture off the ridge.
Then I check the occlusion, with the housings in place, before any acrylic is mixed. If the denture is
propped open by an unrelieved housing, adding acrylic makes that permanent.
Petroleum jelly to the mucosa and to the patient’s lips, because autopolymerising acrylic is unpleasant on
soft tissue and worse on a moustache.
Then the pick-up. I mix autopolymerising acrylic to a flowable consistency and place a small amount
into each recess in the denture — into the denture, not onto the housing. I seat the denture and ask
the patient to close gently into their normal occlusion and hold, without biting hard, until it sets. The
occlusion positions the denture, not my fingers. If I hold it with finger pressure I will seat it off the ridge
and lock in a rock.
When it has set I remove the denture with the housings captured and inspect it. I remove the block-out
spacers, trim and polish the excess acrylic, and make sure there are no sharp edges and no acrylic inside
the housing — acrylic in the housing means the insert will not seat and the retention will be wrong.
Then I exchange the processing inserts for the definitive retention inserts. I start with the lowest
retention available and increase only if the patient wants more. A patient who cannot get their denture
out will not persevere with it, and it is far easier to add retention later than to explain why they cannot
manage.
Then I re-seat, re-check the occlusion and the extension, and I put the denture in the patient’s own
hands — they insert it and remove it in front of me until they can do it reliably.
Instructions. How to clean around each abutment with a single-tufted brush; how to clean the fit surface
and inside the housings; that the inserts wear and will need replacing as routine maintenance, not as a
failure; that the denture will need relining as the ridge resorbs; and to leave it out at night.
And I record the abutment heights, the insert type and the torque values applied, so that whoever sees
this patient next can order the right parts, and I set a maintenance review.”
Marking priority when the clock beats the candidate
Ask for these first (the six that carry the station): 4 block-out spacers placed, and why · 5 generous relief
and venting, verified with pressure paste · 7 patient closes into occlusion to seat, not finger pressure · 1
prerequisites, including remaking an unsatisfactory denture · 9 definitive inserts, lowest retention first ·
10 patient demonstrates insertion and removal; hygiene, maintenance and records.
Accept these late or on prompting: 2 abutments torqued to the manufacturer’s value · 3 processing inserts
in the housings · 6 occlusion checked before acrylic · 8 spacers removed, trimmed and polished.
The commonest way five minutes is wasted here: discussing attachment systems — locators versus balls
versus bars, retention values, resilience — when the instruction is pick up these two housings. That is a
viva answer in a performance station, and none of it is on the checklist. The second loss is silent hands:
candidates place the spacers and relieve the fit surface without a word, and an examiner cannot award
checklists 4 and 5 for something that was merely done. Say “block-out spacers, so acrylic cannot reach
the undercut” as the fingers place them. The third is finishing at the set: checklists 8, 9 and 10 are all
after the acrylic cures, and the definitive inserts and the patient’s own demonstration are worth more
than any amount of preamble.

osce.title: Adjusting and relining a denture over a surgical site
osce.text:
OSCE 45 — Adjusting and relining a denture over a surgical site
Blueprint: postoperative care; awareness of the difference in surgical management of the partially dentate and edentulous patient (OS-P + SCE).
EQUIPMENT
a partial denture, a model with a healing implant/graft site, pressure-indicating paste, acrylic burs, soft liner material.
CANDIDATE INSTRUCTIONS
This patient’s partial denture overlies an implant site grafted 48 hours ago. Adjust and reline it appropriately.
MODEL ANSWER
“The principle is that any pressure on a graft or a submerged implant causes micromotion, dehis-
cence and membrane exposure — denture pressure is one of the commonest causes of early graft
failure.
1. Confirm the patient has followed the instruction to leave the denture out for the first 24 to 48
hours.
2. Examine the site: wound apposition, any dehiscence or exposure, swelling.
3. Identify the pressure areas — seat the denture with pressure-indicating paste on the fit surface
and ask the patient to close gently; the paste shows where it contacts the surgical site.
4. Relieve generously with an acrylic bur — considerably more than seems necessary, because
swelling will change over the next few days. I would aim for clear space over the whole surgical
field, and I would rather the denture be under-extended and slightly loose than press on the
graft.
5. Re-check with paste until there is no contact over the site.
6. Reline the remainder of the fit surface with a soft (tissue conditioner) liner so the load is
distributed onto the sound, non-surgical areas — never a hard reline over a healing site.
7. Check the occlusion and relieve any heavy contact that would transmit load through the denture
onto the site.
8. Smooth and polish all adjusted surfaces so there are no sharp edges.
9. Instructions: wear as little as possible, particularly for the first two weeks; remove at night; clean
the denture and the liner daily with a soft brush and cold water, not hot water, which distorts
liners; and return immediately if it feels tight, rubs, or if anything appears through the gum.
10. Review at one week with the sutures, and plan to replace the soft liner every few weeks as healing
progresses.
Better still: where possible I would have provided a resin-bonded pontic rather than a denture
in the first place, since it removes the problem entirely — and in the aesthetic zone that is my
preference.”
EXAMINER CHECKLIST
1. States the biological rationale
2. Confirms 24–48 h denture-free period
3. Examines the wound
4. Pressure-indicating paste to locate contact
5. Generous relief anticipating swelling
6. Re-verifies with paste
7. Soft liner, not hard reline
8. Checks and adjusts the occlusion
9. Smooths and polishes
10. Instructions, review, liner replacement, and the bonded-pontic alternative
Running this station to time
Time check. The model answer is 454 words, 3 minutes 15 seconds at 140 words per minute — but the
verb is adjust and reline, so paste has to go on, a bur has to run, paste has to go on again and a liner has to
be mixed, all while it is explained. About 100 words must go, and they go by stating the rationale once,
in a sentence, and then narrating each adjustment in a clause as it is made — the biology is one mark,
and the hands earn six.

The five-minute run sheet
Time
The examiner does
What earns the mark

clear space over the whole surgical field,
and the explicit trade-off — I would
rather the denture were under-extended
and slightly loose than pressing on the
graft. Then re-check with paste, and
again, until there is no contact at all
over the site. Mark 6 is a separate mark
from mark 4: the verification has to
happen twice.

“And the rest of the fit surface?”

choice is the mark. Reline the remainder
of the fit surface with a soft liner — a
tissue conditioner — so that load is
distributed onto the sound,
non-surgical areas. Said explicitly: never
a hard reline over a healing site. Then
the occlusion: check it and relieve any
heavy contact, because load applied to
the occlusal surface is transmitted
through the denture base onto the site
regardless of how well the fit surface has
been relieved.

“Finish, and tell the patient what to do.”
Checklists 9 and 10. Smooth and polish
every adjusted surface so there are no
sharp acrylic edges against a healing flap.
Then instructions, specific: wear it as
little as possible, particularly for the
first two weeks; out at night; clean the
denture and the liner daily with a soft
brush and cold water — not hot water,
which distorts a liner; return
immediately if it feels tight, rubs, or if
anything appears through the gum.
Then review at one week with the
sutures, and replace the soft liner every
few weeks as healing progresses. Close
with the judgement mark: a
resin-bonded pontic would have
avoided the problem altogether, and in
the aesthetic zone that is my preference.

The compressed answer — what a strong candidate says in five minutes
“The principle governs everything I am about to do. Any pressure on a graft or a submerged implant
causes micromotion, dehiscence and membrane exposure — and denture pressure is one of the com-
monest causes of early graft failure. So my aim is not to make this denture fit well. It is to make sure it
does not touch the surgical site at all.
First I check she did as she was asked — that the denture was left out for the first 24 to 48 hours.
Then I examine the site before I examine the denture: the wound apposition, any dehiscence, whether
membrane or graft is exposed, the degree of swelling, and the sutures.
Then I find the pressure areas properly. I put pressure-indicating paste on the fit surface, seat the
denture and ask her to close gently — gently, because a firm bite gives me a reading I have created. I take
it out and read where the paste has been displaced: that is where the denture is loading the surgical
field, and it is almost always more extensive than it looks.
Then I relieve, and I relieve generously. With an acrylic bur, considerably more than seems necessary
— because the swelling will change over the next few days, and relief that is just adequate today will be
pressure tomorrow. I aim for clear space over the whole surgical field. And I would say plainly: I would
far rather this denture were under-extended and a little loose for a fortnight than have it pressing on
the graft. A loose denture is an inconvenience; an exposed membrane is a failed graft and a lost site.
Then I check my work with the paste again, and I repeat it until there is no contact whatsoever over the
site.
Then the reline — and the material choice matters. I reline the remainder of the fit surface with a soft
liner, a tissue conditioner, so that the load is spread onto the sound, non-surgical areas and the denture
is stable without recruiting the graft. I would never place a hard reline over a healing site — it sets rigid
against tissue that is still changing shape, and it becomes a stamp on the graft.
Then the occlusion, which candidates forget. I check it and relieve any heavy or premature contact, be-
cause load applied to the teeth is transmitted straight through the base onto the ridge, however carefully
I have relieved the fit surface.
Then I smooth and polish everything I have adjusted. Raw, sharp acrylic against a healing flap will
ulcerate it.
Instructions, and they are as important as the adjustment. Wear it as little as you possibly can, espe-
cially for the first two weeks — for social situations and eating soft food, not all day. Leave it out at night.
Clean it and the liner daily with a soft brush and cold water — not hot water, which distorts the liner.
And come back immediately if it feels tight, if it rubs, or if you can see anything coming through the
gum. I would give that in writing with a number to ring.
Review at one week, with the sutures, and I would plan to replace the soft liner every few weeks as
healing and remodelling change the ridge — a liner left in place hardens, becomes colonised and stops
being soft.
And I would say what I would have preferred. Where the span allows, a resin-bonded pontic rather
than a denture removes this problem entirely — nothing rests on the site, nothing has to be relieved, and
there is nothing to relieve wrongly. In the aesthetic zone that is my routine choice, and I would plan it
before the surgery rather than adjusting a denture afterwards.
I would record the site findings, the areas relieved, the liner used, the occlusal adjustment, the instructions
given and the review interval.”
Marking priority when the clock beats the candidate
Ask for these first (the six that carry the station): 1 pressure causes micromotion, dehiscence and
membrane exposure · 4 pressure-indicating paste used to locate contact · 5 generous relief anticipating
swelling, loose accepted over loaded · 7 soft liner, never a hard reline · 8 occlusion checked and adjusted
· 10 instructions, review, liner replacement and the bonded-pontic alternative.
Accept these late or on prompting: 2 the 24–48 hour denture-free period confirmed · 3 the wound exam-
ined first · 6 re-verified with paste · 9 smoothed and polished.
The commonest way five minutes is wasted here: a lecture on guided bone regeneration and the biology
of membrane exposure, delivered while the denture sits untouched on the bench. The rationale is one
mark and one sentence; the other nine are paste, bur, paste, liner, occlusion, polish and instructions. The
second loss is timidity with the bur — a candidate who relieves conservatively and says “that should be
enough” fails checklist 5 outright, because the mark is specifically for over-relieving in anticipation of

osce.title: Shade taking and communication
osce.text:
OSCE 46 — Shade taking and communication
(Blueprint: prescribe an appropriate type of restoration from the laboratory; evaluate laboratory techniques.)
EQUIPMENT
shade guides (VITA classical and 3D-Master), a camera, a grey card, a model.
CANDIDATE INSTRUCTIONS
Take and communicate the shade for an upper central incisor implant crown.
MODEL ANSWER
“Timing and conditions first, because most shade errors are made here. - Take the shade early in
the appointment, before the teeth dehydrate — dehydrated enamel appears lighter and higher in
value, and can take 20 minutes or more to recover. - Use natural daylight or a colour-corrected light
source of about 5500 K; avoid the operating light. - Remove bright lipstick, ask the patient to remove
strongly coloured clothing or cover it with a grey bib, and work against a neutral background. - Have
the patient at eye level and view for 5 seconds at a time, resting the eye on a neutral grey between
comparisons to avoid fatigue.
Method: 1. Determine value (brightness) first — squint or defocus to compare brightness; then
chroma (saturation); then hue. The 3D-Master guide is designed for this sequence. 2. Select the
shade of the cervical, middle and incisal thirds separately, because a central incisor is rarely one
shade. 3. Note characterisation: translucency of the incisal third, mamelons, white spots, craze
lines, enamel cracks, surface texture, lustre, and any staining. 4. Record the stump shade — the
colour of the underlying abutment — because it determines the opacity and thickness of ceramic
required. This is essential with a titanium abutment.
Communication: 5. Photographs are the most valuable single tool: take images with the selected
shade tab held edge-to-edge in the same plane as the tooth, with a grey card in frame, at least one
polarised or cross-polarised image if available, and one with a black background for translucency.
Include a full-face and a smile view. 6. Written prescription with shade, stump shade, characterisa-
tion, texture and lustre instructions, and the shade guide system used. 7. Consider a custom shade
tab or, ideally, arrangement for the technician to see the patient — the most reliable method of all
for a single anterior unit. 8. If in doubt, request a bisque try-in so adjustments can be made before
glazing.
I would record the shade, the conditions and the guide used in the notes.”
EXAMINER CHECKLIST
1. Takes shade early, before dehydration
2. Correct lighting and neutral surroundings
3. Patient preparation and viewing technique
4. Value, then chroma, then hue
5. Records shade by thirds
6. Notes characterisation and surface texture
7. Records stump shade
8. Photographs with tab in plane, grey card, black background
9. Written prescription and technician contact/custom tab
10. Bisque try-in option; records conditions
Running this station to time
Time check. The model answer is 454 words, 3 minutes 15 seconds at 140 words per minute — comfortable
on paper, but this is a precision station and it is failed by vagueness, not by length. Nothing needs cutting;

what is needed is that every mark is carried by a specific number or a named condition — 5500 K, five
seconds, value then chroma then hue, thirds, stump shade, grey card, black background — rather than by
the phrase “I would take a careful shade”.

Natural daylight or a colour-corrected
source of about 5500 K; the operating
light off. Remove bright lipstick, cover
strongly coloured clothing with a grey
bib, neutral background, patient at eye
level. And the viewing technique: look
for 5 seconds at a time, resting the eye
on neutral grey between comparisons to
avoid retinal fatigue.
1:00–2:00
“Take it.”
Checklists 4 and 5 — the sequence, in the
right order and named. Value —
brightness — first, comparing by
squinting or defocusing, because the eye
discriminates brightness better than hue
at low resolution. Then chroma, the
saturation. Then hue. State that the
3D-Master guide is arranged for exactly
that sequence. Then mark 5: select
separately for the cervical, middle and
incisal thirds, because a central incisor
is never one shade. A single tab quoted
for the whole tooth loses two marks at
once.
2:00–2:50
“Anything else you would record?”
Checklists 6 and 7. Characterisation:
incisal translucency, mamelons, white
spots, craze lines, enamel cracks,
surface texture, lustre and staining —
recorded on a diagram, not in prose.
Then the mark candidates most often
miss entirely: the stump shade — the
colour of the underlying abutment —
because it determines the opacity and
thickness of ceramic the technician
must build. This is essential with a
titanium abutment, which will shine
grey through thin ceramic and thin
tissue.
2:50–4:00
“How do you communicate it?”
Checklists 8 and 9. Photographs are the
single most valuable tool, and the
technique is the mark: the selected tab
held edge-to-edge, in the same plane as
the tooth, a grey card in frame, at least
one polarised or cross-polarised image
if available, and one against a black
background for translucency, plus a
full-face and a smile view. Then the
written prescription: shade by thirds,
stump shade, characterisation, texture
and lustre, and the shade guide system
used — because a number means
nothing without the guide it came from.
And a custom shade tab, or ideally the
technician seeing the patient, which is
the most reliable method for a single
anterior unit.

Time
The examiner does
What earns the mark
4:00–5:00
“And if you are not confident?”
Checklist 10 and the records. Request a
bisque try-in, so shade, characterisation
and texture can be adjusted before
glazing — after glazing the options are
staining or a remake. Then record the
shade, the stump shade, the guide used,
the lighting conditions and the time of
day in the notes, so that if the crown
returns wrong the variables can be
traced, and any second attempt is made
under the same conditions. Tell the
patient the shade may be reviewed at
try-in.
The compressed answer — what a strong candidate says in five minutes
“The conditions first, because that is where shades are lost.
Timing. I take the shade at the start of the appointment, before the teeth dehydrate. Dehydrated enamel
goes lighter and higher in value, and it takes 20 minutes or more to recover — so a shade taken after
isolation is a shade taken from a tooth that no longer exists.
Light. Natural daylight or a colour-corrected source at about 5500 K. The operating light is off — it is too
bright and the wrong colour temperature.
Surroundings. Bright lipstick removed, strongly coloured clothing covered with a grey bib, and a neu-
tral background behind the patient. The patient sits at my eye level.
And the eye itself. I look for five seconds at a time and then rest my eye on neutral grey between
comparisons — hold a comparison longer than that and retinal fatigue shifts what I see.
Now the method, in a fixed order. Value first — brightness. I squint or defocus to compare, because
at low resolution the eye reads brightness far better than it reads hue, and value is the dimension that is
unforgivable to get wrong. Then chroma — the saturation. Then hue. The 3D-Master guide is built for
that sequence, which is why I prefer it here to the classical guide.
Then I stop treating the tooth as one colour. I select separately for the cervical, middle and incisal thirds
— a central incisor is a gradient, and one tab across the whole crown is how a technician is given an opaque,
flat, monolithic tooth.
Then characterisation, which is what makes the crown belong in the mouth: translucency of the incisal
third, mamelons, white spots, craze lines, enamel cracks, surface texture, lustre and any staining. I map
these on a diagram.
Then the stump shade — and this is the one that separates a tooth crown from an implant crown. I
record the colour of the underlying abutment, because it dictates the opacity and thickness of ceramic
the technician needs. With a titanium abutment this is essential: titanium under thin ceramic and a
thin phenotype shows as grey at the margin, and no amount of shade matching in the body of the crown
rescues it. If the stump shade is a problem, the answer is a ceramic abutment or a titanium base with a
ceramic superstructure, and that is a conversation to have now, not at fit.
Communication. Photographs are the most valuable single tool. I take images with the selected tab
held edge-to-edge, in the same plane as the tooth — a tab angled towards the light photographs as a
different colour. A grey card in frame for white balance. At least one polarised or cross-polarised image
to remove surface reflection and show the underlying dentine, and one against a black background to
show incisal translucency. Plus a full-face and a smile view, so the technician sees the tooth in the face it
has to sit in.
A written prescription with all of it: shade by thirds, the stump shade, the characterisation, texture and
lustre instructions, and — crucially — which shade guide system I used, because ‘A2’ and ‘2M2’ are not
interchangeable and a number without its guide is useless.
Best of all, for a single upper central, I would arrange either a custom shade tab or, ideally, for the
technician to see the patient directly. That is the most reliable method there is, and for a single anterior
unit next to a natural central it is worth the appointment.
And if there is any doubt, I request a bisque try-in, so shade, characterisation and surface texture can be
adjusted before glazing — once it is glazed my options are surface stain or a remake.

osce.title: Facebow and jaw registration for an implant case
osce.text:
OSCE 47 — Facebow and jaw registration for an implant case
Blueprint: role of jaw registration when restoring implants (W + SCE, examined practically).
EQUIPMENT
a facebow, a semi-adjustable articulator, record bases, wax rims, bite registration material.
CANDIDATE INSTRUCTIONS
Record a facebow and jaw registration for a patient having a full-arch implant-supported prosthesis planned.
MODEL ANSWER
“Why: without a facebow, casts are mounted arbitrarily and the arc of closure in the articulator does
not match the patient’s, so occlusal contacts developed in the laboratory will be wrong when the
prosthesis is fitted — particularly when the vertical dimension is being altered.
Facebow: 1. Explain to the patient and seat them upright with the head supported. 2. Locate and
mark the reference points — usually the two posterior points at the external auditory meati or the
condylar hinge axis, and an anterior reference point such as the orbitale or a point 43 mm from the
incisal edge, depending on the system. 3. Attach the bite fork to the maxillary arch with a thin,
rigid registration material recording only cusp tips — an over-thick fork record introduces error. 4.
Seat the earpieces or condylar rods, position the nasion relator or anterior reference pin, tighten the
clamps in the correct sequence without displacing the assembly, and check the bow is level and
symmetrical. 5. Remove as a unit and transfer to the articulator to mount the maxillary cast.
Jaw registration: 6. Use rigid, accurately fitting record bases — for a full-arch implant case, ideally
screwed to the implants or to multi-unit abutments, which eliminates the commonest source of
error, the displacement of a resilient mucosa or a flexible base. 7. Adjust the wax rim for lip support,
incisal level at rest and on smiling, the occlusal plane parallel to the interpupillary line anteriorly
and the ala-tragus line posteriorly, and the midline, marking each on the rim. 8. Establish the verti-
cal dimension: measure freeway space by the marks-and-gauge method with phonetic confirmation,
and adjust the rim so freeway space is about 2 to 4 mm. 9. Record the horizontal relationship in
centric relation, guiding the mandible gently, with the rims not in contact — use a low-viscosity
registration material or notches with a small amount of material, so the bases are not displaced. 10.
Verify by re-seating the record and checking it fits without rocking; take a second record and confirm
the two agree. 11. Record the shade, mould and any patient preferences, photograph the rim in
situ, and send with a full written prescription.”

EXAMINER CHECKLIST
1. Explains the purpose of the facebow
2. Correct reference points located and marked
3. Thin, rigid bite fork record
4. Correct assembly, levelling and tightening sequence
5. Rigid record bases, screwed to implants where possible
6. Rim adjusted for lip support, incisal level, occlusal plane, midline
7. Vertical dimension determined with freeway space measurement
8. Centric relation record with bases not displaced
9. Verified with a duplicate record
10. Shade, photographs and written prescription
Running this station to time
Time check. The model answer is 497 words, 3 minutes 33 seconds at 140 words per minute — but a
facebow has to be assembled, seated, levelled and tightened while it is explained, and then a whole jaw
registration follows it. Roughly 140 words must go, and they go by giving the purpose one sentence and
then naming each reference point, material and check in a clause as the hands reach for it. This is a
precision station: the marks are in the named points and the named materials, not in the theory.
The five-minute run sheet

The examiner does
What earns the mark

The examiner does
What earns the mark
1:50–2:50
“Now the jaw registration.”
Checklist 5, the heaviest mark in the
second half, and it is specific to implants.
Rigid, accurately fitting record bases —
and for a full-arch implant case, ideally
screwed to the implants or to multi-unit
abutments. The reason must be said: it
eliminates the commonest source of
error in registration, displacement of a
resilient mucosa or flexure of a poorly
fitting base. A candidate who describes
shellac bases on an edentulous ridge has
missed the point of the station. Then
checklist 6: the rim adjusted for lip
support, incisal level at rest and on
smiling, occlusal plane parallel to the
interpupillary line anteriorly and the
ala-tragus line posteriorly, and the
midline — each marked on the rim
rather than remembered.
2:50–4:00
“How do you determine the vertical and
horizontal relationships?”
Checklists 7 and 8. Vertical: measure
freeway space by the marks-and-gauge
method with phonetic confirmation,
and adjust the rim so freeway space is
about 2 to 4 mm. Horizontal: record in
centric relation, guiding the mandible
gently, with the rims not in contact —
using a low-viscosity registration
material, or notches with a small
amount of material, so that closing onto
the record does not displace the bases.
The phrase “rims not in contact” is
where the mark sits.
4:00–5:00
“Are you confident in that record?”
Checklists 9 and 10. Verify: re-seat the
record and check it fits without rocking,
then take a second, independent record
and confirm the two agree. A
registration taken once is unverified.
Then the transfer: record the shade,
mould and the patient’s preferences,
photograph the rim in situ, and send
everything with a full written
prescription — the articulator type and
settings, the reference points used, and
what is being asked for. Copy retained,
and the patient told what happens next.
The compressed answer — what a strong candidate says in five minutes
“Why a facebow at all. Without one, the maxillary cast is mounted arbitrarily in the articulator, so the arc
of closure on the instrument does not match the patient’s. Any occlusion developed in the laboratory
will then be wrong in the mouth — and the discrepancy grows with every millimetre I change the vertical
dimension, which in a full-arch implant case I always do. So this is not a formality; it is the reason the
prosthesis will need one occlusal adjustment rather than five.
Facebow. I explain it to the patient — it looks alarming — and seat them upright with the head supported.
Reference points, located and marked. Posteriorly, the external auditory meati with an earbow, or the
condylar hinge axis if the system uses one. Anteriorly, an orbitale pointer, or a point 43 mm from the
incisal edge, depending on the system I am using.
The bite fork. I attach it to the maxillary arch with a thin, rigid registration material that records cusp
tips only. An over-thick or soft fork record is the classic error — it flexes, the whole transfer rotates, and
the mounting is wrong from the start.
Then I assemble carefully. Seat the earpieces or condylar rods, position the nasion relator or anterior
reference pin, and tighten the clamps in the correct sequence — without displacing anything I have
already set. I check the bow is level and symmetrical, then remove it as a single unit and transfer it
straight to the articulator to mount the maxillary cast.
Jaw registration — and here the implant case differs from a denture case. I use rigid, accurately fitting
record bases, and for a full-arch implant case I want them screwed to the implants or to multi-unit

osce.title: Oral hygiene instruction for an implant patient
osce.text:
OSCE 48 — Oral hygiene instruction for an implant patient
Blueprint: identify appropriate maintenance care regimes; patient-centred maintenance programmes (W + SCE).
EQUIPMENT
a model with an implant crown, an implant bridge and an overdenture; a range of interdental brushes, single-tufted brush,
superfloss, powered brush, mirror.
CANDIDATE INSTRUCTIONS
Give this patient individualised oral hygiene instruction for their implant restorations.
MODEL ANSWER
“I would make this specific, demonstrated and checked, not generic.

First, assess: disclose plaque so the patient can see where it actually is; record a plaque score; assess
dexterity and whether they can reach the site; and ask what they currently use and when.
Then explain, briefly, why: ‘Implants don’t decay, but the gum and bone around them can get
infected in the same way as around teeth, and that’s the main reason implants are lost. The good
news is it’s almost entirely preventable with daily cleaning.’
Then instruct, site by site:
Single crown: a soft or powered toothbrush twice daily; and the important one — an interdental
brush sized to the space. I would try several sizes on the model and in the mouth, select the largest
that passes without forcing, and have the patient insert it themselves in the mirror while I watch.
A single-tufted brush angled into the sulcus around the emergence.
Implant bridge or splinted units: the same, plus superfloss or a floss threader passed under the
pontic and drawn buccolingually in a shoe-shine motion; interdental brushes through the embra-
sures where they fit.
Overdenture: remove the denture to clean; clean around each abutment with a single-tufted brush;
clean the fit surface of the denture, especially inside the housings, with a denture brush and mild
soap or denture cleaner; leave the denture out at night in water.
Adjuncts: a powered toothbrush is helpful, particularly with reduced dexterity; a water flosser can
help but does not replace mechanical interdental cleaning; chlorhexidine is for short-term use only,
not routine, because of staining and taste disturbance.
Then check: have the patient demonstrate everything back to me, correct their technique, disclose
again to show improvement, and give written instructions with the specific brush sizes noted.
Then set the recall: risk-based — 3 to 4 months for a patient with a history of periodontitis, smoking
or previous peri-implant disease; otherwise 6 months. I would record the sizes prescribed, the
advice given and the plaque score, so I can measure change at the next visit.”
EXAMINER CHECKLIST
1. Discloses and records a plaque score first
2. Assesses dexterity and current routine
3. Explains the rationale in plain language
4. Sizes an interdental brush to the site
5. Single-tufted brush technique
6. Superfloss under pontics
7. Overdenture-specific advice including housings
8. Correct advice on adjuncts and chlorhexidine
9. Patient demonstrates back; technique corrected
10. Written instructions with sizes, risk-based recall, and recorded baseline
Running this station to time
Time check. The model answer is 470 words, 3 minutes 21 seconds at 140 words per minute — but there
are three different prostheses on the model, brushes have to be tried and sized in real time, and the
patient has to demonstrate back. About 120 words must go, and the shape that makes it fit is a fixed
allocation: forty seconds per prosthesis, with the assessment, the check-back and the recall taking the
minutes at either end. This is a taught skill, not a talk.
The five-minute run sheet

Time
The examiner does
What earns the mark
0:00–0:50
Presents a model carrying an implant
crown, an implant bridge and an
overdenture, with interdental brushes of
several sizes, a single-tufted brush,
superfloss, a powered brush and a
mirror: “Give this patient individualised
oral hygiene instruction for their implant
restorations.”

before any advice. Disclose the plaque

0:50–1:50

Checklists 4 and 5 at the single crown,

1:50–2:35

— described as a movement, not as a
product. Interdental brushes through

honest addition that if a brush will not fit,
the prosthesis is not cleansable and that
is a design problem to be addressed, not
a hygiene failure to be blamed on the
patient.
2:35–3:20
“And the overdenture?”
Checklist 7, which is the one candidates
omit altogether. Take the denture out to
clean. Clean around each abutment
with a single-tufted brush. Clean the fit
surface of the denture, and especially
inside the housings, with a denture
brush and mild soap or a denture cleaner.
Leave it out at night, in water. The
housings are the specific mark: plaque
and debris inside them are invisible to
the patient and never mentioned by
candidates.

Time
The examiner does
What earns the mark
3:20–5:00
“Anything else, and when will you see
them?”
Checklists 8, 9 and 10. Adjuncts: a
powered brush, particularly with
reduced dexterity; a water flosser can
help but does not replace mechanical
interdental cleaning; chlorhexidine is
short-term only, not routine, because of
staining and taste disturbance. Then the
check that defines the station: the
patient demonstrates everything back,
technique is corrected, and the plaque
is disclosed again to show the
improvement. Then written instructions
with the specific brush sizes written on
them, a risk-based recall — 3 to 4
months with a history of periodontitis,
smoking or previous peri-implant
disease, otherwise 6 months — and the
sizes, advice and plaque score recorded,
so change can be measured next time.
The compressed answer — what a strong candidate says in five minutes
“I would not give any advice until I know what is actually happening, so I start by disclosing the plaque
— she sees it, I see it, and we are both looking at the same thing rather than at my opinion. I record a plaque
score as a baseline. Then I assess her dexterity and whether she can physically reach these sites, and I
ask what she uses now, how often, and in what order — because I am modifying a routine that already
exists, not issuing a new one.
Then, briefly, why. ‘Implants don’t decay, but the gum and bone around them can get infected in the same way as
around natural teeth, and that is the main reason implants are lost. The good news is it’s almost entirely preventable
with daily cleaning.’ That is the whole rationale, in the patient’s language.
Then I teach it, site by site, with the aids in her hand.
The single crown. A soft or powered toothbrush twice daily — and then the important one, an inter-
dental brush sized to this particular space. I try several sizes: the right one is the largest that passes
without forcing, and I find that by trying, not by guessing. Then I put it in her hand and have her insert
it herself, in the mirror, while I watch and correct the angle. I add a single-tufted brush angled into the
sulcus around the emergence profile, which is where the biofilm actually sits.
The bridge. The same, plus superfloss or a floss threader passed under the pontic and drawn back and
forth buccolingually — a shoe-shine motion, not a saw. Interdental brushes through the embrasures
wherever they fit. And if a brush will not fit anywhere, I say so: that is a prosthesis design problem, and
the answer is to modify or remake the restoration, not to ask her to try harder.
The overdenture. It comes out to be cleaned. Around each abutment with a single-tufted brush, fol-
lowing the contour. Then the denture itself — the fit surface, and especially inside the housings, with a
denture brush and mild soap or a denture cleaner, because debris inside a housing is invisible to her and
is exactly where the mucosa becomes inflamed. Out at night, stored in water.
Adjuncts, with honest limits. A powered toothbrush helps, particularly if dexterity is reduced. A water
flosser can be a useful addition but does not replace mechanical interdental cleaning — it is not a
substitute for the brush. And chlorhexidine is for short-term use only — a fortnight after surgery, or
during an acute episode — not routinely, because of staining and taste disturbance.
Then the part that turns advice into instruction. I have her demonstrate all of it back to me — the brush,
the tuft, the floss, the denture — and I correct the technique in her hand rather than describing it again.
Then I disclose a second time, so she can see the difference she has just made. If she cannot do it, the
answer is a different aid, not a louder explanation.
Then I write it down. Written instructions with the actual brush sizes on them, so she buys the right
ones and so the next clinician knows what was prescribed.
And I set a risk-based recall — 3 to 4 months if there is a history of periodontitis, smoking or previous
peri-implant disease, otherwise 6 months. I record the sizes prescribed, the advice given, that she
demonstrated it back, and the plaque score, so at the next visit I can measure whether any of this worked
rather than repeat it.”

osce.title: Taking a baseline periapical radiograph
osce.text:
OSCE 49 — Taking a baseline periapical radiograph
Blueprint: interpret radiographic findings; assess treatment outcomes and monitoring parameters (OS-P + SCE).
EQUIPMENT
a phantom head, film/sensor holders (paralleling), an X-ray set (may be non-functional), lead apron.
CANDIDATE INSTRUCTIONS
Take a baseline periapical radiograph of a newly restored implant at the LR6, describing your technique and justification.
MODEL ANSWER
“Justification first. A baseline radiograph at the fitting of the prosthesis is the reference against
which every future bone level measurement will be judged, and without it the 2017 diagnostic
criteria for peri-implantitis cannot be applied properly. I would record that justification in the notes,
and confirm that I am acting as referrer, IR(ME)R practitioner and operator, and that I am trained
to do so.
Technique — the paralleling technique, because reproducibility is the whole point: 1. Confirm
the patient’s identity, the site, and check for pregnancy where relevant. 2. Explain the procedure
and gain consent. 3. Select the correct holder with a beam-aiming device — a posterior mandibular
holder here — and assemble it with the sensor or film. 4. Position the sensor parallel to the long
axis of the implant, well away from the crown so the whole implant and the crestal bone on both
sides are included, using cotton wool rolls for comfort if needed. 5. Align the beam-aiming ring
so the central ray is perpendicular to both the sensor and the implant long axis. The key indicator
of correct angulation with an implant is that the implant threads appear crisp and symmetrical
on both sides — if the threads are blurred, the beam is not perpendicular and bone levels cannot
be measured reliably. 6. Use rectangular collimation, which reduces dose substantially compared
with a round collimator. 7. Select the correct exposure factors for the region and the patient. 8.
Ensure everyone else is outside the controlled area; expose. 9. Assess the image quality against the
practice’s quality assurance criteria. If it is non-diagnostic because of positioning, that is a justified
repeat — but repeated errors trigger a quality assurance review. 10. Report the whole image in
writing, measure the bone level mesially and distally relative to the implant shoulder or a known
reference such as the thread pitch, and record those measurements as the baseline. 11. Store the
image in the patient record, and note the settings and holder used so the view can be reproduced at
future reviews.

Future radiographs would be at one year, then only when clinically indicated — increased probing
depth, bleeding, suppuration or symptoms.”
EXAMINER CHECKLIST
1. Justification stated and recorded, with IR(ME)R roles
2. Identity, site, pregnancy check, consent
3. Correct paralleling holder and beam-aiming device
4. Sensor parallel to the implant long axis, whole implant and crest included
5. Beam perpendicular; crisp symmetrical threads as the quality criterion
6. Rectangular collimation
7. Correct exposure factors and radiation safety
8. Image quality assessment
9. Written report and recorded baseline measurements
10. Records settings for reproducibility and states the follow-up regime
Running this station to time
Time check. The model answer is 500 words, 3 minutes 34 seconds at 140 words per minute — but a
holder has to be assembled and positioned on a phantom head while it is described, and the marks at the
end are written ones. Roughly 140 words must go, and they go by compressing the regulatory preamble
into two sentences and giving each positioning step a clause, so that the last ninety seconds are free for
the report, the baseline measurements and the follow-up regime, which are checklists 9 and 10 and are
the ones candidates never reach.
The five-minute run sheet

Checklists 3 and 4, narrated as
performed. The paralleling technique,
and the reason must be said:
reproducibility is the entire point of a
baseline. A posterior mandibular
