osce.title: Writing a referral letter
osce.text:
OSCE 50 — Writing a referral letter
Blueprint: assess the need for referral; recognise the complexity of the case; communicate the planned treatment to the wider team (W + SCE).
EQUIPMENT
a case summary with clinical photographs, radiographs and a CBCT report; blank letterhead.
CANDIDATE INSTRUCTIONS
This patient requires bilateral lateral window sinus elevation, which is beyond your scope. Write the referral letter, reading
it aloud as you write.
MODEL ANSWER

“I would structure it under headings so the receiving clinician can find what they need quickly.
Header: date; my name, practice address, GDC number and contact details; the patient’s full name,
date of birth, address and contact details; and the addressee.
Reason for referral, in the first line: ‘I would be grateful for your opinion and treatment regarding
bilateral sinus floor elevation and implant placement in the posterior maxilla.’ The receiving clinician
should not have to read three paragraphs to find out what I want.
Presenting complaint and the patient’s expectations: what she has asked for, in her words, and
what I have already told her is and is not achievable.
Relevant medical history: conditions, medications with doses, allergies, smoking status in pack-
years, and the results of any liaison I have already undertaken.
Dental and social history: attendance, periodontal history and current status, previous implant
experience.
Clinical findings: extra-oral and intra-oral findings, periodontal status with plaque and bleeding
scores, occlusal findings, the edentulous span, ridge dimensions, keratinised tissue, and the oppos-
ing dentition.
Investigations: ‘I enclose a panoramic radiograph dated…, periapicals of…, clinical photographs, a
small field-of-view CBCT dated… with my report, and mounted study casts with a diagnostic wax-
up.’ Sending the images matters — it prevents repeat exposure and is an IR(ME)R consideration.
My assessment: ‘Residual bone height is 4 mm at the 16 and 3 mm at the 17 with a flat sinus floor
and no septa. On the ITI decision tree this indicates a lateral window approach, which falls outside
my scope of practice.’
What I have already discussed and consented: the options presented — including the shortened
dental arch and no treatment — the risks I have covered, and that she understands the referral is for
an opinion.
What I am requesting: opinion only, or treatment; and who will do what afterwards — ‘I am happy
to undertake the restorative phase and to provide ongoing maintenance, or to refer the whole case,
whichever you prefer.’
Urgency and any access needs: routine; interpreter not required; wheelchair access needed.
Closing: my direct contact details, and an offer to discuss.
I would keep a copy in the notes, tell the patient what I have written and what to expect, and set a
reminder to follow up if I have not heard within a reasonable period — because the referral is my
responsibility until it is picked up.”
EXAMINER CHECKLIST
1. Full identifiers for patient and referrer
2. Reason for referral in the first line
3. Patient expectations in their own words
4. Medical history with medications and smoking
5. Dental, periodontal and social history
6. Structured clinical findings
7. Encloses existing images to avoid repeat exposure
8. States the assessment and why it exceeds scope, with a framework reference
9. States what has been consented and precisely what is requested, including shared-care arrangements
10. Copy retained, patient informed, follow-up arranged
Running this station to time
Time check. The model answer is 554 words, 3 minutes 57 seconds at 140 words per minute — and this
is the one station where the words cannot be spoken at speaking speed, because the instruction is reading
it aloud as you write, and a hand writes at perhaps 25 words a minute. At least 200 words must go. The
shape that works: say each heading aloud and give it one line of content, dictating verbatim only the
two sentences that carry marks — the opening line of the letter and the assessment. Write in headed
notes, not prose.

The compressed answer — what a strong candidate says in five minutes
“I would set it out under headings, so the receiving clinician can find what they need without reading
the whole thing.
Header: today’s date; my name, practice address, GDC number and contact details; the patient’s full
name, date of birth, address and contact details; and the addressee by name.
Then the first line of the letter, because that is where the reason goes: ‘I would be grateful for your opinion
and treatment regarding bilateral sinus floor elevation and implant placement in the posterior maxilla.’ Nobody
should have to read three paragraphs to work out what I want.
Presenting complaint and expectations, in her own words — what she has asked for, and what I have
already told her is and is not achievable, so that the receiving clinician is not blind-sided by an expectation
I created.
Relevant medical history: conditions, medications with doses, allergies, smoking in pack-years, and the
result of any liaison I have already had with her general medical practitioner or specialist.
Dental and social history: attendance pattern, periodontal history and current periodontal status, pre-
vious implant experience and how it went.
Clinical findings, structured: extra-oral and intra-oral findings; periodontal status with plaque and
bleeding scores; occlusal findings; the edentulous span; ridge dimensions; keratinised tissue; and the
opposing dentition.
Investigations, enclosed rather than described: ‘I enclose a panoramic radiograph dated…, periapicals of the…,
clinical photographs, a small field-of-view CBCT dated… with my written report, and mounted study casts with a
diagnostic wax-up.’ Sending the images matters — it spares the patient a repeat exposure, which is an
IR(ME)R consideration, and it stops the receiving clinician starting the assessment from nothing.
My assessment, with the numbers: ‘Residual bone height is 4 mm at the 16 and 3 mm at the 17, with a flat sinus
floor and no septa. On the ITI decision tree this indicates a lateral window approach, which falls outside my scope of
practice.’ That is the sentence the whole letter exists for. I am not referring because I am uncertain; I am
referring because I have measured the site, applied a recognised framework, and identified where my
competence ends. A lateral window is Complex — a general dentist with an interest in implants should
recognise it, plan up to it, and hand it over.
What I have already discussed and consented: the options I presented — including the shortened dental
arch and no treatment at all — the risks I have covered, the costs discussed, and that she understands
this is a referral for an opinion, not a booking for surgery.
What I am requesting, precisely, and who does what afterwards: ‘I am happy to undertake the restorative
phase and to provide ongoing maintenance, or to refer the whole case, whichever you prefer.’ Ambiguity about
shared care is how patients end up with nobody responsible for the maintenance.
Urgency and access needs: routine; no interpreter required; wheelchair access needed.
Closing: my direct contact details and an offer to discuss the case by telephone.

osce.title: Interpreting a BPE chart, and the CPITN/WHO probe
osce.text:
OSCE 51 — Interpreting a BPE chart, and the CPITN/WHO probe
A completed BPE chart of the kind you are handed at this station — simulated illustration, not a clinical image
The WHO/CPITN (BPE) probe, drawn to scale against a millimetre rule — simulated illustration, not a clinical image
Blueprint: patient examination; overall dental health in relation to the provision of dental implants; record keeping.

EQUIPMENT
a completed BPE chart on card or screen, a WHO/CPITN (BPE) probe, a UNC-15 or other graduated probe, a plastic or
titanium peri-implant probe, a blank six-point charting form.
CANDIDATE INSTRUCTIONS
You are shown a completed Basic Periodontal Examination for this patient. The examiner will ask you about the findings,
about the instrument used to obtain them, and about what follows. Answer verbally; you are not asked to examine a patient.
DIRECTION OF THOUGHT
This is a discussion station, not a performance station. You will not be asked to walk a probe round a manikin
and call out numbers — you will be given the numbers and asked what they mean, what you would do next,
and to describe the instrument and the technique in words. That is a harder test of precision, not an easier one:
everything you would normally do with your hands has to be said accurately out loud, including the millimetre
markings on the probe and the force in grams or newtons. Fix the order: read the chart →highest code and
what it obliges →define every code →the probe →the force →the technique →the limitations →what it
means for the implant.
The chart you are shown.
Sextant
UR
UA
UL
Upper
3
1
4*
Lower
2
1
3
MODEL ANSWER
As a discussion
Q
Tell me what this chart shows.
“The highest score is a 4 with an asterisk in the upper left sextant, so that is what drives management for
the whole mouth. There is a code 3 upper right and lower left, a code 2 lower right, and code 1 in both
anterior sextants. In summary: generalised gingival inflammation, a plaque-retentive factor or calculus in one
sextant, moderate pocketing in two, and deep pocketing with either furcation involvement or 7 mm or more
of attachment loss in the upper left.”
Q
Define each of the codes for me.
“0 — probing depth under 3.5 mm, the black band fully visible, no calculus or defective margin, and no bleeding
after probing. 1 — the same, but with bleeding after probing. 2 — the same depth, but supra- or subgingival
calculus or a defective restoration margin is present. 3 — probing depth 3.5 to 5.5 mm, so the black band is
partially visible. 4 — probing depth 6 mm or more, so the black band disappears completely.”
Q
And the asterisk?
“The asterisk is added to any code where there is furcation involvement, or recession plus pocket depth to-
talling 7 mm or more of attachment loss from the cemento-enamel junction. It is not a score in itself — it is a
modifier, and it can sit on a code 1 just as easily as on a code 4.”
Q
What does each code oblige you to do?
“0 — no treatment beyond continued prevention. 1 — oral hygiene instruction. 2 — oral hygiene instruction
plus removal of calculus and correction of any plaque-retentive factor. 3 — as for 2, then six-point charting
of that sextant before and after initial therapy, with review. 4, or any code with an asterisk — six-point
charting of the entire dentition, radiographs as clinically indicated, a full diagnosis with stage and grade, and
consideration of referral. So this patient needs full-mouth charting and radiographs, not simply a scale and
polish.”

Q
Which probe was used, and describe it to me.
“A WHO probe, also called the CPITN probe or BPE probe. It has a 0.5 mm diameter ball at the tip, and a
black band running from 3.5 mm to 5.5 mm from the tip. The extended version — sometimes called the WHO
621 — carries two further markings at 8.5 mm and 11.5 mm, so the second band runs 8.5 to 11.5 mm. The shank
is fine and the working end is lightweight, and it is colour-coded so the band can be read at a glance.”
Q
Why does it have a ball end?
“Three reasons. It stops the tip penetrating the junctional epithelium and over-reading the pocket. It lets me
feel subgingival calculus and defective margins as the ball passes over them, which is how code 2 is detected.
And it is more comfortable and less likely to traumatise the sulcus base than a sharp tip.”
Q
What force do you use, and how do you know you are using it?
“A light force of 20 to 25 grams, which is about 0.2 to 0.25 newtons. I calibrate it by pressing the probe against my
thumbnail until the tip just blanches the nail bed — that is roughly the right force. Too much force pushes
the probe through the inflamed junctional epithelium and over-reads the depth; too little under-reads it and
misses bleeding.”
Q
Take me through how you would actually use it.
“I divide the mouth into six sextants — 17–14, 13–23, 24–27, and the three matching lower sextants; third molars
are excluded unless they are functioning in place of a second molar. A sextant is only scored if it contains two
or more teeth; if it has one tooth or none, that tooth is scored within the adjacent sextant and the sextant is
recorded as X. Within each sextant I insert the probe parallel to the long axis of the tooth, gently to the base of
the sulcus, then walk it in small vertical steps around the whole circumference, covering at least six sites per
tooth — mesiobuccal, mid-buccal, distobuccal and the three matching lingual sites. I keep the ball in contact
with the root surface throughout. I then record only the highest score in that sextant, and once a sextant scores
4 I may move on, since nothing higher can be found — although I would still look for the asterisk.”
Q
What are the limitations of the BPE?
“It is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. It records only the worst site in a sextant, so it hides the distribution
and the number of affected sites; it cannot be used to monitor response to treatment; it gives no information
on recession or attachment loss unless the asterisk is triggered; and it does not by itself let you stage and grade
under the 2017 classification. It also cannot be used around implants.”
Q
Why not around implants?
“Because the peri-implant tissues are different — no periodontal ligament, no perpendicular collagen insertion
into the surface, and a weaker connective tissue seal — so the probe penetrates further for the same force, and
‘normal’ probing depths differ from tooth to tooth depending on how deeply the implant was placed. Peri-
implant probing is a separate examination: six sites per implant, a plastic or titanium probe, a gentle force
of about 0.2 to 0.25 newtons, recording depth, bleeding, suppuration, recession and the width of keratinised
mucosa, and compared against the baseline recorded at prosthesis fitting rather than against an absolute
number.”
Q
What would the six-point chart record?
“For each tooth, probing depth at six sites — mesiobuccal, mid-buccal, distobuccal, mesiolingual, mid-lingual,
distolingual — using a graduated probe such as a UNC-15, rounded to the nearest whole millimetre; recession,
so that clinical attachment loss can be calculated; bleeding on probing and suppuration; mobility by the Miller
grades; furcation with a Nabers probe and the Hamp grades; and a plaque score.”
Q
What does this chart mean for a proposed implant?
“That implants are not on the table yet. A history of periodontitis is the strongest patient-level risk factor for
peri-implantitis, so this patient must be diagnosed, staged and graded under the 2017 classification, treated
through the EFP stepwise approach, and shown to be stable first. Stability means probing depths of 4 mm or
less, no bleeding at those 4 mm sites, and full-mouth bleeding under 10%. If the upper left sextant does not

respond, or if that asterisk turns out to be a Grade C picture, the whole plan may change — including whether
the tooth I am replacing should be replaced at all.”
Q
What would you record?
“The six sextant scores with the asterisk, the date, the probe used, and the fact that the findings were explained to
the patient; then the full chart, the diagnosis with stage and grade, the treatment plan, and the review interval.”
EXAMINER CHECKLIST
1. Reads the chart accurately and identifies the highest score as the driver
2. Codes 0–4 defined correctly, including the band position for each
3. The asterisk defined correctly as a modifier
4. States the action obliged by each code, including full-mouth charting for 4/*
5. Names the WHO/CPITN probe and states the 0.5 mm ball and the 3.5–5.5 mm band, ideally the 8.5/11.5 mm markings
6. Explains why the tip is ball-ended
7. States the force in grams or newtons and how it is calibrated
8. Describes sextants, the two-tooth rule, walking the probe and recording the highest score
9. States the limitations of the BPE and that it is not used around implants, with the peri-implant alternative
10. Relates the findings to implant risk and stability criteria, and states what is recorded
See also OSCE 20 (peri-implant assessment and maintenance) and OSCE 48 (oral hygiene instruction).
Running this station to time
Time check. The model answer in this part runs to 1,186 words, which at 140 words per minute is 8
minutes 28 seconds of unbroken speech before the examiner has asked a single question — so roughly
550 words, nearly half of it, has to go, and it goes by compressing the definitions into single clauses rather
than by dropping any of the ten checklist headings.
The five-minute run sheet

What earns the mark

“What would you record, what have you

Checklist 10, second half — records (six
scores with asterisk, date, probe used,

The compressed answer — what a strong candidate says in five minutes
Q: Tell me what this chart shows. “The highest score is a 4 with an asterisk in the upper left, and
that drives management for the whole mouth. With a 3 upper right and lower left, a 2 lower right and 1
anteriorly, this is generalised gingival inflammation, calculus in one sextant, moderate pocketing in two,
and deep pocketing with furcation or 7 mm of attachment loss upper left.”
Q: Define the codes. “0 — under 3.5 mm, black band fully visible, no calculus, no bleeding. 1 — the
same, but bleeding after probing. 2 — the same depth with supra- or subgingival calculus or a defective
margin. 3 — 3.5 to 5.5 mm, band partially visible. 4 — 6 mm or more, band gone completely. The asterisk
is a modifier, not a score: furcation involvement, or recession plus pocket totalling 7 mm or more of
attachment loss. It can sit on a 1 as easily as on a 4.”
Q: What does each code oblige you to do? “0, prevention only. 1, oral hygiene instruction. 2, plus calculus
removal and correction of the plaque-retentive factor. 3, as for 2, then six-point charting of that sextant
before and after initial therapy. 4, or any asterisk — six-point charting of the whole dentition, radio-
graphs, diagnosis with stage and grade, and consideration of referral. So she needs full-mouth charting,
not a scale and polish.”
Q: Describe this probe. “A WHO probe, also called the CPITN or BPE probe: a 0.5 mm ball at the tip
and a black band from 3.5 to 5.5 mm; the WHO 621 carries further markings at 8.5 and 11.5 mm. The ball
end stops the tip penetrating the junctional epithelium, lets me feel subgingival calculus and defective
margins — which is how code 2 is detected — and is atraumatic.”
Q: What force, and how do you know? “20 to 25 grams, about 0.2 to 0.25 newtons. I calibrate against my
thumbnail until the nail bed just blanches. Too much over-reads through inflamed tissue; too little misses
bleeding.”
Q: How would you use it? “Six sextants — 17 to 14, 13 to 23, 24 to 27 and the three matching lower ones;
third molars excluded unless functioning as second molars. A sextant is scored only if it has two or more
teeth; otherwise that tooth is scored in the adjacent sextant and the sextant recorded as X. Probe parallel
to the long axis, gently to the base of the sulcus, walked in small steps around the whole circumference,
six sites per tooth, recording only the highest score per sextant.”
Q: Limitations? “It is a screening tool, not a diagnosis — worst site only, so it hides distribution; it
cannot monitor treatment; it gives no attachment loss unless the asterisk triggers; and it does not stage
and grade. It is not used around implants: no periodontal ligament and a weaker connective tissue seal,
so the probe penetrates further for the same force. Peri-implant probing is separate — six sites, a plastic
or titanium probe, 0.2 to 0.25 newtons, recording depth, bleeding, suppuration, recession and keratinised
width against the baseline taken at fit.”
Q: What does this mean for her implant? “Implants are not on the table yet. Previous periodontitis is
the strongest patient-level risk factor for peri-implantitis, so she needs diagnosis with stage and grade,
stepwise therapy, and demonstrated stability — pockets 4 mm or less, no bleeding at those sites, full-
mouth bleeding under 10% — first.”
Q: Records and review? “The six scores with the asterisk, the date, the probe used, and that I explained
the findings and told her the implant waits until she is stable; then the six-point chart with recession,
bleeding, mobility, furcation and plaque score, the diagnosis with stage and grade, the plan, and review
after initial therapy.”

stability criteria and what is recorded.

osce.title: Buccally tilted 24 implant with a high smile line: discussion with the technician
osce.text:
OSCE 52 — Buccally tilted 24 implant with a high smile line: discussion with the technician
Blueprint: select the appropriate abutment; difference between screw- and cement-retained restorations and their application; communicate the
planned treatment to the wider team; prescribe an appropriate type of restoration from the laboratory. Marked W + OS-P + SCE.
EQUIPMENT
a working cast with an implant analogue at the 24 angled markedly buccally; a screw-retained trial crown whose access hole
emerges through the buccal surface; a selection of abutments including an angulated screw channel (ASC) abutment, a
straight titanium abutment, an angled abutment and a titanium base; photographs of the patient smiling showing a high
smile line; a laboratory prescription form; a telephone or a role-player acting as the technician.
CANDIDATE INSTRUCTIONS
An implant was placed at the UL4. The implant is tilted buccally. The patient has a high smile line. The laboratory has
returned a screw-retained crown whose access channel emerges through the buccal surface. Discuss the problem and the
possible solutions with the technician, and record your decision.
DIRECTION OF THOUGHT
The problem is a surgical error being presented as a prosthetic problem. Do not start with “I’ll cement it.” Start
by naming the problem, then run through the options in order of preference, and only then arrive at cementation
— with the caveats. This station rewards a structured conversation with a colleague: greet, describe the problem,
state what you have observed, ask for the technician’s view, agree a plan, confirm it in writing.
MODEL ANSWER
As a conversation with the technician
“‘Hello — I’ve got the UL4 crown you made. Can I talk you through a problem? The implant is tilted
buccally, and the screw access is coming out through the buccal surface of the crown, right in the
middle of the visible face. The patient has a high smile line, so I can see the whole crown and about
2 mm of gingiva when she smiles. A composite-filled access hole on the labial surface is going to be
visible and will discolour over time, so I don’t think we can deliver it as it is.’
Then I would set out the options with him.
Option 1 — an angulated screw channel abutment. My first choice. These allow the screw channel
to be redirected, typically by up to about 25 to 30 degrees depending on the system, so the access
can be moved palatally while the restoration stays screw-retained. That keeps retrievability and
eliminates cement entirely. I would ask him to check whether our system offers an ASC solution for
this platform and whether the angulation is within range.
Option 2 — a ‘screwmentable’ or hybrid restoration. The crown is cemented extra-orally in the
laboratory onto a titanium base, and the whole assembly is then delivered as a screw-retained unit.
All the excess cement is removed on the bench where it can be seen, so there is no submucosal
cement, and the restoration remains retrievable. This is my preferred fallback if the ASC angulation
is insuﬀicient.
Option 3 — a cement-retained crown on a custom angled abutment. This solves the aesthetic
problem and is the classic answer, but it introduces the risk that concerns me most: residual sub-
mucosal cement is a well-documented cause of peri-implantitis. If we go this way, I would ask

him for: - a custom CAD-CAM abutment, not a stock one, so I control the emergence profile and
the margin; - the margin placed at or no more than 1 mm below the mucosal margin, following
the gingival scallop, and ideally supramucosal on the palatal aspect where it will not show; - an
adequate abutment height and taper for retention — around 5 mm — because a short abutment
plus a weak cement means the crown will come off; - a Ti-base with a ceramic superstructure rather
than a plain titanium abutment, because with a high smile line and possibly thin tissue, a titanium
abutment can produce grey show-through.
Option 4 — accept the buccal access hole and mask it. I would reject this with a high smile line.
Then: ‘Which of those can you do with this system? If the ASC works, that’s what I’d like. If not,
let’s do the extra-oral cementation on a Ti-base so it comes back as a screw-retained unit.’
Then I would confirm it in writing on a new laboratory prescription, stating the implant system,
platform and connection; the abutment type and material; the margin position; the retention type;
the shade and stump shade; the occlusal scheme; and the date required. I would keep a copy in the
notes.
If I do end up cementing, I would use a radiopaque cement, apply it only to the coronal half of
the intaglio, use an extra-oral replica abutment to extrude the excess before seating, remove excess
meticulously with floss and scalers, and take a periapical radiograph to verify no residual cement.
And I would record the underlying lesson. The real problem here is implant angulation, which is
a planning and surgical issue. I would record it as a significant event, review whether a surgical
guide derived from a diagnostic wax-up was used, and audit my own use of restoratively driven
planning.”
EXAMINER CHECKLIST
1. Names the problem clearly and states why the crown cannot be delivered as made
2. Structured, courteous professional exchange with the technician, inviting their view
3. Angulated screw channel abutment offered first, with the angulation limit
4. Extra-oral cementation on a Ti-base (“screwmentable”) described
5. States the cement risk explicitly
6. If cementing: custom abutment, margin ≤1 mm subgingival, adequate height
7. Ti-base/ceramic to avoid grey show-through with a high smile line
8. Rejects a labial access hole and says why
9. Written laboratory prescription with all required detail, copy retained
10. Identifies the underlying planning/surgical cause and the governance response
Extended by practice stations OSCE 12 (abutment selection), OSCE 13 (screw versus cement) and OSCE 18 (laboratory prescription).
Running this station to time
Time check. The model answer is 985 words, 7 minutes 2 seconds at 140 words per minute — two minutes
over the station before the technician has said a word. Around 280 words must go, and the format does
most of the cutting for you: this is a conversation, so each option gets one sentence and its single decisive
reason, and the technician’s replies carry the alternatives. Only the candidate’s own words spend the
clock, so ask, then listen.

osce.title: Framework try-in with a transfer jig: what if it does not fit
osce.text:
OSCE 53 — Framework try-in with a transfer jig: what if it does not fit
Periapical view at the framework try-in — note the interface at one abutment — simulated illustration, not a clinical image
Blueprint: describe how to manage a mis-fitting prosthesis or framework; evaluate the laboratory techniques involved in implant reconstruction.
EQUIPMENT
a model with four implant analogues; a cast metal framework; a verification (transfer) jig; a set of crowns; screws and a
screwdriver; a periapical radiograph showing a wedge-shaped gap at one abutment; probes.
CANDIDATE INSTRUCTIONS
You are trying in a metal framework and crowns for an implant-supported prosthesis. A transfer jig has been provided.
Demonstrate and describe the try-in, and describe what you would do if the framework does not fit.

DIRECTION OF THOUGHT
Two halves: how to verify fit, and what to do when it fails. Use the jig first — that is why it is on the table and
it is a named checklist item. Be explicit that you never force a framework with a torque wrench.
MODEL ANSWER
“The purpose of a verification or transfer jig is to check that the master cast reproduces the implant
positions in the mouth accurately, before an expensive framework is made. It is usually made of
pattern resin or a rigid material joining copings, sectioned and re-joined to compensate for poly-
merisation shrinkage.
Step 1 — verify the cast with the jig. Remove the healing abutments or provisional. Seat the jig in
the mouth. It should seat passively and completely on all implants with no rocking, and each screw
should engage without resistance. I check visually and with a fine probe at each interface. If the jig
does not seat, the master cast is wrong and there is no point trying the framework — I would take
a new splinted open-tray impression.
Step 2 — try in the framework. Seat it by hand, hand-tighten one screw only, and then verify
passivity: - Visual and tactile: inspect each interface and run a fine probe around each margin. - The
one-screw, or Sheﬀield, test: tighten only the most distal screw and examine the fit at the opposite
end. A visible gap or rocking means the framework is not passive. I repeat the test from the other
end, because a framework can appear to fit from one direction and not the other. - Radiographically:
a paralleling periapical at each abutment. The classic sign of misfit is a wedge-shaped radiolucent
gap between framework and implant. - Patient symptoms: pressure, tightness or pain as the screws
are tightened is a warning sign and I would stop.
Step 3 — check the rest. Contour and cleansability, interocclusal clearance for the ceramic, the
occlusal scheme, the shade, and the position of the screw access channels.
If it does not fit. First, I do not force it. Torquing a non-passive framework transmits static stress to
the implants and components, and causes screw loosening or fracture, marginal bone loss and pain.
Then I identify the cause: - Interference — soft tissue or bone over a platform, or an incompletely
seated component. Remove it and re-try. - A component error — the wrong analogue, or an ana-
logue rotated in the cast. - Impression distortion — unsplinted copings, a coping that moved, a
flexible tray, or a coping not fully seated at the time of impression. - Cast inaccuracy — expansion
or damage. - Laboratory distortion — during casting, soldering or ceramic firing. A framework can
be passive before firing and not afterwards.
The remedies, in escalating order: 1. Remove any interference and re-try. 2. Section the framework
at the point of misfit, lute the sections together intra-orally with pattern resin, and return it for
soldering or laser welding, then re-verify. This is the standard remedy for a framework that is
accurate in its parts but distorted overall. 3. If the error is in the impression or the cast, make a new
verification jig and take a new splinted open-tray impression, and have the framework remade.
Then the professional part. I would explain the delay to the patient honestly and apologise for it,
provide or adjust a provisional so they are not inconvenienced, discuss the case with the technician
to establish where the error arose so it does not recur, and record everything. I would not criticise
the laboratory in front of the patient.”
EXAMINER CHECKLIST
1. Explains the purpose of the verification/transfer jig
2. Uses the jig first and states what a non-seating jig means
3. Sections-and-rejoins principle understood
4. One-screw (Sheﬀield) test performed and repeated from both ends
5. Radiographic verification and the wedge-shaped gap
6. Checks contour, cleansability, clearance, occlusion, shade, access position
7. States explicitly that the framework must not be forced, with the consequences
8. Lists causes systematically
9. Section-and-solder remedy, and the new-impression remedy
10. Patient communication, provisional, technician discussion, records
Extended by practice stations OSCE 14 (implant impression), OSCE 16 (fitting the prosthesis) and OSCE 17 (the mis-fitting framework).

Running this station to time
Time check. The model answer in this part is 556 words, 3 minutes 58 seconds at 140 words per minute —
which leaves barely a minute for the examiner and none for actually handling the jig, the framework and
the screwdriver on the bench; about 100 words of the causes list has to be compressed into a single sweep
so that the demonstration is not sacrificed to the commentary.

The compressed answer — what a strong candidate says in five minutes
“I will start with the jig, not the framework.
The purpose of a verification or transfer jig is to confirm that the master cast reproduces the implant
positions in the mouth accurately, before an expensive framework is made. It is rigid pattern resin joining
copings, sectioned and re-joined to compensate for polymerisation shrinkage.
Step one — verify the cast. I remove the healing abutments, seat the jig, and check it sits passively and
completely on all four implants with no rocking, each screw engaging without resistance. I check visually
and with a fine probe at every interface. If the jig does not seat, the master cast is wrong, and there is no
point trying the framework — I would take a new splinted open-tray impression there and then.

Step two — try in the framework. I seat it by hand and hand-tighten one screw only. Then I verify
passivity four ways. Visually and tactilely, inspecting each interface and running a fine probe round each
margin. With the one-screw or Sheﬀield test — tightening only the most distal screw and examining the
fit at the opposite end; a visible gap or rocking means it is not passive, and I repeat the test from the
other end, because a framework can appear to fit from one direction and not the other. Radiographically,
with a paralleling periapical at each abutment: the classic sign of misfit is a wedge-shaped radiolucent
gap between framework and implant. And by the patient’s symptoms — pressure, tightness or pain as I
tighten is a warning, and I stop.
Step three. Contour and cleansability, interocclusal clearance for the ceramic, the occlusal scheme, the
shade, and where the screw access channels emerge.
If it does not fit, the first thing is that I do not force it. Torquing a non-passive framework transmits static
stress to the implants and components, and causes screw loosening or fracture, marginal bone loss and
pain.
Then I find the cause, systematically. Interference — soft tissue or bone over a platform, or a component
not fully seated; remove it and re-try. A component error — the wrong analogue, or an analogue rotated
in the cast. Impression distortion — unsplinted copings, a coping that moved or was not fully seated, or
a flexible tray. Cast inaccuracy — expansion or damage. Laboratory distortion during casting, soldering
or ceramic firing; a framework can be passive before firing and not afterwards.
The remedies, in escalating order. First, remove any interference and re-try. Second — and this is the
standard remedy for a framework that is accurate in its parts but distorted overall — section it at the point
of misfit, lute the sections together intra-orally with pattern resin, and return it for soldering or laser
welding, then re-verify with the same tests. Third, if the error lies in the impression or the cast, make
a new verification jig, take a new splinted open-tray impression, and have the framework remade. I
would not adjust my way out of a misfit by grinding the intaglio.
Then the professional part. I explain the delay to the patient honestly and apologise for it, and I adjust or
replace the provisional so they leave with something comfortable and are not inconvenienced. I discuss
the case with the technician to establish where the error arose so it does not recur — but I would not
criticise the laboratory in front of the patient. And I record it all: the jig result, which tests I performed
and from which end, the radiographic findings, the cause I identified, the decision taken, what I told the
patient, and the review appointment for the re-try.”
Marking priority when the clock beats the candidate
Ask for these first (the six that carry the station): 2 uses the jig first and states what a non-seating jig
means · 4 one-screw (Sheﬀield) test performed and repeated from both ends · 7 states explicitly that
the framework must not be forced, with the consequences · 5 radiographic verification and the wedge-
shaped gap · 9 section-and-solder remedy and the new-impression remedy · 10 patient communication,
provisional, technician discussion and records.
Accept these late or on prompting: 1 the purpose of the verification jig · 3 the sections-and-rejoins prin-
ciple · 6 contour, cleansability, clearance, occlusion, shade and access position · 8 the systematic list of
causes.
The commonest way five minutes is wasted here: reciting the full causes list as a lecture before the
examiner has asked what to do about it, and — worse — reaching for the framework and the torque
wrench before the jig, which forfeits the two marks the examiner put the jig on the table to test.

osce.title: Chairside provisional implant crown
osce.text:
OSCE 54 — Chairside provisional implant crown
The instruments and materials laid out for this station — simulated illustration, not a clinical image
Blueprint: demonstrate the fitting of a prosthesis; plan the type of prosthesis and translate this into the definitive restoration; different techniques of
restoring implants.
EQUIPMENT
Equipment — laid out on the table in front of you: a study model with a diagnostic wax-up of the 11; silicone putty; a
temporary implant abutment (titanium or PEEK) with its screw and screwdriver; Protemp or another bis-acryl provisional
material with mixing tips; flowable composite; PTFE tape; articulating paper; a polishing bur kit — acrylic burs, discs,
silicone wheels, polishing paste; temporary luting cement (temp bond); dental floss; and a model carrying an implant
analogue at the 11 with matured soft tissue.
CANDIDATE INSTRUCTIONS
An implant has been placed at the 11 and is ready to be provisionalised. Using the instruments and materials on the table,
explain to the examiner, step by step, how you would make the provisional crown. You are not asked to make it
— describe the procedure verbally, say which of these items you would use and which you would not, and explain why.
DIRECTION OF THOUGHT
This is a discussion station: everything you would do with your hands must be said out loud, in order,
naming the material each time. Three things carry the marks. First, the sequence — index, abutment, block
out, form, remove before set, contour, polish, seat, check, seal, review. Second, the reason the provisional exists
at all: it is the instrument that shapes the peri-implant soft tissue, and its subgingival contour is a deliberate
design decision, not an accident of the material. Third — and this is where the tray is testing you — not every
item on the table should be used. Say which you reject and why. Work through the list before you start: “I
would use the wax-up and putty to make an index, the temporary abutment, PTFE, the bis-acryl, flowable, the polishing
kit, articulating paper and floss. I would not use the temporary cement, and I will explain why.”
MODEL ANSWER
“The purposes of an implant provisional are to restore appearance and function temporarily, to pro-
tect the site, and above all to develop and support the peri-implant soft tissue and the emergence
profile, which I will then copy into the definitive restoration.
Steps: 0. Make the index first, before anything goes near the mouth. I take the study model
with the diagnostic wax-up and load silicone putty over the wax-up and two teeth either side, to
make a rigid palatal or labio-palatal index. I trim it so it seats on the adjacent teeth only, and
cut a small vent over the 11 so that excess material and air can escape. The wax-up is the shape
I have already agreed with the patient, so the index transfers an approved contour rather than an
invented one. An alternative index is a vacuum-formed matrix made on the same wax-up. 1. Verify
the implant is integrated and the soft tissue healthy. Remove the healing abutment and clean the
internal connection. 2. Select a temporary abutment — titanium or PEEK — of the correct platform,
and check it seats fully. 3. Block out the screw channel with PTFE tape so that no resin enters the
screw head, and so I can retrieve it. 4. Protect the soft tissue and the interface: I place a small
amount of rubber dam sheet or PTFE around the abutment collar, or apply a separating medium,

so that resin does not lock into the undercut around the abutment or contact the mucosa. 5. Form
the crown. Either load a vacuum-formed matrix taken from the diagnostic wax-up with bis-acryl
and seat it over the abutment; or, in an immediate case, relieve the patient’s own natural crown,
hollow it, and lute it to the abutment; or free-hand with flowable composite and a matrix strip.
6. Remove before full set — unscrew and remove the assembly while the resin is still rubbery,
then allow it to bench-cure fully outside the mouth. Removing it prevents locking into undercuts
and prevents the exotherm from damaging the tissue. 7. Add resin to the subgingival portion
and shape the emergence profile. This is the critical step. Below the mucosal margin I create a
flat or slightly concave (under-contoured) profile, which supports the tissue without pushing it
apically; a convex, over-contoured subgingival form causes recession and inflammation. Above the
margin I develop the correct emergence to support the papillae. 8. Finish and polish to a very
high lustre — any roughness subgingivally becomes a plaque trap and a source of inflammation. I
polish with discs, silicone wheels and a polishing paste. 9. Seat and check. Hand-tighten only, or
torque to the manufacturer’s provisional value. Check the proximal contacts with floss, check the
emergence supports the papillae, and check the occlusion — for an immediate provisional, it must
be completely free of contact in intercuspation and in all excursions; for a conventionally loaded
provisional, light contact is acceptable. 10. Seal the access with PTFE and composite so it can be
removed and modified. 11. Instructions and review. Soft diet, no incising with the tooth, hygiene
around the provisional, and review in 2 to 3 weeks so I can add or remove resin incrementally
to refine the emergence over the following 8 to 12 weeks. 12. When the profile is mature, I take
a customised impression coping copying the provisional’s subgingival contour, so the definitive
restoration reproduces it exactly.
What I would use from this tray, and how. The wax-up and putty for the index. The temporary
abutment and its screw. PTFE for the block-out and, at the end, for the access seal. Bis-acryl
(Protemp) through the index to form the crown, and flowable composite to add and refine the
subgingival contour incrementally. The polishing kit — acrylic bur, disc, silicone wheel, then paste
— because a rough subgingival surface is a plaque trap and the single commonest cause of an in-
flamed provisional site. Articulating paper to confirm the occlusion: for an immediately placed
and immediately restored anterior implant the crown must be completely free of contact in inter-
cuspation and in every excursive movement, and I check protrusion and both lateral excursions,
not just tapping. Floss to check the proximal contacts and, just as importantly, to check that I can
clean under and around the emergence — if floss shreds, the surface is not polished, and if it will
not pass, the contact is too tight.
What I would not use, and why. The temporary cement. This is a screw-retained provisional, and
that is a deliberate choice in an anterior implant: it is retrievable without stressing the interface, it
can be removed repeatedly to add resin as the tissue matures, and — decisively — it eliminates
residual subgingival cement, which is a well-documented cause of peri-implant inflammation and
bone loss and is very diﬀicult to detect radiographically once it is deep. Cement excess is far harder
to remove around an implant than around a tooth because there is no periodontal ligament and the
margin is often deeply subgingival. If the emergence angle made a screw channel impossible — a
labially inclined implant with the channel emerging through the incisal edge — I would either use
an angulated screw-channel abutment or accept a cemented provisional on a customised abutment
with a supragingival or barely subgingival margin, and I would still extra-orally cement it onto the
abutment and clean it outside the mouth wherever possible.
I would record the abutment used, the material, the occlusal arrangement and the review plan.”
EXAMINER CHECKLIST
1. States the purpose, including soft tissue conditioning, and verifies integration and tissue health first
2. Putty or vacuum-formed index taken from the diagnostic wax-up, and says why the wax-up is the source of the contour
3. Correct temporary abutment selected, seated fully, connection cleaned
4. PTFE block-out of the screw channel and protection of the tissue and undercuts from resin
5. Forms the crown in bis-acryl through the index and removes it before full set, with the reason (undercuts, exotherm)
6. Concave or flat subgingival emergence profile, with the reason, refined incrementally in flowable
7. High polish, naming the sequence of burs, wheels and paste
8. Occlusion checked with articulating paper in intercuspation and all excursions, and kept out of contact where required;
floss used for contacts and cleansability
9. Screw-retained, and explicitly rejects the temporary cement, giving residual subgingival cement as the reason, with the
angulated-screw-channel alternative

10. Access sealed with PTFE and composite; instructions, incremental refinement plan and customised impression coping to
transfer the profile
Extended by practice stations OSCE 16 (fitting the prosthesis) and OSCE 14 (implant impression).
Running this station to time
Time check. The model answer in this part runs to about 1,050 words — roughly 7½ minutes at 140 words
per minute before the examiner has asked anything — so about a third has to go. It goes by naming each
step in one clause instead of justifying it, and by keeping the full justification for only three places:
the source of the contour, the subgingival profile, and the refusal of the temporary cement. This is a
discussion station: the candidate is not making the crown, they are talking the examiner through it while
the materials sit on the table between them.
The five-minute run sheet
Time
The examiner does
What earns the mark
0:00–0:30

is in at the 11 and is ready to be
provisionalised. Talk me through how
you would make the provisional.”

purpose first — appearance and
function, protection, and above all

ask it if the candidate has not already

“Finish off.”
Checklists 8 and 10. Articulating paper
— out of contact in intercuspation and all

and composite; then what is recorded,

ending with the customised impression
coping that transfers the matured profile.

The compressed answer — what a strong candidate says in five minutes
“The provisional is not a stop-gap; it is the instrument that shapes the peri-implant soft tissue, and the
definitive crown will copy whatever shape it creates. So before anything else I would confirm the implant
is integrated, the mucosa is healthy, and that I have an agreed target shape.
That shape comes from the diagnostic wax-up. I would load silicone putty over the wax-up on the study
model and two teeth either side, trim the index to seat on the adjacent teeth only, and cut a small vent over
the 11 so excess and air escape. A vacuum-formed matrix on the same wax-up does the same job. The
point is that the contour is one the patient has already seen and approved, not one I invent at the chair.
Then the abutment. I remove the healing abutment, clean the internal connection, and seat the correct-
platform temporary titanium or PEEK abutment, checking it is fully home. I block the screw channel
with PTFE tape so no resin reaches the screw head, and place PTFE or a separating medium around the
collar so resin does not lock into the undercut or contact the mucosa.
Forming it. I load the index with bis-acryl — Protemp — and seat it, then remove the whole assembly
before the material has fully set, while it is still rubbery. Two reasons: resin locks into undercuts if it sets
in the mouth, and the exotherm damages the mucosa. It bench-cures outside the mouth.
The subgingival contour is the critical step. Below the mucosal margin I add flowable composite to
build a flat or slightly concave profile that supports the tissue without pushing it apically. A convex, over-
contoured subgingival form is what causes recession and inflammation. Above the margin I develop the
emergence that supports the papillae.
Then I polish it to a high lustre — acrylic bur, disc, silicone wheel, then paste. Any roughness subgingi-
vally is a plaque trap, and an inflamed provisional site is usually a badly polished one.
Seating and checking. Hand-tighten or torque to the manufacturer’s provisional value. Articulating
paper: if this implant was placed and restored immediately, the crown must be completely free of contact
in intercuspation and in every excursion — I check protrusion and both lateral movements, not just
tapping. Floss for the proximal contacts, and to confirm it will pass and not shred, which tells me the
contact and the polish are both right. I seal the access with PTFE and composite so I can retrieve it.
One thing on this tray I would not use: the temporary cement. This is a screw-retained provisional
deliberately — retrievable without stressing the interface, removable repeatedly so I can add resin as the
tissue matures, and, decisively, no residual subgingival cement, which is a well-recognised cause of peri-
implant inflammation and bone loss and is very diﬀicult to detect or remove once it is deep, because there
is no periodontal ligament and the margin is often well below the tissue. If the screw channel emerged
through the incisal edge I would use an angulated screw-channel abutment, or accept a cemented provi-
sional on a customised abutment with a supragingival margin, cemented extra-orally where possible.
Finally, I would record the abutment, the material, the occlusal arrangement and the plan; tell the patient
soft diet, not to bite into anything with it, and how to clean around it; and review at two to three weeks to
refine the emergence incrementally over the next two to three months. When the profile is mature I take
a customised impression coping that copies it, so the definitive crown reproduces the shape exactly.”
Marking priority when the clock beats the candidate
Ask for these first (the six that carry the station): 1 purpose, including soft-tissue conditioning · 2 index
taken from the diagnostic wax-up, with the reason · 5 forms in the index and removes before full set,
with the reason · 6 flat or concave subgingival profile, with the reason · 9 screw-retained; rejects the
temporary cement because of residual cement · 10 records, patient instructions, review and the customised
impression coping.
Accept these late or on prompting: 3 abutment selection and seating · 4 PTFE block-out and tissue pro-
tection · 7 the polishing sequence by name · 8 articulating paper in excursions and floss for contacts and
cleansability.
The commonest way five minutes is wasted here: describing the material rather than the procedure
— a candidate who spends 90 seconds on the merits of bis-acryl against PMMA and then rushes the
subgingival contour has spent the time on the least examinable part of the station. The other failure is
never mentioning the temporary cement at all: the tray was laid out with a distractor on it, and saying
nothing about it is treated as not having noticed.

osce.title: Post-operative instructions after multiple implant placement
osce.text:
OSCE 55 — Post-operative instructions after multiple implant placement
The surgical site at the end of the appointment — simulated illustration, not a clinical image
Blueprint: suggest appropriate and adequate postoperative care and advice including the use of post-operative painkillers and antibiotics. Marked
OS-P + SCE.
EQUIPMENT
a simulated patient or the examiner acting as the patient; a blank post-operative instruction sheet; a prescription pad.
CANDIDATE INSTRUCTIONS
You have just placed four implants in the mandible in a single visit. Give the patient their post-operative instructions.
DIRECTION OF THOUGHT
This is a spoken station: plain language, no jargon, in a fixed order, ending with warning signs and a contact
number. Multiple implants changes the emphasis compared with a single implant: more swelling and bruis-
ing, more analgesia, a longer flap and more sutures, a greater risk of bleeding, more attention to the denture,
and — because the mandible is involved — an explicit airway warning.
MODEL ANSWER
As spoken to the patient
“That all went to plan — four implants are in. This was a bigger procedure than a single implant, so
I want to go through what to expect, and I’ll give you all of this in writing too.
Bleeding. Some oozing today is normal and can look worse than it is because it mixes with saliva.
If it bleeds, bite firmly on the gauze I’ve given you for 20 minutes without checking it. Don’t rinse
at all today.
Swelling and bruising. Because we’ve worked on both sides, expect more swelling than for a single
implant, and expect bruising that may track down towards your jawline or neck over a few days —
that’s normal and it settles. Swelling is usually worst at two to three days and then improves. Use a
cold pack on the outside, 20 minutes on and 20 off, for the first day, and sleep with an extra pillow.
Pain. Take ibuprofen 400 mg with food, up to four times a day, and paracetamol 1 gram up to
four times a day — you can take them together and that combination works better than either alone.
Take the first dose now, before the numbness wears off. Avoid aspirin.
Medication I’ve prescribed. [If given] Finish the whole antibiotic course. Start the chlorhexidine
mouthwash tomorrow, twice a day for two weeks — hold it in your mouth gently, don’t swill hard.
Cleaning. Brush all your other teeth normally, but do not brush over the stitches until I say so.
Keeping the rest of your mouth clean matters more than usual.
Eating and drinking. Soft food for the first week — you’ve got sutures across a wide area, so nothing
that needs biting or chewing hard. Nothing hot today. Keep well hydrated, and don’t use a straw.

Your denture. Leave it out completely for the next 48 hours. Then bring it in and I’ll adjust and
reline it so it doesn’t press on the implants. Do not wear it until I’ve done that — pressure on a
healing implant is one of the main causes of failure. And leave it out at night from now on.
Activity. No smoking at all — smoking is the single biggest thing that will make these fail. No
alcohol, and no strenuous exercise or heavy lifting for at least three days, because that can restart
the bleeding.
Numbness. Your lip and chin will be numb from the anaesthetic for a few hours. If any numbness
is still there tomorrow, ring me — that’s important and I need to know straight away.
Contact me if: the bleeding doesn’t stop with 20 minutes of firm pressure; the pain gets worse after
day three rather than better; you get a temperature or the swelling spreads towards your eye or down
your neck; a stitch comes away and something feels rough; or you feel unwell.
And this one is an emergency — call 999: if you develop swelling under your tongue, diﬀiculty
swallowing, or any diﬀiculty breathing.
Here is the written sheet, my number, and the out-of-hours number. I’ll see you in a week to take
the stitches out, and I’ll ring you this evening to check how you are.”
EXAMINER CHECKLIST
1. Bleeding advice with a specific duration of pressure
2. Swelling and bruising, anticipating a greater response after multiple implants, with cold pack and head elevation
3. Specific analgesia with drug, dose, frequency and pre-emptive timing
4. Antibiotic and chlorhexidine instructions
5. Hygiene — no brushing over the surgical site
6. Diet, extended to reflect a larger surgical field; no straws
7. Denture out for 48 hours, then relieved and soft-relined; not worn until adjusted
8. Smoking, alcohol, exercise
9. Numbness instruction and the airway emergency warning
10. Written instructions, contact numbers, review appointment and a same-day follow-up call
See also OSCE 10 (post-operative care after a single implant with a graft) and OSCE 45 (denture relief and relining).
Running this station to time
Time check. The model answer in this part is 544 words, 3 minutes 53 seconds of pure speech at 140
words per minute — but a patient interrupts, and a candidate who greets, checks understanding, hands
over the sheet and answers one question will overrun five minutes comfortably; nothing here can be cut
for content, so the compression is in phrasing, and the three items that must survive intact are the airway
warning, the analgesia doses and the contact arrangements.
The five-minute run sheet
Time
The examiner does
What earns the mark

happens now?”

Checklists 5, 6 and 7. No brushing over

because pressure on a healing implant is
a leading cause of failure.

May ask: “When can I have a cigarette?”
Checklists 8 and 9. No smoking at all,
named as the single biggest cause of
failure; no alcohol; no strenuous exercise
or heavy lifting for three days. Then
numbness — normal for a few hours,
but ring me if any numbness is still
there tomorrow — followed immediately
by the airway warning: swelling under

4:00–5:00
“Is that everything?”
Checklist 10 and the close. The warning
signs that prompt a call, then records
(that instructions were given and
understood, and the prescription
written), what the patient is told in
writing (the sheet, the practice number
and the out-of-hours number), and
review — sutures out in a week, plus a
phone call this evening.
The compressed answer — what a strong candidate says in five minutes
“That all went to plan — all four implants are in. This was a bigger procedure than a single implant, so let
me talk you through what to expect, and you will have all of it in writing as well.
Bleeding. A bit of oozing today is normal, and it looks worse than it is because it mixes with saliva. If it
bleeds, bite firmly on the gauze I have given you for twenty minutes without checking it. Do not rinse at
all today.
Swelling and bruising. Because we have worked on both sides, expect more swelling than you would
get with one implant, and expect bruising that may spread down towards your jawline and neck over a
few days. That is normal and it settles. Swelling is usually worst at two to three days and then improves.
Hold a cold pack against the outside of your face, twenty minutes on and twenty minutes off, for the first
day, and sleep with an extra pillow tonight.
Pain. Take ibuprofen four hundred milligrams with food, up to four times a day, and paracetamol one
gram, up to four times a day. You can take them together, and together they work better than either on
its own. Take your first dose now, before the numbness wears off — do not wait for it to start hurting.
Please avoid aspirin.
Medicines I have given you. Finish the whole course of antibiotics. Start the mouthwash tomorrow, twice
a day for two weeks — hold it in your mouth gently, do not swill it hard.
Cleaning. Brush all your other teeth normally, but do not brush over the stitches until I tell you it is safe.
Keeping the rest of your mouth clean matters more than usual just now.
Eating. Soft food for the first week — you have stitches right across the front, so nothing you have to bite
or chew hard. Nothing hot today. Drink plenty, but no straws.
Your denture. Leave it out completely for the next forty-eight hours. Then bring it in to me and I will
ease it and put a soft lining in so it does not press on the implants. Please do not wear it until I have done
that — pressure on a healing implant is one of the main reasons they fail. And from now on, leave it out
at night.
Smoking, alcohol and exercise. No smoking at all — smoking is the single biggest thing that would
make these fail. No alcohol, and no hard exercise or heavy lifting for at least three days, because that can
start the bleeding again.
Numbness. Your lip and chin will feel numb from the injection for a few hours. If any numbness is still
there tomorrow morning, ring me — that is important and I need to know straight away.

osce.title: Three interim prostheses: resin-bonded bridge, spoon denture and Essix retainer
osce.text:
OSCE 56 — Three interim prostheses: resin-bonded bridge, spoon denture and Essix retainer
The three interim prostheses — simulated illustration, not a clinical image
Blueprint: differentiate between the treatment options for tooth replacement; decipher the differences between removable and fixed prostheses;
plan the type of prosthesis during the initial planning.
EQUIPMENT
examples of a resin-bonded bridge, a spoon denture, and an Essix (vacuum-formed) retainer with a pontic tooth; a model
of an anterior edentulous space; photographs.
CANDIDATE INSTRUCTIONS
Describe these three interim prostheses. Give the advantages and disadvantages of each, and state which you would use for
a patient awaiting an implant at the UR1 following extraction and ridge preservation.
DIRECTION OF THOUGHT
Describe →compare →choose, and justify the choice against the clinical situation. The decisive clinical
criterion in an implant case is whether the prosthesis loads the healing site. Say that early and use it as your
organising principle.

MODEL ANSWER
“1. Resin-bonded bridge (adhesive bridge / bonded pontic). A pontic supported by one or more
thin retainer wings bonded to the enamel of an adjacent tooth — for a single anterior unit, the
evidence favours a cantilever design with a single retainer, because fixed-fixed designs debond
at one retainer and allow undetected caries.
Advantages: fixed, so the patient is never without a tooth; excellent aesthetics; applies no pressure
to the healing ridge, which is its decisive advantage over the other two; comfortable; no palatal
coverage; good speech; minimal or no tooth preparation, confined to enamel; well documented,
with good survival for single anterior units. Disadvantages: needs a suitable abutment tooth with
suﬀicient sound enamel and adequate occlusal clearance; may debond, particularly in deep overbite
or parafunction; metal retainer may cause slight greying of the abutment tooth; higher cost and
requires laboratory work, so not immediate; unsuitable where there is heavy occlusal loading on the
pontic; and it may need modification when the implant is restored.
2. Spoon denture. A simple acrylic removable prosthesis with the pontic supported by a ‘spoon’-
shaped palatal acrylic plate that does not engage the teeth with clasps.
Advantages: cheap and quick; easily made and easily added to or modified; no preparation of any
tooth; useful when several teeth may be lost sequentially; can be relieved over a graft. Disadvantages:
poor retention and stability — it relies on the palatal vault and muscular control, so it can dislodge
in function and speech; may traumatise the healing site, so it must be generously relieved; palatal
coverage can cause gagging and affects taste and speech; unsuitable in the mandible; poor patient
acceptance; and, if under-relieved, it presses directly on the ridge, which is exactly what must be
avoided over a graft.
3. Essix retainer (vacuum-formed retainer with a pontic). A clear thermoplastic vacuum-formed
appliance covering the arch, with a denture tooth or composite added at the missing site.
Advantages: very quick and cheap, often same-day; excellent immediate aesthetics; no palatal cov-
erage; retentive because it grips the whole arch; easily relieved over the surgical site; can double
as a retainer; useful as a short-term aesthetic solution after extraction. Disadvantages: full occlusal
coverage, so there is no tooth contact when it is worn and it cannot be worn while eating; wears,
cracks and discolours; not durable beyond a few months; hygiene is poor if worn continuously; can
cause occlusal changes and intrusion if worn full-time for a long period; and, as with the spoon
denture, it can press on the ridge if not relieved.
My choice for this case. For a UR1 site after extraction and ridge preservation, my first choice is the
resin-bonded bridge or bonded pontic, because it is the only one of the three that applies no load
to the healing ridge, it is fixed so the patient does not have to remove anything, and the aesthetics
are the best of the three — which matters in an upper central incisor.
If a bonded bridge is not possible — an unsuitable abutment tooth, a deep overbite, cost, or the need
for something on the day of surgery — I would provide an Essix retainer with a pontic immediately,
generously relieved over the site, and warn the patient not to wear it while eating; and I would
consider converting to a bonded pontic once the site has settled.
I would reserve the spoon denture for situations where several teeth are being lost sequentially and
I need something I can add to repeatedly, and I would relieve it heavily and warn the patient about
pressure.
Whatever I use, I would review it at one week, check for pressure on the site with pressure-indicating
paste, and adjust it as swelling and healing change the contour.”
EXAMINER CHECKLIST
1. Describes the RBB correctly, including cantilever design
2. RBB advantages and disadvantages
3. Describes the spoon denture correctly
4. Spoon denture advantages and disadvantages
5. Describes the Essix retainer correctly
6. Essix advantages and disadvantages, including that it cannot be worn while eating
7. Identifies loading of the healing site as the decisive criterion
8. Makes a clear choice with justification
9. States a fallback and the circumstances for it

10. Review, pressure check and adjustment
See also OSCE 45 (denture relief and relining) and SOE cases 1 and 2.
Running this station to time
Time check. The model answer in this part is 636 words, 4 minutes 33 seconds at 140 words per minute —
which sounds survivable until you add the examiner’s instruction, the handling of three appliances and
the inevitable “why?”, at which point the honest delivery time is well past 7 minutes; the fix is a fixed
60-second frame per prosthesis — what it is, its one decisive advantage, its one decisive disadvantage —
then 60 seconds for the choice, then the close.
The five-minute run sheet
Time
The examiner does
What earns the mark

and disadvantages, and tell me which
you would use for a UR1 awaiting an

“So which would you use for this patient,
and why?”

again as the decisive criterion, a clear
single choice (resin-bonded bridge or
bonded pontic) with justification tied to
the UR1 and the ridge preservation, and
a named fallback with the
circumstances that trigger it (Essix on
the day of surgery if the abutment is
unsuitable, the overbite is deep, or cost
forbids).
4:30–5:00
“How will you follow this up?”
Checklist 10 — records (which appliance,
the relief provided, the instructions
given), what the patient is told (do not
eat in the Essix; report any pressure or
ulceration), and review at one week
with pressure-indicating paste and
adjustment as swelling settles.
The compressed answer — what a strong candidate says in five minutes
“Before I describe them, the criterion that decides this case: in an implant patient the question is whether
the prosthesis loads the healing site. I will use that to organise all three.
First, the resin-bonded bridge. A pontic carried on one or more thin metal wings bonded to the enamel
of an adjacent tooth; for a single anterior unit the evidence favours a cantilever with a single retainer,

osce.title: Severe periodontal bone loss and furcation involvement at 16 and 17
osce.text:
OSCE 57 — Severe periodontal bone loss and furcation involvement at 16 and 17
Blueprint: interpret radiographic findings; assess the need for referral on the basis of clinical findings; arrive at a prognosis of the remaining teeth
and the impact on the treatment options for tooth replacement.
EQUIPMENT
a periapical radiograph of the 16 and 17 showing severe horizontal and angular bone loss; axial CBCT slices showing
furcation involvement of both teeth; a Nabers probe; a periodontal chart.

CANDIDATE INSTRUCTIONS
Report these images. Discuss the management of these teeth and the effect of your findings on the replacement of the teeth.
DIRECTION OF THOUGHT
Three parts, and the third carries most of the marks: report →manage the teeth →what this means for
replacement. The furcation finding is the hinge: grade II–III furcation involvement in maxillary molars carries
a poor prognosis, and the interradicular bone that is being destroyed is exactly the bone an implant would need.
MODEL ANSWER
“Report. A periapical of the upper right molar region. I would state the image type and its diagnostic
quality, then report the whole image before the region of interest.
At the 16 and 17 there is severe bone loss — I would quantify it as a proportion of root length,
and describe whether it is horizontal or angular and whether it is generalised or localised. I would
look at the furcation regions, the periodontal ligament space, the periapical status of both teeth, any
existing restorations and caries, the relationship to the maxillary sinus floor and whether the sinus
is pneumatised, and the bone level on the adjacent 15.
The axial CBCT slices confirm furcation involvement. In the maxilla each molar has three roots and
therefore three furcation entrances — buccal, mesiopalatal and distopalatal — and cross-sectional
imaging lets me see which are involved and how far through. I would state that CBCT is more sen-
sitive than a periapical for furcation involvement, but that it must have been individually justified
and the whole volume reported.
Clinically I would need: full six-point charting with recession so I can calculate attachment loss;
furcation grading with a Nabers probe using the Hamp classification — grade I under 3 mm hor-
izontally, grade II more than 3 mm but not through-and-through, grade III through-and-through;
mobility; bleeding and suppuration; sensibility testing of both teeth; assessment for cracks; plaque
scores; and a full-mouth BPE to establish whether this is localised or generalised. I would then
assign a stage and grade under the 2017 classification.
Management of the teeth. The options are: - Non-surgical periodontal therapy and reassessment
— always the first step, whatever the eventual plan. - Retain with periodontal surgery — furcation
surgery, tunnel preparation or root resection. Grade III furcation with mobility carries a poor long-
term prognosis; root resection in maxillary molars is a Complex procedure with modest survival,
and I would not offer it as a general dentist with an interest in implants. - Extraction of one or both
teeth. - Referral to a periodontist for an opinion before extracting, which I would consider if there
is any prospect of retention.
My likely conclusion, with severe bone loss and confirmed furcation involvement in both molars,
is that both teeth have a poor to hopeless prognosis — but I would not extract before completing
cause-related therapy, reassessing, and having the conversation with the patient about the alterna-
tives.
The effect on replacement — and this is the important part.
1. The bone that is being lost is the bone an implant would need. Furcation involvement means
the interradicular bone is destroyed, so after extraction I should expect a deficient site, not a
simple socket.
2. Immediate implant placement is contraindicated here — there is active infection, and the in-
terradicular septum that would provide primary stability in a molar socket is exactly what the
disease has destroyed.
3. The sinus. The posterior maxilla pneumatises after tooth loss, and periodontal bone loss reduces
the residual height before I even start. I should measure the residual height beneath the sinus
on the CBCT. If it is more than 6 mm with a flat floor, a transcrestal elevation with simultaneous
placement is possible; 6 mm or less, or an oblique floor, indicates a lateral window, which is
outside my scope and would mean referral.
4. Ridge preservation at the time of extraction is therefore particularly valuable here, and I would
section the molars and remove the roots individually to preserve the buccal and palatal plates.

5. Timing. These are large sockets in infected sites; I would allow at least four to six months before
reassessing for implant placement.
6. The periodontal condition governs everything.
A history of periodontitis is the strongest
patient-level risk factor for peri-implantitis, so implants should not be planned until the
periodontal condition is stable by the EFP criteria and the patient has demonstrated compliance
with maintenance.
7. And replacement may not be necessary. If the 15 and the opposing teeth are sound, a shortened
dental arch to the second premolar is a legitimate and well-evidenced outcome that avoids sinus
surgery altogether. I would present that seriously, alongside a partial denture and implants.
On the SAC classification, implant replacement here would be at least Advanced, and Complex
if a lateral window or vertical augmentation were required — in which case I would refer, having
completed the periodontal treatment and the planning myself.”
EXAMINER CHECKLIST
1. Structured report of the whole image, then the region of interest
2. Quantifies bone loss and describes its pattern
3. States the three maxillary furcation entrances and grades with a Nabers probe/Hamp
4. States the CBCT justification and whole-volume reporting requirement
5. Clinical assessment listed, with staging and grading
6. Management options for the teeth, with a reasoned prognosis and appropriate referral
7. Links furcation destruction to the deficient future implant site
8. Rules out immediate placement and gives the reason
9. Sinus assessment against the 6 mm / flat floor threshold, with the referral implication
10. Ridge preservation, timing, the periodontal stability precondition, and offers the shortened dental arch

Nothing is done with the hands here, so every second is speech: findings as a list of clauses, and full
