osce.title: Buccal abscess on a lower implant-supported bridge, with no bone loss
osce.text:
OSCE 58 — Buccal abscess on a lower implant-supported bridge, with no bone loss
Blueprint: suggest appropriate management of complications relating to the provision of implant restorations; recognise clinical situations which
are unsafe or could lead to an adverse event; discuss appropriate management of common complications.
EQUIPMENT
a model or photograph of a mandibular implant-supported bridge with a buccal swelling and a sinus/fistula; a medical
history card stating no relevant medical history; a periapical radiograph. Additional written information given during the
station: there is no bone loss.
CANDIDATE INSTRUCTIONS
This patient has a lower implant-supported bridge and presents with a buccal abscess. The medical history is clear. Discuss
your management.
DIRECTION OF THOUGHT
Build a differential before the extra information arrives, then say out loud how the “no bone loss” statement
changes it. That single sentence is the point of the station: it removes advanced peri-implantitis from the top

of your list and pushes you towards causes that do not destroy bone — a foreign body, residual cement, an
adjacent tooth, a leaking screw joint, or a non-cleansable prosthesis.
MODEL ANSWER
“First, the patient. Is she systemically unwell — fever, malaise, lymphadenopathy, trismus, diﬀiculty
swallowing or breathing? A spreading infection in the floor of the mouth is an airway emergency
and takes priority over everything else. Assuming she is systemically well, I proceed to assessment.
History. When did it start, is it getting worse, is there pain, discharge or a bad taste, has it happened
before, and does it come and go? When was the bridge fitted, by whom, is it screw- or cement-
retained, and have there been previous problems such as a loose screw? What maintenance has she
had? Any food packing or diﬀiculty cleaning? Medical history and smoking — the card says the
history is clear.
Examination. Extra-oral swelling, lymph nodes, temperature. Intra-orally: the site, size and charac-
ter of the swelling; whether it is fluctuant; whether there is a sinus tract, which I would trace with a
gutta-percha point and radiograph; peri-implant probing at six sites with a plastic probe at gentle
force, recording depth, bleeding and suppuration; mobility of the prosthesis and, separately, of
each implant — I would remove the bridge if it is retrievable, which is the single most useful step in
this station; the cleansability of the bridge, the emergence profile and the embrasures; any residual
cement; and sensibility testing and periodontal probing of the adjacent natural teeth.
Radiographs. A standardised paralleling periapical of the implants and the adjacent teeth, com-
pared with any baseline. A small field-of-view CBCT if the periapical is inconclusive.
Differential diagnosis before the extra information. Peri-implantitis with abscess formation; resid-
ual submucosal cement; a foreign body or chronic food impaction under a pontic; an endodontic
or periodontal lesion of an adjacent natural tooth draining buccally; retrograde peri-implantitis
from residual pathology at the site; a retained root fragment or residual cyst; a fractured implant
or abutment, or a loose or fractured screw allowing bacterial leakage through the microgap; and a
soft tissue lesion unrelated to the implants.
Now, given that there is no bone loss — that changes my differential substantially. Peri-implantitis
by definition requires bone loss beyond initial crestal remodelling, so if the bone levels are stable
against baseline, this is not established peri-implantitis. What remains, in order of likelihood:
1. Residual submucosal cement or another foreign body, producing a localised soft tissue abscess
without yet having caused bone loss. Note that a non-radiopaque cement will not appear on
the radiograph, so absence on the film does not exclude it.
2. Chronic food impaction beneath a pontic or in an inaccessible embrasure, particularly with an
over-contoured or ridge-lap prosthesis.
3. An odontogenic infection from an adjacent natural tooth — a periapical abscess or a periodontal
abscess — draining buccally and appearing to arise from the implant. This is why I test the
adjacent teeth.
4. A loose or fractured abutment screw, allowing bacterial colonisation of the internal connection
and leakage through the microgap, which can produce recurrent soft tissue infection with little
or no bone change.
5. Retrograde peri-implantitis or residual pathology, though I would expect an apical radiolu-
cency.
6. A soft tissue lesion — a mucocele, a fistula from another source, or rarely a neoplasm; anything
that does not resolve requires biopsy or referral.
Immediate management. Establish drainage — through the sulcus with a probe, or by incision
of a fluctuant swelling under local anaesthetic — and irrigate. Remove the prosthesis if it is screw-
retained; this gives access, allows me to inspect for cement and to check the screws, and often resolves
the problem in itself. Antibiotics are not the primary treatment and I would prescribe them only
if there were systemic signs, spreading infection or immunocompromise; drainage and removal of
the cause is the treatment. Analgesia. Review at 48 hours.
Definitive management, according to cause. - Cement or foreign body: meticulous removal un-
der magnification with titanium or PEEK instruments, knotted floss drawn circumferentially, and
glycine air-polishing; then replace or modify the prosthesis to a cleansable, screw-retained design

so it cannot recur. - Food impaction / poor contour: recontour or remake with open, cleansable
embrasures and a non-ridge-lap pontic form; re-instruct with correctly sized interdental brushes
and superfloss. - Adjacent tooth: treat the tooth — endodontic or periodontal — as indicated. -
Loose or fractured screw: remove the prosthesis, replace the screw with a new one, inspect for
component or implant fracture, identify and correct the cause (occlusion, cantilever, non-passive
fit), torque to the manufacturer’s value and re-torque at ten minutes. - Persistent or unexplained:
consider microbiological sampling, further imaging, and referral; any lesion that does not resolve
requires biopsy or specialist opinion.
Then prevention and governance. Establish a new baseline radiograph after treatment; place her
on 3- to 5-monthly supportive therapy with peri-implant probing at every visit; record the diagnosis,
the cause, what was done and what was said; and, if this arose from the original prosthetic design,
treat it as a significant event and review my own use of screw retention and cleansable contours.”
EXAMINER CHECKLIST
1. Excludes systemic illness and airway compromise first
2. Structured history including retention type and previous problems
3. Examination including peri-implant probing with a plastic probe, sinus tracing, and separate assessment of implant
versus prosthesis mobility
4. Tests the adjacent natural teeth
5. Radiographs of implants and adjacent teeth, compared with baseline
6. Comprehensive differential offered
7. Explicitly revises the differential when told there is no bone loss, and states why peri-implantitis is excluded
8. Removes the prosthesis and establishes drainage; antibiotics reserved for systemic/spreading infection
9. Cause-specific definitive management, including redesign for cleansability
10. New baseline radiograph, supportive therapy interval, records and governance
Extended by practice stations OSCE 38 (removing a cemented crown and residual cement), OSCE 37 (fractured screw retrieval) and SOE cases 4
and 40.
Running this station to time
Time check. The model answer is 1,136 words, 8 minutes 7 seconds at 140 words per minute — the longest
overrun in the section, with more than three minutes to lose. Nothing is done with the hands, so all of it
is speech, and the cut is made by naming each differential in a single clause rather than a sentence each,
and by holding whole sentences for one thing only: what changes when the examiner says there is no
bone loss. That revision is the station.

lymphadenopathy, trismus, diﬀiculty swallowing or breathing? A spreading infection in the floor of

history is clear; assuming she is also systemically well, I proceed.”

whom, whether it is screw- or cement-retained, and whether there have been previous problems such
as a loose screw. Then maintenance, food packing, whether she can actually clean it, and smoking.
Extra-orally, swelling, nodes and temperature. Intra-orally: the character of the swelling and whether it
is fluctuant, and if there is a sinus tract I would trace it with a gutta-percha point and radiograph it —

recording depth, bleeding and suppuration. Then two things separately: the mobility of the prosthesis,
and the mobility of each implant — and if the bridge is retrievable I would remove it, which is the single
most useful step available to me. I would assess the cleansability, emergence profile and embrasures and
look specifically for residual cement. And I would sensibility test and periodontally probe the adjacent
natural teeth — because the source may not be an implant at all.”
Q: Radiographs? “A standardised paralleling periapical of the implants and the adjacent teeth, com-

Q: Your differential? “Peri-implantitis with abscess formation; residual submucosal cement; a foreign
body or chronic food impaction under a pontic; an endodontic or periodontal lesion of an adjacent
natural tooth draining buccally; retrograde peri-implantitis, a retained root fragment or a residual cyst;
a loose or fractured screw or component allowing bacterial leakage through the microgap; and a soft
tissue lesion unrelated to the implants.”
Q: [Handed the card] There is no bone loss. “That changes my differential substantially, and I would
say so. Peri-implantitis by definition requires bone loss beyond initial crestal remodelling — so if the
bone levels are stable against baseline, this is not established peri-implantitis, and it drops off the top of
my list. What remains, in order:
First, residual submucosal cement or another foreign body, producing a localised soft tissue abscess
before it has caused any bone change. And the trap: a non-radiopaque cement will not show on the film,
so its absence on the radiograph does not exclude it.
Second, chronic food impaction beneath a pontic or in an inaccessible embrasure — particularly with an
over-contoured or ridge-lap prosthesis.
Third, an odontogenic infection from an adjacent natural tooth — periapical or periodontal — draining
buccally and appearing to arise from the implant. That is exactly why I tested those teeth.

Fourth, a loose or fractured abutment screw, allowing colonisation of the internal connection and leakage
through the microgap, which can produce recurrent soft tissue infection with little or no bone change at
all.
Fifth, retrograde peri-implantitis or residual pathology, though I would expect an apical radiolucency.
Sixth, a soft tissue lesion — a mucocele, a fistula from elsewhere, rarely a neoplasm — and anything that
does not resolve requires biopsy or referral.”
Q: Immediate management? “Drainage — through the sulcus with a probe, or incision of a fluctuant
swelling under local anaesthetic — and irrigation. Remove the prosthesis if it is screw-retained: it
gives me access, lets me inspect for cement and check the screws, and frequently resolves the problem in
itself. Antibiotics are not the primary treatment — I would prescribe only for systemic signs, spreading
infection or immunocompromise. Drainage and removal of the cause is the treatment. Analgesia, and
review at 48 hours.”
Q
And definitively? “By cause. Cement or foreign body:** meticulous removal under magnification with titanium or
PEEK instruments, knotted floss drawn circumferentially, glycine air-polishing — then modify or remake the prosthesis
to a cleansable, screw-retained design so it cannot recur. Food impaction or poor contour: remake with open
embrasures and a non-ridge-lap pontic, and re-instruct with sized interdental brushes. Adjacent tooth: treat the tooth.
Loose or fractured screw: replace it, inspect for component fracture, correct the cause — occlusion, cantilever or
non-passive fit — and re-torque at ten minutes. Persistent or unexplained: microbiology, further imaging, **biopsy or
referral.
Then a new baseline radiograph after treatment, 3- to 5-monthly supportive therapy with peri-implant
probing at every visit, the diagnosis, cause and advice recorded — and if this arose from the original
prosthetic design, a significant event review of my own use of screw retention and cleansable contours.”
Marking priority when the clock beats the candidate
Ask for these first (the six that carry the station): 7 the differential explicitly revised on “no bone
loss”, with peri-implantitis excluded by definition · 8 prosthesis removed and drainage established;
antibiotics reserved · 4 the adjacent natural teeth tested · 3 plastic-probe probing, sinus traced, implant
mobility assessed separately from prosthesis mobility · 6 a comprehensive differential offered before the
extra information · 9 cause-specific management, including redesign for cleansability.
Accept these late or on prompting: 1 systemic illness and airway excluded first · 2 structured history
including retention type and previous problems · 5 radiographs of implants and adjacent teeth against
baseline · 10 new baseline, supportive therapy interval, records and governance.
The commonest way five minutes is wasted here: answering the word “abscess” with a peri-implantitis
protocol — surgical debridement, decontamination, implantoplasty, regeneration — before the extra in-
formation arrives, and then failing to unwind it when it does. Checklist 7 is not scored for silently
changing course; it is scored for saying “that changes my differential, and here is why.” The second loss
is forgetting that the source may be a tooth: checklist 4 is a discrete mark, and the adjacent teeth are the
commonest thing a candidate never mentions. The third is reaching for antibiotics — amoxicillin as the
opening move is a marked-down answer, because drainage and removal of the cause is the treatment.
The fourth is stopping at drainage: checklists 9 and 10 are the redesign, the new baseline, the recall
interval and the significant event, and a bridge that cannot be cleaned will simply present again.

soe.title: The bruxist, the posterior maxilla and the
soe.text:
SOE Case 1 — The bruxist, the posterior maxilla and the
occlusal scheme
THE CASE
59-year-old male. Clear medical history. Recent extraction of the 15 and 16 for cracked teeth. The 46 is over-
erupted. OPG shows generalised attritive wear and flattened condylar contours suggestive of bruxism. Cross-
sectional CBCT slices are provided: at the 15, ridge width is 8 mm coronally, 10 mm apically, with 20 mm of
height; at the 16, there is a marked buccal sinus drop with an oblique floor and a pendulum-shaped, “key-
ring” cross-section — approximately 6 mm buccally and 12 mm palatally.
Pace: one structured opening of about 60 seconds, then roughly 35 questions in the remaining 14 minutes. Nothing after the opening earns you
more than a few seconds of thought.
Opening — the 60-second presentation
Q
Present this case.
“A 59-year-old man, medically fit, who has recently lost the 15 and 16 to cracked teeth in a mouth showing
generalised attritive wear and flattened condyles — so my working diagnosis is bruxism, and the cracks are
a symptom of it rather than bad luck. The 46 has over-erupted into the 16 space. Radiographically these are
two quite different sites: the 15 has generous bone in all three dimensions, while the 16 shows a pendulum or
key-ring cross-section with an oblique, buccally dipping sinus floor giving about 6 mm buccally against 12 mm
palatally. My working position is that the 15 is straightforward and the 16 is where the decision lies. What I need
to establish is whether there is restorative space above the over-erupted 46, whether the 16 can be implanted
without a lateral window, and how I protect whatever I place from his parafunction.”
Domain 1 — Clinical interpretation and reasoning
Chain: the anatomical groundwork
Q
Describe the anatomy of the maxillary sinus.
“A pyramidal air-filled cavity in the body of the maxilla, lined by respiratory epithelium. Its base is the lat-
eral nasal wall, its apex points into the zygomatic process, its roof is the orbital floor carrying the infraorbital
nerve, its floor is the alveolar process — often lowest around the first molar — and its anterior wall carries the
infraorbital foramen. It drains through the ostium in the middle meatus, high on the medial wall, which is
why drainage is against gravity.”
Q
What is the Schneiderian membrane, and what thickness concerns you?
“The mucoperiosteal lining of the sinus — thin ciliated respiratory epithelium with periosteum, typically under
1 mm. A very thin membrane tears easily; a membrane thickened beyond about 2 mm suggests inflammation or
an odontogenic source and warrants investigation first. Complete opacification, an air-fluid level, or anything
obstructing the osteomeatal complex changes the plan, because an obstructed sinus becomes an infected one.”
Q
What is a septum, and why do you look for one?
“A Underwood’s septum is a bony ridge projecting from the sinus floor, commonest between the second pre-
molar and first molar. It matters because it compartmentalises the sinus, makes membrane elevation far more
likely to tear, and complicates any window design. Finding one on the CBCT is often the point at which I decide
the case is not mine.”
Q
What bone quality do you expect in the posterior maxilla, and what follows?
“Characteristically D3 or D4 on Misch — thin cortex with fine trabecular bone. That means poor primary
stability, so I under-prepare the osteotomy, stop a drill short, avoid tapping, and lean towards conventional
loading rather than early or immediate. It is the opposite problem to the anterior mandible, where the risk is
overheating dense bone.”

Chain: reading this patient
Q
Why did these teeth crack?
“Heavily restored teeth carrying parafunctional load. That matters for what comes next, because an implant has
no periodontal ligament — no proprioceptive protective reflex and only 3 to 5 micrometres of axial movement
against 25 to 100 for a tooth. So parafunction is a mechanical risk factor, not a biological one: I expect screw
loosening, chipping and component fracture rather than loss of integration.”
Q
What clinical signs would confirm the bruxism?
“Wear facets that match in excursion, masseteric hypertrophy, linea alba, a scalloped tongue, cervical abfraction
and repeatedly fractured restorations. Historically: morning jaw stiffness or headache, and a partner’s report
of night-time grinding, which is more reliable than the patient’s own account.”
Q
Interpret the cross-section at the 16.
“The key-ring or pendulum shape means the sinus floor is oblique and dips buccally, so usable height is asym-
metric — around 6 mm buccally against 12 mm palatally. An implant in the correct prosthetic position meets
far less bone buccally than palatally. A transcrestal elevation is unreliable here, because the ITI decision tree
assumes a flat floor and more than 6 mm of residual height; an oblique floor tips the osteotome and invites
perforation.”
Q
And the 15?
“Generous — 8 mm coronal width, 10 mm apical, 20 mm height. That comfortably accommodates a standard-
diameter implant with more than 1 mm of bone circumferentially, and the height means the sinus is not a
factor. Surgically this site is unremarkable; the challenge at the 15 is prosthetic, not surgical.”
Q
What further information do you want?
“Mounted study casts to measure the restorative space against the over-erupted 46; a full occlusal analysis in
centric relation and in excursion; sensibility and periodontal status of the 14, 17 and 47; confirmation of sinus
health, membrane thickness and septa on the CBCT; and, most importantly, what he actually wants — function,
appearance, or simply to avoid a denture.”
Domain 2 — Clinical decision making and treatment planning
Chain: the occlusal groundwork
Q
Name the recognised occlusal schemes.
“Mutually protected occlusion, also called canine-guided; group function; and bilateral balanced occlusion.
Each describes how load is distributed in intercuspation and, separately, in excursion — and the distinction
between those two states is the thing to keep clear.”
Q
Describe mutually protected occlusion.
“In intercuspation the posterior teeth take the axial load and protect the anterior teeth, which are held out of
heavy contact. In excursion the canine guidance discludes the posterior teeth, protecting them from lateral
load. It is my default wherever a sound natural canine exists, and it is the scheme I would provide here.”
Q
When would you choose group function instead?
“Where the canine is periodontally compromised, worn flat, or is itself an implant. Then I would distribute the
excursive load across several working-side posterior teeth rather than concentrate it on one unit — particularly
on an implant, which cannot feel the overload and cannot move away from it.”
Q
Why is bilateral balanced occlusion wrong for a fixed implant restoration?

“Because it deliberately creates non-working side contacts, and those generate the largest bending moments of
any contact in the mouth. It exists to stop a complete denture tipping — a free body needs contact on both sides.
A fixed implant restoration is not a free body, so balance buys nothing and costs a great deal mechanically.”
Chain: the options for these two sites
Q
What are the options here?
“No treatment, accepting a shortened arch — legitimate in principle, but he has a two-unit gap and an over-
erupting 46 that will worsen. Removable partial denture — cheap and non-surgical, poorly tolerated for two
units in a bruxist. Conventional bridge from 14 to 17 — a long span, heavy loading and a questionable abutment.
Implants — straightforward at the 15; at the 16 the sub-options are a short implant, a transcrestal elevation, a
lateral window, or restoring the 15 alone.”
Q
Which do you choose?
“A standard implant at the 15 and a wide, short implant at the 16 using the buccal height available. Systematic
reviews show short implants of 6 mm or less in the posterior jaws achieve survival comparable to longer
implants placed with augmentation over three to five years, with fewer biological complications and less
morbidity — and it keeps the case within my competence.”
Q
You have chosen a short implant — argue against yourself.
“The honest counter-argument is the crown-to-implant ratio: a short implant under a tall crown in a bruxist
has an unfavourable lever arm, and the medium-term data on short implants specifically in parafunction is thin.
Someone who augments would say I am accepting a mechanical compromise to avoid a procedure. I mitigate
it with a wide diameter, a narrow occlusal table, no cantilever and a splint — but I accept the trade-off is real.”
Q
Would you splint the two implants?
“Yes — joined as two units, screw-retained so it can be retrieved. Splinting a short implant to a standard one
shares load, which matters in a bruxist. The cost is cleansability, so I would design the connector and emergence
profile to admit an interdental brush and would show him how to use it before the restoration is fitted.”
Q
You mentioned splitting — is a ridge split relevant here?
“No. Ridge splitting addresses horizontal deficiency; it needs about 3 mm of width with cancellous bone be-
tween two cortical plates, and is far more predictable in the maxilla than the mandible. Here the width is
adequate at both sites and the deficiency at the 16 is vertical. It is the wrong operation for this problem.”
Q
SAC classification?
“Site 15: surgically Straightforward, prosthodontically Straightforward to Advanced because of the parafunc-
tion. Site 16: surgically Advanced because of the oblique sinus floor and the short-implant decision; prosthodon-
tically Advanced for the crown-to-implant ratio, the parafunction and the opposing over-eruption.”
Q
What is beyond your competence here, and when would you refer?
“A lateral window sinus elevation is outside the scope of a general dentist with an interest in implants, and so is
vertical block grafting. If the CBCT showed a septum, established sinus pathology, or if intra-operatively I met
a frank perforation, I would stop and refer rather than improvise. I would also refer if he insisted on treating
the 16 by augmentation.”
Q
What about the over-erupted 46?
“It is dealt with before the definitive restoration, never after. I measure the space on mounted casts, then in
escalating order: enameloplasty; a new crown at reduced height, which may require elective endodontics;
orthodontic intrusion; or accepting a compromised scheme. I would also consider modest crest reduction
at the 16 if it gains space and a flatter platform — provided it does not cost me height I need.”

Q
What would you tell him, in your own words to him?
“ ‘Your teeth cracked because you grind, and the grinding is not going away — so the new teeth are being built
to survive it rather than to be perfect. The front site is straightforward. The back site has your sinus sitting low
over it, so I plan to use a shorter, wider implant there; if when I open it the sinus is not where I expect, I will
stop and just do the front one rather than take a risk. You will need a hard night guard for as long as you have
these, and screws and porcelain will need attention over the years — that is maintenance, not failure.’ ”
Domain 3 — Decision making in relation to treatment procedures
Chain: implant-protective occlusion
Q
Define implant-protective occlusion.
“The deliberate modification of the occlusal scheme to compensate for the absence of a periodontal ligament
around an implant. It is not a separate scheme — it sits inside whichever scheme the natural dentition dictates,
and modifies only how the implant restorations themselves are contacted.”
Q
What is its biological basis?
“An implant moves about 3 to 5 micrometres axially against 25 to 100 for a tooth, and 10 to 50 laterally against
56 to 108. A tooth moves immediately and in two phases; an implant moves gradually and linearly. And there
are no periodontal mechanoreceptors, so the reflex that makes a patient unload a painful tooth is absent — the
tactile threshold is far higher, and only osseoperception from periosteal, muscular and joint receptors remains.”
Q
What are the practical rules that follow?
“Light centric contacts — the restoration holds shimstock only on heavy clenching, roughly 25 to 30 micrometres
lighter than the adjacent teeth. Contacts centralised over the long axis, with a narrowed occlusal table and
reduced cusp inclination, converting lateral force to axial. No excursive contact on the implant where a natural
tooth can guide. No non-working interferences. No cantilevers. And never connect an implant rigidly to a
natural tooth.”
Q
And what changes specifically because he is a bruxist?
“More or wider implants rather than fewer; monolithic rather than layered ceramic to remove the chipping
interface; splinting where it is cleansable; a hard full-coverage splint; and explicit consent to a higher rate of
mechanical complications with a cost attached. I would also shorten the recall interval.”
Chain: the procedure
Q
Take me through the surgery at the 15.
“Pre-operative chlorhexidine rinse, aseptic technique. Buccal and palatal infiltration. Mid-crestal incision from
the 14 to the 17 with intrasulcular extension and a distal relieving incision if access demands it; full-thickness
flap raised atraumatically. Graded drilling under copious sterile saline with intermittent pressure, direction
indicator check, and — because this is D3 bone — I stop one drill short to under-prepare and raise primary
stability.”
Q
And at the 16?
“I plan the exact buccal height from the CBCT and treat that, not the palatal measurement, as my working depth.
Drill short of the floor, verify with a depth gauge and a periapical, and place a wide, short implant. I would
not attempt to gain height with an osteotome against an oblique floor — that is precisely the anatomy in which
transcrestal elevation fails.”
Q
You breach the membrane. What do you do?
“Stop drilling and assess. Valsalva to test the membrane: no air or bubbling and I may proceed, placing a small
collagen membrane and graft over an intact elevation. If there is a frank perforation, I abandon that site, close
primarily, place the patient on antibiotics and decongestant advice, and re-plan — either restoring the 15 alone
or referring. Improvising a repair is beyond my scope.”

Q
What insertion torque do you want, and what if you achieve 15 Ncm at the 16?
“25 to 45 Ncm. At 15 Ncm with a short implant in D4 bone I would not load early. I would submerge it, extend
healing to four to six months, and re-assess with resonance frequency analysis before restoring — an ISQ above
70 for confidence, and a falling ISQ telling me it is failing.”
Q
One stage or two?
“One stage with healing abutments where primary stability is good, because it avoids a second surgery and
avoids repeatedly disrupting the mucosal seal. Two stage at the 16 if stability is marginal, if I have grafted, or if
soft tissue closure is compromised. I am content to run a one-stage 15 alongside a submerged 16.”
Q
Describe the restorative phase.
“Conventional loading — no immediate or early loading in a bruxist with soft posterior maxillary bone.
Implant-level open-tray impression with splinted copings since the units are being joined, in polyether in a
custom tray. Screw-retained monolithic zirconia on titanium bases. Occlusion set to implant-protective rules,
then a hard full-coverage acrylic night guard at fit.”
Q
Why monolithic zirconia rather than layered porcelain?
“Because the commonest technical complication in a parafunctional patient is chipping of the veneering ce-
ramic, and monolithic material removes that interface entirely. The trade-off is aesthetics and wear of the
opposing dentition, but in a posterior quadrant opposing a heavily worn dentition I accept that. I would polish
rather than glaze any adjusted surface.”
Q
How would you manage the bruxism itself?
“As a condition in its own right. Characterise it from the signs and history. Identify contributors — stress, caf-
feine, alcohol, smoking, recreational drugs, SSRIs. Screen for obstructive sleep apnoea — snoring, witnessed
apnoeas, daytime somnolence — and refer to his GP if present, because sleep bruxism is associated with it and
a mandibular advancement device must never precede that assessment.”
Q
Describe the splint you would provide.
“A hard, heat-cured or milled full-coverage acrylic splint, usually maxillary, covering every tooth so none can
over-erupt. Adjusted to even bilateral contacts in intercuspation with smooth canine guidance so the posterior
teeth disclude in excursion. I review its wear pattern at every recall — it is the only objective measure I have of
the force he generates, and it warns me when the restorations are at rising risk.”
Domain 4 — Interpretation and problem solving of clinical outcomes
Chain: what goes wrong and how you answer it
Q
What will go wrong, and roughly when?
“In order of likelihood: screw loosening; ceramic or acrylic chipping; wear of the night guard; and, if hygiene
lapses, peri-implant mucositis. Less likely but more serious: failure of the short implant at the 16 during
healing, and sinusitis if the membrane was compromised. Mechanical complications dominate in this patient
— that is the shape of the risk.”
Q
He returns at 18 months with a loose restoration and no pain. What do you do?
“I would not simply retighten. Remove the restoration, inspect the screw, the abutment and the implant con-
nection for damage, and exclude implant fracture — pain-free looseness can be a fractured screw or a fractured
fixture. Fit a new screw, find the cause — occlusion, an excursive interference or a non-passive fit — correct it,
torque to the manufacturer’s value and re-torque at ten minutes.”
Q
Your colleague would simply retighten it in five minutes. Why might they be right?

“Because a single early loosening after a torque that was never re-checked is often exactly what it appears to
be, and dismantling a joined screw-retained restoration carries its own risk of damaging the connection. If it
were the first episode, within months of fitting, with a passive fit I had verified myself and an occlusion I had
checked, retightening with a new screw is defensible. It is repetition that makes it negligent.”
Q
At three weeks he has unilateral nasal discharge and cheek pain. Differential and action?
“Acute sinusitis, most likely iatrogenic from the 16, against a displaced graft particle, an oro-antral commu-
nication, or a coincidental viral upper respiratory infection. I would examine for a communication, test with
Valsalva, image if indicated, prescribe according to local antimicrobial guidance with decongestant advice, and
refer to ENT if it fails to settle or recurs. And I would record it as a significant event.”
Q
What would you record?
“The consent discussion including the named material risks and the fallback plan; the CBCT justification under
IR(ME)R and the report; implant make, diameter, length, site and lot number; insertion torque and any ISQ;
the surgical detail including flap design and any membrane contact; the occlusal scheme prescribed and the
shimstock findings; the splint provision; baseline periapical radiographs and probing depths at fitting; and
the recall interval agreed.”
Q
How would you know this treatment had succeeded?
“Survival of both implants; marginal bone levels stable against the baseline taken at fitting; probing depths and
bleeding on probing acceptable with no suppuration; a stable, cleansable prosthesis; a splint that is being worn;
and his own report of comfort and function measured against what he told me at the start that he wanted.”
Q
Maintenance?
“Three to six monthly, at the shorter end for parafunction and a joined restoration. At each visit: plaque
and bleeding scores, six-point peri-implant probing with a plastic probe at gentle force, screw and prosthesis
check, night-guard wear assessment, and professional biofilm removal with titanium or plastic instruments.
Radiographs at one year, then only when clinically indicated.”
WATCH OUT
Ask yourself whether the problem in front of you is biological or mechanical — in this patient it is nearly always
mechanical, and saying so out loud buys you a sentence while you assemble the answer.
Running this case to time
Time check. The flow above holds 38 questions and about 1,905 words of model answer. At examination
pace — 140 words a minute, plus roughly five seconds for each question to be asked — that is a little under
seventeen minutes, so as written it overruns by nearly two. An examiner short of time drops the far end
of Domain 3 — bruxism as a condition in its own right, and the splint description — to protect Domain
4, where the marks in this case sit. If your answers run past thirty seconds you will still be discussing
occlusal schemes when the time ends.

The spine — the twelve answers to have ready if nothing else
1 Sinus anatomy and why drainage is against gravity · 2 Membrane thickness that concerns you, and

Where the marks are lost in this case

Skipping the occlusal groundwork. Domain 2 opens below the implant material. A candidate who
cannot distinguish the three schemes, or who explains balance without saying it exists to stop a denture

Forgetting the 46. The over-erupted 46 is dealt with before the definitive restoration, never after, and the
escalating order — enameloplasty, crown at reduced height, orthodontic intrusion — must be volunteered.
Unprompted, it turns a list of implants into a plan.

soe.title: Missing 22 in a patient who works in the
soe.text:
SOE Case 2 — Missing 22 in a patient who works in the
entertainment industry
Anterior view, interim retainer removed — simulated illustration, not a clinical image
The pre-extraction periapical of the 22 — simulated illustration, not a clinical image

CBCT at the 22 site — simulated illustration, not a clinical image
THE CASE
26-year-old who works in the entertainment industry as a television presenter. The 22 was lost 6 weeks ago.
She is currently wearing an Essix retainer with a pontic. The pre-extraction periapical showed external root
resorption in a virgin, unrestored tooth with an associated radiolucency. Clinically: a narrow ridge at 22; the 23
has a triangular crown form, the 21 rectangular; normal (medium/thick) biotype with adequate keratinised
gingiva. CBCT shows a buccal concavity at the site.
Pace: one structured opening of about 60 seconds, then roughly 37 questions in the remaining 13 minutes. Nothing after the opening earns you
more than a few seconds of thought.
Opening — the 60-second presentation
Q
Present this case.
“A 26-year-old television presenter who lost the 22 six weeks ago to external root resorption in an otherwise
virgin tooth. Her occupation puts her face on camera in high definition, so the aesthetic outcome is unusually
material to her, and that shapes both the consent conversation and my threshold for referral. The site has a
narrow ridge with a buccal concavity, a favourable medium-to-thick biotype with adequate keratinised tissue,
and a crown form discrepancy — a triangular 23 against a rectangular 21. My working position is that this is
an aesthetically demanding single-unit site that will need augmentation, and the three things I must establish
before committing are her smile line, the cause of the resorption and the prognosis of the neighbours, and what
she actually expects.”
Domain 1 — Clinical interpretation and reasoning
Chain: the anatomical and biological groundwork
Q
Describe the anatomy of the anterior maxilla that matters for implant placement.
“The labial plate over the root prominences with the canine eminence, a labial concavity above the apices
deepening towards the lateral, the nasopalatine canal at the midline, the nasal floor above, and scalloped
gingiva whose papillae depend on the bony crest.”
Q
How thick is the labial plate at a lateral incisor, and what is it made of?
“Under 1 mm in most anterior sites, often under 0.5 at a lateral. It is largely bundle bone — ligament-dependent,
with no cancellous core to revascularise from — so it resorbs when the tooth goes, and that loss shows as mid-
facial recession.”
Q
Take me through socket healing and the ridge change that goes with it.

“Clot, granulation tissue within a week, soft tissue closure by four to eight weeks, woven bone from four to six
weeks, lamellar by six months. Meanwhile the ridge loses half its width in a year, two-thirds by three months,
mostly buccally.”
Q
How do you classify her periodontal phenotype, and why do you care?
“Phenotype — gingival thickness, keratinised width, bone morphotype — is the 2017 World Workshop term
replacing biotype, judged by probe transparency. Thin tissue recedes and shows titanium; hers is thick and
flat, which resists recession and masks the abutment.”
Chain: reading this patient
Q
Why would a virgin tooth develop external root resorption, and why does the cause matter?
“Usually previous trauma; also orthodontic resorption, adjacent pathology or invasive cervical resorption. It
matters because trauma means the neighbours may share the prognosis, and I will not place beside a tooth I
expect to lose — so I sensibility test the 21 and 23.”
Q
What else do you need to examine?
“Smile line at full smile and in speech — the biggest aesthetic risk factor. Then lip dynamics, midline, incisal
plane, papilla heights and gingival margins from 21 to 23, probing depths and shade, with photographs and an
ITI Aesthetic Risk Assessment.”
Q
What is the significance of the triangular 23 against the rectangular 21?
“Its contact point sits more coronally, so contact-to-crest distance is greater and the papilla has more to fill.
Tarnow: almost always present at 5 mm, 56% at 6 mm, 27% at 7 mm. And one crown must reconcile two tooth
forms.”
Q
What does the buccal concavity on the CBCT tell you?
“That the bone lies palatal to the ideal prosthetic axis, so an implant following the ridge either perforates the
plate or emerges too buccally. This site needs augmentation — at placement or staged.”
Domain 2 — Clinical decision making and treatment planning
Chain: the options and the argument between them
Q
What are her options?
“No treatment, which must be offered, with a warning about drift. A denture as an interim. A resin-bonded
cantilever from the 23. A conventional bridge. An implant crown with augmentation. Orthodontic space
closure. Each with its biological cost and maintenance.”
Q
Your colleague would place a resin-bonded cantilever and never touch this ridge. Why might they be right?
“Minimally invasive, excellent survival for single anterior cantilevers, delivered in weeks, reversible in a 26-year-
old, and it avoids nine months of treatment in a woman whose living depends on how she looks meanwhile.
Against it: debonding, and a pontic over a concavity. It turns on her smile line, not my preference.”
Q
Why not a conventional bridge — and what about orthodontic space closure?
“Preparing two unrestored teeth in a 26-year-old is irreversible, risks pulpal death and buys nothing over a
cantilever. Space closure deserves raising — the 23 substituted for the 22, guidance moved to the premolar —
but needs an orthodontic opinion.”
Q
Has growth ceased at 26?

“Almost certainly, but I would confirm — stable height, shoe size and dentition, and serial cephalograms a year
apart in real doubt. Implants behave as ankylosed teeth, and infraposition in an on-camera professional would
be a serious failure.”
Q
What is alveolar ridge preservation, and since the tooth is already out, what is your equivalent now?
“Grafting the socket at extraction with a slowly resorbing xenograft; it roughly halves horizontal loss but cannot
prevent bundle bone loss, so it is damage limitation. That moment has gone: my equivalent is guided bone
regeneration, without socket walls to contain the graft.”
Q
SAC classification, and what part of this is within your competence?
“Surgically Advanced, Complex if her smile line is high — aesthetic zone, ridge deficiency, concavity.
Prosthodontically Advanced to Complex. Simultaneous contour grafting is within my competence; a high
smile line, staged horizontal GBR or soft tissue reconstruction I refer — said at the outset.”
Q
What must she be told, specifically because of who she is?
“Materiality under Montgomery is judged from her position. ‘The gum edge may shrink and show a grey line,
a black triangle may appear beside the canine. Six to nine months, mostly in a temporary — I need your filming
dates. Even done well it may not match exactly.’ Then a mock-up before committing.”
Domain 3 — Decision making in relation to treatment procedures
Chain: placement protocol and loading
Q
When would you place, and when would you load?
“Those are two separate decisions. Types 1 to 4 describe when I place relative to the extraction; immediate,
early and conventional describe when a restoration goes into occlusion relative to placement. They are chosen
independently, but the combinations are not equally well documented.”
Q
Give me the four placement types, and say which this site is.
“Type 1 immediate, same day. Type 2 early with soft tissue healing, four to eight weeks. Type 3 early with partial
bone healing, twelve to sixteen weeks. Type 4 late, six months or more. At six weeks with healed mucosa she
is Type 2.”
Q
Why is Type 2 the workhorse of the aesthetic zone?
“The mucosa has healed and can be advanced, giving tension-free primary closure over a simultaneous graft;
infection has resolved; and much of the ridge remains. The price is two surgical episodes and a graft I will
almost certainly need.”
Q
Would immediate placement have preserved her buccal plate?
“No. The buccal wall is bundle bone, dependent on the periodontal ligament, and resorbs whatever I do. Im-
mediate placement saves time and surgical episodes, not bone, and costs me control of the three-dimensional
position — what I least want to lose here.”
Q
So what loading protocol, and what does she wear meanwhile?
“Conventional loading, four to six months after simultaneous grafting, submerged; early loading after early
placement is clinically insuﬀiciently documented. Meanwhile a bonded pontic rather than the Essix, so nothing
presses on the graft. My provisional is restoration, not loading — free of contact in intercuspation and every
excursion, checked with shim stock.”
Chain: choosing an augmentation material

Q
What are the four categories of graft material, and what can each actually do?
“Autograft, allograft, xenograft, alloplast. All four are osteoconductive. Only autogenous bone is osteogenic,
because only it carries living cells, and it is osteoinductive too; demineralised allograft is variably osteoinductive;
xenograft and alloplast are scaffolds only.”
Q
Their advantages and disadvantages?
“Autograft: best biology and fastest incorporation, no ethical objection, but limited volume, donor morbidity, un-
predictable resorption. Allograft: no donor site, unlimited, but human origin and batch variability. Xenograft:
outstanding contour stability, best documented, but conductive only. Alloplast: no origin objection, cheap,
least documented here.”
Q
What would you use to correct this buccal concavity, and why?
“A composite graft — autogenous chips from the osteotomy against the implant surface for their osteogenic
cells, roughly 50:50 with deproteinised bovine bone mineral outside, because a slowly resorbing xenograft
holds buccal contour for years. Covered by a resorbable collagen membrane onto decorticated bone.”
Q
Simultaneous or staged augmentation — and where is the limit of your competence?
“Simultaneous where I can place in the correct prosthetic position and the defect is a contained dehiscence —
my plan here; staged where the ridge cannot house the implant. Placing where bone dictates rather than the
prosthesis is the commonest unrecoverable failure. Staged horizontal GBR, blocks or vertical augmentation I
refer.”
Q
What must she consent to that is specific to the graft materials?
“That the graft is bovine, the membrane porcine collagen, and allograft human donor tissue — raised at
planning, never on the day, because religious, cultural, dietary and vegetarian objections are common and
legitimate. Then the very low transmission risk, the autogenous-plus-synthetic alternative and its weaker
documentation, and that brand and lot number are recorded.”
Chain: timing, position and the graft
Q
Describe your flap.
“A palatally displaced crestal incision with papilla-sparing intrasulcular extensions to the 21 and 23, and one
vertical relief at the mesial line angle of the 24, away from the graft. Full thickness, atraumatic, carrying kera-
tinised tissue buccally.”
Q
Where exactly does the implant go?
“Shoulder 3 mm apical to the planned mid-facial margin, 1 to 2 mm palatal to the neighbours’ emergence line,
1.5 mm from each adjacent root, angled through the cingulum. Given the concavity I angle more palatally and
accept an angulated screw channel.”
Q
What diameter, and why?
“A narrow-diameter implant around 3.3 mm in titanium-zirconium alloy, which gives it strength narrow tita-
nium would lack. A standard diameter would consume the buccal bone I am protecting and over-contour the
emergence.”
Q
You expect a buccal dehiscence over the concavity. Take me through the closure.
“Graft deliberately over-contoured, membrane 2 to 3 mm beyond the defect onto sound bone, then a periosteal
releasing incision and tension-free closure with horizontal mattress and interrupted 5/0 monofilament — ten-
sion causes exposure, and exposure loses the graft.”

Q
Describe the restorative phase, and the occlusion you want.
“Second stage with a palatally repositioned flap, a connective tissue graft if the phenotype is thin, a provisional
developing emergence over 8 to 12 weeks, then a customised coping copying it. Definitive: screw-retained,
titanium base with milled ceramic, reconciling the two crown forms. Light contact in intercuspation, none in
excursion — the canine guides.”
Domain 4 — Interpretation and problem solving of clinical outcomes
Chain: what goes wrong and what you do about it
Q
What are the most likely complications?
“Aesthetic first — mid-facial recession, a black triangle, shade mismatch, and change as she ages while the
implant does not. Biological — graft or membrane exposure, and mucositis. Mechanical — screw loosening or
chipping, least likely in a lateral.”
Q
At two years she has 1.5 mm of mid-facial recession with visible greyness. Diagnose it before you treat it.
“Four questions. Is the implant too buccal — commonest and least recoverable? Is the phenotype thin there
after all? Is inflammation driving it? Has the abutment been repeatedly disconnected? That decides whether
this is treatable or fundamental.”
Q
Give me the options.
“Connective tissue graft with a coronally advanced flap. A zirconia or ceramic abutment to remove the grey.
Recontouring or pink ceramic. Accept and monitor photographically. Or explantation and re-treatment if the
position is fundamentally wrong — discussed frankly.”
Q
You have offered her a connective tissue graft. Argue against it.
“Around an established implant it is far less predictable than the same graft at placement — no ligament, no
interproximal bone to advance against, so complete coverage is not realistic. If the implant is too buccal it treats
appearance, not cause. Better said than over-promised.”
Q
How would you monitor her?
“Standardised photographs at every review — non-negotiable here. Periapical at fitting and one year. Plastic
probing, bleeding, recession from a fixed reference, a papilla index, and her satisfaction asked directly. Review
at two weeks, second stage, fitting, three and twelve months, then six-monthly.”
Q
What would you record?
“The aesthetic risk assessment and smile line; every option including no treatment; the risks discussed with
her occupation in mind, in her words as well as mine; the mock-up; the surgical record with graft lot numbers;
and baseline photographs and radiographs.”

Q
How will you know this has succeeded?
“By her measure — that she works on camera without thinking about her lateral incisor. Objectively: stable bone
levels against baseline, no bleeding or suppuration, margin and papillae unchanged against the photographic
record, and a crown a stranger would not identify.”
WATCH OUT
Come back to the aesthetic risk assessment — smile line, phenotype, crown form, ridge, expectation — and say
which of those this question belongs to. It buys you a sentence and it is nearly always the right frame in an
aesthetic-zone case.
Running this case to time
Time check. The flow above holds 38 questions and about 1,693 words of model answer. At examination
pace — 140 words a minute, plus roughly five seconds for each question to be asked — that comes to a little
over fifteen minutes: it fits, but with nothing to spare. Domain 3 carries three chains, so it compresses
first — an examiner takes the graft categories as one question rather than four. If your answers run past
thirty seconds, you will never reach the aesthetic complications in Domain 4.

Where the marks are lost in this case
Answering as though she were any 26-year-old. Her occupation is the case: it sets materiality under
Montgomery, it sets the referral threshold, and it makes her filming schedule part of the plan. Volunteering
that unprompted is the difference between a 3 and a 5 in Domain 2.
Claiming immediate placement would have saved the plate. It would not — the buccal wall is bundle
bone and resorbs regardless. Say so, and say what immediate placement really costs: control of the three-
dimensional position, the one thing you cannot lose at a lateral incisor.
Never naming the smile line as the referral line. Simultaneous contour grafting at a contained dehis-
cence is within competence; a high smile line, staged horizontal GBR or soft tissue reconstruction is not.
Candidates plan the surgery beautifully and never say where they would stop.

soe.title: A perio-endo lesion in a medically complex
soe.text:
SOE Case 3 — A perio-endo lesion in a medically complex
patient
THE CASE
Middle-aged woman. Medical history: breast cancer treated with radiotherapy, uncontrolled diabetes, on
hormone replacement therapy. Presenting with the 23: 10 mm mid-buccal pocket, 8 mm mesiobuccal; peri-
apical shows a radiolucency extending from the lateral aspect of the root to the apex; a sinus tract is suspected
but hard to identify on a blurred photograph; the tooth is sensitive to cold.
Pace: one structured opening of about 60 seconds, then roughly 35 questions in the remaining 14 minutes. Nothing after the opening earns you
more than a few seconds of thought.
Opening — the 60-second presentation
Q
Present this case.
“A middle-aged woman with three medical issues that all bear on healing — breast cancer treated with ra-
diotherapy, uncontrolled diabetes and HRT — presenting with a 23 that has a 10 mm mid-buccal and 8 mm
mesiobuccal pocket, a radiolucency running from the lateral aspect of the root to the apex, a suspected sinus
tract, and, importantly, a tooth that still responds to cold. My working diagnosis is a lesion of combined
periodontal and endodontic origin, but the cold response argues against a straightforwardly necrotic pulp, so
I would not commit yet. The three things I must establish are the true medical picture — particularly whether
she has had an antiresorptive — her current HbA1c, and where that sinus tract actually leads.”
Domain 1 — Clinical interpretation and reasoning
Chain: the diagnostic groundwork
Q
By what routes can pulp and periodontium communicate?
“Four. The apical foramen, the main pathway in both directions. Lateral and accessory canals, most numerous
in the apical third and in furcations. Dentinal tubules, exposed where cementum is absent or lost, particularly
at the cemento-enamel junction and in cervical areas. And developmental anomalies — palatogingival grooves,
most classically on maxillary incisors, and enamel projections. Iatrogenic routes such as perforations and root
fractures are the fifth.”
Q
Classify the pulpal and periapical diagnoses.
“Pulpally: normal, reversible pulpitis, symptomatic or asymptomatic irreversible pulpitis, pulp necrosis,
and previously treated or previously initiated. Periapically: normal, symptomatic or asymptomatic apical
periodontitis, acute apical abscess, chronic apical abscess — which is the one that presents with a sinus tract
— and condensing osteitis. Naming both halves forces me to be specific rather than saying ‘an infected tooth’.”
Q
What does a cold test actually test, and what are its limits?
“It tests A-delta fibre response, so it tells me there is vital, innervated tissue somewhere in the canal system —
not that the whole pulp is healthy. False negatives occur with calcification, recent trauma, heavy restorations,
immature apices and anxious patients. False positives occur with pulp stones, periodontal ligament stimulation
and multi-rooted teeth where one canal remains vital. It must be interpreted against contralateral and adjacent
controls, never in isolation.”
Q
How would you stage and grade her periodontal condition?
“Under the 2017 World Workshop: stage by severity and complexity, from interdental attachment loss and bone
loss — I would need full charting and radiographs, but a 10 mm pocket suggests at least Stage III. Grade by rate
of progression, using bone loss as a percentage of age, with smoking and diabetes as grade modifiers. Extent
as localised, generalised or molar-incisor pattern. And I would state whether it is currently stable, in remission
or unstable.”

Q
What does her diabetes do to that grade?
“It raises it. An HbA1c of 7.0% or above in a diagnosed diabetic is a grade modifier that takes her to Grade C
under the Workshop criteria, meaning rapid progression and a worse response to treatment. The relationship is
bidirectional — hyperglycaemia impairs neutrophil function, collagen turnover and healing, while periodontal
inflammation worsens glycaemic control. That is the single most useful thing I can tell her.”
Chain: reading this patient
Q
What is your differential for the 23?
“A combined perio-endo lesion; a primary endodontic lesion with secondary periodontal involvement drain-
ing through the sulcus; a primary periodontal lesion in a diabetic with generalised periodontitis; a vertical root
fracture; or invasive cervical resorption or other local pathology. A palatogingival groove would also be on
the list at a maxillary anterior tooth.”
Q
Which finding discriminates most, and how?
“The cold sensitivity. A tooth that responds to cold has vital pulp tissue, which argues against a primary
necrotic endodontic lesion — although a partially necrotic or multi-canalled tooth can still respond. A single
deep narrow isolated pocket in an otherwise reasonable mouth would point me towards a vertical root fracture;
a broad pocket with generalised bone loss elsewhere points to periodontal disease as the primary problem.”
Q
What further investigations?
“Sensibility testing of the 23, 22 and 24 with cold and electric pulp testing, against contralateral controls. Full
six-point charting, mobility, plaque and bleeding scores, and a BPE. Trace the sinus tract with a gutta-percha
point and radiograph with it in place. Good long-cone paralleling periapicals at two horizontal angles. Tran-
sillumination and staining for a crack. And a current HbA1c and full drug list from her GP and oncology
team.”
Q
Why is the gutta-percha point the most useful single test here?
“Because it converts a suspicion into an anatomical answer. The point follows the tract to its origin, and the
radiograph then tells me whether the source is the apex — endodontic — the lateral aspect of the root — a
lateral canal or a fracture — or the sulcus and crest — periodontal. It costs nothing, takes two minutes, and
changes the whole treatment plan.”
Q
The photograph of the tract is blurred. What do you do?
“I say so. An inadequate record is not a basis for a diagnosis, in the clinic or in the examination. Clinically I
would dry the mucosa, palpate along the sulcus and look for a bead of pus on gentle pressure, place a gutta-
percha point, and repeat the photograph properly. I would not commit to a diagnosis on a poor image and I
would record that I had not.”
Domain 2 — Clinical decision making and treatment planning
Chain: taking the medical history apart
Q
The breast cancer and radiotherapy — what exactly do you need to know?
“The field. Radiotherapy to the breast and axilla does not irradiate the jaws and has essentially no bearing on
oral surgery. Head and neck radiotherapy is an entirely different matter, with a risk of osteoradionecrosis
rising above about 50 Gy, in which case elective implants in irradiated bone would need specialist assessment.
I also want the date, whether she had chemotherapy, her current disease status and who is following her up.”
Q
Why do you ask about bisphosphonates and denosumab, and does the route matter?
“Because both are commonly given in breast cancer — intravenously for bone metastases, or orally or subcu-
taneously for treatment-induced bone loss — and the woman herself often does not call them cancer drugs.
Route and indication matter enormously: an intravenous antiresorptive given for malignancy puts her in the

high-risk MRONJ group, and I would regard elective implant placement as contraindicated. A low-dose oral
bisphosphonate for osteoporosis is a much lower risk.”
Q
How would you risk-assess and manage her for MRONJ?
“Following SDCEP: identify the drug, dose, route, indication and duration; place her in the higher-risk group
if it is intravenous for malignancy, if she has had it more than five years, or if there is concurrent steroid or
antiresorptive-plus-antiangiogenic therapy. Then: avoid extractions where a tooth can reasonably be saved, use
atraumatic technique, give clear warning of the risk, and review healing at eight weeks, referring if it has not
healed.”
Q
The uncontrolled diabetes — what do you need and what does it change?
“I need the HbA1c, the type, the treatment, who manages it and whether she has complications. Poor control im-
pairs neutrophil chemotaxis and phagocytosis, collagen synthesis and microvascular perfusion, so it increases
infection risk, slows healing and accelerates periodontal destruction. It partly explains her 10 mm pocket. It is
a relative contraindication to elective implant surgery until improved, not an absolute one.”
Q
What figure would you want before elective implant surgery?
“I would want her stable and under her diabetes team’s control, and in practical terms an HbA1c below about
7%, or at minimum a clear downward trend agreed with her physician. I would not fix on a single number as
a barrier — the evidence is that well-controlled diabetics have implant survival close to non-diabetics, while
poorly controlled patients heal slowly and have more early failures and more peri-implant disease.”
Q
And the HRT?
“Largely a marker of menopausal status and bone metabolism rather than a problem in itself. There is some
association with xerostomia and with gingival changes. It is not a contraindication to any of this treatment.
What I would check is that HRT is not being confused with, or given alongside, an antiresorptive.”
Chain: the plan and the argument about it
Q
Suppose the 23 is unrestorable. What is your plan?
“Phased. Phase 1 — relieve pain, control infection, and get her diabetes controlled in liaison with her GP or
diabetes team, while obtaining a full oncology and drug history and stabilising her periodontal condition with
non-surgical therapy and oral hygiene instruction. Phase 2 — atraumatic extraction with ridge preservation if
an implant is contemplated, plus an interim prosthesis. Phase 3 — re-evaluate. Phase 4 — only then decide the
definitive replacement.”
Q
Would you plan an implant at all, and on what conditions?
“Potentially, but not now and not unconditionally. My conditions would be: confirmed no intravenous an-
tiresorptive for malignancy; HbA1c controlled and stable; periodontal disease treated and stable with good
plaque control, since a history of periodontitis is a risk factor for peri-implantitis; no smoking; and a healed,
adequate ridge. If she remains uncontrolled, the honest plan is a resin-bonded bridge or a denture, and I
would say so.”
Q
A colleague says the evidence shows controlled diabetics do as well as anyone, so why are you delaying?
“They are right about controlled diabetics — that is exactly why I am delaying, because she is not one yet. The
delay is not a punishment, it is a change of the variable that predicts failure. Where they might be right against
me is on timing of the extraction: delaying the extraction of an infected tooth does not help her glycaemic
control and may worsen it, so I would treat the infection promptly and delay only the implant.”
Q
SAC classification, and where is the boundary of your competence?
“Even a single anterior unit becomes Advanced here, because the complexity is medical rather than anatomical
— an uncontrolled diabetic with a possible antiresorptive history and active periodontal disease. The diagnosis,
the medical liaison, the extraction and the interim prosthesis are all within my scope. If she proves to be on

an intravenous antiresorptive, or if head and neck radiotherapy is confirmed, implant treatment is not mine to
provide and I would refer for specialist assessment.”
Q
How would you explain the delay to her, in your own words to her?
“ ‘Your gum and bone heal much more slowly when your blood sugar is high, and an implant depends entirely
on bone healing around it. If we put one in now it is much more likely to fail, and I don’t think that would be
fair to you. What I’d like to do is settle the infection, give you something to fill the gap, and work with your
doctor on your blood sugar. Then we look at the permanent options from a much stronger position.’ Then I
would ask her to tell me back what we have agreed.”
Domain 3 — Decision making in relation to treatment procedures
Chain: the acute phase and the pharmacology
Q
Does she need emergency treatment today?
“If she has pain, a spreading infection, systemic upset, trismus, or swelling threatening the airway or the eye,
then yes. The treatment for a localised fluctuant swelling is drainage — through the tooth if the source is
endodontic, through the pocket or by incision if it is periodontal — with debridement. Drainage plus removal
of the source is the treatment; everything else is an adjunct.”
Q
Does she need antibiotics?
“Only if there are systemic signs — fever, malaise, lymphadenopathy — spreading infection, or significant
immunocompromise. Her uncontrolled diabetes lowers my threshold, because hyperglycaemia impairs neu-
trophil function, but antibiotics are never a substitute for drainage. Prescribing them instead of treating the
source is the commonest antimicrobial stewardship failure in dentistry.”
Q
If you did prescribe, what and for how long?
“Amoxicillin, or metronidazole where anaerobes predominate, for a short course of about five days with a
definite review — not a repeat. If penicillin-allergic, clarithromycin or clindamycin, checking interactions
against her oncology and diabetes medication. I would record the indication in the notes, not just the drug,
and I would arrange to see her rather than leaving the course to run unsupervised.”
Q
What would you tell her about the infection and her diabetes?
“That the two feed each other: ‘An infection like this pushes your blood sugar up, and high blood sugar makes
it harder for you to fight the infection. So please check your levels more often than usual over the next few days,
and let your diabetes team know that you’ve got a dental infection and what we’ve given you.’ That is a safety
instruction, not general advice, and I would record giving it.”
Chain: the operative decisions
Q
If the tooth were treatable, what determines whether you save it?
“Prognosis, and specifically the periodontal component. Treating the endodontic half of a true perio-endo
lesion often resolves the apical portion, but the periodontal attachment loss determines the long-term outcome.
A 10 mm mid-buccal pocket on a vital tooth in an uncontrolled diabetic is a poor prognosis, and a vertical root
fracture is hopeless. I would treat any endodontic component first, re-evaluate at three months, then decide.”
Q
Describe the extraction.
“Confirm the medical position first, antiresorptives specifically. Then periotomes and luxators to preserve
the buccal plate, minimal elevation, forceps with controlled rotation given a conical canine root, thorough
curettage of granulation tissue, inspection of all four socket walls, and irrigation. I would examine the extracted
root under magnification for a fracture line, because that answers the diagnostic question retrospectively and
informs what I do next door.”

Q
Would you preserve the ridge?
“If the buccal plate is intact and an implant is genuinely contemplated later, yes — a slowly resorbing xenograft
with a collagen membrane or socket seal and a figure-of-eight suture. If the site is actively infected with a
large lesion, or if implant treatment is unlikely because of her medical position, grafting adds cost and risk for
no return, and I would simply debride and let it heal.”
Q
She turns out to have had intravenous zoledronate. How does the extraction change?
“Under SDCEP she is high risk. I would first re-examine whether the tooth can be retained instead — root
treatment and decoronation rather than extraction is a legitimate alternative in this group. If extraction is
unavoidable: liaise with her oncologist, minimal trauma, round off sharp bony edges, primary closure where
achievable, explicit warning of MRONJ, and review at eight weeks with referral if unhealed. No implants,
now or later.”
Q
Post-operative instructions and analgesia?
“Written as well as verbal instructions with an emergency contact. Paracetamol first line; I would check before
recommending NSAIDs because of renal function in a long-standing diabetic and any interaction with her other
medication. Standard advice on rinsing from the next day, and specific advice to monitor blood glucose and to
eat as normally as she can rather than skipping meals while sore.”
Q
What interim prosthesis?
“An acrylic removable partial denture as the immediate option — cheap, quick, and easily relieved over a
healing socket — or a bonded pontic on the adjacent teeth if the site allows, which puts no load on the healing
site at all. I would relieve either generously over the graft or socket and review it, since a prosthesis pressing on
a healing site in a diabetic is a genuine risk.”
Domain 4 — Interpretation and problem solving of clinical outcomes
Chain: judging the result and knowing when to stop
Q
If you treat the 23 rather than extract it, how do you monitor?
“Reduction in probing depth and bleeding, resolution of the sinus tract, and radiographic healing of the
radiolucency at six and twelve months against a proper baseline. Alongside that, her HbA1c trend, because
if that does not move, nothing else will. Standardised radiographs, same technique and angulation, or the
comparison is worthless.”
Q
You said you would set a threshold. What is it?
“That I decide in advance, and write it down: if at three months the pocket has not reduced and the sinus tract
persists, the tooth is not being saved and I move to extraction. The failure mode in these cases is repeating the
same treatment hoping for a different result while she loses bone that I will later want for an implant.”
Q
At three months the pocket is 8 mm and the tract is still there. What now?
“I follow my own threshold. I would re-examine for a vertical root fracture — raise a small flap if necessary and
inspect the root surface directly, which is the definitive test — and re-check her HbA1c. Then extract, with the
technique dictated by her antiresorptive status, and move to the interim prosthesis. I would explain that this
was the agreed plan, not a failure of the last three months.”
Q
Her HbA1c comes back at 9.5% and she tells you she cannot change it. What do you offer?
“The same care with different expectations. I would treat her periodontal disease and keep her stable, because
that will help her glycaemia as well as her mouth; extract what is hopeless; and provide a resin-bonded bridge
or a denture, which do not depend on osseointegration. I would not simply withhold treatment. What I would
not do is place an implant and pretend the risk is the same.”

Q
She asks whether she will ever be able to have an implant. What do you say?
“ ‘Possibly, yes — but not while things are as they are. If your blood sugar comes down and stays down, and
your gums are stable, then an implant becomes a reasonable option and I’d be happy to look at it again. If your
cancer team has you on a bone-strengthening drug through a drip, then implants aren’t safe for you and I’d
want us to plan around that rather than risk it.’ Honest, specific, and with the door left open.”
Q
What would you record?
“The medical liaison in full — who I wrote to, what I asked, what I was told and when; the diagnosis and
the evidence for it, including that I would not diagnose from an inadequate photograph; the options discussed
including no treatment; the reasons for deferring implant treatment; any emergency treatment and any pre-
scription with its indication; the threshold I set and when I would re-evaluate; and the review plan. If she later
complains of delay, that record is my defence — and more importantly it is what makes her care coherent for
whoever sees her next.”
WATCH OUT
Come back to the sequence: control the infection, control the medical risk, control the periodontal disease, and
only then replace the tooth. Saying which of those four the question belongs to buys you a sentence and is
almost always the right frame in a medically complex case.
Running this case to time
Time check. The flow above holds 35 questions and about 1,838 words of model answer. At examination
pace — 140 words a minute, plus roughly five seconds for each question to be asked — that is a little over
sixteen minutes, so it overruns by about one. The first thing an examiner drops is the pharmacology
sub-chain in Domain 3 — which antibiotic, for how long. If your answers run past thirty seconds, you
will still be reciting the medical history when the three-month threshold question should be asked.
