Where the marks are lost in this case
Diagnosing from the blurred photograph. The tract cannot be identified on the image given, and saying
so is a mark rather than an evasion. An inadequate record is not a basis for a diagnosis — trace it with
gutta-percha, radiograph it in place, and record that you would not commit until you had.
Treating “radiotherapy” as one thing. Breast and axillary fields do not irradiate the jaws and change
nothing surgically. Candidates who invoke osteoradionecrosis without asking the field look as though
they have memorised a risk rather than understood it — and then miss the antiresorptive, which is the
real hazard here.
Delaying the extraction along with the implant. Poor glycaemic control defers the implant; it does not
defer treating an infected tooth, which will worsen her control if left. Volunteer that separation, and
volunteer the fallback — a resin-bonded bridge or denture — if her HbA1c never moves.

soe.title: The very deeply placed 46 implant, with mesial
soe.text:
SOE Case 4 — The very deeply placed 46 implant, with mesial
drifting of the 47
THE CASE
Middle-aged man, clear medical history. Complains of pus discharge and bleeding on brushing. The 46
implant was placed 12 months ago and carries a cemented crown. Periapical shows residual cement, a very
deeply positioned implant, an abutment that is not fully seated, and the 47 drifting mesially. The implant is
a tissue-level design.
Pace: one structured opening of about 60 seconds, then roughly 35 questions in the remaining 14 minutes. Nothing after the opening earns you
more than a few seconds of thought.
Opening — the 60-second presentation
Q
Present this case.
“A medically fit middle-aged man with suppuration and bleeding around a twelve-month-old cemented crown
on a 46 implant. The radiograph shows residual submucosal cement, a very deeply placed implant, an abut-
ment that is not fully seated, and the 47 drifting mesially. My working diagnosis is peri-implantitis, with at
least three identifiable contributing causes: the cement, the depth of placement — which made cement removal
impossible and created a pocket neither he nor I can clean — and the microgap and plaque trap at the unseated
abutment. The drifting 47 suggests an open contact or an occlusal change. The question I have to answer before
anything else is whether it is rational to keep this implant at all.”
Domain 1 — Clinical interpretation and reasoning
Chain: the peri-implant groundwork
Q
Compare the soft tissue attachment around an implant with that around a tooth.
“Both have a junctional or barrier epithelium of similar length. The difference is below it. Around a tooth,
connective tissue fibres insert into cementum perpendicularly; around an implant there is no cementum, so
the fibres run parallel or circularly around the abutment and are not attached to it. There is no periodontal
ligament, so no ligament blood supply and no proprioception — the vascular supply is from periosteum and
bone alone.”
Q
What are the clinical consequences of those differences?
“The seal is weaker and more easily penetrated, so a probe passes closer to bone and probing depths read
deeper for the same health. Inflammation spreads more readily into bone and the lesion is larger and less well
encapsulated than in periodontitis, so progression is faster and often non-linear. There is no proprioceptive
feedback, so occlusal overload is not felt. And healing after treatment is less predictable because there is no
ligament to regenerate from.”
Q
Define peri-implant health, mucositis and peri-implantitis.
“Under the 2017 World Workshop: health is no erythema, no bleeding on gentle probing, no suppuration
and no bone loss beyond initial crestal remodelling. Mucositis is bleeding on gentle probing with those same
stable bone levels — an inflammatory lesion confined to the mucosa, and reversible. Peri-implantitis is bleeding
and/or suppuration, increased probing depth compared with previous examinations, and bone loss beyond
initial crestal remodelling.”
Q
You have no baseline radiograph. How do you make the diagnosis?
“By the Workshop’s alternative threshold: bleeding or suppuration on probing, plus a probing depth of 6 mm
or more, plus a bone level 3 mm or more apical to the most coronal intraosseous part of the implant. And
I would make a real effort to obtain the original records from whoever placed it, because a genuine baseline
changes both the diagnosis and the medico-legal picture.”

Q
How do you probe an implant, and with what?
“Six sites, gently — around 0.2 to 0.25 newtons, which is lighter than most people use — with a plastic or blunt
periodontal probe to avoid scoring the titanium surface. I record depth, bleeding, suppuration, recession and
the width of keratinised mucosa. Probing an implant is a comparison against previous readings more than an
absolute number, which is why serial charting matters so much.”
Q
What crestal bone change is normal in the first year?
“Around 1 to 1.5 mm in the first year after loading, and thereafter no more than about 0.2 mm per year — the
classical Albrektsson success criteria. That is the yardstick against which ‘beyond initial remodelling’ is judged.
Modern platform-switched designs typically remodel less than that, so I would not use 1.5 mm as an allowance
to excuse loss I have found.”
Chain: reading this radiograph and this mouth
Q
What can this periapical not tell you?
“It is a two-dimensional image of a three-dimensional defect — it shows me mesial and distal bone and tells
me nothing about the buccal and lingual walls, which is where the defect morphology that governs treatment
actually lies. It will not show non-radiopaque cement at all. And without a standardised, reproducible paral-
leling technique I cannot compare it reliably with any future film.”
Q
Why does residual cement cause this?
“Because set cement submucosally is a rough, plaque-retentive foreign body in intimate contact with the
implant surface, sitting in a space that cannot be cleaned by the patient or the hygienist. It provokes both a
plaque-mediated and a foreign-body inflammatory response. The association with peri-implantitis is strong,
and the deeper the margin, the more cement is left and the less likely it is ever to be found.”
Q
Why is the 47 drifting, and what does that tell you?
“Most likely because the proximal contact has opened — loss of contact between implant restorations and
adjacent natural teeth is a well-recognised and common phenomenon, because the tooth continues to erupt
and migrate while the ankylosed implant does not. It tells me there is now a food trap feeding the problem,
that the occlusion has changed, and that the 47 needs assessing in its own right, not just as a contact to be closed.”
Q
What else do you assess clinically?
“Whether the implant itself or only the prosthesis is mobile — a mobile implant has lost integration and the
conversation becomes removal. The occlusion, including whether the drifted 47 has created a heavy or eccentric
contact. The contour and cleansability of the crown and whether he can physically reach the area. His plaque
control, smoking, glycaemic status and periodontal status elsewhere. And what he was told at the time and
what maintenance he has actually had.”
Q
Why does his periodontal status elsewhere matter so much?
“Because a history of periodontitis is one of the strongest risk factors for peri-implantitis, along with poor
plaque control, smoking and lack of supportive maintenance. If he has untreated periodontitis, treating this
implant in isolation will fail — the same pathogens and the same host response are in the rest of his mouth. So
a full periodontal assessment is part of treating the implant, not a separate exercise.”
Domain 2 — Clinical decision making and treatment planning
Chain: keep it or lose it
Q
What is the first decision, and what determines it?
“Whether it is rational or irrational to keep this implant, as the ITI decision tree frames it. That turns on three
things: the extent of bone loss and whether the implant retains adequate support; whether the position permits
a restoration that can be cleaned; and whether decontamination of the exposed surface is actually feasible.
If the answer to any of those is no, treating it is postponing an inevitable removal at the patient’s expense.”

Q
Assume it is rational to keep it. Outline your treatment.
“Step one, cause-related therapy — remove the crown, remove all cement, seat or replace the abutment, and
modify or remake the prosthesis so it is cleansable. Step two, non-surgical therapy with debridement and oral
hygiene instruction. Step three, re-assess at about a month. Step four, surgery if suppuration or bleeding
persists with probing depths of 6 mm or more. Then lifelong supportive care.”
Q
Why is removing the crown not optional here?
“Because I cannot remove submucosal cement, assess whether the abutment is seated, or judge the cleansability
of the emergence profile with the restoration in place. Every one of the identified causes sits under that crown.
Non-surgical debridement around a crown that is itself the cause is treatment of the symptom, and it will fail.”
Q
How do you consent him for crown removal?
“Explicitly, because it is a cemented crown and removal may destroy it. ‘To treat this properly I need to get
underneath the crown, because I think there’s cement left behind that’s causing the infection. The crown is
glued on, so there’s a real chance it’ll be damaged or need remaking, and I need you to agree to that before I
start. If we don’t do it, the infection carries on and you may lose the implant.’ And I would record that in those
terms.”
Q
What else must that consent conversation cover?
“That the underlying implant position may prove unrestorable, so we may be removing the crown to find out
that the implant must come out. That treatment may not arrest the bone loss. That soft tissue recession is a
likely consequence of successful treatment, which the ITI tree specifically requires me to discuss. The cost of
a new restoration. And the alternative — removal of the implant — with what would replace it.”
Q
What does the non-surgical phase actually consist of?
“Mechanical debridement with titanium or plastic-tipped curettes and glycine air-polishing to reach the
threads without scoring the surface. Individualised oral hygiene instruction with correctly sized interdental
brushes and a demonstration in his mouth rather than a leaflet. Risk factor modification — smoking, glycaemic
control, and treatment of periodontitis elsewhere. Local antimicrobials or antiseptics as adjuncts only. Then
re-assess at about one month.”
Q
The implant is very deeply positioned. What does that mean for the outcome?
“It is the fundamental problem. A deep implant creates a peri-implant sulcus that neither he nor I can clean,
and it is why the cement was never retrievable. Even with textbook treatment the site remains vulnerable, and
I would tell him so honestly. It also argues strongly for converting to a screw-retained restoration to eliminate
cement entirely and give me retrievability at every maintenance visit.”
Q
A colleague would simply remove the implant now. Why might they be right?
“Because they would be treating the cause rather than its consequences. If the position is so deep that no
restoration will ever be cleansable, then every step I have described buys twelve or eighteen months at real
cost, with recession and possibly implantoplasty along the way, before he ends up in the same place with less
bone than he has today. Early removal preserves bone for a properly placed replacement. My counter is that
I do not yet know the defect morphology, and that decision should follow crown removal, not precede it.”
Q
SAC classification, and what would you refer?
“Managing established peri-implantitis around a malpositioned implant with a cemented restoration is at least
Advanced, and surgical reconstructive management of a peri-implantitis defect is Complex. I would under-
take the cause-related and non-surgical phase, the crown removal, the cement removal and conversion to a
cleansable screw-retained restoration myself. Surgical management, implantoplasty or explantation I would
refer if beyond my experience — and in the posterior mandible, explantation near the inferior alveolar nerve is
not a procedure to learn on.”

Q
What do you tell him about the likely outcome, in his words?
“ ‘You’ve got an infection in the gum and bone around the implant. Some of it is caused by cement left behind
when the crown was fitted, and some by how deep the implant sits, which I can’t change. I think we can settle
the infection and I’d like to try — but I have to be straight with you: the gum will shrink back and it may look
longer, and there’s a chance this comes back and the implant has to come out. If that happens, I’d rather we
plan for it than be surprised by it.’ ”
Domain 3 — Decision making in relation to treatment procedures
Chain: getting the crown off and the surface clean
Q
How would you remove the cemented crown?
“First the conservative attempts: a crown-removal instrument or an ultrasonic tip applied to the margin to
fatigue the cement lute. If it is firmly cemented, I would section it with a bur, cutting from occlusal to buccal,
protecting the implant shoulder and the soft tissue, and accepting that I am likely to destroy it. I would have
consented for that, and I would have a plan for a provisional before I started.”
Q
And how do you remove the cement?
“Irrigate, then work under magnification and good illumination with titanium or plastic scalers and floss
knotted and drawn circumferentially around the abutment, followed by glycine air-polishing to reach the
threads. Then a periapical to confirm no radiopaque cement remains — while remembering that a non-
radiopaque cement will not appear at all, which is precisely why radiopaque cements should be chosen in
the first place.”
Q
How would you have prevented this at the fitting appointment?
“By keeping the margin at or no more than 1 to 1.5 mm below the mucosa, ideally supramucosal. By using
minimal cement in a vented crown, seating it on an abutment replica extraoradly first to express the excess,
and using a radiopaque cement. By taking a post-cementation radiograph. Or simplest of all, by making it
screw-retained, which removes the cause completely.”
Q
If you proceed to surgery, describe it.
“A full-thickness mucoperiosteal flap for access, extended enough to see the whole defect. Complete removal
of granulation tissue with curettes so I can read the defect morphology. Decontamination of the exposed
implant surface. Then the reconstructive or resective decision based on the defect. Careful flap adaptation and
suturing, post-operative chlorhexidine, and systemic antimicrobials only where genuinely indicated.”
Q
How do you decontaminate the surface?
“Mechanically with titanium brushes, titanium curettes or ultrasonic tips, and air-polishing with glycine or
erythritol powder, which reaches thread depths that instruments cannot. Chemically with saline, chlorhexi-
dine or hydrogen peroxide. Er:YAG laser and photodynamic therapy are alternatives. The honest position is
that no method reliably re-establishes a biologically clean surface, and that uncertainty is part of the prognosis
I give him.”
Q
Reconstructive or resective — how do you choose?
“By defect morphology, which is why I remove granulation tissue before deciding. A contained intrabony
defect with several walls is a reconstructive indication — a bone substitute with a barrier membrane, sub-
merged where possible. A supracrestal or horizontal defect with no containment cannot be reconstructed, so
it is resective: an apically positioned flap, osseous recontouring, and implantoplasty of the exposed threads.
Combined defects get a combined approach.”
Q
You have said you would do implantoplasty here. Argue against it.
“It is irreversible; it weakens the implant, which matters in a narrow implant or where bone loss is already
extensive; it releases titanium particles into the tissues, whose long-term significance is not settled; and it
guarantees a long, exposed, visible implant surface with recession. Against a posterior non-aesthetic site with

a supracrestal defect and good evidence of reduced re-infection, I still favour it — but if the defect turns out to
be contained, reconstruction is the better answer, and I would not have committed beforehand.”
Q
Would you give systemic antibiotics?
“Not routinely.
There is no convincing evidence that systemic antibiotics improve outcomes in non-
surgical peri-implantitis therapy, and the stewardship argument against them is strong. I would consider a
peri-operative course in surgical reconstructive treatment, or where there is spreading infection or systemic
upset. The decisive interventions here are mechanical debridement, decontamination and making the site
cleansable.”
Q
How would you restore it afterwards?
“Screw-retained, without question — no cement, retrievable, and removable by me at maintenance visits. A
custom abutment shaped for cleansability, with generous embrasures for an interdental brush and no over-
contour, and the margin brought as supramucosal as the depth allows. I would correct the occlusion, close the
open contact with the 47, and treat the 47 on its own merits.”
Q
What if you have to remove the implant?
“Reverse-torque removal first — it is the least destructive method and works well in the first years or where
bone loss has already occurred. Trephine only if that fails, accepting the bone it costs, and with the inferior
alveolar canal identified on a CBCT beforehand in this region. Then either spontaneous healing or grafting,
and a discussion about a replacement implant later, a bridge, or accepting a shortened dental arch.”
Domain 4 — Interpretation and problem solving of clinical outcomes
Chain: outcomes, maintenance and the diﬀicult conversation
Q
How will you judge success?
“Absence of suppuration, absence of bleeding on gentle probing, probing depths that have not increased, and
radiographic bone levels stable against a new baseline taken after treatment — because the old level is gone
and the honest measure is stability from here. I would re-assess at one month, three months, and then at each
maintenance visit.”
Q
How successful is treatment of peri-implantitis, honestly?
“Less successful than treatment of periodontitis, and he should be told that. Disease resolution is achieved
in a proportion of cases but recurrence is common, and the strongest predictors of a good result are removal
of the cause, a cleansable restoration and adherence to maintenance — which is exactly why the crown must
come off. I would present this as controlling a condition, not curing it.”
Q
What maintenance would you provide?
“Every three to five months, as the ITI tree specifies after treating peri-implant disease: professional biofilm
removal, reinforcement and re-demonstration of hygiene at every visit, peri-implant probing at six sites com-
pared against the new baseline, occlusal check, and radiographs when there is a clinical indication rather than
routinely. Non-attendance at maintenance is itself a reason to reconsider whether the implant should stay.”
Q
At one year the suppuration is back. What now?
“I would treat that as the answer to the question I asked at the start. Re-examine, re-radiograph against the post-
treatment baseline, and check whether the cause really was removed — is any cement left, is the restoration
genuinely cleansable, is his plaque control adequate, has his periodontitis been treated? If the cause has been
removed and it has still recurred, then it is irrational to keep the implant and I would recommend removal and
discuss what replaces it.”
Q
He asks whether the previous dentist was negligent. What do you say?

“I would not comment on another clinician’s care. I would explain what I have found and what I think is
causing it, factually and without attributing blame. I would tell him he is entitled to raise concerns with the
practice that treated him, or with the GDC, and give him what he needs to do that. I would record exactly
what I found and what I said, and notify my indemnity provider if I were asked to comment formally. If he
wanted a report, I would report only on my own findings.”
Q
What would you record?
“The presenting complaint and his account of the history; six-point probing, bleeding, suppuration and mo-
bility; the radiograph and my interpretation of its limitations; the diagnosis and the criteria I used; the causes
identified; the options including removal; the consent discussion in the words used, particularly the risk to
the crown and the likelihood of recession; what I actually did; the new baseline radiograph and chart; the
maintenance interval agreed; and, verbatim, what I said when he asked about the previous dentist.”
WATCH OUT
Go back to the first question — is it rational or irrational to keep this implant — and then to the three-step
sequence of removing the cause, treating the disease, and making the site maintainable. Saying which of those
the question belongs to buys you a sentence and is nearly always the right frame in a peri-implantitis case.
Running this case to time
Time check. The flow above holds 33 questions and about 1,731 words of model answer. At examination
pace — 140 words a minute, plus roughly five seconds for each question to be asked — that comes to
just over fifteen minutes, so it fits the slot almost exactly as written. There is no slack: Domain 3 runs
from crown removal to explantation without a pause, and an examiner behind time drops the prevention
question rather than the negligence question. If your answers run past thirty seconds you will be arguing
about implantoplasty when you are asked what you would say to the patient.

In his words: some of this is cement left
behind and some is how deep the
implant sits, which cannot be changed;
the gum will shrink and may look longer;
it may come back and the implant may
have to come out — and better planned
for than a surprise.
The spine — the twelve answers to have ready if nothing else
1 Implant versus tooth soft tissue attachment · 2 Health, mucositis, peri-implantitis defined · 3 The diagno-
sis with no baseline radiograph · 4 How you probe an implant, and with what · 5 Normal first-year crestal
remodelling · 6 Why residual cement causes this · 7 Why the 47 has drifted · 8 Rational or irrational to
keep it · 9 Why the crown must come off · 10 Reconstructive against resective, by defect morphology · 11
Implantoplasty, argued against yourself · 12 What you say when he asks about the previous dentist.
Where the marks are lost in this case
Debriding around the crown. Candidates describe glycine air-polishing and interdental brushes while
leaving in place the restoration that is causing the disease. Every identified cause sits under that crown,
so removing it — and consenting for its destruction beforehand — comes before any talk of surgery.
Treating the depth as a detail. The very deep placement is the reason the cement was unretrievable
and the reason the sulcus can never be cleaned. Say plainly that even textbook treatment leaves this site
vulnerable, and convert to screw retention; a candidate who promises resolution has misread the case.
Ducking the negligence question. It will be asked, and the answer is a competence line of its own:
comment on your own findings only, tell him he may raise concerns with the practice or the GDC, notify
your indemnifier, and record what you said verbatim.

soe.title: The long-term denture wearer and the mandibular
soe.text:
SOE Case 5 — The long-term denture wearer and the mandibular
implant overdenture
Intra-oral views, with the dentures in and the lower denture out — simulated illustration, not a clinical image
Panoramic view, dentures in situ — simulated illustration, not a clinical image
CBCT: axial locator and cross-sections at the 33 and 43 regions — simulated illustration, not a clinical image

CBCT: anterior maxilla at the midline — simulated illustration, not a clinical image
THE CASE
Middle-aged man reporting a loose lower denture, worn for 18 years. The denture has a well-extended flange.
Intra-oral photographs are provided with and without the denture. There is a crossbite in the second and
third quadrants. CBCT shows the incisive canal at the maxillary midline, a knife-edge mandibular ridge
with posterior resorption, imaged with the denture in place. Cross-sectional slices are provided at the 33 and
43 regions.
Pace: one structured opening of about 60 seconds, then 38 rapid questions in the remaining 13 minutes. Nothing after the opening earns you
more than a few seconds of thought.
Opening — the 60-second presentation
Q
Present this case.
“A middle-aged man with an 18-year-old lower complete denture, now loose. The flange is well extended, so
this is not a border-moulding failure but progressive residual ridge resorption, which is faster in the mandible
and continues lifelong. The CBCT confirms it — a knife-edge anterior ridge with posterior resorption. The
posterior crossbite is acquired from the differing resorption patterns of the two jaws, not developmental. My
working position is that a two-implant mandibular overdenture is the treatment most likely to solve his prob-
lem. What I need to establish is whether the anterior mandible will safely accept two implants, whether his
existing prostheses are otherwise sound, what maintenance he can commit to, and what he actually wants.”
Domain 1 — Clinical interpretation and reasoning
Chain: the anatomical groundwork
Q
Describe the surface anatomy of the edentulous maxilla.
“Front to back: labial and buccal sulci and frena; residual ridge and crest; maxillary tuberosities; hamular
notches; incisive papilla; rugae; median palatine raphe; palatine fovea; and the vibrating line, the denture’s
posterior limit.”

Q
Which give support, and which give retention?
“Support — hard palate and firm ridge crest. Relief — incisive papilla, median raphe, flabby ridge. Retention
— peripheral seal plus a posterior palatal seal at the vibrating line, holding as the soft palate moves.”
Q
Now the mandible, and its primary stress-bearing area.
“Labial, buccal and lingual sulci and frena; residual ridge; buccal shelf; external and internal oblique ridges;
mylohyoid ridge; retromolar pad; genial tubercles; mental foramina. The buccal shelf bears load — dense
cortical bone perpendicular to it. The resorbing crest is the worst place to load.”
Q
Why does the lower denture always give more trouble?
“A quarter of the bearing area, no palatal vault, a mobile floor of mouth and tongue, active muscle attachments,
continuing resorption. Cawood and Howell: the mandible resorbs about four times as fast as the maxilla.”
Q
What is the significance of the incisive canal here?
“It carries the nasopalatine bundle: relieved in a denture, avoided by any implant, which will not integrate in
it. It widens with resorption — a note for the future, as I am not planning maxillary implants.”
Chain: reading this patient’s radiographs and jaws
Q
Why the posterior crossbite, and what does it mean for the new denture?
“Acquired. The maxilla resorbs upwards and inwards, the mandible downwards and outwards, so the lower
ridge ends up anterior and lateral to the upper. So I set the posterior teeth over the ridges, in crossbite; teeth
outside the crest lever the denture.”
Q
Describe the cross-sections at the 33 and 43, and classify the ridge.
“A knife-edge crest, narrow coronally and wider basally. I would record crest width, width 5 mm apical, height
above the canal, and angulation, often lingual. Cawood and Howell Class IV — adequate height, inadequate
width, so a horizontal deficiency.”
Q
What about bone density?
“D1 or D2 on Misch. Excellent primary stability, hence the classic overdenture site, but poorly vascular —
overheating is the real risk: sharp drills, slow speed, copious irrigation.”
Q
Limitations of a CBCT taken with the denture in place?
“Useful if the denture carries radiopaque markers, relating tooth position to bone. Limiting because the base
creates artefact and the mucosa is displaced, misrepresenting tissue thickness. It must still be justified under
IR(ME)R.”
Q
What else would you examine clinically?
“Lip support, smile line, vertical dimension and freeway space, TMJ; then ridge form, keratinised width,
sulcus depth, floor-of-mouth height, tongue, saliva, stomatitis; and both dentures judged on retention, stability,
support and occlusion.”
Q
How do you measure the freeway space?
“Marks on nose and chin, patient upright. Measure in occlusion; establish rest position by relaxation, swallowing
and the closest speaking space; measure again. Mean of three. The difference is the freeway space — normally
2 to 4 mm.”

Domain 2 — Clinical decision making and treatment planning
Chain: complete denture fundamentals before implants
Q
The three requirements of a complete denture?
“Support — resistance to vertical seating force. Retention — resistance to dislodging force, from peripheral
seal, adhesion, cohesion and muscular control. Stability — resistance to horizontal and rotational force, from
ridge form, neutral-zone tooth position and balanced occlusion.”
Q
What occlusal scheme, and what are the alternatives?
“Balanced articulation — bilateral simultaneous contact in centric and excursion — because a denture is a free
body and any single contact tips it; delivered through Hanau’s quint. Alternatives: anatomical 30-degree teeth,
semi-anatomical, monoplane for an unpredictable jaw relationship, and lingualised occlusion, my choice on a
resorbed ridge.”
Q
Does that change once the denture is implant-retained?
“It matters more. Lingualised occlusion with bilateral balance, narrow occlusal table, anterior teeth free in
centric, denture tissue-supported posteriorly — otherwise the load cantilevers onto two anterior implants.”
Q
What are the options for this man?
“Remake conventional dentures with restored vertical dimension and a neutral-zone technique — must be
offered, but the ridge is the limit. A copy denture. A two-implant overdenture, which McGill and York call
the minimum standard for the edentulous mandible. Four implants and a bar. A fixed prosthesis. Or nothing.”
Q
Which do you recommend?
“A copy-technique lower denture retained by two implants at the 33 and 43 with stud attachments, plus a
new or relined upper. Strong long-term evidence, dense bone away from the mental foramina, modest cost and
morbidity. SAC: Straightforward to Advanced — within my competence.”
Q
He has read about fixed teeth on implants. Argue against yourself.
“Lip support — his flange is doing real work after 18 years of resorption and a fixed prosthesis cannot reproduce
it; I would show him with a trial set-up. Then cleansability. And full-arch fixed work is beyond a general
dentist with an interest in implants — I would refer.”
Domain 3 — Decision making in relation to treatment procedures
Chain: overdenture design and its specific requirements
Q
Take me through the attachment options and the space each needs.
“Studs such as Locators — independent, cheap, cleanable, retention changed by swapping a nylon insert, toler-
ating about 20 degrees of divergence, needing 8 to 10 mm of vertical space. Balls are bulkier. A bar splints and
shares load and suits divergent implants, but needs 12 to 15 mm and is harder to clean.”
Q
How does the knife-edge ridge affect implant choice?
“I need 1 mm of bone circumferentially, so a 4 mm implant wants 6 mm of crest, which he lacks. Options: crest
reduction to a wider basal level; a narrow 3.3 mm implant, acceptable here but with higher fracture risk under
a stud, which transmits load unsplinted; ridge splitting; or GBR.”
Q
Where exactly do you place them?
“Canine regions, 33 and 43, at least 5 mm anterior to the mental foramen or its anterior loop, 20 to 22 mm
apart, as parallel as possible, following a ridge that is often lingually inclined, with room above for the housing
plus 2 mm of acrylic.”

Q
What goes wrong if they are too far forward, or too far back?
“Too far forward, the rotational axis becomes a point: the denture rocks, inserts wear, the base fractures where
acrylic is thinnest. Too far back, the mental nerve is at risk, the posterior extension shortens and cantilevers the
saddles, and a straight implant may perforate the submandibular fossa.”
Q
Take me through the surgery.
“Aseptic technique, infiltration rather than a block so he can report a sharp sensation. Mid-crestal incision
canine to canine, full thickness, both mental bundles identified. Flatten the crest. Graded sharp drills, slow
speed, copious irrigation. 25 to 45 Ncm, one stage with healing abutments. Denture out 48 hours, then relieved
and soft-relined.”
Chain: placement protocol and loading
Q
When would you place, and when would you load? Separate the two.
“Two separate decisions. Placement timing, Types 1 to 4, is when I place relative to the extraction. Loading —
immediate, early, conventional — is when the restoration comes into occlusal contact. Any placement type can
pair with any loading protocol, but the pairings are not equally documented.”
Q
Which placement type applies to this ridge, and why?
“Type 4, late placement. The classification describes socket healing, and after 18 years there is no socket — the
ridge is fully healed. Best documented and most predictable, but maximum resorption has already happened:
that is why the crest is knife-edge.”
Q
And the loading protocol?
“Conventional loading — pick-up beyond two months, about three months in the mandible, confirmed by
clinical stability and ISQ where available. Type 4C is scientifically and clinically validated; no reason to take
risk in a man who has coped for 18 years.”
Q
A colleague loads two mandibular implants on the day. What would have to be true?
“All of: torque above 35 Ncm or ISQ above 70, D1 or D2 bone, no parafunction, no simultaneous graft, a compli-
ant patient on a soft diet. Splinting the implants with a bar, or placing four, strengthens the case; immediate
loading of two independent studs is less well supported. Every criterion exists to control micromotion, above
which fibrous repair replaces bone.”
Q
What would make you abandon early loading on the day?
“Torque under 35 Ncm, a low or falling ISQ, the drill dropping through soft bone, a dehiscence, or a crest needing
reduction or grafting. Then healing abutments, a soft-relined denture and conventional loading — the stability
trough at two to four weeks is unforgiving.”
Chain: choosing an augmentation material
Q
Name the four categories, and be honest about what each does.
“Autograft — osteogenic, osteoinductive and osteoconductive; the only one with living cells. Allograft — osteo-
conductive, demineralised freeze-dried bone variably osteoinductive. Xenograft, deproteinised bovine mineral
— osteoconductive only. Alloplast, 𝛽-tricalcium phosphate or hydroxyapatite — osteoconductive only. A
membrane is osteopromotive.”
Q
Advantages and drawbacks of each?
“Autograft: best biology, fastest incorporation; donor morbidity, small volume, unpredictable resorption. Al-
lograft: no donor site; human origin, batch variability. Xenograft: outstanding volume stability, most docu-
mented; animal origin, particles persisting for years. Alloplast: cheap, no ethical objection; least documented,
resorption too fast or too slow.”

Q
For this knife-edge ridge — graft it, or reduce it?
“Reduce it. Alveoloplasty to a wider basal level avoids grafting altogether, and he has height to spare provided I
clear the canal and keep adequate implant length. I would graft only a residual dehiscence — autogenous chips
against the implant, bovine mineral outside. Ridge splitting, blocks and vertical augmentation are beyond me;
I refer.”
Q
Which barrier membrane, and why?
“Resorbable native collagen for a small contained dehiscence — no second surgery, and if it exposes without
infection, chlorhexidine and no brushing usually sees it heal. Non-resorbable PTFE holds space better but must
be removed, and exposure means removing it early — and a defect that size I would refer.”
Q
What must the consent cover for the graft material specifically?
“The origin — bovine graft, porcine collagen membrane, human if allograft — raised well before the day, be-
cause religious, cultural, dietary and vegetarian objections are legitimate. The theoretical, very low transmission
risk. That autogenous-plus-synthetic alternatives exist and are less documented. And that material, brand and
lot number are recorded.”
Domain 4 — Interpretation and problem solving of clinical outcomes
Chain: complications, their frequency and their prevention
Q
Survival of implants used for a mandibular overdenture?
“Around 95% or better at 10 years in the anterior mandible, among the best-documented figures in implant
dentistry. The consent point is that survival and satisfaction are excellent but maintenance is frequent — the
failures are mechanical, not biological.”
Q
So the prosthetic complications, in order of frequency?
“Worn nylon inserts by a wide margin, typically annually. Then denture base fracture over the housings; abut-
ment loosening; relining as the posterior ridge resorbs; tooth wear with loss of vertical dimension. Mucositis
and peri-implantitis are less frequent but need the same monitoring.”
Q
How do you prevent each?
“Inserts — lowest retention that satisfies him, implants parallel, replaced by schedule. Base fracture — 2 mm of
acrylic over the housing, cobalt-chromium or mesh reinforcement, denture kept tissue-supported. Loosening
— correct torque, rechecked. Relining — expected, so the fit surface is reviewed at every recall.”
Q
At two years it is loose and rocks. Differential?
“Continued posterior ridge resorption, so it is no longer tissue-supported — commonest, and the answer is
a reline, not new inserts. Then worn inserts, a fractured base, a loose abutment, a lost implant, peri-implant
disease, an occlusal error. I check each implant individually, the fit surface with pressure-indicating paste, then
the occlusion.”
Q
What would you monitor, and what would you record?
“Six-monthly: probing at six sites with a plastic probe, bleeding, suppuration, plaque control, denture fit,
extension, occlusion, attachment retention. Recorded: component lot numbers, insertion torque, the consent
discussion, baseline radiographs at fitting, every insert change. Radiographs at one year, then as indicated.”
Q
Explain the maintenance to him, in his words.
“ ‘The two supports should last many years and the denture will feel secure. But it still rests on your gum, and
the gum keeps shrinking slowly — so expect new clips about once a year and a reline every few years. If it clicks,
rocks or feels loose, come in early.’ ”

WATCH OUT
Fall back to the three requirements — support, retention, stability — and say which one this problem belongs
to. It buys you a sentence of thinking time and it is almost always the right frame for a denture question.
Running this case to time
Time check. The flow above holds 39 questions and about 1,760 words of model answer. At examination
pace — 140 words a minute, plus roughly five seconds for each question to be asked — that is close to
fifteen minutes exactly, which is the point: it is written to fill the slot at the speed the slot is actually run.
If your answers are running longer than about thirty seconds, you will reach the end of Domain 2 and no
further, and the marks in Domains 3 and 4 will be awarded on nothing.
The fifteen-minute run sheet
Clock

What earns the mark

images where you can see them

1 Why the denture is loose despite good extension · 2 The landmarks that give a lower denture its support ·
3 What “knife-edge” means for implant placement · 4 Bone density here, and why it matters · 5 The mental
foramen and where it puts your implants · 6 Support, retention, stability — defined · 7 The occlusal scheme,
named and justified · 8 Two implants, and the McGill statement in one sentence · 9 Locator versus bar, with
the specific requirements of each · 10 Placement type and loading protocol, kept apart · 11 The commonest
prosthetic complications and roughly how often · 12 What you record and what you tell him.

Where the marks are lost in this case
Going straight to implants. The first third of this case is undergraduate prosthodontics, and it is marked.
A candidate who cannot define retention or name an occlusal scheme has failed Domain 1 before the CBCT
appears.
Confusing the two protocols. Placement timing and loading protocol are separate decisions. Saying
“immediate” without saying immediate what reads as not knowing the difference.
Under-selling the maintenance. The overdenture is not finished at fit. Volunteer the attachment wear,
the reline interval and the recall — unprompted, this is the difference between a 3 and a 5.

soe.title: Recession and grey show-through at a
soe.text:
SOE Case 6 — Recession and grey show-through at a
malpositioned anterior implant
Anterior view of the implant restoration at the 21 — simulated illustration, not a clinical image
Periapical of the 21 implant — simulated illustration, not a clinical image

CBCT cross-section at the 21 — simulated illustration, not a clinical image
THE CASE
Patient with an implant at the 21, placed immediately after extraction 10 years ago. There is recession with
metal show-through, and the implant is facially malpositioned. There is a history of recurrent soft tissue
infection at the site.
Pace: one structured opening of about 60 seconds, then 36 questions in the remaining 13 minutes. Nothing after the opening earns you more than
a few seconds of thought.
Opening — the 60-second presentation
Q
Present this case.
“An implant at the 21, placed immediately into the socket ten years ago, now facially malpositioned with mid-
facial recession, visible metal and recurrent soft tissue infection. My reading is a chain that began at surgery: a
fixture placed too far buccally where the labial plate is under 1 mm thick and is bundle bone, which resorbs once
the ligament is lost. With no bone buccal to the implant, thin mucosa has receded over a decade and exposed
the shoulder. The recurrent infection may be peri-implantitis, an uncleansable deep sulcus, or residual cement.
What I need to establish is the three-dimensional position on a small-field CBCT, whether there is active disease,
his smile line, and what actually troubles him — because a malpositioned implant cannot be restored into the
right place.”
Domain 1 — Clinical interpretation and reasoning
Chain: the anatomical and biological groundwork
Q
Describe the anatomy relevant to placing an implant at the 21.
“A thin labial cortical plate, often dehisced or fenestrated; the incisive canal palatally; the nasal floor above;
and a scalloped margin whose papillae depend on the crestal bone of adjacent teeth. The alveolus exists only
because the tooth did.”

Q
What is bundle bone, and how thick is that plate at the 21?
“The socket wall into which the periodontal ligament’s Sharpey’s fibres insert; being ligament-supplied, it
resorbs when the tooth goes. Labially at the 21 that plate is usually 1 mm or less and largely bundle bone
— Araújo and Lindhe’s explanation for buccal collapse.”
Q
What happens dimensionally to the socket in the first year?
“Roughly 50% of the ridge width, two-thirds within three months, and greater buccally than palatally, so the
crest migrates palatally.”
Q
What is gingival phenotype, and how do you assess it?
“Gingival thickness plus keratinised width plus bone morphotype; the 2017 World Workshop replaced ‘biotype’
because tissue can be modified. I assess it by probe transparency — if the probe shows through the sulcus it is
thin, under 1 mm. Thin phenotypes recede; thick ones pocket.”
Q
Define peri-implant health, mucositis and peri-implantitis.
“Health — no bleeding or suppuration and no bone loss beyond initial remodelling. Mucositis — bleeding
on gentle probing without that loss, and reversible. Peri-implantitis — adds increased probing depth and
progressive bone loss; without baselines, 6 mm depth with 3 mm bone loss.”
Chain: reading this patient
Q
So what has actually happened here?
“A buccally placed immediate implant, a thin or absent labial plate, a thin phenotype. The bone was never there
to support the mucosa, so tissue crept apically until the shoulder was exposed. The infection is an uncleansable
sulcus or peri-implantitis.”
Q
Why is the smile line pivotal, and what else must you establish?
“It decides whether this is functional with a cosmetic component or purely aesthetic — if his lip covers the
margin, maintenance is legitimate. I also need six-point probing, retention type, keratinised width, papilla
heights against the 11 and 22, and what actually bothers him.”
Q
Would you take a CBCT? Justify it.
“Yes, small field of view. Restoring versus explanting turns on buccal bone volume and angulation, which no
two-dimensional film shows — a diagnostic yield that changes management, which is the IR(ME)R justifica-
tion.”
Domain 2 — Clinical decision making and treatment planning
Chain: what is realistically achievable
Q
How would you record the recession, and do the classifications help you?
“Restoration margin to mucosal margin in millimetres, papilla heights, keratinised width and standardised
photographs. Cairo’s and Miller’s classifications rest on interdental attachment, which around an implant is
set by the adjacent teeth — they predict coverage at teeth, not implants.”
Q
Is coverage around an implant as predictable as around a tooth? Why not?
“No. A tooth has a periodontal ligament with inserting fibres to which a graft reattaches. An implant has
circumferential fibres, no ligament and a poorer supply; the graft lives on periosteum alone, and outside the
bony envelope there is nothing to advance over.”

Q
Start with the least interventive option.
“Treat the infection and maintain — debridement with titanium or PEEK instruments, glycine air-polishing,
single-tufted brush instruction, review. Legitimate where the smile line is low and recession stable — a real
option, not a failure to treat.”
Q
Next — prosthetically, and then soft tissue?
“A ceramic or titanium-base ceramic abutment to take the grey out from under thin mucosa, a recontoured
crown and pink ceramic to mask the deficiency — cheap and reversible, but it does not move the implant. Then
a connective tissue graft: complete coverage is unlikely, but thicker tissue stops further recession.”
Q
And the definitive option? Must the replacement be another implant?
“Explantation and reconstruction — remove the fixture, let soft tissue heal, augment, then re-place correctly
or restore without an implant. It need not be an implant: a cantilever resin-bonded bridge from the 11 over a
grafted ridge is often more reliable aesthetically.”
Q
Which would you recommend?
“It depends on the CBCT and his smile line, and I would say so. Mildly buccal, stable, lip covering it — infection
control, abutment change, thickening, maintenance. Grossly malpositioned, active disease or a high smile line
— explantation.”
Q
A colleague would explant at the first visit. Why might they be right?
“Because everything short of explantation spends his money and tissue on a fixture in the wrong place, and
each intervention scars the site. If he ends up there anyway, the least destructive time to remove it is now.”
Q
SAC classification, and what would you refer?
“Complex, surgically and prosthodontically. Within my competence: diagnosis, the CBCT request, infection
control, abutment change and the discussion.
Beyond it:
explantation, staged augmentation and re-
implantation in the aesthetic zone. I would do the diagnostic work and refer.”
Q
How do you have that conversation with him?
“ ‘The implant sits too far forward in the bone, so the gum has always been thin and has shrunk back until the
metal shows. I can change the part underneath and add gum tissue, but that won’t move the implant. Fixing it
properly means taking it out and rebuilding the area — most of a year, and neither is guaranteed.’ ”
Domain 3 — Decision making in relation to treatment procedures
Chain: placement protocol and loading
Q
This implant was placed immediately. What exactly does “immediate” describe?
“Placement timing and loading are two separate decisions. Types 1 to 4 describe when the implant is placed
relative to the extraction — this was Type 1, the same day. Immediate, early and conventional describe when a
restoration is attached. They are chosen independently.”
Q
What are the pre-requisites for Type 1 placement, and were they met here?
“No acute infection, intact socket walls with a facial wall of at least 1 mm, palatal bone for primary stability, the
socket within the alveolar envelope, and a grafted jumping gap of 2 mm or more. Here the wall was thin and
the fixture went buccally — several were unmet.”
Q
A colleague says immediate placement preserves the buccal plate. Argue against that.

“It does not. The buccal plate is largely bundle bone, dependent on the ligament, and resorbs whatever I put
in the socket. Immediate placement saves time and surgical episodes — not bone — and costs control of the
three-dimensional position.”
Q
If you explanted and re-treated, which placement type, and why not immediate?
“Type 4, late placement into a healed, staged-augmented ridge. Not immediate: an explantation defect has no
intact socket walls, often residual infection and no bony envelope, so neither primary stability nor the correct
position could be guaranteed.”
Q
And the loading protocol on the second attempt?
“Conventional loading beyond two months — Type 4C, scientifically and clinically validated — extended to
six to nine months in staged grafted bone. I would stage it for torque under 35 Ncm or ISQ under 70, D4 bone,
parafunction, or simultaneous augmentation.”
Chain: choosing an augmentation material
Q
Name the four categories of graft material and the properties each has.
“Autograft — osteogenic, osteoinductive and osteoconductive, the only living material, but limited volume,
donor morbidity, unpredictable resorption. Allograft — osteoconductive, variably osteoinductive, human ori-
gin. Xenograft and alloplast are osteoconductive only; xenograft gives outstanding volume stability, alloplast
avoids all human and animal origin.”
Q
What would you graft an explantation defect with, and why that combination?
“Particulate autograft or allograft against the bone where biology matters, layered with a slowly resorbing
xenograft outside for contour, because deproteinised bovine bone mineral barely resorbs and holds the buccal
profile for years. It marries the biology of one to the stability of the other.”
Q
And the membrane?
“A resorbable collagen membrane onto sound bone for a contained defect — no second surgery, and if it exposes
without infection, chlorhexidine and no brushing often see it heal. Non-resorbable PTFE maintains space better,
but exposure means early removal.”
Q
Is that reconstruction within your competence?
“No. A large three-dimensional defect in the aesthetic zone, needing horizontal and often vertical augmenta-
tion, is beyond a general dentist with an interest in implants — vertical augmentation is the least predictable
procedure of all. I would control the infection and refer.”
Q
What must you consent him to specifically about the materials?
“The origin of every material — bovine or porcine xenograft, human donor allograft, porcine collagen mem-
brane — the theoretical transmission risk, that autogenous and synthetic alternatives exist, less well docu-
mented, and that lot numbers are recorded. Religious, cultural and dietary objections must be raised well
before the day of surgery.”
Chain: doing it
Q
Whichever route you take, what comes first?
“Control the infection. Retrieve the restoration if possible, debride with titanium or PEEK curettes and a plastic-
sheathed ultrasonic tip, subgingival glycine air-polishing, re-establish a cleansable emergence. Reassess at four
to six weeks — you do not graft into an inflamed field.”

Q
You find residual cement. What do you do?
“Remove all of it — scaler, air-polishing, flap access if I cannot see it. Residual cement is a recognised cause
of peri-implant disease, and only radiopaque cements show on a film, so a clear radiograph proves nothing.
Then convert to screw retention.”
Q
If you take the graft route, describe the harvest and the recipient site.
“A palatal connective tissue graft, single-incision, between distal of the canine and mesial of the first molar, 5 to
7 mm apical to the gingival margin to spare the greater palatine bundle, 1 to 1.5 mm thick. Recipient: a split-
thickness envelope advanced without tension, under a screw-retained provisional with a deliberately concave
subgingival contour.”
Q
Describe explantation, and what if reverse-torque fails?
“Reverse-torque first, unscrewing the fixture out through the internal connection; it removes almost no bone.
If it fails, piezoelectric surgery around the circumference, then re-attempt. A trephine only as a last resort — it
sacrifices the ring of bone I need for reconstruction.”
Q
What do you do immediately after removal, and what interim prosthesis?
“Debride the granulation tissue and read the defect. If contained, graft immediately; if the buccal plate is absent,
do not chase it — let soft tissue heal six to eight weeks, then stage it. Interim cover is a bonded pontic, never a
denture flange.”
Domain 4 — Interpretation and problem solving of clinical outcomes
Chain: outcome, record and candour
Q
What outcome would you promise him, and how would you judge it?
“None. Partial improvement is likely, complete coverage unlikely. I would judge it on standardised pho-
tographs at baseline and each review, millimetre measurements of mucosal margin, papilla height and kera-
tinised width, the Pink Aesthetic Score, and his own rating in his words.”
Q
What would you record?
“His concern in his own words; the peri-implant chart with bleeding and suppuration; smile line, phenotype,
keratinised width; retention type; the CBCT justification; photographs; every option including no treatment,
with risks, costs and prognosis; and his decision.”
Q
He is dissatisfied, and then complains formally. How do you handle it?
“Listen, examine, review the records with him. If the outcome was consented, I say so and offer a second opinion;
if not, duty of candour — tell him promptly, apologise, put right what I can. Then the practice complaints
procedure, notify my indemnifier, record a significant event.”

Q
If he elects to do nothing, what would you expect in five years?
“Slow further recession: the driver — a fixture outside the bony envelope under a thin phenotype — is un-
changed. Recurrent mucositis and real risk of peri-implantitis, since the sulcus cannot be cleaned. The implant
will probably stay integrated — survival is not success.”
WATCH OUT
Ask yourself whether the problem is bone, soft tissue, or implant position — and say which. Position problems
cannot be restored away, and naming that buys you a sentence and is almost always the right frame in the
aesthetic zone.
Running this case to time
Time check. The flow above holds 37 questions and about 1,646 words of model answer. At examination
pace — 140 words a minute, plus roughly five seconds for each question to be asked — that comes to just
under fifteen minutes, so it fits, with perhaps ten seconds in hand. The answers are short because the
question count is high: this is a case examined in rapid chains, not in paragraphs. If your answers run
past thirty seconds you will still be on graft materials when the candour question arrives, and Domain 4
will be marked on nothing.

Phenotype, and how you assess it · 4 Health, mucositis, peri-implantitis defined · 5 Why the smile line

least interventive option, offered seriously · 9 The Type 1 pre-requisites, and which were unmet · 10 Why
immediate placement did not preserve the plate · 11 Control the infection before anything else · 12 What
outcome you promise — and that survival is not success.
Where the marks are lost in this case
Restoring the position away. Candidates offer a ceramic abutment, pink ceramic and a connective tissue
graft as though they solved the problem. They mask it. Say once, plainly, that the fixture sits outside the
bony envelope and nothing prosthetic will move it — that sentence is the case.
Dismissing maintenance as doing nothing. If his lip covers the margin and the recession is stable, in-
fection control and review is a legitimate treatment, not a failure to treat. Offering it seriously, alongside
explantation, is what shows judgement rather than enthusiasm.

in the aesthetic zone — vertical augmentation above all — are beyond a general dentist with an interest in
implants. Do the diagnostic work, control the infection, and name the referral before you are asked for it.

soe.title: Stage IV Grade C periodontitis and a failing
soe.text:
SOE Case 7 — Stage IV Grade C periodontitis and a failing
dentition
Panoramic radiograph — simulated illustration, not a clinical image
The six-point periodontal chart — simulated illustration, not a clinical image
THE CASE
A patient with generalised periodontitis, Stage IV, Grade C — sometimes loosely called “grade 4C” — with
multiple failing teeth. The question put to you is how to plan tooth replacement.
Pace: one structured opening of about 60 seconds, then roughly 39 questions in the remaining 13 minutes. Nothing after the opening earns you
more than a few seconds of thought.
Opening — the 60-second presentation
Q
Present this case.
“A patient with generalised periodontitis, Stage IV, Grade C and a collapsing dentition — advanced attachment
loss, teeth already lost to the disease, and progression rapid for his age and for the plaque present. The question
asked is tooth replacement, but replacement is the last decision, not the first. A history of periodontitis is the
strongest patient-level risk factor for peri-implantitis, and Grade C means the destruction is active now. So
my plan is periodontal first: diagnosis, risk factor control, extraction of hopeless teeth, non-surgical therapy,
and re-evaluation against the EFP stability criteria. Only if he reaches and holds stability, with attendance
demonstrated rather than promised, would I discuss implants — and even then a well-designed removable
prosthesis or a shortened arch may serve him better.”
Domain 1 — Clinical interpretation and reasoning
Chain: the periodontal groundwork
Q
Name the components of the periodontium.

“Gingiva, periodontal ligament, root cementum and alveolar bone. The dentogingival junction is sulcular
and junctional epithelium, attached by hemidesmosomes. The ligament fibres — crestal, horizontal, oblique,
apical, interradicular — suspend the tooth and carry its proprioception.”
Q
What are the supracrestal attached tissues, and why do they matter?
“The 2017 term for biologic width — junctional epithelium plus connective tissue attachment, about 2 mm
above the crest. A margin within it causes inflammation and attachment loss. The same principle governs
crown margin and implant platform depth.”
Q
How does the peri-implant attachment differ?
“No ligament and no cementum, so no inserting Sharpey’s fibres. Fibres run parallel and circumferentially, the
tissue collagen-rich and fibroblast-poor, the supply periosteal only. A weaker seal — peri-implantitis progresses
faster and less predictably.”
Q
Take me through staging, and what makes him Stage IV?
“Staging is severity and complexity, from interdental attachment loss at the worst site: Stage I one to two
millimetres, II three to four, III five or more with up to four teeth lost. Stage IV is that loss with five or more
lost, plus bite collapse, drifting or degree 2 mobility.”
Q
And grading?
“Grading is rate of progression — bone loss percentage over age — A under 0.25, B 0.25 to 1.0, C over 1.0 — or
destruction exceeding the deposits. Modifiers: smoking ten a day, HbA1c 7.0% or more.”
Q
What completes the diagnosis?
“Extent — localised under 30% of teeth, generalised at 30% or more — and status: stable, in remission or
unstable. So: ‘generalised periodontitis, Stage IV, Grade C, currently unstable’. That last word stops the implant
conversation.”
Chain: what that means for this patient
Q
Why is that diagnosis the single most important fact here?
“Because previous periodontitis is the strongest patient-level risk factor for peri-implantitis, and Grade C
means active destruction now. Implants transplant the same dysbiotic biofilm onto a surface with a weaker seal
and no ligament, and the disease recurs faster.”
Q
What must you know before planning?
“Six-point charting with recession, mobility, furcation and bleeding; plaque scores; full-mouth radiographs;
smoking in pack-years; HbA1c; medical history; his priorities and finances; and what treatment he has had
and how he responded.”
Domain 2 — Clinical decision making and treatment planning
Chain: sequencing
Q
Outline your plan in one sentence.
“Periodontal first, prosthetic later — cause-related therapy, risk factor control, extraction of hopeless teeth with
an interim prosthesis, re-evaluation at three months, replacement only in a stable attending mouth, then three-
monthly supportive therapy indefinitely.”
Q
What does Phase 1 consist of?

“Explain the diagnosis. Smoking cessation — very brief advice, then refer. Liaise with the GP on glycaemic
control. Hygiene instruction with plaque and bleeding scores every visit, so behaviour change is measured.
Extract hopeless teeth, then full-mouth subgingival instrumentation per EFP S3.”
Q
Which teeth are hopeless?
“Grade 3 mobility; bone loss beyond 75% of root length; an unmaintainable Grade III furcation; unrestorable
caries, vertical root fracture or persistent suppuration. Strategic value counts — a hopeless tooth under a denture
saddle goes, a marginal overdenture abutment may stay.”
Q
How do you grade furcation and mobility?
“Hamp — Grade I horizontal loss under 3 mm, II over 3 mm, III through-and-through. Miller — Grade 1
up to 1 mm horizontally, 2 over 1 mm, 3 plus vertical depressibility. Both recorded at charting; both drive
extractions.”
Q
When do you re-evaluate, and against what endpoint?
“At three months, re-charting fully. The endpoint is the EFP definition of stability: pockets 4 mm or less, no
bleeding at any 4 mm site, full-mouth bleeding under 10% — an objective number I can share with him.”
Q
He has not reached it. What then?
“Step 3 — repeated instrumentation of residual pockets, surgery for deep sites, or referral. First re-check the
obvious: cleaning, smoking, HbA1c, missed calculus or a furcation. Non-response is usually compliance or
diagnosis, not instrumentation.”
Chain: whether implants at all
Q
Would you ever place implants in this patient?
“Potentially, on four conditions: periodontitis treated and objectively stable; smoking stopped or substantially
reduced; adequate glycaemic control; and three-monthly compliance demonstrated over 6 to 12 months, not
promised. Even then I consent him to a peri-implantitis risk well above average.”
Q
What would you say to him in his own words?
“ ‘Your gum disease is why you are losing teeth, and it is moving fast. Implants don’t decay, but they catch the
same infection — and around an implant it does more damage, more quickly. So we settle the gums first, then
talk about replacing teeth.’ ”
Q
What are the alternatives?
“A hygienic cobalt-chromium partial denture — maximal gingival clearance, rests on sound teeth — added to
as more teeth are lost. Complete dentures if the dentition is failing. The well-evidenced shortened dental arch.
Or two implants retaining a mandibular overdenture.”
Q
A colleague says extract everything and place implants — the disease then has nothing to live in. Why might they
be wrong?
“Because the pathogens are not confined to pockets — they persist on the tongue, tonsils and mucosa and
recolonise peri-implant sulci within weeks. And the real drivers — host response, smoking, glycaemic control,
plaque control — follow the patient, not the teeth.”
Q
SAC classification, and what is beyond you?
“At least Advanced, and with ridge defects, altered vertical dimension and multiple missing units, likely Com-
plex. Within my scope: diagnosis, cause-related therapy, extractions, interim prostheses, maintenance. Beyond
it: periodontal surgery and the definitive reconstruction — I refer or co-manage.”

Domain 3 — Decision making in relation to treatment procedures
Chain: doing the work
Q
What would you do at the extraction visits?
“Extract atraumatically — periotomes, luxators, and sectioning rather than expanding the socket — preserving
every wall, and debride granulation tissue. Sequence so he is never without anterior teeth or posterior support.
Alveoloplasty only where an undercut would compromise the denture.”
Q
Describe your subgingival instrumentation — and would you use adjunctive antimicrobials?
“Full-mouth, quadrant by quadrant under local anaesthesia, hand instruments and ultrasonics together — no
meaningful difference between them, so access and thoroughness decide. Endpoint: a smooth root, no de-
tectable deposit. Systemic antimicrobials are not indicated routinely; local agents suit isolated non-responding
sites.”
Q
If you eventually restore implants, what would you design differently?
“Screw-retained without exception — retrievable, because I should assume I will remove it to treat peri-
implant disease, and no cement left behind.
Emergence profiles cleansable with an interdental brush,
margins supragingival, and three-monthly recall from fit.”
Q
Does he need keratinised mucosa?
“In a plaque-susceptible patient, yes — at least 2 mm, grafted if necessary. The evidence it is essential to survival
is weak; the evidence it makes brushing comfortable and reduces plaque is reasonable. Comfort while cleaning
determines his outcome.”
Q
How would you design his interim prosthesis?
“Acrylic, hygienic, clear of the gingival margins, easily added to and relined, resting on sound teeth. He will
wear it a year or more, so it must not become the plaque trap that undoes the therapy.”
Chain: placement protocol and loading
Q
When would you place, and when would you load?
“Two separate decisions. Types 1 to 4 describe when I place relative to the extraction; immediate, early and
conventional describe when the restoration comes into occlusion. They are chosen independently, and I grade
the combination against the ITI evidence table.”
Q
Why not Type 1 — immediate placement into a socket lost to periodontitis?
“The pre-requisites are absent: no acute infection, intact socket walls with a facial wall of at least 1 mm, apical
and palatal bone for primary stability, and a jumping gap of 2 mm grafted with xenograft. Periodontitis has
destroyed the walls and infected the site. And immediate placement does not preserve the buccal plate —
bundle bone is ligament-dependent.”
Q
Which type would you use, and how long would you wait?
“Type 4 — late placement at six months or more into a healed ridge; the best-documented protocol, and the
honest choice where infection must resolve. At extraction I would do ridge preservation only where the site is
a realistic future implant site.”
Q
And the loading protocol?
“Conventional loading beyond two months — Type 4C, scientifically and clinically validated; three months
mandible, six maxilla, longer in grafted bone. I would not chase immediate loading: it needs 35 Ncm or ISQ
over 70, and saved weeks do not justify the risk here.”

Chain: choosing an augmentation material
Q
What are the four categories of graft material, and what does each do?
“Autograft — the only osteogenic material, also osteoinductive, but limited volume, donor morbidity, unpre-
dictable resorption. Allograft — human donor, osteoconductive, variably osteoinductive, batch-dependent.
Xenograft — deproteinised bovine mineral, osteoconductive only, but outstanding volume stability and best
documented. Alloplast — synthetic, osteoconductive only, no ethical objection, less documented.”
Q
What would you use for socket preservation, and why?
“A slowly resorbing xenograft — deproteinised bovine bone mineral — with a socket seal or membrane, placed
flaplessly. Its very slow resorption holds the ridge dimension across four to six months of healing, which
autogenous bone or a fast-resorbing alloplast would not.”
Q
The socket walls are already destroyed by the disease. What then?
“Then space maintenance and graft stability are lost: this is staged augmentation, not socket preservation — and
I would not graft an infected site. Debride, heal, reassess on CBCT. Vertical and large horizontal augmentation
in a Stage IV mouth are beyond a general dentist with an interest in implants — I refer.”
Q
Would you use a barrier membrane, and which?
“Yes — a native porcine collagen membrane for a socket or small dehiscence: resorbable, forgiving if it exposes,
extended 2 to 3 mm onto sound bone. Dense PTFE may be left deliberately exposed and removed at three to
four weeks. Titanium-reinforced membranes go with the referral.”
Q
What must you consent him to specifically about the graft?
“The origin — bovine graft, porcine membrane, human donor if allograft — because religious, cultural,
dietary and vegetarian objections are legitimate, raised well before the day of surgery, with an autogenous-
plus-synthetic alternative offered. Also that exposure is the commonest complication, and that the lot number
is recorded.”
Domain 4 — Interpretation and problem solving of clinical outcomes
Chain: monitoring and the long view
Q
How would you monitor him?
“Plaque and bleeding scores every visit, six-point charting at re-evaluation, radiographs against baseline, and
once implants exist six-site peri-implant probing with bleeding and suppuration. I set the intervention thresh-
old in advance and share it.”
Q
What would you record?
“The full 2017 diagnosis with extent and status; charting and scores throughout; smoking, HbA1c and the con-
versations about them; every option including no treatment, with risks, costs and prognosis; that his elevated
peri-implantitis risk and lifelong maintenance were explained; his decision.”
Q
What is your single greatest concern at five years?
“That he stops attending.
Every biological outcome rests on supportive care, and non-attendance is the
strongest predictor of implant loss in treated periodontitis. I build it into the consent and the recall, and say
plainly: ‘The treatment is not the day I place the implant.’ ”
Q
Two years on, one implant probes 7 mm with bleeding, suppuration and 4 mm of bone loss. Your assessment?
“Peri-implantitis, here the disease recurring, not a local accident. Check compliance, smoking, HbA1c and
prosthesis cleansability; remove the restoration; debride with titanium instruments and glycine air-polishing;
reassess at one month. Persistent suppuration with 6 mm or more means surgery — I refer.”

Q
He tells you he has seen the hygienist twice in two years. What does that change?
“Everything. In a Grade C patient that is the principal risk factor realising itself. I would explore why rather
than lecture — cost, time, anxiety, lost sense of benefit — then consider whether further implant treatment is
contraindicated and a removable design more honest.”
Q
How would you know the whole treatment had succeeded?
“By his measure and mine. His: he eats what he wants, loses no more teeth, is not embarrassed. Mine: EFP
stability held, no further teeth or implants lost, stable bone, and maintenance he attends. Prosthesis survival
alone is not success.”
WATCH OUT
Say where the patient is in the sequence — diagnosis, cause-related therapy, re-evaluation, definitive treat-
ment, or maintenance — and answer from there. In a Stage IV Grade C case the answer is almost always that
the periodontal phase is not finished yet.
Running this case to time
Time check. The flow above holds 40 questions and about 1,721 words of model answer — the highest
question count in the notebook. At examination pace — 140 words a minute, plus roughly five seconds
for each question to be asked — that is about fifteen minutes and forty seconds, so it overruns by rather
less than a minute. An examiner behind time compresses the three chains of Domain 3 into two, usually
by taking the graft categories as one question. If your answers run past thirty seconds you will still be
staging and grading when the maintenance questions decide Domain 4.
