modifiers · 6 Extent and status, and why “unstable” ends the conversation · 7 Which teeth are hopeless ·
8 The EFP stability endpoint, in numbers · 9 The four conditions before any implant · 10 Why extracting
everything does not remove the disease · 11 Why not Type 1 into a periodontitis socket · 12 The single
greatest concern at five years.
Where the marks are lost in this case
Answering the question that was asked. He is presented as a tooth-replacement problem and candi-
dates dutifully plan replacements. The mark is in refusing the framing: say in the opening minute that
replacement is the last decision, and that “currently unstable” stops the implant conversation.
Quoting stability without the numbers. “Periodontally stable” is worth nothing; pockets 4 mm or less,
no bleeding at any 4 mm site, full-mouth bleeding under 10% is an endpoint you can share with him
and re-chart against. Volunteer the three-month re-evaluation, and what you do if he has not reached it.
Trusting a promise of attendance. Non-attendance is the principal risk factor realising itself, so compli-
ance must be demonstrated over six to twelve months before implants are considered — and when he
has seen the hygienist twice in two years, the honest answer is that further implant treatment may be
contraindicated.

soe.title: Peri-implantitis at linked LR6 and LR7
soe.text:
SOE Case 8 — Peri-implantitis at linked LR6 and LR7
THE CASE
(The published RCSEd sample scenario, Appendix E.) 45-year-old female, first attendance, routine check-up. Occa-
sional soreness of the gum near the implants, sometimes aware of discharge, otherwise asymptomatic — no
pain, never any bleeding. Brings radiographs from when the implants were restored. Implants placed 3 years
ago by a dentist who has retired; aware of soreness for 1 year, worsening; lost the molars because of failed
crowns. No relevant medical history. Lives alone; never smoked; unaware of grinding or clenching; moderate
stress. Regular attender until 2 years ago; sees the hygienist periodically, last visit over 2 years ago. She wants
to know why she has the soreness and whether her implants are okay. EO: NAD. Soft tissues NAD; oral
hygiene fair to good; gingival tissues healthy except at LR6/7 where the marginal tissues are inflamed with
bleeding and pus discharge. Probing depths generally up to 3 mm; 6 mm around the LR6/7 implants. BPE:
upper 1/1/1; lower 4/1/1. Intact, unrestored dentition. Implants LR6 and LR7 linked by the restoration. Class
I occlusion. Post-surgical radiographs (patient’s own) and radiographs taken at presentation are provided.
Pace: one structured opening of about 60 seconds, then roughly 35 questions in the remaining 14 minutes. Nothing after the opening earns you
more than a few seconds of thought.
Opening — the 60-second presentation
Q
Present this case.
“A 45-year-old woman attending for the first time with a one-year history of worsening soreness and intermittent
discharge around two linked implants placed three years ago. She has an otherwise intact, unrestored, periodon-
tally healthy mouth with fair-to-good hygiene, has never smoked and has no relevant medical history — so the
patient-level risk factors are largely absent. What stands out is that she has had no supportive maintenance
for over two years, and that the two implants are splinted by a single restoration with 6 mm pockets, bleeding
and suppuration confined to that sextant. My working diagnosis is peri-implantitis at the LR6 and LR7. My
priorities are to confirm it against her own baseline radiographs, to establish why it has happened, and to decide
whether the implants are retainable.”
Domain 1 — Clinical interpretation and reasoning
Chain: the periodontal groundwork
Q
Describe the attachment apparatus of a natural tooth.
“From the sulcus apically: junctional epithelium, attached to enamel by hemidesmosomes and a basal lamina,
about 1 mm; then a connective tissue attachment of about 1 mm in which the supracrestal fibre groups —
dentogingival, dentoperiosteal, circular and transseptal — insert perpendicularly into cementum as Sharpey’s
fibres. Below that, the periodontal ligament and alveolar bone. The epithelial plus connective tissue component
is the supracrestal attachment, historically the biologic width, around 2 mm.”
Q
How does the peri-implant soft tissue differ?
“There is no cementum and no periodontal ligament, so nothing inserts into the implant. The junctional ep-
ithelium is longer, and the connective tissue fibres run parallel or circumferential to the implant surface rather
than perpendicular. The tissue is more collagenous and less vascular, and the blood supply comes only from
the periosteum and bone, not from a ligament. The result is a weaker seal with poorer defence.”
Q
What does that mean for this lesion?
“That peri-implantitis behaves worse than periodontitis. The lesion extends closer to the bone crest, is not
encapsulated by a fibrous barrier, and progresses faster and in a non-linear, accelerating pattern. There is
no periodontal ligament proprioception, so she has no pain and no awareness — which is exactly her history:
soreness and discharge but never any bleeding she noticed, over a year.”

Q
How is the BPE recorded?
“Six sextants, using a WHO probe with a 0.5 mm ball end and black band from 3.5 to 5.5 mm, at a force of 20 to
25 grams, walking around every tooth and recording the highest code per sextant. Code 0 healthy, 1 bleeding,
2 plaque retentive factor or calculus, 3 black band partly visible so 4 to 5 mm, 4 black band disappears so 6 mm
or more, and * for furcation involvement or 7 mm attachment loss.”
Q
What does her code 4 tell you?
“That the lower right sextant has probing depths of 6 mm or more while every other sextant is a code 1. That
distribution is the diagnosis in itself: a localised, site-specific problem centred on the implants, not generalised
periodontitis. A code 4 obliges me to record a full-mouth six-point pocket chart with recession, plaque and
bleeding scores, and radiographs where indicated — not just that sextant.”
Q
Define peri-implant health, mucositis and peri-implantitis.
“On the 2017 World Workshop definitions: health — no erythema, no bleeding on probing, no suppuration,
no increase in probing depth, no bone loss beyond initial crestal remodelling. Mucositis — bleeding on gentle
probing with or without erythema, swelling or suppuration, and no bone loss beyond crestal remodelling; it
is plaque-induced and reversible. Peri-implantitis — bleeding and/or suppuration, increased probing depth
compared with previous examinations, and bone loss beyond crestal remodelling.”
Q
Which does she have, and on what evidence?
“Peri-implantitis at the LR6 and LR7 — suppuration, bleeding, 6 mm probing depths against 3 mm elsewhere,
and I expect radiographic bone loss beyond remodelling when I compare with her baseline. The rest of the
mouth is peri-implant and periodontally healthy. Formally I would say localised peri-implantitis at two im-
plants in a patient with clinical gingival health on an intact periodontium.”
Chain: reading her radiographs and her history
Q
Why do her own post-restoration radiographs matter so much?
“Because the case definition is built on change from a previous examination. With her baseline I can apply it
directly and I can estimate the rate of loss, which is what determines urgency and prognosis. Without a baseline
I fall back on the surrogate thresholds: bleeding or suppuration, probing depth of 6 mm or more, and bone level
3 mm or more apical to the most coronal intraosseous part of the implant.”
Q
What are the risk factors in this history?
“The dominant one is absence of supportive maintenance for over two years. She has never smoked, has no
medical history, denies parafunction and cleans reasonably — so the patient-level suspects are largely absent.
That directs me to prosthesis-related factors: two implants splinted by one restoration so an interdental brush
cannot pass, possible over-contour or ridge-lap, possible residual cement if it is cement-retained, implant depth,
emergence profile, and the width of keratinised mucosa.”
Q
How do you probe an implant, and what are the pitfalls?
“Six sites per implant with a plastic, PEEK or titanium probe at a light force of about 0.2 to 0.25 newtons,
recording depth, bleeding and suppuration, plus recession and keratinised width. The pitfalls are that the
restoration contour often prevents the probe reaching the true base, so depths are underestimated; and that
absolute depth means little without a baseline, because a deeply placed implant reads deep when healthy.”
Q
What else would you examine and investigate?
“Mobility — testing the implants themselves, removing the restoration if necessary to distinguish a loose pros-
thesis from a mobile implant. A standardised paralleling periapical compared directly with her films. The
prosthesis: retention type, fit, contour, whether a brush passes, residual cement, abutment seating. Occlusion,
including excursive contacts on the implants. Full-mouth charting with plaque and bleeding scores. And with
her consent I would try to obtain the original records from the retired dentist’s practice.”

Domain 2 — Clinical decision making and treatment planning
Chain: telling her
Q
How do you explain the diagnosis to her, in her words?
“ ‘Implants can get a gum infection just like teeth can, and that is what has happened here. There is an infection
in the gum and bone around both of these implants — that is why it is sore and why you get the discharge. The
rest of your mouth is healthy and you clean well. The two problems are that these implants are joined together,
so you cannot clean between them however hard you try, and that nobody has been checking them for over two
years. I need measurements and an X-ray to compare with yours before I tell you how much bone has been
lost.’ ”
Q
She asks whether it is her fault. What do you say?
“ ‘No. You have been cleaning a restoration that is very diﬀicult to clean, and you were not told this needed
checking every few months. What matters now is what we change.’ I would then be honest that going forward
her cleaning and her attendance are the two things that decide the outcome — so it is not blame, but she does
own part of the solution.”
Chain: the plan
Q
What is your treatment plan, in outline?
“Following the ITI structure: cause-related therapy — explain the disease, discuss costs and adverse effects
including recession, modify risk factors, and above all make the prosthesis cleansable. Then non-surgical
therapy, then re-assessment at about one month. If it has resolved, straight to supportive care. If suppuration
or bleeding persists with depths of 6 mm or more, surgical therapy. Then supportive therapy every three to
five months, indefinitely.”
Q
Why is the linked restoration so central?
“Because the disease is biofilm-driven, and no debridement I perform survives contact with a site she cannot
clean at home. If an interdental brush cannot pass between the LR6 and LR7, the embrasure is a permanent
reservoir. Cleansability is the treatment, not an adjunct to it.”
Q
Would you separate the two implants?
“I would strongly consider it — two individual screw-retained crowns with open, cleansable embrasures. Splint-
ing is sometimes justified mechanically, but here it is very likely causal. The counter-argument is the cost of a
remake, which I would discuss openly. If that is not affordable now, opening the embrasure on the existing
restoration is a legitimate interim measure.”
Q
Your colleague would leave the restoration alone and simply debride and review. Why might he be right?
“Because removing a three-year-old restoration risks fracturing it, stripping a screw or damaging the abutment,
and he may be left with a worse problem and an unrestored implant. He would also argue that debridement
plus proper hygiene instruction resolves a proportion of cases without any prosthetic work, so the reversible
step should be taken first. That is a fair position — I would test cleansability with a brush before condemning
the restoration.”
Q
If it is cement-retained, what changes?
“Residual cement moves to the top of my differential — it is a well-recognised cause of peri-implant disease,
particularly with deep, subgingival margins. I would attempt retrieval, inspect for cement radiographically and
directly, remove every trace, and if I re-restore I would convert to screw retention or use a cementable-screw-
retained design so no cement sits subgingivally.”
Q
What is the SAC classification of this case?
“The prosthetic re-treatment and the non-surgical management are Advanced. Surgical management of peri-
implantitis, and explantation, are Complex — the outcome is unpredictable, the aesthetic and functional
consequences are significant, and the evidence for reconstructive techniques is uncertain.”

Q
So what is within your competence, and when do you refer?
“Within: the diagnosis, the full charting and radiographic comparison, the prosthetic assessment, restoration
removal, converting to a cleansable screw-retained design, non-surgical therapy, and lifelong supportive care.
Beyond: surgical peri-implantitis therapy, particularly reconstructive surgery, and explantation — I would
refer for those unless specifically trained. I would complete the diagnostic work first so the referral is useful
rather than a hand-off.”
Q
What prognosis do you give her?
“Not one until I have the radiograph and the charting. Then I frame it by proportion of bone lost, whether the
disease arrests at the one-month review, and her ability to clean and attend. I would be honest that the aim is to
arrest the disease, not regrow bone, that recession is a likely consequence of successful treatment, and that
with extensive bone loss the right answer may be removal.”
Domain 3 — Decision making in relation to treatment procedures
Chain: the non-surgical appointment
Q
Talk me through that appointment.
“Update the history and record plaque and bleeding scores. Remove the restoration if it is retrievable — that
transforms access and lets me inspect for cement and for an unseated abutment. Debride with titanium or
PEEK curettes and ultrasonics with a plastic-sheathed tip, then glycine or erythritol air-polishing delivered
subgingivally. Irrigate. Modify contours where I can. Re-seat and re-torque. Then oral hygiene instruction,
and book the one-month re-assessment.”
Q
Why air-polishing rather than curettes alone?
“Because the implant surface is threaded and often roughened, and a curette blade cannot reach into the threads
or the microtopography. A low-abrasive glycine or erythritol powder disrupts biofilm in those recesses without
gouging the titanium. The evidence shows it improves biofilm removal; it does not by itself change the need to
make the site cleansable.”
Q
What must you not use on the implant surface, and why?
“Stainless steel curettes and unsheathed metal ultrasonic tips — they scratch titanium, leaving a rougher
surface that accumulates more biofilm, and they shed metal particles. Also avoid conventional abrasive pro-
phylaxis pastes and, on titanium, acidulated fluoride, which can corrode the surface.”
Q
Would you prescribe systemic antibiotics?
“Not routinely for non-surgical therapy — the evidence for benefit is weak and the antimicrobial stewardship
argument is strong. I would consider them for spreading infection, systemic upset, or as a peri-operative
adjunct at reconstructive surgery. Local delivery agents and photodynamic therapy are options, but I would
present the evidence for them as modest.”
Q
What oral hygiene do you actually prescribe her?
“Size an interdental brush to each embrasure and have her demonstrate it in a mirror, not just watch me. Add
a single-tufted brush angled at the implant necks, and superfloss or a floss threader beneath the linked unit
while it remains linked. A powered toothbrush. I would give written instructions and re-check technique at
every visit, because instruction given once is not instruction.”
Q
What would you record?
“The full six-point chart with bleeding and suppuration, plaque and bleeding scores, keratinised width, mobility
of each implant tested separately, the radiographic comparison with her baseline and the bone loss measured
in millimetres, the prosthesis assessment, the diagnosis in 2017 terms, the options discussed with risks, costs
and alternatives, what she chose, the hygiene instruction given, and the review interval. Plus my attempt to
obtain the original records.”

Chain: if it goes to surgery
Q
What would the surgical procedure involve?
“A full-thickness mucoperiosteal flap for access, complete removal of granulation tissue, and decontamination
of the exposed implant surface — mechanically with a titanium brush or ultrasonics, chemically with saline,
chlorhexidine or hydrogen peroxide, or with an Er:YAG laser. Then treatment according to defect morphology,
careful flap adaptation, antiseptic mouthrinse post-operatively, and systemic antimicrobials where indicated.”
Q
What decides reconstructive versus resective?
“Defect morphology. A contained, circumferential intrabony defect with intact walls is the case for reconstruc-
tion with a bone substitute, with or without a membrane. A supracrestal or dehiscence-type defect with lost
walls will not hold a graft, so the answer is resective — recontouring, implantoplasty and an apically positioned
flap. Aesthetic risk is the other determinant.”
Q
Why is this particular site suited to a resective approach?
“Because it is a lower right molar region — not aesthetically visible, with a thick tissue biotype and good access.
The recession and exposed threads that resective surgery produces are far more acceptable here than they would
be anteriorly, and the resulting profile is easier for her to clean, which is the whole point.”
Q
What is implantoplasty, and what are its drawbacks?
“Mechanically smoothing and polishing the exposed threaded surface with burs so it no longer retains biofilm.
Drawbacks: titanium particles shed into the tissues, overheating, weakening of the implant body — a real
fracture concern in a narrow implant — and it is irreversible. It also demands meticulous soft tissue and suction
management to limit particle spread.”
Domain 4 — Interpretation and problem solving of clinical outcomes
Chain: measuring the outcome and dealing with failure
Q
What determines whether this treatment succeeds?
“Three things: whether the prosthesis can be made cleansable, whether she can and does clean it, and whether
she attends three- to five-monthly maintenance. The decontamination technique matters, but it fails without
all three of those.”
Q
What outcomes will you measure, and when?
“At one month: bleeding on probing, suppuration and probing depths. At three months and each maintenance
visit: the same plus plaque scores. Radiographically: a new baseline after treatment, compared at 12 months.
And her own symptoms — the soreness and discharge she presented with — because that is her measure, not
mine.”
Q
Define a successful outcome in one sentence.
“Absence of suppuration, absence of bleeding on gentle probing, no further increase in probing depth and
stable bone levels against the post-treatment baseline — in a patient who is comfortable, can clean the restora-
tion and attends her maintenance.”
Q
What happens at a maintenance visit?
“Update the history, plaque and bleeding scores, six-point peri-implant probing with bleeding and suppu-
ration, check restoration integrity, screw or cement margins and occlusion, professional biofilm removal with
air-polishing, re-instruction, and radiographs only when clinically indicated against baseline. Then reset the
interval by risk — three months if she is not stable, five if she is.”
Q
One implant continues to lose bone despite surgery. What now?

“Then it is irrational to retain it and I would recommend removal, by reverse-torque if possible to preserve
bone. After healing, the options are to convert to a shorter span or a cantilever from the remaining implant if
it is sound and the occlusion permits, to graft and replace, or to accept a shortened arch. I would explain the
position honestly and document the discussion.”
Q
She asks whether the implants should ever have been placed at all.
“I would decline to speculate on another clinician’s treatment planning, explain in general terms what I have
found and why I think it has happened, and set out her options from here. If she wants to pursue it formally I
would tell her how. I would record what I found and what I said, and I would not put a critical opinion of a
colleague into her notes as fact. Duty of candour applies to my own care, not to a retrospective judgement of
someone else’s.”
Q
With hindsight, what would have prevented this?
“Two separate screw-retained crowns with cleansable embrasures rather than a linked cemented unit; adequate
keratinised mucosa and an emergence profile that allows a brush; a documented maintenance programme with
the interval set at handover; and a written recall the patient understands is not optional. Every one of those is
a planning decision, not a surgical one — which is the lesson of this case.”
WATCH OUT
Come back to the three drivers of peri-implant disease — biofilm, access for cleaning, and maintenance — and
say which of the three this question belongs to. It buys a sentence of thinking time and it is almost always the
right frame here.
Running this case to time
Time check. The flow above holds 39 questions and about 2,496 words of model answer. At examination
pace — 140 words a minute, plus roughly five seconds for each question to be asked — that is close to
twenty-one minutes, so it overruns by about six. What goes first is the chain “if it goes to surgery” —
defect morphology, resective versus reconstructive and implantoplasty collapse into one question, because
that surgery is contingent on a re-assessment you have not yet done. If your answers run past thirty
seconds, you will never reach Domain 4 at all.

Where the marks are lost in this case

junctional epithelium, Sharpey’s fibres, BPE technique and probing force. A candidate who reaches for
the 2017 definitions before he can describe a natural attachment apparatus has thrown away free marks.

Debriding and reviewing without touching the prosthesis. The disease here is a splinted restoration
a brush cannot pass. Volunteer that cleansability is the treatment, then volunteer the honest counter-
argument about the risk of removing a three-year-old unit — that pairing, unprompted, is the difference
between a 3 and a 5 in Domain 2.
Never naming the surgical line. Diagnosis, charting, prosthetic assessment, conversion to a cleansable
screw-retained design, non-surgical therapy and lifelong maintenance are yours.

the diagnostic work finished first so the referral is useful. Candidates describe implantoplasty in detail
and never say they would not be doing it.

soe.title: The atrophic posterior maxilla
soe.text:
SOE Case 9 — The atrophic posterior maxilla
THE CASE
62-year-old woman, non-smoker, well-controlled hypertension. Missing 16 and 17 for eight years; wears no
prosthesis. Wants a fixed replacement. CBCT: residual bone height beneath the sinus of 5 mm at the 16 and 4
mm at the 17; ridge width 7 mm; flat sinus floor, no septa, membrane 1 mm, patent ostium. Interarch space is
generous — the 46 and 47 have over-erupted by 2 mm.
Pace: one structured opening of about 60 seconds, then roughly 35 questions in the remaining 14 minutes. Nothing after the opening earns you
more than a few seconds of thought.
Opening — the 60-second presentation
Q
Present this case.
“A healthy 62-year-old non-smoker with well-controlled hypertension, missing the 16 and 17 for eight years and
wearing nothing in the space, who now wants a fixed replacement. The CBCT shows an atrophic posterior
maxilla — 5 mm of residual height at the 16 and 4 mm at the 17 — but with several favourable features: a 7 mm
ridge width, a flat sinus floor with no septa, a healthy 1 mm membrane and a patent ostium. The complication
is that the interarch space is generous only because the 46 and 47 have over-erupted by 2 mm into the space.
So there are two decisions: how to manage the vertical bone deficiency, and how to manage the over-erupted
antagonists. And a prior question — whether she needs upper molars at all.”
Domain 1 — Clinical interpretation and reasoning
Chain: the anatomy of the posterior maxilla
Q
Describe the maxillary sinus.
“A pyramidal air-filled cavity in the maxillary body, roughly 15 millilitres in the adult, with its base the lateral
nasal wall and its apex towards the zygoma. The roof is the orbital floor carrying the infraorbital nerve; the
floor is the alveolar process, often dipping between the molar roots; the anterior wall is the facial surface of the
maxilla. It drains through the ostium on the medial wall, high up, into the middle meatus via the osteomeatal
complex.”
Q
What lines it, and what is its nerve and blood supply?
“The Schneiderian membrane — pseudostratified ciliated columnar respiratory epithelium on a thin perios-
teum, normally 0.8 to 1.5 mm thick. Sensory supply is the posterior, middle and anterior superior alveolar
nerves and the infraorbital nerve, all branches of the maxillary division of the trigeminal. Blood supply is the
posterior superior alveolar and infraorbital arteries, both from the maxillary artery.”
Q
Why does that blood supply matter surgically?
“Because the posterior superior alveolar and infraorbital arteries anastomose in the lateral wall of the sinus as
the alveolar antral artery, with an intraosseous branch typically running around 15 to 20 mm above the crest.
A lateral window is cut straight across it, so it is the source of the troublesome bleed in that procedure. On a
CBCT I can see it and plan the window around it — which is one of the arguments for CBCT before any lateral
approach.”
Q
What does a 1 mm membrane and a patent ostium tell you?
“That the sinus is healthy — a normal-thickness membrane with no mucosal thickening, no polyp, no fluid
level, and clearance working normally. It matters because the mucociliary escalator sweeps towards the ostium;
if the ostium is blocked, anything I introduce into the sinus cannot clear and I create a post-operative sinusitis.
A thickened membrane of more than 2 mm, or a blocked ostium, would send me to an ENT opinion before any
elevation.”

Q
Would a thin membrane worry you at all?
“Yes — thin membranes perforate more readily during elevation. So 1 mm is favourable for sinus health but not
a free pass surgically. A slightly thicker membrane is actually easier to lift intact. The other favourable features
here are the flat floor and the absence of septa, since septa are the commonest anatomical cause of perforation.”
Q
Why is she down to 4 to 5 mm of bone?
“Two processes acting from opposite directions. From below, pneumatisation of the sinus after the molars were
lost — the floor descends as the sinus expands into the space once occupied by the roots. From above, crestal
residual ridge resorption, greatest in the first year and continuing. Eight years of both leaves the thin residual
plate she has. The 17 is worse than the 16 because pneumatisation is typically greatest distally.”
Q
What bone quality do you expect, and why does it matter?
“D4 on Misch, or Lekholm and Zarb type IV — a thin, sometimes absent cortex over sparse, fine trabecular bone.
It matters because it gives the poorest primary stability, the longest healing time and the highest failure rate
of any site. Practically it means under-preparing the osteotomy, choosing a tapered implant with an aggressive
thread, conventional loading, and no immediate loading.”
Q
What exactly do you measure on the CBCT?
“Residual height beneath the sinus floor at each planned site; ridge width at the crest and 5 mm apical; mem-
brane thickness; presence and position of septa; the slope of the floor, since a sloping floor makes transcrestal
elevation unpredictable; the thickness of the lateral wall and the course of the alveolar antral artery; patency
of the ostium; and any sinus pathology. I would also check the exposure is justified under IR(ME)R and report
the whole volume, not just my field of interest.”
Q
What would contraindicate any sinus procedure?
“Acute sinusitis — absolute until resolved. Then chronic rhinosinusitis, nasal polyposis, a mucocele or re-
tention cyst obstructing the ostium, previous Caldwell-Luc surgery with a scarred sinus, and heavy smoking.
Relatives include uncontrolled diabetes, bisphosphonate or antiresorptive therapy, and radiotherapy to the field.
Here the sinus is clean, she does not smoke and her hypertension is controlled — so the sinus itself is not the
problem.”
Q
Does her hypertension change anything?
“Not materially if it is genuinely well controlled. I would record a recent blood pressure, take a full drug history
— a calcium channel blocker can cause gingival overgrowth, and some patients are on an antiplatelet — and
use a local anaesthetic with adrenaline in normal dental doses, which is safe in controlled hypertension. She is
ASA II. I would defer elective surgery if the pressure were uncontrolled.”
Domain 2 — Clinical decision making and treatment planning
Chain: the occlusal groundwork
Q
What is the shortened dental arch concept?
“Käyser’s proposition that a dentition of the anterior teeth and premolars — around 20 teeth, or ten occluding
pairs — provides adequate function, comfort and aesthetics for most patients, without an increase in tem-
poromandibular disorder, drifting or periodontal breakdown in a stable mouth. It is endorsed as a legitimate
treatment goal rather than a failure of care, and it is the reason ‘replace the molars’ is not automatically the right
answer.”
Q
Is a shortened arch acceptable in her?
“Potentially — she has occlusion to the second premolar and has managed eight years without any prosthesis,
which is strong evidence she functions. The condition for a shortened arch is a stable occlusion, and hers is
not entirely stable: the 46 and 47 have over-erupted 2 mm. So the concept applies, but it needs the antagonists
managing whichever route we take.”

Q
What are the over-erupted lower molars actually telling you?
“That the space has not been passively tolerated. Unopposed teeth erupt with their alveolar bone, so the
occlusal plane is now disturbed, and the ‘generous’ interarch space is generous because of the over-eruption
rather than despite it. If I restore the 16 and 17 at the current lower level I build a prosthesis into a deranged
occlusal plane. They must be addressed before any definitive restoration.”
Q
How would you manage them?
“In escalating order: enameloplasty if 2 mm can be removed within enamel and the teeth are unrestored;
crowns at a reduced occlusal height, possibly requiring elective endodontics if the reduction exposes pulp;
or orthodontic intrusion, which is the most conservative of tooth tissue but the slowest and needs anchorage,
often temporary anchorage devices. If she chose a shortened arch I would still manage them, to stop further
drift and interference.”
Chain: the options for the 16 and 17
Q
Apply the ITI decision tree for the atrophic posterior maxilla.
“The first branch asks about the interarch relationship and crest width. Hers is favourable on both — generous
space, 7 mm width — so the branch is sinus floor elevation alone, not a combined vertical augmentation. Then
the sinus elevation tree keys on residual height: with 6 mm or less the indicated approach is the lateral window;
a transcrestal approach needs more than 6 mm with a horizontal floor. So the algorithm gives me a lateral
window at both sites — which is explicitly beyond the scope of this level of practice, so I would refer for it.”
Q
What are your other options?
“Short implants — 6 mm fixtures at both sites with no sinus procedure. A transcrestal elevation of 2 to 3 mm
with simultaneous placement, which might be feasible at the 16 with its 5 mm, though the tree favours a lateral
window below 6 mm. A cantilever from a single implant at the 15. A conventional or resin-bonded bridge.
A removable partial denture. Or accept a shortened dental arch.”
Q
Make the case for short implants.
“Systematic reviews report survival comparable to longer implants placed with augmentation at three to five
years, with fewer complications, less morbidity, lower cost and shorter treatment time. A short implant is
usually taken as 6 mm or less of intrabony length. With 4 to 5 mm of native bone I still need a small gain at
both sites, so it is not augmentation-free here, but it converts a lateral window into a transcrestal procedure —
a much smaller intervention.”
Q
You have argued for short implants. Now argue against them.
“The comparable-survival data are mostly three to five years, not fifteen, and this woman may need forty. A
short implant has an unfavourable crown-to-implant ratio, less surface area in the poorest bone quality in the
mouth, and less reserve — if it loses 2 mm of marginal bone it has lost a third of its length, where a 10 mm
implant has lost a fifth. The technical complication rate is the real cost. My colleague who augments properly
and places a longer implant is buying reserve.”
Q
Why not a cantilever from the 15?
“Because a molar-sized cantilever from a single implant in D4 bone applies a large bending moment to one
fixture at the position of greatest occlusal load. That combination — poorest bone, highest force, no splinting —
is the classic setting for screw loosening, screw fracture and marginal bone loss. I would not do it here.”
Q
Why not a bridge or a denture?
“A conventional bridge from the 15 to the 18 is too long a span and the 18 is very likely absent, so there is
no distal abutment — it would be a two-unit cantilever from an unrestored premolar. A resin-bonded bridge
cannot carry a molar span. A removable partial denture is a genuine option and must be offered, but she has
worn nothing for eight years and specifically wants fixed, so I expect her to decline it.”

Q
So what do you recommend?
“I would put the shortened arch honestly first as the low-risk option, given eight years of comfortable function —
with the lower molars adjusted. If she wants a fixed replacement, I would refer for a lateral window elevation
with staged or simultaneous placement, having done the diagnostic and restorative planning myself. If the
referral centre offered short implants instead, that is also reasonable, and I would be comfortable restoring
either.”
Q
What is the SAC classification?
“The surgical phase is Complex — augmentation of an atrophic posterior maxilla, D4 bone, adjacent to the
sinus. The restorative phase is Advanced — a two-unit posterior implant reconstruction in a modified occlusion.
Naming it that way is how I justify referring the surgery while retaining the restoration.”
Q
What would you tell her, in her own words?
“ ‘You have lost quite a lot of the bone that used to hold those two teeth, and the sinus — the air space above
them — has expanded down into it. There is about four to five millimetres of bone left where I would need ten
or more. There are three honest choices: leave the gap, which you have managed well for eight years; have a
specialist lift the sinus lining and add bone, then place implants — a bigger procedure with a recovery and a
real chance of a blocked or infected sinus; or use shorter implants, which is a smaller operation but with less
long-term evidence. Either way, your lower back teeth have grown up into the space and need reshaping first.’ ”
Domain 3 — Decision making in relation to treatment procedures
Chain: sinus floor elevation
Q
When is a transcrestal elevation indicated?
“Residual height greater than 6 mm, a flat sinus floor, a gain of only 3 to 4 mm required, adequate ridge width,
a healthy sinus with a patent ostium, and no septa in the field. It is a blind procedure, so every one of those
conditions is doing work — a sloping floor in particular makes the osteotome slide and tear the membrane.”
Q
Describe it.
“Flap, then prepare the osteotomy to 1 to 2 mm short of the sinus floor, confirmed radiographically. Then
concave osteotomes of increasing diameter with gentle malleting to green-stick fracture the floor, elevating
the membrane with a plug of graft material pushed ahead of the osteotome as a hydraulic and mechanical
cushion. Confirm membrane integrity, place the implant, close. Modern alternatives are hydraulic elevation
or sequential drills with depth stops, both gentler than malleting.”
Q
How do you confirm the membrane is intact?
“The Valsalva manoeuvre — the patient pinches the nose and blows gently while I watch and listen at the
osteotomy. No air movement and no membrane movement means intact. I would also look directly with good
light and probe gently with a blunt instrument. If it is perforated, I would abandon elevation and either place
without a gain or close and allow four to six months of healing before reattempting.”
Q
What are the complications of the transcrestal approach?
“Membrane perforation is the commonest. Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo from the malleting, caused
by displacement of otoliths — an under-recognised and distressing complication. Then graft migration, sinusi-
tis, oro-antral communication, loss of the implant into the sinus, and failure to achieve the intended gain.”
Q
What are your post-operative sinus precautions?
“No nose-blowing, sneeze with the mouth open, no straws or smoking, avoid air travel and diving, and a soft
diet. Analgesia, a chlorhexidine rinse, and antibiotics with a decongestant such as a topical or systemic nasal
decongestant where appropriate. I would warn her that a small amount of blood-stained nasal discharge on
the first day is expected but that increasing pain, swelling or purulent discharge means she rings me.”

Q
In outline, what would the lateral window involve — so you can consent her for the referral?
“A buccal full-thickness flap, an antrostomy cut in the lateral wall with a round bur or piezosurgery, the
window either hinged inwards or removed. The membrane is elevated from the floor and walls with curved
elevators to create a contained compartment, which is filled with graft — usually a xenograft, alone or mixed
with autogenous bone — a membrane is placed over the window, and it is closed tension-free. Implants are
placed simultaneously if primary stability is achievable, otherwise staged at six to nine months.”
Q
What if the membrane perforates during that procedure?
“Small perforations are managed by folding the membrane on itself or patching with a resorbable collagen
membrane and continuing. Large ones may mean abandoning the graft and closing, then reattempting after
healing. The risk is that graft escapes into the sinus, obstructs the ostium and causes sinusitis or graft infection
— which is why the ostium and membrane assessment beforehand matter so much.”
Q
If short implants were chosen instead, what changes surgically?
“Under-preparation of the osteotomy — stopping short of the final diameter, or using osteotomes rather than
drills, to condense the sparse trabecular bone; a tapered implant with an aggressive thread and a moderately
rough surface; low drill speed with irrigation; and accepting a lower insertion torque than I would in the
mandible. No immediate or early loading. I would also consider splinting the two crowns to share load.”
Q
When would you load in this bone?
“Conventional loading at around six months in a grafted or D4 posterior maxilla, against three months in the
mandible, confirmed clinically and with ISQ if available. Six to eight weeks would be early loading, which I
would not choose here. If a sinus graft has been placed I would follow the surgeon’s protocol, usually longer
again.”
Q
What would you record?
“The medical history and blood pressure, the CBCT findings site by site with measured residual heights, width,
membrane thickness and ostium patency, the justification for the exposure, the SAC assessment, the options
discussed with risks, benefits, costs and alternatives including no treatment and the shortened arch, her
decision, the referral and what it was for, the occlusal management plan for the 46 and 47, and the consent
conversation about sinusitis and altered sensation.”
Domain 4 — Interpretation and problem solving of clinical outcomes
Chain: monitoring and dealing with what goes wrong
Q
What would you monitor, and how often?
“Implant survival and marginal bone levels against a baseline film taken at fitting; peri-implant probing,
bleeding and suppuration; sinus symptoms; the crown-to-implant ratio and any mechanical complications;
and the occlusion, particularly where I have adjusted the opposing teeth. Six-monthly initially, then set by
risk, with radiographs at one year and thereafter as clinically indicated.”
Q
How do you design the prosthesis to protect a short implant?
“Keep the occlusal table narrow so the load stays over the implant axis, avoid excursive contacts on the implant
crowns entirely, no cantilevers, a flatter cusp angle, and splint the two units so they share load. I would also
consent her specifically that a short implant has a less favourable lever arm, so a night guard is likely if any
parafunction emerges.”
Q
At six months she reports a blocked nose and one-sided discharge. What now?
“That is a unilateral sinusitis on the operated side until proved otherwise — likely graft-related or from ostium
obstruction. History, tenderness over the antrum, nasal endoscopy findings if available, and imaging. I would
prescribe antibiotics and a decongestant, and refer to ENT early rather than treating it repeatedly myself. A
displaced implant or migrated graft in the sinus needs removal.”

Q
The implant at the 17 fails to integrate. What do you do?
“Remove it, curette the site, and be honest with her under duty of candour. Then decide whether to replace
it after three to six months of healing — accepting that a second failure at the same site is more likely — or to
restore the 16 alone and accept a shortened arch to the first molar, which in this patient is a perfectly good
outcome. I would not cantilever a second molar from a single short implant.”
Q
She asks why implants fail more often up here than in her lower jaw.
“ ‘The bone at the back of the upper jaw is the softest in the mouth — more like a sponge than a brick — and
there is less of it because the sinus has expanded into it. The implant has less to grip while it is healing. That is
why we take longer before we put the tooth on it, and why the success rate here is a few per cent lower than at
the front of the lower jaw.’ ”
Q
How would you know this treatment had succeeded?
“By her measure first — that she chews comfortably on that side and does not think about it. Objectively:
implants stable with no bleeding or suppuration, marginal bone levels stable against baseline, no sinus
symptoms, an occlusion that is even and free of excursive contacts on the implants, and a maintenance pattern
she attends. And if she chose the shortened arch, success is exactly the same measure with no surgery at all.”
WATCH OUT
Come back to the two questions this case is really asking — how much bone is there, and does she actually
need molars? Naming those buys a sentence of thinking time, and the shortened arch is a legitimate answer to
almost anything here.
Running this case to time
Time check. The flow above holds 40 questions and about 2,864 words of model answer. At 140 words a
minute plus roughly five seconds a question, that is nearly twenty-four minutes — an overrun of about
nine, the largest in this section. The examiner drops from the middle of Domain 3: the step-by-step
transcrestal description and the lateral window mechanics go first, compressed into one question about
what you would consent her for, since you are referring that surgery anyway. Indications, Valsalva and
the sinus precautions stay. If your answers run past thirty seconds, you will never reach Domain 4.

Where the marks are lost in this case
Planning the surgery and ignoring the lower jaw. The 46 and 47 have over-erupted 2 mm and taken their
alveolar bone with them. Restore the 16 and 17 to that level and you have built a prosthesis into a deranged

if she chooses the shortened arch.
Never offering no molars at all. She has worn nothing for eight years and functions. Käyser’s shortened
arch is the low-risk option and should be put honestly first, not produced as an afterthought when the
surgery is questioned. Candidates who only ever argue for treatment lose Domain 2.
Describing a lateral window as though they would do it. This is the competence line and it must be said
out loud: lateral window elevation in an atrophic posterior maxilla is Complex and beyond a general
dentist with an interest in implants — it is referred. What stays yours is the diagnostic work, the occlusal
plan, the consent conversation and the Advanced restorative phase.

soe.title: Nerve proximity and the consent conversation
soe.text:
SOE Case 10 — Nerve proximity and the consent conversation
THE CASE
48-year-old male teacher, fit and well. Missing 36 for two years. OPT suggests 9 mm from crest to the superior
border of the mandibular canal. Ridge width appears adequate. He is a keen wind musician who plays clarinet
in an orchestra.
Pace: one structured opening of about 60 seconds, then roughly 35 questions in the remaining 14 minutes. Nothing after the opening earns you
more than a few seconds of thought.
Opening — the 60-second presentation
Q
Present this case.
“A fit 48-year-old wanting a single lower first molar implant, with an apparent 9 mm of bone above the canal
on a panoramic film and adequate ridge width. Two features dominate. First, 9 mm on an OPT is not 9 mm
of usable bone — the film magnifies, gives no buccolingual information and may not show the true superior
border, so I cannot plan a length from it. Second, he is a clarinettist and a teacher, so altered lip and chin
sensation would be far more than an inconvenience to him. Under Montgomery that makes nerve injury a
highly material risk for this particular patient, and it will shape both the consent conversation and the plan. My
tasks are to image him properly, establish what he wants, and decide whether the safety margin I can guarantee
is one he is willing to accept.”
Domain 1 — Clinical interpretation and reasoning
Chain: the anatomical groundwork
Q
Describe the course of the inferior alveolar nerve.
“It is the largest branch of the posterior division of the mandibular nerve, V3. It descends between the spheno-
mandibular ligament and the ramus, enters the mandibular foramen below the lingula, and runs forward and
downward in the mandibular canal, usually lingual then more buccal as it comes forward. It divides at about
the second premolar into the mental nerve, which exits the mental foramen, and the incisive branch, which
continues in bone to the anterior teeth.”
Q
What does it supply?
“The mandibular molars and premolars and their periodontium via the dental branches. The mental nerve
supplies the skin and mucosa of the lower lip, the labial gingivae from canine to canine, and the skin of the
chin — all unilaterally. It is purely sensory at this point; the mylohyoid nerve, which branches off before the
foramen, is motor to mylohyoid and anterior digastric and can also carry accessory sensation to the chin.”
Q
What is the anterior loop, and why does it matter here?
“The anterior loop is the segment where the incisive branch continues forward beyond the point at which the
mental nerve turns back and up to exit the foramen — so the nerve extends anterior to the radiographic foramen.
It is variable, commonly a couple of millimetres but sometimes considerably more. It matters because it is
not reliably visible on a panoramic film, so a foramen-based safety margin taken from an OPT can be falsely
reassuring.”
Q
What canal variations would you look for?
“A bifid or trifid canal, which is uncommon but well described and means a second bundle may sit outside my
planned margin. Retromolar and accessory foramina. An anterior looping of the mental nerve. And a canal
with an indistinct or absent cortication, which is a reason to be more, not less, conservative — I cannot measure
to a border I cannot see.”

Q
Describe the cross-sectional shape of the posterior mandible in the 36 region.
“Typically a crest that is narrower than the base, with a lingual concavity — the submandibular fossa — below
the mylohyoid ridge, and a buccal fullness towards the external oblique ridge. That concavity is the reason a
drill following the apparent long axis of the ridge can perforate the lingual plate even when the crest looks
wide, which risks the sublingual and submental vessels.”
Chain: reading the imaging
Q
Is the OPT measurement reliable?
“No, not on its own. A panoramic magnifies by roughly 20 to 30% and not uniformly, it is a tomographic image
with distortion outside the focal trough, it gives no buccolingual information, and the superior border of the
canal is often indistinct. It is a good screening film for gross anatomy and pathology, but it is not a planning
film when I am working close to the canal.”
Q
So justify the CBCT.
“Under IR(ME)R every exposure must be justified by a specific clinical question that a lower-dose alternative
cannot answer. Mine is: what is the true vertical height above the canal at the 36, what is the buccolingual
position of the canal, is there a lingual concavity, and is the canal bifid? None of those can be answered by a
panoramic. I would use a small field of view at the smallest volume and resolution that answers the question.”
Q
What exactly would you measure on it?
“Crestal bone width at the crest and 5 mm apical; vertical height from the crest to the superior cortex of the
canal at the planned site, not at the mean of the region; the buccolingual position of the canal relative to my
planned axis; the depth of the submandibular fossa; and the bone density. I would record those numbers in the
notes with the site they were taken at.”
Q
What else would you examine clinically before planning?
“Over-eruption of the 26 and tilting of the 35 and 37 after two years, which may have taken the restorative space.
Inter-arch space and the occlusal scheme. Mouth opening and access to a lower second premolar–molar region.
Periodontal status and plaque control. Smoking and any parafunction. And a baseline sensory examination
of both mental nerve distributions, recorded before I touch him.”
Q
Why does that baseline matter so much?
“Because if he reports altered sensation afterwards I need to know whether it is new. A pre-operative record of
normal light touch, sharp-blunt discrimination and thermal sensation on both sides, documented and ideally
with the patient’s own confirmation, is a few minutes’ work that transforms my ability to manage a complaint
honestly. In a patient for whom this risk is material it is not optional.”
Domain 2 — Clinical decision making and treatment planning
Chain: the options, and the groundwork behind them
Q
What are the options for a single missing 36?
“No treatment or a shortened dental arch; a removable partial denture; a conventional fixed bridge on the 35
and 37; a cantilever or resin-bonded bridge, which is poorly supported in a molar site; or a single implant-
retained crown. Each has to be offered with its risks, benefits and costs, including doing nothing, before I can
say his consent is valid.”
Q
Make the case for the shortened dental arch.
“The shortened dental arch concept holds that occlusal function, comfort and stability are generally maintained
with around 20 teeth — the anteriors and premolars in occluding pairs. Long-term studies show acceptable
function and no major increase in TMD or periodontal breakdown. Here the 36 is a first molar, so he would still
have a second molar contact; the argument is weaker than for a missing 37, but it is still a legitimate option to
place before him.”

Q
You have offered an implant. Argue against it.
“That it introduces a surgical risk to a nerve that currently works perfectly, in a man whose livelihood and
principal pleasure depend on lip sensation, to replace a single tooth he has managed without for two years. It
commits him to lifelong maintenance and a restoration that will need components replaced. The null option
is genuinely reasonable here, and a doctrine that every gap must be filled is exactly the reasoning that gets
criticised in a complaint.”
Q
Your colleague would place a conventional bridge instead. Why might they be right?
“Because it avoids the nerve entirely. If the 35 and 37 are already heavily restored, a bridge sacrifices little
additional tooth tissue and can be delivered predictably in weeks, with a well-understood failure mode. The
counter-argument is that the abutments here may be sound, and preparing sound teeth carries its own long-
term biological cost — but if he places overwhelming value on avoiding nerve risk, a bridge is a defensible and
possibly better answer.”
Q
What is the legal standard for consent?
“Montgomery — the test of materiality is no longer what a body of doctors would disclose but whether a
reasonable person in this patient’s position, or this particular patient, would attach significance to the risk.
So I must know enough about him to know what matters to him. His clarinet playing converts a small risk of
altered lip sensation from a nuisance into a career-relevant one, and I must therefore discuss it in proportion.”
Q
Tell me what you would say to him, in his words.
“ ‘There is a nerve running through your lower jaw that gives feeling to your lip and chin on that side. I’ll take
a 3D scan first so I know exactly where it is, and I plan to keep at least two millimetres away from it. Even so,
there’s a small chance of bruising or damaging it, which can leave numbness, tingling or an unpleasant altered
feeling in your lip and chin. Most of these settle over weeks or months, but occasionally it’s permanent. For
most people that’s an inconvenience — for you, with the clarinet, it could be a real problem, so I want you to
weigh it carefully against simply leaving the gap.’ ”
Q
What would you record?
“The options discussed including no treatment, the specific risks and the fact that I discussed nerve injury in
the context of his clarinet playing — quoting the words, not just the heading. His questions and answers.
The baseline sensory examination. The CBCT justification, the measurements and the planned clearance. The
written information given and the cooling-off period. And his signature, on the understanding that consent is
the conversation and not the form.”
Q
Would his hobby change your plan?
“Possibly. I would consider a shorter, wider implant to increase the safety margin, since contemporary evidence
for short implants in the posterior mandible is good over the medium term and avoids grafting altogether. I
would consider a fully guided approach. And I would explicitly re-offer the bridge and the shortened arch,
because a plan chosen after hearing his priorities is a different plan from one chosen for him.”
Q
SAC classification?
“Normatively Straightforward — a single posterior implant in a healed site with adequate bone volume, non-
aesthetic. But the anatomical risk modifier of nerve proximity and the patient expectation modifier created by
his occupation and hobby raise it, and I would treat it as Advanced.”
Q
Is this within your competence, and when would you refer?
“A single posterior mandibular implant with a CBCT-verified clearance is within the scope of a general dentist
with implant training, so yes — provided I have the CBCT and, ideally, a guide. I would refer if the clearance
were under about 2 mm at any point, if the canal were bifid or uncorticated, if he wanted a guarantee I cannot
give, or if he wished the case to be done somewhere that guided surgery and immediate specialist support are
routine. That is a legitimate reason to refer even when the case itself is not complex.”

Domain 3 — Decision making in relation to treatment procedures
Chain: designing the safety margin
Q
How much clearance do you want from the canal, and why that figure?
“At least 2 mm from the superior cortex of the canal to the implant apex. That covers the accuracy limits of the
imaging, the guide or free-hand technique and the drill itself, and it allows for the fact that the neurovascular
bundle can be compressed or heated without ever being touched. If my CBCT height is 9 mm true, I am planning
an implant of no more than about 7 mm at that site.”
Q
Are you comfortable with a 7 mm implant in a molar site?
“Yes. Short implants of 6 to 8 mm in the posterior mandible perform comparably to longer implants with
vertical augmentation over the medium term, with fewer complications, because they avoid a graft procedure
entirely. The trade-off is that I must protect them: a wider diameter, a favourable crown-to-implant ratio, a
narrow occlusal table and no cantilever.”
Q
Guided or free-hand?
“Fully guided is my preference here, because it carries the CBCT plan into the mouth and controls both depth
and angulation — which is exactly what I am worried about. Free-hand with drill stops is acceptable in experi-
enced hands, but if a small angular error could put me into the canal in a patient for whom that is career-altering,
the guide is the proportionate answer.”
Q
What are the limitations of a guide?
“It is only as good as the scan, the merge and the seating. A poorly fitting guide, an unstable mucosa-borne
guide, or a merge error between the CBCT and the intra-oral scan all introduce error, and the guide gives false
confidence because it feels definitive. Reported deviations of a millimetre or more at the apex are not unusual,
which is another reason the 2 mm margin exists rather than being spent.”
Q
Would you use an inferior alveolar block?
“I would prefer infiltration with an articaine-based solution, so that he retains enough lip sensation to report
a sharp electric sensation if the drill approaches the bundle. Articaine infiltration in the posterior mandible is
often suﬀicient for implant placement.”
Q
Your colleague blocks every posterior mandibular case. Why might they be right?
“Because patient movement from inadequate anaesthesia is itself a hazard when a drill is 2 mm from a nerve,
and because the ‘warning sign’ argument is weak — by the time the patient reports a sensation, the injury may
already have occurred, so it should never be relied on as a safety mechanism. The honest position is that a block
is acceptable if the planning is sound; the infiltration is a supplement to good planning, not a substitute for it.”
Q
Take me through the drilling.
“Aseptic technique, chlorhexidine rinse. Mid-crestal incision with the releasing incision kept well away from
the mental foramen, full-thickness flap, and I palpate and visualise the lingual concavity. Then graded drilling
with new sharp drills, slow speed, copious irrigation and intermittent pressure, using drills with physical
stops or a guided sleeve system, and a depth gauge check at each stage rather than only at the end.”
Q
How do you verify depth intra-operatively?
“A direction indicator and a periapical after the pilot drill, with a paralleling technique so the geometry is
interpretable, comparing the indicator tip against the canal. Then depth gauges at each increment. If the
periapical is ambiguous I stop and reassess rather than take one more drill — the point at which you are tempted
to press on is exactly the point at which you should not.”
Q
How do you avoid perforating the lingual plate?

“Plan the axis on the cross-sectional CBCT slice, not on the crest form. Angle the implant slightly buccally
where the fossa is deep, keep the flap raised so I can palpate the lingual plate directly with a finger, and be
alert to the drill suddenly losing resistance. Perforation risks bleeding into the sublingual and submandibular
spaces, which is a genuine airway emergency.”
Q
What would you do if you did get a floor-of-mouth bleed?
“Direct pressure, bimanual compression with a finger in the floor of mouth, and place the implant or a haemo-
static agent to tamponade the site. Sit him up, keep him talking, and observe closely. If there is any swelling
of the floor of mouth, tongue elevation or diﬀiculty swallowing, that is an evolving airway obstruction and I
call 999 and transfer to hospital — this can develop over hours, so I would not discharge him early.”
Domain 4 — Interpretation and problem solving of clinical outcomes
Chain: the nerve injury, if it happens
Q
He telephones the next day reporting numbness. What do you do?
“See him that day — this is the one complication where delay changes the outcome. Take a history: is it
anaesthesia, paraesthesia or painful dysaesthesia, when did it start, and is it changing. Examine and map it.
Then image the site immediately to establish whether the implant is in or on the canal, because that determines
whether I act surgically in the next 24 to 36 hours.”
Q
How do you map and record it?
“Draw the affected area on a facial diagram with measurements, and photograph it. Test light touch with a
cotton wisp, sharp-blunt discrimination, two-point discrimination and thermal sensation, comparing with
the contralateral side and with his recorded baseline. Ask him to score it, for example on a visual analogue
scale, and note the functional effect — speech, drooling, and specifically his clarinet embouchure.”
Q
Classify nerve injuries for me.
“Seddon — neurapraxia, a conduction block with an intact axon and full recovery; axonotmesis, axonal damage
with the endoneurium intact and recovery over weeks to months; neurotmesis, complete disruption with poor
spontaneous recovery. Sunderland subdivides this into five degrees by which layer is disrupted, first degree
being neurapraxia and fifth being complete transection. The clinical value is prognostic: the further down the
scale, the less likely spontaneous recovery becomes.”
Q
The radiograph shows the implant apex in the canal. Now what?
“Remove or back the implant out immediately — ideally within 24 to 36 hours, and certainly within days.
Compression and a foreign body in the canal produce ongoing injury, so the priority is decompression rather
than preserving the fixture. I would explain this honestly, do it under local anaesthetic, and plan a shorter
implant later once sensation has been reassessed.”
Q
And if the implant is clear of the canal?
“Then it is more likely a drill, retraction or injection injury, or oedema and haematoma compressing the bundle
— which carries a better prognosis, and I would manage it conservatively with close review. A short course of
corticosteroid and an NSAID in the first few days are commonly suggested to reduce perineural oedema and are
reasonable if started early, though I would be honest that the evidence is limited. I would not simply reassure
and discharge, because the review pattern is what lets me refer at the right moment.”
Q
When and where do you refer?
“Urgently to oral and maxillofacial surgery if the implant is in the canal and I cannot remove it, if there is
painful dysaesthesia from the outset, or if there is no meaningful improvement by around four weeks. The
window in which surgical exploration or repair can help is measured in weeks to a few months, not years —
so referring late is itself a failure. I would refer with my baseline, my maps and my imaging.”

Q
What do you say to him at that first review?
“ ‘I’m sorry — the feeling in your lip and chin has been affected, and that’s the risk we discussed. The scan
shows where the implant is and I’m acting on that today. Most of these improve, many completely, but it can
take weeks or months and I can’t promise you it will fully recover. I’m going to see you weekly to start with,
I’m going to record exactly how it changes, and if it isn’t improving by a month I’ll refer you to a specialist unit.’
Then duty of candour in writing, and I would notify my indemnifier the same day.”
Q
What would success look like, and what would you audit?
“Success is an integrated implant with stable bone levels, a cleansable crown that he can floss and that carries no
excursive contacts — and normal sensation. For audit I would set a standard that 100% of posterior mandibular
implant cases have a recorded pre-operative sensory baseline, a CBCT-derived height at the planned site, and
a documented planned clearance, then measure my own compliance and my incidence of altered sensation, and
re-audit after any change. That is a legitimate quality improvement project.”
WATCH OUT
Come back to the margin: state the true bone height, the clearance you are protecting and how you will verify
it. Nearly every question in this case is really asking how you keep 2 mm between a drill and a nerve, and how
you would tell the patient if you failed.
Running this case to time
Time check. The flow above holds 39 questions and about 2,846 words of model answer. At 140 words
a minute plus roughly five seconds a question, that runs to nearly twenty-four minutes — an overrun of
about eight and a half. What goes first is the lingual plate and floor-of-mouth bleed sub-chain in Domain
3 — real, but this case is about a nerve, and Domain 4 is entirely the nerve injury. If your answers run past
thirty seconds you will never reach Domain 4, which here means never being asked what you do when
he telephones.
