The spine — the twelve answers to have ready if nothing else
1 The inferior alveolar nerve, and what the mental nerve supplies · 2 The anterior loop, and why an OPT
hides it · 3 Canal variations that change your margin · 4 The submandibular fossa and lingual perforation
· 5 Why the 9 mm cannot be used, and how you justify the CBCT · 6 The baseline sensory examination · 7
All the options, including no treatment · 8 Montgomery, and materiality judged from his position · 9 The
2 mm clearance, and the arithmetic that follows · 10 Short implants, and how you protect them · 11 The
limitations of a guide · 12 The telephone call the next day.
Where the marks are lost in this case
Measuring 9 mm off the panoramic and planning a 9 mm implant. The film magnifies by 20 to 30% and
not uniformly, gives no buccolingual information and often shows no reliable superior cortex. Say out
loud that you cannot plan a length from this image, then justify the CBCT by the question it answers, not
by habit.
Skipping the baseline. A recorded pre-operative sensory examination of both mental distributions takes
minutes and transforms your position if he telephones. Candidates plan a beautiful guided case, never
volunteer it, and then have no way to say whether anything is new. In a patient for whom this risk is
material, volunteering it is the difference between a 3 and a 5.
Consenting the procedure instead of the man. Under Montgomery the test is what a person in his
position would attach significance to, and he plays clarinet in an orchestra — so the record must show the
risk discussed in those terms and the null option genuinely re-offered. The competence line follows: a
CBCT-verified single posterior implant is yours, but a clearance under about 2 mm, a bifid or uncorticated
canal, or a patient who wants a guarantee, is a referral — and a nerve injury not improving at four weeks
goes urgently to oral and maxillofacial surgery.

soe.title: The medically complex patient on
soe.text:
SOE Case 11 — The medically complex patient on
antiresorptives
THE CASE
71-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis, taking methotrexate, prednisolone 5 mg daily and denosumab
60 mg every six months for osteoporosis. Warfarin for atrial fibrillation, INR 2.8 last week. She wants two
implants to stabilise a lower denture. She has limited manual dexterity.
Pace: one structured opening of about 60 seconds, then roughly 35 questions in the remaining 14 minutes. Nothing after the opening earns you
more than a few seconds of thought.
Opening — the 60-second presentation
Q
Present this case.
“A 71-year-old woman requesting a two-implant mandibular overdenture, with four medical issues and one
major functional one. She is on denosumab for osteoporosis, so there is an MRONJ risk; on long-term pred-
nisolone, which both impairs healing and, importantly, changes her MRONJ risk category; on methotrexate,
which is immunosuppressive and dictates my choice of analgesic; and on warfarin with an INR of 2.8, which
is manageable but must be verified. Overlying all of that, her rheumatoid arthritis has reduced her manual
dexterity, and implants demand lifelong daily cleaning. My position is that the request is entirely reasonable in
principle — a two-implant overdenture transforms quality of life — but that I must take each issue in turn, and
that the dexterity may prove decisive.”
Domain 1 — Clinical interpretation and reasoning
Chain: the pharmacology groundwork
Q
How does denosumab work?
“It is a fully human monoclonal antibody against RANK ligand. RANK-L, produced by osteoblasts and
stromal cells, binds RANK on osteoclast precursors and drives their differentiation, activation and survival.
Denosumab sequesters RANK-L, so it acts like an excess of the natural decoy receptor osteoprotegerin, and
osteoclastic resorption is profoundly suppressed. At 60 mg six-monthly it is used for osteoporosis; at 120 mg
monthly for skeletal metastases and giant cell tumour.”
Q
How does that differ from a bisphosphonate?
“A bisphosphonate binds to hydroxyapatite and is incorporated into bone, so its effect persists for years after
the last dose and a ‘drug holiday’ achieves little in the short term. Denosumab is a circulating antibody that is
not incorporated into bone, so its effect wanes towards the end of each six-month cycle and is fully reversible
on stopping. Stopping it, though, causes rebound bone loss and vertebral fracture — which is why the decision
is never mine.”
Q
Define MRONJ.
“Exposed bone, or bone that can be probed through an intra-oral or extra-oral fistula, in the maxillofacial
region, persisting for more than eight weeks, in a patient who is taking or has taken an antiresorptive or
antiangiogenic drug, and who has no history of radiotherapy to the jaws and no obvious metastatic disease at
that site. The three limbs all have to be satisfied — the eight weeks and the exclusion of radiotherapy are the
parts candidates drop.”
Q
What risk group is she in?
“This is the trap. The osteoporosis dose is the lower-risk indication, and on that alone she would be lower
risk. But under SDCEP a patient taking an antiresorptive for osteoporosis moves into the higher-risk group
if they have taken it for more than five years or if they are also on a systemic glucocorticoid — and she is on

prednisolone 5 mg daily. So I would treat her as higher risk, and I would establish how long she has been on
denosumab.”
Q
What does prednisolone 5 mg daily mean for you otherwise?
“Long-term low-dose steroid causes adrenal suppression, impaired wound healing and increased infection
risk, and contributes to her osteoporosis. For routine dentistry and minor oral surgery under local anaesthetic,
steroid supplementation is generally not required — I would ensure she takes her normal morning dose, treat
early in the day, and be alert to hypotension or collapse. If in doubt I would ask her rheumatologist rather than
guess.”
Q
Methotrexate — mechanism and dental relevance.
“It is a folate antagonist, inhibiting dihydrofolate reductase; in rheumatology it is given weekly at low dose as a
disease-modifying immunosuppressant. Dental relevance: immunosuppression and possible myelosuppres-
sion, so meticulous asepsis, awareness of oral ulceration and infection, and a lower threshold for antibiotic cover.
Critically, NSAIDs reduce its renal excretion and increase methotrexate toxicity, so they must be avoided.”
Q
How does warfarin work, and what is the INR?
“Warfarin is a vitamin K antagonist, inhibiting vitamin K epoxide reductase and so the synthesis of the vitamin
K–dependent clotting factors II, VII, IX and X, plus proteins C and S. The INR is the patient’s prothrombin time
divided by a control, raised to the power of the international sensitivity index of the reagent — a standardised
ratio, so an INR of 2.8 means her extrinsic pathway takes 2.8 times as long as normal.”
Q
What features of rheumatoid arthritis itself matter to you?
“Cervical spine involvement, including atlanto-axial subluxation, so I must not extend her neck or tip her
far back. TMJ involvement limiting opening. Reduced tolerance of long appointments and of maintaining a
fixed posture. Secondary Sjögren’s syndrome giving xerostomia, which affects both caries risk and denture
retention. Anaemia of chronic disease. And the hand deformity itself.”
Q
What would you ask her rheumatologist and GP?
“In writing: the indication, dose and duration of the denosumab and when the next dose is due; her disease
activity and whether it is stable; her current steroid dose and any advice on cover; her full blood count and
renal function; whether her INR has been stable and her target range; and whether they foresee any change of
therapy. I would put my own plan and my reasoning in the letter, and file the reply.”
Domain 2 — Clinical decision making and treatment planning
Chain: from dexterity to the treatment decision
Q
How would you assess her dexterity?
“Directly, not by assumption. I would ask her to remove and reinsert her denture in front of me, to demonstrate
cleaning it, and to use an interdental brush and a toothbrush on her remaining teeth or the ridge. I would look
at her grip, her wrists and her ability to sustain a task. I would also ask who helps her at home, and what her
plaque control is like now — her current oral hygiene is the best predictor of her future oral hygiene.”
Q
What are her options?
“A remade conventional lower denture with correct extension, a neutral-zone technique and a restored vertical
dimension; a copy denture preserving what she has adapted to; a permanent soft liner for a resorbed or
tender ridge; denture adhesive and dietary advice, which are legitimate and not a failure; or a two-implant
mandibular overdenture, which the McGill and York consensus statements describe as the minimum standard
of care for an edentulous mandible.”
Q
Where do you start?

“With the conventional denture, properly made. A significant proportion of ‘my denture is loose’ cases are
extension, occlusion or vertical dimension errors rather than a biological limit, and a remake is reversible, cheap
and carries no MRONJ risk. If a well-made denture solves it, the medical debate never has to happen. I would
only move on when I can say her denture is technically as good as it can be and still fails.”
Q
Suppose it is not enough. Would you place the implants?
“Not myself. Two implants in the anterior mandible would ordinarily be Straightforward work, but a higher-
risk MRONJ categorisation combined with immunosuppression, anticoagulation and reduced dexterity
takes this beyond what I would undertake single-handed. I would refer for a joint opinion — while being
clear to her that referral is not refusal, and that the treatment may well be entirely appropriate for her in the
right setting.”
Q
You said the MRONJ risk is small. Argue against treating at all.
“That this is elective surgery creating a lifelong hygiene burden in a woman who may not be able to meet it.
That MRONJ, though uncommon, is disabling and diﬀicult to treat, and that its risk here is not the reassuring
osteoporosis figure but the higher-risk category. That peri-implant mucositis in a patient who cannot clean is
close to inevitable. And that a well-made conventional denture with a soft liner and adhesive carries none of
these risks.”
Q
And argue the other way.
“That a lower complete denture on a resorbed ridge is genuinely miserable, that it affects nutrition, speech and
confidence in an elderly woman who may have limited years to enjoy the improvement, and that withholding
a well-evidenced, modest intervention because of a small risk is itself a harm. Two implants and stud attach-
ments are among the least invasive implant treatments there are. The honest answer is that this is her decision
to make on properly presented information.”
Q
If she were on 120 mg denosumab monthly for malignancy?
“I would decline outright and explain why. That is the high-risk oncology dosing, MRONJ risk is an order of
magnitude greater, and elective implant surgery cannot be justified. I would optimise her denture, keep her
under close preventive care, and make sure any necessary extractions were done in a specialist setting.”
Q
Bar or studs, if implants do go ahead?
“Studs — Locator-type attachments. With her dexterity a bar is the wrong answer: it needs a floss threader or
superfloss passed underneath, more vertical space, and it is far harder to clean. Two independent studs allow a
single-tufted brush around each abutment and a denture fit surface she can brush. Simplicity and cleansability
outrank theoretical load-sharing here.”
Q
SAC classification?
“Surgically and prosthodontically a two-implant mandibular overdenture is normatively Straightforward. Her
medical risk modifier — antiresorptive therapy, immunosuppression and anticoagulation — and the patient-
factor modifier of impaired plaque control take it to Complex in my assessment, and that is why it should be
delivered with specialist input.”
Q
What would you say to her, in her own words?
“ ‘Your osteoporosis injection works by switching off the cells that break bone down, which is what makes your
bones stronger. Very occasionally, in people on that injection, the jawbone doesn’t heal properly after surgery
and a small area of bone stays exposed — that’s called osteonecrosis of the jaw. It’s uncommon, but because
you’re also on steroid tablets your risk is a bit higher than average, and it can be diﬀicult to treat. That doesn’t
mean you can’t have implants, but it does mean I’d like to try getting your denture right first, and if we do go
ahead I’d want a specialist involved. I would not want you to stop your injection — that would risk your spine.’ ”
Q
What would you record?

“Every drug with dose, indication and duration — not just the name. The MRONJ risk category and my
reasoning for it. The written liaison with her rheumatologist and the reply. My direct assessment of her
dexterity, described. The options discussed including no treatment and a conventional remake, the specific
risks discussed, and the words I used about MRONJ. Her questions. And the decision, whose it was, and the
referral if made.”
Domain 3 — Decision making in relation to treatment procedures
Chain: making the surgery as safe as it can be
Q
Does the timing within the denosumab cycle matter?
“It is often suggested that elective surgery is best placed in the later part of the six-month cycle, when the
antibody’s effect has waned, and that the next dose is deferred until healing is established. It is biologically
plausible and worth discussing with her physician, but I would be honest that the evidence for it is limited
and I would not present it as established practice.”
Q
Would you stop the denosumab?
“No — not my decision and not my drug. Stopping denosumab causes rebound-associated vertebral fractures,
which is a far greater harm than the risk I would be trying to avoid. Any alteration is for her rheumatologist, in
writing, and I would make clear in my letter that I am not requesting cessation but asking about timing.”
Q
How do you manage the warfarin?
“Under SDCEP: do not interrupt it. Check the INR within 24 hours of the procedure, or up to 72 hours if she is
stably anticoagulated. If it is below 4.0, proceed with local haemostatic measures. Treat early in the day and
early in the week, limit the initial surgical area, and give her written post-operative instructions and a contact
number.”
Q
The INR on the day is 4.2. What now?
“Postpone and refer back to her anticoagulation service or GP for adjustment, then re-check and rebook. I
would not proceed and I would not adjust her dose myself. I would also use the delay to ask whether her
control has been unstable, because that is relevant to whether elective surgery is wise at all.”
Q
What local haemostatic measures?
“Atraumatic technique first — the less trauma, the less bleeding. Then oxidised regenerated cellulose or a
collagen sponge in the socket or under the flap, sutures to approximate the wound, and firm pressure with a
damp gauze pack for at least twenty minutes. Tranexamic acid mouthwash if oozing persists. Avoid vigorous
rinsing for 24 hours and no hot drinks or alcohol that day.”
Q
What analgesia would you prescribe, and what would you avoid?
“Paracetamol, regularly and by the clock, with codeine added if needed. I would avoid all NSAIDs — twice
over: they increase methotrexate toxicity, and they potentiate warfarin both pharmacokinetically and by their
antiplatelet effect and gastric irritation. I would tell her this explicitly, including that she must not buy ibuprofen
over the counter.”
Q
Antibiotic prophylaxis?
“I would give it here — a single pre-operative dose, for example amoxicillin 3 g orally one hour before, or
clindamycin if penicillin-allergic. The justification is her immunosuppression from methotrexate and pred-
nisolone plus her antiresorptive status, not implant surgery per se. I would avoid metronidazole and micona-
zole for anything else, because both markedly potentiate warfarin.”
Q
Describe your surgical modifications.
“Minimise trauma throughout. A flapless or minimal-flap approach if the CBCT allows, or a small mid-crestal
incision with careful atraumatic elevation. Avoid unnecessary bone removal and smooth any sharp edges. Co-

pious irrigation and sharp drills to avoid thermal injury. Primary closure wherever possible, because exposed
bone is precisely what I am trying to prevent. Pre-operative chlorhexidine rinse.”
Q
How would you plan the appointment around her arthritis?
“A morning appointment, short, with her usual medication taken. Do not extend her neck — treat her close
to upright, support the head and neck, and let her change position; if she has known atlanto-axial instability
I would be especially careful. Allow time for her to get into and out of the chair. Ask about her hands before
handing her anything, and check she can manage the journey.”
Q
What post-operative instructions would you give her?
“Written as well as spoken, and a contact number. Do not rinse for 24 hours, then warm salt-water rinses.
Paracetamol only — no ibuprofen or aspirin. Leave the denture out for 24 to 48 hours and then only wear it
after I have relieved and relined it. Soft diet, no smoking, no alcohol that day. And specifically: come back if
bleeding does not stop with 20 minutes of pressure, or if the site has not healed over.”
Domain 4 — Interpretation and problem solving of clinical outcomes
Chain: watching for what can go wrong
Q
What are you watching for, and when?
“Bleeding in the first 48 hours. Infection in the first week. And then, specifically, a review at eight weeks
for delayed healing or exposed bone, because that is the point at which non-healing meets the definition of
MRONJ. In the longer term, peri-implant mucositis driven by her plaque control, and denture-induced trauma
over a healing site.”
Q
She telephones on day two with bleeding. Manage it.
“Reassure, sit her up, and have her bite firmly on a damp gauze or a clean handkerchief for twenty minutes
without checking. If that fails, see her: identify whether it is oozing from the mucosa or a vessel, clean the site,
remove any liver clot, re-suture and pack with a haemostatic agent, and use tranexamic mouthwash. Check
the INR and ask about ibuprofen. If it still will not settle, or if there is airway swelling, she goes to hospital.”
Q
At ten weeks there is a 4 mm area of exposed bone. What is your diagnosis and what do you do?
“That is MRONJ, and by definition — exposed bone beyond eight weeks in a patient on an antiresorptive with-
out jaw radiotherapy. I would take a radiograph, not debride it, prescribe chlorhexidine 0.2% mouthwash,
treat any secondary infection with antibiotics, remove any sharp bony edge causing trauma only if clearly
necessary, keep the denture off the area, and refer to oral and maxillofacial surgery. And I would inform
her rheumatologist.”
Q
How is MRONJ staged?
“Broadly: stage 0 with non-specific symptoms or radiographic change but no exposed bone; stage 1 exposed or
probeable bone that is asymptomatic and uninfected; stage 2 exposed bone with pain and infection; and stage
3 with exposed bone plus extension beyond the alveolar bone — pathological fracture, extra-oral fistula, oro-
antral communication or osteolysis to the inferior border. Management is conservative at the lower stages and
increasingly surgical at stage 3.”
Q
She develops mucositis around both abutments at six months. What does that tell you and what do you do?
“That plaque control has failed, which is exactly the risk I identified at the outset. Peri-implant mucositis is re-
versible — bleeding on gentle probing without bone loss — so I would treat it before it becomes peri-implantitis:
professional debridement with instruments that will not damage the abutment surface, chlorhexidine locally,
and above all re-teach the cleaning with adapted aids — a powered brush with a wide handle, single-tufted
brushes, and involving whoever helps her at home.”

Q
What recall would you set, and what would you record at each visit?
“Three-monthly, with hygienist support, given her dexterity and immunosuppression. At each visit: probing
at six sites per implant with a plastic probe, bleeding and suppuration, mucosal health, plaque scores, denture
fit, extension and occlusion, attachment retention, and a check of the ridge for any exposed bone. Radiographs
at one year against the baseline taken at fitting, then as clinically indicated.”
Q
How would you know this had gone well?
“By her own account — that she eats a normal diet and does not think about the denture. Objectively: both im-
plants stable with no bleeding or suppuration, bone levels matching baseline, mucosa intact with no exposed
bone at any review, a denture she can insert, remove and clean herself or with help, and a maintenance interval
she attends. If any of those fail, the honest conclusion may be that the conventional denture would have served
her better.”
WATCH OUT
Take the drugs one at a time — denosumab, prednisolone, methotrexate, warfarin — and say for each what it
does, what it means for healing or bleeding, and what you would change. It buys a sentence of thinking time
and it is almost always the frame the question is really asking for.
Running this case to time
Time check. The flow above holds 38 questions and about 2,646 words of model answer. At 140 words a
minute plus roughly five seconds a question, that comes to about twenty-two minutes — an overrun of
seven. What goes first is the appointment-logistics material in Domain 3: the morning slot, the atlanto-
axial precaution, the post-operative instructions. It is good practice and it will be taken as one question,
because the marks here sit in the drugs and in the eight-week review. If your answers run past thirty
seconds, you will never reach Domain 4 — and Domain 4 is where MRONJ is actually diagnosed.
The fifteen-minute run sheet
Clock
The examiner does
What earns the mark
0:00–0:20
Settles you, confirms the case, puts the
drug list in front of you
Nothing. Do not talk into this.
0:20–1:20
Lets you present, uninterrupted
A 71-year-old requesting a two-implant
mandibular overdenture, presented as
four medical issues and one functional
one, each named with what it does:
denosumab — MRONJ risk;
prednisolone 5 mg — impairs healing
and changes her risk category; methotrexate
— immunosuppression and the analgesic
it forbids; warfarin at INR 2.8 —
manageable but verified. Then the one
that may decide it: rheumatoid hands,
and implants demand lifelong daily
cleaning. Working position — the
request is reasonable in principle, but
each issue is taken in turn and the
dexterity may prove decisive.

Clock
The examiner does
What earns the mark
1:20–4:30
Domain 1: the pharmacology
groundwork
Mechanisms, not names. Denosumab as
a monoclonal antibody against
RANK-L, acting like excess
osteoprotegerin; not incorporated into
bone, so its effect wanes across the cycle
and is reversible — unlike a
bisphosphonate bound to hydroxyapatite
for years. MRONJ defined in all three
limbs — exposed or probeable bone,
more than eight weeks, antiresorptive
exposure, no jaw radiotherapy —
because the eight weeks and the
radiotherapy exclusion are what
candidates drop. Then the trap: the
osteoporosis dose is the lower-risk
indication, but SDCEP moves her to
higher risk on the concurrent
glucocorticoid. Methotrexate as a folate
antagonist — and NSAIDs raise its
toxicity. Warfarin against II, VII, IX, X,
and what an INR is. Then the cervical
spine and secondary Sjögren’s.
4:30–7:30
Domain 2: from dexterity to the
treatment decision
Dexterity assessed directly, not assumed
— she removes, reinserts and cleans the
denture in front of you, and her present
hygiene predicts her future hygiene. All
the options, starting with a properly
remade conventional denture, because
that is reversible, cheap and carries no
MRONJ risk — and if it works the
medical debate never happens. Then the
case argued both ways: elective surgery
creating a hygiene burden she may not
meet, against the misery of a lower
complete denture and the harm of
withholding a well-evidenced
intervention. Studs, not a bar —
cleansability outranks load-sharing in
these hands. SAC Straightforward
normatively, Complex here.
7:30–11:30
Domain 3: making the surgery as safe as
it can be
You do not stop the denosumab — not
your drug, and stopping causes rebound
vertebral fracture; timing within the
cycle goes to her physician, offered
honestly as limited evidence. Warfarin
under SDCEP: do not interrupt, check
the INR within 24 hours (72 if stable),
proceed below 4.0 with local measures —
and at 4.2, postpone and refer back,
never adjust it yourself. Haemostasis in
order, ending in twenty minutes’
pressure and tranexamic mouthwash.
Analgesia: paracetamol and codeine, no
NSAIDs — twice over, for methotrexate
and for warfarin — said explicitly,
including over the counter. Single-dose
amoxicillin 3 g, justified by
immunosuppression rather than by
implant surgery; metronidazole and
miconazole avoided. Surgically:
minimal flap, primary closure —
exposed bone is the thing being
prevented.

Clock
The examiner does
What earns the mark
11:30–14:30
Domain 4: watching for what can go
wrong
The three windows: bleeding at 48
hours, infection in the first week, and a
review at eight weeks for delayed
healing — because eight weeks is where
non-healing becomes MRONJ. The
day-two bleed managed by twenty
minutes of pressure without checking,
then liver clot, re-suture, haemostatic
agent, INR, and a question about
ibuprofen. Then: 4 mm of exposed bone
at ten weeks is MRONJ by definition —
radiograph, do not debride,
chlorhexidine 0.2%, denture off the area,
refer to OMFS, and inform her
rheumatologist. Staging 0 to 3.
Mucositis at six months read as plaque
control having failed — reversible, so
treated now, with adapted aids and
whoever helps her at home.
Three-monthly recall.
14:30–15:00
Closes on the patient and the record
What you say to her: the injection
switches off the cells that break bone
down; very occasionally the jaw does
not heal after surgery; her risk is higher
than average because of the steroid
tablets; that does not mean no implants,
but the denture is optimised first and a
specialist is involved; and — plainly — “I
would not want you to stop your
injection.” Recorded: every drug with
dose, indication and duration, the risk
category and the reasoning for it, the
written liaison and reply, and whose
decision it was.
The spine — the twelve answers to have ready if nothing else
1 How denosumab works · 2 How it differs from a bisphosphonate, and why that matters · 3 MRONJ
defined, all three limbs · 4 Her risk category, and why the steroid moves it · 5 Methotrexate, and the drug
you must not prescribe · 6 Warfarin, the factors, and what an INR is · 7 The features of rheumatoid arthritis
that change your appointment · 8 How you assess her dexterity · 9 Why the conventional remake comes
first · 10 The INR rules, and what you do at 4.2 · 11 Studs rather than a bar, and why · 12 Exposed bone at
ten weeks — diagnosis, and what you do not do.
Where the marks are lost in this case
Reading “denosumab” and stopping there. The mark is in the drug, the indication and the route to-
gether: 60 mg six-monthly for osteoporosis is the lower-risk indication, and the same molecule at 120 mg
monthly for skeletal metastases is a case you decline outright. Say which one she is on, say what would
change if she were on the other, and say how long she has been taking it.
Missing the escalation the case is built on. Under SDCEP she is not lower risk, because she takes
prednisolone 5 mg daily — a concurrent systemic glucocorticoid moves an osteoporosis patient into the
higher-risk group. Candidates recite the reassuring osteoporosis figures and never notice that this patient
does not qualify for them. Volunteering that unprompted is the difference between a 3 and a 5.
Planning the surgery and forgetting the hands. Rheumatoid dexterity is not a footnote — it decides
the attachment choice, the recall interval and arguably whether to treat at all. And the competence line
must be said: two anterior mandibular implants would normally be Straightforward, but higher-risk
MRONJ status plus immunosuppression plus anticoagulation plus impaired plaque control is not
work to undertake single-handed — refer for a joint opinion, making clear to her that referral is not
refusal.

soe.title: The early failure
soe.text:
SOE Case 12 — The early failure
THE CASE
You placed a single implant at the UR5 eight weeks ago in a healthy 52-year-old. At the review the patient reports
mild discomfort. The healing abutment is loose and the implant rotates with light finger pressure. Radiograph
shows a peri-implant radiolucency.
Domain 1
“This is an early implant failure — failure to achieve or maintain osseointegration before loading. The implant
is mobile and there is a peri-implant radiolucency, so the diagnosis is not in doubt. My tasks are to explain it to
the patient, remove the implant, understand why it happened, and decide what to do next.”
Q
What are the causes of early failure?
“Grouped: surgical — inadequate primary stability, overheating during preparation, contamination, excessive
insertion torque causing compression necrosis, or placement into an infected site; patient — smoking, uncon-
trolled diabetes, poor bone quality, previous irradiation; loading — micromotion from a denture pressing on
the site, or premature loading; and site — residual infection or placement into non-osseous tissue such as
the incisive canal. I would go back through my own operative record: the bone quality recorded, insertion
torque, drill sequence and irrigation, whether the denture was relieved, and whether the patient smoked or
was unwell.”
Domain 2
Q: What do you tell the patient?
“Duty of candour applies. Promptly, honestly and without excessive self-flagellation: ‘I’m sorry — the implant
hasn’t attached to the bone as it should have. That happens in a small percentage of cases, around two to five
per cent, even when everything is done correctly. It’s not dangerous, but the implant has to come out. Once it’s
out and the area has healed for a couple of months, we can look at putting another one in, and I would expect
that to work — though I have to be honest that the chance of a second failure at the same site is a bit higher than
the first time. There will be no further charge from me for the replacement implant.’ I would then set out the
alternatives again, in case she now prefers a bridge or a denture, and record the conversation.”
Q
Would you charge?
“That is a practice policy and a professional judgement rather than a regulatory rule, but I would have set it out
in writing before treatment. My own position would be to replace the implant without charging for the fixture
and the surgery, while being clear about laboratory and component costs. What matters for the examination is
that the arrangement was agreed and documented in advance, so that this conversation is not a negotiation at
a diﬀicult moment.”
Domain 3
Q: Describe removal and re-treatment.
“Removal is straightforward with a mobile implant — often by hand or with a reverse-torque device. Then
thorough curettage of all granulation tissue, irrigation, and inspection of the bony walls. If there is a contained
defect I would graft with a xenograft and a collagen membrane and close primarily; if the walls are intact I might
allow spontaneous healing. An interim prosthesis — a bonded pontic or an acrylic partial denture generously
relieved. Re-entry at 2 to 3 months, or 4 to 6 months if I grafted. At re-placement I would use a wider and/or
longer implant to engage fresh bone, take particular care with irrigation and drill sharpness, and consider a
two-stage submerged protocol with an extended healing period.”

Domain 4
Q: What would you do to prevent recurrence in your practice?
“Treat it as a significant event. Review the operative record against my protocol; check drill usage counts and
replacement intervals; check irrigation flow; review my primary stability threshold; review my denture-relief
protocol. Then audit: my early failure rate over the last two years against a standard — the literature suggests
early failure of the order of 2 to 5% — with a re-audit after any change. That would be a legitimate quality
improvement project for the entrance requirements.”
Running this case to time
Time check. This case is written in the older format — five long answers, about 563 words. At 140 words
a minute plus five seconds a question that is barely four and a half minutes: it does not overrun, it leaves
ten minutes unaccounted for. Read that the right way round — the printed answers are far longer than
anything you would say out loud, and each is really three or four short questions in the mouth of an
examiner. Expect the causes of early failure alone to be four. If your answers run past thirty seconds you
will still never reach Domain 4, which here is the audit — the easiest mark in the case to earn and the
easiest to miss.
The fifteen-minute run sheet
Clock
The examiner does
What earns the mark
0:00–0:20
Settles you, confirms the case, puts the
radiograph in front of you
Nothing. Do not talk into this.
0:20–1:20
Lets you present, uninterrupted
Name it in the first clause: an early
implant failure — failure to achieve or
maintain osseointegration before
loading. Then the evidence, briefly: a
loose healing abutment, an implant that
rotates on light finger pressure, and a
peri-implant radiolucency at eight
weeks, so the diagnosis is not in doubt.
Then the four tasks that structure
everything that follows — explain it to
the patient, remove the implant,
understand why it happened, and
decide what to do next — in that order,
because the order is itself the answer.
1:20–4:30
Domain 1: the biology, then the causes,
drilled one group at a time
Expect this to open below the implant
material: osseointegration, how bone
heals round a fixture, and primary
versus secondary stability with the dip
between them — the exact window this
implant has fallen into at eight weeks.
Then the causes, delivered as four
named groups, not a list: surgical —
poor primary stability, overheating,
contamination, excessive torque causing
compression necrosis, an infected site;
patient — smoking, uncontrolled
diabetes, poor bone quality, irradiation;
loading — micromotion from an
unrelieved denture; site — residual
infection or non-osseous tissue. Then the
move that earns the domain: go back
through your own operative record.

Clock
The examiner does
What earns the mark
4:30–7:30
Domain 2: telling her, and the money
Duty of candour, named as a duty:
promptly, honestly, without excessive
self-flagellation. The words themselves
— the implant has not attached; this
happens in around two to five per cent
of cases even when everything is done
correctly; it must come out; a
replacement after a couple of months;
and the honest qualifier that a second
failure at the same site is more likely
than the first. Then the alternatives
re-offered, because she may now prefer a
bridge or a denture. On charging: a
practice policy set out in writing before
treatment, not a regulatory rule — the
mark is that it was agreed and
documented in advance.
7:30–11:30
Domain 3: removal, the site, and
re-treatment
Removal is easy in a mobile implant —
by hand or reverse-torque. Then the
part candidates skip: thorough curettage
of all granulation tissue, irrigation, and
inspection of the bony walls, because
the walls decide what happens next. A
contained defect takes a xenograft and a
collagen membrane; intact walls can
heal spontaneously. An interim
prosthesis generously relieved, since an
unrelieved denture is one of the causes
you just listed. Re-entry at two to three
months, or four to six if grafted; a wider
or longer implant into fresh bone, and a
two-stage submerged protocol.
11:30–14:30
Domain 4: the significant event and the
audit
Treat it as a significant event, and say
the words. Then the systems review,
itemised: the operative record against
protocol, drill usage counts and
replacement intervals, irrigation flow,
the primary stability threshold you
work to, and the denture-relief protocol.
Then the audit proper — your own early
failure rate over two years against a
standard of roughly 2 to 5%, with a
re-audit after any change, offered as a
quality improvement project. This is the
domain where a prepared candidate
simply outperforms an unprepared one.
14:30–15:00
Closes on the patient and the record
What you say: “I’m sorry — the implant
hasn’t attached to the bone as it should have…
it has to come out… once the area has healed
we can look at putting another one in, and I’d
expect that to work, though the chance of a
second failure at the same site is a bit higher.”
What you write: the candour
conversation and its date, the words used
about the failure rate and the higher
second-attempt risk, the alternatives
re-offered, the charging arrangement as
previously agreed, and the significant
event logged.
The spine — the twelve answers to have ready if nothing else
1 Early failure defined, and the evidence for it here · 2 Osseointegration, and the primary-to-secondary
stability dip · 3 The surgical causes · 4 The patient causes · 5 The loading causes, including the unrelieved
denture · 6 The site causes · 7 What you look for in your own operative record · 8 Duty of candour, and the
actual words · 9 The two-to-five per cent figure, and the higher second-attempt risk · 10 Charging, agreed
and documented in advance · 11 Removal, curettage, and what the bony walls decide · 12 The significant
event, the systems review and the audit standard.

Where the marks are lost in this case
Removing the implant and moving on. The examiner is not testing whether you can unscrew a loose
fixture — that part is trivial and takes one sentence. The case is about why it happened and what you
change, and a candidate who spends three minutes on removal technique has spent them in the cheapest
domain in the case.
Listing causes instead of grouping them. Say surgical, patient, loading, site and then populate each.
Then volunteer the thing candidates almost never volunteer: that you would audit your own operative
record first — bone quality, torque, irrigation, denture relief — before reaching for the patient’s smoking.
Looking at your own technique before the patient’s habits is the professional instinct being marked.
Treating candour as an apology rather than a duty. It is a regulatory duty, discharged promptly, honestly
and in writing, with the failure rate quoted and the higher risk of a second failure stated rather than
hidden. And the line to name is when to stop: after a repeated failure at the same site the answer is not a
third fixture but the bridge or denture, re-offered honestly — and a defect at re-entry that is not contained
goes on for an opinion.

soe.title: Repeated mechanical failure in a bruxist
soe.text:
SOE Case 13 — Repeated mechanical failure in a bruxist
THE CASE
44-year-old man with implant crowns at the 36 and 46, both fitted 2 years ago. He has returned three times with
screw loosening at the 36 and has now fractured the porcelain on the 46. Masseteric hypertrophy, linea alba,
marked wear facets on the anterior teeth. He works long hours and reports high stress.
Pace: one structured opening of about 60 seconds, then roughly 35 questions in the remaining 14 minutes. Nothing after the opening earns you
more than a few seconds of thought.
Opening — the 60-second presentation
Q
Present this case.
“A 44-year-old man with recurrent mechanical complications at two posterior implants, two years after fitting,
in the presence of clear clinical signs of parafunction — masseteric hypertrophy, linea alba and anterior wear
facets. Three episodes of screw loosening at the 36 and now veneer fracture at the 46. I would not read repeated
loosening as a nuisance to be re-tightened; it tells me the screw joint is being overloaded or is not passively
fitting, and untreated it progresses to screw fracture and ultimately implant fracture. So my priorities are to
establish why the joint is failing — occlusion, fit, component handling or all three — to confirm the implants
themselves are osseointegrated and the bone levels stable, and to correct the cause before I repair the effect.”
Domain 1 — Clinical interpretation and reasoning
Chain: the groundwork — parafunction and the periodontal ligament
Q
Define bruxism.
“Repetitive masticatory muscle activity characterised by clenching or grinding of the teeth and by bracing or
thrusting of the mandible. The international consensus separates sleep bruxism from awake bruxism, because
they have different aetiologies. In an otherwise healthy person it is a behaviour rather than a disorder — but
it becomes a risk factor when it damages teeth or restorations, which it clearly has here.”
Q
How certain is your diagnosis?
“Graded. Possible bruxism is self-report alone. Probable is self-report plus positive clinical findings — which
is where this man sits, with hypertrophy, linea alba and wear facets. Definite requires instrumental confirma-
tion, portable electromyography or polysomnography. I would call this probable sleep bruxism with an awake
clenching component, and I would say so in the notes rather than overclaim.”
Q
Describe the periodontal ligament.
“A collagenous connective tissue about 0.2 mm wide between cementum and alveolar bone, with organised
principal fibre groups — alveolar crest, horizontal, oblique, apical and interradicular — a rich vascular plexus,
and mechanoreceptors supplying proprioceptive feedback. It transmits and dissipates occlusal load, allows
physiological tooth movement, and remodels in response to force.”
Q
How does a tooth move under load compared with an implant?
“A tooth moves 25 to 100 micrometres in two phases — an initial rapid phase within the ligament, then a
slower phase of bone deformation. An osseointegrated implant has no ligament, so it moves only by elastic
deformation of bone, some 3 to 5 micrometres, and only in one phase. Its centre of rotation sits apically, not in
the middle third.”
Q
What follows clinically from that difference?
“Three things. The implant has no shock absorption, so load goes straight into the components and the crestal
bone. It has no ligament proprioception, so the protective reflex is blunted and tactile thresholds are far higher

— he cannot feel that he is overloading it. And connecting an implant rigidly to a natural tooth risks intrusion
of the tooth, which is why I avoid it.”
Q
Define osseointegration.
“A direct structural and functional connection between ordered living bone and the surface of a load-carrying
implant, in Brånemark’s terms; clinically, as Albrektsson set out, an implant that is immobile, symptomless,
without peri-implant radiolucency and with bone loss within accepted limits. The important word for this case
is load-carrying — integration is maintained or lost according to how it is loaded.”
Q
What is preload, and why does it matter here?
“Tightening the screw stretches it elastically; that stored tension is the preload, and it clamps the abutment to
the implant. The joint stays together while the separating forces are less than the preload. Loosening happens
when preload is never achieved, when it is lost to embedment relaxation as microscopic surface roughness
settles, or when eccentric load and bending exceed it — all three are plausible in this man.”
Chain: reading this patient
Q
What would you assess in the occlusion?
“Intercuspal contacts with shimstock and two thicknesses of articulating paper, checking whether the implant
crowns hold more heavily than the adjacent teeth. Then all excursions — working, non-working and protrusive
— looking specifically for non-working interferences on the implants. And the crown form: occlusal table
width, cusp inclines and any cantilever relative to the implant platform.”
Q
Why should an implant crown be lighter in contact than the neighbouring teeth?
“Because the natural teeth intrude within their ligaments under firm closure — of the order of 28 micrometres
— while the implant does not. So a contact that is even under light tapping becomes a premature contact under
clenching. I aim for the implant to hold shimstock only on firm clenching, and to be free in all excursions with
the canines providing guidance.”
Q
What else would you examine, and what radiographs?
“Muscles of mastication and TMJ, tongue scalloping, tooth wear and its distribution, and whether the abutments
are fully seated. History of sleep quality, morning jaw ache or headache, stress, caffeine, alcohol, recreational
drugs, SSRIs. Radiographically, parallel-technique periapicals of both implants to check bone levels against
baseline, seating of the abutment, and any radiolucent line suggesting a fractured screw or implant body.”
Domain 2 — Clinical decision making and treatment planning
Chain: what is actually causing the failure
Q
List the causes of repeated screw loosening.
“Inadequate initial torque or no re-torque; a re-used or damaged screw; a non-passive or misfitting abutment-
crown assembly; excessive occlusal load, including cantilevers, a wide occlusal table and steep cusps; eccentric
loading off the implant axis; a joint design with poor anti-rotation, such as an external hex; and wrong or
mismatched components. Bone loss lengthening the lever arm compounds all of them.”
Q
Is bruxism a contraindication to implants?
“Not an absolute one. The evidence links it convincingly to mechanical and technical complications — screw
loosening, veneer chipping, component fracture — rather than to loss of osseointegration, where the association
is much weaker. So it changes the design, the material, the occlusal scheme, the consent and the maintenance
interval, rather than the decision to treat.”
Q
Classify this case on SAC.

“The original treatment — two single posterior implant crowns in a healed site — would be Straightforward
to Advanced. Managing recurrent mechanical failure in a diagnosed bruxist is Advanced, because of the para-
function modifier and the need for occlusal and prosthodontic re-planning. It is still within my scope.”
Q
What would take it beyond your competence?
“A fractured implant body needing explantation, a fractured screw I could not retrieve, evidence that the arch
needs full occlusal reorganisation at an altered vertical dimension, or a co-existing painful temporomandibular
disorder that was not settling. Those I would refer — to a specialist in restorative dentistry or oral surgery as
appropriate — and I would say so at the outset rather than after a failed attempt.”
Q
Give me your plan in order.
“Correct the cause before repairing the effect. First, occlusal correction and a definitive parafunction diagnosis.
Second, disassemble, inspect and replace both screws with new ones at correct torque. Third, remake the frac-
tured 46 restoration in a more fracture-tolerant material. Fourth, a hard full-coverage occlusal splint for night
wear. Fifth, address the contributing factors — stress, sleep, and screening for sleep-disordered breathing.”
Q
What material for the new 46, and why?
“Monolithic zirconia, screw-retained. The commonest technical failure of implant crowns is chipping of lay-
ered veneering ceramic, and removing the veneer removes that failure mode. It is strong in thin section, which
suits his limited clearance, and screw retention keeps it retrievable so I can service the joint without destroying
the crown.”
Q
Argue against monolithic zirconia.
“It is unrepairable in the mouth — a fracture means a remake. Its wear behaviour against natural enamel
depends heavily on polish, and a rough or adjusted surface will abrade his opposing teeth, which already show
facets. It is stiff and unforgiving, so it transmits rather than absorbs load. And it hides the very early cracks
that a layered ceramic would show as chips. I mitigate by polishing every adjusted surface and reviewing the
antagonists.”
Q
A colleague would provide a metal occlusal surface instead. Why might they be right?
“Because cast metal is the most forgiving occlusal material we have — it does not chip, it wears at a rate close
to enamel, it is easy to adjust and polish, and in a heavy bruxist in a non-visible molar site aesthetics cost him
nothing. In a patient who has already fractured one ceramic, that is a genuinely defensible choice, and I would
offer it as an option.”
Q
Would you splint the two implants together?
“Not here — they are in different quadrants, so splinting is not even possible. Splinting adjacent implants does
share load and reduce screw loosening, but it compromises cleansability and complicates retrievability, so I
reserve it for short implants, poor bone quality or a cantilevered segment. In this case the better load control
comes from the occlusion and the splint.”
Domain 3 — Decision making in relation to treatment procedures
Chain: servicing the screw joint
Q
Take me through disassembly at the 36.
“Confirm which system and screwdriver, isolate with a throat pack or floss ligature so nothing is swallowed
or inhaled, remove the access filling, clean the screw head thoroughly so the driver seats fully, and unscrew.
Then inspect the abutment, the screw threads and the implant connection under magnification for wear or
deformation, and check the fit surface for a marginal discrepancy.”
Q
Why must the screw be replaced rather than re-tightened?

“Because it has already been stretched into its plastic range and its threads and head have deformed and abraded.
A fatigued screw cannot generate or hold full preload, so it will loosen again sooner. A new screw is cheap; a
fractured one retained in the implant is not.”
Q
How exactly do you torque it?
“With a calibrated torque wrench to the manufacturer’s stated value for that screw and connection — commonly
30 to 35 Ncm for an abutment screw, but system-specific. Then re-torque after about ten minutes to compensate
for embedment relaxation. Never torque with a hand driver, and never guess.”
Q
The screw fractures in the implant. What now?
“Stay calm, isolate, and magnify. Try to rotate the fragment out with an ultrasonic tip or a fine probe running
anticlockwise, sometimes after a drop of lubricant. If that fails, use the manufacturer’s screw retrieval kit
with its guide and reverse-cutting drill. Avoid anything that damages the internal threads. If the threads are
destroyed the implant may become unrestorable — which is when I refer.”
Q
Screw-retained or cement-retained for the new crown here — argue it.
“Screw-retained. In a patient who needs repeated access to the joint, retrievability is worth more than anything
cementation offers, and it removes any risk of residual subgingival cement, which is a recognised trigger for
peri-implant disease. Cement retention only wins where the screw channel would emerge through a cusp or a
facial surface, or where interocclusal space is very limited — neither applies at the 46.”
Q
The access channel emerges through the central fossa. Any concerns?
“It removes occlusal material at the point of heaviest loading, so I keep the channel as narrow as the driver
allows, seal it with PTFE tape and composite, and ensure the occlusal contacts sit on sound ceramic away
from the channel margin. An angulated screw channel is an alternative if the emergence would otherwise be
unacceptable.”
Q
Describe the splint you would make.
“A hard heat-cured acrylic full-coverage splint, usually maxillary, about 1 to 1.5 mm thick at the posteriors,
made on articulated casts with a facebow and a centric record at a comfortable vertical dimension. Full coverage
is non-negotiable — a partial-coverage appliance permits over-eruption of the uncovered teeth.”
Q
How do you adjust it at fit and afterwards?
“Check it seats fully and retains without rocking. Adjust to even, simultaneous point contacts on all opposing
cusp tips in the retruded position, with shallow canine ramps giving immediate posterior disclusion in excur-
sion and no working or non-working interferences. Then review it at intervals — the pattern of shiny wear
facets on the acrylic is my objective measure of how much he is grinding.”
Q
A colleague would give him a soft vacuum-formed splint. Respond.
“It is quicker and cheaper and he would tolerate it, and for short-term protection that has some value. But a
soft splint is not adjustable to a defined occlusal scheme, it wears rapidly, and there is a reasonable body of
opinion that a resilient surface can increase muscle activity in some bruxists — the ‘chewing gum’ effect. For a
diagnosed bruxist with a fractured restoration I want a hard, adjustable appliance.”
Q
What would you record?
“The parafunction diagnosis and its certainty level. Baseline and current radiographs and bone levels. The
component batch and the torque value with date for every screw placed. Occlusal findings before and after
adjustment, with photographs. The splint design, its adjustment and its wear at each review. And the consent
discussion — specifically that mechanical complications are likely to recur and carry a cost.”

Domain 4 — Interpretation and problem solving of clinical outcomes
Chain: when it goes wrong again
Q
What do you tell him, in his words?
“ ‘The implants themselves are healthy. The problem is the force you put through them at night — it is well
beyond what a normal crown is built for. I can make the crowns much tougher and even up your bite, but I
can’t switch off the grinding, so the night guard isn’t optional. You should expect parts to need replacing over
the years, and I’d rather you planned for that cost than were surprised by it.’ And I would put that in writing.”
Q
Two years on, the screw loosens again despite all of this. Differential?
“In order: occlusal load not adequately controlled — check the splint is being worn and the contacts have
not drifted; a misfitting or non-passive component; a damaged internal connection from the earlier episodes;
progressive crestal bone loss lengthening the lever arm; a cracked screw already partly failed; or the wrong
component from a previous repair. I would radiograph, disassemble and inspect rather than simply re-tighten
a fourth time.”
Q
When would you worry the implant body itself will fracture?
“Implant fracture is rare — of the order of 0.2 to 1% — but the risk rises with a narrow-diameter implant
under heavy load, with progressive bone loss increasing the lever arm, and with repeated untreated screw
loosening, because a loose joint transfers bending stress into the implant wall. Screw fracture is often the
warning shot before implant fracture.”
Q
It has fractured. How do you manage it?
“Explain honestly what has happened and that it is not restorable. A fractured implant almost always has to be
removed — by reverse-torque device or trephine — or, if removal would be destructive, the apical portion left
submerged as a sleeper with the coronal part smoothed below the soft tissue. Then reassess whether to replace
it, immediately or after healing, and whether the same design would fail again. Removal in a mandibular molar
site near the canal is where I would refer.”
Q
There is 2 mm of bone loss at the 36. Is that overload?
“I would not assume so. The dominant cause of progressive peri-implant bone loss is biofilm-associated in-
flammation, and I would first probe for bleeding and suppuration, check for residual cement and assess plaque
control. Occlusal overload alone, in the absence of inflammation, is not a proven cause of bone loss, though
it plausibly accelerates it once inflammation is present. So I treat the inflammation and correct the occlusion —
both, not one.”
Q
How and how often would you review him?
“Six-monthly, given his risk. At each visit: peri-implant probing with bleeding and suppuration, plaque control,
occlusal check with shimstock, screw and crown integrity, examination of the splint for wear and fit, and the
antagonist teeth. Radiographs at one year after any remake and then as clinically indicated, always compared
with baseline.”

Q
How would you know you had succeeded?
“No further loosening or ceramic fracture over successive reviews; stable bone levels and healthy peri-implant
tissues; a splint that is worn, wearing evenly and being replaced on schedule; and the man himself reporting
that his jaw is more comfortable in the morning. If loosening recurs despite all of it, the honest conclusion is
that the design is wrong for the forces, not that he needs another screw.”
WATCH OUT
Go back to the screw joint: preload against separating force. Ask yourself whether the preload was ever
achieved, whether it has been lost, or whether the separating force is too great — one of those three is nearly
always the answer in a mechanical failure question.
Running this case to time
Time check. The flow above holds 37 questions and about 2,352 words of model answer. At 140 words a
minute plus roughly five seconds a question, that is close to twenty minutes — an overrun of about five.
What goes first is the splint construction material in Domain 3: the thickness, the facebow, the adjustment
and the soft-splint argument compress into one question, because the marks in this case sit in the screw
joint and in Domain 4’s differential when it loosens again. If your answers run past thirty seconds, you
will never reach Domain 4 — and Domain 4 is where the implant fractures.
