Where the marks are lost in this case
Re-tightening the screw a fourth time. The examiner has given you three episodes of loosening precisely
to see whether you treat the symptom. Say in the opening that repeated loosening means the joint is
overloaded or not passively fitting, that it progresses to screw then implant fracture, and that you correct
the cause before you repair the effect. Candidates who reach for a torque wrench first have lost Domain
1 in the first thirty seconds.
Blaming the bruxism for the bone loss. When the 2 mm at the 36 appears, the volunteered answer
is that progressive peri-implant bone loss is biofilm-driven, and that occlusal overload alone is not a
proven cause in the absence of inflammation — so you probe, check for residual cement, and treat both
the inflammation and the occlusion. Reaching straight for “he grinds” is the trap the question is set to
catch.
Never naming what you would not attempt.
Managing recurrent mechanical failure in a bruxist is
Advanced and yours. What is not: a fractured implant body needing explantation, a fractured screw
you cannot retrieve, an arch needing full occlusal reorganisation at an altered vertical dimension, or a
painful temporomandibular disorder that is not settling — those go to a specialist in restorative dentistry
or oral surgery. Say it at the outset, not after a failed attempt.

soe.title: Immediate placement in an intact anterior socket
soe.text:
SOE Case 14 — Immediate placement in an intact anterior socket
THE CASE
35-year-old woman, non-smoker, low lip line. The 11 has a vertical root fracture below a post crown and is
unrestorable. CBCT shows intact socket walls, a facial wall 1.2 mm thick, 6 mm of bone apical and palatal
to the socket apex, the socket lying within the alveolar envelope, and no infection. Thick phenotype, no
recession on the adjacent teeth.
Pace: one structured opening of about 60 seconds, then roughly 35 questions in the remaining 14 minutes. Nothing after the opening earns you
more than a few seconds of thought.
Opening — the 60-second presentation
Q
Present this case.
“A healthy 35-year-old non-smoker with an unrestorable upper central incisor — a vertical root fracture be-
neath a post crown, which is not repairable and means the tooth must come out. What makes this case worth
discussing is that the site is anatomically about as favourable as an anterior socket gets: the walls are intact,
the facial wall is 1.2 mm, there is 6 mm of bone apical and palatal for stability, the socket sits within the bone
envelope, and there is no infection. She has a thick phenotype, a low lip line and no recession on the neighbours,
so her aesthetic risk is low. My working position is that this satisfies the criteria for immediate placement, but
I need to establish what she wants, what she can accept if the contour changes, and whether the case sits within
my own competence.”
Domain 1 — Clinical interpretation and reasoning
Chain: the anatomical and biological groundwork
Q
Describe the anatomy of an anterior maxillary extraction socket.
“Four bony walls lined by bundle bone — the alveolar bone proper, which is the cribriform plate the periodontal
fibres insert into. Buccally it is often the whole thickness of the wall; palatally it is backed by thick cancellous
and cortical bone. The socket contains the periodontal ligament, its blood supply and the clot. Above the crest
sits the supracrestal attachment, and the incisive canal lies palatal and medial.”
Q
What is bundle bone, and why does it matter here?
“It is tooth-dependent bone. Its blood supply and its reason for existing are the periodontal ligament, so when
the tooth is removed the ligament goes and the bundle bone resorbs — regardless of how atraumatic you were.
Since the facial wall in the anterior maxilla is largely bundle bone, that is why the buccal contour collapses.
Immediate implant placement does not prevent this, which is the single most important thing to say about
this case.”
Q
What happens dimensionally if you extract and do nothing?
“Around 50% of the ridge width is lost in the first year, and roughly two-thirds of that in the first three months.
Systematic review figures put horizontal loss at about 3.5 to 4 mm and vertical loss at about 1 to 1.5 mm at six
months, and the loss is predominantly buccal, so the ridge migrates palatally as well as shrinking.”
Q
Where does the buccal plate get its blood supply from?
“Three sources — the periodontal ligament, which is lost with the tooth; the periosteum overlying it; and the
intra-osseous supply, which in a 1 mm wall is negligible. So once the ligament has gone, the periosteum is
essentially all that is left. That is the argument for a flapless approach: raising a flap strips the one remaining
blood supply from a wall that has just lost its other one.”
Q
How thick is the facial wall in the anterior maxilla usually?

“Thin. In the large majority of anterior maxillary sites it is under 1 mm, and in around half of them under 0.5
mm. That is precisely why 1.2 mm here is favourable — she is in the minority, and a wall of that thickness has
some chance of surviving as a wall rather than resorbing entirely.”
Q
How would you assess her periodontal phenotype chairside?
“The simplest reproducible method is to place a periodontal probe in the sulcus and see whether it shows
through the tissue — if it is visible, the phenotype is thin, under about 1 mm. I would combine that with the
gingival appearance and the crown form: thick phenotype tends to give square crowns, flat scallop and a broad
band of keratinised tissue, thin gives triangular crowns and high scallop.”
Q
Why does her lip line matter so much?
“Because it determines what she will actually see if the outcome is imperfect. A low lip line means the mid-
facial gingival margin and the transition line are hidden at maximum smile, so recession or a visible crown
margin is far less consequential. It is one of the strongest modifiers in any aesthetic risk assessment, and it
converts this from a high-stakes case into a manageable one.”
Chain: reading this patient
Q
How would you have diagnosed the vertical root fracture?
“Clinically: a narrow, isolated, deep probing defect on an otherwise healthy tooth, often a sinus tract at or near
the gingival margin, tenderness to bite, and a post-crowned root — post-retained teeth are the classic setting.
Radiographically a J-shaped or halo radiolucency. CBCT can show a fracture line but the post generates beam-
hardening artefact, so a negative scan does not exclude one; direct vision after flap or on removal is definitive.”
Q
What does the CBCT add here, and what are its limits?
“It gives me the facial wall thickness, the apical and palatal bone available for stability, the position of the incisive
canal, and whether the socket sits within the envelope — none of which I can get from a periapical. Its limits
are artefact from the post and core, that it does not show soft tissue thickness, and that it must be justified
individually under IR(ME)R.”
Q
Give me a formal aesthetic risk assessment on her.
“Using the ITI ERA headings: medical status healthy, non-smoker, expectations to be established, low lip line,
thick phenotype, tooth shape to be assessed, no infection, bone levels on the adjacent teeth normal, adjacent
teeth unrestored, a single-tooth span, and intact soft tissue anatomy. Almost every parameter is low risk. The
only unknown is her expectation, and that is the one I have to explore before I promise anything.”
Q
What is the SAC classification, and is this within your competence?
“A single implant in the aesthetic zone is Advanced at best; immediate placement with immediate restoration
in the aesthetic zone is Complex on both the surgical and the restorative axis. So the honest answer is that
I would complete the assessment, the wax-up and the options conversation myself and refer the surgical
phase. What I must be able to do at my level is recognise why this site is favourable, understand the protocol
well enough to consent her properly, and manage her afterwards.”
Domain 2 — Clinical decision making and treatment planning
Chain: the options, and the timing decision
Q
What are her options for replacing the 11?
“No treatment, accepting a space — rarely acceptable at a central incisor. A removable partial denture, which
replaces soft tissue as well but is removable. A resin-bonded bridge from the 21, minimally invasive and
reversible. A conventional bridge, which I would not do on unrestored abutments. Or an implant-retained
crown. Orthodontic space closure is not realistic for a central incisor here.”

Q
You have chosen an implant. Argue against yourself — why might a resin-bonded bridge be better?
“Because it is cheap, quick, reversible and does not depend on a healing ridge. She is 35 with an intact adjacent
tooth and thick tissue, so the abutment preparation is minimal or nil and survival at ten years is respectable. It
avoids surgery, avoids the lifelong mucositis and peri-implantitis risk, and if it debonds I have lost nothing. If
she is at all uncertain about surgery, it is the better first answer — and it does not close the implant door.”
Q
Classify the timing options for implant placement after extraction.
“Type 1 — immediate, into the fresh socket at the time of extraction. Type 2 — early with soft tissue healing,
at about 4 to 8 weeks. Type 3 — early with partial bone healing, at about 12 to 16 weeks. Type 4 — late, at six
months or more, into a healed ridge. Loading is classified separately as immediate, early or conventional.”
Q
Take me through the pre-operative criteria for immediate placement.
“Patient factors — thick soft tissue phenotype, no recession on the site or the neighbours, and low aesthetic risk.
Radiographic factors on CBCT — an intact socket with a facial wall of at least 1 mm; enough bone apical and
palatal to achieve primary stability; the socket lying within the bone envelope; a horizontal gap of at least 2
mm anticipated at the implant shoulder; and no acute infection. She meets all of them.”
Q
And the intra-operative criteria?
“Three, checked after the tooth is out and not before. The socket wall is confirmed intact on probing. Primary
stability is achievable in the apical and palatal bone. And the ideal three-dimensional implant position is
achievable. If any one of those fails, I abandon immediate placement on the table and convert to early placement
or ridge preservation — that decision must be made in advance and consented for in advance.”
Q
What are the loading criteria?
“For an immediate restoration I want an insertion torque above about 35 Ncm or an ISQ above 70, no direct
occlusal contact in intercuspation or in any excursion, and no parafunction. If those are not met I place a healing
abutment or a custom healing abutment and load conventionally.”
Q
How well validated is that protocol?
“Type 1 placement with immediate restoration is graded clinically documented — it works in selected hands
and selected cases, but it is not scientifically and clinically validated. Type 4 late placement with conventional
loading is the SCV protocol. That distinction belongs in the consent conversation: I am offering her the faster
option and telling her it carries the thinner evidence base.”
Q
What are the risks specific to immediate placement?
“Mid-facial recession is the principal one, driven by a thin wall or a buccally positioned implant. Then diﬀiculty
achieving the ideal position because the drill skids off the palatal wall; unpredictable bone fill of the gap;
reduced primary stability; and the fact that it does not prevent bundle bone resorption, so the buccal contour
may still flatten even when everything is done correctly.”
Q
Suppose the facial wall were 0.6 mm, the phenotype thin and the smile line high. What changes?
“Immediate placement comes off the table. I would move to Type 2 early placement at 4 to 8 weeks with
simultaneous contour augmentation, or, if the site were incompatible with Types 1 to 3, ridge preservation at
extraction and Type 4 placement at 4 to 6 months. And the aesthetic risk assessment would read high, so the
case is unambiguously Complex and referred.”
Q
Your colleague would extract, preserve the ridge and place at four months anyway. Why might they be right?
“Because they get the healed soft tissue, a keratinised band and a predictable envelope to work into, they
avoid the risk of misjudging stability on the table, and the evidence base for late placement is the strongest we
have. The cost is time, a second surgery and an interim prosthesis. In an aesthetically low-risk mouth like hers,
the argument for immediacy is convenience — which is a legitimate reason, but I should say so rather than dress
it up as biology.”

Q
What do you tell her, in her own words?
“ ‘This tooth has a crack running down the root, and there’s no way of repairing that, so it has to come out. The
good news is the bone around it is in unusually good shape, which means we may be able to put the implant
in the same day and give you a temporary tooth that looks right straight away. Two things I want you to know.
The gum and bone at the front always shrink a little after a tooth is removed — the implant slows that down
but doesn’t stop it, so the shape may change slightly. And this is the more technically demanding way of doing
it, so I’ll be arranging the surgery with a colleague who does this routinely.’ ”
Domain 3 — Decision making in relation to treatment procedures
Chain: the surgical sequence and its detail
Q
Take me through the extraction.
“Flapless and atraumatic. Sever the periodontal fibres with a periotome or fine luxator, work circumferentially,
and deliver with rotational rather than buccal force — no elevation against the buccal plate. Because the root is
fractured, I expect it to come out in pieces: section it and remove the fragments individually, using a physics
forceps or root-removal system rather than levering. The buccal plate is the whole game; I would rather spend
twenty minutes than lose it.”
Q
Flap or flapless — justify it.
“Flapless. The buccal plate has just lost its periodontal ligament supply, and raising a mucoperiosteal flap
removes the periosteal supply as well; flap elevation is independently associated with greater crestal resorption.
Flapless also preserves the soft tissue architecture and the papillae, which in an aesthetic site I cannot rebuild
reliably. I would only raise a flap if I found a wall defect that needed grafting under direct vision.”
Q
How do you confirm the buccal wall is intact?
“Debride the socket fully of granulation tissue and periodontal ligament remnants, irrigate, then probe circum-
ferentially inside the socket with a blunt probe, feeling for any dehiscence or fenestration, and confirm the
crestal height on all four walls. Direct vision with good light and suction. If the wall is breached, the intra-
operative criteria have failed and I change plan.”
Q
Where do you start the osteotomy, and why?
“Against the palatal wall, not in the centre of the socket. A drill placed in the socket follows the path of least
resistance and skids buccally, which is exactly how immediate implants end up in the wrong place. I make a
purchase point on the palatal wall with a small round bur or precision drill, then follow the palatal wall apically,
engaging 3 to 5 mm of native bone apical and palatal to the socket for stability.”
Q
Where exactly does the implant shoulder sit, in three dimensions?
“Apico-coronally, about 3 mm apical to the planned mid-facial gingival margin. Bucco-palatally, 1 to 2 mm
palatal to the emergence point of the adjacent teeth, leaving the buccal gap. Mesio-distally, at least 1.5 mm from
each adjacent root. That is Buser’s comfort zone; outside it — too shallow, too buccal, too close to a neighbour
— you get recession, a visible margin or loss of papilla.”
Q
What is the jumping gap, and what do you do with it?
“The horizontal gap between the implant surface and the inner aspect of the buccal wall. I want it to be at
least 2 mm, and I graft it with a slowly resorbing xenograft — deproteinised bovine bone mineral — condensed
but not over-packed, up to the crest. The graft is not there to osseointegrate; it is there to support the contour
while the bundle bone resorbs.”
Q
Why a xenograft rather than her own bone?
“Because I want a material that resorbs slowly or barely at all, so it holds the buccal profile for years. Autoge-
nous bone is osteogenic but remodels and shrinks, which is the opposite of what a contour graft needs to do.
Deproteinised bovine bone mineral is osteoconductive, dimensionally stable and very well documented in this
indication.”

Q
When would you place an immediate provisional, and how is it designed?
“Only if the loading criteria are met — torque above 35 Ncm, no parafunction. It should be screw-retained,
so there is no cement anywhere near a fresh socket; completely free of contact in intercuspation and in every
excursion; with a concave subcritical contour to allow tissue thickness and a critical contour that supports the
mid-facial margin and papillae. It is a soft tissue former that happens to look like a tooth.”
Q
You achieve only 20 Ncm. What now?
“I do not provisionalise. Options in order: a healing abutment or custom healing abutment with the socket
sealed and grafted and a submerged or transmucosal healing period; a removable interim prosthesis or an
Essix retainer relieved off the site; or a resin-bonded temporary pontic bonded to the neighbour, which is my
preferred interim because it loads nothing. Then conventional loading at three to four months.”
Q
Post-operative instructions and prescribing?
“Soft diet and absolutely no incising with the front teeth for eight weeks. No brushing over the site for two
weeks — chlorhexidine 0.2% mouthwash or gel applied locally instead. Analgesia with ibuprofen and parac-
etamol. Antibiotics are not routine for me, though there is reasonable evidence for a single pre-operative dose of
amoxicillin in implant surgery; I would follow local antimicrobial stewardship guidance. Written instructions
and a contact number.”
Domain 4 — Interpretation and problem solving of clinical outcomes
Chain: judging and salvaging the aesthetic result
Q
How would you monitor the aesthetic outcome?
“Standardised clinical photographs at every stage from baseline. Objectively, the pink and white aesthetic
scores, or at minimum a papilla index and the mid-facial margin level measured against the adjacent teeth.
Plus peri-implant probing and bleeding, and radiographic bone levels against the baseline film taken at fitting.
Review at one week, three weeks, at each provisional adjustment, at definitive fitting, then three and twelve
months.”
Q
When would you declare success?
“Not at six months. Mid-facial recession in immediate anterior implants characteristically appears over the first
one to three years, so my judgement point is at least a year out, and I tell her that at the start so a good six-month
result is not oversold.”
Q
What actually determines whether the papilla fills?
“The bone level on the adjacent tooth, not on the implant — which is why an intact neighbour is such an asset
here. Tarnow’s measurement is the one to quote: where the distance from the contact point to the interproximal
bone crest is 5 mm or less the papilla is present almost always, at 6 mm about half the time, at 7 mm rarely.
So the lever I have is the contact point position in the definitive crown, and the provisional is where I shape it.”
Q
At one year there is 1.5 mm of mid-facial recession. Why?
“Most likely the implant is slightly too buccal, or the buccal wall resorbed despite the graft, or the tissue
was over-contoured by the provisional and pushed apically. Less commonly, mucositis with tissue loss, or an
occlusal overload she has developed. I would examine the emergence profile, probe the site, check the occlusion,
and take a periapical against baseline.”
Q
What would you actually do about it?
“In order of invasiveness: re-contour the restoration to reduce a bulky critical contour and let the tissue rebound,
and re-shape with a provisional. Then a connective tissue graft to thicken and coronally reposition, which is
the most reliable single measure. Then remaking the crown with a longer clinical crown or pink ceramic to
disguise it. Explantation is the last resort and I would refer before that point. With a low lip line, watchful
monitoring and honest discussion may well be the right answer.”

Q
What would you record?
“Baseline photographs and the aesthetic risk assessment; the consent discussion including the specific words
used about contour change and about the evidence grading of the protocol; the CBCT justification and report;
the intra-operative findings — wall intact, insertion torque, gap size, graft used, batch number; the implant
make, diameter, length and lot; the loading decision and why; the post-operative instructions given; and at
every review, probing, bleeding, margin level and bone level against baseline.”
Q
How would you know this treatment had succeeded?
“By her measure first — that she smiles without checking the tooth. Objectively: an osseointegrated, asymp-
tomatic implant with no bleeding or suppuration, bone levels stable against baseline, a mid-facial margin
within about 1 mm of the contralateral 21, papillae she does not notice, a cleansable emergence profile, and no
prosthetic complication at one year.”
WATCH OUT
Go back to the two intra-operative gates — is the socket wall intact, and can I achieve the ideal position with primary
stability? Almost every question in an immediate placement case is a variation on one of those, and saying it
aloud buys you a sentence of thinking time.
Running this case to time
Time check. The flow above holds 40 questions and about 2,818 words of model answer. At 140 words a
minute plus roughly five seconds a question, that runs to about twenty-three and a half minutes — an
overrun of eight and a half. What goes first is the surgical detail in Domain 3: the extraction technique,
the flapless justification and confirming the wall compress into one question, because you are referring that
surgery and the marks sit in the three-dimensional position, the jumping gap and the loading decision.
If your answers run past thirty seconds, you will never reach Domain 4 — and Domain 4 is the recession
at one year.

What earns the mark

CBCT up

discussing — the site is about as
favourable as an anterior socket gets:
walls intact, facial wall 1.2 mm, 6 mm of
bone apical and palatal, socket within
the envelope, no infection, with a thick
phenotype and a low lip line. Working
position: this meets the criteria for
immediate placement, but three things
remain — what she wants, what she can
accept if the contour changes, and
whether the case is within your own
competence.

Clock
The examiner does
What earns the mark
1:20–4:30
Domain 1: the anatomical and biological
groundwork, then reading this patient
Undergraduate biology first. Four walls
lined by bundle bone —
tooth-dependent, fed by the ligament,
therefore resorbing when the tooth goes
— and the sentence the whole case turns
on: immediate placement does not
prevent this. The figures: about 50% of
ridge width in the first year, two-thirds
of it in three months, roughly 3.5–4 mm
horizontal and 1–1.5 mm vertical at six
months, predominantly buccal. The
buccal plate’s three blood supplies, one
already lost — the argument for flapless.
Anterior facial walls under 1 mm in most
sites, so her 1.2 mm is the minority.
Phenotype by probe transparency; the
low lip line as a risk modifier, because it
decides what she will see. Then the ITI
aesthetic risk assessment, with
expectation the only unknown.
4:30–7:30
Domain 2: the options, and the timing
decision
Every option, including no treatment
and the resin-bonded bridge argued at
its strongest — cheap, quick, reversible,
and it does not close the implant door.
Then the classification kept clean: Types
1 to 4 by timing, loading classified
separately. The pre-operative criteria
matched to her, including the 2 mm
horizontal gap; then the three
intra-operative gates checked after the
tooth is out — wall intact, primary
stability achievable, ideal position
achievable — with the abandonment
plan consented in advance. Loading:
>35 Ncm or ISQ >70, no occlusal
contact anywhere, no parafunction.
And the evidence grading said out loud
— Type 1 with immediate restoration is
clinically documented, not scientifically
and clinically validated.
7:30–11:30
Domain 3: the surgical sequence and its
detail
Compressed at the front — flapless,
periotome, sectioned and delivered
rotationally, no elevation against the
buccal plate, then the socket debrided
and probed circumferentially to confirm
the wall. Then what the examiner will
spend time on: the osteotomy started
against the palatal wall with a purchase
point, because a drill in a socket skids
buccally, engaging 3–5 mm of native
bone apical and palatal. Position in
three dimensions — 3 mm apical to the
planned mid-facial margin, 1–2 mm
palatal, 1.5 mm from each root. The
jumping gap at 2 mm or more, grafted
with deproteinised bovine bone
mineral chosen because it barely resorbs
— a contour graft, not an osteogenic one.
The provisional screw-retained and out
of contact in every excursion. And at 20
Ncm you do not provisionalise.

Clock
The examiner does
What earns the mark
11:30–14:30
Domain 4: judging and salvaging the
aesthetic result
Standardised photographs from
baseline, pink and white aesthetic scores,
and the mid-facial margin measured
against the neighbour. Then the timing
judgement: do not declare success at six
months — recession in immediate
anterior implants appears over one to
three years, and she is told that at the
start so a good early result is not oversold.
Tarnow for the papilla, with the point
that it depends on the bone level of the
adjacent tooth, so the lever you hold is
the contact point position. Then 1.5 mm
of recession at a year, with causes in
order — too buccal, the wall resorbed
despite the graft, or over-contoured by
the provisional — and treatments in
order of invasiveness: re-contour first,
then a connective tissue graft, then pink
ceramic, with explantation referred.
14:30–15:00
Closes on the patient and the record
In her words: the crack cannot be
repaired, so the tooth comes out; the
bone is unusually good, so the implant
and a temporary tooth may go in the
same day; the gum and bone at the front
always shrink a little, and the implant
slows that but does not stop it; and —
plainly — “this is the more technically
demanding way of doing it, so I’ll be
arranging the surgery with a colleague who
does this routinely.” Recorded: baseline
photographs and the risk assessment, the
words used about contour change and
about the evidence grading, torque, gap
size and graft batch, and the margin and
bone level at every review.
The spine — the twelve answers to have ready if nothing else
1 Bundle bone, and why immediate placement does not save the wall · 2 The dimensional change after
extraction, with the figures · 3 The three blood supplies of the buccal plate · 4 How thin an anterior facial
wall usually is, and why 1.2 mm matters · 5 Phenotype assessed chairside · 6 Why the low lip line changes
the case · 7 The resin-bonded bridge argued at its strongest · 8 Types 1 to 4, and loading kept separate · 9
The pre-operative criteria, and the three intra-operative gates · 10 Implant position in three dimensions ·
11 The jumping gap, and why a xenograft rather than her own bone · 12 Tarnow, the contact point, and
what to do about recession at a year.
Where the marks are lost in this case
Claiming the immediate implant preserves the buccal plate. It does not. The facial wall is largely bundle
bone, its blood supply left with the ligament, and it resorbs whatever you place in the socket. Say that
in the first thirty seconds and then say what immediate placement does buy — one surgery, a shorter
treatment time and immediate soft tissue support — because that is an honest answer and the other one
is not.
Losing the position to the socket. The single technical point this case is built on is that a drill placed in
the centre of a socket skids buccally off the palatal wall, and a buccally placed implant is the commonest
cause of the mid-facial recession that arrives at one to three years. Volunteer the palatal purchase point,
the 1–2 mm palatal shoulder and the 2 mm jumping gap unprompted — that is the difference between a
3 and a 5 in Domain 3.
Planning a Complex case as though it were yours. A single implant in the aesthetic zone is Advanced at
best; immediate placement with immediate restoration in the aesthetic zone is Complex on both axes,
and at this level the surgical phase is referred. What stays yours is the diagnosis, the risk assessment,
the wax-up, the options conversation, the consent — including the evidence grading — and the lifelong
aftercare. Candidates describe the palatal osteotomy beautifully and never say who is holding the drill.

soe.title: The smoker with treated periodontitis
soe.text:
SOE Case 15 — The smoker with treated periodontitis
THE CASE
50-year-old woman, smokes 15 cigarettes a day for 30 years. History of generalised periodontitis Stage III
Grade C, treated non-surgically 3 years ago, now with probing depths mostly 4 mm or less, full-mouth bleeding
score 18%, plaque score 30%. Missing 15, 25, 36, 46. Wants “all of them replaced with implants”.
Pace: one structured opening of about 60 seconds, then roughly 35 questions in the remaining 14 minutes. Nothing after the opening earns you
more than a few seconds of thought.
Opening — the 60-second presentation
Q
Present this case.
“A 50-year-old woman who smokes 15 a day and has a treated history of generalised periodontitis, Stage III
Grade C, requesting four implants to replace the 15, 25, 36 and 46. Her pockets have responded, but her bleeding
score of 18% and plaque score of 30% are above the thresholds for periodontal stability, which are bleeding
under 10% and, ideally, plaque under 20%. So the honest interpretation is that she is improved but not stable.
She also carries the two strongest patient-level risk factors for peri-implantitis — a history of periodontitis
and smoking — operating together. My priorities are to establish stability, to address the smoking, to reduce
the scope of what she is asking for, and to make sure she understands the risk before anything is placed.”
Domain 1 — Clinical interpretation and reasoning
Chain: the periodontal groundwork
Q
What does Stage III Grade C mean?
“Under the 2017 World Workshop classification, the stage describes severity and complexity at presentation
and the grade describes the rate of progression and risk of further progression. Stage III is severe disease with
the potential for additional tooth loss; Grade C is rapid progression. The extent — generalised — means 30%
or more of teeth are affected.”
Q
How is the stage determined?
“By the interdental clinical attachment loss at the worst-affected site, supported by radiographic bone loss
and tooth loss due to periodontitis. Stage III is CAL of 5 mm or more, bone loss extending to the middle third
of the root and beyond, and four or fewer teeth lost. Complexity factors then may raise the stage — pockets
of 6 mm or more, vertical defects of 3 mm or more, furcation involvement grade II or III, and ridge defects.”
Q
And the grade?
“By evidence of progression. Direct evidence is radiographic bone loss over five years. Indirect evidence is
the ratio of percentage bone loss to age — under 0.25 is Grade A, 0.25 to 1.0 Grade B, over 1.0 Grade C. Grade
is then modified upward by risk factors: smoking 10 or more cigarettes a day, or HbA1c of 7.0% or above in
diabetes, both push a patient to Grade C. At 15 a day, her smoking alone places her there.”
Q
Define a successfully treated, stable periodontitis patient.
“No probing depths of 4 mm or more that bleed on probing, no sites of 5 mm or greater, and a full-mouth
bleeding score below 10%. Bone levels stable. The patient remains a periodontitis patient for life — the
diagnosis is not cured, it is controlled, and she moves into supportive periodontal care rather than back to
routine recall.”
Q
Is she stable?
“No. Her bleeding score of 18% is nearly twice the threshold, and her plaque score of 30% tells me the cause
of that bleeding is unresolved. Pockets of 4 mm or less is encouraging, but stability is defined by inflammation,

not depth alone. I would describe her as in remission but not stable, and that distinction is the entire basis of
my treatment plan.”
Q
How do you record a full-mouth bleeding score and a plaque score?
“Six sites per tooth, all teeth, scored dichotomously — present or absent — and expressed as a percentage of
sites. Bleeding is recorded after gentle probing to the pocket base with a light force of about 0.25 N; plaque is
recorded by running a probe along the gingival margin or after disclosing. The same indices repeated at every
visit are what let me and the patient see whether anything is changing.”
Chain: smoking and the tissues
Q
How does smoking affect the periodontium?
“Local vasoconstriction and reduced gingival blood flow, so the tissues look fibrous and pale and bleed less
than the underlying inflammation warrants. Impaired neutrophil chemotaxis and phagocytosis. Reduced
fibroblast attachment and proliferation, so healing and reattachment are poorer. A shift towards a more anaero-
bic subgingival microbiota. The net effect is more attachment loss for the same plaque and a blunted response
to treatment.”
Q
So does her bleeding score mislead you?
“Almost certainly — it understates her inflammation. In a smoker, 18% bleeding probably represents more
disease activity than the same figure in a non-smoker, which makes it even less acceptable as a starting point
for implants. It also means that if she stops smoking her bleeding score may temporarily rise, and I would warn
her of that so she does not read it as failure.”
Q
And on implants and healing specifically?
“It impairs early wound healing and osseointegration — reduced oxygen tension, impaired osteoblast function,
nicotine-induced vasoconstriction — and it substantially reduces the predictability of bone augmentation and
membrane procedures, where wound dehiscence and graft loss are markedly more common. It is a dose-
dependent effect: heavier smokers do worse, and the maxilla appears more affected than the mandible.”
Q
What is her overall risk profile in one sentence?
“A Grade C periodontitis history that is not yet stable, combined with a 30 pack-year smoking habit — the
two risk factors most consistently associated with peri-implantitis, in a patient asking for four implants at once.
That is not a refusal, but it is a mandate to change the sequence and the scope.”
Domain 2 — Clinical decision making and treatment planning
Chain: what she is told and what is planned
Q
What do you tell her?
“I would not say no, and I would not say yes. ‘Implants are possible for you, but the conditions aren’t right
today, and if I placed them now I think there is a real chance of losing them. Two things are working against us.
You’ve had gum disease, and the same disease happens around implants — where it actually moves faster and
is harder to treat. And smoking roughly doubles the chance of an implant failing. So let’s get your gums to a
stable point, help you stop smoking, then reassess — and start with fewer than four.’ ”
Q
What figures would you quote?
“That smoking roughly doubles to two-and-a-half times the implant failure rate and increases peri-implantitis
risk in a dose-dependent way. That a history of periodontitis is the strongest patient-level risk factor for peri-
implantitis. And that peri-implantitis affects in the region of 22% of patients overall — while making clear that
her personal risk sits above that, and that these are ranges from the literature, not predictions about her.”

Q
Give me your plan.
“Four steps. One, re-treat to stability. Two, smoking cessation. Three, reassess and reduce the scope, consid-
ering alternatives to implants at every site. Four, only then place a small number of implants with cleansable,
screw-retained restorations and committed three-monthly supportive care. Each step is a gate — I do not move
to the next until the previous one is met.”
Q
Take step one further.
“Step 2 of the EFP S3 guideline — reinforced oral hygiene and risk factor control, then subgingival instru-
mentation of the residual pockets, targeted rather than full-mouth if only a few sites remain. Re-evaluate at
three months, aiming for plaque under 20% and bleeding under 10%. If she has not responded, step 3 and
consideration of referral to a periodontist rather than repeating the same non-surgical treatment indefinitely.”
Q
Why reduce the scope? Which teeth would you actually replace?
“Because four implants in a high-risk mouth quadruple both the biological risk and the maintenance burden for
a benefit she may not need. I would ask which spaces actually trouble her. The 15 and 25 are single premolar
units affecting appearance and are the strongest candidates. The 36 and 46 are molar spaces where a shortened
dental arch — premolar-to-premolar occlusion — is well evidenced as functionally adequate and would avoid
two implants altogether.”
Q
What are the alternatives at the 15 and 25?
“Nothing, if she is functioning and the space is not visible. A resin-bonded bridge, minimally destructive and
reversible, where the abutment teeth are sound and periodontally stable — though her attachment loss may
limit crown-to-root ratio. A conventional bridge, which I would be reluctant to prescribe on periodontally
compromised abutments. Or a removable partial denture, though plaque retention in this patient is a genuine
objection.”
Q
Classify this case on SAC.
“The surgery — single implants in healed premolar sites with adequate bone — would be Straightforward to
Advanced. But the patient risk profile raises it to Advanced: SAC explicitly recognises patient-level modifiers,
and active or unstable periodontitis plus heavy smoking are exactly that. If augmentation were needed at any
site, it becomes Complex in a smoker and I would refer.”
Q
What is beyond your competence here?
“Periodontal surgery or regenerative treatment of residual defects if she fails to respond. Bone augmentation
in a heavy smoker. Established peri-implantitis requiring surgical management. And any suggestion that
the whole dentition needs reorganising rather than four spaces restoring. I would refer for those, and I would
tell her at the outset which parts of the pathway I would not be doing myself.”
Q
If she refuses to stop smoking, would you place implants?
“Smoking is not an absolute contraindication, and refusing all treatment to every smoker is not a defensible
position. I would treat if she achieved periodontal stability, but I would reduce the scope, avoid augmentation
entirely, use maximally cleansable designs, insist on three-monthly maintenance, and consent her explicitly
and in writing that her failure risk is materially higher and that I have advised cessation. I would record that I
re-offered cessation support at every visit.”
Q
She says her friend smokes 20 a day and has had implants for ten years. Respond.
“ ‘That’s genuinely true for some people, and I’m glad it worked for her. Risk isn’t a certainty — it’s a change in
the odds. What I can’t do is tell you which group you’re in beforehand, and you have a second risk your friend
may not have, which is the gum disease. So I’d rather stack the odds in your favour than rely on you being
lucky.’ Honest, non-confrontational, and it keeps her engaged rather than defensive.”

Domain 3 — Decision making in relation to treatment procedures
Chain: getting her ready, then placing
Q
How would you actually deliver smoking cessation advice?
“Very brief advice at every visit — Ask, Advise, Act. Ask and record smoking status; advise that the best way
to stop is with a combination of behavioural support and pharmacotherapy; act by referring to the local stop-
smoking service, which roughly triples quit rates compared with willpower alone. I would mention nicotine
replacement therapy and note that prescribing beyond that is her GP’s or the service’s role, not mine.”
Q
How long before surgery would you want her to have stopped?
“Ideally permanently. The pragmatic protocol frequently cited is stopping at least one to two weeks before
surgery and for eight weeks afterwards, covering the critical early healing and osseointegration period. I
would frame it as an opportunity — implant treatment gives many patients a concrete reason to quit — rather
than as a condition I am imposing.”
Q
How will you decide she is ready to proceed?
“Objective criteria, agreed in advance and written down: plaque score consistently under 20%, full-mouth
bleeding under 10%, no residual pockets of 5 mm or more, no bleeding at any 4 mm site, and demonstrated
attendance at supportive care. Setting the numbers in advance stops the decision becoming an argument, and
it makes the target hers rather than mine.”
Q
What would you do differently at surgery because she is a smoker?
“Nothing exotic, but I would be meticulous about the soft tissue: flap design that guarantees tension-free
primary closure, careful handling, and no elective augmentation. Chlorhexidine rinse pre-operatively and
for the healing period, and clear instructions on abstaining around surgery. And I would favour a two-stage
approach if there were any doubt about soft tissue healing.”
Q
What implant and site factors would you choose for her?
“A site with adequate native bone so no grafting is needed. A standard-diameter implant with a well-
documented surface and a conical connection with platform switching, on the reasoning that it keeps the
microgap away from the crest. Placed at the correct three-dimensional position — not too deep, because deep
placement makes a future peri-implantitis defect far harder to manage in a patient likely to develop one.”
Q
How much keratinised mucosa do you want, and what if it is inadequate?
“At least 2 mm of keratinised mucosa, ideally with an adequate band of attached tissue. Where it is deficient,
plaque control is more painful, tissue recession and inflammation are more common, and this patient in partic-
ular cannot afford that. I would consider a free gingival graft or an apically repositioned flap at second stage
— soft tissue augmentation, unlike bone augmentation, remains reasonable in a smoker.”
Q
What loading protocol?
“Conventional loading, at around three months in the mandible and four in the maxilla, confirmed by clinical
stability. In a heavy smoker with a periodontitis history I would not use immediate or early loading — I gain
little and I remove my margin for error. I would explain that the wait is deliberate, not a delay.”
Q
What restoration design follows from her risk profile?
“Screw-retained, always, so I can retrieve and inspect and there is no risk of retained subgingival cement.
Shallow, cleansable emergence profiles that admit an interdental brush, with margins at or just below the
mucosal level, never deep. No unnecessary splinting. Contours that she can actually clean, even where that
costs some aesthetic ideal.”
Q
What would you record?

“Her diagnosis with stage, grade and extent, and the smoking history in pack-years. Serial plaque and bleed-
ing scores and a six-point pocket chart at each re-evaluation. Every cessation discussion and referral. The
consent conversation including the specific elevated risk figures. Implant details, batch numbers, torque, and a
baseline periapical at fitting against which all future radiographs are compared.”
Domain 4 — Interpretation and problem solving of clinical outcomes
Chain: peri-implant disease, recognised and treated
Q
Define peri-implant health, mucositis and peri-implantitis.
“Health — no erythema, swelling, bleeding on probing or suppuration, and no bone loss beyond initial crestal
remodelling. Mucositis — bleeding on gentle probing, with or without erythema and swelling, and no ad-
ditional bone loss; it is reversible and plaque-induced. Peri-implantitis — bleeding or suppuration, increased
probing depths compared with baseline, and radiographic bone loss beyond crestal remodelling.”
Q
How do you diagnose peri-implantitis without a baseline?
“By the threshold definition: bone levels 3 mm or more apical to the most coronal portion of the intra-osseous
part of the implant, together with bleeding or suppuration on probing and probing depths of 6 mm or more.
It is a fallback, not a substitute for having taken a baseline radiograph and pocket chart at the time of fitting —
which is precisely why I take one.”
Q
Three years on there is a 7 mm pocket with bleeding and 3 mm of bone loss at the 15. First steps?
“Confirm the diagnosis — probe six sites, check suppuration, take a parallel-technique periapical and compare
it with baseline. Check the implant is not mobile, that the restoration is not loose, and that there is no retained
cement or over-contoured emergence. Reinforce her plaque control, review her smoking status, and begin
non-surgical management: mechanical debridement with instruments that will not damage the surface, plus
antiseptic adjuncts.”
Q
The non-surgical phase fails. Now what?
“Then surgical access is indicated — open flap debridement with decontamination, with either resective and
implantoplasty management for a horizontal or one-walled defect, or reconstructive management with a graft
where the defect is contained and intra-bony. In a patient who is still smoking, the outcome of a reconstructive
approach is markedly poorer, so I would favour access and resection for cleansability. This is the point at which
I refer.”
Q
When would you remove the implant?
“When it is mobile, when bone loss exceeds roughly half to two-thirds of the implant length, when a defect is
unmanageable or the implant is malpositioned so that it cannot be cleaned, when the patient has already failed
surgical treatment, or when the patient does not want further intervention. Removing an implant early can be
the kinder decision — leaving a failing implant to destroy the adjacent site helps nobody.”
Q
What maintenance would you set, and why three-monthly?
“Three-monthly supportive care, at least initially. The rationale is that the periodontal literature shows the
reformation of a pathogenic subgingival biofilm within about three months, and her risk profile gives no margin.
Each visit: plaque and bleeding scores, six-point probing of implants and teeth with a light force, suppuration,
mucosal condition, restoration integrity, and reinforcement of cleaning around each implant with a single-tufted
brush and interdental brush.”
Q
How would you know the plan had worked?
“That she is stable rather than merely improved — bleeding under 10%, no pockets of 5 mm or more, stable bone
levels against baseline, healthy peri-implant tissues, and a maintenance pattern she keeps. If she has stopped
smoking, that is a bigger clinical gain than any implant I could place. And by her own measure: that she can
eat and smile without thinking about it, having had fewer implants than she originally asked for.”

WATCH OUT
Come back to the sequence: stabilise the disease, control the risk factor, reduce the scope, then treat. Say
which of those four steps the question belongs to. It buys a sentence of thinking time and it is nearly always the
right frame in a periodontally compromised patient.
Running this case to time
Time check. The flow above holds 37 questions and about 2,485 words of model answer. At 140 words a
minute plus roughly five seconds a question, that is close to twenty-one minutes — an overrun of about
six. What goes first is the implant and site selection material in Domain 3: connection design, platform
switching, keratinised mucosa and loading protocol compress into one question, because the marks here
sit in readiness criteria and cleansable design, not hardware. If your answers run past thirty seconds,
you will never reach Domain 4 — and Domain 4 is where she gets peri-implantitis.
The fifteen-minute run sheet
Clock
The examiner does
What earns the mark

charting in front of you
Nothing. Do not talk into this.

Lets you present, uninterrupted

reduce the scope, and the risk

Very brief advice at every visit — Ask,
Advise, Act — with referral to the

Then the part that earns Domain 3:

recognised and treated
The 2017 triad defined, then diagnosis

intra-osseous portion, with bleeding or
suppuration and 6 mm depths — named
as a fallback, which is why you took a
baseline. The 7 mm pocket at the 15

and a periapical against baseline,
exclude a loose restoration, retained
cement or over-contour, then
non-surgical therapy. When that fails,
surgical access — and in a continuing

Three-monthly supportive care, justified
by biofilm reformation at about three
months.

Clock
The examiner does
What earns the mark
14:30–15:00
Closes on the patient and the record
In her words: “Implants are possible for
you, but the conditions aren’t right today…
you’ve had gum disease, and the same disease
happens around implants, where it moves
faster and is harder to treat… smoking
roughly doubles the chance of an implant
failing. Let’s get your gums stable, help you
stop, then reassess — and start with fewer
than four.” And to the friend who smokes
20 a day: “risk isn’t a certainty, it’s a
change in the odds”, said without
confrontation. Recorded: stage, grade
and extent, pack-years, serial plaque and
bleeding scores, every cessation
discussion and referral, the

and a baseline periapical at fitting.
The spine — the twelve answers to have ready if nothing else
1 What Stage III Grade C means, and how each is determined · 2 The grade modifiers, and why her smoking
alone gives Grade C · 3 Stability defined, and why she does not meet it · 4 How a bleeding and plaque score
is actually recorded · 5 What smoking does to the periodontium · 6 Why her bleeding score understates
her disease · 7 The figures you would quote her, as ranges · 8 The four gates, in order · 9 Why you reduce
the scope, and the shortened arch at the 36 and 46 · 10 The written readiness criteria · 11 The restoration
design her risk profile dictates · 12 Peri-implantitis diagnosed without a baseline.
Where the marks are lost in this case
Calling 4 mm pockets a success. Stability is defined by inflammation, not depth — bleeding under 10%,
nothing 5 mm or more, no bleeding at any 4 mm site — and at 18% and 30% she meets none of it. Say
“in remission but not stable” and say that the whole plan follows from that distinction; a candidate who
reads “mostly 4 mm or less” as ready to place has lost Domain 1.
Missing that the bleeding score flatters her. Smoking causes vasoconstriction, so the tissues bleed less
than the underlying inflammation warrants — 18% in a smoker represents more disease than 18% in a
non-smoker. Volunteer that, and volunteer the corollary she must be warned about: her bleeding score
may rise when she quits, and that is not failure. Unprompted, that is the difference between a 3 and a 5.
Agreeing to four implants. She asked for four; the answer is fewer, and the argument is hers to hear —
four implants in a high-risk mouth quadruple both the biological risk and the maintenance burden, and
the 36 and 46 are answered by a shortened dental arch. Then name the competence line at the outset,
not after a failure: periodontal surgery or regeneration if she does not respond, bone augmentation in
a heavy smoker, and surgical management of peri-implantitis are all referred — and if she will not stop
smoking, treatment is conditional on stability, scoped down, ungrafted, and consented in writing that
her risk is materially higher.

soe.title: The edentulous maxilla and the fixed-prosthesis
soe.text:
SOE Case 16 — The edentulous maxilla and the fixed-prosthesis
request
THE CASE
66-year-old man, edentulous upper for 12 years, wearing a complete upper denture against natural lower teeth.
He wants “teeth that don’t come out”. Examination: moderate maxillary resorption, well-extended denture
with a full labial flange, high smile line, generous freeway space. CBCT shows adequate anterior bone but
pneumatised sinuses posteriorly with 3 mm of residual height.
Pace: one structured opening of about 60 seconds, then roughly 35 questions in the remaining 14 minutes. Nothing after the opening earns you
more than a few seconds of thought.
Opening — the 60-second presentation
Q
Present this case.
“A 66-year-old man, edentulous in the maxilla for 12 years, wearing a complete upper denture against a natural
lower dentition — a high-load and therefore high-risk combination — who is asking for a fixed prosthesis.
Three findings dominate. He has a high smile line, so any transition between prosthesis and mucosa will be
visible. He has a full labial flange after 12 years of resorption, so his lip support is very probably prosthesis-
dependent. And his posterior maxilla has 3 mm of residual bone height beneath pneumatised sinuses, so
posterior implants would require lateral window sinus elevation. My task is to establish whether a fixed pros-
thesis is achievable, whether it is within my scope, and whether it is actually the right answer for him.”
Domain 1 — Clinical interpretation and reasoning
Chain: the anatomical and biological groundwork
Q
Describe the maxillary sinus.
“A pyramidal air-filled cavity in the body of the maxilla, lined by the Schneiderian membrane — thin, ciliated,
pseudostratified columnar respiratory epithelium. Its base is the lateral nasal wall, its apex extends towards the
zygoma, and its floor is the alveolar process. It drains through the ostium in the middle meatus, positioned
high on the medial wall, so drainage is against gravity. Bony septa of Underwood may divide the floor.”
Q
What vessels matter during a lateral window approach?
“The posterior superior alveolar artery and its anastomosis with the infraorbital artery, which runs in the
lateral wall of the sinus, often within bone, at a variable height above the crest. Cutting it during a window
osteotomy produces brisk, obscuring bleeding. It can be identified on CBCT beforehand, which is one of the
arguments for cross-sectional imaging in these cases.”
Q
Why has his sinus pneumatised?
“Loss of the teeth removes the functional stimulus to the alveolar bone, so the ridge resorbs from above
while the sinus expands from below by osteoclastic activity on the sinus floor. Positive intra-sinus pressure on
expiration and the absence of loading both contribute. The result is exactly what the CBCT shows — a thin
residual floor with only 3 mm of bone.”
Q
How would you assess whether the sinus itself is healthy?
“History of sinusitis, allergy, nasal obstruction or previous nasal surgery, and smoking. Radiographically I
would look for mucosal thickening, complete opacification, polyps, retention cysts, and patency of the ostium,
plus septa and the position of the artery. A sinus that cannot drain is a contraindication to elevation until it is
managed — that is an ENT decision, not mine.”

Q
What is combination syndrome?
“Kelly’s description of the changes seen when a complete maxillary denture opposes a natural anterior
mandibular dentition with free-end saddles.
Five features:
resorption of the anterior maxillary ridge,
downgrowth of the maxillary tuberosities, papillary hyperplasia of the hard palate, over-eruption of the
lower anterior teeth, and loss of bone under the mandibular free-end saddles. Loss of occlusal vertical
dimension and an anteriorly displaced occlusal plane follow.”
Q
Why does the opposing natural dentition matter mechanically?
“Because a dentate mandible generates substantially greater and less evenly distributed bite forces than an
opposing complete denture — a complete denture wearer produces a fraction of the force a dentate patient does.
So the maxillary prosthesis is loaded harder, more anteriorly, and less predictably. That raises the mechanical
demand on any implant-borne restoration and makes occlusal design a central rather than a peripheral issue.”
Q
What is the bone quality likely to be, and how do you classify it?
“Lekholm and Zarb type III or IV, or D3 to D4 on Misch — a thin cortex around low-density trabecular bone.
The maxilla is characteristically less dense than the mandible, so primary stability is harder to achieve and
healing takes longer. That drives my surgical technique and my loading protocol rather than my decision to
treat.”
Q
Classify his residual ridge.
“On Cawood and Howell, moderate maxillary resorption with adequate anterior bone is around Class IV to
V — the anterior ridge losing width and then height. Naming it matters because it tells me the deficiency
is progressive and three-dimensional, and because in the maxilla resorption is upwards and inwards, which
moves the ridge palatally away from where the teeth need to sit.”
Q
What does that resorption pattern mean for his appearance?
“That the residual ridge lies well palatal and superior to the original tooth position, so the prosthetic teeth
must be set forward and downward of it. The labial flange fills that space — it restores the lost alveolus and
supports the upper lip, the nasolabial angle and the philtrum. Remove the flange and you remove the tissue
replacement, not just an edge of acrylic.”
Q
How do you assess the smile line and lip support?
“Smile line by asking him to smile broadly and speak — a high smile line displays the gingival margins and
the whole transition zone. Lip support by viewing him in profile and three-quarters with the denture in and
out, assessing philtrum length, vermilion display, nasolabial angle and the depth of the labiomental fold, and
by supporting the lip manually with and without the flange. I would photograph all of it.”
Q
What would you measure on the CBCT?
“Residual bone height beneath each sinus — here 3 mm — and the ridge width and height anteriorly at each
proposed site. The position of the incisive canal and the nasal floor. Any septa, the position of the posterior
superior alveolar artery, and the sinus membrane thickness. And I would relate all of it to a radiographic guide
reproducing the planned tooth position, so I am planning from the prosthesis backwards.”
Domain 2 — Clinical decision making and treatment planning
Chain: options, and the decision that actually matters
Q
What are the options?
“Remake the complete denture, with attention to extension, the posterior palatal seal, the neutral zone and
the vertical dimension — this must be offered and may well be adequate. An implant-retained maxillary
overdenture, typically four or more anterior implants with a bar or studs, which retains the labial flange and is
cleansable. A fixed full-arch implant prosthesis, which is what he is asking for. Or no treatment, with denture
adhesive and advice.”

Q
What would a fixed prosthesis actually require here?
“Enough implants with adequate anteroposterior spread — which with 3 mm of posterior bone means bilateral
lateral window sinus elevation, or tilted implants, or zygomatic implants. And a design that manages the
transition line between prosthesis and mucosa in a man with a high smile line, either by having enough bone
that no flange is needed or by using pink ceramic or acrylic that will be visible when he smiles.”
Q
What is the single most important thing to establish before he commits?
“Whether his appearance depends on the labial flange. With 12 years of resorption and a high smile line it
almost certainly does, and this is the classic cause of profound dissatisfaction after a fixed maxillary prosthe-
sis. Everything else — bone, implants, sinuses — is secondary to that finding, because it determines which
prosthesis type is correct.”
Q
How would you establish it?
“Duplicate his existing denture and remove the flange from the duplicate, or produce a diagnostic wax-up
without a flange, and try it in so he can see it himself in a mirror, with photographs taken from the front, in
profile and smiling. Let him make the judgement. If his lip support and transition line collapse without the
flange, then a fixed prosthesis without a flange will not satisfy him, and an implant-retained overdenture is
the correct answer — not a compromise.”
Q
Which do you recommend?
“A four-implant maxillary overdenture in the anterior maxilla, retaining the labial flange, with the palate
reduced if support permits. It gives him the security he is asking for, preserves the appearance he already has,
avoids two lateral window sinus lifts, remains cleansable in a man of 66 who will age with it, and is within my
scope where a fixed full-arch reconstruction is not.”
Q
Argue against your own recommendation.
“That he asked for teeth that do not come out and I am offering him something that does — that is a real failure
to meet the stated goal, and there is evidence that patients value fixed prostheses highly. A well-planned fixed
prosthesis with adequate bone gives excellent function and no daily removal. My defence is that I am not
refusing it, I am making him see the aesthetic consequence before he chooses, and offering referral if he still
wants it.”
Q
Classify the options on SAC.
“Remaking the complete denture — Straightforward. A four-implant anterior maxillary overdenture — Ad-
vanced, because of the aesthetic zone, the reduced bone density and the multiple-implant prosthodontics. A
fixed full-arch maxillary rehabilitation with bilateral sinus grafting — Complex in both the surgical and the
restorative dimension, and outside the scope of this level of practice.”
Q
So what is beyond your competence?
“Lateral window sinus elevation, particularly bilateral with only 3 mm of residual height. Tilted or zygomatic
implants. Full-arch fixed maxillary reconstruction. Any reorganisation of his lower occlusion at an altered ver-
tical dimension. I would refer for those, and I would make that clear before he becomes emotionally committed
to a plan I cannot deliver.”
Q
He insists on the fixed option. What do you do?
“Refer him — properly, not reluctantly. I would send the photographs, the flangeless try-in, the CBCT and my
assessment of his lip support, so that the specialist begins from the same evidence rather than repeating it. I
would make sure he understands the surgical burden, the cost, the healing time and the maintenance. Refusing
to refer because I disagree would be paternalistic; referring without the aesthetic evidence would be careless.”
Q
What if he cannot afford implants at all?
“Then a properly made conventional denture is a legitimate and often very successful treatment, and I would say
so without apology. Copy technique to preserve the polished surfaces he has adapted to, corrected extension

and posterior palatal seal, neutral zone recording, restored vertical dimension, and a review of his lower arch.
Many patients in his position are transformed by a well-made denture alone.”
Domain 3 — Decision making in relation to treatment procedures
Chain: delivering the overdenture
Q
Outline the sequence.
“Prosthetically driven from the start. Remake or copy the denture first to establish correct tooth position,
vertical dimension and lip support, and prove it clinically. Duplicate that denture as a radiographic and then
surgical guide. Plan on CBCT. Place four anterior implants. Allow conventional healing. Second stage if
needed, then pick up the attachments into the proven denture design.”
Q
How many implants, and where?
“Four, in the anterior maxilla between the sinuses and clear of the incisive canal — broadly the lateral incisor
and premolar regions — with the widest anteroposterior spread the bone allows. Two unsplinted implants
in the maxilla are not comparable to two in the mandible: the bone is softer, the denture-bearing area behaves
differently, and outcomes are poorer. Four, and I would consider splinting them.”
Q
Why avoid the incisive canal?
“Because it contains fibrous tissue and the nasopalatine neurovascular bundle, and an implant engaging it
will not osseointegrate — it will be surrounded by soft tissue. It also enlarges with age and resorption, so it can
occupy much of the midline. Where it obstructs an ideal position, the answer is to reposition the implant, not
to drill through it.”
Q
Bar or studs — how do you decide?
“By available restorative space, implant divergence and his ability to clean. Studs need about 8 to 10 mm from
platform to occlusal plane, are independent, cheap and easy to clean, and tolerate divergence up to roughly 20
degrees. A bar needs 12 to 15 mm, splints the implants, shares load, and creates a common path of insertion
despite divergence — but it is bulkier and harder to clean. In a maxilla with four implants I lean towards a bar
for load sharing.”
Q
How do you measure the available restorative space?
“On the articulated diagnostic set-up at the correct vertical dimension, measuring from the planned implant
platform level to the occlusal or incisal plane of the wax-up. Not by eye in the mouth. He has a generous freeway
space, which suggests his vertical dimension may be under-restored — restoring it correctly will change the
space available, which is another reason the denture must be made first.”
Q
What surgical modifications for D3 to D4 bone?
“An undersized osteotomy to improve primary stability, use of osteotomes or bone condensers rather than
full drilling to compact rather than remove trabecular bone, avoiding countersinking, and engaging the cortical
plates — nasal floor or palatal cortex — where possible. Slow speed and irrigation still apply, though overheating
is less of a risk than in dense mandibular bone.”
Q
What loading protocol, and why?
“Conventional loading at four to six months in this bone quality, confirmed clinically and, if available, by
resonance frequency analysis. I would not use early or immediate loading here — the bone is soft, the opposing
dentition is natural, and I have no need to take that risk. His existing denture is relieved generously and relined
with a tissue conditioner during healing.”
Q
Can you remove the palate?
“Only if the implants provide enough support and retention to replace what the palate was contributing, which
with four splinted implants is usually achievable. I would reduce rather than eliminate it initially, keeping

a horseshoe with adequate rigidity, and reinforce the base with a cast metal framework — an unreinforced
horseshoe denture in a man opposing natural teeth will flex and fracture across the midline.”
Q
Does his lower arch need any treatment?
“Very possibly. I would assess for over-eruption of the lower anteriors, an unlevel occlusal plane, posterior
tooth loss and the periodontal condition — the combination syndrome picture. If the lower occlusal plane is
disordered, restoring the maxilla against it simply repeats the original problem. Minor equilibration or restoring
lower posterior support may be needed first, and a major reorganisation would be a referral.”
Q
What would you record and consent for?
“The photographs and the flangeless try-in and his own reaction to it — that record is what protects both of us.
The options offered including no treatment, and the reasons for the recommendation. The CBCT report and its
justification under IR(ME)R. Implant details, batch, torque and a baseline periapical or panoramic at fitting.
And explicit consent to the lifelong maintenance and its cost.”
Domain 4 — Interpretation and problem solving of clinical outcomes
Chain: maintenance, complications and judging success
Q
What do you tell him, in his own words?
“ ‘I understand you want teeth that stay in. Before we decide, let me show you something.’ Then the flangeless
try-in. Then: ‘What holds your lip out at the moment is this part of the denture. A fixed bridge cannot have that
part, so your lip would sit differently and you would see a join where the bridge meets your gum when you
smile — and you have quite a high smile line. There is an option that is very secure and keeps your appearance:
implants the denture clips onto firmly. It comes out for cleaning but does not move when you eat or talk. The
fully fixed option would also need major bone grafting in both sinuses, which is a much bigger operation and
one I would refer you for.’ ”
Q
What complications should he expect, and how often?
“Mechanical maintenance is frequent and biological failure is uncommon. Replacement of worn attachment
inserts or matrices, typically annually. Relining as the posterior ridge continues to resorb. Denture base or
framework fracture, particularly if the palate has been reduced. Attachment or screw loosening. Wear of
the acrylic teeth with loss of vertical dimension. Then the biological ones — mucositis, hyperplasia around
abutments and peri-implantitis — which are less frequent but need the same monitoring.”
Q
One implant fails to integrate at second stage. What now?
“Explain it honestly and without defensiveness — a proportion of implants do not integrate and it is not a
disaster. Remove it, debride, and allow the site to heal. Then decide whether three implants can carry the
design, which with a bar and good spread they often can, or whether to replace it after two to three months,
possibly with a wider implant or in a slightly different position. I would review why it failed before repeating
the same thing.”
Q
At 18 months the denture is loose and rocks. Differential?
“Continued posterior ridge resorption so the denture is no longer tissue-supported — the commonest cause,
and the answer is a reline, not new inserts. Then worn inserts; a fractured base or housing; a loose abutment
or bar screw; loss of an implant; peri-implant disease; or an occlusal error. I would examine each in turn with
pressure-indicating paste, individual implant testing, and radiographs if indicated.”
Q
He develops papillary hyperplasia of the palate. Manage it.
“Recognise it as denture-induced hyperplasia with a likely candidal component. Leave the denture out as
much as tolerated, especially at night; scrupulous denture and palatal hygiene; disinfect the denture; correct
the fit surface with a tissue conditioner and correct the occlusion, because the cause is usually chronic trauma
from an ill-fitting or over-loaded base. Antifungal therapy if candida is confirmed. Surgical reduction and
biopsy only if it does not resolve — and any non-resolving lesion is referred.”

Q
What would you monitor, and how often?
“Three- to six-monthly initially. Peri-implant probing at six sites with a light force, bleeding and suppuration,
plaque control around the abutments or under the bar, mucosal health of the whole denture-bearing area,
denture fit, extension, occlusion and vertical dimension, and attachment retention. Radiographs at one year
and then as clinically indicated, always compared with the baseline taken at fitting.”
Q
How would you know this had succeeded?
“By his measure first — that he eats, speaks and smiles without thinking about the prosthesis and no longer feels
it move. Objectively: stable implants with no bleeding or suppuration, bone levels stable against baseline,
a retentive comfortable denture, healthy palatal mucosa, an intact lower dentition, and a maintenance pattern
he attends and can afford. And that he is content with an outcome different from the one he first asked for —
which is the real test of the consent conversation.”
WATCH OUT
Come back to the flange: ask whether his appearance depends on it. Almost every decision in this case — fixed
against removable, referral against treating, what you say to him — follows from that single finding, and stating
it buys you a sentence of thinking time.
Running this case to time
Time check. The flow above holds 39 questions and about 2,698 words of model answer. At 140 words a
minute plus roughly five seconds a question, that comes to about twenty-two and a half minutes — an
overrun of seven and a half. What goes first is the sinus anatomy sub-chain in Domain 1: the description,
the posterior superior alveolar artery and the assessment of sinus health compress into one question,
because the plan you will recommend avoids the sinus altogether. Combination syndrome, Cawood
and Howell and the flange stay. If your answers run past thirty seconds, you will never reach Domain 4.
