implants. And if he still insists, the answer is to refer properly — sending the photographs, the flangeless
try-in, the CBCT and your lip-support assessment — not to refuse, and not to hand him on with nothing.

soe.title: Two adjacent missing central incisors
soe.text:
SOE Case 17 — Two adjacent missing central incisors
THE CASE
40-year-old woman, missing 11 and 21 following trauma 6 months ago. Medium smile line, medium pheno-
type. CBCT shows a ridge width of 5 mm and a vertical deficiency of 3 mm relative to the adjacent CEJs. She
wants implants.
Pace: one structured opening of about 60 seconds, then roughly 35 questions in the remaining 14 minutes. Nothing after the opening earns you
more than a few seconds of thought.
Opening — the 60-second presentation
Q
Present this case.
“A healthy 40-year-old woman who lost both upper central incisors to trauma six months ago and would like im-
plants. The findings that matter are a medium smile line, a medium phenotype, a ridge that is 5 mm wide and,
critically, 3 mm vertically deficient against the adjacent cemento-enamel junctions. So this is a two-adjacent-
tooth aesthetic case with a combined horizontal and vertical defect — the most demanding situation short
of a whole anterior segment. The central biological problem is that two adjacent implants cannot support an
inter-implant papilla predictably, because the inter-implant bone crest sits lower than an inter-dental crest. A
black triangle between two implant crowns is the expected outcome, not the exception. What I need to establish
is exactly what she wants to see, what she will accept prosthetically, and whether an implant is the right vehicle
at all.”
Domain 1 — Clinical interpretation and reasoning
Chain: the anatomical and biological groundwork
Q
Describe the anatomy of the anterior maxilla relevant to implant placement here.
“The labial plate, which in the anterior maxilla is thin — under 1 mm in the great majority of central incisor sites
and often under 0.5 mm. Behind it the incisive canal at the midline, carrying the nasopalatine bundle, which
sits directly palatal to the central incisor roots and enlarges with resorption. Superiorly the nasal floor and the
anterior nasal spine. Laterally the canine eminence and the roots of the 12 and 22. And the labial concavity
above the root apices, which dictates implant angulation.”
Q
Why does the thinness of the labial plate matter so much?
“Because that plate is largely bundle bone — bone whose blood supply depends on the periodontal ligament.
When the tooth is lost the bundle bone resorbs. Araújo and Lindhe showed the buccal wall loses height pref-
erentially, and Schropp showed roughly a 50% loss of ridge width in the first year, two-thirds of it in the first
three months. That is exactly what has produced her present ridge form six months on.”
Q
Describe the dentogingival junction around a natural tooth.
“From the crest upwards: connective tissue attachment of about 1 mm, in which the fibres insert perpendicu-
larly into cementum; junctional epithelium of about 1 mm; then the gingival sulcus. Together the attachment
components form the supracrestal attachment — what used to be called biologic width — of roughly 2 mm,
and the body defends that dimension. Above that sits the free gingival margin and the papilla.”
Q
How does the peri-implant soft tissue differ?
“There is no cementum and no periodontal ligament, so the collagen fibres run parallel and circular around
the abutment rather than inserting into it. The attachment is longer — commonly around 3 to 4 mm in total —
and the blood supply is poorer, coming only from the supraperiosteal vessels rather than also from the PDL.
The result is a seal that is weaker, less well vascularised and less resistant to inflammatory breakdown.”

Q
What are the practical consequences of that for this patient?
“First, the tissue is more prone to recession, especially with a thin phenotype and a buccally placed implant.
Second, the peri-implant tissue takes its vertical position from the bone crest, so if the crest is 3 mm low, the
soft tissue margin will be low too. Third, an inflammatory lesion spreads faster and further apically around an
implant than around a tooth.”
Q
What determines whether a papilla is present?
“The distance from the contact point to the bone crest. Tarnow showed that between two teeth a papilla fills the
space essentially always at 5 mm, about 56% at 6 mm and about 27% at 7 mm. Between an implant and a tooth
the papilla takes its support from the tooth’s attachment level, so the figure is roughly 4.5 to 5 mm. Between
two implants the soft tissue height above the crest is only about 3.5 mm, which is why this case is diﬀicult.”
Q
Why is the inter-implant crest lower?
“Because each implant generates its own circumferential remodelling. Tarnow showed that where the inter-
implant distance is under 3 mm the lateral crestal loss is around 1 mm, against about 0.45 mm at 3 mm or more.
Two adjacent implants therefore produce overlapping saucers of bone loss, the crest between them drops, and
the soft tissue drops with it.”
Chain: reading this patient’s ridge
Q
Is a 5 mm ridge width adequate?
“Marginally, and not for two implants side by side. I want at least 1 mm of bone circumferentially, and in the
aesthetic zone I want 1.5 to 2 mm on the buccal to resist recession. A 4 mm implant in a 5 mm ridge leaves half
a millimetre buccally. So even for a single implant I would plan contour augmentation; for two, the width is
the lesser of my problems.”
Q
And the 3 mm vertical deficiency — what does that actually mean for the result?
“It means the soft tissue zenith of any implant crown will sit roughly 3 mm apical to where her natural centrals
sat, so the crowns will be long, and the papillae will start from a lower base. I cannot restore that with pros-
thetics alone without pink material. Vertical ridge augmentation is the least predictable of all augmentation
procedures and carries the highest morbidity and exposure rate.”
Q
How would you formalise the aesthetic risk?
“With the ITI Aesthetic Risk Assessment. In her favour: healthy, non-smoker, medium rather than high smile
line, medium rather than thin phenotype. Against her: an extended edentulous span of two adjacent teeth, a
combined horizontal and vertical soft and hard tissue defect, and a triangular tooth form if that is what she has.
That places her firmly in the high aesthetic risk group.”
Q
What else would you want to know before planning?
“Her smile line at full smile and in speech; tooth form — triangular teeth give longer contacts and more visible
black triangles; the interproximal bone levels on the 12 and 22, because those determine the outer papillae
and I cannot recreate them; sensibility and any resorption of the adjacent traumatised teeth; occlusion and any
parafunction; her expectations in her own words; and standardised photographs plus a diagnostic wax-up.”
Domain 2 — Clinical decision making and treatment planning
Chain: the options and the argument between them
Q
What are her options?
“Two implants, two crowns — the option she has come asking for, and the one most likely to produce a visible
black triangle between them.
One implant with a cantilever pontic — an implant at the 11 with a cantilevered 21, or the reverse.
A two-pontic resin-bonded bridge from the 12 and 22, with soft tissue augmentation under ovate pontics.
A conventional fixed bridge — I would not prepare two sound teeth for it.

A removable partial denture with a labial flange — the only option that reliably replaces lost hard and soft
tissue volume.
Implants plus pink ceramic, accepting prosthetic replacement of the missing tissue.
No treatment, with the site kept under review.”
Q
Why would a single implant with a cantilever pontic give a better papilla than two implants?
“Because a papilla between an implant crown and a pontic is supported by the ridge tissue under the pontic and
by the implant on one side only — it behaves far more predictably than a papilla between two implant platforms
with their overlapping remodelling. You trade a diﬀicult biological problem for a manageable mechanical one,
which is a cantilever in the anterior region.”
Q
What are the mechanical risks of that cantilever?
“Screw loosening first, then abutment or screw fracture, then ceramic chipping. I would mitigate them by
keeping the pontic narrow and out of excursive contact, screw-retaining where possible so it is retrievable,
torquing to the manufacturer’s specification, and checking the occlusion so that the cantilever carries no lateral
guidance. In a bruxist I would not do it.”
Q
Make the case for the resin-bonded bridge.
“It replaces two teeth with no surgery to the ridge, no implant risk and no biological compromise of the
adjacent teeth beyond minimal enamel preparation. With soft tissue augmentation under ovate pontics the
emergence can look excellent, and a pontic papilla is more predictable than an inter-implant papilla. In a 40-
year-old with intact, unrestored 12 and 22 it is a genuinely strong choice, and it is reversible in a way an implant
is not.”
Q
And the case against it?
“Debonding is the main issue — it is the commonest complication, though a single retainer per pontic and a
cobalt-chromium framework improve on older designs. It is also technique-sensitive for moisture control, the
metal can shine through thin incisal edges, and a two-pontic span is a bigger biomechanical ask than a single
cantilever.”
Q
So which do you recommend?
“Given the 3 mm vertical deficiency and a medium smile line, I would be very cautious about two implants.
My preference is either a single implant with a cantilever pontic, combined with contour augmentation and a
connective tissue graft, or a resin-bonded bridge with soft tissue augmentation under ovate pontics. I would
present both, with a mock-up, and let her decide with her eyes rather than on my description.”
Q
She insists on two implants. What do you say?
“That I will not refuse her, but that she must choose it knowing the outcome. I would say: ‘I can put two implants
in and I can make you two very good-looking teeth. What I cannot promise you is the little triangle of gum
between them. On the evidence, that space is likely to be dark, and if it is, we would fill it with pink ceramic
rather than your own gum.’ Then I would show her that on a mock-up before she commits, and record that I
did.”
Q
What is the SAC classification?
“Complex surgically — an extended edentulous span in the aesthetic zone with a combined horizontal and ver-
tical defect. Complex prosthodontically — two adjacent units in the aesthetic zone with a soft tissue deficiency.
There is no reading of this case that makes it Straightforward.”
Q
What is within your competence and what is not?
“Within: the full assessment, the risk assessment, the wax-up and mock-up, the options conversation, an interim
resin-bonded or removable prosthesis, and long-term maintenance. Beyond me: vertical ridge augmentation
and the two-implant aesthetic reconstruction. I would complete the assessment and the consent conversation
myself and refer for the definitive surgical and prosthetic treatment, staying involved as the referring clini-
cian.”

Domain 3 — Decision making in relation to treatment procedures
Chain: how you would actually deliver it
Q
Where does the planning start?
“From the teeth backwards. A diagnostic wax-up of the two centrals in the position her lip and smile need,
converted to an intra-oral mock-up, then a CBCT with a radiographic guide so I can see the planned tooth
position against the available bone. Only then do I know how much bone is missing and in which direction —
which is a different question from how much bone is there.”
Q
Where would you place a single implant, in three dimensions?
“Mesiodistally, at least 1.5 mm from the adjacent root and centred in the tooth position. Buccopalatally, with
the platform about 1.5 to 2 mm palatal to the line joining the adjacent CEJs, leaving 2 mm of buccal bone for
contour grafting. Apicocoronally, about 3 mm apical to the planned gingival margin of the future crown —
not to the existing bone crest, which is 3 mm low. The comfort zone concept: shallow and buccal is the position
that produces recession.”
Q
How would you augment the buccal contour?
“Simultaneous guided bone regeneration at placement, provided the implant is fully within bone and stable:
a slowly resorbing xenograft over the buccal surface to over-contour it, covered with a resorbable collagen
membrane, with tension-free closure achieved by periosteal release. I would combine that with a subepithelial
connective tissue graft from the palate to thicken the phenotype, which is the single most reliable thing I can
do to protect the mid-facial margin.”
Q
Why a connective tissue graft rather than more bone?
“Because soft tissue thickness predicts mid-facial stability better than an extra millimetre of graft particulate
does. Converting a medium phenotype to a thick one reduces recession, masks any grey show-through from
the abutment, and gives the papillae more tissue to work with. It is a lower-risk procedure than vertical aug-
mentation with a much better evidence base.”
Q
How would you manage the site while it heals?
“With a prosthesis that does not load the graft. A resin-bonded temporary bridge with ovate pontics relieved
off the ridge is my first choice, or an Essix retainer with the ridge fully relieved. I would specifically avoid a
removable acrylic denture pressing on a fresh graft — that is a common cause of membrane exposure and graft
loss.”
Q
How would you develop the emergence profile before the definitive crown?
“With a screw-retained provisional crown worn for at least two to three months. I would shape it progressively
— starting concave subgingivally to allow tissue in, then adding flowable composite to push the tissue into
the desired zenith and papilla form. When she and I are both happy with the soft tissue, I capture it with a
customised impression coping so the laboratory reproduces exactly that emergence.”
Q
What abutment and crown material?
“In the aesthetic zone with a medium phenotype, a zirconia abutment or a titanium base with a zirconia super-
structure rather than a plain titanium abutment, to avoid grey show-through. A screw-retained crown where
the access channel allows, because it is retrievable and avoids subgingival cement. If it must be cemented, I
would use a customised abutment with the margin no more than 1 mm subgingivally and clean meticulously.”
Q
Why is subgingival cement such a concern?
“Because residual cement is a well-recognised cause of peri-implant mucositis and peri-implantitis, and it is
very diﬀicult to detect radiographically or to remove once it is deep. The deeper the margin, the more cement
is left. That is the argument for screw retention wherever the trajectory permits.”

Q
What would you record?
“The options discussed and declined, in her own words where possible; the specific risks named — black
triangle, long crowns, recession, grey show-through, graft exposure and failure; that a mock-up was shown,
photographed and approved; the ITI Aesthetic Risk Assessment; the CBCT justification and report under
IR(ME)R; implant details, lot numbers, torque values and graft materials; and the timescale and cost given.
A signed form is not consent — the note of the discussion is.”
Domain 4 — Interpretation and problem solving of clinical outcomes
Chain: outcomes, disappointment and its management
Q
What would you tell her to expect, in your own words to her?
“‘The teeth themselves we can make look excellent. The diﬀiculty is the gum between them — you have lost
about three millimetres of bone there and I cannot reliably grow that back. We should plan on the basis
that some of what looks like gum will be pink porcelain. If grafting is involved this will take nine to twelve
months. There is a real chance a graft becomes exposed and has to be redone. And the mock-up we make
is the honest preview — I would far rather you turned it down at that stage than were disappointed at the
end.’”
Q
How would you measure the result objectively?
“Standardised photographs against baseline; the Pink and White Aesthetic Score; the papilla index; the mid-
facial margin level compared with the 12 and 22; peri-implant probing depths, bleeding and suppuration;
radiographic bone levels against the baseline taken at fitting; and, most importantly, her own rating against
what she said she wanted at the start.”
Q
At one year the mid-facial margin on the 11 has receded 1 mm. Why?
“Most likely a thin buccal plate or a buccally positioned implant, with or without a phenotype that was never
thick enough. Contributing factors are an over-contoured crown, a deep cement margin causing chronic inflam-
mation, and traumatic brushing. I would examine for inflammation first, because inflammatory recession may
partly resolve once it is controlled.”
Q
And how would you manage it?
“Control the inflammation, correct an over-contoured or cement-retentive restoration, and reinforce hygiene. If
the margin is still unacceptable and the implant is otherwise healthy, a connective tissue graft with or without
a coronally advanced flap can improve it, though it is less predictable than around a tooth. If the implant
is fundamentally malpositioned, no soft tissue procedure will correct it and the honest answer is prosthetic
camouflage with pink ceramic, or explantation.”
Q
What is the commonest long-term disappointment in this specific case?
“A black triangle between the two units, and crowns that are longer than her natural centrals were. Both are
predictable from the outset, which is precisely why they belong in the consent conversation and the mock-up
rather than in the complaint letter.”
Q
How would you prevent that disappointment?
“By agreeing the endpoint before the drill: wax-up, mock-up, photographs, and an explicit agreement about
whether pink ceramic is acceptable to her. Then by choosing the design that biology supports — a single implant
with a cantilever, or a resin-bonded bridge — rather than the one she first asked for. Prevention here is almost
entirely a communication and planning task.”
Q
How would you know the treatment had succeeded?
“That she smiles without covering her mouth and does not think about the teeth. Objectively: stable implants
with no bleeding or suppuration, bone levels stable against baseline, an acceptable Pink and White Aesthetic
Score, and a maintenance regime she attends and can manage at home.”

WATCH OUT
Come back to the papilla: state the contact-point-to-crest distance and whether the supporting attachment
belongs to a tooth, an implant or a pontic. That single frame explains almost every aesthetic decision in this
case and buys you a sentence of thinking time.
Running this case to time
Time check. The flow above holds 37 questions and about 2,545 words of model answer. At 140 words a
minute plus roughly five seconds a question, that comes to about twenty-one minutes — an overrun of
six. What goes first is the provisionalisation and abutment-material sub-chain in Domain 3: emergence
shaping, the customised impression coping, zirconia versus titanium and the cement argument compress
into one question, because the definitive work here is referred and the marks sit in position, graft choice
and the papilla. If your answers run past thirty seconds, you will never reach Domain 4 — which in this
case is the disappointment, and the whole point.
The fifteen-minute run sheet

What the 3 mm vertical deficiency actually costs her · 8 The ITI aesthetic risk assessment on her · 9 Why one
implant and a cantilever beats two implants · 10 The resin-bonded bridge argued both ways · 11 Implant

two implants.
Where the marks are lost in this case
Planning two implants because she asked for two teeth. The inter-implant crest remodels from both
sides, the soft tissue above it is only about 3.5 mm, and the black triangle follows. Volunteer that in the
opening presentation — not when the examiner produces it in Domain 4 — and then offer the design
biology supports: one implant with a cantilever pontic, or a resin-bonded bridge with ovate pontics.
Measuring the implant depth from the bone you can see. Her crest is 3 mm low, so an implant placed 3
mm below it is 6 mm below where the margin needs to be. The position is planned from the wax-up —
3 mm apical to the planned gingival margin — which is exactly why the sequence runs mock-up, then
CBCT with a guide, then surgery. Candidates who plan from the CBCT alone build the deficiency into
the result.
Never saying where you stop. Assessment, wax-up and mock-up, the options conversation, an interim
bonded or removable prosthesis and long-term maintenance are yours. Vertical ridge augmentation and
the two-implant aesthetic reconstruction are not — they are referred, with the consent conversation
completed first and you staying involved as the referring clinician. And if she insists on two implants
the answer is not refusal: it is “I can make you two very good-looking teeth; what I cannot promise you
is the triangle of gum between them”, shown on a mock-up, and recorded.

soe.title: The adolescent with missing lateral incisors
soe.text:
SOE Case 18 — The adolescent with missing lateral incisors
THE CASE
15-year-old girl with congenitally absent 12 and 22. Orthodontic treatment has just been completed, creating
spaces of 6.5 mm at each site. Her mother is pressing for implants “before she starts college”.
Pace: one structured opening of about 60 seconds, then roughly 35 questions in the remaining 14 minutes. Nothing after the opening earns you
more than a few seconds of thought.
Opening — the 60-second presentation
Q
Present this case.
“A 15-year-old girl with hypodontia of both maxillary lateral incisors, orthodontically created 6.5 mm spaces,
and family pressure for a rapid definitive solution. The overriding issue is skeletal and dento-alveolar growth.
An implant behaves as an ankylosed tooth: it does not move with the developing alveolus, so it becomes progres-
sively infra-occluded, which in the anterior maxilla is a conspicuous and effectively irreversible aesthetic failure.
Craniofacial growth continues into the late teens in girls and later in boys, and continues at a low level into
adulthood. So my position is that implants are the right long-term plan but the wrong treatment today. What
I need to establish is whether growth has ceased, whether space opening was the right orthodontic decision at
all, what interim prosthesis she will accept, and how to manage her mother’s expectations.”
Domain 1 — Clinical interpretation and reasoning
Chain: the developmental groundwork
Q
Define hypodontia and tell me how common it is.
“Hypodontia is the developmental absence of one to six teeth excluding third molars; oligodontia is six or more;
anodontia is complete absence. Excluding third molars, hypodontia affects roughly 5 to 6% of the population,
and it is somewhat commoner in females. Third molars are absent in a further quarter or so.”
Q
Which teeth are most commonly absent, and what else would you look for?
“Most commonly the mandibular second premolars, then the maxillary lateral incisors, then the maxillary
second premolars. Associated findings are microdontia and peg-shaped laterals — often on the contralateral
side to an absent one — delayed eruption and delayed dental development, retained deciduous teeth, tau-
rodontism, and ectopic or palatally displaced canines. I would also ask about a family history and about hair,
nails and sweating, because oligodontia can signal ectodermal dysplasia.”
Q
Why does hypodontia matter for the bone at these sites?
“Because alveolar bone develops in response to the tooth germ and the erupting tooth. Where a tooth has
never formed, the alveolar process never fully develops, so the ridge is characteristically narrow buccopalatally
and sometimes deficient vertically. That is quite different from an extraction site, which had normal alveolus
and then resorbed. It means I should expect to need augmentation, and it is one reason orthodontic space
opening can leave a knife-edge ridge.”
Q
How does the anterior maxilla grow?
“By sutural growth at the circummaxillary sutures displacing the maxilla downwards and forwards, by surface
remodelling — with resorption on the anterior surface of the premaxilla and deposition posteriorly — and by
alveolar growth with dental eruption, which continues as long as the teeth continue to erupt. It is that last
component, vertical alveolar development with continuous eruption, that keeps changing after skeletal growth
has largely finished.”

Q
So why does an implant behave like an ankylosed tooth?
“Because it is osseointegrated with no periodontal ligament. A natural tooth erupts and drifts with the alveolus
throughout life because the PDL remodels the socket. An implant is locked to the bone it was placed in, so as
the adjacent teeth continue to erupt and the alveolus grows, the implant crown is left behind — infra-occlusion,
with the margin exposed, the incisal edge short, and the crown appearing to sink.”
Q
When does growth actually stop?
“Skeletal growth is essentially complete around 17 or 18 in girls and 20 or 21 in boys, roughly two years
after peak height velocity, which in girls is usually a year or so after menarche. But vertical alveolar change
continues at a low level into the third and fourth decades, particularly in patients with a long face pattern
or continued eruption, so I cannot promise her that infra-occlusion will never occur — only that the risk falls
sharply once growth is complete.”
Chain: assessing this patient
Q
How would you determine whether growth has ceased?
“Not by chronological age alone. Most practically, a period of clinical observation with serial study casts
and standardised photographs showing stable facial height and a stable dentition, alongside the history of
menarche and when she last grew in height or shoe size. Serial cephalometric radiographs 6 to 12 months
apart showing superimposable growth are the classical method, but I would have to justify that exposure.
Hand-wrist radiographs or cervical vertebral maturation on an existing cephalogram are the alternatives.”
Q
What would you assess clinically at the two sites?
“Space at the crest and at the incisal level — they are often different — and the mesiodistal width in relation
to the contralateral tooth and the golden proportion. Ridge width and contour by palpation, the height and
thickness of keratinised tissue, the papilla height and bone level on the adjacent teeth, the smile line and lip
dynamics, and the root angulation of the 11, 13, 21 and 23 — orthodontists frequently leave adequate crown
space but converging roots.”
Q
What imaging would you take today?
“Today, none beyond what orthodontics has already produced. A periapical or the existing panoramic tells
me about root angulation and space. A CBCT is not justified now because it would not change management
for several years and she is 15 — IR(ME)R justification and ALARP apply with particular force in a growing
child. I would take the CBCT when she is ready for surgical planning.”
Q
Classify this case on SAC.
“Complex. Anterior maxilla, high aesthetic risk, a growing patient, an expected horizontal ridge deficiency at a
site where the alveolus never developed, narrow-diameter implants and thin adjacent roots. Under ITI, a single
anterior implant in an aesthetic zone is at best Advanced; adding growth and a probable augmentation makes
it Complex, and outside what I would undertake alone.”
Domain 2 — Clinical decision making and treatment planning
Chain: revisiting the orthodontic decision
Q
Was space opening the right decision?
“It may not have been, and I would want that re-opened with the orthodontist before anything is committed.
Canine substitution — closing the space, bringing the canines into the lateral position, reshaping and recon-
touring them, and building up the first premolars as canines — avoids a prosthesis altogether and gives a result
that grows with her. In a 15-year-old, that is a real advantage.”
Q
When does canine substitution work best?
“When the canine is narrow, pale and not markedly bulbous, when the patient is Class II or Class I with crowd-
ing so space closure helps the occlusion, when the smile line is not high so a slightly gingivally-positioned

canine margin is hidden, and where the first premolar is of reasonable shape and colour to serve as a canine. It
works less well in a Class III patient, where the space is needed, or where the canine is dark and heavily built.”
Q
You have argued for canine substitution — argue against it.
“It converts a group-function or canine-guided occlusion into premolar guidance, which some regard as less
protective. It requires irreversible enamel reduction and composite or veneer work on four teeth, which is
lifelong maintenance in a 15-year-old. The gingival margins can be uneven, and if it fails aesthetically it is very
hard to undo. Space opening preserves the option of an ideal-looking lateral incisor later.”
Q
Your orthodontic colleague says the spaces are already open, so just prosthetically restore them. Why might she
be right?
“Because re-treating orthodontically means another 18 months in appliances for a 15-year-old who has just
finished, with the burden of demineralisation and root resorption risk that carries. Space opening also gives a
restoration in the correct anatomical position rather than a reshaped canine, and it keeps the definitive plan
simple. If she is happy with the spaces and the occlusion is good, re-opening the debate may cause more harm
than good.”
Chain: the interim prosthesis
Q
What do you offer her in the meantime?
“An interim prosthesis that is aesthetic, reversible and adjustable. A resin-bonded cantilever bridge from each
canine — excellent aesthetics, minimal or no preparation, adjustable, and it maintains the space; my preferred
option. The orthodontic retainer with prosthetic teeth added — practical, and she needs a retainer anyway. A
removable acrylic partial denture — simple and cheap but less well accepted socially. Composite build-ups
or a composite-and-fibre splint — quick, cheap and easily repaired.”
Q
Why a cantilever rather than a fixed-fixed resin-bonded bridge?
“Because a fixed-fixed design fails by debonding at one retainer, which then goes undetected and caries devel-
ops beneath it. A single-retainer cantilever either stays on or comes off cleanly, and the evidence for cantilever
resin-bonded bridges in the anterior maxilla is good — survival in the region of 80 to 90% at five years. It also
avoids the problem that the abutments have different mobilities and paths of insertion.”
Q
Which abutment would you choose, and how would you prepare it?
“The canine, because it has the largest bonding area and the best enamel. Preparation is minimal and con-
fined to enamel: a supragingival chamfer or none at all, a defined path of insertion, cingulum rest seats for
support, and adequate wrap-around for resistance form. A cobalt-chromium or nickel-chromium framework,
sandblasted and cemented with a 10-MDP-containing resin cement under rubber dam or good isolation.”
Q
How does the interim prosthesis interact with retention?
“It must not compromise it. Space maintenance is the priority — if the space closes even a millimetre, the
implant plan is lost. So the retainer regime continues, and either the pontic is incorporated into the retainer or
the resin-bonded bridge itself acts as a fixed retainer for those teeth, with a bonded retainer elsewhere as the
orthodontist prescribes. I would agree the plan with the orthodontist in writing rather than assume.”
Chain: communication and consent
Q
What do you say to the mother, in your own words?
“ ‘If we put an implant in now, it will stay exactly where we put it while the rest of her face and jaw keep growing.
In a few years that tooth would look short and high compared with the ones next to it, and the only way to fix it
would be to take it out and start again. What I would like to do is give her something that looks good now and
can be adjusted as she grows, and place the implant once we are confident she has finished growing — probably
in her late teens or early twenties.’ ”

Q
What are the consent issues with a 15-year-old?
“I assess whether she has capacity to consent for herself. At 15 she may well be Gillick competent; if she is, her
consent is valid and I would still involve her mother with her agreement. If she is not competent, consent comes
from someone with parental responsibility. Either way, a competent young person’s refusal must be taken
very seriously, and I would never proceed with elective aesthetic treatment because a parent is keen and the
patient is reluctant.”
Q
What would you record?
“The history including growth and menarche, the clinical findings and space measurements, photographs and
study casts as the growth baseline, the options discussed including canine substitution, the reasons for defer-
ring implants, the specific warning about infra-occlusion, that I spoke to the patient separately and assessed her
competence, that her mother was present and what she was told, the agreed interim prosthesis, and the review
interval. I would also write to the orthodontist and the GDP.”
Domain 3 — Decision making in relation to treatment procedures
Chain: eventually placing the implant
Q
At what point would you finally place?
“When serial records over at least 12 months show no change in facial height or dental relationships, she is at
least in her late teens, and she herself is asking for it rather than her mother. I would rather be a year late than a
year early — the cost of waiting is an interim prosthesis, and the cost of being early is an unrestorable aesthetic
failure.”
Q
What is specific about the lateral incisor site dimensionally?
“A 6.5 mm space demands a narrow-diameter implant, around 3.3 mm, ideally in a titanium-zirconium alloy
for strength at that diameter. I need 1.5 mm of bone between the implant and each adjacent root and at least
1 mm of buccal bone — ideally 2 mm. That arithmetic barely works in 6.5 mm, so root angulation must be
corrected orthodontically first if the roots converge.”
Q
Give me the three-dimensional position.
“Apico-coronally, the shoulder 3 mm apical to the planned mid-facial gingival margin. Bucco-palatally,
within the comfort zone, roughly 1 to 2 mm palatal to the line joining the emergence of the adjacent teeth,
with the buccal plate preserved. Mesio-distally, centred, with at least 1.5 mm to each adjacent root. Angulation
through the cingulum of the planned crown so the access can be screw-retained.”
Q
You expect to augment. What and when?
“Contour augmentation with guided bone regeneration — a deproteinised bovine bone mineral with a re-
sorbable collagen membrane, placed simultaneously with the implant if the defect is a dehiscence with an intact
envelope and the implant has primary stability. If the ridge is a knife edge that will not accept the implant in the
correct position, I would stage it: graft first, wait four to six months, then place. Soft tissue is often the greater
problem — a connective tissue graft may be needed for thickness.”
Q
Where is the boundary of your competence here?
“Placing a straightforward single implant in an adult with adequate bone is within my scope. This is not
that. A high-aesthetic-risk site in a young patient, needing a narrow implant between converging roots with
simultaneous or staged augmentation, is Complex — I would refer to a specialist in restorative dentistry or
oral surgery with an implant practice, and stay involved for the interim prosthesis, the orthodontic liaison and
the long-term maintenance.”

Q
If you were doing it, guided or freehand?
“Static guided surgery from a CBCT merged with an intra-oral scan and a diagnostic wax-up. The tolerances
here are a millimetre or so between roots, so a fully guided protocol is worth the cost. I would still raise a flap
for the augmentation and to visualise the buccal plate, and I would use the guide for the osteotomy rather than
trusting it blindly.”
Q
Immediate, early or conventional restoration?
“Conventional or early, not immediate. There is no soft tissue advantage worth the risk of losing a narrow
implant in a site that has just been grafted. I would allow three to four months, longer if grafted, then a screw-
retained provisional crown to develop the emergence profile before the definitive.”
Q
Why does the provisional matter so much at this site?
“Because the emergence profile and the papillae are created by the provisional, not by the definitive crown.
I use it to shape the peri-implant mucosa progressively over several weeks, then capture that contour with a
customised impression coping so the technician reproduces it. Going straight to a definitive crown means the
tissue dictates the crown rather than the reverse.”
Q
Screw-retained or cement-retained?
“Screw-retained wherever the angulation allows, because there is no risk of retained subgingival cement — a
well-recognised cause of peri-implantitis — and it is retrievable, which matters enormously in a patient who
may need the crown remade for infra-occlusion in twenty years. If the access would come through the labial
face, I would use an angulated screw channel before I resorted to cement.”
Q
Which material for the definitive crown?
“A zirconia or lithium disilicate crown on a titanium base, screw-retained. Ceramic gives the translucency
needed at a lateral incisor, and the titanium base preserves a metal-to-metal implant connection rather than
ceramic on titanium. I would shade-match with the contralateral central and canine and check it under different
lighting, because a single anterior unit is the hardest shade match in dentistry.”
Domain 4 — Interpretation and problem solving of clinical outcomes
Chain: living with the result
Q
Ten years on, the implant crown looks short. What has happened and what do you do?
“Continued vertical alveolar development and eruption of the adjacent teeth — infra-occlusion. First I quan-
tify it against the baseline photographs and casts. If it is under about a millimetre, I would remake the crown
with a longer incisal edge and adjusted contours. If it is greater, options are a new crown with modified
emergence, composite additions to the adjacent teeth to re-level, orthodontic intrusion of the adjacent teeth,
or — as a last resort — removal and replacement of the implant. This is exactly why I warned her at consent
and why the crown is screw-retained.”
Q
How much infra-occlusion should she expect?
“It varies too much to promise a figure, but the concept is that it is progressive and lifelong, greater the younger
the patient at placement and greater in long-face growth patterns. It is measurable in millimetres over decades
rather than years. The honest consent line is that the crown will probably need to be remade at least once in her
lifetime, and that the implant itself will very likely still be sound when it is.”
Q
She develops a black triangle mesial to the implant crown. Why, and what can you do?
“Because papilla height at an implant depends on the bone level on the adjacent natural tooth, not on the
implant — Tarnow’s work shows the papilla fills predictably when the contact point is within about 5 mm of
the crest. So I would measure that distance. Management is prosthetic first: lengthen and lower the contact
point and adjust the emergence. Surgical papilla reconstruction is unpredictable, and composite addition to the
adjacent tooth is often the kindest answer.”

Q
The resin-bonded bridge debonds three times in eighteen months. What are you thinking?
“Something is wrong with isolation, design or occlusion, not with the technique in principle. I would check
for a protrusive or excursive contact on the pontic, inadequate wrap-around or no defined path of insertion,
contamination at cementation, and parafunction. Remedies: re-prepare with better resistance form, remove all
excursive contact from the pontic, rebond under rubber dam with an MDP cement, and consider a removable
retainer with a pontic if it keeps failing.”
Q
What would you monitor, and how often?
“Before placement, six-monthly review with standardised photographs and casts to track growth and confirm
the space is maintained. After placement, review at three and six months and then annually: peri-implant
probing at six sites, bleeding and suppuration, radiographic bone level against the baseline taken at fitting, the
crown margin and contacts, and — specifically in her — the incisal and gingival levels compared with the
contralateral central and canine.”
Q
How would you know this treatment had succeeded?
“That she reached her early twenties with the space intact, an implant placed once in the right position, stable
bone and healthy tissues, and a crown she does not think about when she smiles. And that she understands the
maintenance ahead of her — a successful outcome here is measured over decades, not at the fit appointment.”
WATCH OUT
Come back to the single organising principle: implants do not grow. Say which part of the problem that
principle governs — timing, the interim prosthesis, the consent conversation, or the long-term maintenance —
and the rest of the answer follows.
Running this case to time
Time check. The flow above holds 38 questions and about 2,730 words of model answer. At 140 words
a minute plus roughly five seconds a question, that comes to nearly twenty-three minutes — an overrun
of seven and a half. What goes first is the restorative detail in Domain 3: guided versus freehand, provi-
sionalisation, screw versus cement and crown material compress into one question, because that surgery
is years away and referred, and the marks in this case sit in timing, the interim prosthesis and the consent.
If your answers run past thirty seconds, you will never reach Domain 4 — which is the infra-occlusion at
ten years, and the reason for the whole plan.
The fifteen-minute run sheet

1 Hypodontia defined, its prevalence and its associated findings · 2 Why the ridge at these sites was never

you would actually determine growth has ceased · 7 Why no CBCT today · 8 Canine substitution, argued
both ways · 9 The interim prosthesis, and cantilever rather than fixed-fixed · 10 Space maintenance as the

Where the marks are lost in this case
Answering the mother’s question. She wants implants before college, and the mark is for declining while
keeping everyone on side — something that looks good now and can be adjusted, with the implant when
growth is complete. And the consent point is not decoration: at 15 the patient may be Gillick competent,
her consent is then valid, and her refusal must be taken very seriously. Never proceed with elective
aesthetic treatment because the parent is keen.
Never questioning the orthodontics. The spaces exist because someone chose to open them, and canine
substitution — a result that grows with her and needs no prosthesis — should be re-opened with the or-
thodontist before anything is committed. Volunteer that unprompted, argue it honestly in both directions,
and grant the colleague’s point that re-treatment means another 18 months in appliances. Candidates
who accept the 6.5 mm spaces as a fixed premise have skipped the best question in the case.
Planning surgery that is not yours. A single anterior implant in an aesthetic zone is Advanced at best;
a narrow implant between converging roots, in a site whose alveolus never developed, with augmen-
tation, in a patient whose growth must first be proved complete, is Complex — and at this level it is
referred to a specialist in restorative dentistry or oral surgery. What stays yours, and matters for a decade:
the interim prosthesis, the space maintenance, the orthodontic liaison, the growth records and the
long-term maintenance. Say where you stop before you describe the osteotomy.

soe.title: The free-end saddle and the shortened dental
soe.text:
SOE Case 19 — The free-end saddle and the shortened dental
arch
THE CASE
58-year-old man, fit and well, non-smoker. Missing 35, 36 and 37 on the lower left; the 34 and the whole upper
arch are intact and unrestored. He manages well and has “got used to chewing on the other side”, but his dentist
has told him he should replace the teeth.
Pace: one structured opening of about 60 seconds, then roughly 35 questions in the remaining 14 minutes. Nothing after the opening earns you
more than a few seconds of thought.
Opening — the 60-second presentation
Q
Present this case.
“A healthy 58-year-old non-smoker with a lower left free-end saddle — a Kennedy Class II — who is functioning
satisfactorily and attending because he has been told he should have treatment, not because he wants it. That
framing matters, because the first question is whether he needs anything at all, and ‘no treatment’ is a genuine
contender here rather than a formality. In his favour: he is medically fit, a non-smoker, has an unrestored
opposing arch, and has already adapted. Against: the upper 26 and 27 are unopposed and may over-erupt, and
the 34 may drift. What I need to establish is what he actually wants to be able to do, the periodontal and occlusal
status of the remaining dentition, and whether the anterior loop of the mental nerve and the lingual concavity
would permit implants if he chose them.”
Domain 1 — Clinical interpretation and reasoning
Chain: the groundwork — classifying and understanding the saddle
Q
Classify this edentulous arch.
“Kennedy Class II, modification 0 — a unilateral free-end saddle with no other edentulous areas. Applegate’s
rules apply: classification is determined after any extractions, the most posterior edentulous area determines
the class, and additional areas are modifications, of which there are none here. The upper arch is complete.”
Q
Why does the Kennedy class matter clinically?
“Because it determines the support. Classes I and II are tooth- and mucosa-borne, so the saddle can move
independently of the abutment teeth as the mucosa is displaced. That produces rotation about the fulcrum
line through the most distal rests, torquing forces on the abutment, and progressive resorption under the saddle.
Classes III and IV are entirely tooth-borne and behave predictably. A free-end saddle is the design problem in
removable prosthodontics for exactly this reason.”
Q
Describe the anatomy relevant to implants in the lower left posterior mandible.
“The inferior alveolar canal running forwards in the body of the mandible and exiting at the mental foramen,
usually below and between the premolar apices, often with an anterior loop running mesial to the foramen
before turning back. The external oblique ridge buccally and the mylohyoid ridge lingually. Below the mylo-
hyoid ridge, the submandibular fossa — a lingual concavity that undercuts the molar region. And the lingual
nerve running close to the lingual plate at the level of the third molar.”
Q
What is the anterior loop and why does it matter?
“It is the portion of the inferior alveolar nerve that passes anterior to the mental foramen before looping back to
exit. It is present in a substantial proportion of patients and can extend several millimetres. It matters because if
I measure only to the radiographic foramen on a panoramic, I may place an implant into the loop and produce
altered sensation of the lower lip and chin. It is one of the reasons a CBCT is justified here rather than a
panoramic alone.”

Q
And the lingual concavity?
“The submandibular fossa creates a lingual undercut in the molar region, so the ridge is often much narrower
than it looks on a panoramic. Drilling along the perceived long axis of the crest can perforate the lingual plate —
which risks damage to the sublingual or submental vessels and, in the worst case, a floor-of-mouth haematoma
with airway compromise. It is the reason I want cross-sectional imaging and why I would angle the osteotomy
slightly buccally in the molar region.”
Q
What would you examine clinically?
“The periodontal status of the whole dentition with a six-point chart, because the plan is worthless if the
remaining teeth are not sound. The 34 for drift, tipping and mobility. The 26 and 27 for over-eruption and
whether they still have an occlusal contact. Ridge form and width by palpation, keratinised tissue width, and
the inter-arch space and vertical dimension. His occlusion — the scheme in excursions, the guidance, and any
signs of parafunction. And plaque control and caries risk, since implants demand more of both.”
Q
What imaging?
“Periapicals or a panoramic first to see the bone levels, the canal, any retained roots and the 26/27 position. If
he is seriously considering implants, a CBCT of the left posterior mandible, justified under IR(ME)R because
it is the only way to assess the canal position, the anterior loop and the lingual concavity in cross-section. I
would take it with a radiographic guide or a scan appliance so the planned tooth position is visible.”
Q
What are you measuring on that CBCT?
“Bone height above the canal at each planned site, ridge width at the crest and 5 mm apical, the buccolingual
angulation of the ridge and the depth of the lingual concavity, the position of the foramen and any anterior
loop, and the bone density. I would also check the contralateral side and the sinus incidentally, and report the
whole volume — I am responsible for the entire field of view.”
Q
What bone quality do you expect and why does it matter?
“D2 to D3 on Misch in the posterior mandible — thick to thin cortex with coarse to fine trabecular bone. That is
favourable: enough cortex for primary stability without the heat and vascularity problems of D1. If it turns out
to be D3 or D4 I would under-prepare the osteotomy to improve stability and extend the healing period before
loading.”
Q
Classify this case on SAC.
“Restoratively, a posterior mandibular free-end saddle with an intact opposing arch and no aesthetic demand is
Straightforward to Advanced. Surgically, it is Advanced because of the proximity of the inferior alveolar canal
and the lingual concavity — the anatomical risk, not the prosthodontics, is what raises it.”
Domain 2 — Clinical decision making and treatment planning
Chain: does he need treatment at all?
Q
Explain the shortened dental arch concept.
“That a dentition of about 20 teeth, including four occluding premolar pairs, provides adequate function,
comfort and appearance for most adults without replacement of the molars. It comes from Käyser’s work and
has been supported by long-term follow-up: no measurable increase in temporomandibular disorder, no accel-
erated periodontal breakdown, and patient satisfaction comparable with restored arches. The World Health
Organization has endorsed it as an acceptable treatment goal.”
Q
So is this man a shortened dental arch?
“Not quite — he has a unilateral shortening, with occlusion to the 34 on the left and to the molars on the right.
That is an asymmetric arch rather than the classical bilateral shortened arch, so the evidence applies less directly.
But he is asymptomatic, has adapted, and has occluding contacts on both sides, so the principle still holds:
accepting it is a legitimate positive choice, not a failure to treat.”

Q
What are the risks of leaving it?
“Over-eruption of the 26 and 27, which are unopposed distal to the 34 — this is the real risk and it can eventually
make prosthetic replacement impossible without enameloplasty, elective root treatment or extraction. Drifting
or tipping of the 34. Occlusal instability and loss of vertical dimension on that side if the right side then breaks
down. And a slow increase in load on the remaining teeth.”
Q
You have argued for the shortened arch — argue against it.
“He is only 58, so he has perhaps thirty years in which the right side may fail; replacing the left now while the
bone is good and he is fit is easier than doing it at 75 with a compromised right side. Unopposed upper molars
are a real and progressive problem. And he has not actually said he is happy — he came because he was told
to, but I have not yet asked him what he cannot do.”
Q
A colleague says you should simply make him a denture and be done with it. Why might he be right?
“Because it is reversible, cheap, non-surgical and immediately available, it restores the occlusion to the upper
molars and prevents over-eruption, and if the patient dislikes it nothing has been lost. It also serves as a diag-
nostic trial of whether he actually wants posterior teeth — if he wears it, implants are justified; if he abandons
it in a drawer, that answers the question for both of us.”
Chain: the options
Q
Set out the options.
“Shortened dental arch with active monitoring — accept it, review with photographs and study casts. A
removable partial denture — cheapest, reversible, but a free-end saddle design is the least well tolerated.
Implants — one, two or three, restoring anything from a single 36 to the full span. A cantilever bridge from
the 34 — which I would not do for a molar span. And no treatment with no monitoring, which I would not
offer.”
Q
If he wanted a denture, how would you design it?
“A cobalt-chromium framework, not acrylic. RPI or RPA clasping on the 34 — mesial rest, distal guide plate,
gingivally approaching I-bar — so that under load the clasp disengages rather than torquing the abutment.
Indirect retention anterior to the fulcrum line through a rest on the contralateral side, cross-arch bracing with
a lingual bar, and an altered cast or functional impression for the free-end saddle so it is supported by displaced
mucosa. Broad coverage of the buccal shelf and retromolar pad.”
Q
Why not a cantilever bridge from the 34?
“Because a single premolar abutment cannot support a molar cantilever. The bending moment at the abut-
ment is proportional to the cantilever length, and a molar pontic is both long and heavily loaded. I would
expect debonding, or worse, root fracture or loss of the abutment. Cantilevers are for small pontics on sound
abutments in low-load positions — a lateral incisor from a canine, not a molar from a premolar.”
Q
If he chooses implants, how many and where?
“I would not place three implants for three teeth. My preferred plan is two implants at the 35 and 36 positions,
restored as two separate crowns, accepting occlusion to the first molar — which is itself a shortened arch and
functionally suﬀicient. If bone dictates otherwise, two implants supporting a three-unit fixed prosthesis with
an intervening pontic is reasonable. I would site them by the prosthetic plan and then check the anatomy permits
it, not the other way round.”
Q
Why not a distal cantilever to a 37?
“Because a distal cantilever generates large bending moments on the terminal implant, and the evidence asso-
ciates cantilevers with increased screw loosening, framework and porcelain fracture, and marginal bone loss. A
37 adds little function — the second molar contributes least to masticatory eﬀiciency — for a disproportionate
mechanical cost. I would rather stop at the 36.”

Q
How do you have the conversation with him?
“ ‘You are managing well and there is nothing here that is harming you. There are three honest options. The first
is to leave it and keep an eye on it — a lot of people function perfectly well with teeth back to the premolars, and
there is good evidence for that. The second is a removable denture, which is the cheapest but the one people
are least likely to wear. The third is implants, which would give you back a fixed chewing surface on that side; it
is the most expensive, involves surgery, and commits you to lifelong cleaning and maintenance. Which appeals
to you — and what would you like to be able to do that you cannot do now?’ ”
Q
Why is that last question the important one?
“Because if he cannot answer it, the shortened arch is almost certainly right. Implants are justified by a problem
to solve, not by the existence of a gap. If he says he avoids steak, or he bites his cheek, or he is worried about
the right side failing, that is a reason to treat. If he says nothing, treating him is meeting my expectation rather
than his need.”
Domain 3 — Decision making in relation to treatment procedures
Chain: doing it safely
Q
Where is the boundary of your competence in this case?
“Two implants in a posterior mandible with adequate bone height above the canal and no need for grafting
is within my scope. If the CBCT shows less than about 2 mm of clearance above the canal, a marked lingual
concavity, or a need for vertical augmentation or nerve lateralisation, that is beyond me and I would refer —
nerve injury is the complication that does the most harm and generates the most litigation, and it is entirely
avoidable by not attempting the case.”
Q
What would you specifically warn him about at consent?
“Altered sensation of the lower lip, chin and gum — that it is uncommon, usually temporary, but can be
permanent; that it is not painful in most cases but is intrusive. Also failure to integrate, infection, the need for
lifelong maintenance and hygiene, screw loosening, the cost of maintenance, and peri-implant disease. I would
give written information and a cooling-off period, and record that the nerve risk was specifically discussed.”
Q
Take me through the surgery.
“Chlorhexidine rinse, aseptic technique, infiltration rather than a block so he can report a sharp sensation as
an early warning. Mid-crestal incision with a distal relieving incision kept away from the mental foramen; full-
thickness flap; identify the external oblique ridge and, if it is close, the mental bundle. Sequential drilling with
a drill stop set from the CBCT, slow speed, copious irrigation, sharp drills, checking depth and angulation with
direction indicators and a periapical. Angle slightly buccally in the molar region to stay off the lingual plate.
Insert at 25 to 45 Ncm.”
Q
What is your safety margin above the canal?
“At least 2 mm between the implant apex and the superior border of the canal, and I plan the drill length to that,
not to the implant length. I add a margin for CBCT measurement error and for drill overshoot beyond the tip.
If that arithmetic leaves me a shorter implant than I would like, I use a short implant — 6 to 8 mm implants
have good evidence in the posterior mandible — rather than augment or take the risk.”
Q
You perforate the lingual plate with the drill. What do you do?
“Stop immediately, do not advance further, and assess for bleeding. Most perforations are uneventful, but a
torn sublingual or submental vessel can produce a rapidly expanding floor-of-mouth haematoma with airway
obstruction, which is a medical emergency. I would apply pressure, monitor the floor of mouth and the airway
actively, abandon or reposition the implant, and if there is any swelling or elevation of the tongue, call for
emergency help and arrange urgent transfer rather than watch.”
Q
One stage or two?

“One stage with healing abutments, given good primary stability and adequate keratinised tissue — it avoids
a second surgical episode and lets the soft tissue mature around the abutment. Two stage if primary stability
is poor, if I have grafted, or if I cannot achieve tension-free closure over an adequate cuff.”
Q
When would you load?
“Conventional loading at about three months in the mandible, confirmed by clinical stability and, if I have it,
ISQ. Early loading at six to eight weeks is defensible in D2 bone with good primary stability, but conventional is
what I would do and what I would say. He keeps the arch as it is in the interim — there is no interim prosthesis
needed since he is already functioning.”
Q
Splint the two crowns or leave them separate?
“Separate if the implants are well positioned, of adequate diameter and in good bone — it allows flossing
between them, permits independent assessment and re-treatment, and simplifies any future repair. Splint
them if the implants are short, narrow, in poor bone, or if there is parafunction, because splinting distributes
load and reduces screw loosening. Here, with D2 bone and a fit non-smoker, I would leave them separate.”
Q
Screw-retained or cement-retained, and what occlusal scheme?
“Screw-retained — retrievable and no risk of retained subgingival cement. Occlusally: a narrow occlusal table
to reduce the lever arm, light contact in intercuspation so the crowns come into contact only under firm closure,
given that implants lack the periodontal ligament and its proprioception, no excursive contacts with guidance
kept on the canines and natural teeth, and no cantilever.”
Q
Why light contact rather than equal contact?
“Because a natural tooth intrudes about 25 to 100 microns under load through its periodontal ligament, whereas
an implant moves only 3 to 5 microns by bone deformation. If they are set to equal contact at rest, the implant
takes disproportionate load once the natural teeth depress. Leaving the implant crowns fractionally light means
they share load only when the whole arch is loaded.”
Q
What would you record?
“The full history and examination including the periodontal chart, the imaging justification and findings with
the canal measurements, the options discussed including no treatment and the shortened dental arch, the
specific nerve risk discussion, his stated goals in his own words, the consent, and then surgically the implant
make, diameter, length, batch number, torque achieved, and any complication. Plus the baseline radiograph at
fitting.”
Domain 4 — Interpretation and problem solving of clinical outcomes
Chain: outcomes and their management
Q
What survival would you quote him?
“In the region of 95% at five years and around 90 to 95% at ten years for single implants in a healthy non-
smoker with good bone — the posterior mandible is among the more predictable sites. But I would be careful
to distinguish implant survival from complication-free survival: the implant staying in the bone is likely, while
some prosthetic or biological event over a decade is close to expected.”
Q
The next day he reports a numb lower lip. Walk me through it.
“Reassure and see him urgently. Map and record the affected area with a diagram, test light touch, sharp-blunt
and two-point discrimination, and ask whether it is numbness alone or painful dysaesthesia. Take a periapical
and, if in doubt, a CBCT to see whether the implant impinges on the canal. If it does, remove or back off the
implant within 24 to 36 hours — that is time-critical. Consider a short course of corticosteroids and NSAIDs.
Document everything, review at intervals, and refer early if there is no improvement by about a month or if
there is dysaesthesia.”

Q
Why is early referral so important there?
“Because the window for any surgical intervention is short and the prognosis worsens with delay, and because
persistent dysaesthesia is disabling. Sensory recovery, if it happens, largely occurs in the first three months
and is usually judged permanent by about a year. Beyond that, management becomes symptomatic and psy-
chological support becomes part of it. Delay is the single thing that turns a manageable injury into a permanent
one.”
Q
Two years on, one crown feels loose. What is your differential and your sequence?
“Abutment screw loosening is by far the commonest — check with a periapical and by testing the crown against
the abutment. Then fracture of the screw, loss of integration, a fractured crown or ceramic chip, or simply
a loose adjacent contact. My sequence is: radiograph, remove the crown through the access channel, inspect
the screw and the interface, check for mobility of the implant itself, then re-torque with a new screw at the
manufacturer’s torque and — crucially — find out why it loosened, which is usually an occlusal overload or
an unsplinted narrow implant.”
Q
He develops bleeding and 5 mm probing depths around the 36 implant. What is going on and what do you do?
“That is peri-implant mucositis if there is no bone loss beyond initial remodelling, and peri-implantitis if there
is progressive bone loss against the baseline radiograph. Mucositis is reversible: non-surgical debridement
with appropriate instruments, oral hygiene instruction focused on the implant, correction of any prosthetic
contour that prevents cleaning, and review. Peri-implantitis needs the same first, then reassessment, and
surgical access or referral if it does not resolve. And I would look for a cause — plaque, an over-contoured
crown, or lack of keratinised tissue.”
Q
What would you monitor and how often?
“Annually as a minimum: peri-implant probing at six sites, bleeding and suppuration, plaque control, mobility,
screw and crown integrity, and the occlusion. Radiographs at one year and thereafter as clinically indicated,
compared with the baseline. And if he chose the shortened arch instead, I would still review annually with
photographs and study casts for over-eruption of the 26 and 27 and drift of the 34 — so the decision remains
an active one rather than a drift into a worse position.”
Q
How would you know the treatment had succeeded?
“By whether he can do the thing he told me he wanted to do. Objectively: stable implants, no bleeding or
suppuration, bone levels stable against baseline, an intact prosthesis, and an occlusion that has not changed.
And if the right answer turned out to be no treatment, success is that he reaches 70 with the same arch, no
over-eruption and no regret.”
WATCH OUT
Return to the question the whole case turns on: what problem am I solving, and for whom? State whether the
driver is the patient’s function, the dentist’s expectation, or the risk of future deterioration — that names the
issue and usually points straight at the answer.
Running this case to time
Time check. The flow above holds 41 questions and about 3,077 words of model answer. At 140 words a
minute plus roughly five seconds a question, that is close to twenty-five minutes — an overrun of about
ten, the longest in this section. What goes first is the removable partial denture design material in Domain
2: the cobalt-chromium framework, the RPI clasping, the altered cast impression and the argument against
a cantilever from the 34 collapse into a single question, because the marks in this case sit in the shortened
dental arch and in the canal and lingual concavity. The Domain 1 anatomy will also be sampled rather
than recited. If your answers run past thirty seconds, you will never reach Domain 4 — and Domain 4 is
where the numb lip appears.
The fifteen-minute run sheet

1 Kennedy Class II modification 0, and Applegate’s rules · 2 Why the class matters — tooth- and mucosa-
borne, and the fulcrum line · 3 The anterior loop, and what it costs you if you miss it · 4 The submandibular
fossa, and the floor-of-mouth haematoma · 5 What you measure on the CBCT, and why it is justified · 6
The shortened dental arch, with Käyser and the WHO · 7 Why this man is not quite a classical shortened
arch, and why it still holds · 8 The risks of leaving it — over-eruption of the 26 and 27 first · 9 Two implants
