of a graft · 11 The numb lip — map it, image it, back the implant out within 36 hours · 12 What you say to
him, and the one question you ask him.
Where the marks are lost in this case
Treating the gap instead of the patient. The examiner has told you he came because his dentist sent him,
and that he has adapted. A candidate who opens with implant options has answered a question nobody
asked. Say in the opening that no treatment is a genuine contender, name the shortened dental arch
with Käyser and the WHO behind it, and offer it as a positive plan — then let the over-eruption of the 26
and 27 be the argument that reopens it.
Under-reading the mandible.
This is an Advanced surgical site and the reason is anatomical, not
prosthodontic. Volunteer the anterior loop and the submandibular fossa before you are asked, say that
a panoramic will not show either, and give the 2 mm clearance above the canal as an arithmetic you
plan the drill length to. Candidates who talk about implant length rather than drill length have told the
examiner they have never planned one.
Never naming what you would not attempt. Two implants in adequate native bone with a healthy non-
smoker is yours. What is not: less than 2 mm above the canal, nerve lateralisation, vertical augmenta-
tion, or a lingual concavity you cannot drill around. Say it before the surgery question rather than after
it, and say where it goes. Reaching for a short implant instead of a graft is the mark of judgement here;
reaching for a graft you cannot do is the mark of a fail.

soe.title: The dissatisfied patient and the governance
soe.text:
SOE Case 20 — The dissatisfied patient and the governance
response
THE CASE
A patient returns 4 months after you fitted an implant crown at the 11. She is unhappy: the crown “looks longer
and greyer” than her own tooth and there is a black triangle mesially. She says she “was never told this could
happen” and is threatening to complain. Your records show a signed consent form but no detailed note of the
discussion.
Pace: one structured opening of about 60 seconds, then roughly 35 questions in the remaining 14 minutes. Nothing after the opening earns you
more than a few seconds of thought.
Opening — the 60-second presentation
Q
Present this case.
“A patient four months after fitting an implant crown at the 11, dissatisfied with an aesthetic outcome she says
she did not expect — a crown that looks longer and greyer than the contralateral tooth, and a black triangle
mesially — and threatening to complain. My records contain a signed consent form but no contemporaneous
note of the discussion. There are two entirely separate problems here and I must not let them contaminate
each other. The clinical problem is establishing the cause of each of the three complaints and whether each is
remediable. The professional problem is how I respond to her dissatisfaction, how I handle a records deficiency
I cannot retrospectively repair, and what I change in my practice so it does not recur. My first action is neither
of those: it is to listen properly.”
Domain 1 — Clinical interpretation and reasoning
Chain: the groundwork — why implant crowns look different
Q
Describe the peri-implant soft tissue and how it differs from that around a tooth.
“There is no periodontal ligament and no cementum, so the collagen fibres run parallel and circular around
the abutment rather than inserting into it. The supracrestal attachment is longer than the roughly 2 mm around
a tooth — commonly 3 to 4 mm — and the blood supply is poorer, arising only from the supraperiosteal vessels.
It is a weaker seal, and its vertical position is dictated by the bone crest beneath it.”
Q
What determines the presence of a papilla?
“The contact point to bone crest distance. Tarnow showed that between two teeth the papilla fills the embrasure
essentially always at 5 mm, about 56% at 6 mm and about 27% at 7 mm. Between an implant and a tooth the
papilla is supported by the tooth’s attachment level, so the critical distance is roughly 4.5 to 5 mm, and it is the
adjacent tooth’s interproximal bone that governs it — not the implant.”
Q
So what has probably produced her black triangle?
“Either the contact point is too far incisal relative to the interproximal crest on the 12, or the interproximal bone
on that adjacent tooth was already reduced before I started, or there has been crestal remodelling around the
implant. It may also simply be that the papilla is still maturing — some papillary rebound occurs over the first
one to two years, so four months is early.”
Q
Why might the crown look grey?
“Three candidates. Show-through of a titanium abutment through thin buccal mucosa — the commonest and
the most easily fixed. Loss of buccal bone or a buccally placed implant, so there is no white tissue behind the
mucosa. Or the restorative material itself — a metal-ceramic or high-opacity core with poor translucency at
the cervical third, or a shade mismatch against a natural tooth that has its own internal translucency.”

Q
How would you distinguish those clinically?
“Transillumination and blanching — greyness that changes with light angle and tissue tension suggests show-
through rather than an intrinsic shade problem. Probing the buccal tissue thickness, and probing the implant
to assess the depth of the margin. Radiographs and, if needed, CBCT to see the implant’s buccopalatal position
and any buccal plate. And direct comparison of the crown against the 21 with a shade guide and standardised
photographs.”
Q
And why might the crown be longer than her natural tooth?
“Because the soft tissue margin sits apical to the contralateral zenith — from crestal bone loss after extraction,
a buccally or deeply placed implant, or recession over the four months. The restoration is then made longer to
reach the tissue. Sometimes it is not the implant crown that is wrong at all but a discrepancy in the gingival
zenith levels that was there before treatment and was never pointed out.”
Chain: examining this patient
Q
What exactly would you examine?
“Crown length against the 21; the mid-facial gingival margin level against the 21 and 12; papilla height and
the contact point to crest distance; soft tissue phenotype and thickness; the abutment material and margin
depth; peri-implant probing at six sites with bleeding and suppuration, to exclude inflammation as a cause
of recession; the implant’s three-dimensional position on radiograph and, if needed, CBCT; the occlusion; and
standardised photographs compared with any pre-operative images.”
Q
Why does inflammation matter to an aesthetic complaint?
“Because inflamed tissue is oedematous, red and prone to further recession, and because some apparent reces-
sion resolves once inflammation is controlled. If I remake a crown against an inflamed baseline I will get the
tissue level wrong. Inflammation also raises the possibility of retained cement, which would be both a cause
and something I am responsible for.”
Q
What would you look for on the radiograph?
“Bone levels mesially and distally compared with the film taken at fitting; the interproximal bone level on
the adjacent 12, because that determines the papilla; any radiopaque residual cement; the abutment–implant
interface for a gap or misfit; and the implant’s angulation. A single periapical with a paralleling technique, not
a panoramic.”
Q
She has no pre-operative photographs in her record. Does that change your position?
“Yes — it weakens it considerably. Without a baseline I cannot demonstrate what the zeniths and papillae looked
like before, so I cannot show that a discrepancy pre-existed. That is a records failure of the same family as the
missing consent note, and I would treat it as such rather than argue around it.”
Domain 2 — Clinical decision making and treatment planning
Chain: the clinical options
Q
If the greyness is titanium show-through, what do you do?
“Replace the abutment with a zirconia abutment, or a titanium base with a zirconia superstructure, and re-
make the crown. It is a straightforward change with a large visual effect. I would combine it with a connective
tissue graft to thicken the buccal tissue if it is thin, because that both masks the underlying metal and protects
the margin long term.”
Q
And for the black triangle?
“In order of invasiveness: modify the crown to move the contact point apically, which shortens the contact-to-
crest distance and is often enough on its own; add composite or ceramic to the mesial of the 12 to close the
embrasure from the other side; orthodontic movement to approximate the roots; or a connective tissue graft,

which is far less predictable for papillae than for mid-facial recession. I would also allow time, since papillary
maturation continues.”
Q
And if the crown is simply too long?
“Remake it with a modified emergence profile and, if the tissue cannot be brought coronally, pink ceramic at
the cervical margin to restore the apparent length. That is a legitimate solution, not a failure — but it has to be
shown to her and agreed, not sprung on her at the fit.”
Q
What if the implant is fundamentally malpositioned?
“Then I say so plainly: no restoration will fully correct a malpositioned implant. The options become prosthetic
camouflage with pink ceramic, or explantation and re-treatment with grafting and a new implant, or removal
and conversion to a resin-bonded bridge. I would set out the time, the cost, who would do it, and who would
pay for it — and I would take advice from my indemnity provider before discussing the financial side.”
Q
What is the one thing you would do before committing to any of these?
“Make a provisional or a mock-up first, so she can see the proposed improvement in her own mouth before she
commits. It converts an argument about my description into a decision she makes with her eyes. It also protects
both of us: if the mock-up does not satisfy her, we have learned that before spending her money.”
Q
What is the SAC classification of what is now in front of you?
“The original single implant in the aesthetic zone was Advanced prosthodontically at best. The corrective
treatment is Complex — revision in the aesthetic zone with a soft tissue deficiency and a dissatisfied patient
— and if explantation and regrafting are involved it is unequivocally Complex. Re-treatment is always harder
than treatment.”
Q
What is within your competence here and what is not?
“Within: the assessment, the abutment and crown revision, contact point modification, hygiene and inflam-
mation management, the complaint handling and the governance response. Beyond me: explantation with
regrafting and re-implantation in the aesthetic zone. If that is where this goes, I would refer, and I would say
so early rather than after another failed attempt. Referring a case I have already restored is not an admission of
incompetence — persisting is.”
Chain: the professional response
Q
What do you do first, on the day she comes in?
“I listen. A proper appointment, not a doorstep conversation — private, unhurried, no one waiting — and I let
her tell the whole story without interrupting. Then I acknowledge it genuinely: ‘I’m sorry you’re unhappy with
how this looks. That matters to me, and I want to understand exactly what’s bothering you.’ Only then do I
examine. Most complaints escalate because the patient did not feel heard, not because of the clinical outcome.”
Q
How do you handle the complaint formally?
“Follow the practice complaints procedure: acknowledge in writing within the stated timescale, offer a meeting,
investigate properly, and respond in writing with what I found, what I propose, and what she can do if she
remains dissatisfied — naming the relevant ombudsman or regulator. I would inform my indemnity provider
early, before I write anything formal, and take their help with the wording.”
Q
What about the records problem?
“I cannot and would not alter them. A signed form is not consent — consent is the discussion, and my note
of that discussion is not as detailed as it should have been. I would tell her that honestly and apologise for
it. If I add anything now it is clearly dated and signed as a late entry recording only today’s conversation.
Retrospectively backfilling a consent note would be dishonest and, if discovered, far more serious than the
original omission.”

Q
Does duty of candour apply to an aesthetic complaint?
“Yes. The professional duty of candour applies when something goes wrong and a patient is harmed or dis-
tressed. It requires me to tell her promptly, apologise, explain what happened as far as I know it, and put
right what can be put right. An apology is not an admission of liability — that is explicit in the Compensation
Act and in the regulators’ guidance, and it is the single most useful thing to know in this room.”
Q
You said the signed form is not consent. Argue against yourself — what use is it?
“It is evidence that a process took place and that documentation was given, and it usually lists the material risks,
which is worth something. But it is a record of an event, not of an exchange. It cannot show what she asked,
what mattered to her, or what she understood — and those are precisely what Montgomery makes the test.”
Q
State the Montgomery standard.
“That the clinician must take reasonable care to ensure the patient is aware of any material risk in the proposed
treatment and of any reasonable alternative. Materiality is judged from the patient’s perspective — what a
reasonable person in her position would attach significance to, or what this particular patient would. In aesthetic
implant dentistry, a black triangle and a colour mismatch are unambiguously material.”
Domain 3 — Decision making in relation to treatment procedures
Chain: doing the corrective work properly
Q
Take me through the abutment and crown revision.
“Remove the crown, retrieve the abutment, and assess the tissue at rest before deciding anything. Fit a screw-
retained provisional with a modified emergence and let the tissue respond for at least eight to twelve weeks.
Refine the provisional with flowable composite until she and I are both satisfied. Then capture that contour
with a customised impression coping so the laboratory reproduces exactly what she approved, and only then
make the definitive crown.”
Q
How would you shape the emergence to help the papilla?
“Keep the subgingival contour concave or flat rather than over-contoured, so tissue has room to occupy the
embrasure, and place the contact point more apically and slightly longer. Over-contouring the cervical third
pushes tissue apically and is a common self-inflicted cause of exactly this appearance.”
Q
If you graft connective tissue, where from and how?
“A subepithelial connective tissue graft from the palate, taken with a single-incision or trap-door technique
from the premolar region, staying anterior to the greater palatine bundle and away from the rugae. Placed
through a tunnel or an envelope flap buccal to the implant, sutured coronally, and left undisturbed. I would
warn her about donor site discomfort and the need for a palatal stent.”
Q
What could go wrong with the corrective treatment?
“Graft necrosis or shrinkage; further recession; donor site bleeding or discomfort; failure of the tissue to fill the
black triangle despite everything; a shade that still does not match; and — the risk that matters most here —
spending her money and her goodwill for a small improvement. So I would set the expectation deliberately
low and demonstrate it on a provisional first.”
Q
What would you record from now on in this case?
“Every contact contemporaneously and factually: what she said, in her words where I can; what I examined
and found; the options offered and declined; the risks named; that a provisional was shown, photographed and
approved; and the financial arrangement. No opinion about her character and no defensive commentary —
the record will be read by others.”
Q
Who else should know about this?

“My indemnity provider, early. My practice owner or clinical lead, under the practice’s complaints and sig-
nificant event procedures. The laboratory, if the technical work is part of the problem. And the whole team,
through a significant event analysis — because the systems failures here are the practice’s, not only mine.”
Domain 4 — Interpretation and problem solving of clinical outcomes
Chain: closing the loop
Q
What would you change in your consent process?
“A written, implant-specific consent document naming the material risks — recession, grey show-through,
black triangles, crown length discrepancy, long-term aesthetic change, biological and mechanical complications
— given at a separate visit with a cooling-off period, and, crucially, a contemporaneous note of the discussion,
recording what was discussed, what was given, what she asked, and what she said mattered to her.”
Q
What would you change in your aesthetic case protocol?
“A mock-up or provisional shown, photographed and approved before the definitive restoration in every
anterior case, with the approval recorded. Standardised pre-operative photographs as a mandatory record.
And an ITI Aesthetic Risk Assessment completed and shared with the patient for every anterior implant, so
the risk conversation is structured rather than remembered.”
Q
Design the audit.
“Standard: 100% of implant cases have a contemporaneous note of the consent discussion and a pre-operative
photographic record. Sample: my last 20 implant cases. Measure against the standard, identify the gap, im-
plement the new proforma and photographic protocol, then re-audit the next 20 cases at six months to close
the loop. That is the shape of a quality improvement project, and it is what the entrance requirements for this
qualification are asking for.”
Q
What is the difference between that audit and a significant event analysis?
“Audit measures practice against a defined standard over a sample and closes a loop with re-audit. Significant
event analysis examines a single episode in depth — what happened, why, what went well, what did not, and
what will change — with the team, and is recorded and reviewed. Both belong here: the SEA for this case, the
audit for the system.”
Q
How would you know your changes had worked?
“The re-audit reaching the standard is the process measure. The outcome measures are fewer aesthetic com-
plaints, patients approving provisionals before definitive work, and — the one I would actually watch — patients
arriving at the fit appointment with no surprises, because everything they see they have already seen.”
Q
What do you say to her at the end of the first appointment?
“‘I’ve heard what you’re unhappy about, and I can see it too. I want to find out exactly why each of those
three things has happened before I promise you anything. I’ll examine, take some photographs and an X-ray,
and I’ll see you again with a proper explanation and some options. In the meantime, if you want to make a
formal complaint, that’s absolutely your right and it won’t affect how I look after you.’”

Q
What is the single most important lesson from this case?
“That in aesthetic implant dentistry the outcome is judged against the patient’s expectation, not against my
technical standard. The work that determines whether a case succeeds is done before the drill — establishing
what she wanted, showing her honestly what was achievable, and recording that conversation.”
WATCH OUT
Separate the two threads and say which one you are answering: the clinical cause and its remedy, or the pro-
fessional response — listen, apologise, investigate, be candid, involve indemnity, change the system. Naming
the thread buys you a sentence and is almost always the frame the examiner wants.
Running this case to time
Time check. The flow above holds 37 questions and about 2,410 words of model answer. At 140 words a
minute plus roughly five seconds a question, that is a little over twenty minutes — an overrun of about
five. What goes first is the connective tissue graft material in Domain 3: the donor site, the single-incision
technique, the greater palatine bundle and the palatal stent compress into one question, because this case
is not marked on soft tissue surgery. The marks sit in the professional response — listening, candour,
Montgomery, the records, the indemnity provider and the audit — and an examiner will protect those. If
your answers run past thirty seconds, you will never reach Domain 4 — and Domain 4 is where the audit
and the closed loop live.

Where the marks are lost in this case
Defending the dentistry instead of answering the complaint. The examiner has given you a records
deficiency deliberately. Candidates who explain that the black triangle was unavoidable, or that she signed
the form, have lost the case in the first minute. Say in the opening that there are two problems and that
the first action is to listen — then handle the clinical cause and the professional response as separate
threads, naming which one you are in.
Trying to make the record better than it is. The volunteered answer is that consent is the discussion, not
the signature, that your note was inadequate, that you would tell her so and apologise for it, and that
anything added now is a dated late entry about today only. Candidates who hedge — “I would clarify
my notes” — have described the thing that ends careers. Say retrospective alteration is dishonest and
more serious than the omission before you are pushed to it.

the assessment, the abutment and crown revision, contact point modification, inflammation control, and
the complaint handling and governance response. Beyond it: explantation with regrafting and re-
implantation in the aesthetic zone, which is referred — and, separately, anything touching liability or
the financial settlement, which goes to your indemnity provider before you speak to her about money.
Referring a case you have already restored is not an admission of incompetence; persisting is.

soe.title: Failed endodontics in the aesthetic zone
soe.text:
SOE Case 21 — Failed endodontics in the aesthetic zone
THE CASE
38-year-old teacher, fit and well, non-smoker. The 21 has had two root canal treatments and an apicectomy;
there is a buccal sinus, a post crown, and a 6 mm buccal probing depth. CBCT shows a large periapical lesion
with buccal plate loss over 8 mm. Medium smile line, medium phenotype.
Pace: one structured opening of about 60 seconds, then roughly 35 questions in the remaining 14 minutes. Nothing after the opening earns you
more than a few seconds of thought.
Opening — the 60-second presentation
Q
Present this case.
“A fit, non-smoking 38-year-old teacher with a failed, apicected upper left central incisor. It has had two root
canal treatments and an apicectomy, it has a chronic buccal sinus, a post crown, and a 6 mm buccal probing
depth. The CBCT is the decisive finding: a large periapical lesion with loss of the buccal plate over 8 mm.
The tooth is not salvageable — three endodontic attempts have failed and the supporting wall is gone. So the
decision is not whether to extract, but how to manage a site that has already lost its buccal wall in a patient
with a medium smile line and an occupation that puts her in front of people all day. My immediate questions
are how much interproximal bone remains on the adjacent 11 and 22, what her smile actually shows, and what
she is expecting.”
Domain 1 — Clinical interpretation and reasoning
Chain: the endodontic and periapical groundwork
Q
What is the likely periapical diagnosis?
“Chronic apical periodontitis with a sinus tract — previously called a chronic apical abscess — arising from
a persistently infected root canal system. It is chronic, so it is asymptomatic; the sinus is the reason she has no
pain. There is no pulp to test: the tooth is previously treated, so pulpal diagnosis is by history, not by sensibility
testing.”
Q
Why do endodontic treatments fail?
“Persistent intraradicular infection — untreated canals, an inadequately disinfected apical third, or resistant
organisms such as Enterococcus faecalis — is the commonest by far. Then coronal leakage past a restoration
or post. Then extraradicular infection or a true apical cyst that will not resolve non-surgically. And non-
endodontic causes: a vertical root fracture, a perforation, or a foreign body reaction. After two orthograde
attempts and an apicectomy I would be considering a root fracture or a true cyst.”
Q
How would you confirm a vertical root fracture?
“A narrow, isolated, deep probing defect on one aspect — which is what a 6 mm buccal pocket could represent;
a J-shaped or halo radiolucency tracking along the root; a sinus at or near the gingival margin rather than at
the apex; and direct visualisation after raising a flap or after extraction. CBCT can suggest it but metal artefact
from a post makes it unreliable.”
Q
What does the 6 mm buccal probing actually represent here?
“Most probably a sinus tract draining along the buccal root surface through the sulcus, rather than true pe-
riodontal attachment loss. I would confirm by tracing the sinus with a gutta-percha point and radiographing
it. The distinction matters: a resolving endodontic lesion leaves a site with better regenerative potential than
genuine periodontal attachment loss, and it changes what I expect from the adjacent papillae.”

Q
What is the significance of the buccal plate in this region normally?
“In the anterior maxilla the buccal plate is thin — under 1 mm in the large majority of central incisor sites,
and often under 0.5 mm. It is largely bundle bone, dependent on the periodontal ligament for its blood supply,
so it resorbs once the tooth is lost. Here she has already lost 8 mm of it to disease, which means she starts the
extraction with the deficiency most patients only develop afterwards.”
Q
What happens to a socket after extraction?
“Remodelling that is greatest on the buccal aspect. Schropp showed roughly a 50% reduction in ridge width in
the first year, about two-thirds of it in the first three months. Araújo and Lindhe showed the buccal wall loses
height preferentially because of bundle bone resorption. Superimposed on an existing 8 mm dehiscence, that is
a very substantial defect.”
Q
What actually determines the papillae around the future restoration?
“The interproximal bone height on the adjacent teeth — the 11 and 22 — not the implant. Tarnow’s work gives
the rule: a papilla fills the embrasure essentially always at a 5 mm contact-to-crest distance, about 56% at 6 mm,
about 27% at 7 mm. Between an implant and a tooth the papilla is supported by the tooth’s attachment. So if
the 11 and 22 have intact interproximal bone I can still get papillae; if they do not, I cannot recreate it.”
Chain: reading this patient
Q
What further information do you want?
“Her smile line at full smile and during speech; the exact vertical and horizontal extent of the buccal defect
and whether the palatal wall is intact; the interproximal bone levels on the 11 and 22; sensibility of the 11 and
22, since the 21 may not have been the only tooth traumatised; her expectations in her own words and what her
job demands aesthetically; occlusion and any parafunction; and standardised photographs plus a diagnostic
wax-up.”
Q
Why does the palatal wall matter?
“Because it determines whether an implant can be placed at all in the correct prosthetic position and whether
it will have primary stability. In the anterior maxilla the implant is engaged in the palatal wall and the apical
bone, not the buccal plate. If the palatal wall is intact I have a scaffold to graft against; if it is lost as well, the
defect becomes a two-wall or non-contained one and predictability falls sharply.”
Q
What is her aesthetic risk?
“On the ITI Aesthetic Risk Assessment: in her favour, healthy, non-smoker, medium rather than high smile
line, medium phenotype, and a single tooth space with adjacent teeth present. Against her, acute or chronic
infection at the site and a major hard tissue defect. Those two alone move her to high aesthetic risk.”
Q
Why does the CBCT change your management here, when a periapical would show the lesion?
“Because the periapical shows the lesion in two dimensions but tells me nothing about the buccal plate, which
is superimposed on the root. The buccal loss is precisely the finding that rules out an immediate implant and
dictates a staged approach. The exposure is justified under IR(ME)R because it changes management, and I
would report the whole volume, not just the region of interest.”
Domain 2 — Clinical decision making and treatment planning
Chain: choosing between the options
Q
What are her options?
“No treatment — not realistic with a discharging sinus.
Retreatment or re-apicectomy — it has failed twice already, so the prognosis is poor.
Extraction plus a removable prosthesis — reasonable as an interim, not as the endpoint for a 38-year-old
teacher.
Extraction plus a resin-bonded cantilever bridge from the 11, with soft tissue augmentation under an ovate

pontic.
Extraction plus ridge preservation, then a delayed implant at 4 to 6 months with simultaneous or staged GBR.
Immediate implant placement — which I would rule out.”
Q
Why do you rule out an immediate implant?
“Because the ITI decision tree for immediate placement requires an intact socket with a facial wall of at least
1 mm, adequate apical and palatal bone for primary stability, a thick phenotype and no acute infection. This
site has an 8 mm buccal dehiscence and a chronic draining sinus. Placing into it risks failure of osseointegration,
and if it does integrate it will do so in a position with no buccal support and a predictable mid-facial recession.”
Q
What would you actually do, and why?
“Extract atraumatically without a flap, curette the lesion and the sinus tract thoroughly, and perform ridge
preservation — recognising that with 8 mm of buccal plate missing this is an Elian Type 3 socket where
preservation can only be partially effective. Provide a bonded pontic immediately. Reassess at four months
with a CBCT: if I can place an implant in the correct prosthetic position with simultaneous contour GBR, I will;
if a staged augmentation is needed, I stage it or refer.”
Q
Explain the socket classification you have just used.
“Elian: Type 1 — intact buccal plate and intact soft tissue. Type 2 — soft tissue present but the buccal plate is
partly or wholly missing beneath it. Type 3 — both the buccal plate and the overlying soft tissue are deficient.
It is useful because it tells you immediately whether you are managing a hard tissue problem, a soft tissue
problem, or both. Here it is both.”
Q
Make the case for the resin-bonded bridge instead.
“It avoids implanting into a compromised site altogether. With soft tissue augmentation under an ovate pontic
the emergence can be excellent, and a pontic papilla is more predictable than an implant papilla. The prepa-
ration on the 11 is minimal and essentially reversible. In a site that has lost 8 mm of buccal wall, it may well
give a better aesthetic result for less biological risk — and I would say that honestly rather than assume she has
come for an implant.”
Q
Argue against it.
“Debonding is the principal complication, and a teacher who talks all day will notice it at the worst moment; a
single-retainer cantilever design in cobalt-chromium reduces but does not eliminate it. It also commits the 11
to being part of the restoration, it can grey the incisal third of the abutment tooth, and it does not maintain the
ridge. It is a good option, not a free one.”
Q
Your colleague says he would place an immediate implant with simultaneous grafting. Why might he be right?
“Because immediate placement with simultaneous contour grafting preserves the soft tissue architecture, re-
duces the number of surgical episodes, and in experienced hands with an intact palatal wall and good primary
stability it has respectable outcomes even in compromised sockets. Extraction site infection of endodontic origin
is not an absolute contraindication if the site is thoroughly debrided. My answer is that the evidence supports
it in selected cases with an intact facial wall — and this site has none — and that it sits beyond my level of
practice.”
Q
What is the SAC classification?
“Surgically Complex — aesthetic zone, an extensive buccal defect, and infection at the site. Prosthodontically
Advanced to Complex for a single anterior unit with a soft tissue deficiency. The extraction and ridge preser-
vation on their own are Advanced.”
Q
What is within your competence and what is not?
“Within: the diagnosis, the CBCT interpretation, the atraumatic extraction, thorough debridement, ridge preser-
vation, the immediate bonded pontic, and the maintenance. Beyond me: staged vertical augmentation, and

implant placement into a site that still has a major defect at reassessment. I would do the extraction and
preservation myself and co-manage or refer for the reconstruction, having had the options conversation first.”
Q
What would you tell her, in your words to her?
“‘This tooth has been treated three times and it is not going to get better — the infection has eaten away the
bone at the front of it. I need to take it out, clean the area properly and put a graft in to hold the shape.
You will not be without a tooth at any point. In about four months I will scan it again and we will decide
together whether an implant is sensible or whether a bridge would give you a better-looking result. What
I cannot promise you is that the gum will look identical to the other side, and I would rather tell you that
now than at the end.’”
Domain 3 — Decision making in relation to treatment procedures
Chain: the surgery and the graft
Q
Describe the extraction.
“Flapless wherever possible, to preserve what soft tissue blood supply remains. Remove the post crown first
if it improves access. Sever the ligament with a periotome or fine luxators, section if necessary, and deliver
with rotational movements — no buccal luxation against a wall that is already missing. Then curette all the
granulation tissue and the sinus tract thoroughly, irrigate copiously with saline, and inspect and probe the
defect to map its walls.”
Q
Why is complete removal of the sinus tract important?
“Because epithelialised tract tissue left behind will not heal, it maintains a route of contamination into the graft,
and it can produce a persistent soft tissue depression or fistula. The graft has no chance in an incompletely
debrided site — debridement is the step that determines whether everything after it works.”
Q
What do you graft with, and why?
“A slowly resorbing xenograft — deproteinised bovine bone mineral — because in a site I want to hold di-
mensionally for four months, slow substitution is the point. It maintains ridge contour better than a rapidly
resorbing material. I would cover it with a resorbable collagen membrane tucked under the buccal soft tissue,
and seal the coronal aspect.”
Q
How do you seal the socket without primary closure?
“With a free gingival punch graft from the palate or a collagen matrix over the entrance, secured with a figure-
of-eight or crossed mattress suture. I avoid advancing a flap for primary closure because it drags keratinised
tissue coronally and flattens the vestibule, which then has to be undone before the definitive restoration. Keep-
ing the mucogingival line where it is saves a procedure later.”
Q
What are the principles of successful guided bone regeneration?
“The PASS principles: Primary wound closure or a stable seal; Angiogenesis, so decortication of the recipient
bed and preservation of blood supply; Space maintenance, so a graft or membrane that will not collapse; and
Stability of the clot and the graft, meaning fixation and no micromovement. If any one of those four fails, the
graft fails.”
Q
What temporary restoration would you provide?
“An immediate bonded pontic — her own crown or a denture tooth bonded to the 11 and 22 — with the tissue
surface fully relieved off the graft. It is aesthetic from day one, it does not load the site, and it avoids the acrylic
denture pressing on a fresh graft, which is a common cause of membrane exposure and graft loss. An Essix
retainer with the ridge relieved is the alternative.”
Q
At four months the ridge is still deficient buccally. What then?

“Staged horizontal augmentation: decortication of the recipient bed, a composite graft of autogenous bone
and xenograft, a collagen membrane, and tension-free primary closure, with 6 to 9 months of healing before
implant placement. That is at the upper limit of what I would undertake. If the defect were vertical as well
as horizontal, I would refer — vertical augmentation is the least predictable procedure in the field and has the
highest complication rate.”
Q
The membrane becomes exposed at two weeks. What do you do?
“Do not attempt to re-cover it by advancing a flap over infected tissue. Manage it conservatively: chlorhexidine
gel applied locally, no brushing over the site, weekly review, and antibiotics only if there is spreading infection.
A small exposure of a resorbable membrane over a xenograft often heals with partial graft loss. If it becomes
purulent and the graft is mobile, remove the graft, let the site heal, and re-plan.”
Q
What would you record?
“The diagnosis and the reasoning for extraction; the CBCT justification and full report under IR(ME)R; the
options discussed and declined, including the bridge, in her words; the specific risks named — graft exposure
and failure, a shorter crown, a flatter contour, a black triangle, the possibility that an implant proves impossible;
the materials, lot numbers and batch details of graft and membrane; photographs; and the timescale and costs
given.”
Domain 4 — Interpretation and problem solving of clinical outcomes
Chain: judging and salvaging the result
Q
What will you measure at reassessment?
“Resolution of the sinus first — that is the primary indicator that the infection is gone. Then radiographic
healing of the periapical area; ridge width and height at four months against the pre-extraction CBCT; soft
tissue quality and the width of keratinised tissue; and, after restoration, the mid-facial margin level and papilla
index against the 11 and 22, standardised photographs, and peri-implant probing and bone levels against a
baseline taken at fitting.”
Q
The sinus has not resolved at four months. What is going on?
“Incomplete debridement of the tract or of granulation tissue, most likely. Then a retained root fragment or
foreign body, an infected graft, or a pathology I have misdiagnosed — so I would consider whether this was
ever purely endodontic. I would re-image, explore and re-debride, and I would not place an implant into a site
with an unresolved sinus under any circumstances.”
Q
What is the most likely long-term disappointment?
“A shorter clinical crown and a flatter buccal contour than the contralateral central, and possibly a black tri-
angle mesially or distally. Those follow directly from 8 mm of lost buccal plate — they are predictable, which
is why they belong in the consent conversation.”
Q
How do you prevent that becoming a complaint?
“By showing her at the mock-up stage and agreeing in advance whether pink ceramic is acceptable, rather than
discovering her view at the fit appointment. Photograph the mock-up, record her approval, and give her the
option of stopping at that point. The mock-up is the honest preview — I would far rather she rejected the plan
there than be disappointed at the end.”
Q
At two years the implant crown has 1 mm of mid-facial recession. Your approach?
“Exclude inflammation first, with probing, bleeding and a radiograph, and treat it if present — some apparent
recession resolves. Check for an over-contoured crown or residual cement. If it persists and the implant
is otherwise healthy, a connective tissue graft with a coronally advanced flap may improve it, though less
predictably than around a tooth. If the implant is malpositioned, the honest answer is prosthetic camouflage or
explantation.”

Q
How would you know this treatment had succeeded?
“That she teaches all day without thinking about the tooth. Objectively: the sinus resolved and never recurred,
the implant stable with no bleeding or suppuration, bone levels stable against baseline, an acceptable Pink and
White Aesthetic Score, and her own rating measured against what she told me she wanted at the very first visit.”
WATCH OUT
Go back to the defect: name which walls are missing, whether the deficiency is horizontal, vertical or both, and
whether the problem is hard tissue, soft tissue or infection. That frame answers most questions in this case and
buys you a sentence of thinking time.
Running this case to time
Time check. The flow above holds 37 questions and about 2,590 words of model answer. At 140 words
a minute plus roughly five seconds a question, that is a little over twenty-one minutes — an overrun of
about six and a half. What goes first is the staged augmentation material in Domain 3: decortication, the
composite autograft-and-xenograft, tension-free primary closure and the 6-to-9-month wait compress into
one question, because that procedure sits above your competence line anyway and the examiner would
rather hear you say so than describe it. The endodontic aetiology in Domain 1 gets sampled rather than
recited. If your answers run past thirty seconds, you will never reach Domain 4 — and Domain 4 is where
the unresolved sinus is.
The fifteen-minute run sheet
Clock
The examiner does
What earns the mark
0:00–0:20
Settles you, confirms the case, puts the
CBCT slices up
Nothing. Do not talk into this.
0:20–1:20
Lets you present, uninterrupted
A fit, non-smoking 38-year-old teacher
with a failed, apicected 21 — two root
treatments, an apicectomy, a chronic
buccal sinus, a post crown and a 6 mm
buccal pocket — and the decisive CBCT
finding: a large periapical lesion with
loss of the buccal plate over 8 mm. Then
the interpretation: the tooth is not
salvageable, so the decision is not
whether to extract but how to manage a
site that has already lost its buccal wall,
in a medium smile line and an
occupation that puts her in front of
people all day. What you must still
establish: the interproximal bone on the
11 and 22, what her smile actually shows,
and what she expects.

Clock
The examiner does
What earns the mark
1:20–4:30
Domain 1: the endodontic and periapical
groundwork, then reading this patient
Chronic apical periodontitis with a
sinus tract, and the point that scores —
the sinus is why she has no pain, and
there is no pulp to test because the tooth
is previously treated. Failure causes
ranked: persistent intraradicular
infection first, then coronal leakage, then
extraradicular infection or a true cyst,
then non-endodontic causes — and after
two orthograde attempts and an
apicectomy you are thinking root
fracture or true cyst. The 6 mm pocket
reinterpreted: most probably a sinus
tract draining along the root through
the sulcus, not attachment loss —
confirmed by tracing with a
gutta-percha point — and why the
distinction changes what you expect of
the papillae. Then the buccal plate:
under 1 mm in most central incisor sites,
largely bundle bone, and Schropp’s 50%
width loss in the first year, two-thirds
of it in three months superimposed on
an existing 8 mm dehiscence. And
Tarnow again: the papilla belongs to the
11 and 22, and if their interproximal
bone is gone you cannot recreate it.
4:30–7:30
Domain 2: choosing between the options
The options listed with no treatment
named and dismissed for a reason,
retreatment given its poor prognosis, and
the two real contenders set against each
other. Immediate placement ruled out
against the ITI decision tree — an intact
socket with at least 1 mm of facial wall,
adequate apical and palatal bone, thick
phenotype, no acute infection — none of
which she has. The plan: flapless
atraumatic extraction, thorough
curettage of the lesion and the tract,
ridge preservation recognised as only
partially effective in an Elian Type 3
socket, a bonded pontic the same day,
and reassessment at four months with a
CBCT. Elian given properly — Type 1
intact, Type 2 plate missing beneath
intact soft tissue, Type 3 both deficient.
Then the honesty that separates a 3 from
a 5: the resin-bonded cantilever with an
ovate pontic argued for on its merits —
a pontic papilla is more predictable
than an implant papilla — before it is
argued against on debonding. The
colleague’s immediate implant granted
its evidence in selected cases with an
intact facial wall, and refused because
this site has none. SAC: surgically
Complex.

Clock
The examiner does
What earns the mark
7:30–11:30
Domain 3: the surgery and the graft
The competence line volunteered here,
not extracted: yours are the diagnosis,
the CBCT interpretation, the atraumatic
flapless extraction, thorough
debridement, ridge preservation, the
immediate bonded pontic and the
maintenance; beyond you are staged
vertical augmentation and implant
placement into a site still holding a
major defect at reassessment — do the
extraction and preservation yourself and
co-manage or refer the reconstruction.

periotome or fine luxators, no buccal
luxation against a wall that is already
missing; complete removal of the tract,
because debridement is the step that
determines whether everything after it
works; a slowly resorbing xenograft
chosen precisely because you want the
site held dimensionally for four months;
a resorbable collagen membrane; and
the socket sealed with a free gingival
punch or collagen matrix rather than an
advanced flap, because advancing drags
keratinised tissue coronally and flattens
the vestibule you will need later. PASS
named and expanded. The provisional a
bonded pontic fully relieved off the
graft, not a denture pressing on it.
11:30–14:30
Domain 4: judging and salvaging the
result
What is measured at reassessment,
resolution of the sinus first — that is the
primary indicator the infection is gone.
Then the unresolved sinus given a
differential in order: incomplete
debridement most likely, then a
retained fragment or foreign body, an
infected graft, or a misdiagnosis — and
the absolute: you would not place an
implant into a site with an unresolved
sinus under any circumstances. The
membrane exposed at two weeks
managed conservatively —
chlorhexidine gel, no brushing, weekly
review, antibiotics only for spreading
infection, and no attempt to re-cover it
by advancing a flap over infected tissue.

disappointment named before you are
asked: a shorter clinical crown, a flatter
buccal contour, and possibly a black
triangle — predictable, which is exactly
why they belong in the consent
conversation.

The examiner does
What earns the mark

In her words: “This tooth has been treated
three times and it is not going to get better —
the infection has eaten away the bone at the
front of it… You will not be without a tooth at
any point. In about four months I will scan it
again and we will decide together whether an
implant is sensible or whether a bridge would
give you a better-looking result. What I
cannot promise you is that the gum will look
identical to the other side, and I would rather
tell you that now than at the end.”
Recorded: the diagnosis and reasoning,
the IR(ME)R justification and a report
of the whole volume, the options
including the bridge in her words, the
specific risks — graft exposure, a shorter
crown, a flatter contour, a black triangle,
the possibility that an implant proves
impossible — the lot numbers of graft
and membrane, photographs, timescale
and costs.
The spine — the twelve answers to have ready if nothing else
1 Chronic apical periodontitis with a sinus tract, and why she has no pain · 2 Why root treatments fail, and
what two failures plus an apicectomy suggest · 3 What the 6 mm buccal pocket actually is, and how you
prove it · 4 The buccal plate — thickness, bundle bone, and what happens after extraction · 5 Tarnow, and
why the papilla belongs to the 11 and 22 · 6 Why the palatal wall decides whether an implant is possible
at all · 7 The ITI criteria for immediate placement, and which ones she fails · 8 Elian Type 1, 2 and 3 · 9
The resin-bonded cantilever argued for, then against · 10 Debridement of the tract, and why it decides
everything after it · 11 PASS, and why you seal rather than advance a flap · 12 The sinus that has not
resolved at four months.
Where the marks are lost in this case
Racing to the implant. The examiner has put 8 mm of missing buccal plate and a discharging sinus in
front of you to see whether you notice that this is a grafting and infection problem before it is an implant
problem. Volunteer that immediate placement is ruled out against the ITI criteria, name Elian Type 3,
and say that the four-month reassessment is a genuine decision point, not a formality — because it may
still end in a bridge.
Never offering the bridge honestly. The resin-bonded cantilever with soft tissue augmentation under
an ovate pontic is a real answer here, and in a site that has lost its buccal wall it may give a better aesthetic
result for less biological risk — a pontic papilla is more predictable than an implant papilla. Candidates
who list it and move on have missed the mark; argue it properly, then argue it down on debonding in a
teacher who talks all day.
Never naming what you would not attempt. Extraction, debridement, ridge preservation and the bonded
pontic are yours. Staged vertical augmentation is not — it is the least predictable procedure in the field
with the highest complication rate — nor is placing into a site that still has a major defect at four months,
nor into one where the sinus has not resolved. Say it at the outset and say who it goes to. Describing an
augmentation you would never perform is worse than admitting you would refer it.

soe.title: The furcation-involved molar
soe.text:
SOE Case 22 — The furcation-involved molar
THE CASE
55-year-old, non-smoker, well-controlled hypertension. The 46 has a grade III buccal and lingual furcation
involvement, 9 mm pockets, grade II mobility and a failed crown. The rest of the mouth is periodontally stable
(BPE 1/1/1 elsewhere).
Pace: one structured opening of about 60 seconds, then roughly 35 questions in the remaining 14 minutes. Nothing after the opening earns you
more than a few seconds of thought.
Opening — the 60-second presentation
Q
Present this case.
“A 55-year-old non-smoker with well-controlled hypertension and a single failing lower first molar. The 46 has
a through-and-through furcation, 9 mm pockets, grade II mobility and a failed crown, while the rest of the
mouth charts at BPE 1. That mismatch is the striking feature: advanced localised destruction in an otherwise
healthy mouth is not the pattern of generalised periodontitis, so my working diagnosis is a local cause —
an endodontic-periodontal lesion, a vertical root fracture or an iatrogenic perforation — and I would establish
which before condemning the tooth. Whatever the cause, a grade III furcation with grade II mobility carries a
poor long-term prognosis. The questions I need to answer are why this tooth alone has failed, whether it is
restorable at all, and what he wants done about the space.”
Domain 1 — Clinical interpretation and reasoning
Chain: the periodontal groundwork
Q
What is a furcation involvement?
“Loss of attachment and bone in the inter-radicular area of a multi-rooted tooth, such that a probe passes into
the space between the roots. It is not a separate disease — it is periodontitis, or a local lesion, reaching an
anatomical site that cannot be instrumented properly and that the patient cannot clean. That is why furcation
involvement is treated as a prognostic marker and not simply as another measurement.”
Q
How do you classify it?
“Hamp classifies it horizontally: Degree I is horizontal loss of less than a third of the tooth width, Degree II is
more than a third but not through-and-through, and Degree III is through-and-through. Glickman’s classifica-
tion is comparable, with Grade IV being a through-and-through that is clinically visible because the tissue has
receded. I measure with a Nabers probe, buccally and lingually, and record both.”
Q
Why is a lower first molar so vulnerable to this?
“The furcation entrance is frequently narrower than a curette blade — commonly under 1 mm — so it cannot
be debrided properly. The roof of the furcation lies only 3 to 4 mm below the amelocemental junction, so little
attachment loss is needed to reach it. Add root concavities, cervical enamel projections or enamel pearls,
and accessory canals in the furcation floor, and it becomes the classic site for both periodontal and endodontic
involvement.”
Q
Grade II mobility — define the grades.
“On Miller, Grade I is horizontal movement up to 1 mm, Grade II is horizontal movement of more than 1 mm,
and Grade III is horizontal movement plus vertical depressibility. Mobility is a sign, not a diagnosis. I would
separate mobility from irreversible attachment loss, which will not improve, from mobility due to an inflamed
periodontium or occlusal trauma, which often does improve with treatment.”
Q
How would you diagnose him under the 2017 World Workshop?

“With a single affected tooth in a BPE 1 mouth, I would first exclude a non-periodontitis cause, because periodon-
titis requires interproximal attachment loss at two or more non-adjacent teeth. If periodontitis were confirmed,
a grade III furcation and the anticipated tooth loss put it at Stage III or IV, graded by rate of progression against
age and risk factors, with an extent descriptor of localised.”
Q
Does the hypertension matter?
“Not to the diagnosis. To the treatment in three ways: a blood pressure reading before any surgery and a
threshold above which I defer; awareness that some antihypertensives cause xerostomia or postural hypoten-
sion; and that calcium channel blockers cause gingival overgrowth. I would confirm the actual drug, the last
recorded reading and who monitors him, and record all three.”
Chain: reading this particular tooth
Q
What is your differential for a single tooth behaving like this?
“A primary endodontic lesion draining through the furcation, which is common in molars with accessory
canals in the furcation floor. A vertical root fracture beneath the crown. An iatrogenic furcation perforation
from a post or crown preparation. Or genuinely localised periodontitis driven by a plaque-retentive factor —
an overhang or an open margin on that failed crown.”
Q
What investigations?
“Sensibility testing with cold and electric pulp test, compared against adjacent and contralateral teeth. Periapi-
cals at two horizontal angles. Six-point charting with Nabers probing buccally and lingually, and a check for a
narrow isolated defect suggesting fracture. Assessment for a crack under magnification and transillumination,
with the crown removed if need be. And a small field-of-view CBCT if fracture or perforation is suspected,
which also gives me the implant planning data.”
Q
If it proves non-vital and the lesion is endodontic in origin, does that change things?
“Potentially. A primary endodontic lesion with secondary periodontal involvement can respond dramatically
to root canal treatment, and I would reassess at three months before condemning the tooth. But a genuine
through-and-through furcation with grade II mobility rarely resolves. I would be honest that this is buying
time rather than curing, and only attempt it if he understood that.”
Domain 2 — Clinical decision making and treatment planning
Chain: can the tooth be kept?
Q
What are the options for the 46?
“Retain and treat — non-surgical therapy, then possibly furcation surgery, root resection or a tunnel preparation.
Extract and leave the space, accepting a shortened arch. Extract and place an implant. Extract and bridge
from the 45 to the 47. Extract and provide a partial denture. Each has to be set against the fact that this tooth’s
prognosis is already poor before I start.”
Q
Talk me through root resection and tunnelling.
“Root resection removes one root and its part of the crown, leaving a restorable remainder — but survival
figures are modest, root fracture and recurrent caries are common, and it demands root canal treatment plus a
complex restoration. Tunnel preparation opens the furcation for an interdental brush, at high risk of root caries.
Both are Complex procedures, both are declining in use, and neither is what I would offer here.”
Q
Tell me about the shortened dental arch.
“The concept that a dentition of around 20 teeth, with premolar-to-premolar occlusion, gives adequate function,
comfort and stability without replacing molars. There is good long-term evidence for it. Here, if the 47 is sound
and in occlusion and the arch is stable, extracting the 46 and leaving the space is a legitimate definitive plan,
not a failure — and it must be offered.”

Q
You said the shortened arch is legitimate. Argue against it in this patient.
“At 55 he has a long time to live with the consequences. If the 47 is unopposed or already tilted, the space may
not stay stable — I would expect over-eruption of the 16 and mesial tipping of the 47. If he is a heavy function
patient the load redistributes onto fewer units. And if he later wants the tooth replaced, the ridge will have
resorbed further and the site will be harder.”
Q
What do you recommend?
“Extraction with ridge preservation, given the volume of interradicular bone likely already lost, then reassess-
ment at four months and a single implant at the 46 if the site allows. I would section the tooth to preserve the
plates. If the residual height or width is inadequate at reassessment, I would revert to the shortened arch rather
than escalate to grafting.”
Q
Would you place immediately into the molar socket?
“No. Immediate placement in a molar site relies on the inter-radicular septum for primary stability, and in a
grade III furcation the septum is precisely what has been destroyed. There is also active infection. Immediate
placement is contraindicated here, and forcing it risks a malpositioned implant with poor stability.”
Q
A colleague would still place immediately into the septum with a wide implant and graft the gaps. Why might they
be right?
“Because in a molar socket with a substantial intact septum and no suppuration, immediate placement shortens
treatment, preserves the socket walls, and there is reasonable evidence for it in experienced hands. Their
argument is that waiting guarantees resorption. My answer is that it is Advanced on SAC and dependent
on a septum this patient does not have — the technique is defensible, the case selection is not.”
Chain: scope, consent and the conversation
Q
What is the SAC classification here?
“The extraction with ridge preservation and a delayed single implant in a healed posterior mandible is
Straightforward to Advanced — Straightforward prosthodontically in a non-aesthetic site, Advanced surgically
because of proximity to the inferior alveolar canal and an unpredictable healed volume. Immediate placement,
block grafting or vertical augmentation at this site would be Complex and beyond my competence — I would
refer.”
Q
What would you tell him, in your own words to him?
“ ‘The bone between the roots of this tooth has been destroyed, and the tooth is loose. I don’t think we can keep
it reliably. My plan is to take it out carefully, put a graft into the socket to hold the shape, and let it heal for about
four months. Then we look again. If there’s enough bone, an implant is a good option. If there isn’t, leaving the
gap is a perfectly reasonable place to stop — plenty of people function very well without that tooth.’ ”
Q
What would you record at this appointment?
“The six-point chart and the Nabers readings buccally and lingually, the mobility grade, the sensibility results,
the radiographs and their report, the blood pressure and medication, my diagnosis and prognosis for the 46,
every option discussed including no treatment and the shortened arch, the risks I named, the costs quoted, and
that he was given time and written information before consenting.”
Domain 3 — Decision making in relation to treatment procedures
Chain: what happens to a socket
Q
What happens to an extraction socket if you do nothing?
“A clot organises into granulation tissue, then provisional woven bone, then remodels to lamellar bone over
months. Externally the ridge resorbs — most of the dimensional change occurs in the first three to six months,
with horizontal loss of the order of half the ridge width and greater loss buccally than lingually. The socket is
radiographically filling long before the ridge stops shrinking.”

Q
Why does the buccal plate resorb the most?
“Because in most sites it is thinner, and because a significant part of it is bundle bone — the bone into which
the periodontal ligament fibres insert. Bundle bone is tooth-dependent; when the tooth goes, its blood supply
and its function go with it, so it resorbs. That is the mechanism behind the classic loss of buccal contour.”
Q
So what does ridge preservation actually achieve?
“It does not prevent resorption — it reduces and slows it, typically limiting horizontal and vertical loss by a few
millimetres compared with unassisted healing, and it makes the volume more predictable. That is enough to
change whether a site can take an implant without further grafting. It is a socket management technique, not
an augmentation, and I would not oversell it to him.”
Q
Describe the extraction.
“Local anaesthetic, atraumatic technique. I would section the tooth at the furcation with a bur and deliver
each root separately using periotomes and root forceps, rather than trying to lever out a mobile, furcated molar
whole — sectioning protects the buccal and lingual plates, which are what I need. Then thorough curettage of
all granulation tissue and irrigation, and I would inspect the socket walls directly.”
Q
And the ridge preservation itself.
“Once the socket is clean and the walls assessed, I graft with a slowly resorbing xenograft placed to the level of
the crest without over-packing, and seal it — a resorbable collagen membrane tucked under the flap margins,
or a collagen plug or free gingival socket seal graft. Secure with a figure-of-eight suture. No primary closure
that drags keratinised tissue across, and no flap advancement that shifts the mucogingival line.”
Q
How long would you wait?
“A molar socket is large, so at least four months, and I would prefer five to six. I want the graft consolidated
enough to drill without it crumbling. I would reassess clinically and with a CBCT at that point rather than
assuming the healed volume — a furcation lesion may leave a defect well below the level of the surrounding
crest.”
Q
Implant selection at reassessment?
“From the CBCT: a wide-diameter implant of around 5 mm if the width allows 1.5 to 2 mm of bone buccally
and lingually, and a length that leaves at least 2 mm of clearance above the inferior alveolar canal. A molar
occlusal table on a narrow implant is a mechanical mistake — I want diameter here rather than length. Bone is
likely D2, so I would countersink and watch the insertion torque.”
Q
If that leaves only 7 mm of usable height?
“Then I use a short, wide implant. The evidence for short implants in the posterior mandible is now good —
survival comparable to longer implants with augmentation, and fewer complications, because the graft is what
carries the risk. I would keep the crown-to-implant ratio in mind, keep the occlusal table narrow, and accept a
short implant in preference to vertical augmentation, which I would refer.”
Q
How do you keep away from the nerve?
“Plan from the CBCT, not the panoramic, and measure from the crest to the superior border of the canal at the
exact planned site. Build in a 2 mm safety margin above the canal for measurement error and drill overshoot.
Identify the mental foramen if the incision runs forward. Use drill stops and a surgical guide, check with a
direction indicator and periapical, and use infiltration rather than a block so he can report a sharp sensation.”
Q
One stage or two?
“One stage with a healing abutment if primary stability is good, there is adequate keratinised tissue and I
have not grafted at placement. Two stage if primary stability is poor, if I have had to graft simultaneously, or if
soft tissue closure would be compromised. In a posterior mandible with a healed preserved ridge, one stage is
usually achievable and saves him a second procedure.”

Domain 4 — Interpretation and problem solving of clinical outcomes
Chain: what can go wrong, and what you do about it
Q
What are the main risks in this case?
“Nerve injury, because it is a molar site whose height may be reduced by the furcation destruction. Inadequate
primary stability if the grafted socket has not consolidated. A residual defect at reassessment forcing simulta-
neous grafting or abandonment. And restoratively, the mechanical complications of molar loading — screw
loosening, ceramic chipping — on a single implant carrying a wide occlusal table.”
Q
The day after surgery he reports numbness of the lower lip. What do you do?
“See him the same day. Map and record the affected area, test with light touch, sharp-blunt and two-point
discrimination, and document it — including whether it is anaesthesia, paraesthesia or painful dysaesthesia.
Take a radiograph or CBCT to see whether the implant is impinging on the canal; if it is, remove or back it out
promptly, within about 36 hours. Reassure, review, prescribe as indicated, and refer early if it is not settling.”
Q
How would you restore it?
“Conventional loading at about three months, implant-level impression or intraoral scan with a scan body. A
screw-retained monolithic zirconia crown with a narrow occlusal table, light contact in intercuspation, no
working or non-working excursive contact, a cleansable emergence profile, and no cement subgingivally. Screw
retention because retrievability matters most in exactly the site where mechanical complications happen.”
Q
At three years the crown feels loose. Differential and management?
“Abutment screw loosening is much the commonest and is what I expect. Then a fractured screw, a fractured
abutment, a failed cement seal if it were cemented, or a failing implant. I would take a periapical, remove the
crown, inspect the components, check the occlusion and the excursive contacts for the cause, replace the screw
and torque it to the manufacturer’s value. Repeated loosening means the occlusion or the design is wrong, not
the screw.”
Q
How would you monitor him?
“Six-monthly, given a stable periodontal condition. Six-point peri-implant probing with bleeding and suppu-
ration, plaque control, marginal bone level against the baseline periapical taken at fitting, occlusal review and
screw integrity, and the periodontal status of the remaining dentition. Radiographs at one year and then as
clinically indicated.”
Q
How would you know this had succeeded?
“That he chews comfortably on that side and has stopped thinking about the tooth. Objectively: the implant
stable with no bleeding or suppuration, bone levels stable against baseline, the crown intact with a maintained
occlusion, the adjacent 45 and 47 unharmed, and the rest of the mouth still at BPE 1 — because in this patient
the untouched periodontal health of the other teeth is the real measure.”
WATCH OUT
Fall back to four questions about the failing tooth — is it restorable, is it endodontically treatable, is it periodon-
tally maintainable, and what does the patient actually want — and say out loud which of the four fails. It buys
a sentence and it is nearly always the right frame for a questionable tooth.
Running this case to time
Time check. The flow above holds 36 questions and about 2,412 words of model answer. At 140 words a
minute plus roughly five seconds a question, that is a little over twenty minutes — an overrun of about
five. What goes first is the root resection and tunnelling material in Domain 2: both are declining in
use, both are Complex, and neither is what you would offer, so they compress into one sentence of
acknowledgement. The marks here sit in the differential for a single failing tooth in a BPE 1 mouth,
in the shortened dental arch offered as a definitive plan, and in the canal. If your answers run past
thirty seconds, you will never reach Domain 4 — and Domain 4 is where the numb lip appears.
