leave a defect well below the crest.
Implant selection: wide, around 5 mm,
with 1.5 to 2 mm of bone buccally and
lingually, and at least 2 mm above the
canal — diameter here rather than
length, because a molar occlusal table on
a narrow implant is a mechanical
mistake. At 7 mm of height, a short wide
implant in preference to vertical
augmentation, which you refer. Nerve
safety: CBCT not panoramic, 2 mm
margin, drill stops and a guide,
infiltration rather than a block.
11:30–14:30
Domain 4: what can go wrong, and what
you do about it
The risks named in order — nerve
injury, inadequate primary stability in
an unconsolidated graft, a residual
defect at reassessment, and the
mechanical complications of molar
loading on a single implant. The numb
lip the next day: see him the same day,
map and record, anaesthesia versus
paraesthesia versus painful
dysaesthesia, radiograph or CBCT, and
back the implant out within about 36
hours, then refer early if it is not
settling. The restoration: conventional
loading at three months, screw-retained
monolithic zirconia, narrow occlusal
table, light contact, no excursive
contact, cleansable emergence, no
subgingival cement — screw retention
because retrievability matters most in
exactly the site where mechanical
complications happen. The loose crown
at three years given a differential, with
the volunteered line: repeated loosening
means the occlusion or the design is
wrong, not the screw. Six-monthly
review, six-point probing, bone level
against the baseline periapical taken at
fitting.

Clock
The examiner does
What earns the mark
14:30–15:00
Closes on the patient and the record
In his words: “The bone between the roots of
this tooth has been destroyed, and the tooth is
loose. I don’t think we can keep it reliably… If
there’s enough bone, an implant is a good
option. If there isn’t, leaving the gap is a
perfectly reasonable place to stop — plenty of
people function very well without that tooth.”
Recorded: the six-point chart and the
Nabers readings buccally and lingually,
mobility grade, sensibility results,
radiographs and their report, the blood
pressure and the medication, the
diagnosis and prognosis for the 46, every
option including no treatment and the
shortened arch, the risks, the costs, and
that he had time and written information
before consenting. And the measure of
success: the rest of the mouth still at
BPE 1 — in this patient, the untouched
periodontal health of the other teeth is
the real outcome.
The spine — the twelve answers to have ready if nothing else
1 Why one tooth failing in a BPE 1 mouth changes the diagnosis · 2 Furcation involvement defined, and
why it is a prognostic marker · 3 Hamp, the Nabers probe, and both aspects recorded · 4 Why a lower
first molar is the classic site · 5 Miller mobility, and mobility as a sign not a diagnosis · 6 The differential
— endo-perio, vertical fracture, perforation, plaque-retentive factor · 7 Hypertension in three lines · 8 The
shortened dental arch offered as a definitive plan, then argued against · 9 Why immediate placement fails
here — the septum is what has been destroyed · 10 Ridge preservation reduces, it does not prevent · 11
Wide and short in preference to augmenting, with 2 mm above the canal · 12 The numb lip, and the 36-hour
window.
Where the marks are lost in this case
Extracting the tooth in the first sentence. The examiner has deliberately given you advanced destruction
at one tooth in a BPE 1 mouth. Say in the opening that this pattern is not generalised periodontitis and
name the local differential — endo-perio lesion, vertical root fracture, iatrogenic perforation — then
say you would sensibility-test and reassess at three months if it proves endodontic. Candidates who
condemn the 46 before testing it have failed Domain 1 in thirty seconds.
Treating the gap as a foregone conclusion. The shortened dental arch is a legitimate endpoint here
and it must be offered, in Käyser’s terms, as a positive plan rather than the option of last resort — and
it is also your fallback if the reassessment CBCT is disappointing, which is the judgement the case is
really testing. Say out loud that you would revert to the shortened arch rather than escalate to vertical
augmentation.
Never naming what you would not attempt. Sectional extraction, ridge preservation and a delayed single
implant in adequate native bone are yours. What is not: immediate placement into this socket — the
septum has gone — block grafting, vertical augmentation, or any plan that needs less than 2 mm above
the inferior alveolar canal. Say it before the surgical chain begins, and say that a short wide implant is
the answer you would reach for instead of a graft.

soe.title: The failing three-unit bridge
soe.text:
SOE Case 23 — The failing three-unit bridge
THE CASE
62-year-old woman with an upper right 14–16 conventional bridge placed 18 years ago. The 16 abutment has
recurrent caries to the gingival level and is non-vital; the 14 abutment is sound. She is anxious about “losing
more teeth” and wants “something permanent”.
Pace: one structured opening of about 60 seconds, then roughly 35 questions in the remaining 14 minutes. Nothing after the opening earns you
more than a few seconds of thought.
Opening — the 60-second presentation
Q
Present this case.
“A 62-year-old woman with an 18-year-old three-unit bridge from the 14 to the 16 that has failed at the distal
abutment. The 16 has recurrent caries to gingival level and is non-vital; the 14 appears sound. Eighteen years
is respectable service, and the mode of failure — caries at the margin of an abutment — is the commonest way
conventional bridges end. The decision turns on two things: whether the 16 is restorable, which I cannot judge
until the bridge is off, and what the 14 needs once it loses its retainer. She is anxious about losing more teeth
and wants something permanent, so expectation management is as much a part of this case as the restorative
decision. My immediate need is to remove the bridge, assess both abutments directly, and give her a provisional
so she is never without teeth.”
Domain 1 — Clinical interpretation and reasoning
Chain: fixed prosthodontic groundwork
Q
Name the components of a conventional fixed bridge.
“The abutment is the tooth; the retainer is the restoration cemented to it; the pontic replaces the missing tooth;
and the connector joins pontic to retainer, either rigid or non-rigid. This one is a fixed-fixed design with rigid
connectors and two abutments, which means a failure at one end effectively condemns the whole unit.”
Q
What are the commonest reasons a conventional bridge fails?
“Caries at an abutment margin is the commonest, followed by loss of vitality and periapical disease, then loss
of retention or decementation, then periodontal breakdown of an abutment, then mechanical failure — porce-
lain fracture or connector fracture. Around 90% survive to ten years, so failure at eighteen is not a treatment
error; it is the natural history.”
Q
What is Ante’s law, and do you believe it?
“That the root surface area of the abutments should equal or exceed that of the teeth being replaced. It is a useful
instinct rather than a rule — the evidence does not support it as a hard predictor of survival, and periodontally
reduced but stable abutments can carry bridges successfully. I use it as one factor alongside mobility, crown-to-
root ratio and occlusal load.”
Q
How do you decide whether the 16 is restorable?
“Four things: how far the caries extends subgingivally and whether I can reach a sound margin; how much
ferrule remains; the root and furcation anatomy; and whether it is endodontically treatable. I would remove
all caries first and then judge — deciding restorability with the bridge still on is guesswork.”
Q
What is the ferrule effect, and how much do you need?
“A circumferential band of the crown that grips sound tooth structure coronal to the preparation finish line,
so that occlusal load is transferred to the root rather than levering the post. I want at least 1.5 to 2 mm of height
with a 1 mm wall thickness, circumferentially. Ferrule is a better predictor of survival of a post-retained tooth
than the post design itself.”

Q
If the margin is subgingival, what is the biological constraint?
“The supracrestal tissue attachment — what used to be called biologic width — roughly 2 mm of junctional
epithelium and connective tissue attachment above the bone crest. I need about 3 mm from the restoration
margin to the alveolar crest to allow for that plus a sulcus. Violating it gives chronic inflammation, bleeding
and unpredictable recession.”
Q
So crown lengthening or orthodontic extrusion?
“Extrusion preserves bone and the interdental papillae and is kinder to the adjacent 15, but it is slow and needs
a period of stabilisation. Surgical crown lengthening is quicker, but on an upper first molar removing 3 mm of
bone circumferentially will often expose the furcation, and a tooth with an exposed furcation carrying a bridge
retainer is a poor long-term bet. That single fact usually decides this tooth.”
Q
How would you classify a furcation involvement?
“Hamp: Class I is horizontal loss of less than a third of the tooth width, Class II more than a third but not through-
and-through, Class III is through-and-through. The 2017 World Workshop also grades furcation involvement
as part of periodontitis staging. Anything beyond Class I in an abutment I am about to root-treat and crown
makes me much more inclined to extract.”
Q
What radiographs would you take?
“Periapicals of the 14, 16 and 17 with a paralleling technique — I need bone levels, root morphology, the
periapical status of the 16 and the depth of the caries. If an implant becomes the plan I would then consider a
CBCT of the 16 site specifically to measure residual bone height beneath the sinus, justified separately under
IR(ME)R.”
Q
What does her anxiety about “losing more teeth” tell you?
“That the consent conversation is the diﬀicult part of this case, not the dentistry. She may be assuming an
implant is permanent and maintenance-free. If I do not correct that gently and before treatment, every future
complication will feel to her like a betrayal rather than an expected event.”
Domain 2 — Clinical decision making and treatment planning
Chain: generating and testing the options
Q
Give me the options.
“First, remove the bridge and assess — nothing is decidable until then. If the 16 is restorable: root canal
treatment, core and adequate ferrule, then either two separate crowns or a new bridge. If the 16 is unrestorable:
extract it, restore the 14 separately, and for the space either a cantilever from the 14, a new 14–17 bridge, an
implant at the 16, a partial denture, or no replacement.”
Q
What would you recommend?
“Assuming the 16 is unrestorable: extract with ridge preservation, crown the 14 as a single unit, and then give
her a genuine choice between an implant at the 16 and accepting the space with monitoring. She is 62, medically
well and wants something fixed, so an implant is reasonable — but I would confirm the residual height beneath
the sinus first, because an 18-year-old failing molar is usually accompanied by a pneumatised sinus.”
Q
You have not offered a new 14–17 bridge. Argue for it.
“It avoids surgery, is quicker and cheaper, and she already accepts fixed work. But it requires me to prepare
a sound, unrestored 17 — destroying tissue on a healthy tooth to replace one that has already failed — and it
puts three teeth at risk instead of one. In a patient with a sound 14 and a sound 17, that is the argument that
defeats it.”
Q
A colleague would place a cantilever pontic from the 14. Why might they be right?

“Because it involves only a tooth that already needs crowning, avoids surgery entirely, and cantilever bridges
do have acceptable survival — around 80% at ten years — particularly with a single premolar-sized pontic. My
hesitation is that a molar-sized pontic cantilevered from a single premolar creates a substantial lever arm on
an abutment that is already compromised, and the failure mode is decementation or abutment fracture.”
Q
Make the case for leaving the space.
“Shortened dental arch thinking — Käyser’s work showed that an arch of premolars and one molar pair gives
adequate function, comfort and stability without progressive deterioration. If she has a sound 17 in occlusion,
she has a functional arch. That is a positive, evidence-based plan, not a failure to treat, and I would present it
that way rather than as the option of last resort.”
Q
What must you warn her about if she accepts the space?
“Over-eruption of the opposing 46, drifting or tilting of the 15 and 17, and food packing. I would take study
models or a scan as a baseline, review at six and twelve months, and be explicit that if drifting begins, the
implant option becomes harder — so the decision is not indefinitely reversible.”
Q
Classify this case on SAC.
“The 16 site is Advanced if the sinus is pneumatised and grafting is needed, and Straightforward to Advanced
if there is adequate native bone — it is a single posterior unit, non-aesthetic, adjacent teeth intact. Prosthodon-
tically Straightforward. The whole case is complex in decision-making rather than in execution.”
Q
What if there were only 4 mm below the sinus?
“Then the realistic options narrow to a short implant, a lateral window sinus elevation, or no replacement. A
lateral window graft is beyond my competence and I would refer it — as is a transcrestal lift at that residual
height, where the gain required is large and the membrane is at real risk. Given a sound 14 and 17, I would
present the shortened arch positively rather than steer her into a major graft.”
Q
What do you know about short implants?
“Implants of 6 mm or so placed in native bone have shown outcomes comparable with longer implants placed
alongside sinus augmentation at medium-term follow-up, with fewer complications and lower morbidity. The
caveats are a shorter track record, sensitivity to crown-to-implant ratio and occlusal overload, and the need for
a wide diameter and a narrow occlusal table. It is a legitimate option to discuss, not a compromise to apologise
for.”
Q
How would you explain “permanent” to her?
“ ‘Nothing in dentistry is permanent, and I’d rather be honest now than have you disappointed later. An implant
will very likely still be there in ten years — around nine in ten are. But the crown on top is a mechanical thing:
screws can loosen, porcelain can chip, and parts get replaced. And it needs cleaning and check-ups just like a
tooth. What I can promise is that I’ll tell you what’s likely to happen and what it will cost.’ ”
Domain 3 — Decision making in relation to treatment procedures
Chain: taking the bridge off and getting to a stable position
Q
How would you remove the bridge?
“I would try conservative removal first — a crown-and-bridge remover or ultrasonic scaler on the retainer
margins — because the 14 retainer may then be reusable as a provisional. If that fails, section the connector
and section over the 14 retainer, cutting through the metal and lifting it off rather than levering, so I preserve
every millimetre of tooth structure on an abutment I still want.”
Q
What do you do immediately after removal?

“Assess and stabilise. Caries removal on both abutments, a vitality test and a periapical for the 14, and an
honest look at the 16. Then a provisional — a temporary bridge or a temporary crown on the 14 with the space
held — cemented with temporary cement. She must not leave with a visible gap or an unprotected preparation.”
Q
Describe the extraction of the 16.
“Atraumatic and section-based: raise a minimal or no flap, section the tooth into its three roots with a fine bur,
and elevate each root individually along its own path. Periotomes and physics-style forceps rather than crude
luxation. The aim is to preserve the buccal plate and the interproximal bone, because those determine what I
can do next.”
Q
What is ridge preservation, and what does it actually achieve?
“Grafting the socket — typically a slowly resorbing xenograft with a collagen membrane or a resorbable dressing
over it — to limit the dimensional change of the ridge. It does not prevent resorption; it reduces it, typically
preserving 1 to 2 mm of width and height compared with unassisted healing. In a molar site with an intact
septum I would still do it, because the sinus floor drops as the socket resorbs.”
Q
How long before implant placement?
“Four months for a grafted molar socket — enough for soft tissue closure and organisation of the graft, before
significant ridge collapse. Immediate placement in a three-rooted molar socket with an infected apex is not
something I would attempt; the primary stability is unpredictable and the site is contaminated.”
Q
Give me the treatment sequence.
“Remove bridge and assess →provisional on the 14 →extract the 16 with ridge preservation if unrestorable
→interim provisional bridge or denture →re-evaluate at four months, clinically and radiographically →
definitive crown on the 14 →implant at the 16 if indicated and possible →healing and definitive implant
crown →maintenance programme.”
Q
Describe your ideal three-dimensional implant position at the 16.
“Mesiodistally centred in the space with at least 1.5 mm to each adjacent root and enough room for a cleansable
emergence. Buccolingually with 1.5 to 2 mm of bone buccally, positioned so the screw access emerges through
the central fossa. Apico-coronally about 3 mm apical to the intended gingival margin. A wide-platform implant,
and at least 2 mm of clearance from the sinus floor.”
Q
You catch the Schneiderian membrane during the osteotomy. What now?
“If I am simply preparing an osteotomy and I perforate, I stop, reassess with a Valsalva test, and decide honestly
whether I can still achieve primary stability in the remaining bone without displacing anything into the sinus.
If I cannot, I abandon and close, cover with antibiotics and decongestant advice, warn the patient not to blow
their nose, and refer. A perforation is not a disaster; improvising a repair I am not trained for is.”
Q
Screw-retained or cement-retained crown here?
“Screw-retained, because it is retrievable and because it eliminates residual subgingival cement, which is a
well-recognised cause of peri-implant disease. At the 16 the access hole falls in the central fossa where it is
neither aesthetic nor occlusally critical. I would only cement if the angulation made the access emerge through
a cusp, and then I would use a custom abutment with a supragingival or just-subgingival margin.”
Q
How would you design the occlusion on that crown?
“Narrow occlusal table, cusp inclines reduced, light contact in maximum intercuspation — holding shimstock
only under firm closure — and no working or non-working excursive contact. Implants have no periodontal
ligament and so no proprioceptive protection, and the mesial component of force is what loosens screws.”

Domain 4 — Interpretation and problem solving of clinical outcomes
Chain: outcomes, records and learning from the failure
Q
What survival figures would you quote her?
“Conventional fixed bridges: around 90% at ten years, with about a fifth having had some complication. Single
implant crowns: around 95% survival at ten years, but with a comparable rate of technical complication —
screw loosening, ceramic chipping — and a significant rate of biological complication. I would say plainly that
the implant is not more permanent, it is differently maintained.”
Q
What would you record for this case?
“The pre-operative findings and photographs, the restorability assessment and my reasoning, the options dis-
cussed including no treatment and the shortened arch, the risks and costs given in writing, her questions and
her decision, the implant system, diameter, length and lot number, the insertion torque, the baseline periapical
at fitting, and the maintenance interval agreed.”
Q
She returns at five years with a loose implant crown. Differential and approach?
“Most likely a loose abutment screw — I would remove the crown, inspect the screw and the internal connection,
replace the screw, torque to the manufacturer’s value and re-check the occlusion, because an occlusal error is
usually why it loosened. If the implant itself is mobile, that is loss of integration and the implant is removed.
I would radiograph and probe before I touch anything.”
Q
And if the 14 fractures in ten years?
“Then I assess it exactly as I assessed the 16 — caries extent, ferrule, restorability — and if it is unrestorable I
have a single implant at the 16 that stands alone, which is precisely why I restored the 14 as an individual
crown rather than splinting it into a new bridge. Keeping units independent limits the size of the next failure.”
Q
What is within your competence here, and what is not?
“Within: removal and assessment of the bridge, endodontics and restoration of the 14, sectional extraction with
ridge preservation, and a single posterior implant in adequate native bone with a screw-retained crown. Beyond:
lateral window sinus elevation, significant vertical augmentation, and management of a displaced implant or a
large perforation. I would refer those, and I would say so to her before starting rather than mid-procedure.”
Q
What would you audit from a case like this?
“The longevity and mode of failure of conventional bridges in my own practice. If mine are failing at the
margins, that is a lesson about margin placement, moisture control at cementation and the maintenance advice
I give. It is a legitimate quality improvement project: set a standard, take a sample, measure, change something
specific, and re-audit.”
Q
How would you know this treatment had succeeded?
“That at five years she has a stable, cleansable arch she can eat with, that she has not needed unplanned treatment,
and that when something does need replacing she is not surprised by it — because that was the actual clinical
problem she presented with.”
WATCH OUT
Go back to restorability: caries extent, ferrule, furcation, endodontic prognosis. Deciding whether the tooth
stays or goes is the hinge of this whole case, and saying so out loud buys you a sentence of thinking time.
Running this case to time
Time check. The flow above holds 38 questions and about 2,406 words of model answer. At 140 words a
minute plus roughly five seconds a question, that is a little over twenty minutes — an overrun of about five.
What goes first is the bridge removal material at the head of Domain 3: the crown-and-bridge remover,
sectioning the connector and the temporary cement compress into one question, because the marks in
this case sit in restorability — ferrule, supracrestal attachment, furcation — in the argument between the

options, and in the conversation about the word “permanent”. If your answers run past thirty seconds,
you will never reach Domain 4 — and Domain 4 is where the survival figures and the audit are.

the history alone. The answer that scores is that restorability is judged after complete caries removal,
not through a retainer — and then the four tests, with the specific reason this tooth usually loses: 3 mm
of crown lengthening on an upper first molar exposes the furcation. Candidates who reach a verdict in
the opening have skipped the whole of Domain 1.
Selling the implant as permanent. She has asked for “something permanent” and the examiner is watch-
ing what you do with the word. Volunteer that an implant is not more permanent, it is differently
maintained, give both survival figures side by side, and say that the complication rates are comparable.
Correcting that expectation before treatment is the difference between an expected event and a betrayal
— and it is the answer the closing question is set up to reward.
Never naming the referral line at the sinus. A single posterior implant in adequate native bone is yours.
What is not: lateral window sinus elevation, significant vertical augmentation, a transcrestal lift where
the required gain is large, and management of a displaced implant or a large perforation — all referred,
and said to her before starting rather than mid-procedure. The candidate who describes a lateral window
at this level has told the examiner they do not know where the line is.

soe.title: Well-controlled diabetes and a single posterior
soe.text:
SOE Case 24 — Well-controlled diabetes and a single posterior
implant
THE CASE
57-year-old man, type 2 diabetes, HbA1c 47 mmol/mol, on metformin. Non-smoker, regular attender, excellent
oral hygiene. Missing 36 for 6 months following extraction for a vertical root fracture. Bone height 12 mm above
the canal, width 8 mm.
Pace: one structured opening of about 60 seconds, then roughly 35 questions in the remaining 14 minutes. Nothing after the opening earns you
more than a few seconds of thought.
Opening — the 60-second presentation
Q
Present this case.
“A 57-year-old man missing the 36 for six months after extraction for a vertical root fracture, with a single
systemic factor — type 2 diabetes on metformin. His HbA1c of 47 mmol/mol is below the diagnostic threshold
for diabetes, so this is excellent control and places him at essentially the same risk as a non-diabetic. He is a
non-smoker, attends regularly and cleans well. The site has 12 mm of height above the canal and 8 mm of
width, which is generous in both dimensions, and the adjacent teeth are sound. This is the profile of a patient
who does well with implants. My job is to confirm that impression with a proper medical and site assessment,
to plan his appointment around his diabetes rather than around his diagnosis, and not to over-complicate a
straightforward case.”
Domain 1 — Clinical interpretation and reasoning
Chain: the medical groundwork
Q
What is HbA1c and what does it actually measure?
“Glycated haemoglobin — the fraction of haemoglobin that has been non-enzymatically glycated in proportion
to the ambient glucose concentration. Because red cells live around 120 days, it reflects average glycaemia over
roughly the preceding two to three months, weighted toward the most recent weeks. It is not affected by
whether he ate breakfast, which is why it is the measure we use.”
Q
Interpret his figure of 47.
“In IFCC units, 48 mmol/mol is the diagnostic threshold for diabetes and equates to 6.5% in the old DCCT
units. At 47 he is below that threshold — his glycaemia is currently in the non-diabetic range. A typical
treatment target is around 48 to 53 mmol/mol, and above about 69 mmol/mol I would regard control as poor.
He is doing better than most people without a diagnosis.”
Q
What is HbA1c unreliable in?
“Anything that changes red cell lifespan or haemoglobin: anaemia, haemoglobinopathies, recent transfusion,
haemolysis, chronic kidney disease and pregnancy. In those situations the figure can mislead in either direc-
tion, and I would ask his physician what they are using instead rather than treat the number as gospel.”
Q
How does diabetes affect implant outcomes?
“Well-controlled diabetes shows implant survival close to that of non-diabetics. Poor control is associated
with delayed healing, higher early failure and a higher incidence of peri-implantitis. The consistent message
across the literature is that it is control, not the diagnosis, that matters — and that a well-controlled diabetic is
not a contraindication.”
Q
What is the biological mechanism?

“Chronic hyperglycaemia produces advanced glycation end products which stiffen collagen and alter the in-
flammatory response through the RAGE receptor. There is impaired neutrophil chemotaxis and phagocytosis,
reduced collagen synthesis and turnover, and microvascular disease reducing perfusion and oxygen delivery
to the wound. The net effect is slower, less reliable healing and reduced resistance to infection.”
Q
Tell me about metformin.
“A biguanide — it reduces hepatic gluconeogenesis and improves peripheral insulin sensitivity. It is first line
in type 2 diabetes. Importantly for me, metformin alone rarely causes hypoglycaemia because it does not
stimulate insulin secretion; the drugs that do are sulfonylureas and insulin. Its rare serious adverse effect is
lactic acidosis, usually in renal impairment.”
Q
How would you recognise and manage a hypoglycaemic episode in the chair?
“Sweating, tremor, tachycardia, confusion, aggression, drowsiness. Stop treatment, sit him up, check capillary
blood glucose — below 4 mmol/L is hypoglycaemia. If conscious and cooperative, 15 to 20 g of oral glucose
repeated after 10 to 15 minutes, then a longer-acting carbohydrate. If unconscious or unable to swallow, 1 mg
glucagon intramuscularly, oxygen, and call an ambulance.”
Q
What else would you confirm about his diabetes?
“Who manages it and when he was last reviewed; whether he has microvascular complications — retinopa-
thy, nephropathy, neuropathy — since those indicate longer-standing disease regardless of his current figure;
his full drug list; his renal function, which matters for my analgesic choice; and whether he has ever had a
hypoglycaemic episode. I would write to his GP setting out the plan.”
Chain: the site
Q
Describe the anatomy you must respect at the 36.
“The inferior alveolar canal and its neurovascular bundle running below the site; the mental foramen and its
anterior loop further forward, which I must identify if my incision or flap extends mesially; the submandibular
fossa, a lingual concavity below the mylohyoid ridge that can cause a straight drill to perforate the lingual plate;
the lingual nerve, superficial to the periosteum lingual to the third molar region; and the external oblique
ridge buccally.”
Q
What would perforation of the lingual plate cause?
“At best a benign perforation. At worst haemorrhage into the floor of the mouth from the sublingual or sub-
mental vessels, which can produce a rapidly expanding haematoma and airway compromise. That is why I
angle the osteotomy to follow the lingual concavity, palpate the lingual plate through the flap, and consider a
CBCT where the cross-sectional form is uncertain.”
Q
Interpret his bone dimensions.
“12 mm of height above the canal lets me place a 10 mm implant with a 2 mm safety margin, which is what I
want as a minimum. 8 mm of width allows a 4.5 to 5 mm diameter implant with 1.5 to 2 mm of bone buccally
and lingually. Both dimensions are adequate without augmentation — this is native-bone surgery.”
Q
Why did the tooth fracture vertically, and does it matter now?
“Vertical root fracture is typically a root-filled, post-restored or heavily loaded tooth, with the classic signs of a
narrow deep isolated probing defect, a sinus tract near the gingival margin and a J-shaped or halo radiolucency.
It matters now for two reasons: it usually means chronic infection was present, so I want the site properly
healed and radiographically clear before placing; and it tells me something about his occlusal load, which I will
build into the crown design.”
Domain 2 — Clinical decision making and treatment planning

Q
Give me the options.
“No treatment with monitoring for over-eruption of the 26 and tilting of the 35 and 37; a partial denture; a
conventional bridge from the 35 and 37, which means preparing two sound unrestored teeth; a resin-bonded
cantilever, which is unreliable at a molar span; or an implant. Given intact adjacent teeth and generous bone,
the implant is clearly the option of choice.”
Q
Why is the bridge the wrong answer here specifically?
“Because the biological cost falls on two sound, unrestored teeth. Preparation removes a substantial volume
of dentine and carries a real risk of pulpal death over time, and if either abutment later fails I have converted
a one-tooth problem into a three-tooth problem. When the adjacent teeth are unrestored, that is the strongest
single argument for an implant.”
Q
Your colleague would defer until the HbA1c is confirmed by the GP within three months. Why might they be right?
“Because a figure I have been told is not a figure I have verified, and HbA1c can drift. Confirming a current,
GP-sourced value costs one letter and a few weeks, documents that I checked, and protects the patient if control
has slipped since. I would in fact do exactly that — I would obtain written confirmation before surgery while
proceeding with planning.”
Q
At what level of control would you decline?
“I would be reluctant above about 69 mmol/mol, and would decline elective implant surgery in someone poorly
controlled or with unstable disease until they had been optimised with their physician. That is not a permanent
refusal — it is a deferral with a route back, which I would frame to the patient as working together with their
doctor.”
Q
Classify this case on SAC.
“Surgically Straightforward — a single posterior site, adequate height and width, healed ridge, no augmenta-
tion, non-aesthetic. Prosthodontically Straightforward — a single unit between two sound teeth with adequate
restorative space. His diabetes is a general modifier, but at this level of control it does not raise the classification.
Well within my competence.”
Q
What would raise it beyond your competence?
“Inadequate height requiring vertical augmentation or nerve lateralisation; a severely resorbed site needing
block grafting; poorly controlled or complicated diabetes; a bisphosphonate or antiresorptive history with
MRONJ risk; or head and neck radiotherapy. Any of those and I refer — and I would say so at the outset
rather than discover it mid-surgery.”
Q
What would you consent for specifically?
“The standard risks — failure to integrate, infection, need for further procedures, cost. Plus site-specific ones:
altered sensation of the lip and chin, though with 12 mm of clearance the risk is low; the need for a morning
appointment having eaten and taken his metformin; that healing may be marginally slower; the possibility
of screw loosening or ceramic chipping; and the lifelong maintenance commitment. Written estimate and a
cooling-off period.”
Q
How would you explain the diabetes issue to him, in his words?
“ ‘Your diabetes is very well controlled — your last blood test was actually in the normal range, and at that
level your healing should be just like anyone else’s. What I’d ask is that we do this in the morning, that you
eat normally and take your tablet as usual beforehand, and that you keep an eye on your sugars for a few days
afterwards, because surgery and eating less can unsettle them. If your control slips in future, tell me, because
it changes how closely I watch the implant.’ ”
Domain 3 — Decision making in relation to treatment procedures

Q
How do you schedule and prepare the appointment?
“A morning appointment, not last thing in the afternoon, so he is not fasting and I am not rushing. Confirm on
arrival that he has eaten and taken his metformin. A capillary blood glucose if he is unwell, symptomatic or
unsure. Keep it short. Have oral glucose available. Chlorhexidine rinse and aseptic technique.”
Q
Would you give antibiotic prophylaxis?
“Yes — the evidence supports a single pre-operative dose of amoxicillin 2 to 3 g an hour before, with a number
needed to treat of around 25 to prevent one early failure. Well-controlled diabetes does not by itself justify
a post-operative course, and I would not give one. Prolonged courses add resistance and side effects without
benefit.”
Q
What local anaesthetic, and why?
“Buccal and lingual infiltration with articaine rather than an inferior alveolar block, so that he retains protective
sensation and can report a sharp shooting pain if I approach the bundle. With 12 mm of clearance the risk is
low, but the principle holds. I would avoid excessive adrenaline load only if there were a cardiac indication; his
diabetes is not one.”
Q
Take me through the surgery.
“Mid-crestal incision over keratinised tissue with a sulcular extension, full-thickness flap raised atraumatically,
mental foramen identified if I extend mesially. Graded drilling with copious sterile saline, sharp drills, slow
speed and intermittent pressure, direction indicator checked in two planes, depth gauge to confirm. Bone here
is likely D2, so I would watch torque and countersink if needed.”
Q
Implant dimensions and torque?
“A 4.5 to 5.0 mm diameter, 10 mm long implant — wide enough for a molar occlusal table, leaving 2 mm above
the canal and 1.5 to 2 mm of bone buccally and lingually. Insertion torque 25 to 45 Ncm; I would not chase
high torque in dense bone because over-compression causes crestal necrosis and early bone loss.”
Q
One stage or two?
“One stage with a healing abutment, given good primary stability, adequate keratinised tissue and no graft.
It avoids a second surgical episode and lets the soft tissue mature around the emergence profile from the start.
Two stage if stability were poor, if I had grafted, or if I could not achieve tension-free closure.”
Q
Closure and post-operative care?
“4/0 monofilament interrupted sutures, removed at 7 to 10 days. Written post-operative instructions, ice, no
rinsing for 24 hours then warm saline, chlorhexidine, and analgesia. And one instruction specific to him — to
monitor his blood glucose over the next few days, because surgery, soreness and reduced intake can disturb
control in either direction.”
Q
What analgesia, and is there a caution?
“Paracetamol with ibuprofen is my default. The caution is that NSAIDs plus metformin in someone who
becomes dehydrated can precipitate renal impairment and, rarely, lactic acidosis — so I would check his renal
function is normal, keep the NSAID course short, and tell him to keep his fluid intake up. If renal function were
impaired I would use paracetamol alone.”
Q
How and when would you restore it?
“Conventional loading at about three months, confirmed by clinical stability and ISQ if available. An implant-
level impression — closed tray in polyether, or a digital scan with a scan body. A screw-retained monolithic
zirconia crown on a titanium base, with a narrow occlusal table, a cleansable emergence profile and no subgin-
gival cement.”

Q
How would you set the occlusion?
“Light contact in maximum intercuspation — shimstock held only under firm closure, so that under normal
load the implant carries less than the adjacent teeth, which have a periodontal ligament and intrude slightly.
No working or non-working excursive contacts. Given his history of a vertical root fracture, I would look hard
for parafunction and consider a night guard.”
Domain 4 — Interpretation and problem solving of clinical outcomes
Q
What parameters would you monitor, and how often?
“Survival; marginal bone level against the baseline periapical taken at fitting; six-point probing depths, bleed-
ing and suppuration with a plastic probe; plaque score; the prosthesis for screw integrity, contour and occlusion;
and his HbA1c trend, which I would ask about at every recall. Six-monthly, moving to four-monthly if control
deteriorated or if I saw bleeding on probing.”
Q
He returns at 4 years with bleeding on probing and 4 mm pockets, no bone loss. Diagnosis?
“Peri-implant mucositis — bleeding on gentle probing, with or without increased probing depth, but no bone
loss beyond initial crestal remodelling. It is reversible, it is caused by biofilm, and it is the precursor of peri-
implantitis. That is why the baseline radiograph at fitting earns its keep.”
Q
Manage it.
“Remove the crown if retrievable to assess and clean properly. Debride with titanium, PEEK or plastic instru-
ments and glycine air-polishing — never steel on the implant surface. Review the crown contour and whether
an interdental brush can actually pass. Re-instruct with a correctly sized interdental brush and have him
demonstrate it. Check his glycaemic control. Review at one month, with resolution of bleeding as the target.”
Q
It does not resolve at one month. Now what?
“I look for the reason rather than repeating the same treatment. Is the prosthesis cleansable — over-contoured,
deep margin, residual cement? Is his technique actually working — disclose and watch him. Has his control
slipped — recheck the HbA1c. Repeat non-surgical debridement, and if bleeding persists with deepening
probing depths and bone loss on radiograph, I have moved to peri-implantitis and a different pathway.”
Q
If it were peri-implantitis, what would you do?
“Diagnose it properly — probing depth increase, bleeding or suppuration, and radiographic bone loss beyond
initial remodelling. Non-surgical debridement and risk factor control first, then referral for surgical manage-
ment if it did not respond, because regenerative or resective peri-implant surgery is beyond my competence.
And I would be honest with him about the prognosis rather than repeatedly re-cleaning a losing site.”
Q
His HbA1c comes back at 80 mmol/mol at the next recall. What changes?
“My recall interval shortens to three or four months, my threshold for radiographs falls, and I reinforce hygiene
actively rather than passively. I would write to his GP flagging the periodontal and peri-implant risk, because
there is a bidirectional relationship — treating the inflammation can help his glycaemic control as well as the
other way round.”
Q
What would you record for this case?
“The medical history and the source and date of the HbA1c, the GP correspondence, the options discussed
including no treatment, the consent conversation and written estimate, the implant system, diameter, length
and lot number, insertion torque, the surgical protocol and the antibiotic given, the baseline radiograph at
fitting, and the agreed maintenance interval.”
Q
How would you know this treatment had succeeded?
“That at ten years he still has a stable, symptom-free, cleansable implant, bone levels unchanged against base-
line, no bleeding or suppuration, an intact crown he has not needed unplanned appointments for, and two

adjacent teeth still sound and unprepared. That last point is the real measure — I solved the problem without
spending any healthy tissue.”
WATCH OUT
Come back to the principle that in diabetes it is control, not diagnosis, that determines risk — then say what
you would check, what you would modify, and what would make you defer. It buys a sentence and it is almost
always the right frame.
Running this case to time
Time check. The flow above holds 39 questions and about 2,389 words of model answer. At 140 words a
minute plus roughly five seconds a question, that is a little over twenty minutes — an overrun of about five.
What goes first is the generic surgical sequence in Domain 3: the incision, the flap, the graded drilling and
the closure compress into one question, because none of it is specific to this patient. The marks sit in the
HbA1c arithmetic, in the modifications that are actually about his diabetes — the morning appointment,
the metformin, the glucose monitoring, the NSAID caution — and in Domain 4’s mucositis pathway.
If your answers run past thirty seconds, you will never reach Domain 4 — and Domain 4 is where the
HbA1c comes back at 80.

Where the marks are lost in this case
Treating the diagnosis instead of the control.
The examiner has chosen 47 mmol/mol deliberately,
because it sits below the diagnostic threshold. Candidates who launch into diabetic risk, deferral and

antibiotic cover have failed to read the number and have over-complicated a Straightforward case. Say
the arithmetic out loud — 48 is the threshold, he is at 47, this is normal glycaemia — and then say that
it is control, not the diagnosis, that the evidence says matters.

still show what changes: a morning appointment with his metformin taken and a meal eaten, glucose
available in the surgery, glucose monitoring for a few days afterwards, and the NSAID-with-metformin

bone are referred — and so is surgical management of peri-implantitis if it ever comes to that. The
candidate who never names a line has not shown the examiner they know where theirs is.

soe.title: Early peri-implant mucositis in a new patient
soe.text:
SOE Case 25 — Early peri-implant mucositis in a new patient
THE CASE
49-year-old woman registers at your practice. She has four implants — 15, 25, 36, 46 — placed 4 years ago.
She is asymptomatic. On examination: bleeding on probing at all four implants, probing depths 4 mm, no
suppuration, plaque score 45%, no radiographic bone loss beyond the first thread. She has not seen a hygienist
for 3 years.
Pace: one structured opening of about 60 seconds, then roughly 35 questions in the remaining 14 minutes. Nothing after the opening earns you
more than a few seconds of thought.
Opening — the 60-second presentation
Q
Present this case.
“A 49-year-old woman new to the practice with four implants placed four years ago, asymptomatic, but with
bleeding on gentle probing at all four sites, probing depths of 4 mm, no suppuration, and no radiographic
bone loss beyond initial crestal remodelling. Her plaque score is 45% and she has had no professional main-
tenance for three years. On the 2017 case definitions that is peri-implant mucositis at all four implants — a
plaque-induced, reversible inflammation of the peri-implant mucosa. The generalised pattern and the plaque
score point to a maintenance and plaque-control failure rather than four separate local problems, though I
must still check the cleansability of each restoration. What matters is that this has been caught at the reversible
stage: mucositis is the precursor of peri-implantitis, and my whole plan is aimed at making sure I never have
that second conversation with her.”
Domain 1 — Clinical interpretation and reasoning
Chain: the peri-implant tissues from first principles
Q
Describe the soft tissue attachment around an implant.
“A junctional epithelium of around 2 mm attached by hemidesmosomes to the titanium oxide layer, and below it
a zone of connective tissue about 1 to 1.5 mm deep in contact with the surface. Together they form a supracrestal
seal of roughly 3 to 4 mm — somewhat longer than around a tooth.”
Q
How does it differ from the attachment to a natural tooth?
“Three critical differences. There is no cementum and no periodontal ligament, so no inserting Sharpey’s
fibres — the collagen runs parallel to the implant surface rather than perpendicular into it. The connective
tissue is more collagen-rich and less vascular, more scar-like. And the blood supply comes only from the
supraperiosteal vessels, without the periodontal plexus.”
Q
What is the clinical consequence of that?
“The seal is adherent rather than attached, so it resists apical spread of biofilm less well, and the reduced
vascularity means a less effective inflammatory and reparative response. Once inflammation is established it
spreads more rapidly and further apically than around a tooth, and peri-implantitis lesions are typically larger,
non-self-limiting and closer to the bone.”
Q
Should you probe implants at all?
“Yes. Probing is the only practical way to detect inflammation early, and the concern about damaging the seal
is unfounded — the epithelium re-adheres within days. I use a plastic or blunt probe with light force, around
0.25 N, at six sites per implant, recording depth, bleeding and suppuration. Depth alone means little without
a baseline; change is what I am watching.”
Q
Define peri-implant health.

“Absence of erythema, swelling, suppuration and bleeding on gentle probing. Health can exist with reduced
bone support — a previously treated site can be healthy at a lower bone level. Probing depths in health vary
with the depth of the tissue at placement, so there is no single normal number; absence of bleeding is the
criterion, not a millimetre value.”
Q
Distinguish mucositis from peri-implantitis here.
“Mucositis: bleeding on gentle probing, with or without increased probing depth from swelling, but no bone
loss beyond initial crestal remodelling. Peri-implantitis additionally requires increased probing depth com-
pared with a previous examination and bone loss beyond initial remodelling — or, without baseline data,
bleeding or suppuration plus a probing depth of 6 mm or more plus a bone level 3 mm or more apical to the
coronal intraosseous part of the implant. She meets none of those.”
Q
What is “initial crestal remodelling”, and how much is acceptable?
“The physiological bone loss in the first year of function as the biological width establishes — conventionally
accepted up to about 1.5 to 2 mm, and thereafter no more than around 0.2 mm per year, which are essentially
the Albrektsson success criteria. Her radiographs show loss no further than the first thread, which is consistent
with normal remodelling and not with disease.”
Q
Do you have a baseline?
“Not yet — and I would work hard to get one. With her consent I would write to the placing practice for the
surgical records, the implant system, diameters and lot numbers, and any radiographs taken at placement and
at fitting. Without a baseline I am relying on surrogate thresholds and my own records start today, which makes
future interpretation harder.”
Q
What radiographs would you take now?
“Long-cone paralleling periapicals of each implant, angled so the threads are clearly resolved on both sides —
if the threads are blurred the geometry is wrong and I cannot measure bone level. These become her baseline,
dated and stored. A CBCT is not justified for this diagnosis; it adds dose and suffers scatter artefact from the
implants.”
Q
What else would you assess?
“Full periodontal charting and a BPE of her natural teeth — mucositis with a 45% plaque score usually sits
alongside gingivitis or periodontitis. Smoking, medical history including diabetes, medication, dexterity, and
what cleaning aids she actually uses. And critically, the cleansability of each restoration: contour, embrasure
size, margin position, whether they are cemented, and whether an interdental brush can physically pass.”
Q
Her natural teeth show 5 mm pockets and 30% bone loss. Classify that.
“On the 2017 classification: bone loss in the coronal third at 30% and interdental attachment loss of that order
puts her at Stage II, generalised in extent. Grade comes from the bone loss percentage divided by age — 30 over
49 is about 0.6, so Grade B, moderate progression, modified upward if she smokes or is diabetic. That diagnosis
is not incidental: a history of periodontitis is the strongest risk factor for peri-implantitis.”
Q
Name the other risk factors.
“Poor plaque control and no supportive maintenance — both present here. Smoking. Poorly controlled
diabetes. Residual submucosal cement. Restorations that cannot be cleaned — over-contoured or with deep
margins. Lack of keratinised mucosa. And occlusal overload as a contributory rather than initiating factor.”
Domain 2 — Clinical decision making and treatment planning
Q
How common is what you are looking at?
“Common. Meta-analysis of the prevalence puts peri-implant mucositis at around 43% of implants and peri-
implantitis at around 22% — so roughly one implant in five eventually develops the bone-losing form. That

figure is worth quoting to her, because it reframes maintenance from an optional expense into the thing that
determines which group she joins.”
Q
Give me your management plan.
“Cause-related therapy — explain the disease and that it is reversible, assess and modify risk factors, assess
each prosthesis for cleaning access and modify contours where needed, and assess her ability to perform
plaque control. Non-surgical therapy — professional biofilm removal, treatment of the periodontitis on her
natural teeth, and individualised oral hygiene instruction. Re-assess at one month. Then supportive therapy
at 3 to 5 monthly intervals if resolved.”
Q
Why treat her natural teeth at the same time?
“Because periodontal pockets are a reservoir of pathogens that recolonise the peri-implant sulcus, and because
the two conditions share the same cause and the same behavioural fix. Treating the implants while leaving 5
mm pockets untouched is treating half a mouth. I would follow the EFP S3 stepwise approach — behaviour
change, then subgingival instrumentation, then re-evaluation, then supportive care.”
Q
What if the crowns are over-contoured and cannot be cleaned?
“Then the restorations are the cause and no amount of instruction will fix it. I would recontour where the
material allows, or discuss remaking them as screw-retained, cleansable designs with the cost explained
honestly. With a patient who has just registered, I would present that as a finding about the shape of the
crown, not as a criticism of the previous clinician.”
Q
How would you check whether they are cemented, and why does it matter?
“Look for a screw access channel under a composite plug, transilluminate, and take a well-angled periapical
which often shows the abutment–crown junction and sometimes the cement itself. It matters because residual
submucosal cement is a recognised cause of peri-implant disease, and it is a cause I can actually remove —
which makes it worth ten minutes of looking.”
Q
Does she need more keratinised tissue?
“Not on this presentation. Less than 2 mm of keratinised mucosa is associated with more plaque, more brushing
discomfort and more recession, and a graft can be justified where a patient genuinely cannot clean because it
hurts. But her problem is 45% plaque and three years without maintenance, and I would not offer surgery for
what is a hygiene and access problem.”
Q
Your colleague would prescribe a course of antibiotics. Why might they be right, and would you?
“They might argue that four inflamed sites represent an established infection. But mucositis is a biofilm disease
and biofilm is removed mechanically, not chemically — systemic antibiotics show no benefit in mucositis, and
prescribing them here risks resistance and side effects and, worse, teaches her that a tablet solves it. I would
not prescribe. I would use a chlorhexidine mouthwash as a short-term adjunct at most.”
Q
Classify this case on SAC, and where does your competence end?
“As a maintenance and non-surgical case it is Straightforward and entirely within my competence — diagnosis,
debridement, hygiene instruction, contour assessment and supportive care. Beyond my competence: surgical
management of peri-implantitis, whether resective or regenerative, implant surface decontamination protocols
at open flap, implantoplasty, and explantation. If she progressed to established peri-implantitis unresponsive
to non-surgical care, I would refer.”
Q
How would you explain this to her, given she has no symptoms?
“ ‘Your gums are bleeding around all four implants when I test them gently. That’s an infection in the gum — it
doesn’t hurt, which is exactly why people don’t notice it. The important thing is that at this stage it’s completely
reversible. If it’s left, it can spread to the bone that holds the implants in, and that stage is much harder to treat
and can end with losing them. So what I’d like to do is clean them properly, show you how to clean around
them, and see you again in a month.’ ”

Q
She says she cannot afford three-monthly hygienist visits. What do you do?
“I do not treat that as a refusal. I would find the minimum viable interval she will actually attend, make her
home care carry more of the load with a disclosed, supervised technique, and be explicit that a longer interval
means a higher risk which I will monitor for. And I would record the conversation, because a patient who
cannot afford maintenance needs to have understood the trade-off, not just been told it.”
Domain 3 — Decision making in relation to treatment procedures
Q
Describe the professional cleaning.
“Titanium or PEEK curettes and an ultrasonic with a plastic-sheathed tip on the abutment and any exposed im-
plant surface. Glycine or erythritol air-polishing delivered submucosally, which reaches thread and abutment
surfaces far better than a curette can. Polish with a non-abrasive paste. Then the part that actually determines
the outcome — disclose, size an interdental brush to each embrasure, and have her demonstrate it in a mirror
while I watch and correct her.”
Q
Why never steel?
“Because a steel instrument scratches the titanium oxide layer, leaving a roughened surface that retains biofilm
more readily than the original machined or polished collar, and it can smear metal onto the surface. The damage
is permanent and it makes every subsequent clean less effective. On the crown or the abutment above the
mucosa conventional instruments are acceptable; on the implant surface they are not.”
Q
Why is air-polishing better than curettage on an implant?
“Because an implant surface is threaded and convex, not a flat root surface — a curette blade cannot adapt to it
and physically cannot reach between threads or into a concave transmucosal contour. A low-abrasive glycine
or erythritol powder follows the surface hydrodynamically, disrupts biofilm effectively, and does not roughen
titanium. It is also more comfortable, which matters for a treatment she must accept repeatedly.”
Q
What about lasers, local antimicrobials and probiotics?
“For mucositis, the evidence does not show a consistent added benefit over thorough mechanical biofilm
removal with good oral hygiene. Local antimicrobials have some role as adjuncts in peri-implantitis; lasers
and probiotics remain unproven. I would not spend her money on adjuncts before I had proved that the
mechanical and behavioural basics were being achieved.”
Q
Take me through the oral hygiene instruction in detail.
“Disclose first, so she sees the plaque rather than hears about it. Demonstrate in her own mouth, in a mirror. A
powered toothbrush angled at the mucosal margin. Interdental brushes sized individually to each embrasure
and written down by colour, passed straight through rather than forced. Superfloss or a floss threader under
a splinted or bridge-form restoration. Then have her do it back to me — instruction she has not performed is
instruction she has not received.”
Q
How would you recontour an over-contoured crown intra-orally?
“Fine diamonds under copious water to reduce the emergence and open the embrasure, working from the
mucosal margin outward, then a graded polishing sequence to a high lustre — a rough surface is worse
than the original contour. On zirconia I would use zirconia-specific polishers. If the required reduction would
perforate to the abutment or destroy the contact point, the crown needs remaking, not adjusting.”
Q
You need to remove a cemented crown to assess a site. How?
“Ideally I do not — I try to manage it in situ. If I must, I would attempt a crown remover or an ultrasonic on
the margin, accepting that a definitively cemented crown may have to be sectioned and remade, and that must
be consented and costed before I start. That risk is one of the strongest practical arguments for screw retention
in the first place.”

Q
What do you do at the one-month re-assessment?
“Re-probe six sites per implant and record bleeding, re-disclose and re-score plaque, re-check the periodontal
charting on her natural teeth, and ask her to demonstrate her cleaning. Compare directly with the figures
recorded today. Resolution of bleeding is the endpoint; if plaque control has improved but bleeding has not,
the prosthesis or the anatomy is the problem, not her.”
Q
How would you plan her supportive care?
“A defined 3 to 5 monthly recall, tailored to her risk — and with a history of periodontitis, a 45% plaque score
and four implants, I would start at three months. Each visit: plaque score, six-point peri-implant probing and
bleeding, periodontal charting, professional biofilm removal, re-instruction, and radiographs when clinically
indicated rather than routinely.”
Domain 4 — Interpretation and problem solving of clinical outcomes
Q
What would you record today?
“Six-point probing and bleeding at each implant and each tooth, the plaque score, the prosthetic assessment
site by site, the periapical radiographs as baseline, the diagnosis in the words of the 2017 classification, the
advice given, the interdental brush sizes prescribed, the recall interval agreed, and the letter requesting the
original records.”
Q
How do you define success at one month?
“Absence of bleeding on gentle probing at all four implants, with no increase in probing depth. I would tell her
that plainly at the outset — that this is our shared target and it is a target she controls more than I do. Reduced
but persistent bleeding is a partial response and means further non-surgical therapy and another look at the
prostheses.”
Q
At the one-month review three sites have resolved but the 46 still bleeds. What is going on?
“Something local to the 46. My differential in order: an over-contoured or unreachable emergence profile;
residual cement; an open or deficient margin; inaccessibility because of the tongue or a shallow vestibule;
or that she genuinely cannot get the brush there. I would re-examine the site with a radiograph and disclose it
specifically, rather than simply repeating the debridement.”
Q
Two years on, that site has 6 mm pockets, suppuration and 3 mm of bone loss. Diagnosis and action?
“Peri-implantitis at the 46. I would confirm against my own baseline, restate the risk factors, remove or modify
the prosthesis if it is contributory, and carry out non-surgical debridement with air-polishing and risk-factor
control. If it did not respond, surgical management is beyond my competence and I would refer. And I would
be honest with her about the prognosis rather than re-cleaning a losing site indefinitely.”
Q
She asks whether the implants will have to come out. What do you say?
“ ‘Not at this stage, and I don’t want to alarm you. What you have now is treatable, and most implants in this
situation settle down completely with cleaning. If it ever did get to the bone, we’d treat that too and I’d get a
specialist involved. Implants only come out when the bone loss can’t be stopped, and we are a long way from
that — which is why I’d like to see you regularly rather than in three years’ time.”’
Q
What would you audit from a case like this?
“The proportion of my own implant patients who are actually in a defined maintenance programme, and
their bleeding and plaque scores. If patients are drifting out of recall, that is a systems failure in my practice,
not a patient failure — and the change I would test is a recall protocol with active follow-up, then re-audit the
attendance and the bleeding scores.”
Q
What is the single most important thing in this case?

“That it has been caught at the reversible stage. Mucositis is the last point at which the disease can be turned
round completely. Everything I do — the debridement, the contour modification, the instruction and, above
all, getting her into a 3- to 5-monthly maintenance programme — is aimed at making sure the peri-implantitis
conversation never happens.”
WATCH OUT
Go back to the case definitions — bleeding, probing depth, bone loss — say which of the three are present and
which are absent, and the diagnosis and the plan follow from it.
Running this case to time
Time check. The flow above holds 39 questions and about 2,535 words of model answer. At 140 words
a minute plus roughly five seconds a question, that is a little over twenty-one minutes — an overrun of
about six. What goes first is the restoration-handling material in Domain 3: intra-oral recontouring with
fine diamonds and the removal of a definitively cemented crown compress into one question, and the
lasers, local antimicrobials and probiotics get sampled rather than listed. The marks sit in the 2017 case
definitions, in probing an implant properly, in the risk factors and the prevalence figures, and in the
one-month reassessment. If your answers run past thirty seconds, you will never reach Domain 4 — and
Domain 4 is where the 46 is still bleeding.

tion, no bone loss beyond the first thread — is chosen so that the case definitions are the answer. Name
peri-implant mucositis in the words of the 2017 classification, say what she would need to meet to be
peri-implantitis including the no-baseline thresholds, and say that this is the last point at which the
disease can be turned round completely. A candidate who overcalls the diagnosis has thrown away the
whole frame of the case.

teeth, and that is not background detail: a history of periodontitis is the strongest risk factor for peri-
implantitis, and untreated pockets are a reservoir that recolonises the peri-implant sulcus. Stage and
grade her, treat both together under the EFP S3 approach, and volunteer that treating the implants alone
is treating half a mouth.
