line here is unusually clean: non-surgical management, contour assessment, instruction and supportive
care are yours; resective or regenerative peri-implantitis surgery, open-flap decontamination, implan-
toplasty and explantation are not — refer. Say it before Domain 4 forces it. And there is a second line of
the same kind: you would not prescribe antibiotics for mucositis, and you would not spend her money
on lasers, local antimicrobials or probiotics before proving the mechanical and behavioural basics were
being achieved. Restraint, said out loud, is what a 5 looks like here.

soe.title: Progressive bone loss at five years
soe.text:
SOE Case 26 — Progressive bone loss at five years
THE CASE
60-year-old male, ex-smoker (stopped 3 years ago, 25 pack-years). Implant at the 26 placed 5 years ago with
a cement-retained crown. Baseline radiograph available. Current: bleeding and suppuration, probing 8 mm
mesially, bone loss of 5 mm — approximately 50% of the implant length. Implant is not mobile.
Pace: one structured opening of about 60 seconds, then roughly 35 questions in the remaining 14 minutes. Nothing after the opening earns you
more than a few seconds of thought.
Opening — the 60-second presentation
Q
Present this case.
“A 60-year-old ex-smoker with a five-year-old cement-retained crown on an implant at the 26. He has bleeding
and suppuration, an 8 mm pocket mesially, and 5 mm of bone loss against a documented baseline radiograph
— roughly half the implant length. The implant is not mobile. My diagnosis is advanced peri-implantitis, and
with a baseline available I can say that confidently rather than by inference. The likely drivers are residual
submucosal cement, a 25 pack-year smoking history and the absence of supportive care. The implant is still
integrated, so the central question is whether it is rational to keep it, and that decision needs to be made
explicitly, with an endpoint agreed in advance, rather than drifting into open-ended treatment.”
Domain 1 — Clinical interpretation and reasoning
Chain: the peri-implant tissues
Q
Describe the soft tissue attachment around an implant.
“A junctional epithelium of around 2 mm attached by hemidesmosomes, and below it a connective tissue zone
of about 1 to 1.5 mm in contact with the implant surface. Together they form the supracrestal attachment —
what used to be called the biologic width. The collagen fibres in that connective tissue run parallel or circular
to the implant surface; they do not insert into it.”
Q
How does that differ from a tooth, and why does it matter?
“Around a tooth, Sharpey’s fibres insert perpendicularly into cementum, and the periodontal ligament sup-
plies a second vascular plexus, proprioception and progenitor cells. The implant has none of that. Its blood
supply is supraperiosteal only, and the tissue is more collagenous and less cellular — closer to scar. So the seal
is weaker mechanically and the defence is poorer.”
Q
What is the clinical consequence of those differences?
“Peri-implant lesions extend further apically and closer to bone than periodontal lesions, they are less well
contained by the tissues, and untreated peri-implantitis tends to progress in a non-linear, accelerating pattern.
There is also no proprioception, so occlusal overload is not signalled, and the patient feels nothing until suppu-
ration or mobility appear.”
Q
How do you probe an implant, and what is normal?
“Gently — around 0.2 to 0.25 N — with a plastic or a fine conventional probe at six sites. A depth of 3 to 4 mm
can be entirely healthy, because depth reflects mucosal thickness and prosthetic emergence as much as disease.
What matters is change from the baseline recorded at fitting, together with bleeding and suppuration.”

Q
Define peri-implant health, mucositis and peri-implantitis using the 2017 World Workshop.
“Health — no erythema, swelling, suppuration or bleeding on gentle probing, and no bone loss beyond initial
crestal remodelling. Mucositis — bleeding on probing with no bone loss beyond that remodelling; it is re-
versible. Peri-implantitis — bleeding or suppuration, increased probing depth compared with baseline, and
progressive bone loss beyond crestal remodelling.”
Q
And if you have no baseline records?
“Then the case definition is probing depth of 6 mm or more, bleeding or suppuration, and bone levels 3 mm
or more apical to the most coronal intra-osseous part of the implant. I would use that threshold and note in
the record that the diagnosis was made without baseline data.”
Q
Which do you have here?
“Peri-implantitis, and advanced. I have suppuration, an 8 mm pocket and 5 mm of bone loss measured against
a documented baseline. The absence of mobility does not soften the diagnosis — mobility means complete loss
of integration and is a late, terminal sign, not a screening test.”
Q
How do you quantify the bone loss?
“Against the baseline film, measuring from a fixed reference — the implant shoulder — to the first bone-to-
implant contact, mesially and distally, using the thread pitch as an internal scale. Fifty per cent of a 10 mm
implant is 5 mm, and that figure is what will drive the retain-or-remove decision.”
Q
What radiographic technique, and would you take a CBCT?
“A long-cone paralleling periapical with a holder, reproducing the original geometry so the two films are
comparable. I would only add a CBCT if the buccal or palatal defect morphology would change my surgical
plan, and I would justify that exposure under IR(ME)R — scatter from the implant degrades the image, so it is
not a free decision.”
Q
What has caused this?
“In order of likelihood: residual submucosal cement; his smoking history; the absence of any structured main-
tenance; and a prosthesis or implant position that cannot be cleaned. I would look at the film specifically for
radiopaque cement at the margin, and assess the depth of the crown margin and the emergence profile once
the crown is off.”
Domain 2 — Clinical decision making and treatment planning
Chain: risk factors and the periodontal groundwork
Q
List the recognised risk factors for peri-implantitis.
“A history of periodontitis — the strongest — poor plaque control, and absence of supportive maintenance.
Then smoking, poorly controlled diabetes, submucosal cement, prostheses that cannot be cleaned, implant
malposition, and a lack of keratinised mucosa. Most of them are present or plausible in this man.”
Q
He stopped smoking three years ago. Does 25 pack-years still count against him?
“Yes, but less than it did. Smoking impairs the microvasculature, neutrophil function and collagen turnover,
and it is dose-related. Three years of cessation is a genuinely favourable prognostic factor and I would say so
to him, because it makes him more likely to engage. But his tissues carry the history, and I would still class him
as higher risk than a lifelong non-smoker.”
Q
If he had residual periodontitis on his own teeth, how would you stage and grade it?
“Stage by severity and complexity from interproximal bone loss or attachment loss at the worst site — I to IV,
Stage III and IV involving tooth loss. Grade by rate of progression — A slow, B moderate, C rapid — modified
by smoking of ten or more a day and by HbA1c of 7% or above, which push you to Grade C. His history
would have graded him C while he smoked.”

Q
Why is submucosal cement so damaging?
“It is a rough, retentive foreign body sitting below the mucosa where neither the patient nor the hygienist can
reach it. It holds a biofilm directly against the implant surface and provokes a sustained inflammatory response.
The deeper the crown margin, the more cement is left and the less likely it is to be detected — which is why the
damage is often extensive before anything is noticed.”
Q
How should it have been avoided?
“Keep the margin at or no more than 1 mm below the mucosa, use minimal cement, seat the crown first on a
replica abutment or a cementation jig to extrude the excess extra-orally, clean thoroughly with floss and a probe,
and take a post-cementation radiograph. Or avoid the problem entirely with a screw-retained restoration,
which is what I would do at a posterior site.”
Chain: retain or remove
Q
Is it rational to keep this implant?
“It is borderline, and I would set out criteria rather than guess. Against — 50% bone loss, suppuration, a possibly
uncleanable restoration, and a smoking history. For — it is still integrated, and the site is posterior and non-
aesthetic, so resective therapy with recession is an acceptable outcome. Removal means either grafting and a
new implant, or no molar at all.”
Q
So what is your position?
“I would attempt treatment with a clearly defined endpoint agreed in advance and put in writing: if suppu-
ration and bleeding persist after surgical therapy, or if bone loss progresses at review, the implant comes out.
Setting that threshold now prevents it being renegotiated in eighteen months when we are both invested in
having tried.”
Q
A colleague would remove it today. Why might they be right?
“Because at 50% bone loss the published outcomes of surgical therapy are unreliable — recurrence is common
— and every month of treatment costs him money and destroys more bone, which makes the eventual grafting
harder. Removing now, while the surrounding bone is better, gives the cleanest site for a replacement. That is
a defensible position, and if he did not want a treatment attempt I would support it.”
Q
What is the SAC classification, and what is within your competence?
“The non-surgical and prosthodontic management is Straightforward to Advanced, and I would do all of it
— diagnosis, removal of the crown and cement, debridement, and conversion to a cleansable screw-retained
restoration. Surgical management of a 50% defect is Complex on SAC: a compromised site, reduced bone,
a systemic risk factor, uncertain outcome. That phase I would refer, having completed and documented the
cause-related therapy first.”
Q
Tell him what is happening, in his words.
“ ‘The gum and bone around this implant are infected. You’ve lost about half the bone that was supporting it,
and there’s pus coming from the gum. The most likely cause is a small amount of cement left under the gum
when the crown was fitted, and the smoking history hasn’t helped. We can try to stop it getting worse, but we
can’t grow the bone back, and the gum will shrink so more of the implant shows. If it doesn’t settle, the implant
has to come out.’ ”
Q
What must the consent cover?
“That treatment aims to arrest the disease, not regenerate bone; that recession and exposure of the implant
surface are expected consequences of successful treatment, not complications; the total cost including remak-
ing the crown; that treatment may fail and removal may still be needed; the alternative of removing it now; and
what replacement would involve and cost.”

Domain 3 — Decision making in relation to treatment procedures
Chain: cause-related and non-surgical therapy
Q
What is the first phase of treatment?
“Cause-related therapy. Remove the crown, find and remove all residual cement, and assess whether the restora-
tion and the implant position are cleansable. Reinforce his smoking cessation. Detailed oral hygiene instruction
with interdental brushes and a single-tufted brush aimed specifically at this site, and full treatment of any
periodontitis elsewhere, because the mouth is one ecosystem.”
Q
The crown is cemented and will not come off. What then?
“I would attempt controlled removal with a crown remover or by sectioning the crown, accepting that it will
be destroyed — the crown is not the asset here, the implant is. If the abutment screw channel can be located
from the original records or a radiograph, I would cut down to it. If I genuinely cannot retrieve it, I would treat
around it and factor that uncleanable margin into the prognosis I give him.”
Q
What would the replacement restoration look like?
“Screw-retained, so there is no cement at all. A cleansable emergence profile — flat or slightly concave, no
ridge-lap — with the margin at mucosal level, a narrow occlusal table, and enough embrasure space for an
interdental brush. In a compromised site I would accept a slightly less pretty contour in exchange for access.”
Q
Describe non-surgical debridement of an implant.
“Mechanical disruption of the biofilm with titanium or carbon-fibre curettes or a PEEK-tipped ultrasonic,
avoiding steel on the machined surface, plus glycine or erythritol air-polishing submucosally, which is the
most effective way of reaching threads. Then irrigation and chlorhexidine, and reinforcement of home care.”
Q
Would you use antibiotics or local antimicrobials?
“Not routinely. Systemic antibiotics have no reliable role in non-surgical peri-implantitis therapy and I would
not prescribe them simply because there is pus — antimicrobial stewardship applies. Local delivery agents may
give a small additional benefit as an adjunct to mechanical debridement, not instead of it. I would reserve
systemic antibiotics for spreading infection or as a peri-operative adjunct at surgery.”
Q
When do you reassess, and what counts as resolution?
“At six to eight weeks. Resolution would be absence of suppuration, no bleeding on gentle probing, and probing
depths reduced. With an 8 mm pocket and suppuration I expect non-surgical therapy alone will not resolve
it — its realistic function here is to reduce inflammation and prove his engagement before I commit him to
surgery.”
Chain: surgical therapy
Q
What are the surgical options, and how do you choose between them?
“Access surgery alone for debridement; resective therapy with osseous recontouring, implantoplasty and an
apically positioned flap; or reconstructive therapy with a bone substitute and possibly a membrane. The
choice is driven by defect morphology and aesthetics: contained intrabony defects with three or four walls
suit reconstruction; supracrestal, horizontal or one-wall defects suit resection.”
Q
Which applies here?
“This is a posterior, non-aesthetic site, so recession is tolerable and resective therapy with implantoplasty is
my default. If the defect proves to be a contained circumferential crater once the flap is raised, I would consider
a reconstructive approach — but I would not promise regeneration in advance.”
Q
Describe the resective surgery.

“Intrasulcular and relieving incisions preserving keratinised tissue; full-thickness flap; complete removal of
granulation tissue; surface decontamination mechanically with a titanium brush and chemically with saline or
chlorhexidine; osseous recontouring to eliminate the residual craters; implantoplasty of the exposed threads;
then an apically positioned flap so the smoothed surface is cleansable. Sutures, chlorhexidine post-operatively,
no brushing at the site for two weeks.”
Q
What are the risks of implantoplasty?
“It weakens the implant by reducing its wall thickness, which matters if the implant is narrow or the loss is
extensive, and it disperses titanium particles into the tissues, whose long-term significance is uncertain. So I
use copious irrigation and high-volume suction, protect the flap, and I would think hard before doing it on a
narrow implant.”
Q
What determines whether reconstruction has a chance?
“Defect containment above everything — a circumferential intrabony crater with intact walls has the blood
supply and space maintenance to fill; a dehiscence does not. Then a decontaminated surface, primary closure
without tension, no smoking, and a patient who will attend maintenance. Even in ideal conditions I would
describe it as defect fill, not re-osseointegration.”
Q
Post-operative regime?
“Chlorhexidine 0.2% mouthwash twice daily for two weeks in place of brushing at the site, analgesia, and
no denture or removable appliance pressure. Peri-operative systemic antimicrobials only if clinically indicated.
Suture removal at 7 to 14 days, and no probing for three months so the healing attachment is not disrupted.”
Domain 4 — Interpretation and problem solving of clinical outcomes
Chain: outcome, failure and what happens next
Q
How will you judge success at one year?
“Absence of suppuration, absence of bleeding on gentle probing, probing depths no greater than the post-
treatment baseline, and stable bone levels on a new baseline radiograph taken after surgery. Recession and a
visibly longer crown are expected, not failures. If bone loss has progressed, the treatment has failed.”
Q
How likely is that, honestly?
“Less likely than I would want. Surgical therapy for advanced peri-implantitis achieves disease resolution in
only a proportion of cases, and recurrence over the following years is common — so I would present this as
a treatment attempt with real uncertainty, not a cure. That is exactly why the endpoint is agreed in writing
beforehand.”
Q
What is his maintenance regime afterwards?
“Three-monthly supportive care indefinitely. At each visit: plaque and bleeding scores, six-point probing
with a gentle force, check for suppuration, check the abutment screw and the restoration, professional biofilm
removal with glycine air-polishing, and reinforcement of interdental cleaning. Radiographs at one year and
then as indicated. Failure to attend maintenance is itself a reason to revisit the retain-or-remove decision.”
Q
What would you record?
“The full six-point chart with bleeding and suppuration, the measured bone loss with the reference points
used, both radiographs and their dates, the diagnosis in World Workshop terms, the risk factors, the options
discussed including removal, the agreed endpoint for abandoning treatment, the words used with the patient,
the consent, and the review interval.”
Q
If it progresses, how do you remove an integrated implant?
“Counter-torque with a reverse-torque device first, because it is the most bone-conserving method and often
works in a compromised implant. If that fails, piezo-surgery around the neck, and only then the smallest

trephine that will pass, under copious irrigation because trephining generates a great deal of heat. Then
debride, irrigate and assess the residual defect.”
Q
Would you place another implant in that site?
“Only after healing and grafting, with him fully informed that an implant placed in a previously infected site
in a former smoker carries a higher risk of the same outcome. The honest alternative is a shortened dental
arch to the 25, which for a 60-year-old with an intact opposing arch and this history may be the wiser long-term
answer.”
Q
How would you present that choice to him?
“Neutrally, with the numbers I have. ‘Once the implant is out we can rebuild the bone and try again, which
takes about a year, costs this much, and carries a higher-than-normal risk of the same problem. Or we can leave
the gap — most people chew perfectly well on the teeth in front of it. There isn’t a wrong answer here, and I’d
rather you chose than I did.’ ”
WATCH OUT
Come back to the three questions in order — what is the diagnosis in World Workshop terms, what is the cause,
and is it rational to keep this implant. Almost every question in this case is a sub-question of one of those three.
Running this case to time
Time check. The flow above holds 41 questions and about 2,438 words of model answer. At 140 words a
minute plus roughly five seconds a question, that is close to twenty-one minutes — an overrun of about six.
What goes first is the surgical technique chain in Domain 3: the resective sequence, the implantoplasty
risks, the containment criteria for reconstruction and the post-operative regime compress into one question
— for the good reason that you have already said you would refer that phase, so the examiner would
rather hear the referral than the flap design. The marks sit in the diagnosis against a baseline, the cement,
and the retain-or-remove decision with an endpoint agreed in advance. If your answers run past thirty
seconds, you will never reach Domain 4 — and Domain 4 is where the implant comes out.

1 The peri-implant attachment, and the three things a tooth has that it does not · 2 Why peri-implant

· 4 The 2017 definitions, with and without a baseline · 5 Why the absence of mobility does not soften the

it should have been avoided · 9 Retain or remove — the criteria, and the endpoint agreed in writing · 10
Non-surgical therapy, and why you do not prescribe antibiotics for pus · 11 What success at one year looks
like, recession included · 12 How you remove an integrated implant, in the bone-conserving order.

Where the marks are lost in this case
Starting treatment before making the decision. The examiner has given you 50% bone loss and an
implant that is not mobile precisely to see whether you will drift. The answer that scores is to say, in the
opening, that the central question is whether it is rational to keep this implant, and that you would agree
an endpoint in writing before you begin — if suppuration and bleeding persist after surgical therapy, or
bone loss progresses at review, it comes out. Candidates who describe debridement without ever making
that decision have answered a different case.
Promising bone. Two things must be volunteered and are routinely not. First, treatment aims to arrest
the disease, not regenerate bone — even a reconstructive result is defect fill, not re-osseointegration.
Second, recession and a longer-looking crown are expected consequences of successful treatment, not
complications — and that must be in the consent, with the cost of remaking the crown, before anything
starts. A patient who is surprised by the recession will experience a successful outcome as a failure.
Never naming the split. The competence line here divides the case in half, and the split is the answer.
Yours: the diagnosis against baseline, crown removal, finding and removing the cement, debridement,
hygiene, smoking-cessation reinforcement, and conversion to a cleansable screw-retained restoration.
Not yours: surgical management of a 50% defect — resective or regenerative — implantoplasty, and the
reconstruction of the site afterwards, all referred, having completed and documented the cause-related
therapy first. Say it before Domain 3 asks for a flap design.

soe.title: Sinus membrane perforation during a
soe.text:
SOE Case 27 — Sinus membrane perforation during a
transcrestal elevation
THE CASE
You are performing a transcrestal sinus floor elevation at the UL6 with 7 mm of residual bone height. After
the third osteotome, the Valsalva manoeuvre produces bubbling in the osteotomy. The patient is comfortable
and unaware.
Pace: one structured opening of about 60 seconds, then roughly 35 questions in the remaining 14 minutes. Nothing after the opening earns you
more than a few seconds of thought.
Opening — the 60-second presentation
Q
Present this case.
“This is an intra-operative complication. I am performing a transcrestal sinus floor elevation at the UL6 with 7
mm of residual height, and bubbling in the osteotomy on Valsalva tells me I have a Schneiderian membrane
perforation — the commonest complication of sinus elevation. The patient is comfortable and unaware, so I
have time to think rather than react. What I need to establish is the size and containment of the tear, whether any
graft has entered the sinus, and whether I can still achieve primary stability in the residual bone. My working
position is that with 7 mm of native bone I do not need this elevation at all — a short implant converts the
complication into an acceptable and well-evidenced treatment. The governing principle is that if I am uncertain,
I abandon the elevation rather than push graft against a torn membrane.”
Domain 1 — Clinical interpretation and reasoning
Chain: the anatomical groundwork
Q
Describe the maxillary sinus.
“A pyramidal air-filled cavity in the body of the maxilla, the largest paranasal sinus, with its base at the lateral
nasal wall and its apex towards the zygoma. The floor is the alveolar process, often dipping between the roots of
the premolars and molars; the roof is the orbital floor carrying the infra-orbital nerve; the anterior wall carries
the anterior superior alveolar nerve. It drains through the ostium into the middle meatus, high on the medial
wall — which is why drainage is against gravity and why it obstructs so readily.”
Q
What lines it?
“The Schneiderian membrane — pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium with goblet cells on a thin
lamina propria and periosteum. It is typically 0.8 to 1.5 mm thick. The cilia beat towards the ostium, which is
the sinus’s self-clearance mechanism, and that is precisely what is impaired when you fill it with graft or blood.”
Q
What is the blood supply, and why does it matter surgically?
“Chiefly from the posterior superior alveolar and infra-orbital arteries, which anastomose in the lateral wall as
an intraosseous vessel — the alveolar antral artery. It matters most for a lateral window, where cutting it causes
brisk bleeding that obscures the field; on a CBCT I look for it and site my window below it. In a transcrestal
approach it is less relevant, but the anastomosis explains why sinus membrane bleeding can be surprisingly
vigorous.”
Q
What anatomy would you have assessed on the CBCT before starting?
“Residual bone height and width at the site, the contour of the sinus floor — flat, oblique or with a concavity
— the presence of septa and their orientation, membrane thickness and any existing pathology, patency of the
ostiomeatal complex, and the position of the lateral wall artery. Septa and an oblique floor are the two findings
that most raise perforation risk with osteotomes.”

Q
What membrane thickness concerns you?
“A very thin membrane — under about half a millimetre — tears easily. A thickened membrane over about 2
mm suggests chronic inflammation or an obstructed ostium and, although it is more robust, it signals that the
sinus may not tolerate grafting; that is a case for ENT assessment before surgery rather than a surgical challenge
on the day.”
Chain: reading this complication
Q
What exactly does bubbling on Valsalva tell you?
“That there is a communication between the sinus and the osteotomy — the membrane is breached. It is a
highly specific sign. Its limitation is that it tells me nothing about the size of the tear, and a negative Valsalva
does not exclude a perforation, because a small tear can be sealed by blood or by the graft already placed.”
Q
How do you assess it further?
“Direct vision with good illumination down the osteotomy; gentle probing with a blunt instrument to feel for
the defect rather than to enlarge it; repeat Valsalva watching for membrane movement — an intact membrane
billows, a torn one does not; and an assessment of how much graft I have already placed and whether any has
entered the sinus.”
Q
How would you classify the perforation?
“Pragmatically by size and containment: small, under about 5 mm and contained within the osteotomy, where
the membrane still tents and the tear can be covered; large or uncontained, where I cannot see the margins, the
membrane has collapsed, or graft has passed into the antrum. A transcrestal approach gives poor visibility, so
my threshold for calling it ‘uncertain’ is deliberately low — and uncertain is managed as large.”
Q
Why is a perforation a problem at all — what actually goes wrong?
“Three things. Graft particles enter the sinus and act as a foreign body, risking chronic sinusitis or a fungal
ball. The graft loses containment, so it disperses and the elevation fails. And ciliary clearance and drainage
are impaired, so a low-grade sinusitis can establish. The perforation itself, if left clean and small, usually heals
— the membrane has good regenerative capacity.”
Q
What is the reported incidence?
“It is the commonest complication of sinus floor elevation, and it is more frequent with the lateral window
than with the transcrestal approach — although with the transcrestal technique it is more often missed rather
than genuinely absent, because you cannot see it. Risk rises with a thin membrane, septa, an oblique or narrow
sinus floor, and previous sinus surgery.”
Domain 2 — Clinical decision making and treatment planning
Chain: the decision on the day
Q
What are your options right now?
“Seal and proceed — if the perforation is small and contained, fold a resorbable collagen membrane into the
osteotomy to cover the tear, then elevate cautiously with reduced graft volume, or place the implant with no
further elevation.
Abandon — if it is large, if I cannot see it, or if graft has entered the sinus: remove loose graft, close, and re-plan
at three to six months.
Place a short implant into the residual 7 mm with no elevation at all — which turns a complication into a
perfectly acceptable definitive treatment.”
Q
Which do you choose, and why?
“A 6 to 7 mm short implant in the residual bone with no further elevation. Seven millimetres of native bone
is enough for primary stability; the evidence for short implants in the posterior maxilla is good; it stops me

compounding an error; and it removes the graft-in-sinus risk entirely. I would not push more graft against a
torn membrane to rescue a plan.”
Q
You said short implants. Argue against yourself.
“The counter-argument is crown-to-implant ratio and the poor bone quality of the posterior maxilla — a short
implant in D3 or D4 bone carrying a molar crown is loaded unfavourably. The mitigation is a wider implant if the
ridge allows, a narrow occlusal table with no cusp interferences in excursion, a cemented or screw-retained
single crown rather than a distal cantilever, and unsplinted only if stability is good. The systematic reviews
nonetheless show survival comparable to longer implants in grafted sinuses, with fewer complications.”
Q
Your colleague would seal the tear and carry on with the graft. Why might they be right?
“Because a small contained perforation covered with collagen genuinely does heal, and completing the elevation
gives a longer implant in more bone, which is a better long-term biomechanical position — and it avoids a
second procedure if the short implant later fails. If they had clear direct vision of a small tear, minimal graft
placed and good experience of the technique, that is a defensible decision. My reservation is that transcrestally
I usually do not have that vision.”
Q
What is the SAC classification here?
“The original plan — transcrestal elevation with simultaneous implant placement in the posterior maxilla — is
Advanced surgically. A short implant in 7 mm of residual bone is Advanced too, but the moment there is a
perforation with graft displacement or a need for lateral window repair, it becomes Complex and I would refer.”
Q
So what is within your competence and what is beyond it?
“Within: transcrestal elevation of a few millimetres with a flat floor and adequate residual height, recognising
and managing a small perforation, and placing a short implant. Beyond: lateral window elevation, repair of
a large perforation, and retrieval of graft or an implant from the antrum — those go to an oral surgeon or a
colleague with a specialist interest, and displaced material with sinus symptoms goes to ENT.”
Q
What do you tell the patient?
“Immediately and honestly under duty of candour, but calmly and after the procedure rather than mid-
operation while she is comfortable.
‘The lining of your sinus is a very thin membrane, and during the
procedure a small tear occurred.
That’s a recognised complication and it usually heals without trouble.
Because of it I’ve changed the plan slightly and used a shorter implant instead of lifting the sinus floor, which
is a well-proven approach. I’ll give you some antibiotics and some specific instructions about not blowing your
nose, and I’ll see you in a week.’ ”
Q
Was this covered in your original consent?
“It should have been — sinus membrane perforation, sinusitis, the possibility of abandoning the elevation
and the possibility of a different implant or none at all are all foreseeable and material risks that a reasonable
patient would want to know. Under Montgomery the test is materiality to this patient, not what I consider
significant, so ‘the plan may change on the day’ has to be said in advance, not explained afterwards.”
Domain 3 — Decision making in relation to treatment procedures
Chain: technique, repair and aftercare
Q
Take me through the transcrestal technique you were using.
“Crestal incision and flap, a pilot osteotomy stopping 1 to 2 mm short of the sinus floor, then progressive
osteotomes used with light malleting to greenstick-fracture the floor and elevate the membrane hydraulically
or with graft acting as a cushion. Small increments of graft, each one lifting the membrane a little further, with
Valsalva and radiographic checks. It is a blind technique — you are working by feel, which is exactly why the
perforation happened and why my elevation ambition should be modest.”

Q
How much elevation is realistic transcrestally?
“Around 3 to 4 mm reliably, and I would want at least 6 mm of residual height with a flat floor before attempting
it, which is why the case selection here was borderline-acceptable but the ambition must stay small. If I need
more than that, the answer is a lateral window — and that is a referral.”
Q
If you had decided to repair it, how?
“A resorbable collagen membrane, trimmed and folded, introduced through the osteotomy and unfolded to
lie against the sinus floor covering the tear, with the graft then contained beneath it. Collagen is the material
of choice because it is haemostatic, adheres to the wet membrane and needs no fixation. Fibrin sealant or a
platelet-rich fibrin membrane are alternatives.”
Q
What graft material would you have used, and why does the choice matter here?
“Deproteinised bovine bone mineral is the best-evidenced sinus graft — slow-resorbing, good space mainte-
nance, excellent long-term data. It matters here because a particulate xenograft that escapes into the sinus
does not resorb; it sits there as a foreign body. Autogenous bone or an allograft would at least remodel. That
asymmetry is another reason to abandon rather than persist.”
Q
What post-operative management?
“Sinus precautions — no nose-blowing, sneeze with the mouth open, no straws, no smoking, avoid flying
and diving, sleep with the head elevated. Antibiotics — amoxicillin, or clarithromycin if penicillin-allergic. A
decongestant such as xylometazoline nasal drops for a few days plus steam inhalation. Analgesia. Review at
one week.”
Q
Justify the antibiotic.
“The sinus is now in communication with the mouth, cilial clearance is impaired and there is a foreign body —
an implant — at the interface, so this is one of the genuine indications for therapeutic prophylaxis rather than
routine cover. I would prescribe it as a defined short course, document the indication, and be clear that this is
a specific-risk situation, not a habit — antimicrobial stewardship still applies.”
Q
What specifically do you ask at the one-week review?
“Nasal discharge, facial pain or pressure, a blocked nose, a bad taste or smell, nosebleed, and altered sensa-
tion. Plus the usual wound review: healing, dehiscence, swelling, and whether the healing abutment or cover
screw is undisturbed. I would also check she has actually managed the sinus precautions.”
Q
What would make you refer, and to whom?
“Acute sinusitis not settling — purulent discharge, facial pain, fever — goes to ENT. Displacement of the
implant or a significant volume of graft into the antrum is an urgent referral for retrieval, because retained
foreign material risks chronic sinusitis or a fungal ball. A large perforation needing lateral window repair goes
to an oral surgeon. I would make the referral the same day where there are systemic signs.”
Q
The implant disappears into the sinus during placement. What do you do?
“Stop. Do not fish for it blindly through the osteotomy — that enlarges the defect and pushes it further. Obtain
imaging to localise it, close the site, cover with antibiotics and sinus precautions, inform the patient under
duty of candour, and arrange urgent referral for retrieval, usually via a lateral antrostomy or endoscopically.
Retrieval is not something I would attempt at this level.”
Domain 4 — Interpretation and problem solving of clinical outcomes
Chain: outcomes, records and learning
Q
How would you record this?
“Contemporaneously: what happened, when and how it was identified; the size and appearance of the perfora-
tion; what I did and why; the graft volume placed and whether any was retrieved; what I said to the patient and

when; the implant actually placed with its lot and batch number; medication prescribed; instructions given;
and the review arranged. This is exactly the kind of entry that protects both the patient and me.”
Q
Does this need reporting beyond the notes?
“I would treat it as a significant event, log it in the practice’s significant event system, and discuss it at a
team meeting. It is a recognised complication managed appropriately rather than an incident of harm, but the
duty of candour conversation and the change of plan should both be visible in the record and in the practice’s
governance.”
Q
What is the prognosis for a perforation managed this way?
“Good. The Schneiderian membrane heals reliably when the tear is left clean and the sinus is not loaded with
displaced graft. The literature does not show a consistent reduction in implant survival where a perforation is
recognised and appropriately managed — the poor outcomes cluster around unrecognised perforations with
graft displacement and subsequent sinusitis. Recognition is the variable that matters.”
Q
At two weeks she has a blocked nose, a bad taste and unilateral facial pain. Differential?
“Acute maxillary sinusitis, most likely — secondary to the perforation, graft material or impaired drainage.
Also consider a wound infection or dehiscence over the implant, an oro-antral communication if the crestal
wound has broken down, and less likely a failing implant. I would examine the site, test for air passage, take
a periapical or CBCT if I suspect displaced material, and refer to ENT if it is not settling on antibiotics and
decongestants.”
Q
How would you distinguish an oro-antral communication from simple sinusitis?
“Air or fluid passing between mouth and nose — regurgitation of liquids nasally, a change in voice, inability
to inflate the cheek, and a positive Valsalva at the wound. Sinusitis alone gives pain, congestion and discharge
without air passage. A communication over about 5 mm or persisting beyond three weeks needs surgical closure,
which is a referral.”
Q
What would you change in your practice?
“Review my case selection — transcrestal elevation is indicated for a flat floor with adequate residual height,
so I would recheck how I assess floor contour and septa on CBCT. I would consider whether a short implant
should have been my first plan rather than my rescue plan at 7 mm. And if I found a pattern across my cases
I would audit my sinus elevations against those criteria.”
Q
How would you know, a year on, that this had ended well?
“The implant osseointegrated and restored, with stable bone levels against the baseline radiograph taken at
fitting; no sinus symptoms and no ENT involvement needed; the patient chewing comfortably; and a record
that shows the complication was recognised, disclosed and managed. Success here is measured by the absence
of the sinus becoming a problem, not by whether I completed the operation I planned.”
WATCH OUT
Come back to the three questions this complication always reduces to: how big is the tear, has anything gone
into the sinus, and do I still need the elevation at all? Saying them out loud buys thinking time and is almost
always the right frame.
Running this case to time
Time check. The flow above holds 35 questions and about 2,399 words of model answer. At 140 words a
minute plus roughly five seconds a question, that is a little over twenty minutes — an overrun of about
five. What goes first is the sinus blood supply material in Domain 1: the posterior superior alveolar and
infra-orbital anastomosis matters chiefly to a lateral window, which you have already said you would
refer. What must not be compressed is the sequence on the day — this is an intra-operative complication,
and the examiner is marking whether you act in a safe order, not whether you can recite the sinus. If your
answers run past thirty seconds, you will never reach Domain 4 — and Domain 4 is where the sinusitis
and the oro-antral communication are.

the short implant is the answer · 9 The limits of transcrestal elevation: 3 to 4 mm, and 6 mm of floor · 10

do not fish · 12 Sinusitis versus oro-antral communication, distinguished by air passage.

Where the marks are lost in this case
Trying to finish the operation you planned. The examiner has engineered a moment where persisting
is tempting and wrong. The safe sequence beats the complete one: stop, assess without enlarging the
tear, establish whether anything has entered the sinus, then abandon the elevation and place a short
implant in the 7 mm you already have. Say the governing principle in the opening, and say that uncertain
is managed as large, because transcrestally you cannot see. Candidates who fold in a collagen membrane
and carry on have chosen completeness over safety in front of an examiner watching for exactly that.
Failing to tell her, and failing to have told her. Two candour points, both routinely missed. After the
procedure she is told plainly and calmly that a recognised complication occurred and the plan changed
— not mid-operation, and not never. Before it, the consent should already have named perforation,
sinusitis, abandonment of the lift, and the possibility of a different implant or none at all, because
under Montgomery those are material to her. Conceding that scores far better than defending the record.
Never naming the line the case is built across. It is crossed twice. Yours: a modest transcrestal lift with a
flat floor and adequate height, recognising a perforation, and a short implant. Not yours: lateral window
elevation, repair of a large perforation, and retrieval of graft or an implant from the antrum — to an
oral surgeon; and sinusitis that is not settling, or displaced material with sinus symptoms — to ENT,
the same day where there are systemic signs. An implant in the antrum is an ENT and oral surgery
problem, not yours. Say it before you are asked, and say that you would not fish for it.

soe.title: An implant displaced into the maxillary sinus
soe.text:
SOE Case 28 — An implant displaced into the maxillary sinus
THE CASE
A colleague refers a patient urgently. During placement at the 16, the implant was lost into the maxillary sinus.
The patient is well, with mild epistaxis and no other symptoms. A CBCT shows the implant lying free on the
sinus floor.
Pace: one structured opening of about 60 seconds, then roughly 34 questions in the remaining 14 minutes. Nothing after the opening earns you
more than a few seconds of thought.
Opening — the 60-second presentation
Q
Present this case.
“This is an urgent referral following an implant displaced into the maxillary sinus during placement at the 16 —
an uncommon but recognised complication, usually the result of inadequate residual bone height, overzealous
elevation, or attempting placement into an elevated site without primary stability. The patient is systemically
well with only mild epistaxis, so this is urgent but not an emergency. A free foreign body in the sinus cannot
be left: it predisposes to chronic sinusitis, oro-antral communication and, in some cases, a fungal ball, and it
may migrate. My role is to establish the implant’s position and mobility, look for an oro-antral communication,
start interim medical management and sinus precautions, and make a prompt, complete referral to oral and
maxillofacial surgery — not to attempt retrieval myself. Alongside that sit the professional issues of candour
and record-keeping.”
Domain 1 — Clinical interpretation and reasoning
Chain: the anatomical and physiological groundwork
Q
Describe the maxillary sinus and its drainage.
“A pyramidal air-filled cavity in the body of the maxilla, the largest paranasal sinus. Its floor is the alveolar
process, its roof the orbital floor carrying the infra-orbital nerve, its medial wall the lateral wall of the nose. It
drains through the ostium into the middle meatus via the ostiomeatal complex — and critically the ostium sits
high on the medial wall, so drainage works against gravity and depends entirely on ciliary transport.”
Q
What lines it, and why does that matter with a foreign body inside?
“Pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium with goblet cells — the Schneiderian membrane. The mu-
cociliary escalator sweeps mucus towards the ostium. A foreign body disrupts that transport locally, mucus
stagnates, the ostium can obstruct, and you get the classic sequence of stasis, obstruction and infection. That
is the mechanism by which a retained implant produces chronic sinusitis.”
Q
What is a fungal ball, and why does an implant predispose to one?
“An aspergilloma — a dense non-invasive tangle of fungal hyphae, usually Aspergillus, colonising a chronically
obstructed sinus. Any retained foreign material provides a nidus and a stagnant environment; dense radiopaque
foreign bodies in particular are classically associated. It is non-invasive in an immunocompetent patient but
needs surgical clearance, which is another reason retrieval is the standard of care.”
Q
Why is she bleeding from the nose?
“Because the Schneiderian membrane and the sinus floor have been breached and blood has drained through
the ostium into the nasal cavity. Mild epistaxis in this context is expected and reassuring. Persistent or heavy
bleeding would make me think of the posterior superior alveolar and infra-orbital anastomosis in the lateral
wall, and that would change this from urgent to emergency.”
Q
How would you classify the sinus as healthy or not on the CBCT?

“I look at membrane thickness — a few millimetres of thickening is common and not necessarily pathological,
but generalised thickening over about 2 to 3 mm, an air-fluid level, complete opacification, or an obstructed
ostiomeatal complex all indicate disease. I would also check the contralateral sinus for comparison and look
for septa and any retention cyst.”
Chain: reading this patient’s situation
Q
What exactly do you need to establish?
“The exact position and mobility of the implant on the CBCT; whether it is free in the antrum or still contained
beneath an intact membrane; whether there is an oro-antral communication at the crest; whether there is pre-
existing sinus disease or ostium obstruction; her symptoms and any systemic signs; and what the referring
colleague has already done and already told her.”
Q
Does it matter whether the implant is free in the antrum or sub-antral?
“Yes. If it is beneath an intact membrane it is technically extra-sinus, contamination risk is lower, and there is
more time. If it is free in the antral cavity it will move with head position and mucociliary flow, it can migrate
towards the ostium or into other sinuses, and the contamination risk is immediate. Free means urgent retrieval.”
Q
How would you check for an oro-antral communication clinically?
“Direct inspection of the crest with good light and suction; a gentle Valsalva watching for air or bubbling at the
socket; asking about fluid passing into the nose on drinking and any change in voice; and the nose-blowing
test only cautiously, because it can enlarge a small defect. I would not probe it, because probing converts a small
communication into a larger one.”
Q
Why can this not simply be left and watched?
“Because a free foreign body in the sinus predisposes to chronic sinusitis, oro-antral communication and fun-
gal ball formation, and it may migrate to a site that is harder to retrieve. There is no evidence that leaving it is
safe, and the standard of care is retrieval. Watchful waiting is only entertained where retrieval carries a greater
risk than the foreign body, which is not the situation here.”
Domain 2 — Clinical decision making and treatment planning
Chain: management and referral
Q
What is your management?
“Refer urgently to an oral and maxillofacial surgery unit for retrieval. In the interim: antibiotics and a de-
congestant, sinus precautions, suture or close the crestal site if it is open, analgesia, and clear safety-netting
instructions to attend urgently with facial swelling, purulent discharge, visual disturbance or fever. I would
speak to the unit by telephone as well as writing, so the urgency is understood.”
Q
Why not attempt retrieval yourself?
“Because blind retrieval through the osteotomy risks pushing the implant further, creating a larger communica-
tion, damaging the membrane or the lateral wall vessel, and converting a straightforward endoscopic retrieval
into a bigger operation. I have neither the visibility nor the instrumentation. Recognising the limit of my
competence is the correct answer here, and it is the answer the patient is best served by.”
Q
What is the SAC classification?
“Placement at the 16 with a deficient sinus floor was Advanced at best. Once the implant is displaced into the
antrum, management is Complex — it sits outside the scope of a general dentist with an interest in implant
dentistry and belongs in a specialist unit.”
Q
What goes in the referral letter?

“What happened and when; the implant system, diameter and length; the CBCT itself, not just a report; the
current symptoms and findings including the epistaxis and the state of the crestal wound; her medical history
and medication, including any anticoagulant or bisphosphonate; what has been prescribed and when; what
she has already been told; and my contact details. An incomplete referral is the commonest reason for delay.”
Q
How would the retrieval be performed?
“Typically by a transnasal endoscopic approach through the middle meatus, or by an intraoral antrostomy — a
Caldwell-Luc type lateral window — under local or general anaesthesia, with the implant retrieved under direct
or endoscopic vision and the sinus irrigated. The endoscopic route is generally preferred where the anatomy
allows because it is less morbid.”
Q
What are the professional issues?
“For the referring colleague: duty of candour — the patient must be told promptly and honestly, with an apology
and an explanation, and it must be recorded; their indemnity provider should be informed. For me: manage
her immediate care and referral, and describe my findings factually without speculating about the colleague’s
technique in front of her. If she asks how to raise concerns, I explain the route neutrally.”
Q
She asks you directly whether the colleague did something wrong. What do you say?
“ ‘This is a recognised complication of implant treatment in the upper back jaw — it can happen even when things
are done carefully. I wasn’t there, so I can’t tell you what happened in your particular case, and it wouldn’t be
fair for me to guess. What I can do is make sure you’re looked after now, and your dentist should explain to
you exactly what happened. If you want to take it further afterwards, I can tell you how.’ Honest, neutral and
it does not close down her options.”
Q
What do you tell her about what happens next, in her words?
“ ‘The implant has moved into the sinus — the air space above your back teeth. It can’t stay there, because over
time it would cause infection, so it needs to be taken out. That’s a routine procedure for a hospital surgical
team, usually done through the nose with a camera or through a small window in the bone. In the meantime
I’m giving you antibiotics and a nasal spray, and I need you not to blow your nose. You’re not in danger, but
this needs doing soon rather than later.’ ”
Domain 3 — Decision making in relation to treatment procedures
Chain: the oro-antral communication and interim care
Q
If there is also an oro-antral communication, how do you manage it?
“Assess the size. Under about 2 mm may close spontaneously with a suture and sinus precautions. Larger
defects need surgical closure — most commonly a buccal advancement flap, sometimes a buccal fat pad or a
palatal rotation flap. Given she also needs retrieval, I would let the receiving unit manage both at the same
operation rather than close it and have them reopen it.”
Q
What is the difference between a communication and a fistula?
“A communication is the acute, unepithelialised defect. If it persists — conventionally beyond about two to three
weeks — it epithelialises and becomes an oro-antral fistula, which will not close spontaneously and requires
excision of the epithelial tract before flap closure. That time window is why prompt referral matters.”
Q
Describe a buccal advancement flap.
“A broad-based trapezoidal buccal mucoperiosteal flap raised over the defect, with the periosteum scored
horizontally at its base to release it so the flap advances passively over the defect and is sutured tension-free
to the palatal margin, on sound bone. Its drawback is loss of buccal sulcus depth, which matters if implants or
a denture are planned later — a relevant consideration for this patient.”

Q
What antibiotic and decongestant would you prescribe, and why?
“Amoxicillin, or clarithromycin or doxycycline if penicillin-allergic, as a defined short course — the indication
is a contaminated communication with a foreign body in a sinus with impaired clearance, which is a genuine
therapeutic indication rather than routine cover. A decongestant such as xylometazoline nasal spray for no
more than five to seven days, to reduce mucosal oedema and keep the ostium patent; longer use causes rebound
congestion. Steam inhalation as an adjunct.”
Q
What sinus precautions do you give?
“No nose-blowing; sneeze with the mouth open; no straws, no smoking, no playing wind instruments; avoid
flying and diving; sleep with the head elevated; soft diet and avoid vigorous rinsing for the first day. I would
give these in writing, because verbal instructions in a distressed patient are not retained.”
Q
What are the red flags you would safety-net?
“Facial swelling, purulent nasal discharge, fever, severe or increasing pain, visual disturbance or diplopia,
and heavy bleeding. Periorbital swelling with any eye sign is an emergency — orbital involvement — and goes
straight to hospital rather than back to me.”
Q
How could this have been prevented?
“Adequate CBCT assessment of residual height, floor contour and septa; respecting the thresholds for transcre-
stal elevation — a flat floor with adequate residual height, otherwise a lateral window and a referral; never
seating an implant that lacks primary stability into an elevated site; and abandoning rather than persisting
when the anatomy does not cooperate. A short implant is usually the honest alternative in a deficient posterior
maxilla.”
Q
What if the patient refuses referral?
“I would establish why — usually fear, cost or loss of trust in dentistry after this experience. I would explain
the specific consequences of leaving it in plain terms: chronic sinusitis, possible fungal infection, and a bigger
operation later. I would document the discussion and the refusal, give written safety-netting, offer to arrange
the appointment myself, and keep the door open with a defined review rather than discharging her.”
Domain 4 — Interpretation and problem solving of clinical outcomes
Chain: aftermath, records and the future
Q
What would you record?
“Contemporaneously and factually: the history as given, my clinical findings including the state of the crest
and the presence or absence of a communication, the CBCT findings, the medication prescribed with doses,
the instructions and written advice given, the referral made and the time it was made, what I told the patient
and in what words, and her questions. No opinion about the colleague’s competence in the clinical record.”
Q
Does this need reporting beyond the notes?
“It should be logged as a significant event by the practice where it occurred, with a team discussion and a review
of case selection and scope of practice. The referring colleague should notify their indemnity provider. If there
were a pattern of similar events, that becomes a concern about a colleague’s practice and there is a professional
duty to act on it — but on a single recognised complication, appropriately disclosed and referred, it is significant
event learning.”
Q
The unit retrieves it. What is the expected outcome?
“Generally very good — a single implant retrieved promptly from an otherwise healthy sinus, with the commu-
nication closed, usually resolves completely. Persistent problems cluster around delayed retrieval, pre-existing
sinus disease, or an unclosed fistula. She should expect the sinus to settle over a few weeks and to be discharged
from ENT or maxillofacial follow-up.”

Q
Six weeks later she has facial pain and a foul-tasting discharge. What has happened?
“Most likely chronic maxillary sinusitis, from residual contamination, an unclosed oro-antral fistula, retained
graft material, or obstructed drainage. I would examine the site, test for air passage, take imaging, and refer
back to the treating unit rather than manage repeated antibiotic courses myself. A dense opacity with flecks of
calcification would raise the possibility of a fungal ball.”
Q
What will you tell her about the future of that site?
“That the priority is retrieving the implant and settling the sinus, and that replacement should not be consid-
ered until the sinus is healthy — typically several months. Then the options are a lateral window elevation by
a specialist, a short implant if enough bone remains, or a non-implant solution such as a bridge or a partial
denture. I would not promise her an implant in that site.”
Q
What is within your competence in her ongoing care?
“Interim medical management, wound care, oral hygiene support, and the eventual prosthodontic conversation
— including a conventional solution if she chooses one. Beyond me: retrieval, sinus surgery, flap closure of a
significant communication, and any subsequent lateral window elevation. I would also be honest that if she
wants a second implant attempt there, it should be done by someone doing sinus surgery routinely.”
Q
How would you judge that you handled this well?
“That she was retrieved promptly and without complication, that she understood at every stage what was
happening and why, that the referral was complete enough that nothing had to be repeated, that my record
would stand up to scrutiny — and that she still has confidence in dental care, which after an event like this is
not a trivial outcome.”
WATCH OUT
Come back to the frame: is she safe now, is the foreign body coming out and who by, and is the mouth-to-sinus
pathway closed? Saying those three aloud buys thinking time and is almost always the right structure here.
Running this case to time
Time check. The flow above holds 33 questions and about 2,158 words of model answer. At 140 words a
minute plus roughly five seconds a question, that is a little over eighteen minutes — an overrun of about
three, the shortest in this section, because the case is built on judgement rather than technique. What
goes first is the flap closure material in Domain 3: the buccal advancement flap and the periosteal scoring
compress into one question, since you have already said you would let the receiving unit close the defect
at the same operation as the retrieval. If your answers run past thirty seconds, you will never reach
Domain 4 — and Domain 4 is where the candour, the records and the future of the site are.

1 Urgent but not an emergency — and a free foreign body cannot be left · 2 The ostium high on the medial
