whether her dentist did something wrong.

Where the marks are lost in this case
Reaching into the sinus. The single thing that fails this case is a candidate who describes retrieving the
implant. Blind retrieval through the osteotomy pushes it further, enlarges the communication, and can
turn an endoscopic procedure into an antrostomy. Say plainly that an implant in the antrum is an ENT
and oral surgery problem and that recognising the limit of your competence is the correct answer here
— then show what you do do: position and mobility, the communication check, interim medication and
precautions, and a complete, telephoned referral. Doing the safe things in the right order beats knowing
the retrieval technique.
Getting the urgency wrong in either direction. She is well with mild epistaxis: urgent, not an emergency
— but a free implant is more urgent than a sub-antral one, and periorbital swelling or any eye sign goes
straight to hospital. Volunteer the calibration and the red flags together, and volunteer that a communi-
cation left beyond two to three weeks becomes a fistula that will not close on its own. Candidates who
neither escalate nor de-escalate have shown no judgement at all.
Talking about the colleague. The professional line here is as marked as the surgical one. Describe
findings factually, do not speculate about another clinician’s technique in front of the patient or in
the record, and do not write an opinion about their competence in the notes. Say that duty of candour
and the indemnity notification belong to the referring colleague, that you would log this as a significant
event, and that if she wishes to raise concerns you explain the route neutrally — advocating neither way.
The answer that scores is honest, neutral, and leaves her options open.

soe.title: Fracture of a narrow implant in a molar site
soe.text:
SOE Case 29 — Fracture of a narrow implant in a molar site
THE CASE
A 58-year-old man with a 3.3 mm narrow implant at the 46, restored seven years ago. He reports the crown
feels loose. On examination the crown moves together with the abutment; the radiograph shows a fracture
line across the implant body at the level of the third thread, with bone loss to that level.
Pace: one structured opening of about 60 seconds, then roughly 35 questions in the remaining 14 minutes. Nothing after the opening earns you
more than a few seconds of thought.
Opening — the 60-second presentation
Q
Present this case.
“A 58-year-old man with a fractured implant body at the 46, seven years after restoration. The crown and
abutment move as one unit and the radiograph shows a fracture across the implant at the third thread with
bone loss to that level. Implant fracture is uncommon — of the order of a fraction of a per cent — and it is
always the end of that implant’s life; there is no repair. The important part of this case is understanding why
it fractured, because the same forces will act on whatever I place next. My working explanation is a narrow
3.3 mm implant in a molar position, crestal bone loss lengthening the lever arm, and very probably a history
of repeated screw loosening. What I need to establish is his occlusion, any parafunction, and what he actually
wants for that site.”
Domain 1 — Clinical interpretation and reasoning
Chain: the mechanical groundwork
Q
The patient says the crown is loose. What is your differential, before you look?
“Loosening of the abutment or prosthetic screw — much the commonest. Decementation of a cemented crown.
Fracture of the abutment or the screw. Loss of osseointegration, so the whole implant is mobile. And fracture
of the implant body itself. They are distinguished by what moves relative to what, and by the radiograph.”
Q
How do you distinguish them clinically?
“If the crown alone moves off a stable abutment, it is decementation. If the crown and abutment move together
but the implant is stable, it is screw loosening or screw fracture. If the whole assembly including the implant
moves, it is either loss of integration or a fracture below the crest. Here the crown and abutment move together,
which pointed me at the screw — and the radiograph corrected me.”
Q
How does a screw joint actually work?
“Tightening the screw stretches it elastically and generates preload — a clamping force holding the abutment to
the implant. The joint is stable while the functional load stays below the preload. Repeated micromovement,
settling of machining irregularities in the first hours, and any misfit all reduce preload, and once it is exceeded
the joint opens, micromoves and loosens.”
Q
So how do you maintain preload in practice?
“Torque to the manufacturer’s specification with a calibrated torque driver, then retorque after about ten
minutes to compensate for the settling effect. Ensure a passive, accurately fitting component, clean threads, and
no interposed debris. And design the occlusion so the functional load stays axial and modest — the occlusion
is what protects the screw joint.”
Q
Why is repeated screw loosening a warning rather than an inconvenience?
“Because it means the loading exceeds the joint’s capacity, and the escalation is predictable: loosening, then
screw fracture, then abutment or implant fracture. A loose joint also transfers bending stress from the screw

into the implant body, so retightening without investigating the cause is actively harmful. Every episode should
trigger review of the occlusion, the fit and the crown design.”
Q
What is the implant made of, and why does that matter here?
“Commercially pure titanium — usually grade 4 — or a titanium-zirconium or Ti-6Al-4V alloy. Grade 4 cp
titanium has good biocompatibility but modest strength, so in a narrow-diameter implant the wall thickness
at the internal connection becomes the weak point. Titanium-zirconium alloys were developed precisely to
allow narrow implants with better fatigue strength, and they matter when diameter is constrained.”
Q
Explain the mechanics of why this one failed.
“Bending stress rises with the cube of the reduction in radius, so diameter dominates strength — a 3.3 mm
implant is far weaker than a 4.8. Molar occlusal loads are the highest in the arch. Crestal bone loss to the third
thread removed the coronal support, lengthening the lever arm and shifting peak stress to an unsupported
section of a thin wall. Add cyclic loading over seven years and you get fatigue fracture — which is why it
happened at seven years and not at one.”
Q
What else would you check?
“His history of previous problems with this crown, especially loosening; parafunctional signs — masseteric
hypertrophy, wear facets, linea alba, a scalloped tongue; the occlusion including excursive contacts on this
crown; the width of the occlusal table and any cantilever; the opposing dentition and whether it is natural,
restored or implant-borne; and the general periodontal and peri-implant status.”
Q
How would you classify the bone loss you can see?
“Radiographically I would state it against the baseline film at fitting if I can get one, and describe it as bone
loss to the level of the third thread. If the implant had been intact, loss of that magnitude with bleeding and
probing depth would meet the 2017 World Workshop definition of peri-implantitis. Here it is academic for
this implant, but it matters because peri-implant bone loss is what set up the fracture, and the same host and
plaque factors will apply to a replacement.”
Domain 2 — Clinical decision making and treatment planning
Chain: what to do about it
Q
What are the options?
“The implant must come out; there is no repair.
Remove and replace with a wider implant after healing and grafting, accepting that there will be a defect at the
fracture level.
Remove and leave a sleeper — if the apical fragment cannot be retrieved without excessive bone destruction,
it may be left submerged provided it is asymptomatic and fully covered.
Remove and do not replace, accepting a shortened dental arch to the 45 if the occlusion permits.
Remove and bridge from the 45 and 47 — destructive if those teeth are sound.”
Q
What do you recommend?
“Removal — ideally by counter-torque if the coronal fragment can be engaged, otherwise piezo-surgery or a
small trephine — then a healing period and reassessment. If I replace, it must be a wide-diameter implant
appropriate to a molar, with the occlusion corrected and a night guard if there is parafunction. I would also
put the shortened dental arch genuinely on the table, because this site has already failed once.”
Q
Make the case for the shortened arch.
“Käyser’s work supports the shortened dental arch as a legitimate endpoint: a functional dentition of the an-
terior teeth and premolars gives acceptable masticatory function, comfort and stability for most patients, and
the second molar contributes little. Here it avoids re-treating a site that has already failed mechanically, avoids
grafting, and costs him nothing further. If he chews adequately on the 45 and the contralateral side, it is the
lowest-risk answer.”

Q
You have argued for the shortened arch. Now argue against it.
“He is 58, not 80, and he has already invested in this site. Leaving the space risks overeruption of the opposing
tooth and drifting of the 45 and 47, and a single wide implant in a healed, grafted site with corrected occlusion
has a good prognosis. The mechanical failure was a design error, not a biological one, and correcting the design
corrects the risk. If his function or his expectations require the molar, replacement is reasonable.”
Q
What is the SAC classification?
“Removal of a fractured implant is Complex — the fragment may be unretrievable without significant bone loss,
and the outcome is unpredictable. Replacement into a healed, grafted molar site with a vertical and horizontal
defect is Advanced to Complex. A straightforward counter-torque removal of an engageable fragment is within
my scope; a trephine removal with a large resulting defect and simultaneous grafting is where I would refer.”
Q
So when would you refer?
“If the fragment cannot be engaged and removal would require substantial bone sacrifice near the inferior
alveolar canal; if the resulting defect needs vertical augmentation, which is beyond me; if there is a large non-
contained defect; or if I am uncertain about the mandibular canal proximity on the CBCT. Removal near the
canal in a resorbed posterior mandible is exactly the situation where a second opinion is cheaper than a nerve
injury.”
Q
What do you tell him about cost and responsibility?
“I would first establish what he was told at the outset and whether there was any written arrangement about
failure. Then be honest: ‘The implant has fractured. That’s uncommon, and I think it happened because a
narrow implant was used in a position that takes heavy chewing forces and because the bone level dropped. It
has to come out. Here’s what replacing it involves and what it would cost, and here’s the alternative of leaving
the space.’ I would not blame the previous clinician, but I would not pretend the implant choice was ideal
either — I describe the mechanics factually.”
Q
He asks whether he should complain. What do you say?
“That a fractured implant is a recognised complication and I was not there, so I cannot say what was or was not
reasonable in his case. I would encourage him to raise it with the treating practice first, since they may well wish
to contribute, and explain the formal routes neutrally if he wants them. Factual, no speculation, no advocacy
either way, and all of it recorded.”
Q
What would you record?
“The history including any previous loosening, the mobility findings and what moved relative to what, the
radiographic findings with the film dated, the diagnosis, the options I discussed and their risks and costs, his
questions and his decision, what I said about causation and in what words, and the plan with review dates. If
I retrieve a fragment I record the implant system, diameter and length, and whether anything was left in situ.”
Domain 3 — Decision making in relation to treatment procedures
Chain: removal and rebuilding
Q
Describe the removal.
“Flap access. Attempt to engage the coronal fragment with a counter-torque device; if the internal connection
is damaged, engage the outer surface with a fragment-removal device. If neither works, piezo-surgery circum-
ferentially, and only then a trephine of the smallest diameter that will pass. Copious irrigation throughout,
because trephining generates significant heat in dense bone. Then debride, irrigate and assess the residual
defect.”
Q
Why is counter-torque preferred?
“Because it removes the implant without sacrificing surrounding bone — the reverse torque breaks the interface
and the fragment unscrews, leaving a socket rather than a crater. A trephine removes a cylinder of host bone with

the implant, which enlarges the defect, may approach the inferior alveolar canal, and turns a straightforward
replacement into a grafting case. Counter-torque first, trephine last, always.”
Q
What do you do about the defect?
“Assess containment. If the defect is contained, I would graft at the same visit with a particulate graft and a
resorbable membrane. If it is non-contained or the soft tissue is compromised, allow six to eight weeks of
soft tissue healing and then graft as a staged procedure, which gives a keratinised soft tissue envelope to close
over. Vertical defects are a referral.”
Q
What interim prosthesis?
“For a lower first molar, often nothing is needed — he can function on the remaining teeth for the healing
period. Otherwise a simple acrylic partial denture relieved over the surgical site, or an adhesive bridge if
aesthetics demanded it, which here they do not. I would warn about overeruption of the opposing tooth if the
interval is going to be long.”
Q
If you replace it, what would you do differently?
“A wide-diameter implant of 5 mm or more, correctly positioned in three dimensions; a screw-retained mono-
lithic zirconia crown with a narrow occlusal table, light centric contact and no excursive contact; a night guard
if there is parafunction; and a maintenance regime that includes checking screw integrity at every recall, so
that loosening is investigated rather than repeatedly retightened.”
Q
Why screw-retained rather than cemented here?
“Retrievability, chiefly — this is a site with a history of mechanical problems, and I want to be able to remove
the crown to inspect and retorque without destroying it. It also eliminates residual excess cement, which is a
recognised cause of peri-implant disease and would compound the bone loss risk in a patient who has already
lost crestal bone.”
Q
Describe the occlusal scheme you want on the replacement crown.
“Light contact in maximum intercuspation — noticeably lighter than the adjacent teeth on shimstock, so that
under load it shares rather than leads, because the implant has no periodontal ligament and no proprioceptive
protection. No contact in lateral or protrusive excursion — guidance on the canines and anterior teeth. Narrow
occlusal table, cusp inclines reduced, contacts centred over the implant axis, and no cantilever.”
Q
Why does the absence of a periodontal ligament matter?
“A tooth has around 25 to 100 microns of physiological mobility and rich proprioception; an implant has roughly
3 to 5 microns of viscoelastic bone deformation and far poorer tactile sensitivity. So an implant does not intrude
to share load and the patient does not feel that they are overloading it. That is the whole rationale for implant-
protected occlusion — deliberately lightening the contact.”
Q
Does a night guard prevent implant fracture?
“It reduces the risk rather than eliminating it — it distributes load, protects the ceramic and gives me a diag-
nostic record of the wear pattern. The evidence base for splints preventing implant mechanical complications
is not strong, so I would present it as a sensible precaution rather than a guarantee, and be clear that correct
diameter and correct occlusion do far more work than the splint does.”
Domain 4 — Interpretation and problem solving of clinical outcomes
Chain: prognosis, monitoring and learning

Q
How common is implant fracture?
“Uncommon — well under one per cent of implants, and typically a late event after five years or more, since it
is a fatigue phenomenon. It clusters in narrow implants, molar sites, bruxists, cantilevered or long-span pros-
theses, and implants with prior crestal bone loss or repeated screw loosening. That risk profile is essentially
a description of this patient.”
Q
What is the prognosis for a replacement implant in this site?
“Reasonable, but poorer than a virgin site. Implants placed into previously failed sites have a measurably
higher failure rate, and the site will have a healing defect and altered bone quality. That said, the failure here
was mechanical and explicable, so correcting the diameter and the occlusion addresses the actual cause —
which is a better position than a site that failed for unexplained biological reasons.”
Q
You leave an apical fragment as a sleeper. What do you tell him and what do you monitor?
“That a small piece of the implant remains in the bone because removing it would have destroyed more bone
than leaving it, that it is inert titanium fully covered by bone and gum, and that it is expected to cause no trouble
— but that I will review it and radiograph it periodically, and that it must be flagged to any future clinician. I
record its position clearly and monitor for symptoms, exposure through the mucosa, or radiolucency around
it.”
Q
If a sleeper becomes exposed or symptomatic, what then?
“Then it is no longer a sleeper — an exposed fragment is a plaque-retentive foreign body that cannot be main-
tained. It needs removal, and if that is diﬀicult it goes to an oral surgeon. That possibility is part of the consent
for leaving it in the first place.”
Q
What would you monitor on the replacement, and how often?
“Six-monthly initially: peri-implant probing at six sites, bleeding and suppuration, plaque control, mucosal
health, radiographs at one year against a baseline taken at fitting and thereafter as indicated, and — specifically
for this patient — occlusal check on shimstock, inspection for wear facets, and confirmation that the screw is
tight at each recall.”
Q
What is the wider lesson from this case?
“Two. First, implant diameter must match the loading demands of the site — narrow implants belong in
lateral incisor and lower incisor positions, not molar sites. Second, repeated screw loosening is a warning, not
an inconvenience: each episode should prompt investigation of the occlusion and the fit, because the escalation
runs loosening, screw fracture, implant fracture.”
Q
How would you know you had handled this well?
“That he understood what had happened and why, without being handed either a blame narrative or a false
reassurance; that removal was achieved with minimal bone loss; that whichever endpoint he chose — replace-
ment or a shortened arch — he is chewing comfortably and can maintain it; and that the mechanical cause was
corrected rather than repeated.”
WATCH OUT
Come back to the mechanics: what force, on what lever arm, through what diameter? Naming those three buys
you a sentence of thinking time and is almost always the right frame for a mechanical implant failure.
Running this case to time
Time check. The flow above holds 35 questions and about 2,391 words of model answer. At 140 words
a minute plus roughly five seconds a question, that is twenty minutes — an overrun of about five. What
goes first is the interim prosthesis and night guard pair in Domain 3: for a lower first molar the honest
answer is that often nothing is needed, and the splint reduces rather than eliminates the risk, so the
two compress into one question. The marks sit in the mechanics — diameter, lever arm, fatigue — in the
escalation from loosening to fracture, and in the shortened arch offered against a site that has already

failed. If your answers run past thirty seconds, you will never reach Domain 4 — and Domain 4 is where
the sleeper is.
The fifteen-minute run sheet
Clock

Domain 1: the mechanical groundwork,

The differential given before looking and

The options with the constraint first —

45 and 47, which is destructive if those

with its sequence: counter-torque if the

otherwise piezo-surgery or a small

— and if replacing, a wide implant
appropriate to a molar with the
occlusion corrected. Then the honesty
the case is built on: the shortened dental

because this site has already failed once

mechanically, avoids grafting, and costs

The removal in strict order with the

Why the order matters: counter-torque
removes the implant without sacrificing

cylinder of host bone with it, enlarges
the defect, may approach the canal, and
turns a straightforward replacement
into a grafting case — counter-torque
first, trephine last, always. The defect
judged by containment: contained, graft
at the same visit with particulate and a
resorbable membrane; non-contained or
with compromised soft tissue, allow six
to eight weeks of soft tissue healing
and stage it, so you have a keratinised
envelope to close over — vertical
defects are a referral. Then what you
would do differently, which is the answer
to the whole case: a wide-diameter
implant of 5 mm or more, a
screw-retained monolithic zirconia
crown for retrievability in a site with a
history of mechanical problems and no
residual cement, a narrow occlusal table
with light centric contact and no

— with the qualification that matters: the

and the occlusion addresses the actual

explained to him plainly, recorded with

Closes on the patient and the record
To him, factually and without a blame
narrative: “The implant has fractured.
That’s uncommon, and I think it happened
because a narrow implant was used in a
position that takes heavy chewing forces and
because the bone level dropped. It has to come
out. Here’s what replacing it involves and
what it would cost, and here’s the alternative
of leaving the space.” On whether to
complain: a recognised complication,
you were not there, raise it with the
treating practice first since they may
wish to contribute, and the formal
routes explained neutrally — no
speculation, no advocacy either way,
and all of it recorded. Recorded: the
history including any previous
loosening, the mobility findings and
what moved relative to what, the dated
radiograph, the diagnosis, the options
with risks and costs, his decision, what
you said about causation and in what
words, and if you retrieve a fragment,
the system, diameter and length, and
whether anything was left in situ.
The spine — the twelve answers to have ready if nothing else
1 The differential for a loose crown, resolved by what moves relative to what · 2 Preload, and the three ways
a joint loses it · 3 Torque value, torque driver, and the ten-minute retorque · 4 Why repeated loosening is
a warning: loosening, screw fracture, implant fracture · 5 Grade 4 titanium, and why titanium-zirconium
exists · 6 Bending stress and the cube of the radius — why 3.3 mm failed here · 7 How bone loss to the
third thread lengthened the lever arm · 8 Why it happened at seven years — fatigue, not overload on the
day · 9 The shortened arch offered against a site that has already failed · 10 Counter-torque first, trephine
last, always · 11 What you would do differently: 5 mm, screw-retained, narrow table, no excursive contact
· 12 The sleeper — what he is told, what you record, what you monitor.

Where the marks are lost in this case
Explaining the fracture as bad luck. The examiner has specified 3.3 mm, a molar site, seven years and
bone loss to the third thread because together they are a complete mechanical explanation. Volunteer it:
bending stress rises with the cube of the reduction in radius, crestal bone loss lengthened the lever
arm, and cyclic loading produced a fatigue fracture — which is why it failed then and not at one year.
And volunteer the history you have not been given: ask about repeated screw loosening, because the
escalation runs loosening, screw fracture, implant fracture, and retightening without investigating the
cause is actively harmful.
Replacing it without changing anything. The site has already failed once. A candidate who says “remove
and place another implant” and stops has learned nothing from the case. Say what changes — 5 mm or
more, screw-retained for retrievability and no cement, narrow occlusal table, light centric contact, no
excursive contact, screw integrity checked at every recall — and then say the harder thing: the shortened
dental arch to the 45 is a legitimate endpoint here and must be offered, because it avoids re-treating a
site that has already failed. Offering it, then arguing honestly against it, is what a 5 looks like.
Never naming the removal line. Removal is where this case can do real harm. Counter-torque on an
engageable fragment is yours. What is not: a trephine removal that would sacrifice substantial bone
near the inferior alveolar canal, a large non-contained defect, vertical augmentation, or any uncertainty
about canal proximity on the CBCT — all referred. Say the sequence with its reason — counter-torque
leaves a socket, a trephine leaves a crater — and say that near the canal in a resorbed posterior mandible,
a second opinion is cheaper than a nerve injury.

soe.title: Aesthetic failure: the implant crown that looks
soe.text:
SOE Case 30 — Aesthetic failure: the implant crown that looks
too long
THE CASE
44-year-old woman, 8 months after fitting of an implant crown at the 11 by another dentist. She is distressed:
the crown is 2 mm longer than the 21, there is a black triangle mesially, and the mucosal margin is 2 mm apical
to that of the 21. She has a high smile line. The implant is healthy — no bleeding, no bone loss.
Pace: one structured opening of about 60 seconds, then roughly 35 questions in the remaining 14 minutes. Nothing after the opening earns you
more than a few seconds of thought.
Opening — the 60-second presentation
Q
Present this case.
“A 44-year-old woman with a biologically successful but aesthetically failed implant restoration at the 11, eight
months after fitting elsewhere. The implant is healthy — no bleeding, no suppuration, no bone loss — so this
is entirely a problem of tissue position and crown proportion: a crown 2 mm longer than the 21, a mid-facial
margin 2 mm apical to its neighbour, and a mesial black triangle. Her high smile line makes every millimetre of
that visible, so her distress is proportionate and I would not minimise it. My tasks are to establish why it looks
like this — most importantly whether the implant is malpositioned — to work out what is genuinely recoverable,
and to be honest with her about the difference between improvement and correction.”
Domain 1 — Clinical interpretation and reasoning
Chain: the aesthetic groundwork
Q
Describe the normal gingival architecture around an upper central incisor.
“A scalloped margin following the CEJ, with the gingival zenith — the most apical point of the margin — sitting
slightly distal to the long axis of a central incisor and on the axis for a canine. The margins of the two centrals
should be level with each other and with the canines, with the laterals about 1 mm coronal. Between the teeth
the interdental papilla fills the embrasure to the contact point, and there is a band of firm keratinised attached
tissue apical to a free gingival groove.”
Q
What is the supracrestal attachment, and what are its dimensions?
“It is the soft tissue attachment between the bone crest and the base of the sulcus — what used to be called
biologic width, renamed supracrestal attached tissue at the 2017 World Workshop. Gargiulo’s figures are
roughly 1 mm of junctional epithelium and 1 mm of connective tissue attachment, with a sulcus of about 0.7
mm above it. It re-establishes itself at a constant dimension, which is why a margin placed too deep produces
either inflammation or recession.”
Q
How does the peri-implant equivalent differ?
“It is longer and weaker. The junctional epithelium is around 2 mm and the connective tissue zone 1 to 1.5 mm,
so the total is greater than around a tooth. Crucially the collagen fibres run parallel to the implant surface, not
inserted perpendicularly, because there is no cementum and no Sharpey’s fibres. Vascularity is reduced, coming
only from the supraperiosteal vessels. That is precisely why soft tissue around implants is less stable and less
correctable than around teeth.”
Q
What decides whether a papilla fills the embrasure?
“The distance from the contact point to the underlying bone crest. On Tarnow’s data, at 5 mm the papilla is
present almost always, at 6 mm about half the time, and at 7 mm only about a quarter. Around an implant the
critical bone is the crest on the adjacent tooth, not the implant, so I cannot create a papilla by anything I do to
the implant — I can only shorten the distance by lowering the contact point.”

Q
Classify smile lines.
“On Tjan’s classification: a low smile shows less than three-quarters of the upper anterior teeth; an average smile
shows three-quarters to all of the clinical crown plus the interdental papillae; a high smile shows the full crown
length plus a continuous band of gingiva. Roughly a fifth of patients have a high smile line, more commonly
women. It is the single biggest determinant of aesthetic risk, and it is why this restoration is a problem rather
than an observation.”
Q
What are the normal proportions of an upper central incisor?
“A width-to-length ratio of about 80%, typically around 8.5 mm wide by 10.5 to 11 mm long. Her crown is 2
mm longer than the 21, so the ratio has dropped to roughly two-thirds and the eye reads it as a long tooth even
before it registers the margin discrepancy. Proportion, symmetry with the contralateral, and the level of the
gingival margins are what an observer actually notices.”
Chain: reading this particular failure
Q
So what has gone wrong here?
“Most likely the implant is malpositioned — too shallow, too buccal, or both — so the mucosal margin sits api-
cally and the crown had to be lengthened to reach the contact. Contributing factors would be a thin phenotype
with recession over the first year, a contact point more than 5 mm from the adjacent crest producing the black
triangle, loss of interproximal bone on the 12, and a pre-existing tissue deficit that was never augmented.”
Q
Which single cause is most likely, and why?
“Three-dimensional implant position. A crown that is 2 mm too long with a margin 2 mm too apical, in a
healthy implant with no bone loss, is the signature of a platform placed too far coronally or too far buccally —
the restoration is simply following where the implant told it to go. Recession alone would not usually give both
findings together to that degree.”
Q
What would you measure and record at that first visit?
“Crown length at the 11 and 21 and the mid-facial margin discrepancy in millimetres; the papilla level against
Jemt’s index; the contact point to crest distance radiographically; phenotype and the width of keratinised tissue;
full peri-implant probing depths, bleeding and suppuration; the smile line on video, at rest and animated. Plus
standardised photographs, study casts, and — with her consent — the previous clinician’s records.”
Q
What would a CBCT add?
“The buccolingual and apicocoronal position of the platform and the thickness of any remaining buccal bone
— neither of which I can determine clinically or from a periapical. That is the finding that decides everything:
if the implant sits within a restorable envelope I can work prosthetically and surgically; if it does not, no crown
and no graft will fix it. I would justify the exposure on that basis under IR(ME)R.”
Q
Define the envelope a central incisor implant should sit in.
“Mesiodistally, at least 1.5 to 2 mm from the adjacent root. Orofacially, the shoulder about 1 to 2 mm palatal
to the emergence line drawn between the adjacent teeth, so the restoration emerges rather than the implant.
Apicocoronally, about 3 mm apical to the planned mucosal margin of the definitive crown. Buser describes
these as comfort and danger zones — outside them, the prosthesis cannot compensate.”
Domain 2 — Clinical decision making and treatment planning
Chain: the conversation before the treatment plan
Q
She is in tears. What do you do first?
“Listen, uninterrupted. I would let her say the whole of it before I look in her mouth, and then acknowledge it
explicitly rather than moving straight to examination. Distress that is dismissed becomes a complaint; distress
that is heard usually becomes a working relationship. Only then would I examine, and I would tell her at the
outset that I am going to need records before I can say anything useful.”

Q
Tell me in your own words what you would say to her.
“ ‘I can see this is really affecting you, and I don’t think you’re being unreasonable — with the way you smile,
this shows. What I can tell you already is that the implant itself is healthy, so we’re not dealing with an infection
or something failing. The problem is where the gum sits and how long the tooth looks. Before I promise you
anything I need a three-dimensional scan, because the position of the implant under the gum decides what’s
realistically possible.’ ”
Q
She asks whether the previous dentist did something wrong. Answer her.
“ ‘I wasn’t there, I haven’t seen the planning records, and it wouldn’t be fair for me to judge a colleague’s work
from the outside. What I can do is tell you exactly what I find and what your options are now.’ I would not
criticise him — but I would not defend the result either, and I would not tell her it looks fine when it does not.”
Q
Do you have a duty of candour here?
“The statutory duty falls on the clinician whose care caused the harm, so it sits with him, not me, for anything
that happened before I met her. My professional duty is to be open and honest with her about what I find,
to support her if she wishes to raise it with him or with the GDC, and to apply candour fully to anything that
arises from my own subsequent treatment.”
Chain: the options
Q
Set out her options.
“Accept and monitor with a full explanation — legitimate, but unlikely to satisfy a high smile line. Prosthetic
modification alone — a new crown with a lowered contact point, altered proportions and cervical pink ceramic.
Soft tissue augmentation with a connective tissue graft, alone or with a new crown. Orthodontic levelling of
the adjacent gingival margins. Explantation and reconstruction if the implant is malpositioned. Or removal
and a resin-bonded bridge with an ovate pontic over a grafted site.”
Q
Which do you recommend?
“It depends entirely on the CBCT. Within a restorable envelope, I would stage prosthetic modification plus a
connective tissue graft, working through a screw-retained provisional so she can see the result before commit-
ting to anything definitive. Grossly malpositioned, I would tell her plainly that no crown will fix it and set out
explantation or removal and a bonded bridge, with honest timescales and cost.”
Q
You said prosthetic modification first — argue against it.
“Fairly: a longer crown with pink ceramic at the neck is camouflage, not correction, and in a high smile line
at conversational distance pink ceramic can read as false. It also commits her to a crown she may still dislike,
having spent money. The counter-argument is that it is reversible, cheap relative to the alternatives, carries no
surgical morbidity, and can be trialled in a provisional first — which is why I would still start there.”
Q
A colleague would go straight to explantation. Why might they be right?
“Because if the implant is buccally positioned, every intermediate step is delay: the graft will relapse, the crown
will still be long, and she will have spent a year and considerable money arriving at the option she could have
started with. If the CBCT shows the platform outside the envelope, they are right and I would say so — the
mistake is grafting a position problem.”
Q
How predictable is soft tissue grafting around an implant compared with a tooth?
“Considerably less. Around a tooth with an intact interproximal attachment, root coverage is highly predictable.
Around an implant there is no cementum, no perpendicular fibre insertion and reduced blood supply, so the
realistic aim is thickening the phenotype and gaining perhaps 1 mm, not complete coverage. Complete cor-
rection of a 2 mm mid-facial discrepancy is unlikely, and I would say that in those words before she consents.”

Q
What is the SAC classification of what you are proposing?
“The original case was Complex — a single central incisor in a high smile line always is. Correcting an estab-
lished aesthetic failure is Complex as well, and arguably harder than the primary case, because I am working
against a fixed implant position and scarred tissue. Explantation of an osseointegrated anterior implant with
reconstruction is beyond straightforward practice.”
Q
Where do your own limits sit?
“Within my competence: the assessment, the CBCT interpretation, the provisional, the new definitive crown,
the maintenance, and the conversation. Beyond it: explantation of an integrated anterior implant, and advanced
mucogingival surgery or contour augmentation in the aesthetic zone. I would refer those, and I would tell her
where the boundary is at the first appointment rather than discovering it mid-treatment.”
Domain 3 — Decision making in relation to treatment procedures
Chain: the prosthetic route
Q
Take me through remaking the crown.
“Remove the definitive crown, place a screw-retained provisional with a concave subgingival contour so the
tissue is not being pushed apically, and let it rebound for several weeks. Then adjust it incrementally to develop
the emergence profile and the margin position I want, review it against photographs and with her, and only
when both of us are satisfied convert it with a customised impression coping into a definitive screw-retained
crown.”
Q
How do you lower the contact point without making a bulbous crown?
“By moving the contact apically and slightly palatally and lengthening it vertically rather than thickening it
buccally, so the embrasure closes from beneath while the labial contour and the width at the incisal third stay
correct. If the contact-to-crest distance is 7 mm I cannot close a black triangle with proportion alone, and I would
be honest that a small triangle may remain.”
Q
What subgingival contour do you want, and why?
“Concave, or at least flat, in the critical zone immediately below the margin — a convex or over-contoured
emergence displaces the mucosa apically and is a common iatrogenic cause of the very recession she has. Below
that, in the subcritical zone, the contour is freer. The principle is that the tissue is supported, not pushed.”
Q
When would you use pink ceramic, and what are its drawbacks?
“Where the vertical tissue deficit cannot be closed surgically and the alternative is an unacceptably long tooth
— so, potentially here. Drawbacks: the transition line between ceramic and mucosa is visible in a high smile,
the colour match is diﬀicult and does not change as her own tissue does, and it is unforgiving if further recession
exposes the join. I would trial it in the provisional before committing.”
Q
Screw or cement retained, and why?
“Screw-retained wherever the access hole allows it. It is retrievable, which matters enormously in a case I
may need to revise repeatedly, and it eliminates subgingival cement, which is a well-recognised cause of peri-
implant disease. If the angulation forces a cingulum-emerging channel I would use an angulated screw channel
system rather than accept cement in the aesthetic zone.”
Q
What abutment material?
“A titanium base with a zirconia or ceramic superstructure. Titanium alone shows through thin mucosa as a
grey band, which in her phenotype and smile line would compound the problem. Zirconia bonded to a titanium
base gives the optical result without the risk of a full ceramic abutment fracturing at the connection.”
Chain: the surgical route

Q
If you graft, describe the sequence.
“Provisional in place with a concave contour and the tissue rebounded. Then a subepithelial connective tissue
graft placed through a split-thickness envelope or tunnel with a coronally advanced flap, secured with sling
sutures, and the provisional relieved so it does not compress the graft. Allow 3 to 6 months of maturation,
adjusting the provisional incrementally, then a customised impression coping and the definitive crown.”
Q
Where would you harvest the graft from?
“The palate, between the distal of the canine and the mesial of the first molar, staying about 2 mm from the
gingival margin and superficial enough to avoid the greater palatine neurovascular bundle, which lies further
apically and closer in a shallow vault. The maxillary tuberosity is an alternative with denser tissue and less
morbidity. A xenogeneic collagen matrix avoids a donor site but gains less thickness.”
Q
What would you consent her for, specifically?
“Donor site pain and bleeding, and the possibility of a palatal bleed needing a stent; graft shrinkage and incom-
plete correction; colour or texture mismatch of the grafted tissue; relapse over the following one to three years;
the number of visits and the total timescale of roughly nine to twelve months; the cost; and, most importantly,
that the realistic aim is improvement rather than symmetry with the 21.”
Q
How long before you would judge the result?
“Not before six months, and I would tell her that at the start so she does not panic at three weeks when it
looks over-corrected and swollen. Peri-implant soft tissue continues to remodel and mid-facial change typically
declares itself over the first one to three years, so the six-month appearance is an interim reading, not the
verdict.”
Domain 4 — Interpretation and problem solving of clinical outcomes
Chain: judging and recording the outcome
Q
How would you measure the outcome objectively?
“With standardised photographs taken at the same distance, magnification and lighting throughout, and a
numerical score — the pink and white aesthetic scores, or at minimum Jemt’s papilla index, the mid-facial
margin level measured against the 21 in millimetres, and the crown length ratio. Alongside that, peri-implant
probing, bleeding and bone levels against baseline, and her own rating of how she feels about it.”
Q
What would you promise her at the outset?
“Improvement, not perfection — in those words, and recorded in those words. I would say that I expect to
make it noticeably better, that I cannot make it identical to the 21, and that if she needs it to be identical then
the honest answer is that this implant is not the route to that. Promising symmetry in this situation is how a
diﬀicult case becomes a complaint.”
Q
At six months the mid-facial margin has relapsed 1 mm. What now?
“First, compare against the standardised photographs rather than her recollection or mine, and confirm it is
genuine relapse and not remodelling. Then check the implant is still healthy and that the crown contour is
not over-contoured and pushing the tissue. Options are a second graft with diminishing returns, prosthetic
recontouring with cervical pink ceramic, or acceptance — and I would present them in that honest order.”
Q
When would you tell her to stop?
“When the marginal gain from each further intervention has become smaller than its cost, morbidity and risk of
making things worse — usually after one graft and one crown remake. Recognising the point of diminishing
returns is a clinical skill, and continuing to operate on an unhappy aesthetic patient rarely ends well. At that
point I would offer a second opinion rather than another procedure.”

Q
What would you record throughout?
“Her presenting concern in her own words; all measurements and the CBCT findings; the options discussed
including doing nothing, with the risks and realistic outcomes of each; the explicit statement that the aim is
improvement not perfection; that a mock-up or provisional was used as the decision tool and that she saw and
approved it; costs; the limits of my competence and any referral; and standardised photographs at every stage.”
Q
What is the lesson for your own practice?
“That anterior implant aesthetics are decided before the drill — by the three-dimensional position, by pheno-
type modification at placement or second stage, and by a mock-up agreed with the patient in advance. Every
corrective option here is less predictable than getting it right at placement. I would make sure my own aesthetic
consent explicitly covers recession, black triangles and long-term change, with a contemporaneous note, and I
would audit that.”
WATCH OUT
Fall back to the question “is this a position problem, a tissue problem or a prosthetic problem?” — say which,
and say what evidence would tell you. That is the frame the whole case hangs on, and it buys you a sentence
of thinking time.
Running this case to time
Time check. The flow above holds 39 questions and about 2,723 words of model answer. At 140 words a
minute plus roughly five seconds a question, that is close to twenty-three minutes — an overrun of seven
to eight. What goes first is the front of Domain 1: normal gingival architecture and the supracrestal
attachment collapse into a single question, and the harvest site and abutment material questions in
Domain 3 disappear entirely. What never goes is Tarnow, the three-dimensional envelope, the CBCT
that decides everything, and improvement not perfection. If your answers run past thirty seconds you
will never reach Domain 4 — and Domain 4 here is where the case is actually won.
The fifteen-minute run sheet

The spine — the twelve answers to have ready if nothing else
1 Biologically successful, aesthetically failed — said in the first clause · 2 The supracrestal attachment, and
how the peri-implant version differs · 3 Tarnow: contact point to crest, and why the crest is on the tooth · 4
Tjan’s high smile line, and why it makes this a problem not an observation · 5 Why position, not recession,
explains both findings · 6 The three-dimensional envelope, in millimetres · 7 What the CBCT decides, and
the IR(ME)R justification · 8 Candour — whose duty it is, and what yours actually is · 9 The six options,
and the one the CBCT would rule out · 10 Grafting round an implant: 1 mm, not coverage · 11 Concave
contour, screw retention, and the provisional as decision tool · 12 Improvement not perfection — and when
to stop.
Where the marks are lost in this case
Treating it as a crown problem. The examiner has given you a healthy implant with no bone loss, a
crown 2 mm long and a margin 2 mm apical — that combination is the signature of three-dimensional
implant position, and a candidate who goes straight to remaking the crown has missed the question the
case is built on. Say the frame out loud: is this a position problem, a tissue problem or a prosthetic
problem — and say that the CBCT decides it, because within the envelope you can work and outside it
no crown and no graft will fix it.
Over-promising the graft. Volunteer, unprompted, that soft tissue grafting round an implant is consid-
erably less predictable than round a tooth — no cementum, no perpendicular fibre insertion, reduced
blood supply — and that the realistic gain is thickening the phenotype and perhaps a millimetre, not
correction of a 2 mm mid-facial discrepancy. Then say the harder thing: the colleague who would go
straight to explantation may be right, because grafting a position problem simply spends her year and
her money arriving at the option she could have started with.
Never naming the limit. Within your competence: the assessment, the CBCT interpretation, the pro-
visional, the definitive crown, the maintenance and the conversation. Not within it: explantation of an
integrated anterior implant, and advanced mucogingival or contour augmentation in the aesthetic zone
— both referred, and both named at the first appointment rather than discovered mid-treatment. The
second limit is temporal: knowing when to stop treating an unhappy aesthetic patient and offer a second
opinion instead of another procedure.

soe.title: The severely anxious patient who asks for an
soe.text:
SOE Case 31 — The severely anxious patient who asks for an
implant
THE CASE
42-year-old woman, dental phobic, has avoided dentistry for 12 years. Presents with pain from a grossly carious
36, which is unrestorable. She is otherwise fit and well. She has heard that implants are “done under sedation”
and asks for one.
Pace: one structured opening of about 60 seconds, then roughly 35 questions in the remaining 14 minutes. Nothing after the opening earns you
more than a few seconds of thought.
Opening — the 60-second presentation
Q
Present this case.
“A 42-year-old dental phobic woman who has avoided dentistry for twelve years and now presents in pain from
an unrestorable 36, asking for an implant because she believes it can be done under sedation. My immediate
priority is relief of pain, delivered in a way that begins to rebuild rather than confirm her fear. The implant
question is a much later one. Implant treatment is a long, multi-visit surgical undertaking followed by lifelong
maintenance, so it is one of the least suitable ways to begin treating a phobic patient, and I would say that to
her kindly rather than simply refusing. What I need to establish is the nature and severity of her anxiety, the
state of the rest of her mouth, whether the underlying disease is controlled, and whether she can realistically
sustain implant maintenance.”
Domain 1 — Clinical interpretation and reasoning
Chain: the undergraduate groundwork — her pain and her tooth
Q
She is in pain. How do you establish the diagnosis?
“History first — site, onset, character, radiation, duration, exacerbating and relieving factors, whether it wakes
her, whether hot or cold provokes it and whether it lingers, and whether she can bite on it. Then examination
and special tests: sensibility testing with cold and electric pulp test on the suspect and control teeth, percussion,
palpation, mobility, periodontal probing, and a periapical radiograph.”
Q
Distinguish irreversible pulpitis from apical periodontitis on those findings.
“Irreversible pulpitis — spontaneous, poorly localised, often worse lying down, an exaggerated response to
cold or heat that lingers beyond ten seconds, and typically not tender to percussion until the inflammation
reaches the periodontal ligament. Apical periodontitis — well localised because the periodontal ligament is
proprioceptive, tender to percussion and biting, the tooth may feel high, sensibility testing is usually negative,
and there may be a widened periodontal ligament space or a periapical radiolucency.”
Q
What makes a tooth unrestorable?
“Insuﬀicient sound coronal tissue to obtain a ferrule of 1.5 to 2 mm circumferentially on sound dentine; caries
extending well subcrestally or into the furcation; an unfavourable crown-to-root ratio; a vertical root fracture;
inaccessible or unnegotiable canals; or a periodontal prognosis that is hopeless regardless. It is also a judgement
about strategic value and about what the patient can sustain — a heroic restoration in someone who has not
attended for twelve years is not a kindness.”
Q
How would you anaesthetise that tooth?
“An inferior alveolar nerve block, needle entering at the coronoid notch level with the barrel over the contralat-
eral premolars, about 1 cm above the mandibular occlusal plane, advancing 20 to 25 mm to bone contact and
withdrawing 1 mm before aspirating. Plus a long buccal infiltration for the buccal soft tissue. Blocks fail more
often in irreversible pulpitis, so I would plan supplementary techniques from the start.”

Q
Why do blocks fail in irreversible pulpitis, and what do you do about it?
“Because the inflamed tissue is acidic, so less of the anaesthetic exists in the un-ionised form that crosses the
nerve membrane; because inflamed nerves show altered, tetrodotoxin-resistant sodium channels; and because
of central sensitisation. The answers are a buccal infiltration of 4% articaine as a supplement, then intraliga-
mentary, intraosseous, or as a last resort intrapulpal anaesthesia — and telling her in advance that I have those
options, because unexpected pain is what created the phobia in the first place.”
Q
Maximum safe dose of lidocaine?
“4.4 mg/kg with adrenaline, to a usual adult maximum of around 300 mg. A 2.2 ml cartridge of 2% lidocaine
contains 44 mg, so for a 70 kg adult that is about seven cartridges — far more than I would need. The practical
point in a phobic patient is not the ceiling; it is warming the cartridge, applying topical properly, and injecting
slowly and out of her line of sight.”
Chain: assessing the anxiety itself
Q
What do you need to establish about her anxiety?
“Its origin and its trigger — needles, the drill, gagging, loss of control, a specific previous traumatic experience,
or a fear of judgement about the state of her mouth, which is very common after long avoidance. Whether she
has had sedation or general anaesthesia before and how she found it. Her medical and psychiatric history and
medication. Who supports her, and what she actually wants.”
Q
How would you measure it?
“With a validated instrument — the Modified Dental Anxiety Scale. Five questions, each scored one to five,
giving a total of five to twenty-five, with nineteen or above indicating severe anxiety or dental phobia. It takes
a minute, it gives me a baseline I can re-measure, and it demonstrates to her that I take it seriously as a clinical
finding rather than a personality trait.”
Q
Is anxiety a contraindication to implant treatment?
“No — but untreated anxiety that prevents maintenance is. The implant will integrate regardless of how she
feels about it. What it will not survive is a patient who cannot attend for peri-implant monitoring, cannot tolerate
professional debridement, and presents years later with advanced peri-implantitis. So the question I am asking
is not ‘can she cope with the surgery’ but ‘can she cope with the next twenty years’.”
Q
What else about a twelve-year absence concerns you?
“That the 36 is unlikely to be the only problem. I would expect active caries elsewhere, undiagnosed periodontal
disease, and possibly oral mucosal lesions that have gone unexamined. I would want a full mouth examination
with a basic periodontal examination, bitewings and appropriate radiographs, and a soft tissue and cancer
screening — she is in a group where late presentation is the norm.”
Domain 2 — Clinical decision making and treatment planning
Chain: the pharmacology and the escalation ladder
Q
Define conscious sedation.
“A technique in which one or more drugs produce a depression of the central nervous system suﬀicient to
allow treatment, but during which verbal contact with the patient is maintained throughout. The drugs and
techniques used must carry a margin of safety wide enough to render loss of consciousness unlikely. If verbal
contact is lost, that is general anaesthesia, and it must be managed as such.”
Q
Set out the anxiety management options from least to most invasive.
“Behavioural techniques first — calm environment, tell-show-do, an agreed stop signal, giving her control over
pace, relaxation and distraction, careful appointment timing and a longer appointment so nothing is rushed.
Then inhalation sedation. Then intravenous conscious sedation with midazolam. General anaesthesia only

in a hospital setting and very rarely for elective treatment. Running alongside all of it, referral for cognitive
behavioural therapy.”
Q
Tell me about inhalation sedation.
“Nitrous oxide and oxygen, titrated, typically at 30 to 40%, delivered through a nasal hood with a minimum
30% oxygen and active scavenging. It is anxiolytic and mildly analgesic, has a very wide margin of safety,
and recovers in minutes so she needs no escort. It is excellent for needle phobia. Contraindications are nasal
obstruction, first-trimester pregnancy, recent middle ear or intraocular surgery, and previous bleomycin.”
Q
And intravenous midazolam?
“Titrated to effect — typically 2 mg over 30 seconds, then 1 mg increments at 60-second intervals, most adults
settling around 5 to 7 mg, with much smaller doses and slower titration in the elderly or medically compromised.
End points are slurred speech, relaxation, delayed response and Verrill’s sign. It gives anterograde amnesia,
which is a genuine advantage in a phobic patient. She needs a responsible escort and cannot drive or work for
the rest of the day.”
Q
What monitoring and what standards?
“Continuous pulse oximetry and blood pressure, clinical observation of colour, respiration and responsiveness,
and a trained second appropriate person present throughout. Compliance with the IACSD standards — ap-
propriate training and continuing education, a designated sedationist, documented pre-operative assessment
and consent, emergency drugs and equipment immediately available, and audit.”
Q
What is flumazenil and how do you use it?
“A competitive benzodiazepine antagonist for reversal of over-sedation or respiratory depression. 200 micro-
grams intravenously over 15 seconds, then 100 micrograms at one-minute intervals, to a usual maximum of
1 mg. It must be immediately available whenever midazolam is used. The critical point is that its half-life
is shorter than midazolam’s, so re-sedation can occur and the patient must be observed, not discharged on
reversal.”
Q
When would general anaesthesia be appropriate?
“For emergency treatment where sedation has genuinely failed, for severe learning disability, or where the surgi-
cal requirement is beyond what sedation can cover — and always in a hospital setting with an anaesthetist. It is
almost never appropriate for elective implant placement, because a patient who requires general anaesthesia
to accept a single visit cannot sustain the twenty years of maintenance that follow.”
Chain: the plan for this patient
Q
What is your plan, in phases?
“Phase one, relief of pain — extraction of the 36 with whatever anxiety management she needs today. Phase
two, stabilisation and acclimatisation — treat the remaining disease by graded exposure across several short
appointments, and address the cause: diet, fluoride, hygiene. Phase three, re-evaluation — only once she is
attending reliably and the disease is controlled do I raise replacing the 36. Phase four, replacement options, of
which an implant is one.”
Q
What are the options for replacing the 36?
“No replacement — a shortened arch to the 35 if the occlusion is stable, requiring no surgery at all. A removable
partial denture. A bridge from 35 to 37 if both are sound, though that is destructive of unrestored teeth. Or
an implant. Given her anxiety I would present the shortened arch first and genuinely, not as a token gesture
before steering her elsewhere.”
Q
You’ve put the shortened arch first — argue against it.
“Fairly: she is 42, so she may live another forty years without a first molar; the 37, if present, may tip and the 26
over-erupt; and there is an argument that a patient should not be denied the definitive option simply because

she finds dentistry frightening — that risks being paternalistic. My counter is that the evidence for functional
adequacy of a shortened arch is good, and I would monitor drifting and over-eruption rather than assume they
will not happen.”
Q
She insists on an implant today. What do you actually say to her?
“ ‘I can hear how much you want this dealt with in one go, and I’m not saying no. But an implant isn’t one
appointment — it’s the surgery, then three or four months of healing, then impressions, then the crown, and
then a check-up every few months for the rest of your life. Sedation makes each visit easier; it doesn’t make there
be fewer of them. Let’s get you out of pain today, and let’s find out together whether coming here is something
you can do. Then we’ll talk about the implant properly.’ ”
Domain 3 — Decision making in relation to treatment procedures
Chain: delivering treatment to this patient
Q
How would you modify today’s extraction appointment?
“First appointment of the day, minimal waiting, a quiet surgery. Explain everything before starting and agree
a stop signal that I actually honour. Topical anaesthetic left in place long enough to work, a warmed cartridge,
slow injection out of her sight. Inhalation sedation if she accepts it. Headphones and music, a companion if she
wants one, continuous narration of what is happening, and no time pressure.”
Q
Would you socket-preserve at the extraction?
“I would extract as atraumatically as possible — periotomes, sectioning rather than levering, preserving the
buccal and lingual plates — because that keeps the implant option open at no extra burden to her. Formal ridge
preservation with a graft I would only do if she had already engaged with the idea of an implant; performing
an extra procedure on a phobic patient for a treatment she may never have is hard to justify.”
Q
If she does proceed to an implant, how would you modify the surgical visit?
“A pre-operative visit to see the room and the equipment with nothing done. Then: first appointment of the
day, sedation as agreed with escort arranged, the same stop signal, instruments kept out of her line of sight,
drapes positioned so she is not covered, warning her before every noise and every vibration, and generous time.
A phone call from me that evening — which does more for a phobic patient than almost anything else.”
Q
Would you place an implant under intravenous sedation?
“Yes, if she needs it and she is suitable — sedation and implant surgery combine well. But I would make two
things explicit to her first: sedation makes the appointment tolerable, it does not shorten the treatment or make
maintenance optional; and a patient who requires sedation for every visit will find a three- to six-monthly
lifelong recall very diﬀicult. That is a genuine clinical argument for the simpler solution.”
Q
What must be in place before you sedate her intravenously?
“A documented pre-operative assessment including ASA status, medical history, medication, allergies, airway
and body mass index, and a plan for the treatment itself. Written consent for both sedation and the procedure,
taken at a separate prior visit and confirmed on the day. Fasting advice per local policy, an escort confirmed,
escort and post-operative instructions given in writing beforehand, and cannulation site checked.”
Q
What are your discharge criteria?
“She is fully conscious and orientated, vital signs stable and back to baseline, able to stand and walk unaided,
no bleeding, pain controlled, and in the care of her responsible escort who has had the written instructions
explained. No driving, no operating machinery, no alcohol, no important decisions or legal documents for the
rest of the day, and a contact number for the evening.”
Q
Halfway through, she becomes distressed and wants to stop. What do you do?

“Stop. Immediately, and completely — because honouring the stop signal is the single most important thing I
will do for her long-term relationship with dentistry. Make the site safe, remove instruments, sit her up, and
let her recover. Then find out what specifically triggered it, and either resume on her terms or stage the rest to
another visit. Overriding a stop signal once destroys everything I have built.”
Q
What is the SAC classification of a single implant at the 36?
“Surgically Straightforward in adequate bone with good access, and prosthodontically Straightforward for a
single posterior crown. But the SAC classification recognises patient modifiers, and severe dental phobia with
a twelve-year absence and unproven maintenance capacity is a significant one — so in practice I would treat
this case as Advanced in its management, even though the drilling is simple.”
Q
Where does the limit of your competence sit here?
“The extraction, the acclimatisation, the restorative care and the implant itself are within my scope. Beyond it:
intravenous sedation unless I hold current IACSD-compliant training and work within a compliant team, and
any general anaesthetic, which needs a hospital referral. Managing the phobia itself is also beyond me — I
would refer for cognitive behavioural therapy, which is the only intervention that treats it rather than working
around it.”
Domain 4 — Interpretation and problem solving of clinical outcomes
Chain: judging whether this was the right decision
Q
How would you judge whether implant treatment was right for her?
“Not by whether the implant integrates, but by whether she is attending, cleaning and maintaining it at two
and five years, and by whether the experience improved or worsened her relationship with dentistry. If a patient
completes implant treatment and then never returns, that is a failure regardless of what the radiographs show.
I would also re-measure her anxiety score and expect it to have fallen.”
Q
At one year she has not attended for ten months and there is bleeding around the implant. Assessment?
“Probe six sites with light force, record bleeding and suppuration, and take a periapical against baseline.
Bleeding with no bone loss is peri-implant mucositis — reversible, and managed by professional debridement
and re-establishing her oral hygiene. Bleeding with progressive bone loss beyond initial remodelling is peri-
implantitis, which is much harder to arrest and which non-attendance predicts.”
Q
How would you have prevented that?
“By making maintenance part of the consent, not an afterthought — agreeing the recall interval before placing
anything, booking the appointments in advance rather than relying on recall letters, keeping the visits short
and predictable, and using the same behavioural approach for hygiene visits as for surgery. And by choosing a
cleansable design — screw-retained, no residual cement, accessible embrasures.”
Q
She now says she wishes she had never had it done. How do you respond?
“By listening first, then reviewing honestly what was discussed and recorded at the outset. If the consent
conversation genuinely covered maintenance and she has decided she cannot sustain it, the discussion is about
how to make it manageable, not about blame. If something I did fell short, I would say so and apply duty of
candour. Either way I would offer a second opinion rather than become defensive.”
Q
What would you record?
“Her anxiety score and its date; the discussion of all options including no treatment and the shortened arch;
the specific conversation that maintenance is lifelong and her stated ability to attend, in her own words; the
sedation assessment, consent taken at a prior visit, drugs and doses titrated, monitoring, recovery and discharge;
her escort’s name; and the written instructions given.”

Q
What is the lesson you take from this case?
“That the hardest clinical decision here is not surgical. The implant is straightforward; the judgement is
whether this particular person can carry it for the next twenty years, and that judgement is made by watching
her attend rather than by asking her whether she will. Acclimatisation first, disease control second, implants
last — and sometimes never, which is a legitimate outcome.”
WATCH OUT
Fall back to the phased frame — pain relief, stabilisation, re-evaluation, then replacement — and say which
phase the question belongs to. It buys you a sentence and it is almost always the right ordering for a neglected,
anxious mouth.
Running this case to time
Time check. The flow above holds 37 questions and about 2,557 words of model answer. At 140 words
a minute plus roughly five seconds a question that is a little over twenty-one minutes — an overrun of
about six. What goes first is the pharmacology detail: the lidocaine maximum dose and the flumazenil
regimen compress into one question, and the discharge criteria and pre-sedation requirements merge.
What never goes is conscious sedation defined, the escalation ladder, the phased plan, and the sentence
the whole case turns on — sedation makes each visit easier; it does not make there be fewer of them. If
your answers run past thirty seconds you will never reach Domain 4, which here is where the judgement
is marked.

today, and let’s find out together whether
coming here is something you can do.” What
you write: her anxiety score and its date;
all options including no treatment and
the shortened arch; the maintenance
conversation and her stated ability to

The spine — the twelve answers to have ready if nothing else
1 Pain relief first, and why the order is the answer · 2 Irreversible pulpitis against apical periodontitis on the
findings · 3 Unrestorable — ferrule, and what she can sustain · 4 Why blocks fail in pulpitis, and the three
supplementary techniques · 5 The Modified Dental Anxiety Scale, and the score that matters · 6 Anxiety
is not the contraindication; unmaintainable anxiety is · 7 Conscious sedation defined — verbal contact
throughout · 8 The ladder: behavioural, inhalation, intravenous, GA, with CBT alongside · 9 Midazolam
titration, and why flumazenil does not permit discharge · 10 The four phases, and the shortened arch
offered first and genuinely · 11 The stop signal, honoured absolutely · 12 Success measured at five years
by attendance, not by integration.
Where the marks are lost in this case
Answering the sedation question instead of the case. The examiner is not asking whether you can titrate
midazolam — that is one question and it is worth one answer. The case is about whether this woman can

carry an implant for twenty years, and the sentence that scores is that sedation makes the appointment
tolerable, not the treatment shorter or the maintenance optional. A patient who needs sedation for every
visit will struggle with a lifelong three- to six-monthly recall, and saying so is the clinical argument, not
a soft one.
Skipping the undergraduate third. The first three minutes are pulp diagnosis, unrestorability and local
anaesthetic physiology, and they are marked. Volunteer the part candidates never do: blocks fail more
often in irreversible pulpitis, for named reasons, so you plan supplementary techniques from the start
and tell her you have them — because unexpected pain is what created the phobia in the first place.
And volunteer the shortened arch to the 35 first and genuinely, then argue against it fairly, rather than
producing it as a token before steering her to an implant.
Never naming the limit. The extraction, the acclimatisation, the restorative care and the implant itself are
yours. Not yours: intravenous sedation unless you hold current IACSD-compliant training and work
in a compliant team, and any general anaesthetic, which is a hospital referral. And the limit candidates
miss entirely — the phobia itself, which is treated by cognitive behavioural therapy, the only intervention
that treats it rather than working around it. Acclimatisation first, disease control second, implants last, and
sometimes never — which is a legitimate outcome.

soe.title: High smile line, thin phenotype, immediate
soe.text:
SOE Case 32 — High smile line, thin phenotype, immediate
implant request
THE CASE
29-year-old model. The 11 has a horizontal root fracture below the crest following trauma 3 weeks ago and
is unrestorable. High smile line, thin scalloped phenotype, triangular crown forms. CBCT: buccal plate 0.6
mm thick, intact. She has read about “same-day teeth” and wants the tooth out and an implant placed with a
temporary crown at the same visit.
Domain 1
“This is the highest-risk aesthetic scenario in implant dentistry: an upper central incisor in a young patient with a
high smile line, thin scalloped phenotype, triangular crowns and a 0.6 mm buccal plate, in a profession where
appearance is her livelihood. She is asking for the protocol that carries the greatest aesthetic risk in exactly the
situation where risk is least acceptable.”
Q
Work through the ITI immediate placement decision tree.
“The pre-operative assessment requires a thick soft tissue phenotype, absence of recession and low aesthetic
risk. She fails all three. It then requires CBCT confirmation of an intact socket with a facial wall of at least
1 mm — hers is 0.6 mm — enough apical and palatal bone, the socket within the bone envelope, a horizontal
defect of at least 2 mm, and no infection. She therefore falls into the second branch: facial wall under 1 mm.
The tree directs to Type II–III placement at 4 to 16 weeks, or, if the situation is incompatible with Type I to III
placement, ridge preservation or a formal graft followed by Type IV late placement at 4 to 6 months. On the
SAC classification this is Complex surgically and prosthodontically.”
Q
What else would you assess?
“Exact smile line and lip dynamics on video, not just at rest; papilla heights and interproximal bone levels on
the 12 and 21, which determine the papillae and which I cannot recreate; sensibility of the adjacent teeth after
trauma; the position of the fracture relative to the crest; her occlusion, particularly overbite and protrusive
contacts; her expectations in her own words; and comprehensive photographic records.”
Domain 2
Q: What do you tell her?
“Honestly and without condescension. ‘I understand why same-day teeth appeal, and in the right mouth they
work well. Yours isn’t the right mouth for it, and I’d be doing you a disservice if I pretended otherwise. The
bone on the front of your tooth is about half a millimetre thick — thinner than a fingernail — and your gum is
thin too. If I place an implant today, the most likely result over the next couple of years is that the gum shrinks
back and you see a grey line or a longer tooth. In your job that’s not a small thing. What I’d like to do instead
is take the tooth out very carefully, preserve the socket, give you a temporary tooth that looks good and that
nobody will notice, and place the implant once the site is right.’ ”
Q
What is your plan?
“Atraumatic extraction without a flap, preserving the buccal plate absolutely — periotomes, sectioning if
needed, no buccal levering. Ridge preservation with a slowly resorbing xenograft and a socket seal. An
immediate resin-bonded provisional bridge or a bonded pontic — not a denture, which would press on the
site and is unacceptable to her professionally. Reassess at 8 weeks clinically and, if needed, with CBCT. Then
either early placement (Type 2–3) with simultaneous contour augmentation and a connective tissue graft, or
late placement at 4 to 6 months if the ridge needs staged augmentation.
Two-stage submerged healing, then a screw-retained provisional to develop the emergence over 8 to 12 weeks,
then a customised impression coping and a definitive screw-retained restoration on a Ti-base with a ceramic
superstructure.”

Q
Would you treat her yourself?
“This is Complex in both dimensions. I would undertake the extraction and ridge preservation and the restora-
tive planning, and I would refer or co-manage the implant placement with contour augmentation and connective
tissue grafting in this aesthetic zone. Saying that to her early is better than discovering my limits mid-treatment.”
Q
What must the consent cover, given who she is?
“Under Montgomery, materiality is judged from her position. So: mid-facial recession; grey show-through;
black triangles, which her triangular crown form makes more likely; that the appearance may change over
years; the total treatment time of nine to twelve months and what she will wear during it — which for a model
is a material fact; the possibility that the result will not match the 21 exactly; the cost including maintenance;
and that no one can guarantee an aesthetic outcome. I would use a mock-up so she can see the achievable result
before committing, and record all of it.”
Domain 3
Q: How does the thin phenotype change your surgical plan?
“It makes phenotype modification part of the plan, not a rescue procedure. I would perform a connective
tissue graft at placement or at second stage — the two windows when it is most predictable — to convert a
thin phenotype to a thicker one. I would also position the implant palatally, use a narrow-diameter implant to
leave more buccal bone, over-contour the buccal graft slightly to allow for resorption, and use a Ti-base with a
ceramic superstructure rather than a titanium abutment to avoid grey show-through.”
Domain 4
Q: How would you monitor the aesthetic outcome?
“Standardised photographs at every stage; pink and white aesthetic scores, or at minimum the papilla index
and the mid-facial margin level measured against the 21; peri-implant probing, bleeding and bone levels. Re-
views at 1 week, 3 weeks, second stage, provisional adjustments, fitting, 3 months, 12 months, then maintenance.
I would counsel her that mid-facial recession, if it occurs, typically appears over the first one to three years,
so I would not declare success at six months.”
Q
What if, despite everything, she develops recession at two years?
“I would have prepared her for that possibility. Management would be a connective tissue graft, a change of
abutment material, prosthetic recontouring with cervical pink ceramic, or — if the implant position is the prob-
lem — explantation and reconstruction. I would be honest, apply duty of candour if anything I did contributed,
and involve a colleague for a second opinion. And I would use the photographs to have that conversation
objectively.”
Running this case to time
Time check. This case is written in the older format — nine long answers, about 903 words. At 140 words
a minute plus five seconds a question that is barely seven and a quarter minutes: it does not overrun, it
leaves almost eight minutes unaccounted for. Read that the right way round — the printed answers
are far longer than anything you would say out loud, and each is really three or four short questions in
the mouth of an examiner. The decision tree alone is four: the pre-operative criteria, which ones she fails,
which branch that puts her in, and what the branch directs you to. If your answers run past thirty seconds
you will still never reach Domain 4 — and Domain 4 here is the one-to-three-year recession window, which
is the easiest mark in the case to earn.

with a plan attached and in her own words — half a millimetre, thinner than a fingernail, a gum that

nobody will notice, and the implant when the site is right.

at a time and say which she fails and by how much — thick phenotype, no recession, low aesthetic risk,
then the 1 mm facial wall against her 0.6 mm — and then name the branch and what it directs to. Then
