and 21, and nothing you do to the implant can create them. And volunteer that phenotype modification
is part of the plan, not a rescue — a connective tissue graft at placement or second stage, because those
are the two predictable windows.

Taking the whole case on. This is Complex in both dimensions and it sits beyond a general dentist
with an interest in implants. The extraction, the ridge preservation, the provisional and the restorative
planning are yours. Immediate or early placement in a thin phenotype with a high smile line, with
simultaneous contour augmentation and connective tissue grafting in the aesthetic zone, is not — that
is referred or co-managed with someone who does it regularly, and, as the case says, saying so early is
better than discovering your limits mid-treatment.

soe.title: Multiple missing posterior teeth on a limited
soe.text:
SOE Case 33 — Multiple missing posterior teeth on a limited
budget
THE CASE
51-year-old builder. Missing 16, 17, 26, 27, 36, 37, 46, 47 — all four posterior sextants. He has an intact anterior
dentition from 15 to 25 and 35 to 45, all sound. He has marked wear on the anterior teeth and masseteric
hypertrophy. He can afford approximately the cost of two implants.
Domain 1
“A patient with a shortened dental arch to the second premolars in all four quadrants, intact and sound anterior
teeth, clear signs of parafunction, and a limited budget. This is a case where the correct answer may be to do
very little, and where the temptation to fill every space is the trap.”
Q
What is his functional status?
“I would ask rather than assume: can he eat what he wants, does he have pain or discomfort, does he have any
TMJ symptoms, and what actually brought him in? A patient with premolar occlusion and no complaint may
not need any posterior replacement at all.”
Q
What is the significance of the anterior wear?
“It tells me he is loading his anterior teeth heavily, partly because of parafunction and partly because he has no
posterior support. That is an argument for some posterior replacement — to protect the anterior teeth — and
simultaneously a warning about the mechanical risk of anything I place.”
Domain 2
Q: What are the options?
“Shortened dental arch — accept the current situation. Evidence from Käyser onwards indicates that around 20
teeth with four occluding premolar pairs gives adequate function and satisfaction, without increased TMD or
periodontal breakdown. He already has that. This is the default and the cheapest option, and I would present
it as a positive choice.
Removable partial dentures — bilateral free-end saddles, the least well tolerated design; in a builder with
parafunction, unlikely to be worn.
Implants — but eight units is far beyond his budget. The question becomes: if I can only place two, where?
A combination — implants in the two most valuable positions, accepting the shortened arch elsewhere.”
Q
If you place two implants, where and why?
“I would place them at the first molar positions in the arch where he has the greatest functional deficit, most
likely the 36 and 46 — restoring lower first molars gives the greatest functional return, mandibular bone is more
favourable, and it re-establishes posterior support to protect the anterior teeth. I would not place single implants
at the 17 or 27 positions, which contribute least. But I would say honestly that the marginal functional gain
over a well-managed shortened arch may be small, and that spending his money on a protective splint, occlusal
management of the anterior wear, and prevention may serve him better. That is a legitimate recommendation,
not a cop-out.”
Q
What about his parafunction?
“It must be addressed regardless of what else I do. A hard, full-coverage occlusal splint for night-time wear,
adjusted to give even contacts and canine guidance. Discussion of stress and sleep, and screening for obstructive
sleep apnoea if there are symptoms, with referral to his GP. Anything I place will be loaded heavily, so I would
design for it: wide implants, monolithic zirconia, narrow occlusal tables, no cantilevers, and consent to a higher
mechanical complication rate.”

Q
SAC?
“Individual posterior implants in adequate bone would be Straightforward surgically. Prosthodontically, the
parafunction is a modifier that raises it to Advanced. The overall case management — deciding what not to do
— is the harder part.”
Domain 3
Q: What would you check before placing at the 36 and 46?
“CBCT for residual height above the canal and ridge width; the position of the mental foramina and any anterior
loop; the lingual concavity; and the restorative space, because unopposed upper teeth may have over-erupted,
though here the uppers are also missing so the space is likely generous. Also mouth opening and access — he
is a large man and posterior access matters.”
Q
Surgical and restorative plan?
“Standard placement with 2 mm canal clearance, wide-diameter implants if width allows, conventional loading
at three months, screw-retained monolithic zirconia crowns, narrow occlusal tables, light centric contacts, no
excursive contacts, and a night guard fabricated after the crowns are fitted and adjusted to include them.”
Domain 4
Q: How would you judge success in this case?
“By his function and comfort, not by the number of teeth. I would ask him at each review what he can eat now
that he could not before. I would monitor the anterior wear with photographs and casts, because arresting that
is arguably the main clinical objective. And I would monitor the implants conventionally.”
Q
What is the risk of the alternative approach — filling every space?
“Eight implants he cannot afford, in a heavy parafunctional loader, with a high mechanical complication rate and
a maintenance burden he may not sustain — a worse outcome than a well-managed shortened arch. Knowing
when not to treat is an examinable clinical skill, not a failure of ambition.”
Running this case to time
Time check. This case is written in the older format — ten long answers, about 691 words. At 140 words a
minute plus five seconds a question that is under six minutes: it does not overrun, it leaves nine minutes
unaccounted for. Read that the right way round — the printed answers are far longer than anything you
would say out loud, and each is really three or four short questions. The options answer alone is four:
the shortened arch and its evidence, the free-end saddle denture, the arithmetic that eight implants do
not fit the budget, and the combination. If your answers run past thirty seconds you will still never reach
Domain 4, which here is the question the whole case exists for — the risk of filling every space.

tables, no cantilevers · 12 Knowing when not to treat, said in those words.
Where the marks are lost in this case
Planning eight implants he cannot have. The candidate who starts costing a full posterior reconstruction
has failed the case in the first minute. He has four occluding premolar pairs and sound anterior teeth,
and Käyser’s evidence says that is functionally adequate. Present the shortened dental arch first, as a
positive choice, name the evidence, and only then move to what two implants could add — 36 and 46, for
functional return and posterior support, and never the 17 or 27.
Ignoring the wear. The marked anterior wear and masseteric hypertrophy are not scenery; arresting
that wear is arguably the main clinical objective of the case. Volunteer the hard full-coverage splint
with even contacts and canine guidance, the discussion of stress and sleep, the screen for obstructive
sleep apnoea with GP referral, and the design consequences — wide implants, monolithic zirconia,
narrow occlusal tables, no cantilevers, and explicit consent to a higher mechanical complication rate.

implant in adequate bone is within any implant dentist’s scope. The line is honest sequencing: saying
out loud that a splint, occlusal management and prevention may serve him better than two implants,
and that a well-made partial denture or an accepted shortened arch is a legitimate endpoint, not a
consolation. Refer if the parafunctional occlusal management runs beyond you — but say the cheaper
option genuinely, or the examiner will read it as a token.

soe.title: Adult hypodontia
soe.text:
SOE Case 34 — Adult hypodontia
THE CASE
26-year-old woman with hypodontia: congenitally absent 12, 22, 35, 45, with retained but infra-occluded decid-
uous 75 and 85. She has completed orthodontic treatment, with spaces opened at the lateral incisor sites (6 mm
each) and the deciduous molars retained. She wants “everything sorted”.
Domain 1
“An adult hypodontia case with four missing permanent units and two retained, infra-occluded deciduous
molars. This is a multidisciplinary case, and my first job is to establish who else needs to be involved and
what the endpoint is, rather than to start treating the easiest bit.”
Q
What are the specific issues in a hypodontia patient?
“The alveolus never developed fully around teeth that never formed, so the sites are typically narrow buc-
colingually and may be reduced in height — augmentation is more likely than in an acquired edentulous site.
Infra-occluded deciduous teeth are ankylosed and take the surrounding alveolar bone down with them, so their
sites are often vertically deficient. There is often a microdont or unusual crown form in the remaining teeth
requiring restorative harmonisation. And there are psychological and long-term maintenance dimensions in a
young patient who will need this care for sixty years.”
Q
What would you assess?
“Smile line and lip dynamics; the exact space at each site and whether it matches the ideal tooth width; the
crown form and shade of the adjacent teeth; the vertical position of the deciduous molars and the extent of infra-
occlusion; occlusion and vertical dimension; CBCT for ridge dimensions at all four sites; periodontal status; and
her expectations. I would also want the orthodontist’s records and retention plan, because implants cannot be
placed until the position is stable and retained.”
Domain 2
Q: What are the options at the lateral incisor sites?
“Implants — 6 mm of space allows a 3.3 mm narrow implant with 1.5 mm each side, which is feasible, but
hypodontia sites are often narrow and may need contour augmentation.
Resin-bonded cantilever bridges from the canines — minimally invasive, well evidenced for single anterior
units, reversible in principle, and avoiding surgery in a 26-year-old. Often the better choice.
Composite build-ups or veneers on the canines with orthodontic space closure — the canine substitution
route, though the orthodontics is complete and reopening that discussion has costs.
Removable prosthesis — interim only.”
Q
And at the deciduous molar sites?
“First, decide the fate of the 75 and 85. A well-retained, minimally infra-occluded deciduous molar in an adult
can serve for many years and is often best retained and monitored, sometimes with onlay build-up to restore
the occlusal plane. If they are significantly infra-occluded, ankylosed, submerging further, or damaging the
adjacent periodontium, they should be extracted — but I must warn her that extraction reveals a vertically
deficient site that may need augmentation. If they are retained, no replacement is needed at all.”
Q
What would you recommend overall?
“A staged, conservative plan:
1. Multidisciplinary discussion with the orthodontist and, given the complexity, a restorative specialist.
2. Retain the deciduous molars if sound, monitoring with annual photographs and radiographs; restore the
occlusal plane with composite if needed.
3. At the lateral incisor sites, offer resin-bonded cantilever bridges as first line and implants as the alternative,

with a mock-up to show her the achievable aesthetics either way.
4. Defer any decision about the deciduous molar sites until they actually fail. This preserves options, avoids
irreversible surgery in a 26-year-old, and can be revisited as she ages.”
Q
SAC?
“The lateral incisor implants: surgically Advanced — narrow sites likely needing contour augmentation, aes-
thetic zone. Prosthodontically Advanced — crown form harmonisation across the anterior segment. The overall
case is Complex by virtue of being multidisciplinary and lifelong, and I would want it managed within a team.”
Domain 3
Q: If you place implants at the 12 and 22, describe the key considerations.
“Space: 6 mm allows a 3.3 mm implant with 1.5 mm to each root; I would confirm root positions and divergence
on CBCT and, if the roots converge, ask the orthodontist for root divergence before placement.
Bone: hypodontia sites are often narrow; I would expect to need simultaneous contour augmentation and
would plan for a two-stage submerged protocol.
Position: shoulder 3 mm apical to the planned mid-facial margin, 1 to 2 mm palatal, angled through the cingu-
lum.
Phenotype: consider a connective tissue graft at placement or second stage.
Retention: the orthodontic retainer must be designed to allow the implant crowns, and she must remain in
retention.
Restoration: screw-retained on Ti-bases, with the crown form harmonised to the canines — which may itself
require composite or ceramic modification of the canines.”
Domain 4
Q: What is the lifelong picture you must explain to her?
“That she will be maintaining these restorations for sixty years; that implant crowns will need replacing more
than once in that time; that continued eruption of the natural dentition relative to an ankylosed implant can
produce infra-occlusion and open contacts even in adults, requiring modification; and that she will need regular
review with photographs to detect these changes. I would rather she heard that now than at 45.”
Q
What would you monitor specifically?
“Standardised photographs and study casts at intervals, to detect relative infra-occlusion and open proximal
contacts; the deciduous molars for progressive submergence and root resorption; peri-implant health; and the
periodontal condition of the canines carrying any bonded bridge.”
Running this case to time
Time check. This case is written in the older format — nine long answers, about 767 words. At 140
words a minute plus five seconds a question that is a little over six minutes: it does not overrun, it leaves
nearly nine minutes unaccounted for. Read that the right way round — the printed answers are far longer
than anything you would say out loud, and each is really three or four short questions. The hypodontia
issues answer alone is four: the undeveloped alveolus, the infra-occluded deciduous teeth, the microdont
crown forms, and the sixty-year horizon. If your answers run past thirty seconds you will still never reach
Domain 4, which here is the lifelong picture — the domain most candidates never get to and the one that
distinguishes them.

one printed answer, and it is really six

if the roots converge, ask the

ankylosed implant can produce

Closes on the patient and the record
What you say: “I know you want

But you’re 26, and whatever we do here you’ll

so sites are narrow and often need augmentation · 3 Infra-occluded deciduous teeth are ankylosed and
take the bone down with them · 4 The orthodontist’s retention plan, and why implants wait for stability ·
5 6 mm allows a 3.3 mm implant with 1.5 mm each side · 6 Resin-bonded cantilever bridges — minimally
invasive, well evidenced, often better here · 7 Retaining the 75 and 85, and what extraction would reveal · 8

· 10 Root divergence requested before placement · 11 The retainer redesigned around the implant crowns ·

Where the marks are lost in this case

the candidate who reads that as an instruction to place two implants has skipped the decision. In a 26-
year-old, the resin-bonded cantilever bridge from the canine is first line — minimally invasive, well
evidenced for single anterior units, reversible in principle, and it avoids irreversible surgery in a young
patient whose options should be preserved. Implants are the genuine alternative, shown alongside it on
a mock-up, not the default.
Extracting the 75 and 85 on sight. A well-retained, minimally infra-occluded deciduous molar in an
adult can serve for many years and is often best retained, monitored with annual photographs and
radiographs, and built up in composite to restore the occlusal plane. Volunteer the consequence of
the alternative — extraction reveals a vertically deficient site that may need augmentation — and then

volunteer the conclusion candidates never reach: if they are retained, no replacement is needed at all,
and the decision on those sites can be deferred until they actually fail.

will need replacing more than once, that continued eruption of the natural dentition relative to an
ankylosed implant produces infra-occlusion and open contacts even in adults, and that this is why she
needs standardised photographs and casts at intervals. And name the line: this is Advanced at the lateral
sites and Complex overall by virtue of being multidisciplinary and lifelong — it belongs in a team with
the orthodontist and a restorative specialist, and the placement of narrow implants into unaugmented
hypodontia sites in the aesthetic zone is not solo work.

soe.title: The patient who will not commit to maintenance
soe.text:
SOE Case 35 — The patient who will not commit to maintenance
THE CASE
47-year-old sales director who travels internationally 40 weeks a year. Missing 36 and 46. Medically fit, non-
smoker, moderate plaque control, no periodontal disease. He wants implants but says frankly that he “cannot
commit to appointments every few months” and is “away too much”.
Domain 1
“A medically and dentally suitable candidate whose limiting factor is entirely behavioural and practical: he is
telling me, honestly, that he cannot attend maintenance. That honesty is valuable, and I should treat it as clinical
information rather than as an obstacle to be talked around.”
Q
Why does this matter so much?
“Because the strongest predictor of long-term peri-implant health is supportive maintenance combined with
daily plaque control. Peri-implantitis affects around 22% of patients, and the risk is substantially higher in
those without regular supportive care. An implant placed in a patient who never returns is an implant I am
likely to be removing in ten years.”
Q
What would you assess?
“His actual plaque control, disclosed and scored, not his description of it. His periodontal status and BPE. His
dexterity and technique. What his travel pattern really is — whether he is home at predictable intervals, which
may be perfectly workable. Whether he has a dentist wherever he spends most time. And what he actually
wants replaced and why.”
Domain 2
Q: How do you approach the conversation?
“Not as a refusal. ‘Thank you for being straight with me — that helps. Let me be equally straight. Implants don’t
decay, but they can get gum disease, and that’s the main way people lose them. The single thing that protects
them is being seen regularly and cleaning them properly every day. If you genuinely can’t be seen every few
months, that changes the risk substantially, and it changes what I’d recommend. Let’s work out what is actually
possible for you.’ Then problem-solve: could he be seen twice a year when he is home? Could he see a dentist
in the city he most often works in, with a shared care arrangement and my records sent? Could his hygiene be
made robust enough with a simpler prosthesis design?”
Q
What are the options?
“No treatment — a shortened arch to the second premolars, which requires no maintenance beyond his normal
dentistry. Given he is missing only the first molars, this is genuinely reasonable and I would present it first.
Removable partial denture — low biological risk if he cleans it, easily replaced.
Bridges from 35–37 and 45–47 if those teeth are sound — but destructive, and they also require maintenance.
Implants with a modified plan — fewer implants, maximally cleansable screw-retained designs, and a docu-
mented shared-care maintenance arrangement.”
Q
Would you place implants?
“Yes, potentially — but only with three things in place: a realistic, agreed maintenance arrangement, even if
that is twice yearly rather than quarterly, possibly with a second clinician abroad; demonstrated improvement
in his plaque control at a review before I commit; and explicit written consent that his risk of peri-implant
disease is higher because of reduced maintenance, with the consequences spelled out. If his plaque score does
not improve at review, I would decline and say why.”

Q
How do you design for a low-maintenance patient?
“Screw-retained, always — retrievable, and no cement. Wide embrasures and a cleansable emergence profile
that an interdental brush passes through easily. No deep subgingival margins. Separate crowns rather than
splinted units, so he can clean between them. Adequate keratinised mucosa, grafted if necessary, since it
makes brushing more comfortable and is associated with less inflammation. And a tissue-level implant in a
non-aesthetic posterior site, which keeps the microgap supracrestal and simplifies cleaning.”
Domain 3
Q: What would you actually do at the placement and restoration stages differently?
“Nothing exotic — the differences are in design rather than technique. I would ensure at least 2 mm of keratinised
mucosa, using an apically positioned flap at second stage if needed. I would use a custom abutment shaped
for cleansability rather than for maximum tissue support, and I would spend disproportionate time on the
hygiene instruction appointment, sizing brushes, watching him use them, and giving written instructions with
the sizes noted.”
Domain 4
Q: How would you structure his maintenance realistically?
“Agree a fixed pattern he can actually keep — for example, two long appointments a year timed to when he
is home, each including full peri-implant probing, professional biofilm removal and re-instruction, with radio-
graphs at one year and then as indicated. Provide him with a written record and his implant card so that any
clinician anywhere can pick up his care. Set a recall reminder system that reaches him, and record every failed
or cancelled appointment.”
Q
If he stops attending altogether and returns at five years with peri-implantitis, what then?
“I would treat him without recrimination, following the decision tree, and I would use the consent record to
have an honest conversation about how we got here and what needs to change. Blaming him achieves nothing;
but a clear, documented record of what was agreed protects the therapeutic relationship as well as me.”
Running this case to time
Time check. This case is written in the older format — nine long answers, about 721 words. At 140
words a minute plus five seconds a question that is under six minutes: it does not overrun, it leaves nine
minutes unaccounted for. Read that the right way round — the printed answers are far longer than
anything you would say out loud, and each is really three or four short questions. The design answer
alone is five: screw retention, embrasures, margin depth, splinting, keratinised mucosa and the tissue-
level implant. If your answers run past thirty seconds you will still never reach Domain 4, which here is
the realistic maintenance schedule and the five-year return — the part of the case where the earlier consent
conversation either saves you or does not.

has ignored that he is missing only two first molars and is otherwise fit and disease-free. The mark is
in problem-solving: twice a year when he is home, a shared-care clinician in the city he works in with
records sent, and a design robust enough to survive imperfect attendance — with the shortened arch
put on the table first and genuinely.

at a review before you commit, and explicit written consent that his risk of peri-implant disease is
higher because of reduced maintenance, with the consequences spelled out. Then volunteer the harder

a single implant at the 36 or 46 is Straightforward. The line is whether you will proceed at all with
reduced maintenance, and it is drawn by design as much as by conversation: screw-retained always, no

supracrestal. A patient you will see twice a year needs a prosthesis that forgives — and if he will not
attend at all, the shortened arch or a well-made denture is the right answer, recorded as a considered
decision.

soe.title: Failing lower denture in an elderly patient with
soe.text:
SOE Case 36 — Failing lower denture in an elderly patient with
early dementia
THE CASE
81-year-old woman with mild Alzheimer’s dementia, living with her daughter. Edentulous for 20 years. Her
lower complete denture is loose and she is losing weight. Her daughter asks whether implants would help. She
takes donepezil and an antihypertensive; she is otherwise well and mobile.
Domain 1
“An 81-year-old with early dementia, a loose lower denture and weight loss — which makes this a nutritional
and quality-of-life problem, not merely a prosthetic one. The clinical question of whether a two-implant
overdenture would help is straightforward; the harder questions are capacity, the trajectory of her dementia,
and who will maintain the prosthesis in five years.”
Q
What do you need to establish about her dementia?
“Its severity and rate of progression; whether she has decision-specific capacity for this decision, assessed by
the four-part functional test — can she understand, retain, weigh and communicate a decision about implant
treatment; her insight; whether she can cooperate for a surgical appointment; and her manual dexterity and
ability to manage a prosthesis. I would seek information from her general medical practitioner and her daughter,
while remembering that the patient, not the daughter, is my patient.”
Q
What about the weight loss?
“It must be taken seriously and not assumed to be dental. I would ask about appetite, swallowing, dry mouth,
taste changes, mood and depression, and refer to her GP for assessment. Dental causes — an unstable denture,
sore spots, reduced masticatory eﬀiciency — may be contributory but are rarely the sole cause. Referral to a
dietitian may help regardless of what I do.”
Domain 2
Q: What are the options?
“Optimise the existing prosthesis first: assess extension, occlusion, vertical dimension and fit; consider a reline,
a copy denture — which preserves the tooth position and polished surfaces she has adapted to over twenty years
— or a remake using neutral zone technique. Denture adhesive and dietary advice. This is low-risk, reversible
and may be suﬀicient.
Two-implant mandibular overdenture — the McGill and York consensus position that this is the minimum
standard of care for the edentulous mandible, and the intervention with the best evidence for improving satis-
faction and, in some studies, nutritional outcomes.
No further intervention with supportive dietary care.”
Q
How does the dementia change the decision?
“It does not automatically preclude implants — but it changes the calculus in three ways.
Capacity: she must be able to consent. If she lacks capacity, elective implant treatment in her best interests
would be very diﬀicult to justify, and I would be extremely cautious.
Trajectory: dementia is progressive. In five years she may be unable to clean around abutments, may not
tolerate examination, and may be in residential care. A prosthesis that becomes unmaintainable is a liability —
peri-implant disease in a patient who cannot cooperate with treatment is a real problem.
Simplicity: if I proceed, the design must be as simple and cleanable as possible — two implants with stud
attachments, not a bar, so that a carer can clean around two abutments with a single-tufted brush.”

Q
What would you recommend?
“I would optimise the conventional denture first, using a copy technique, and see whether that resolves the
problem — many do. If it does not, and if she has capacity and her daughter can support daily cleaning, I would
offer a two-implant overdenture with Locator-type attachments as a modest, well-evidenced intervention,
undertaken sooner rather than later while she can still consent and cooperate. I would be explicit that the
argument for acting now rather than in two years is precisely her dementia — the window for a treatment that
requires her cooperation is closing.”
Q
How do you handle the daughter?
“With her mother’s agreement, involve her fully — she is likely to be the person supporting daily cleaning
and attendance. But I would address my questions and explanations to the patient, check the patient’s own
understanding, and ensure the decision is hers while she has capacity. If mother and daughter disagree, the
patient’s own decision prevails while she has capacity.”
Domain 3
Q: Describe the surgical modifications.
“Short, calm appointments at a time of day when she is at her best — usually the morning. A familiar accompany-
ing person present. Clear, simple explanations repeated as needed. Two implants in the canine regions, at least 5
mm anterior to the mental foramina; a simple mid-crestal incision; a one-stage protocol with healing abutments
to avoid a second surgery; minimal grafting; and conventional loading at about three months. Careful denture
relief and soft relining afterwards.”
Domain 4
Q: What is the maintenance plan?
“Written, simple and shared with her daughter: remove the denture at night; clean around each abutment with
a single-tufted brush; clean the housings in the denture fit surface; review every three to six months. I would
demonstrate to the daughter as well as to the patient, and give written instructions with pictures. I would record
who is providing daily care.”
Q
When would you decide not to proceed?
“If she lacked capacity; if she could not tolerate a surgical appointment; if her dementia were progressing rapidly;
if there were no reliable daily support; or if optimising the conventional denture solved the problem. Any of
those would make a conventional denture the right answer — and I would document the reasoning so that it is
clear this was a considered decision, not neglect.”
Running this case to time
Time check. This case is written in the older format — nine long answers, about 778 words. At 140 words
a minute plus five seconds a question that is a little over six minutes: it does not overrun, it leaves nearly
nine minutes unaccounted for. Read that the right way round — the printed answers are far longer than
anything you would say out loud, and each is really three or four short questions. The capacity answer
alone is four: the four-part functional test, decision-specific capacity, who you take information from, and
whose patient she is. If your answers run past thirty seconds you will still never reach Domain 4, which
here is the carer-delivered maintenance plan and the decision not to proceed — the two easiest marks in
the case to earn.

soe.title: The severely atrophic mandible
soe.text:
SOE Case 37 — The severely atrophic mandible
THE CASE
74-year-old man, edentulous for 30 years, wearing complete dentures. He cannot tolerate the lower denture.
Panoramic radiograph and CBCT show a severely atrophic mandible of 7 mm height in the symphysis, with
the mandibular canal at the crest posteriorly. He is medically fit.
Domain 1
“A severely atrophic mandible — 7 mm of height in the anterior region and a posteriorly superficial canal — in
a patient with genuine functional diﬀiculty. This is a Complex case in which the principal risks are iatrogenic
mandibular fracture and nerve injury, and in which the temptation to help must be balanced against the
potential to do serious harm.”
Q
How would you classify this ridge?
“On the Lekholm and Zarb quantity classification this is Class D or E — advanced resorption of basal bone.
Cawood and Howell would classify it as Class V or VI. The key figures are the residual height and the posi-
tion of the canal, and 7 mm in the symphysis is at the threshold where standard implant placement becomes
hazardous.”
Q
What else would you assess?
“The existing dentures critically — extension, occlusion, vertical dimension, polished surface form, and whether
the neutral zone has been respected, because a poorly made denture on an atrophic ridge is a common and
correctable cause of intolerance. Floor of mouth height relative to the crest, mentalis and mylohyoid attachments,
tongue position and size, saliva, mucosal quality, and whether there is denture-induced hyperplasia. And what
he actually finds intolerable — pain, looseness, or both.”
Domain 2
Q: What are the options?
“Remake the conventional denture using a neutral zone technique and careful attention to extension, with a
soft liner. On a severely atrophic ridge this is frequently the single most effective intervention and it carries no
surgical risk. I would do this first regardless.
Two-implant overdenture in the symphysis — the standard-of-care option, but with 7 mm of height it carries
a genuine risk of fracture and would require short implants and careful case selection.
Four implants with a bar, distributing load — more surgery, more risk.
Augmentation before implants — vertical augmentation of an atrophic mandible is Complex and
unpredictable.
Specialist options — nerve lateralisation, or extraoral bone grafting — firmly outside my scope.
Continue with conventional dentures and adhesive, with dietary support.”
Q
What would you recommend?
“Remake the lower denture properly first, with a neutral zone technique and a soft liner, and reassess. If he
remains intolerant and wants to proceed, I would refer for a specialist opinion rather than place implants
myself, because with 7 mm of height the risk of mandibular fracture is real, the case is Complex, and I would
want it assessed by someone who manages atrophic mandibles regularly. I would explain that clearly and not
present referral as abandonment.”
Q
Why is mandibular fracture such a concern?
“Because in a mandible of this height, an osteotomy removes a substantial proportion of the remaining bone, and
the atrophic mandible has poor vascularity and poor healing capacity. A fracture in this situation is a serious

injury, often requiring open reduction and internal fixation, sometimes with non-union. Patients can be warned,
but the risk is best avoided by not creating it.”
Q
What would you consent for if implants were placed?
“Beyond the standard risks: mandibular fracture, both during surgery and afterwards under function, and
what its management would involve; mental and inferior alveolar nerve injury, with the canal superficial poste-
riorly; failure to integrate in poorly vascularised atrophic bone; and the maintenance burden of an overdenture.
I would give this in writing.”
Domain 3
Q: If a specialist placed two short implants, what would your restorative plan be?
“Stud attachments rather than a bar if the implants are parallel and space permits, because a bar demands
12 to 15 mm of vertical space and adds a further stress concentration; but with divergent implants in atrophic
bone a bar may distribute load better and I would take the surgeon’s view. The overdenture must be implant-
retained and tissue-supported, with full extension so the posterior saddles continue to carry load — an implant-
supported design would concentrate all the load on two short implants in fragile bone. Conventional loading,
careful occlusal balance, and a soft liner if needed.”
Domain 4
Q: What are you watching for at review?
“Any sign of mandibular fracture — pain, altered occlusion, mobility; peri-implant health; attachment wear; and
continued resorption requiring relines. I would review him more frequently than usual in the first year.”
Q
What is the lesson of this case?
“That the best intervention is often the least invasive one, and that recognising a case as beyond one’s compe-
tence is a clinical skill in its own right. A well-made conventional denture in a severely atrophic mandible is
not a failure of ambition — it may be the safest and most effective thing I can offer.”
Running this case to time
Time check. This case is written in the older format — nine long answers, about 687 words. At 140
words a minute plus five seconds a question that is under six minutes: it does not overrun, it leaves over
nine minutes unaccounted for. Read that the right way round — the printed answers are far longer than
anything you would say out loud, and each is really three or four short questions. The options answer
alone is six, one per option, each with its own follow-up on risk. If your answers run past thirty seconds
you will still never reach Domain 4 — and Domain 4 here is one line, that recognising a case as beyond
your competence is a clinical skill in its own right, which is the mark the whole case is built to award.

soe.title: Failure to integrate in a previously grafted site
soe.text:
SOE Case 38 — Failure to integrate in a previously grafted site
THE CASE
You placed an implant at the UR5 six months after a staged guided bone regeneration procedure. At the 4-
month review the implant is mobile, with a peri-implant radiolucency. The patient is a 55-year-old non-smoker
with no medical history.
Domain 1
“An implant that has failed to integrate in a previously grafted site. The immediate management is clear — the
implant must come out. The valuable part of this case is working out why, because a failure in grafted bone has
a different differential from a failure in native bone.”
Q
What are the possible causes?
“Graft-related: the regenerated bone was immature or of low density, with a lower bone-to-implant contact and
slower remodelling than native bone; the healing period after the graft may have been too short — staged GBR
usually requires 6 to 9 months; or the graft may have been largely residual xenograft particles with little vital
bone.
Surgical: inadequate primary stability at placement; overheating; contamination.
Loading: micromotion from a denture pressing on the site.
Patient: an undisclosed factor — smoking, undiagnosed diabetes, medication.
Site: residual infection from the original pathology or a retained membrane fragment.”
Q
How would you investigate?
“Review my own operative records: the healing period allowed after grafting, the insertion torque recorded,
the drilling protocol, whether primary stability was documented, and whether a denture was worn. Re-take
the medical history including a specific question about smoking and any new diagnoses. Take a periapical,
and consider a biopsy or histological assessment of the removed tissue if there is any suggestion of unusual
pathology.”
Domain 2
Q: What do you tell the patient?
“Duty of candour. Promptly, honestly and without excessive self-criticism: ‘I’m sorry — the implant hasn’t
attached to the bone. That’s more likely in an area where we’ve had to rebuild bone first, and it happens in a
small proportion of cases even when everything is done properly. It has to come out. Once the area has healed
we can look at whether to try again, and I need to be honest that a second attempt in a site that’s already needed
grafting carries a higher risk than the first.’ I would then set out the alternatives afresh, in case she now prefers
a bridge or a denture.”
Q
What about the fee?
“That should have been agreed in writing before treatment — my own position would be to replace the implant
without charging for the fixture and the surgery, while being clear about laboratory and component costs. What
matters is that the arrangement was documented in advance rather than negotiated now.”
Q
What is your plan?
“Remove the implant — with a mobile implant this is usually simple. Curette all granulation tissue thoroughly
and inspect the bony walls; send tissue for histology if anything is unexpected. Assess the residual defect. If
contained, graft with a composite graft and a membrane; if the walls are intact, allow spontaneous healing.
Provide an interim prosthesis that does not press on the site — a bonded pontic in preference to a denture.
Re-entry at 4 to 6 months, since this is a grafted site rather than a simple socket, with reassessment by CBCT. At
replacement, use a wider and/or longer implant to engage the maximum available bone, take particular care

with drill sharpness and irrigation, and use a two-stage submerged protocol with an extended healing period.
I would also consider whether the right answer is not to re-implant — a resin-bonded bridge in this premolar
site may be the more predictable option after a failure.”
Domain 3
Q: What would you do differently at the second attempt?
“Allow a longer healing period after grafting — closer to 9 months than 6. Document insertion torque and
ISQ at placement, and use serial ISQ during healing so that a falling trend gives early warning. Under-prepare
the osteotomy to maximise primary stability in low-density regenerated bone. Submerge the implant. Avoid
any denture pressure on the site. And extend the healing period before loading.”
Domain 4
Q: What governance actions follow?
“Treat it as a significant event. Review my grafting protocol, my healing intervals, my drill replacement policy
and my irrigation. Then audit my implant survival, separating implants in native bone from those in grafted
sites, against a standard drawn from the literature, and re-audit after any change. That would be a legitimate
quality improvement project. I would also inform my indemnity provider if the patient raised a concern, and
record everything contemporaneously.”
Q
How would you decide whether to keep doing GBR at all?
“By looking at my own outcomes honestly. If my grafted-site failure rate were materially higher than published
figures, the right responses would be more mentoring, a narrower case selection, or referring augmentation
cases — not doing more of the same and hoping. Working within one’s competence includes knowing one’s
own results.”
Running this case to time
Time check. This case is written in the older format — eight long answers, about 704 words. At 140
words a minute plus five seconds a question that is under six minutes: it does not overrun, it leaves over
nine minutes unaccounted for. Read that the right way round — the printed answers are far longer than
anything you would say out loud, and each is really three or four short questions. The causes answer
alone is five, one per group, and the plan answer is six. If your answers run past thirty seconds you will
still never reach Domain 4, which here is the audit that separates grafted from native sites — the easiest
mark in the case to earn and the easiest to miss.

soe.title: Recurrent ceramic fracture on a screw-retained
soe.text:
SOE Case 39 — Recurrent ceramic fracture on a screw-retained
bridge
THE CASE
56-year-old male with a three-unit screw-retained implant bridge at the 45–47 on two implants (45, 47), placed
4 years ago in layered zirconia. The veneering ceramic has fractured three times. He has no pain and the
implants are healthy. He grinds his teeth and has an intact, heavily worn natural dentition elsewhere.
Domain 1
“A recurring technical complication — chipping of veneering ceramic — on an otherwise healthy implant bridge
in a parafunctional patient. Three fractures in four years is not bad luck; it is a design and load mismatch that
will continue until I change something.”
Q
Why does veneering ceramic chip on implant restorations?
“Several reasons, and usually more than one: absence of a periodontal ligament, so the load is transmitted
without the damping and proprioceptive protection a tooth would give; parafunctional loading; inadequate
or uneven framework support for the veneer — the ceramic must be supported in even thickness, and un-
supported ceramic over a poorly designed connector or a flat framework is where fractures start; residual
thermal stresses from an inappropriate cooling protocol during firing; and occlusal interferences, particularly
in excursion.”
Q
What would you examine?
“The occlusion in detail: contacts in intercuspation with shimstock and articulating paper of two thicknesses,
and all excursive movements including non-working interferences. Whether the implant bridge is contacting
more heavily than the adjacent natural teeth. The framework design on a radiograph and, if the bridge is
removed, directly — is the veneer evenly supported? Whether there is a cantilever. Whether the screws have
loosened previously, which would indicate overload. Signs of parafunction — masseteric hypertrophy, linea
alba, wear facets, and whether he has ever had or worn a splint.”
Domain 2
Q: What are the options?
“Repair with composite — a temporary measure at best, and it has already failed as a strategy.
Polish and monitor — appropriate only for a very minor chip.
Remake in monolithic zirconia — removing the weak veneering layer entirely. This is the definitive answer for
a parafunctional patient and is what I would recommend.
Remake in metal-ceramic with reduced veneer or a metal occlusal surface — an alternative, less aesthetic but
very robust.
Redesign — reconsider the span, connector dimensions and whether a cantilever is present.”
Q
What is your plan?
“Correct the cause before remaking, otherwise I will remake it again. 1. Adjust the occlusion so the bridge holds
shimstock only under heavy clenching and has no excursive contacts, with guidance on the natural canine. 2.
Confirm the implants and screws are sound; replace the screws with new ones and torque correctly, re-torquing
at ten minutes. 3. Remake in monolithic zirconia, screw-retained, with a narrow occlusal table, reduced cusp
inclination, generous connector dimensions and no cantilever. 4. Provide a hard, full-coverage occlusal splint
for night-time wear, adjusted after the new bridge is fitted, and review its wear as an objective measure of his
parafunction. 5. Discuss the contributing factors — stress, sleep, caffeine, alcohol — and screen for obstructive
sleep apnoea, referring to his GP if there are symptoms, since sleep bruxism and OSA are associated.”

Q
How would you discuss the cost?
“Honestly and early. I would establish what was originally agreed, explain that the material choice was rea-
sonable at the time but has not withstood his bite, and set out what a remake in monolithic zirconia would
cost. I would also make clear that even monolithic zirconia is not immune — he generates forces beyond what
restorations are designed for — and that the splint is not optional. I would put the maintenance expectation in
writing so future component replacement is not a surprise.”
Domain 3
Q: What would you specify to the laboratory?
“Monolithic zirconia, screw-retained, with the implant system, platform and connection specified; connector
dimensions adequate for the span; a narrow occlusal table with reduced cusp inclination; occlusal contacts
light in intercuspation and absent in excursion; a cleansable emergence with open embrasures; and a request
for a bisque or design preview before final milling. I would also send photographs and my occlusal instructions,
and ask the technician to advise if he sees a design problem — a good technician will often identify the reason
a restoration keeps failing.”
Q
How would you adjust and finish the zirconia occlusally?
“With fine diamonds under copious water, then polish thoroughly with a dedicated zirconia polishing system.
An adjusted but unpolished zirconia surface causes rapid wear of the opposing dentition, which in a bruxist
with an already worn dentition would be a serious harm.”
Domain 4
Q: How would you monitor?
“Six-monthly review with occlusal assessment, screw integrity checks, examination of the splint for wear as a
proxy for his parafunctional activity, and photographs of the restoration. Radiographs at one year and then as
clinically indicated. I would record the torque values and dates of any component replacement, so I can see
whether the pattern is improving.”
Q
What would you audit?
“The incidence of technical complications in my own implant restorations, separated by material and by whether
the patient has diagnosed parafunction. If layered restorations in bruxists are failing in my hands, the change
is to specify monolithic materials for that group as a matter of protocol — and re-audit.”
Running this case to time
Time check. This case is written in the older format — nine long answers, about 748 words. At 140
words a minute plus five seconds a question that is a little over six minutes: it does not overrun, it leaves
nearly nine minutes unaccounted for. Read that the right way round — the printed answers are far longer
than anything you would say out loud, and each is really three or four short questions. The five reasons
ceramic chips are five questions on their own, and the plan is five more, one per numbered step. If your
answers run past thirty seconds you will still never reach Domain 4, which here is the audit by material
and by parafunction — a straightforward mark that most candidates never arrive at.

canine, new screws torqued correctly and re-torqued at ten minutes, the framework and any cantilever
reconsidered, and only then a monolithic zirconia remake. A candidate who names the material and
stops has answered a laboratory question, not a clinical one.

natural dentition, and he has broken the same restoration three times. Volunteer the hard, full-coverage
night splint, fabricated after the new bridge is fitted and adjusted to include it, and then volunteer

are associated — and say to him that the splint is not optional.

is in the finishing and the honesty. Adjusted but unpolished zirconia causes rapid wear of the opposing
dentition, and in a bruxist whose remaining teeth are already worn that is a serious harm you would have
caused — so fine diamonds under water, then a dedicated zirconia polishing system, every time. And
be honest on cost before you start: the original material choice was reasonable but has not withstood
his bite, even monolithic zirconia is not immune, and the maintenance expectation goes in writing so
future component replacement is not a surprise.

soe.title: Residual cement discovered incidentally
soe.text:
SOE Case 40 — Residual cement discovered incidentally
THE CASE
50-year-old woman attends for a routine examination. She has an implant crown at the 24, cemented 3 years
ago elsewhere. She is asymptomatic. A bitewing taken for caries screening shows an obvious radiopaque mass
at the implant–abutment junction mesially. Probing at that site is 5 mm with bleeding, no suppuration, and
there is 1.5 mm of bone loss compared with a radiograph she has brought from the time of fitting.
Domain 1
“An incidental finding of residual cement with early peri-implant disease in an asymptomatic patient. The
diagnosis is peri-implantitis — she has bleeding on probing, increased probing depth and, against her own
baseline, bone loss beyond initial remodelling. Because I have a baseline and the disease is early, this is a case
where intervention now is likely to be effective.”
Q
Confirm the diagnosis against the 2017 criteria.
“The criteria are bleeding and/or suppuration on gentle probing, increased probing depth compared with pre-
vious examinations, and bone loss beyond crestal remodelling. She has bleeding, 5 mm probing depth, and 1.5
mm of loss against a documented baseline. She does not meet the surrogate thresholds used when no baseline
exists — probing depth of 6 mm or more and 3 mm of bone loss — but I do not need those, because I have her
baseline. That is exactly why the baseline radiograph matters.”
Q
Would you have found this without the bitewing?
“Probably, on probing — which is why peri-implant probing at six sites is part of every implant recall, not an
optional extra. The lesson is that an asymptomatic implant is not a healthy implant until it has been probed and
compared with a baseline.”
Domain 2
Q: What is your management?
“Cause-related therapy first, and here the cause is identified and removable. 1. Explain the finding and obtain
consent to remove the crown, including the real possibility of damaging or destroying it and the cost of a
remake. Without that consent I cannot treat the cause. 2. Remove the crown — ultrasonic first, then a crown
remover, sectioning only if necessary. 3. Remove all residual cement under magnification with titanium or
PEEK instruments, knotted floss drawn circumferentially, and glycine air-polishing. Verify radiographically,
noting that non-radiopaque cement would not show. 4. Assess the abutment: is it fully seated? Is the margin
excessively subgingival? Is the emergence over-contoured? 5. Debride the peri-implant tissues, deliver indi-
vidualised oral hygiene instruction with a correctly sized interdental brush. 6. Replace the restoration with
a screw-retained, cleansable design — this removes the cause permanently. 7. Re-assess at one month. With
early disease and the cause removed, I would expect resolution of bleeding. 8. Supportive therapy at 3 to 5
monthly intervals, with a new baseline radiograph.”
Q
What if she declines to have the crown removed because of the cost?
“I would explain the consequences clearly and without pressure: that the cement is the cause, that non-surgical
treatment without removing it is unlikely to resolve the disease, and that continued bone loss risks losing the
implant, which would be more costly. I would offer to stage the work. If she still declines, I would record
the informed refusal, treat as well as I can non-surgically, monitor closely at three-monthly intervals with
radiographs when indicated, and revisit the discussion. Her refusal is her right; my job is to make sure it is
informed and documented.”
Q
Would you tell her the previous dentist made an error?

“No. I would describe my findings factually — ‘there is cement material left under the gum, which is a recognised
complication of the cemented technique and a known cause of this kind of gum infection’ — explain what I
propose, and tell her how she can raise concerns formally if she wishes. I would not put a critical opinion of a
colleague into her notes as fact.”
Domain 3
Q: How, practically, do you remove submucosal cement you cannot see?
“Magnification and good illumination first. Then knotted dental floss drawn around the abutment and worked
in a see-saw motion, which engages set cement in the sulcus remarkably effectively. Titanium or PEEK curettes
and scalers worked circumferentially — never steel. Glycine or erythritol air-polishing delivered subgingivally
to reach threads and residual particles. If access remains inadequate and cement persists, a small flap for direct
vision is justified. Then a verification radiograph.”
Domain 4
Q: What is the prognosis?
“Good, precisely because it has been caught early and the cause is removable. Studies of cement-associated
peri-implant disease show that removal of the cement resolves the inflammation in a substantial proportion of
cases. My success criteria at re-assessment are absence of bleeding on gentle probing, no further increase in
probing depth, and stable bone levels against a new baseline.”
Q
What does this case change in your own practice?
“Three things. Screw retention by default wherever angulation allows. If cementing is unavoidable, margins at
or within 1 mm of the mucosal margin, minimal radiopaque cement and an extra-oral replica technique, with
a verification radiograph. And peri-implant probing at six sites at every recall, with a baseline radiograph
taken and recorded at every prosthesis fitting — I would audit my compliance with that last point, since it is
the single measure that made this diagnosis possible.”
Running this case to time
Time check. This case is written in the older format — eight long answers, about 721 words. At 140
words a minute plus five seconds a question that is under six minutes: it does not overrun, it leaves over
nine minutes unaccounted for. Read that the right way round — the printed answers are far longer than
anything you would say out loud, and each is really three or four short questions. The management
answer is eight questions on its own, one per numbered step, and the diagnosis answer is three. If your
answers run past thirty seconds you will still never reach Domain 4, which here is the prognosis and the
three changes to your own practice — the cheapest marks in the case.

bridement without removing the cement is unlikely to resolve the disease, so the sequence is cause-

and say the consequence: without that consent I cannot treat the cause.

“cement material left under the gum, a recognised complication of the cemented technique and a
known cause of this kind of gum infection” — explain what you propose, and tell her how she can

beyond this level and goes on for an opinion.

soe.title: Post-orthodontic lateral incisor spaces
soe.text:
SOE Case 41 — Post-orthodontic lateral incisor spaces
THE CASE
19-year-old female, orthodontic treatment completed 3 months ago. Congenitally absent 12 and 22; spaces
opened to 6.2 mm each. She is in fixed retainers bonded 13 to 23. Medium smile line, medium phenotype,
canines of normal shade and shape. She is at university and will be abroad for a year from next September.
Domain 1
“A recently completed orthodontic case with bilateral lateral incisor spaces in a 19-year-old. Three issues de-
termine the plan: whether growth has ceased, whether the roots are adequately divergent, and the practical
constraint of a year abroad, which affects timing and continuity of care.”
Q
Has growth ceased at 19?
“In a female, very probably. But I would confirm rather than assume — a history of stable height and shoe size
for at least two years, stable dentition, and if there were real doubt, serial cephalometric radiographs a year
apart or hand-wrist films, though I would need to justify the exposure. Craniofacial growth continues at a low
level into adulthood, and late infra-occlusion of anterior implants is a recognised long-term problem that I
would warn her about regardless.”
Q
What do you need from the orthodontist?
“Confirmation that treatment is complete and the position is stable; the retention plan and its duration; the root
positions and divergence at the 12 and 22 sites — I need at least 1.5 mm from each adjacent root, and converging
roots are a common reason an apparently adequate space cannot take an implant; and whether the space was
distributed to the ideal tooth width, checked against the golden proportion and the contralateral side.”
Q
What else would you assess?
“Smile line and lip dynamics on video; papilla heights and the interproximal bone levels on the 11, 13, 21 and
23; phenotype; CBCT for ridge width at both sites, since hypodontia sites are typically narrow because the
alveolus never developed around a tooth; and photographs and study casts with a diagnostic wax-up.”
Domain 2
Q: Options?
“Resin-bonded cantilever bridges from the canines — minimally invasive, excellent published survival for
single anterior units, no surgery, and readily repaired or replaced if she debonds while abroad. My first-line
option for a 19-year-old.
Implants — definitive and preserving the adjacent teeth, but committing a 19-year-old to a restoration she will
maintain for sixty years, in sites likely to need contour augmentation, with a real risk of late infra-occlusion.
Canine substitution — the orthodontics is complete, so reopening that would mean further treatment; and her
canines are of normal shade and shape, which makes substitution less attractive aesthetically. Worth mentioning
but not pursuing.
Composite build-ups on the canines with orthodontic space closure — as above.
Removable prosthesis — interim only.”
Q
What would you recommend, and how does the year abroad affect it?
“The year abroad is decisive for timing. Implant treatment would take six to twelve months if augmentation
is needed, and would leave her mid-treatment when she leaves — with a provisional, no local clinician, and
no continuity of care. That is not acceptable. So I would recommend resin-bonded cantilever bridges now,
which can be delivered in two or three visits, look excellent, and are robust enough to survive a year abroad. I
would tell her explicitly that this is not a compromise but a legitimate long-term option, and that if she later
wants implants, the bridges have preserved the option entirely. If she strongly prefers implants, I would either

complete the whole treatment before she leaves — which is only realistic if no augmentation is needed and I
can use a conventional protocol with time in hand — or defer until she returns.”
Q
SAC?
“Implants here would be surgically Advanced — aesthetic zone, narrow hypodontia sites likely requiring con-
tour augmentation, 6.2 mm spaces requiring narrow implants with tight tolerances. Prosthodontically Ad-
vanced. Resin-bonded bridges are Straightforward and within my competence comfortably.”
Domain 3
Q: If she chooses resin-bonded bridges, describe the key points.
“Cantilever design from the canine, single retainer — the evidence favours cantilevers over fixed-fixed designs,
which fail by debonding at one retainer with undetected caries beneath. Minimal or no preparation, confined to
enamel, with a defined path of insertion and a supragingival margin. A cobalt-chromium or nickel-chromium
framework sandblasted and treated with a metal primer, or a zirconia framework, bonded with a resin cement
under good moisture control. An ovate pontic shaped to support the tissue, with soft tissue augmentation
beneath it if the ridge is deficient — a connective tissue graft under a pontic is far more predictable than around
an implant. Occlusion: no contact in intercuspation or excursion on the pontic, particularly important with
her fixed retainer in place. I would also coordinate with the orthodontist about the bonded retainer, since it
may need modifying to accommodate the retainers.”
Q
If she chooses implants, what would you plan?
“3.3 mm narrow-diameter implants in a titanium-zirconium alloy, with 1.5 mm to each adjacent root — 6.2 mm
makes this feasible but tight, and I would confirm root divergence first. Position: shoulder 3 mm apical to the
planned mid-facial margin, 1 to 2 mm palatal, angled through the cingulum. Expect to need simultaneous
contour augmentation and a connective tissue graft. Two-stage submerged healing, then a screw-retained
provisional to develop the emergence over 8 to 12 weeks, then a definitive screw-retained restoration on a Ti-
base.”
Domain 4
Q: What would you warn her about for the long term?
“That whichever option she chooses, this is maintenance for life, not a one-off procedure. For bridges: debond-
ing, and the need for periodic replacement. For implants: that continued eruption of the natural dentition
relative to an ankylosed implant can produce relative infra-occlusion and open contacts over decades, that
crowns will need replacing more than once, and that recession may occur. I would arrange standardised
photographs and study casts at intervals so those changes are detected rather than discovered.”
Q
How would you handle continuity of care while she is abroad?
“Give her a written summary of what has been done, photographs, and my contact details; advise her to register
with a dentist wherever she is; and, if she has implants, give her the implant card with the system, diameter,
length and lot numbers so any clinician can service them. I would set a recall reminder for her return.”

Time check. This case is written in the older format — ten long answers, about 905 words. At 140 words
a minute that is six and a half minutes, and ten questions at five seconds each adds fifty seconds: call
it seven and a half minutes. It does not overrun; it leaves the better part of eight minutes unaccounted
for. Read that the right way round — the printed answers are far longer than anything you would say out
loud, and each is really three to six short questions. The options answer alone is five; the resin-bonded
bridge answer is six. If your answers run past thirty seconds you will still never reach Domain 4, which
here is the warning about late infra-occlusion and the continuity of care while she is abroad.

the implant option entirely. Say it before it is drawn out of you.

prosthodontically Advanced, and a candidate at this level should say so and consider referral or co-
management. But the sharper line is temporal: starting a six-to-twelve-month treatment on a patient
who leaves the country mid-course, with a provisional and no local clinician, is not acceptable care.
Say that plainly, then close the loop she will live with — the written summary, the photographs, the
implant card if relevant, and a recall set for her return.

soe.title: Parafunction and an anterior implant
soe.text:
SOE Case 42 — Parafunction and an anterior implant
THE CASE
45-year-old male, implant at the 11 restored 2 years ago. He presents with the screw access composite lost and
the crown loose. He has an edge-to-edge incisal relationship, marked incisal wear on all upper and lower
anteriors, and reports “clenching at work”. The implant is healthy radiographically.
Domain 1
“A loose screw-retained anterior crown in a patient with an edge-to-edge incisal relationship and heavy ante-
rior wear — that is, an implant placed in the position that receives the greatest excursive load in the mouth, in
a patient with parafunction. The looseness is a symptom; the anterior guidance is the disease.”
Q
Why is an anterior implant particularly vulnerable in this patient?
“Because an edge-to-edge relationship means the upper incisors take substantial load in protrusion and in in-
cising, and the implant has no periodontal ligament to damp that load or to provide protective proprioceptive
feedback. Implant axial movement is 3 to 5 micrometres against 25 to 100 for a tooth. Combined with clenching,
that concentrates fatigue at the screw joint.”
Q
What would you examine?
“Whether it is the screw or the implant that is loose — I would remove the crown and test the implant separately.
The screw and internal connection for damage, and the implant body for fracture. Occlusion in detail: contacts
in intercuspation with shimstock, protrusive and lateral excursions, and specifically whether the implant crown
carries protrusive guidance. Signs of parafunction — masseteric hypertrophy, linea alba, scalloped tongue, wear
facets that match in excursion. Whether he has ever had a splint. Peri-implant probing and bone levels. And I
would ask about sleep quality, snoring and daytime somnolence.”
Domain 2
Q: What is your management?
“Never simply retighten. 1. Remove the crown; inspect all components and the implant; replace the screw with
a new one — a screw that has loosened has been fatigued. 2. Correct the occlusion. The implant crown should
hold shimstock only under heavy clenching in intercuspation, and — critically here — should carry as little
protrusive guidance as possible. In an edge-to-edge relationship that is diﬀicult, so I would aim to distribute
protrusive guidance across as many natural incisors as possible and minimise the implant’s share, adjusting the
crown’s palatal contour. 3. Re-torque to the manufacturer’s value and re-torque at ten minutes. 4. Reseal with
PTFE tape and composite, then re-check the occlusion because the composite adds height. 5. Provide a hard,
full-coverage occlusal splint for night-time wear, and consider a daytime habit-awareness programme given
he clenches at work. 6. Consider whether the crown should be remade in a more robust design — monolithic
material, modified palatal contour — if loosening recurs. 7. Screen for obstructive sleep apnoea and refer to
his GP if there are symptoms.”
Q
What if it loosens again despite this?
“Then I would escalate the investigation rather than the tightening. Check for a non-passive fit, an unrecognised
implant fracture, or a damaged internal connection. Consider remaking with a different abutment design. And
I would have a frank conversation about the mechanical limits of an anterior implant in his occlusion, including
the possibility that repeated loosening will progress to screw fracture and eventually implant fracture — which
is the natural history if the cause is not corrected.”
Q
What should have been done differently at the planning stage?
“The edge-to-edge relationship and the wear would have been visible at assessment. Ideally the plan would
have included occlusal management before the implant — assessment of the vertical dimension, possible

reorganisation of the anterior guidance, and a splint from the outset — and consent that explicitly covered a
higher mechanical complication rate. The wear pattern should also have prompted an assessment of the whole
dentition, not just the missing 11.”
Domain 3
Q: Describe the splint you would provide.
“A hard, heat-cured or milled acrylic full-coverage splint, usually maxillary, covering all teeth so none can
over-erupt, with even bilateral contacts in intercuspation and smooth canine guidance in excursion so the
posterior teeth disclude. It must be adjusted at fit and reviewed, and its wear pattern monitored at each recall
as an objective measure of his parafunctional activity. A soft splint is not appropriate — it can increase muscle
activity.”
Domain 4
Q: What would you monitor?
“Screw integrity at every recall — I would check it deliberately rather than wait for him to report looseness; the
occlusion; the splint for wear; peri-implant health and bone levels against baseline; and the wear of his natural
anterior teeth with photographs and study casts. Six-monthly review.”
Q
What would you record?
“The cause identified, the occlusal adjustments made, the screw replacement with date and torque value, the
splint provided and its review, the discussion about mechanical risk and the possibility of eventual implant
fracture, and the maintenance expectation. If loosening recurs a third time, that record becomes the basis for a
considered decision about redesign or removal.”
Running this case to time
Time check. This case is written in the older format — eight long answers, about 699 words. At 140
words a minute that is five minutes, and eight questions at five seconds each adds forty seconds: call it
five and three-quarter minutes. It does not overrun; it leaves more than nine minutes unaccounted for.
Read that the right way round — the printed answers are far longer than anything you would say out
loud, and each is really three to seven short questions — the management answer alone is seven, printed
as a numbered list an examiner will take one item at a time. If your answers run past thirty seconds you
will still never reach Domain 4, which here is the deliberate screw check at every recall and the record that
eventually justifies removal.

cause identified as occlusal overload in
an edge-to-edge relationship with
parafunction; the adjustments and the

The spine — the twelve answers to have ready if nothing else
1 The looseness is a symptom; the anterior guidance is the disease · 2 No periodontal ligament: 3–5 𝜇m
against 25–100 𝜇m · 3 Test screw and implant separately; inspect the connection and body · 4 Shimstock,
protrusive and lateral excursions, and whether the crown guides · 5 Masseteric hypertrophy, linea alba,
scalloped tongue, matching wear facets · 6 Sleep quality, snoring, daytime somnolence · 7 Never simply
retighten — always a new screw · 8 Distribute protrusive guidance across the natural incisors · 9 Re-torque
to the manufacturer’s value and again at ten minutes · 10 Hard full-coverage splint, canine guidance, never
soft · 11 Escalate investigation, not torque: non-passive fit, implant fracture, damaged connection · 12
Deliberate screw check at every recall, and the record that justifies removal.
Where the marks are lost in this case
Retightening and calling it management. A candidate who says “I’d remove the crown, clean it, retighten
to torque and reseal” has described the trivial half of the case. Say never simply retighten, say a screw
that has loosened has been fatigued and is replaced, and spend your words where the marks are —
correcting the occlusion so the implant carries as little protrusive guidance as possible, and the hard
full-coverage splint with canine guidance. Treating the joint without treating the load is why this crown
will be loose again by the next recall.
Never mentioning sleep. The case asks about sleep quality, snoring and daytime somnolence, and about
a daytime habit-awareness programme, because he clenches at work and may be clenching at night for a
reason. Almost nobody volunteers obstructive sleep apnoea screening and referral to his GP — a free
mark that also shows you are treating a patient rather than a screw joint.
Not knowing when to stop tightening. The competence line here has two limbs. First: after a second
episode you escalate the investigation, not the torque — non-passive fit, implant fracture, a damaged in-
ternal connection — saying plainly that the natural history of uncorrected overload is screw fracture and
then implant fracture. Second: rebuilding the vertical dimension and the anterior guidance across a
worn dentition is beyond this level and belongs with a restorative colleague. And take the retrospective
mark the case hands you: this should have been managed before the implant was placed, with consent
that named the higher mechanical complication rate — professional honesty, not self-incrimination.

soe.title: Head and neck radiotherapy and xerostomia
soe.text:
SOE Case 43 — Head and neck radiotherapy and xerostomia
THE CASE
61-year-old man, 3 years after chemoradiotherapy (66 Gy) for a right tonsillar squamous cell carcinoma, in
remission. He has severe xerostomia, rampant cervical caries, and has lost several teeth. He wears an upper
partial denture he cannot tolerate because of mucosal soreness. He asks about implants.
Domain 1
“A patient three years after high-dose head and neck radiotherapy with severe xerostomia, radiation caries and
denture intolerance. The 66 Gy dose is well above the level at which the risk of osteoradionecrosis becomes
significant, and I need to know precisely which structures were in the field.”
Q
What determines whether implants are possible?
“The radiation field and dose to the specific jaw site. A right tonsillar tumour field will have included the
right posterior mandible at or near full dose, while the anterior mandible and the maxilla may have received
considerably less. I would obtain the radiotherapy planning records from his oncology centre — the dose-
volume data for the mandible and maxilla — rather than guess. That single piece of information changes the
answer more than anything I can determine clinically.”
Q
What else is relevant?
“Time since radiotherapy — the risk of osteoradionecrosis persists lifelong but the tissues are most hostile in
the first year, and three years is more favourable. Whether he had a neck dissection. Current oncological status
and surveillance. Smoking and alcohol, which are both risk factors for ORN and for second primaries. Trismus,
which affects access. Xerostomia severity and whether saliva substitutes or pilocarpine have been tried. His
caries risk and prevention regime. And his nutritional status and weight.”
Q
Why is his denture causing soreness?
“Irradiated, xerostomic mucosa is atrophic, poorly lubricated and fragile, and a denture that would be comfort-
able in a normal mouth causes ulceration. This is a common and very diﬀicult problem, and it is one of the
strongest arguments for implant support in irradiated patients — an implant-retained prosthesis can reduce
mucosal loading substantially.”
Domain 2
Q: What is your approach?
“This is specialist care and I would refer, but I would do so having completed a proper assessment and having
managed what is within my scope.
Within my scope: intensive prevention — high-fluoride toothpaste 5000 ppm, fluoride varnish, dietary advice,
saliva substitutes and stimulants, meticulous caries management, and treatment of any candidal infection; op-
timisation of the existing denture with a soft liner and careful extension; and liaison with his oncology team.
Referral: to a restorative consultant or a hospital-based implant service with experience of irradiated patients,
for assessment of implant provision. The decision will depend on the site doses. I would not place implants in
a field that received 66 Gy in general practice.”
Q
What are the specific risks you would explain?
“Osteoradionecrosis — the most serious, potentially requiring major surgery; higher implant failure rates in
irradiated bone, particularly the mandible and particularly at higher doses; impaired soft tissue healing; and
that any implant will be harder to maintain in a xerostomic mouth with a high caries and infection risk. I would
also explain that the alternative — continuing with an intolerable denture — is not benign either, and that
this is a balance of risks rather than a simple prohibition.”

Q
What about hyperbaric oxygen?
“It has been used to improve tissue oxygenation before surgery in irradiated bone, but the evidence is contested
and it is not routinely recommended. It is a specialist decision, not a general practice one, and I would neither
promise it nor dismiss it — I would say that the receiving unit would advise.”
Q
If implants were provided, what design would you favour?
“Wherever possible, in the site that received the lowest dose — often the anterior mandible. Fewest implants
that will do the job, since each osteotomy is a risk. An overdenture rather than a fixed prosthesis, because
it is removable, cleansable, allows mucosal inspection, and can be relined or converted if an implant is lost.
Maximum cleansability, and a rigorous preventive and maintenance regime.”
Domain 3
Q: What would your role be after specialist placement?
“Shared care: intensive prevention, three-monthly recall, peri-implant monitoring, denture maintenance and
relining, and prompt referral of any non-healing mucosal lesion — because in a patient with a previous head
and neck malignancy, any ulcer persisting beyond two weeks requires urgent referral to exclude recurrence
or a second primary. That surveillance responsibility is arguably the most important part of my role.”
Domain 4
Q: What would you monitor?
“Peri-implant health and bone levels; mucosal condition, with a low threshold for referral; caries and the effec-
tiveness of the prevention regime; xerostomia and its management; his weight and nutrition; trismus; and his
oncological follow-up. Three-monthly review, and I would document every mucosal examination.”
Q
What is the overriding principle in this case?
“That his cancer surveillance and his prevention matter more than his implants, and that any implant decision
belongs in a team that manages irradiated patients regularly. My most valuable contributions are the referral,
the prevention, and the vigilance.”
Running this case to time
Time check. This case is written in the older format — ten long answers, about 706 words. At 140
words a minute that is five minutes, and ten questions at five seconds each adds fifty seconds: call it six
minutes. It does not overrun; it leaves nine minutes unaccounted for. Read that the right way round
— the printed answers are far longer than anything you would say out loud, and each is really three to
five short questions. “What else is relevant?” alone is eight separate risk factors an examiner will take
one at a time. If your answers run past thirty seconds you will still never reach Domain 4, which here is
the three-monthly surveillance and the two-week ulcer rule — the part of the case where the marks are
highest and the clinical stakes are highest too.
