soe.title: Nerve injury caused by another clinician
soe.text:
SOE Case 44 — Nerve injury caused by another clinician
THE CASE
A patient attends your practice 6 weeks after implant placement at the 36 by a dentist she has since stopped
attending. She has persistent numbness and burning pain in the left lower lip and chin. A periapical shows
the implant apex apparently within the mandibular canal. She is angry and asks you to “sort it out” and to
write a report for her solicitor.
Domain 1
“A patient with a persistent neurosensory disturbance six weeks after implant placement, with radiographic
evidence suggesting the implant is within the mandibular canal, presenting with both a clinical problem and
a medico-legal one. My priorities, in order, are: her clinical care, an accurate independent assessment, and
appropriate professional conduct regarding the report.”
Q
What is the clinical significance of six weeks?
“It is late. The evidence favours decompression within 24 to 36 hours where an implant is impinging on
the nerve, and the window for any surgical intervention is generally measured in weeks. At six weeks the
prognosis for full recovery is substantially reduced, and the presence of burning pain — dysaesthesia — is a
poor prognostic sign suggesting neuropathic pain rather than simple conduction block.”
Q
How would you assess her?
“A structured neurosensory assessment. Map the affected area onto a diagram with measurements and pho-
tograph it. Characterise the disturbance: anaesthesia, hypoaesthesia, paraesthesia or dysaesthesia; whether
there is allodynia or hyperalgesia. Perform mechanoceptive tests — light touch with cotton wool, static two-
point discrimination, brush stroke direction — and nociceptive tests — sharp/blunt discrimination and thermal.
Compare with the contralateral side. Ask about functional impact: eating, drinking, speech, shaving, dribbling,
and psychological effect. And obtain a small field-of-view CBCT to establish definitively whether the implant
is within or adjacent to the canal.”
Domain 2
Q: What would you do?
“Refer urgently to an oral and maxillofacial surgery unit with experience in trigeminal nerve injury — today,
not by routine letter. The decisions about whether to remove the implant now, and about any nerve exploration,
belong there. In the meantime: explain honestly what I have found and what I do not know; discuss manage-
ment of neuropathic pain — which may require medication such as a tricyclic or gabapentinoid, prescribed by
the appropriate clinician, and which is not managed by removing the implant alone; and provide support and
clear information. I would not remove the implant myself at six weeks without specialist advice, since removal
at this stage may not improve the sensory outcome and may cause further injury.”
Q
Would you remove the implant if it is clearly in the canal?
“That is a specialist decision at this stage. Early removal — within 24 to 36 hours — is well supported. At six
weeks, the injury is established; removal may still be indicated if the implant is causing ongoing compression,
but it should be done on specialist advice and with the patient’s understanding that it may not restore sensation.
I would not act unilaterally.”
Q
She asks you to write a report for her solicitor. How do you respond?
“Carefully and professionally. I would explain that I am happy to provide a factual report of my own findings
— what she told me, what I examined, what I measured, what the imaging showed, and what I did — and
that this is a factual report, not an expert opinion on another clinician’s care. I would explain that a report
commenting on whether the previous treatment fell below an acceptable standard requires an appropriately

instructed independent expert, and that I am not in that role. I would contact my own indemnity provider
before writing anything, obtain her written consent for disclosure, and ensure the report is dated, signed, and
based only on my own records. I would not speculate, would not use emotive language, and would not put an
opinion about a colleague into her clinical record as if it were a finding.”
Q
She asks you directly whether the previous dentist was negligent.
“ ‘I understand why you’re asking, and I’m sorry this has happened to you. I can tell you what I’ve found: the
implant appears to be very close to or within the nerve canal, and you have a significant sensory disturbance.
What I can’t do is give you an opinion about another dentist’s decisions — that isn’t my role, and I don’t have
their records or their reasoning. What I can do is make sure you’re seen quickly by the right specialist, give you
a factual report of what I’ve found, and tell you how to raise a formal concern if you want to.’ ”
Domain 3
Q: What information would you give her about prognosis?
“Honestly and without false reassurance: that some sensory disturbances improve over weeks to months; that
recovery after six weeks with dysaesthesia is less likely to be complete; that the specialist assessment will give
a better estimate; and that even where sensation does not fully recover, neuropathic pain can often be managed.
I would avoid both minimising and catastrophising.”
Domain 4
Q: What would you record?
“Everything, contemporaneously and factually: her account in her own words, the date of the original surgery,
my examination findings with the mapped diagram and measurements, the imaging and my report of it, my
advice, the referral made and its urgency, what I said about the report and about raising concerns, and her
consent to disclosure. This record may be scrutinised, and its value lies in its being contemporaneous and
neutral.”
Q
What is the wider lesson for your own practice?
“That posterior mandibular implants demand CBCT planning with a documented 2 mm safety margin, drill
stops, direction indicators with radiographic verification, and a recorded pre-operative baseline sensory
assessment — and that any report of post-operative numbness must be seen the same day, not at a routine
review. I would audit my own compliance with those standards.”
Running this case to time
Time check. This case is written in the older format — nine long answers, about 818 words. At 140 words
a minute that is five minutes fifty, and nine questions at five seconds each adds forty-five seconds: call
it six and a half minutes. It does not overrun; it leaves eight and a half minutes unaccounted for. Read
that the right way round — the printed answers are far longer than anything you would say out loud,
and each is really three to six short questions — the neurosensory assessment alone is six, the solicitor’s
report five. If your answers run past thirty seconds you will still never reach Domain 4, which here is the
contemporaneous record and the audit of your own posterior mandibular protocol.

gence. What you owe this patient: a full independent neurosensory assessment, mapped, measured
and photographed; a small field-of-view CBCT; an urgent referral; honest prognostic information; and
a factual report of your own findings with her written consent. What you must not do: speculate about a
colleague, give an expert opinion you were never instructed to give, or record an opinion about another
clinician in her notes as though it were a finding. Have the sentence ready — saying it fluently is the
mark.
Writing anything before ringing your indemnity provider. Candidates offer the report willingly and
forget the sequence: indemnity provider first, then her written consent, then a dated, signed report
based only on your own records. And do not stop there — the last domain hands you the governance
mark: CBCT planning with a documented 2 mm safety margin, drill stops, direction indicators with ra-
diographic verification, a recorded pre-operative baseline sensory assessment, and any post-operative
numbness seen the same day — followed by an audit of your own compliance.

soe.title: The patient who wants a healthy implant crown
soe.text:
SOE Case 45 — The patient who wants a healthy implant crown
removed
THE CASE
35-year-old woman with a screw-retained implant crown at the 21, fitted 18 months ago. It is biologically and
mechanically healthy — no bleeding, no bone loss, correct occlusion. She dislikes it: she says it is “half a shade
too yellow” and “doesn’t quite match”. You and two colleagues consider the match good. She has had two
previous crowns remade elsewhere for the same reason. She has a low smile line.
Domain 1
“A biologically and mechanically successful restoration with which the patient is dissatisfied, in the context of a
low smile line and a history of two previous remakes elsewhere for the same complaint. That pattern is the
significant finding here, and it changes the case from a technical problem into one about expectation, perception
and possibly psychological factors.”
Q
What concerns you about the history?
“Serial dissatisfaction with successive clinicians, a focus on a defect that others cannot perceive, a discrepancy
between the objective finding and her distress, and a low smile line meaning the tooth is barely visible in
function. These are recognised features that should prompt consideration of body dysmorphic disorder or
another underlying dissatisfaction. I would not diagnose that myself, but I would recognise the pattern and
behave accordingly.”
Q
How would you assess this properly rather than dismissively?
“I would take her complaint seriously and examine objectively. Standardised photographs in controlled lighting;
shade assessment under a colour-corrected light with the teeth hydrated, comparing cervical, middle and incisal
thirds; cross-polarised photographs if available; assessment of value, chroma, hue, translucency and surface
texture separately, since a mismatch is often in value or texture rather than hue; assessment of the emergence,
contour and the mucosal margin; and a genuine attempt to identify what specifically she is seeing. Sometimes
the patient is right and three clinicians are wrong — a difference in surface lustre or incisal translucency can be
real and hard to articulate.”
Q
What would you ask her?
“What specifically bothers her, and in what circumstances — is it in a mirror, in photographs, in particular
lighting? What happened with the previous two remakes and why they did not satisfy her. What she is hoping
will be different this time. And, gently, how much she thinks about it and whether it affects her daily life —
because the answer to that last question is the one that matters most.”
Domain 2
Q: What are the options?
“Do nothing, with an honest explanation and support.
Modify — external staining and reglazing, or surface texture adjustment and repolishing, which is minimally
invasive and occasionally solves it.
Remake the crown, potentially with the technician present at a shade appointment or with a custom shade tab.
Whiten the adjacent natural teeth — if she perceives the crown as too yellow, and the natural teeth are the
reference, bleaching the natural teeth and then remaking the crown to the new shade may be the actual answer
she is looking for.
Decline further treatment and, with her agreement, seek an opinion from a colleague or suggest she discuss
her concerns with her general medical practitioner.”

Q
What would you do?
“I would not proceed straight to a third remake. My approach would be: 1. Take proper records and demon-
strate them to her — showing her the photographs and the shade analysis is often more powerful than telling her.
2. Offer a reversible trial: a provisional crown made to the shade she believes she wants, worn for a few weeks.
If it satisfies her, I have a clear target for the definitive restoration. If it does not, that is important information
for both of us, gathered without destroying anything. 3. Discuss bleaching the natural teeth if the mismatch is
directional. 4. Be honest about the possibility that a further remake may not resolve her dissatisfaction, given the
history — and say that kindly, not as an accusation. 5. If the pattern is that of body dysmorphic concern, decline
elective aesthetic re-treatment, explain why, and suggest, carefully and non-judgementally, that a discussion
with her doctor may help.”
Q
How do you have that last conversation without offending her?
“ ‘I want to be honest with you, because I think that’s more use to you than another crown. Three of us have
looked at this and we can’t see what you’re seeing, and you’ve had two remade already without it feeling right.
That tells me that another remake might not solve it either, and I’d rather not take your money and your time
for something that may leave you feeling the same. What I’d like to do is try a temporary version first so we can
test it without committing. And I’d gently say — if this is on your mind a lot, it might be worth mentioning to
your doctor, because that’s a very common thing and there is help for it.’ ”
Q
Is she entitled to insist you remake it?
“She is entitled to request it. Patient autonomy allows a patient to refuse treatment, not to compel a clinician
to provide treatment that is not in their interest. If I judge that a further remake is unlikely to help and may
reinforce the preoccupation, I may decline — provided I explain my reasoning, offer to help her obtain another
opinion, and record the discussion. Declining must never be dismissive.”
Domain 3
Q: If you do remake it, how would you maximise the chance of success?
“Involve the technician directly, ideally with the patient present for shade selection. Take shade early in the
appointment with hydrated teeth under corrected lighting, recording value, chroma and hue separately plus
translucency, texture and lustre. Photograph with the tab in the same plane, with a grey card, and cross-
polarised. Communicate the stump shade. Use a provisional at the target shade first. Request a bisque try-in
so adjustments precede glazing. And agree in writing, in advance, what would constitute an acceptable result.”
Domain 4
Q: What would you record?
“Her complaint in her own words; my objective findings and those of my colleagues; the photographs and shade
analysis; the options offered including no treatment; the reversible trial proposed; my reasoning if I decline
further remakes; the suggestion of a medical discussion and how it was received; and her response. This record
protects her — by making the reasoning visible to any future clinician — as much as it protects me.”

Q
What is the general principle?
“That the outcome of an aesthetic restoration is judged against the patient’s perception, and that when per-
ception and objective finding diverge repeatedly, more dentistry is rarely the answer. Recognising that is a
clinical skill, and handling it with kindness rather than dismissal is a professional one.”
Running this case to time
Time check. This case is written in the older format — ten long answers, about 955 words. At 140 words
a minute that is six minutes fifty, and ten questions at five seconds each adds fifty seconds: call it seven
and a half minutes. It does not overrun; it leaves seven and a half minutes unaccounted for. Read that
the right way round — the printed answers are far longer than anything said out loud, and each is really
three to six short questions: the shade assessment alone is six. If your answers run past thirty seconds

principle that more dentistry is rarely the answer.

soe.title: The second opinion
soe.text:
SOE Case 46 — The second opinion
THE CASE
A 58-year-old man attends for a second opinion. Another practice has proposed bilateral lateral window sinus
elevation with block grafting and eight implants to restore his upper posterior teeth, at considerable cost. He
has an intact upper anterior dentition 15 to 25, a stable lower arch with all teeth present to the second molars,
and no complaints — he attended for a routine check-up and was offered the plan. CBCT shows 4 mm of bone
bilaterally below the sinuses.
Domain 1
“A man with no symptoms and no complaint who has been offered extensive, expensive and irreversible surgery.
My first task is to establish what problem the proposed treatment is meant to solve, because if he has a stable,
functional shortened arch and no complaint, the starting point is not which technique but whether any treatment
is needed at all.”
Q
What would you assess?
“His function and symptoms in his own words — can he eat what he wants, is there pain, is anything changing?
The occlusal stability — over-eruption of the lower molars into the upper spaces, drifting, wear, and whether
the anterior teeth are being overloaded. Periodontal status and the prognosis of the remaining teeth. The CBCT,
independently. His expectations and what he was told. And what has changed recently, if anything, that led to
this proposal.”
Q
How do you approach giving a second opinion without criticising a colleague?
“By confining myself to my own assessment and by describing options rather than passing judgement. ‘I can’t
comment on another dentist’s reasoning because I don’t have their records or their discussion with you. What I
can do is examine you myself, tell you what I find, and set out the options as I see them, including doing nothing.
Then you’ll have two views and can decide.’ That is both professionally correct and more useful to him than an
opinion about someone else.”
Domain 2
Q: What are the options?
“No treatment with monitoring. He has occlusion to the second premolars bilaterally — a shortened dental
arch, for which the evidence indicates adequate function, comfort and satisfaction in most people, without
increased TMD or periodontal breakdown. He is asymptomatic. This is the baseline against which everything
else must justify itself, and I would present it first and seriously.
Limited treatment — for example, managing over-eruption of the lower molars if present, or replacing one first
molar per side if there is a genuine functional deficit.
The proposed plan — bilateral lateral window elevation, block grafting and eight implants. It is technically
feasible but represents major surgery, substantial cost, months of treatment, significant morbidity, and a lifelong
maintenance burden, to treat a situation causing him no trouble.
Intermediate options — short implants where residual height allows, though at 4 mm that is marginal; or a
removable prosthesis, which he is unlikely to want or need.”
Q
What would you recommend?
“That he does nothing for now, with active monitoring: photographs and study casts to detect over-eruption
and drift, periodontal maintenance, and review. I would tell him that if his function deteriorates or the occlusion
becomes unstable, the options remain open and we can revisit them. I would be explicit that this is a positive
recommendation based on evidence, not a refusal to treat — and that the fact a treatment is possible does not
make it necessary.”

Q
How would you explain the risk-benefit balance?
“ ‘The plan you’ve been offered would work, technically. But it’s a big undertaking — two sinus operations, bone
grafting, eight implants, the best part of a year, a lot of money, and a commitment to cleaning and check-ups for
the rest of your life. And at the moment, you have no symptoms and you can eat what you like. There’s good
evidence that a set of teeth back to the premolars gives most people all the function they need. So my honest
advice is to leave it alone, keep an eye on it, and treat if something changes. If you want the fuller reconstruction,
it’s available — but I’d want you to choose it because you want it, not because you’ve been told you need it.’ ”
Q
What if he says he does want it?
“Then I would take him seriously, and make sure he is choosing it fully informed: the number of procedures,
the risks of lateral window elevation and block grafting including membrane perforation, sinusitis, graft failure
and donor-site morbidity, the timescale, the total cost including maintenance, and the alternatives. Bilateral
lateral window sinus elevation with block grafting is Complex and firmly outside my scope, so I would refer
him — to a specialist unit, with a full assessment and my own records — rather than provide it. I would also
suggest he ask the receiving clinician the same question: what problem is this solving?”
Domain 3
Q: If treatment were eventually undertaken, what would your role be?
“Assessment and planning, the restorative phase if agreed with the surgical team, and long-term maintenance.
I would want the shared-care arrangement documented from the outset — who does what, who provides
maintenance, and who manages complications.”
Domain 4
Q: What would you record?
“That he attended for a second opinion; his symptoms and function in his own words; my independent findings
including the CBCT; the options I presented including no treatment and the evidence for the shortened arch;
my recommendation and reasoning; that I made no comment on the other practice’s plan; and his decision. I
would also give him a written summary, so that whatever he decides, he decides with the reasoning in front of
him.”
Q
What is the underlying principle?
“That the ability to perform a treatment is not an indication for it. The examination is explicitly about safe,
risk-assessed, harmless overall patient care — and the most important word in that phrase is ‘harmless’. Recom-
mending no treatment, with monitoring and a clear rationale, is a defensible and often correct clinical decision.”
Running this case to time
Time check. This case is written in the older format — nine long answers, about 837 words. At 140 words
a minute that is six minutes, and nine questions at five seconds each adds forty-five seconds: call it six
and three-quarter minutes. It does not overrun; it leaves eight and a quarter minutes unaccounted for.
Read that the right way round — the printed answers are far longer than anything said out loud, and each
is really three to five short questions: the options answer alone is four. If your answers run past thirty
seconds you will still never reach Domain 4, which here is the written summary you hand him and the
principle that ability is not indication.

shortened-arch evidence recorded first;
your recommendation and reasoning;
the explicit note that you offered no
comment on the other plan; the written
summary handed over; and his
decision, with the monitoring interval
and what would trigger a review.
The spine — the twelve answers to have ready if nothing else
1 What problem is the proposed treatment meant to solve? · 2 His function and symptoms in his own
words · 3 Over-eruption, drift, wear and anterior overload as the objective test of stability · 4 The shortened
dental arch, and the evidence behind it · 5 Presenting no treatment first, and seriously · 6 Active monitoring:
photographs, casts, periodontal maintenance, review · 7 A positive recommendation, not a refusal to treat
· 8 The words for the risk-benefit conversation · 9 If he wants it: procedures, risks, timescale, total cost,
alternatives · 10 Lateral window with block grafting is Complex and outside scope — refer · 11 Shared care
documented: who does what, who maintains, who manages complications · 12 The ability to perform a
treatment is not an indication for it.
Where the marks are lost in this case
Debating the technique instead of the indication. The CBCT is interesting — 4 mm bilaterally, sinus
elevation, short implants — and a candidate can spend eight minutes on lateral windows in a man with no
complaint. The examinable move is the first one: establish what problem the treatment is meant to solve,
then present no treatment first and seriously, with the shortened dental arch evidence — adequate
function, comfort and satisfaction in most people, without increased TMD or periodontal breakdown
— named as the baseline everything else must justify itself against.

Being drawn into judging the other practice. He will invite it and the examiner will let him. Neither
criticise nor defend: confine yourself to your own assessment and describe options rather than pass
judgement, with the sentence ready — “I can’t comment on another dentist’s reasoning because I don’t have their
records or their discussion with you.” Then volunteer the two things candidates forget: that you recorded
explicitly that you made no comment on the other plan, and that you would suggest he put the same
question to the receiving clinician.
Turning a recommendation into a refusal. If he wants the reconstruction after a proper discussion, that is
his decision. Consent him fully — membrane perforation, sinusitis, graft failure, donor-site morbidity,
the timescale, the total cost including maintenance — then draw the competence line plainly: bilateral
lateral window sinus elevation with block grafting is Complex in both dimensions and firmly outside
the scope of a general dentist with an interest in implants, so he goes to a specialist unit with your full
assessment and the shared-care arrangement documented from the outset. The principle to say before
the bell: the ability to perform a treatment is not an indication for it.

soe.title: Maxillary overdenture versus fixed prosthesis
soe.text:
SOE Case 47 — Maxillary overdenture versus fixed prosthesis
THE CASE
68-year-old woman, edentulous maxilla for 8 years, dentate mandible (all teeth present, 35 to 45 plus first
molars). Her upper complete denture is unstable and she gags. CBCT: adequate bone anteriorly (10–12 mm
height, 6–7 mm width from 15 to 25), pneumatised sinuses posteriorly with 3 mm. Medium smile line. She
wants “teeth fixed in so I don’t gag”.
Domain 1
“An edentulous maxilla opposing a complete natural mandibular dentition — a high-load situation — with
adequate anterior bone but severe posterior pneumatisation, in a patient whose principal complaint is gagging
and instability rather than appearance. That distinction matters: her problem may be solvable by removing
palatal coverage, which does not require a fixed prosthesis.”
Q
Why does the opposing natural dentition matter?
“Because a maxillary prosthesis opposing a full natural mandibular dentition generates substantially higher and
less evenly distributed loads than one opposing a denture. It increases the mechanical demand on any implant
prosthesis and is a recognised setting for accelerated maxillary ridge resorption.”
Q
What would you assess?
“Her existing denture critically — extension, post-dam, occlusion, vertical dimension, and whether the gagging
is related to palatal coverage, over-extension or an incorrect vertical dimension, because many gaggers are made
worse by a poorly fitting denture. Smile line and lip dynamics. Whether her appearance depends on the
labial flange — the single most important planning question. Interarch space. The condition and prognosis of
her lower teeth. Her expectations, and what”fixed” means to her — many patients mean “doesn’t move”, not
“cannot be taken out”.”
Domain 2
Q: What are the options?
“Remake the conventional denture with attention to extension, post-dam and vertical dimension, and desensi-
tisation techniques for gagging. Low risk and may be suﬀicient.
Implant-retained maxillary overdenture, typically four to six implants in the anterior maxilla with a bar or
studs. This can be palate-free, which directly addresses her gagging, retains the labial flange for lip support,
and is removable and cleansable. This is my leading option.
Fixed full-arch implant prosthesis — would require bilateral sinus elevation given 3 mm posteriorly, or tilted
implants; it is Complex, expensive, harder to clean, and cannot provide a labial flange.
No change with adhesive and dietary advice.”
Q
How do you decide between the overdenture and the fixed option?
“By testing the flange question objectively. I would duplicate her denture, remove the flange from the duplicate,
and try it in — with photographs — so she can see for herself what a fixed prosthesis without a flange would
look like. After eight years of resorption and with a medium smile line, the transition line and lip support will
very likely be compromised. I would also explain that her actual complaint — gagging — is caused by palatal
coverage, and that a palate-free implant overdenture solves that completely, whereas a fixed prosthesis solves
it at far greater surgical and biological cost.”
Q
What would you say to her?
“ ‘I think I can solve the gagging without needing to graft your sinuses. The reason you gag is the plate across
the roof of your mouth. If we put four implants in the front of your upper jaw, we can make a denture that clips
on very firmly and has no palate at all — it won’t move when you eat or speak, and you take it out to clean it.

The fully fixed option would mean two sinus operations and much bigger surgery, and it also can’t have the little
lip that supports your top lip, which I think you’d notice. Let me show you what that would look like first.’ ”
Q
SAC?
“Four anterior maxillary implants for an overdenture: surgically Advanced, prosthodontically Advanced. A
fixed full-arch maxillary rehabilitation with bilateral sinus grafting is Complex in both dimensions and outside
the scope of this level of practice — I would refer if she pursued it after understanding the alternatives.”
Domain 3
Q: Outline the treatment plan for the overdenture.
“1. Remake or copy the upper denture first, establishing the correct tooth position, vertical dimension, occlu-
sion and lip support. That denture becomes the radiographic and surgical guide and the interim prosthesis. 2.
Duplicate in clear acrylic with radiopaque markers; CBCT; plan four implants between the 15 and 25 regions,
avoiding the incisive canal, with adequate anteroposterior spread. 3. Surgery: crestal incision, full-thickness
flap, graded drilling with copious irrigation; the anterior maxilla is typically D3, so I would under-prepare
to improve primary stability. Two-stage submerged healing given the denture will be worn over the site. 4.
Conventional loading at 4 to 6 months in maxillary D3 bone. Relieve and soft-line the denture throughout.
5. Second stage, then attachment selection: studs need 8 to 10 mm, a bar needs 12 to 15 mm of vertical space.
With divergent implants or if maximum stability is needed against a natural lower dentition, a bar distributes
load better; if space is limited and cleaning ability is a concern, studs. 6. Palate-free design with a cast metal
framework for strength, since removing the palate weakens an acrylic base considerably. 7. Occlusion: balanced
or lingualised, carefully developed against her natural lower teeth.”
Domain 4
Q: What maintenance would you set out?
“Attachment inserts replaced as they wear, typically annually or more often; the framework and base checked for
fracture; relines as the ridge resorbs; peri-implant probing at every recall; and daily cleaning of the abutments
with a single-tufted brush and of the fit surface including the housings. I would give this in writing with costs,
because unexpected maintenance charges are the commonest source of later dissatisfaction.”
Q
What would you monitor in the opposing arch?
“Her natural lower teeth — for wear, mobility, and periodontal change under the increased load — and the
occlusion, since changes in the lower arch will alter the loading on the maxillary prosthesis. That surveillance
is as much a part of the plan as the implants themselves.”
Running this case to time
Time check. This case is written in the older format — nine long answers, about 850 words. At 140 words
a minute that is six minutes, and nine questions at five seconds each adds forty-five seconds: call it just
under seven minutes. It does not overrun; it leaves eight minutes unaccounted for. Read that the right
way round — the printed answers are far longer than anything said out loud, and each is really three to
seven short questions: the treatment plan alone is seven, printed as a numbered sequence an examiner
will take one item at a time. If your answers run past thirty seconds you will still never reach Domain 4,
which here is the maintenance schedule given in writing with costs, and the surveillance of her natural
lower teeth.

soe.title: “Teeth in a day”
soe.text:
SOE Case 48 — “Teeth in a day”
THE CASE
55-year-old businessman with a failing upper dentition: generalised periodontitis Stage IV Grade B, several
mobile teeth, a failing anterior bridge, and caries. He has researched “All-on-4” online, wants his upper teeth
removed and fixed teeth fitted the same day, and has booked a holiday in six weeks. He is a non-smoker,
medically fit.
Domain 1
“A patient with a failing upper dentition requesting immediate full-arch fixed rehabilitation, with a fixed dead-
line. Two things are immediately clear: full-arch fixed rehabilitation is explicitly outside the scope of my
practice at this level, and the six-week deadline is driving the request rather than the clinical need. My job is
to give him a proper assessment and an honest account of the options, not to accommodate the timetable.”
Q
What would you assess?
“Full periodontal charting and radiographs; the prognosis of every tooth individually, because ‘failing’ does
not necessarily mean ‘hopeless’; caries and restorability; the occlusion and vertical dimension; smile line and
lip support; the opposing arch; CBCT for bone volume and anatomy; and his medical history, parafunction
and smoking status. And critically, his expectations — what he thinks ‘teeth in a day’ involves, and what he
understands about maintenance.”
Q
What does Stage IV Grade B mean here?
“Stage IV: interdental attachment loss with bone loss to the apical third, tooth loss due to periodontitis of five
or more teeth, and complexity such as masticatory dysfunction, secondary occlusal trauma, bite collapse or
drifting. Grade B: progression at a moderate rate, bone loss to age ratio between 0.25 and 1.0. The Grade B is
relatively reassuring — this is not the galloping destruction of Grade C — and it raises a genuine question about
whether some teeth could be saved rather than clearing the arch.”
Domain 2
Q: What are the options?
“Periodontal treatment with strategic extractions and a partial denture or partial fixed prosthesis — preserv-
ing what can be saved. This must be assessed properly before anything is cleared.
Full clearance and a conventional complete denture, with or without later implant support.
Full clearance with an implant-retained overdenture — fewer implants, removable, cleansable, and it retains
the labial flange for lip support.
Full clearance with a fixed full-arch implant prosthesis, immediately loaded or conventionally loaded.
No treatment — not viable given active disease.”
Q
What would you tell him about the six-week deadline?
“That it cannot drive the clinical decision. ‘I understand the holiday matters, and I’ll make sure you’re not
without teeth. But taking out a whole arch and fixing teeth in on the same day is a big, irreversible decision,
and it isn’t one to make because of a date in the diary. What I can do in six weeks is get you comfortable, stable
and looking presentable. What I’d rather not do is clear an arch that might not all need clearing.’ ”
Q
What are the specific concerns about immediate full-arch loading?
“First, whether it is necessary — some of his teeth may be salvageable, and a full-arch prosthesis is irreversible.
Second, the loss of the labial flange: after clearance and alveoloplasty, a fixed prosthesis without a flange may
not support the lip, and with a medium or high smile line the transition line may show. This must be tested
with a trial denture before he commits. Third, immediate loading criteria must be met — adequate primary
stability across the arch, no parafunction, and cross-arch splinting; and the ITI evidence grading rates immediate

protocols as less well validated than conventional ones. Fourth, maintenance: a fixed full-arch prosthesis is
diﬀicult to clean and requires lifelong professional maintenance and periodic removal. Fifth, scope — this is
Complex in both surgical and prosthodontic dimensions and outside what I would undertake.”
Q
What is your plan?
“Phase 1, within six weeks: full assessment; emergency treatment; extraction of genuinely hopeless teeth with
immediate additions to a provisional prosthesis so he is never without teeth; non-surgical periodontal therapy;
oral hygiene instruction. He goes on holiday comfortable and presentable.
Phase 2: re-evaluation at three months against the EFP stability criteria — probing depths of 4 mm or less with
no bleeding at those sites, and full-mouth bleeding under 10%.
Phase 3: with a stable periodontal condition and a clear picture of which teeth have a good prognosis, present
the definitive options properly — including a trial denture to test the flange question.
Phase 4: refer for the surgical phase if he chooses a full-arch implant solution, having done the assessment, the
periodontal stabilisation and the prosthodontic planning myself.”
Domain 3
Q: If he proceeds with a fixed full-arch prosthesis elsewhere, what is your continuing role?
“Shared care: periodontal maintenance of the opposing arch, peri-implant monitoring at three- to six-monthly
intervals, hygiene reinforcement, and prompt referral of complications. I would want the responsibilities docu-
mented at the outset, and I would want to know who removes the prosthesis for maintenance and how often.”
Q
What would you insist on before any clearance?
“A trial denture set-up tried in the mouth, photographed and approved by him, testing tooth position, lip
support, smile line, speech and the transition line with and without a flange. Clearing an arch without that is
planning blind, and it is the commonest route to an unrecoverable aesthetic disappointment.”
Domain 4
Q: What would you record?
“The full assessment and the individual prognosis of every tooth; the options presented including preserving
teeth; the discussion about the deadline and why it should not determine the plan; the trial denture and his
approval; the scope discussion and the referral; and what I told him about maintenance and cost. I would give
him a written summary.”
Q
What is the principle underlying this case?
“That irreversible treatment should never be driven by a timetable, and that a request for a specific technique
is not a diagnosis. The examination’s stated aim is ‘harmless, independent overall patient care’ — and the harm
most available in this case is clearing an arch that did not all need clearing.”
Running this case to time
Time check. This case is written in the older format — ten long answers, about 853 words. At 140 words a
minute that is six minutes, and ten questions at five seconds each adds fifty seconds: call it seven minutes.
It does not overrun; it leaves eight minutes unaccounted for. Read that the right way round — the printed
answers are far longer than anything said out loud, and each is really three to five short questions: the
concerns about immediate loading are five, and the plan is four phases. If your answers run past thirty
seconds you will still never reach Domain 4, which here is the record of the deadline conversation and the
principle that irreversible treatment is never driven by a timetable.

1 Full-arch fixed rehabilitation is outside my scope at this level · 2 The deadline is driving the request, not
the clinical need · 3 “Failing” does not mean “hopeless” — every tooth prognosed individually · 4 Stage IV

three months: ≤4 mm with no bleeding, full-mouth bleeding <10% · 11 A trial denture, photographed
and approved, with and without a flange, before clearance · 12 Irreversible treatment is never driven by a
timetable.
Where the marks are lost in this case
Accepting the request as the diagnosis. He has researched All-on-4 and asks for it, and the weak answer
discusses All-on-4. A request for a specific technique is not a diagnosis. What scores is prognosing every
tooth individually and then saying the inference out loud: Stage IV Grade B is moderate progression,
not the galloping destruction of Grade C, and it raises a genuine question about whether some teeth
could be saved. The harm most available here is clearing an arch that did not all need clearing — name
it.
Negotiating with the six weeks. Candidates either squeeze a plan into the deadline or refuse outright. Do
neither: the deadline cannot drive the clinical decision, and it does not have to be defied either — Phase
1 delivers emergency treatment, extraction of the genuinely hopeless teeth with immediate additions
to a provisional, non-surgical therapy and hygiene instruction, and he goes away comfortable. Then
re-evaluate at three months against the EFP criteria — 4 mm or less with no bleeding at those sites,
full-mouth bleeding under 10% — before any irreversible decision.
Consenting to a clearance without testing the face. The competence line is in the case and must be
stated by you: a fixed full-arch implant prosthesis is Complex in both dimensions and outside what
you would undertake — you do the assessment, the periodontal stabilisation and the prosthodontic
planning, and refer the surgical phase. But the point candidates never volunteer is the one immediately
before it: nothing is cleared until a trial denture set-up has been tried in, photographed and approved
by him, testing tooth position, lip support, smile line, speech and the transition line with and without
a flange — because after clearance and alveoloplasty a fixed prosthesis cannot carry a flange.

soe.title: Imminent explantation in the aesthetic zone
soe.text:
SOE Case 49 — Imminent explantation in the aesthetic zone
THE CASE
47-year-old woman with an implant at the 11, placed 6 years ago. She presents with suppuration, 9 mm probing,
and radiographic bone loss to the apical third — approximately 70% of the implant length. There is 3 mm
of mid-facial recession with visible threads. She has a high smile line. The adjacent 12 and 21 are sound with
good bone levels.
Domain 1
“An implant in the most aesthetically critical position with 70% bone loss, suppuration and visible threads,
in a patient with a high smile line. This implant is not retainable — no treatment will produce a maintainable,
restorable, aesthetically acceptable result — and the clinical work now is about how to remove it and what to
replace it with, and about managing a conversation that will be diﬀicult.”
Q
How do you determine that it is “irrational to keep”?
“The ITI decision tree makes this an explicit decision point. Against retention: bone loss beyond half the im-
plant length; suppuration; exposed threads in the aesthetic zone; and a high smile line, so that even successful
resective treatment — which produces recession and exposes more metal — would leave an unacceptable ap-
pearance. Reconstructive therapy in a 70% defect is not predictable. Taken together, removal is the correct
recommendation, and I would state that clearly rather than offer treatment I do not believe will work.”
Q
What would you establish first?
“Whether the implant is mobile; the exact defect morphology on CBCT; the bone levels and periodontal status
of the 12 and 21, because the interproximal bone on those teeth determines the papillae in whatever replaces
the implant and I cannot recreate it; the phenotype; her smile line on video; the cause — cement, position,
maintenance, smoking, systemic factors — because whatever I place next will face the same environment; and
her expectations.”
Domain 2
Q: What are the replacement options after removal?
“A new implant after ridge reconstruction. This is the option patients expect, but the site will have a substantial
combined horizontal and vertical defect after removal, and vertical augmentation in the aesthetic zone is the
least predictable of all augmentation procedures. It would mean staged grafting, a year or more, and a real
chance of an inferior aesthetic result.
A resin-bonded cantilever bridge from the 21, with soft tissue augmentation under an ovate pontic. Frequently
the most aesthetically reliable outcome after an anterior implant failure: a pontic site can be sculpted with
connective tissue grafting far more predictably than peri-implant tissue can be regenerated, and the papillae
are supported by the natural adjacent teeth.
A conventional bridge from the 12 and 21 — destructive to two sound teeth.
A removable prosthesis with a flange — the only option that replaces lost hard and soft tissue volume reliably,
and worth mentioning honestly.
No replacement — not realistic in this position.”
Q
What would you recommend?
“Removal by counter-torque to preserve as much bone as possible, thorough debridement, and then — after
healing — a resin-bonded cantilever bridge with soft tissue augmentation under an ovate pontic as my first
recommendation, with a new implant as the alternative if she wants it and accepts the longer, less predictable
route. I would be explicit that I am recommending the bridge not as a compromise but because it is more
likely to give her a good result, and I would show her the reasoning.”

Q
How do you have this conversation?
“Sit down, allow time, and lead with the finding rather than the solution. ‘I’m sorry — I have some diﬀicult
news. The bone around this implant has been lost to about two-thirds of its length and there’s an active infection.
I don’t think it can be saved, and I don’t want to put you through treatment that I don’t believe will work. It
needs to come out.’ Then pause, and let her respond, before moving to options. Then: ‘The good news is that the
teeth on either side are healthy, and there are good ways to replace it. The one I’d recommend might surprise
you, because it isn’t another implant…’ and explain why. I would give written information, allow her time, and
offer a second opinion.”
Q
SAC and referral?
“Explantation with ridge reconstruction in the aesthetic zone is Complex in both dimensions. I would undertake
the diagnosis, the options discussion and, if she chooses it, the resin-bonded bridge with soft tissue grafting —
the last only if within my experience. For explantation and any implant re-treatment I would refer, having done
the assessment and the conversation myself.”
Domain 3
Q: Describe the removal and the immediate aftermath.
“Counter-torque device first — least destructive and preserves bone for reconstruction. Escalate to piezo-
surgery if needed, and only as a last resort to a trephine. Thorough removal of granulation tissue, irrigation, and
assessment of the residual defect. Then either allow 6 to 8 weeks of soft tissue healing before staged grafting, or
graft immediately if the defect is contained. The interim prosthesis matters enormously to her: a resin-bonded
provisional bridge or a bonded pontic rather than a denture, so nothing presses on the site and so she is never
without a tooth in the front of her mouth. I would arrange this before the removal appointment, not after.”
Q
If she chooses a new implant, what would you tell her about the sequence?
“Removal; 6 to 8 weeks of soft tissue healing; staged horizontal and probably vertical augmentation; 6 to 9
months of graft maturation; implant placement, possibly with further contour augmentation; 3 to 6 months of
integration; second stage with a connective tissue graft; 8 to 12 weeks of provisional soft tissue conditioning;
then the definitive crown. Fourteen to twenty months, with several surgical episodes, and no guarantee that
the papillae or the mid-facial margin will match the 21. She should hear that timeline before she chooses.”
Domain 4
Q: How would you monitor whichever route she takes?
“Standardised photographs at every stage; the papilla index and mid-facial margin level against the 21; peri-
implant or periodontal parameters as appropriate; and her own satisfaction recorded at intervals. For a bonded
bridge, the abutment tooth’s vitality and the bond integrity.”
Q
What is the principle you would take from this case?
“That recognising an unsalvageable situation early and saying so plainly is better care than optimistic treat-
ment — and that after an anterior implant failure, the reflex to place another implant should be questioned. The
aim is a result she can live with for twenty years, not a particular technique.”
Running this case to time
Time check. This case is written in the older format — ten long answers, about 932 words. At 140 words
a minute that is six minutes forty, and ten questions at five seconds each adds fifty seconds: call it seven
and a half minutes. It does not overrun; it leaves seven and a half minutes unaccounted for. Read
that the right way round — the printed answers are far longer than anything said out loud, and each is
really three to six short questions: the replacement options are five, and the re-implant sequence nine
consecutive stages. If your answers run past thirty seconds you will still never reach Domain 4 — the
papilla index against the 21, and the principle that recognising an unsalvageable situation early is better
care than optimistic treatment.

soe.title: Governance, audit and the quality improvement
soe.text:
SOE Case 50 — Governance, audit and the quality improvement
project
THE CASE
You are asked to discuss your own clinical governance arrangements for implant dentistry, including your
quality improvement project, your audit activity, and how you assure the quality of your implant care. (The
Regulations require a completed quality improvement project as an entry condition, so a case of this kind is entirely
foreseeable — it must be prepared, not improvised.)
Domain 1 — Interpretation and reasoning
Q: What does clinical governance mean in the context of implant dentistry?
“A framework through which I am accountable for the quality of the implant care I provide and for continuously
improving it. In practice it has several strands: evidence-based practice; audit and quality improvement; risk
management, including significant event analysis and duty of candour; education and training, with verifiable
CPD and reflection, mentoring, and working within competence under GDC Principle 7; patient involvement,
including consent, information and complaints handling; information governance, covering records, confiden-
tiality and data protection; and staﬀing and team training, including medical emergencies and decontamina-
tion.”
Q
How do you know whether your implant treatment is any good?
“By measuring it, not by assuming it. The parameters are implant survival; marginal bone level change against
a baseline taken at prosthesis fitting; peri-implant health — probing depths, bleeding, suppuration; prosthetic
complication events, such as screw loosening, ceramic fracture and component replacement; early failure rate;
and patient-reported outcomes, using a validated measure such as OHIP-14 alongside satisfaction with func-
tion and appearance. Without a baseline radiograph and a recall system, none of that can be measured — which
is why those two things are foundational.”
Domain 2 — Decision making
Q: Describe your quality improvement project.
(Candidates must give their own. A model structure:) “The problem: I noticed that when patients returned for
maintenance, I could not always find a baseline radiograph or a recorded insertion torque in the notes, which
made it impossible to apply the 2017 diagnostic criteria for peri-implantitis.
The standard: 100% of implant cases should have a contemporaneous surgical record including system, di-
ameter, length, lot number and insertion torque, and a standardised baseline periapical radiograph taken at
prosthesis fitting with a written report and recorded bone level measurements. The standard is drawn from the
FGDP training standards, GDC Standards on record keeping, and the 2017 World Workshop case definitions.
The method: retrospective review of the records of 30 consecutive implant cases over 18 months, against a data
collection sheet.
The finding: surgical records were complete in 63%; insertion torque was recorded in 40%; a baseline radio-
graph existed in 77% but bone level measurements were recorded in only 13%.
The change: I introduced a structured implant surgical proforma and a fitting proforma, both integrated into
the practice software, with the baseline radiograph and its measurements as mandatory fields; and I briefed the
whole team.
The re-audit at 6 months: 28 consecutive cases — surgical record completeness 100%, insertion torque 100%,
baseline radiograph with recorded measurements 96%.
The reflection: the omissions were not knowledge failures but system failures, and the fix was structural rather
than educational. It also improved my ability to diagnose peri-implant disease, because I now have compara-
tors.”
Q
Why is re-audit essential?
“Because without it there is data collection but no improvement. Closing the loop is what distinguishes audit
from a survey, and it is the part most often omitted.”

Q
Give three other implant audit topics you could undertake.
“Radiographic justification and reporting — the proportion of implant-related exposures with a documented
justification and a written report of the whole image, against a standard of 100% under IR(ME)R.
Consent documentation — the proportion of implant cases with a contemporaneous note of the consent dis-
cussion, not merely a signed form, including the risks material to that patient and the provision of written
information with a cooling-off period.
Antibiotic prescribing — the proportion of implant placements with a recorded indication for any antibiotic,
against SDCEP and antimicrobial stewardship standards.”
Domain 3 — Procedures and systems
Q: What systems assure quality in your surgical practice?
“Decontamination compliant with HTM 01-05, with validated cycles, retained records and periodic testing.
Medical emergency drugs and oxygen checked and in date, with annual whole-team training in medical emer-
gencies and immediate life support. Radiography quality assurance — image quality rating, analysis of repeats,
equipment testing, and dose audit. Medical device traceability — implant, graft and membrane lot numbers
recorded and a patient implant card issued. Torque wrench calibration at the manufacturer’s recommended
intervals, with a record. Surgical safety checks — patient, site, consent, implant availability including back-up
sizes, allergies, and instrument and swab counts. And structured recall with risk-based intervals.”
Q
How do you handle an adverse event?
“Duty of candour first: tell the patient promptly, apologise, explain what happened and what I will do, and
record it. Notify my indemnity provider early. Then significant event analysis with the team — what hap-
pened, why, what went well, what should change, and who is responsible for implementing it, with a review
date. Where a systemic change results, follow it with an audit to confirm it has worked.”
Domain 4 — Outcomes
Q: How do you keep your knowledge current?
“Verifiable CPD with written reflection, which the entry requirements specify — at least 30 hours of implant-
related CPD with reflection in the preceding 18 months. Structured reading of the primary literature and of the
ITI Treatment Guides and consensus statements, rather than relying on courses alone. A mentor for cases at the
edge of my experience. Peer review and case discussion. And I would say that the most useful learning comes
from reviewing my own outcomes, including the failures.”
Q
How do you decide whether to add a new technique to your practice?
“Against GDC Principle 7.1 — good quality care based on current evidence and authoritative guidance. I would
ask: what is the evidence base, and is it more than manufacturer-sponsored case series? Is the technique
within my competence or would it require formal training and mentoring? Is the manufacturer stable and
will components be available in ten years — the FGDP standards require me to satisfy myself of that. What are
the failure modes, and can I manage them? And can I explain it honestly to a patient, including how well
documented it is? If a technique is only ‘clinically insuﬀiciently documented’ on the ITI grading, I would say so
to the patient rather than present it as established.”

Q
Final question — what does good governance actually achieve for the patient?
“It converts good intentions into reliable care. The consent discussion happens because the proforma prompts it;
the baseline radiograph exists because the system requires it; the peri-implantitis is caught at the mucositis stage
because the recall interval is risk-based and probing is routine. Almost every serious implant complication I
have described in this examination is either preventable or detectable early by a system rather than by an
individual remembering. That is what governance is for.”
Running this case to time
Time check. This case is written in the older format — ten long answers, about 972 words. At 140 words a
minute that is seven minutes, and ten questions at five seconds each adds fifty seconds: call it just under
eight minutes. It does not overrun; it leaves seven minutes unaccounted for. Read that the right way
round — the printed answers are far longer than anything said out loud, and each is really three to seven
short questions: the quality improvement project alone is seven — problem, standard, method, finding,
change, re-audit, reflection — asked in exactly that order. If your answers run past thirty seconds you
will never reach Domain 4. And this is the one case that must be prepared rather than improvised: the
project is an entry condition, and the examiner knows you have one.

Clock
The examiner does
What earns the mark
1:20–4:30
Domain 1: what governance is, and how
you know your work is any good — two
printed answers that become nine
Expect the strands to be taken one at a
time — what does risk management mean in
your practice? — so have a concrete
example for each rather than the noun
alone. Then the better question: How do
you know whether your implant treatment is
any good? — the principle first: by
measuring it, not by assuming it. Then
the parameters, one per question:
survival; marginal bone level change
against a baseline taken at fitting;
peri-implant health — probing,
bleeding, suppuration; prosthetic
complications — screw loosening,
ceramic fracture, component
replacement; early failure rate;
patient-reported outcomes, on a
validated measure such as OHIP-14.
Then the sentence that ties the domain
together: without a baseline radiograph
and a recall system none of that can be
measured — which is why those two
are foundational.

Clock
The examiner does
What earns the mark
4:30–7:30
Domain 2: the audit cycle, in your own
project — three printed answers that
become eleven
The heart of the case, examined as a cycle,
one stage per question. The problem? —
on maintenance visits I could not
always find a baseline radiograph or a
recorded insertion torque, making it
impossible to apply the 2017 diagnostic
criteria for peri-implantitis. The standard,
and its source? — 100% of cases to have a
contemporaneous surgical record —
system, diameter, length, lot number,
insertion torque — and a standardised
baseline periapical at fitting with a
written report and recorded bone levels
— drawn from the FGDP training
standards, GDC Standards on record
keeping, and the 2017 World Workshop
case definitions. Method and sample? — a
retrospective review of 30 consecutive
implant cases over 18 months, against a
data collection sheet. The findings? —
the numbers, exactly: surgical records
complete in 63%; insertion torque in
40%; a baseline radiograph in 77%, but
bone level measurements in only 13%.
The change? — a surgical proforma and a
fitting proforma in the practice
software, with the baseline radiograph
and its measurements as mandatory
fields, and the team briefed. The
re-audit? — at 6 months, 28 consecutive
cases: record completeness 100%,
insertion torque 100%, baseline
radiograph with measurements 96%.
The reflection? — the insight that lifts the
mark: the omissions were not
knowledge failures but system failures,
and the fix was structural rather than
educational — with the dividend, I can
now diagnose peri-implant disease
against comparators. Why is re-audit
essential? — without it there is data
collection but no improvement; closing
the loop is what distinguishes audit
from a survey, and it is the part most
often omitted. Three other topics? — each
with its standard: radiographic
justification and reporting, against
100% under IR(ME)R; consent
documentation — a contemporaneous
note of the discussion, not merely a
signed form, with the risks material to
that patient; antibiotic prescribing — a
recorded indication, against SDCEP
and stewardship standards.
