The examiner does
What earns the mark
7:30–11:30
Domain 3: the systems, and the adverse
event — two printed answers that
become eleven
What systems assure quality in your surgical
practice? — seven, each with its standard
or its record: decontamination
compliant with HTM 01-05, validated
cycles, retained records, periodic
testing; emergency drugs and oxygen
checked and in date, with annual
whole-team emergency and immediate
life support training; radiography
quality assurance — image quality
rating, analysis of repeats, equipment
testing, dose audit; device traceability
— implant, graft and membrane lot
numbers recorded, a patient implant
card issued; torque wrench calibration
at the manufacturer’s intervals, with a
record; surgical safety checks — patient,
site, consent, implant availability
including back-up sizes, allergies,
instrument and swab counts; structured
recall at risk-based intervals. How do
you handle an adverse event? — in
sequence, because the sequence is the
answer: duty of candour first — tell the
patient promptly, apologise, explain,
record it; notify my indemnity provider
early; significant event analysis with
the team — what happened, why, what
went well, what should change, who
implements it, a review date; and where
a systemic change results, audit it to
confirm it has worked — the same loop,
closed in a different context.

Clock
The examiner does
What earns the mark
11:30–14:30
Domain 4: currency, new techniques,
and what it is all for — three printed
answers that become nine
How do you keep your knowledge current? —
verifiable CPD with written reflection,
as the entry requirements specify — at
least 30 hours of implant-related CPD
with reflection in the preceding 18
months; structured reading of the
primary literature and the ITI
Treatment Guides, not courses alone; a
mentor for cases at the edge of my
experience; peer review; and the honest
one — the most useful learning comes
from reviewing my own outcomes,
including the failures. How do you decide
whether to add a new technique? — anchor
it in GDC Principle 7.1, then five
questions of the technique: is the
evidence more than
manufacturer-sponsored case series?; is
it within my competence, or does it
need formal training and mentoring?; is
the manufacturer stable, and will
components be available in ten years —
the FGDP standards require me to
satisfy myself of that; what are the
failure modes, and can I manage them?;
can I explain it honestly, including how
well documented it is — saying so if it
is only “clinically insuﬀiciently
documented” on the ITI grading, rather
than presenting it as established? What
does good governance achieve for the patient?
— it converts good intentions into
reliable care: the consent discussion
happens because the proforma prompts
it, the baseline radiograph exists
because the system requires it, the
peri-implantitis is caught at the
mucositis stage because the recall is
risk-based — then finish on almost
every serious implant complication is
either preventable or detectable early
by a system rather than by an
individual remembering.
14:30–15:00
Closes on the patient and on what
changed as a result
The patient is not in the room here, so
put her there. What you say to the
patient the audit changed: “When we fit
your crown I’ll take a radiograph and
measure the bone level, and that goes in your
notes as the starting point. Every time you
come back I’ll measure it again against that.
It means if anything starts to go wrong
around the implant, I’ll see it while it’s still
gum inflammation and easy to treat, rather
than years later when there’s bone missing.”
What you write, and what changed as a
result: the completed audit cycle with
its dates, standard, sample, findings,
change and re-audit figures; the
proformas now mandatory in the
software; the team briefing and who
owns the change; the re-audit date
already set; and — the point of the
exercise — that the 13% of records
carrying a measurable baseline is now
96%, so peri-implant disease here is
diagnosed against a comparator rather
than guessed at.
The spine — the twelve answers to have ready if nothing else
1 Governance defined, and its strands named · 2 Measure it, don’t assume it: survival, bone level change,
peri-implant health, prosthetic complications, early failures, PROMs · 3 A baseline radiograph and a recall
system are foundational · 4 Your project’s problem, in one sentence · 5 The standard, and its three sources

· 6 The sample — 30 consecutive cases over 18 months · 7 The findings, with the actual percentages · 8
The change — proformas with mandatory fields, and the team briefed · 9 The re-audit figures, and why
closing the loop is the point · 10 Three further audit topics, each with its standard · 11 The systems: HTM
01-05, emergencies, radiography QA, traceability, torque calibration, safety checks, risk-based recall · 12
Candour, indemnity, significant event analysis, then audit the change.
Where the marks are lost in this case
Improvising a project you were required to have finished. This case is entirely foreseeable — a completed
quality improvement project is an entry condition — and it is asked for by its stages. A candidate who
describes a vague “look at my records” exercise, or who cannot give the standard, the sample size, the
percentages before and after, and the re-audit date, has failed the domain in the one case where prepara-
tion is guaranteed to pay. Know your own numbers, and know where your standard came from — FGDP
training standards, GDC Standards on record keeping, the 2017 World Workshop case definitions —
because “best practice” is not a standard.
Stopping before the loop closes. The commonest omission is the second half: without re-audit there
is data collection but no improvement — closing the loop is what distinguishes audit from a survey.
Do not stop at the numbers either: volunteer the reflection that shows you understood your own result —
the omissions were not knowledge failures but system failures, and the fix was structural rather than
educational — and apply the same reflex to adverse events, where a systemic change is followed by an
audit to confirm it has worked.
Treating governance as paperwork rather than as competence. The competence line here is not a referral
threshold but GDC Principle 7 — working within your competence — drawn explicitly when a new
technique is offered: is the evidence more than manufacturer-sponsored case series; is it within my
competence or does it need formal training and mentoring; will the components still exist in ten years;
can I manage its failure modes; and can I say honestly that a technique is only “clinically insuﬀiciently
documented” on the ITI grading? Then close where the case closes — on the patient: almost every
serious implant complication is either preventable or detectable early by a system rather than by an
individual remembering, and the audit’s real product is a measurable baseline in 96% of records where
it existed in 13%.

soe.title: The lawyer: replacement of the 21, six weeks
soe.text:
SOE Case 51 — The lawyer: replacement of the 21, six weeks
after extraction
THE CASE
44-year-old solicitor. The 21 was extracted six weeks ago because of a failed root canal treatment with a per-
sistent apical infection; it had been root-treated twice and had a post crown. He is currently wearing a spoon
denture, which he dislikes and says “clicks when I speak in court”. Medical history clear; non-smoker; regular
attender; good oral hygiene. Medium smile line. The adjacent 11 and 22 are unrestored and vital. The ridge
is healing but there is a visible buccal concavity. He wants “the best long-term solution” and asks specifically
what the risks are and what happens if it fails.
Domain 1 — Clinical interpretation and reasoning
Q
Summarise this case.
“A 44-year-old solicitor, six weeks after extraction of an upper central incisor for failed endodontic treatment,
wearing an interim spoon denture he finds unsatisfactory, with unrestored adjacent teeth, a medium smile line
and a buccal concavity in a healing ridge. He is articulate, engaged and asking directly about risk and about
failure. Three things stand out: the timing, which places him exactly at the Type 2 early placement window;
the spoon denture, which may be loading the healing site; and his occupation, which tells me that the consent
discussion and my records need to be exemplary.”
Q
Why does his occupation matter clinically?
“Two reasons, and both are legitimate clinical reasons rather than defensive ones. First, under Montgomery,
a risk is material if a reasonable person in this patient’s position would attach significance to it, or if I should
be aware that this particular patient would. A solicitor who speaks professionally will attach significance to
anything affecting speech and appearance in public — so a visible interim prosthesis that clicks, the aesthetic
outcome, and the treatment duration are all material to him in a way they might not be to someone else. Second,
he is asking precise questions about risk and failure, which tells me he wants to make an informed decision. That
is not a threat — it is exactly the patient I should find easiest to consent properly. I would answer fully, give
written information, allow a cooling-off period, and record the discussion contemporaneously in detail — not
because he is a lawyer, but because that is the standard for everyone and he has made it easy to demonstrate.”
Q
What do you make of the spoon denture?
“It is doing three things I would want to change. It is unretentive — that is inherent to the design, since it relies
on the palatal vault with no clasps — which explains the clicking in speech and is why he dislikes it. It has
palatal coverage, which affects speech and taste. And most importantly, it may be pressing on the healing
ridge. Pressure on a healing extraction site or a graft causes soft tissue trauma and, if a graft is present, can
cause dehiscence. I would check it with pressure-indicating paste, relieve it generously, and consider replacing
it. My preferred interim option here is a resin-bonded cantilever bridge or a bonded pontic, because it is fixed,
it does not click, the aesthetics are far better, and — decisively — it applies no load to the healing ridge. An
Essix retainer with a pontic is the quick alternative, but he cannot wear it while eating and it would not solve
the speech problem.”
Q
What else do you need to know and examine?
“History: why the endodontic treatment failed — a vertical root fracture, a missed canal, a perforation, or
persistent apical periodontitis; whether the extraction was atraumatic and whether ridge preservation was
performed; whether there was a flap; and whether he had any post-operative infection.
Examination: smile line at full smile and in speech, since he speaks professionally; lip dynamics; the soft tissue
phenotype; papilla heights and the interproximal bone levels on the 11 and 22, which determine the papillae
and which I cannot recreate; the ridge width and the extent of the buccal concavity; keratinised tissue; the shade,
form and translucency of the 11 and 22; the occlusion, particularly overbite, overjet and protrusive contacts; and
sensibility testing of the adjacent teeth, since they were adjacent to a chronic apical infection.
Investigations: standardised photographs; mounted study casts and a diagnostic wax-up; a periapical of the
site and the adjacent teeth; and a small field-of-view CBCT, justified because I need the ridge width, the extent

of the buccal concavity and the position of the incisive canal, and those will determine whether augmentation
is needed and whether the case is within my competence.
Risk assessment: I would complete an ITI Aesthetic Risk Assessment and share it with him.”
Domain 2 — Clinical decision making and treatment planning
Q
What are the options?
“I would give him all of them, including no treatment.
No treatment / continue with the removable prosthesis — he has rejected this in practice, but it must be
offered.
A new, better interim removable prosthesis — an Essix or an improved acrylic partial. Interim only.
Resin-bonded cantilever bridge from the 11 — minimally invasive, no surgery, excellent published survival
for a single anterior unit, and it preserves every future option. Its weakness here is that a pontic over a concave
ridge may look poor unless the ridge contour is augmented; a connective tissue graft under an ovate pontic
addresses that and is more predictable than augmenting around an implant.
Conventional bridge from the 11 and 22 — I would advise against it: both are unrestored and vital, and
preparing two sound anterior teeth in a 44-year-old is a substantial and irreversible biological cost.
Implant-retained crown — preserves the adjacent teeth, best long-term function, and the option he is most
likely expecting. It requires management of the buccal concavity.
Orthodontic space closure — not realistic for a central incisor.”
Q
What would you recommend, and what is the timing?
“An implant, provided the site allows the implant to be placed in the correct prosthetic position — with the
resin-bonded bridge presented as a genuine alternative rather than a consolation. On timing, six weeks post-
extraction places him in the Type 2 window — early placement with soft tissue healing, four to eight weeks.
That is often the ideal compromise in the aesthetic zone: the soft tissue has healed and can be advanced for
tension-free closure, any residual infection has resolved, but the major phase of ridge resorption — about two-
thirds of the horizontal loss occurs in the first three months — has not yet completed. The decision at surgery
is whether I can achieve the correct three-dimensional position with at least 2 mm of buccal bone, using
simultaneous contour guided bone regeneration. If I can, I place now and graft simultaneously, submerged. If
the concavity means I cannot achieve position or primary stability, I stop and stage — graft first, place at six to
nine months. Placing an implant where the bone allows rather than where the crown needs it is the commonest
cause of an unrecoverable aesthetic failure, and I would rather abandon and stage than compromise the position.
I would consent him for both possibilities in advance, so that a staged approach is a planned contingency rather
than a disappointment.”
Q
SAC classification?
“Surgically Advanced, potentially Complex: aesthetic zone, a buccal concavity requiring simultaneous or
staged augmentation, and a post-infection site. Prosthodontically Advanced: a single central incisor between
two unrestored, vital adjacent teeth, in a patient with high expectations and a medium smile line.
The
modifying factors that raise it are his aesthetic expectations and the bone deficiency. If his smile line proved
high, or if a vertical component to the defect emerged, it would move to Complex and I would refer or
co-manage — and I would say so to him at the outset rather than discovering it mid-treatment.”
Q
He asks you directly: “What are the risks, and what happens if it fails?” Answer him.
“ ’Let me take those separately, and I’ll give you all of this in writing as well.
The risks during and just after surgery are pain, swelling, bruising, bleeding and infection — all common and
manageable. Because this is your upper jaw, there is no significant nerve risk. There is a small risk of damage
to the roots of the teeth either side, which I minimise by planning from a scan and using a guide.
The risk that it does not attach to the bone is around two to five in a hundred. That usually shows up in the
first few weeks.
The risks specific to the front of the mouth are the ones I would want you to weigh most carefully. The gum
can shrink back over the years, which can show as a longer tooth or a grey line at the margin. There may be a
small dark triangle between the new tooth and its neighbour — that depends on the bone level on your own
teeth either side, which I can measure but cannot change. And the appearance can drift over ten or twenty years
as your gums and face change, even if it looks perfect on the day.

There is also a risk in the other direction: that when I open the site, the bone at the front is too thin to put the
implant exactly where the tooth needs to be. If that happens I will stop, rebuild the bone, and place the implant
six to nine months later. I would rather do that than put it in the wrong place.
If it fails — and I mean if the implant itself is lost — I would remove it, let the site heal for two to three months,
rebuild the bone if needed, and we would decide together whether to try again or to use a bonded bridge instead.
I have to be honest that a second implant in the same site has a somewhat higher risk of failing than the first.
Here is what that would cost and what is included in my original fee.
And the alternative that carries none of the surgical risk is a bonded bridge from the tooth next door, which
in a site like yours can look extremely good, particularly if we build the gum contour underneath it. It is not a
second-best option; it is a different set of trade-offs.’
Then I would give him written information, ask him to take it away, and ask him to tell me back in his own
words what we have agreed and what could go wrong, so I can be sure I have explained it clearly. And I would
record all of that.”
Domain 3 — Decision making in relation to treatment procedures
Q
Take me through the surgery.
“Restoratively driven throughout. I start from the diagnostic wax-up of the 21, duplicated into a surgical guide,
and I would use a CBCT-planned tooth-supported guide.
Flap: a palatally displaced crestal incision over the edentulous site, with papilla-sparing intrasulcular exten-
sions to the 11 and 22 to protect the papillae, and a single vertical relieving incision at the mesial line angle
of the 23, away from where the graft and membrane will sit. Full-thickness, atraumatic elevation with a sharp
periosteal elevator working against bone, retracting on bone and never crushing the flap margin, keeping the
flap moist.
Position: the shoulder about 3 mm apical to the planned mid-facial gingival margin, 1 to 2 mm palatal to the
point of emergence of the adjacent teeth, at least 1.5 mm from each adjacent root, angled so the screw channel
emerges through the cingulum.
Preparation: graded drilling with copious sterile saline, intermittent pressure, sharp drills, direction indicator
checked mesiodistally and buccolingually. Bone here is likely D3, so I would under-prepare to raise primary
stability. I would aim for 25 to 45 Ncm.
Augmentation: I expect a buccal dehiscence over the concavity. I would decorticate the buccal plate, place
autogenous chips collected from the osteotomy directly against the implant surface, layer a deproteinised
bovine bone mineral over it for volume stability, and cover with a native collagen membrane extending 2 to 3
mm onto sound bone.
Closure: a periosteal releasing incision for tension-free primary closure, tested by checking the flap passively
reaches beyond the closure line. Two-stage submerged healing because of the membrane. 5/0 or 6/0 monofil-
ament — horizontal mattress plus interrupted — removed at 10 to 14 days.
Interim prosthesis: a bonded pontic, not the spoon denture, so nothing presses on the graft.”
Q
And the restorative phase?
“Second stage at four to six months with a palatally displaced or roll flap to preserve and reposition keratinised
tissue, and a connective tissue graft at that point if the phenotype is thin. Then a screw-retained provisional to
develop the emergence profile over 8 to 12 weeks, adjusted incrementally, with a concave subgingival contour.
Then a customised impression coping copying the provisional’s subgingival form, an implant-level impression,
and a definitive screw-retained restoration on a titanium base with a milled ceramic superstructure. Shade
taken early with photographs and a stump shade, ideally with the technician present. Occlusion: light contact
in intercuspation, no contact in protrusion or excursion — the canines guide.”
Domain 4 — Interpretation and problem solving of clinical outcomes
Q
How will you know whether it has succeeded?
“Against parameters, and against what he told me at the start. Standardised photographs at every stage, com-
pared with the contralateral 11; the mid-facial mucosal margin level and papilla index measured against the 11
and 22; peri-implant probing, bleeding and suppuration; marginal bone level against the baseline periapical
taken at fitting; and his own rating of the appearance and of speech. Reviews at 1 week, 2 weeks, second stage,
provisional adjustments, fitting, 3 months, 12 months, then risk-based maintenance.”

Q
At two years he has 1 mm of mid-facial recession. What do you do?
“Diagnose the cause first — is there inflammation, is the phenotype thin, is the implant too buccal, has the
abutment been repeatedly disconnected? Then the options are: treat any inflammation; change the abutment
to a ceramic or Ti-base-plus-ceramic to remove any greyness; a connective tissue graft to thicken the tissue,
which is more reliable at arresting further recession than at achieving coverage; prosthetic recontouring with
cervical pink ceramic; or, if the implant is fundamentally malpositioned, explantation and reconstruction. I
would be honest that soft tissue procedures around an established implant are less predictable than around
teeth, and I would use the photographs from the start to discuss it objectively. And I would have warned him
at consent that this could happen, which is why the consent record matters.”
Q
What would you record throughout?
“Everything, contemporaneously: his expectations in his own words; the options presented including no treat-
ment and the bonded bridge; the risks discussed, specifically identifying the ones material to him as someone
who speaks professionally; the written information given and the cooling-off period; his questions and my an-
swers; the aesthetic risk assessment; the surgical record with implant system, diameter, length, lot number and
insertion torque; the graft and membrane with lot numbers; the abutment, torque value and occlusal scheme;
the baseline radiograph and its measurements; and the maintenance plan, with his implant record card. If a
complication arises, I would apply duty of candour — tell him promptly, apologise, explain, and put right what
I can.”
Running this case to time
Time check. This is the outlier of the set — thirteen questions, about 2,298 words, roughly two and a half
times the length of its neighbours. At 140 words a minute that is sixteen and a half minutes, and thirteen
questions at five seconds each adds just over a minute: call it seventeen and a half minutes. Read out
in full it overruns by about two and a half minutes — the only case in this group that does. But it is not
too long: it is already close to rapid-fire, and the printed answers still exceed what would be said aloud.
What an examiner drops is predictable — the suturing detail, the risk answer delivered as a monologue,
and the second half of the restorative sequence. What an examiner never drops is the timing decision,
the stop-and-stage contingency, and the consent record. If your answers run past thirty seconds you
will not reach Domain 4 — where the consent conversation from Domain 2 either saves you or does not.
The fifteen-minute run sheet

PART 6 • OSCE
PART 6 — OSCE: 58 PRACTICAL & PROCEDURAL STATIONS
Format reminder: 10 stations, 2 minutes reading + 5 minutes inside, 10 marks each, checklist-marked,
equal weighting, examiner silent unless the task requires interaction.
How to work a 5-minute station. Say what you are doing as you do it. Work in a fixed order — indication
→preparation →procedure →completion →what I would record and warn about. If you cannot complete the
physical task, keep describing. If you finish early, stay and add the post-operative advice, the records, and
the complications — those are almost always unclaimed checklist marks.
Read “Where the marks are” below before you start. The 58 stations that follow cover every learning
outcome that Appendix A marks in the OS-P column, together with the practical skills listed in the FGDP
training standards. They are deliberately weighted towards restorative and prosthodontic procedure, tem-
porisation and communication, because that is where the blueprint places most of its procedural outcomes
and where candidates most often under-prepare.
Each station below gives: the RCSEd-style station brief, the candidate instruction sheet, your direction
of thought (what to do in the 2 minutes of reading), a model answer, a 10-point checklist as an examiner
would use it, and the common pitfalls.
Where the marks are in the OSCE
The OSCE is the component candidates most often misjudge. It is easy to assume that a practical examina-
tion in implant dentistry must be an examination in surgery. Read Appendix A carefully and it is clear that
this is not so: the OS-P column is spread across assessment, radiographic interpretation, prosthodontic
procedure, temporisation, communication with the dental team, post-operative care and the management
of complications, and the FGDP training standards list the same range. Six points follow, and they should
shape the way you prepare.
1. The circuit is weighted towards restorative and prosthodontic procedure, not surgery. Far more of
the procedural learning outcomes concern impressions and scans, framework and crown fit, retention
decisions, occlusal adjustment, temporisation and the handling of an existing restoration than concern
flaps, osteotomies and sutures. Know the surgical stations — flap design, site preparation, suturing and
minor augmentation all sit in the blueprint and can appear — but do not let them consume your revision.
If you can describe an osteotomy sequence fluently but cannot explain what you would do when a
metal framework does not seat, you have prepared the wrong half of this component.
2. Several stations are conversations, not silent tasks. The published sample station in Appendix D
states that no interaction with the examiner is required, and that is true of some stations — but not of all.
A station may ask you to discuss management, or to talk to a role-player representing a dental technician,
a colleague or a patient. Prepare to talk to a member of the team, not only to perform in front of an observer.
Rehearse saying what you want from the laboratory in the words you would actually use on a prescription.
2a. Expect to be handed the findings and questioned on them, rather than asked to obtain them. This is
the single most common way a “clinical skill” station is actually run, and candidates prepare for the wrong
version of it. You may be shown a completed BPE chart, a set of probing depths, a radiographic report
or a laboratory work ticket and then asked, in quick succession: what does this tell you, what does each
figure mean, what does it oblige you to do, what instrument produced it, describe that instrument, what
force did you use, how do you know it was the right force. Everything you would ordinarily do with
your hands then has to be said accurately out loud — the millimetre markings on a probe, the diameter
of its ball tip, the force in grams or newtons, the calibration trick you use to judge it, the sequence of sites.
That is a harder test than performing the task, not an easier one, because vague description is immediately
visible where competent hands are not. For every instrument in your working week, be able to say what
it is called, what is marked on it, how hard you press, and why.
3. Information may be released during a station, not all at the start. A station may hand you an additional
piece of written information partway through — a radiographic finding, a result, a change in the history.
This is deliberate, and it tests whether you can revise a differential when new data arrives. When it
happens, say out loud what it changes: “That changes my differential — with no bone loss, this is far more
likely to be residual cement, a foreign body or a problem with the adjacent tooth than peri-implantitis.” Silence loses
the mark; narration earns it.

PART 6 • OSCE
4. Basic clinical skills are examined, and they are where marks are quietly lost. A station built on
something you have done thousands of times — a BPE, a six-point chart, oral hygiene instruction, post-
operative instructions — is not a gift. It is a station where full marks are available and expected, and
where candidates lose them by working fast, silently and imprecisely. The examiner is marking a checklist
that includes the instrument, the force, the sequence, the codes and what each finding obliges you to do
next. Slow down and say the numbers.
5. Temporisation is a named topic and is chronically under-revised. The interim prosthesis over a graft,
the provisional that shapes an emergence profile, and the thing the patient wears for the nine months in
between all sit squarely in the blueprint. Be able to describe, compare and justify a resin-bonded bridge,
a spoon denture, an Essix retainer, an immediate partial denture and a screw-retained provisional —
indications, advantages, disadvantages, and the effect of each on a healing site.
6. The stations are drawn from ordinary practice, not from the literature. Everything in this component
is something a general dentist with an interest in implants does, or should do, in a normal working week.
That is the level. If your answer needs a systematic review to justify it, you are pitching too high; if it
does not include what you would record and what you would tell the patient, you are pitching too low.
KEY POINT
Revision priority for the OSCE, in order: temporisation and provisionals →prosthetic retention decisions and
communication with the technician →framework and restoration fit and how you verify it →post-operative
care →periodontal and peri-implant assessment →radiographic interpretation and its effect on the replace-
ment plan →complications of existing implant restorations →then the surgical stations.
How to work a station
Minute
What to do
Reading time
Read the instruction twice. Identify the verb — carry out,
describe, discuss, explain to the patient. That verb tells you who
you are talking to and what will be marked.
First 30 seconds
State your framework aloud before you start doing anything: “I
will check the medical history and consent, then work through X, Y
and Z, and finish with what I would record and review.”
Body of the station
Narrate everything. Say the instrument, the force, the material,
the reason. An examiner cannot award a mark for something
you did silently.
If new information is given
Stop, read it, and say explicitly what it changes.
Last 30 seconds
Close with records, patient instructions and review — three
marks that sit at the end of almost every checklist and are
routinely left unclaimed when candidates run out of time.
How the five minutes is actually spent, and how to use the run sheets
The station model answers in this part are written to be complete, so that you can revise from them. They
are not written to be said — several of them run to seven or eight minutes of unbroken speech, and you
have five. That gap is where marks are lost, and closing it is a separate skill from knowing the material.
So every station in this part carries its own run sheet, printed immediately after the model answer and
the checklist. Each one has the same four parts:
Running this station to time. How long the model answer actually takes at speaking pace, how much of
it has to go, and — specifically for that station — how it goes.
The five-minute run sheet. A minute-by-minute table: what the examiner is doing in each block, and
which checklist points must have been spoken by the time that block ends.
The compressed answer. What a strong candidate actually delivers inside the five minutes — the same
content as the model answer, in about a third of the words, ordered for the clock. This is the artefact you
rehearse.
Marking priority when the clock beats the candidate. The six points that carry the station, the four an
examiner will accept late or on prompting, and the commonest way five minutes is wasted at that particular
station.

PART 7 — STRUCTURED ORAL EXAMINATION: 51 CLINICAL
SCENARIOS
Read the three set-pieces first. They precede the cases and cover the technical ground that recurs in almost
every scenario: placement timing and loading protocol; bone grafting materials with their advantages,
disadvantages and complications; and incision and flap design. The 51 cases that follow include RCSEd’s
own published sample case (Appendix E), worked in full, and cover the breadth of the blueprint. Each
is structured across the four marked domains with a full examiner question flow — enough material to
sustain the 15 minutes.

5 marks each = 20 marks per examiner per case, pass = mean of 3 across all domains and cases.

PART 7 • SOE
Where the marks are in the SOE
The structured oral examination is not a viva about implant dentistry in general. It is a structured assess-
ment of whether you reason safely about a specific patient, across four declared domains, at the level of
a general dentist with an interest in implants. Seven observations about how cases at this level are built
should shape your preparation.
1. Expect single-tooth and small-span problems, not full-arch reconstruction. Full-arch and complex
reconstructive work is explicitly outside the scope of this Membership. The examinable material is the set
of decisions a general dentist makes about one tooth, one site, one existing implant. Prepare depth on
the single unit rather than breadth on the complex case.
2. Expect cases where something has already gone wrong. A large proportion of realistic scenarios
present after treatment — a malpositioned implant placed by someone else, recession and metal show-
through, a deeply placed fixture, a failing restoration, peri-implant disease. These test whether you can
diagnose a failure, identify its cause, decide whether the situation is retrievable, and have an honest
conversation about it. That is a different skill from planning a virgin case, and it is examined at least as
often.
3. If an occupation is given, it is not decoration. A patient described as a lawyer, a teacher, a musician or
someone working in the entertainment industry is there to test Montgomery: materiality of risk is judged
from the position of this patient. Build the consent discussion around the occupation explicitly — what
this particular person needs to know, and why a risk that is immaterial to one patient is material to another.
4. The medical history is either the pivot of the case or deliberately clear. When a complex history
is given — antiresorptives, radiotherapy, poorly controlled diabetes, anticoagulation — that is the case.
When you are told the medical history is clear, that escape route has been closed deliberately, and the
examiners want your local, occlusal and prosthetic reasoning instead. Notice which kind of case you are
in.
5. Occlusion is examined in its own right. Occlusion, interocclusal space and parafunction appear re-
peatedly across the blueprint and are routinely under-prepared. You must be able to describe an occlusal
examination, name and justify an occlusal scheme, explain implant-protective occlusion and its biological
basis, and manage a bruxist prosthodontically — including what you would say to him about prognosis.
6. Periodontal disease is examined in its own right. Be fluent in the 2017 staging and grading, the EFP
stepwise approach and its stability criteria, and the relationship between a history of periodontitis and
peri-implantitis. A failing periodontal dentition is a legitimate implant case, and the examinable question
is usually whether, when and on what conditions — not which implant.
7. Interim prostheses are part of the case data. If you are told what the patient is wearing while the site
heals, you are expected to comment on it: what it is doing to the healing tissues, whether it is the right
choice, and what you would change. The same applies to anything else stated in passing — a smile line,
an attendance pattern, a stated expectation.
KEY POINT
Preparation priority for the SOE, in order: the single missing anterior tooth in a demanding patient →the
failing or malpositioned existing implant →occlusion and parafunction →the periodontally compromised
dentition →the edentulous and overdenture patient →the medically complex patient →everything else.
How the fifteen minutes is spent, and what the examiner is holding
The cases in this part are written to be worked from, so each carries more questions than any single oral
will use. This short section is the other half of that: how the time is actually divided, what the examiner
is looking at while you speak, and how to rehearse a case against the clock rather than reading it.
Every case in this part then carries its own run sheet, printed after the question flow: a time check
that says plainly whether the printed material fits fifteen minutes; a clock table setting the four domains
against the minutes they are actually given; the spine — the twelve answers to have ready if the case had
to be run in half the time; and where the marks are lost in that particular case. Rehearse from those, not
from the full flow.

The single most useful number in that table is thirty to forty questions. It tells you that the unit of currency
is a short answer, not a discourse — an answer of ninety seconds costs you three questions you will never
be asked, and each of those was a mark you might have had. If you have said your point, stop talking.
The four domains, and how a case moves through them
An examiner works the case across the four published domains, and each of the cases in this part is laid
out in the same order so that you can rehearse the transitions:
Domain 1 — clinical interpretation and reasoning. Nearly always opens with groundwork below the
implant material: surface anatomy, denture principles, occlusal schemes, periodontal staging, healing
biology, reading the images. Candidates who have revised only implantology are caught here.
Domain 2 — clinical decision making and treatment planning. The options, the argument between them,
the SAC classification, and the point at which you refer.
Domain 3 — decision making in relation to treatment procedures. How you would actually do it, in
sequence, with the specific numbers and materials.
Domain 4 — interpretation and problem solving of clinical outcomes. What goes wrong, how often,
how you would detect it, how you would prevent it, what you would record and what you would tell the
patient.
Each domain carries five marks, marked independently; the descriptors and the difference between a 3
and a 5 are set out in §1.6. The practical consequence is that a case is not one performance but four, and a
weak Domain 4 cannot be rescued by a strong Domain 1. If you notice that ten minutes have gone and
nobody has asked you about complications, expect them now and have the prevalence figures ready.
How to rehearse a case properly
KEY POINT
Work a case out loud, timed, with a colleague holding the page. Give them these instructions: let me open for
sixty seconds without interrupting; then ask questions from the flow as fast as I answer them; move me on as soon as I have
made the point; and mark down every time you had to prompt me. Then compare the number of prompts against the
descriptors — a prompted answer is a pass, an unprompted one is a good mark, and the count of prompts is the
most honest feedback available to you before the day.
Three things to watch for in your own rehearsal, in order of how often they cost marks:
Not volunteering the risk. The competent-sounding answer that never mentions what could go wrong is
a 3 at best.
Not stopping at the competence line. Every case in this part contains a point beyond which the right

THREE SET-PIECE ANSWERS TO PREPARE BEFORE ANY CASE

• “When would you place the implant, and when would you load it?”
• “What would you graft with, and why that material?”
• “Describe the flap you would raise.”

Type 1 — immediate. Advantages: fewest surgical episodes; shortest overall treatment time; the socket

the drill skids off the palatal wall so ideal position is harder to achieve; primary stability is less predictable;
it does not prevent resorption of the buccal bundle bone, which is ligament-dependent and disappears
with the tooth; the highest aesthetic complication rate; technique-sensitive. Absolute pre-requisites: no acute
infection with suppuration, intact socket walls with a facial wall of at least 1 mm, suﬀicient apical and
palatal bone for primary stability, the socket within the alveolar bone envelope, and a horizontal “jumping”
gap of at least 2 mm at the implant shoulder which is grafted with a slowly resorbing xenograft.

tension-free primary closure over a simultaneous graft is achievable; any infection has resolved and can
be assessed; a substantial proportion of the ridge is still present because most of the horizontal resorption

Type 3 — early with partial bone healing. Advantages: more bone in the socket, so better primary stability
and less need for grafting than Type 2; useful in large or multi-rooted sockets. Disadvantages: more ridge
resorption has occurred, particularly buccally; longer for the patient.
Type 4 — late. Advantages: a fully healed, predictable site; the best-documented protocol; no compromise
from residual infection; simple surgery. Disadvantages: maximum ridge resorption — roughly 50% of the
width is lost by 12 months, of which about two-thirds occurs in the first three months, so augmentation
is frequently required; the longest treatment time; the patient wears an interim prosthesis throughout.
The examiner’s favourite trap. “Why not place immediately, it saves time?” The scoring answer names the
pre-requisites and then says: “Immediate placement does not preserve the buccal plate. The bundle bone is dependent
on the periodontal ligament and resorbs whatever I do. What immediate placement saves is time and surgical episodes —
it does not save bone, and it costs me control of the three-dimensional position, which in the aesthetic zone is the thing I am
least willing to lose.”

The biological basis, which you should be able to give in one sentence:
“The threshold is micromotion. Above roughly 50 to 150 micrometres at the interface, fibrous repair replaces bone formation,
so every criterion for immediate loading — the torque, the ISQ, the absence of occlusal contact, the absence of parafunction
— exists to keep micromotion below that threshold during the vulnerable period.”
And the vulnerable period itself:
“Total stability is primary mechanical stability plus secondary biological stability. Primary stability falls as the bone at the
interface remodels, and secondary stability rises as new bone forms. The trough is at about two to four weeks, which is
why an implant that felt solid at placement can be mobile at three weeks, and why early loading protocols must be selected
rather than assumed.”

1.5 Delivering it in the SOE
When asked “when would you place and load this implant?”, answer in this order and you cannot go wrong:
1. Separate the two decisions in one sentence.
2. State the placement type with its number and its timing, and say what in this case determines it —
socket integrity, buccal wall thickness, infection, phenotype, aesthetic risk.
3. State the loading protocol, and check the criteria out loud against this patient — torque, ISQ, occlusion,
parafunction, bone quality.
4. Grade it against the ITI evidence table.
5. State your fallback — what you would do if the intra-operative findings differ from the plan.
Model sentence. “I would plan a Type 2, early placement at six to eight weeks, because the buccal wall is under 1
mm so immediate placement is excluded by the decision tree, and the soft tissue will have healed enough for tension-free
closure over a simultaneous graft. I would use conventional loading beyond two months, which is Type 2–3C and
scientifically and clinically validated — early or immediate loading here would be Type 2–3B or A, which are clinically
insuﬀiciently documented. My fallback is that if at surgery I cannot achieve the correct three-dimensional position with at
least 2 mm of buccal bone, I stop, graft, and place at six to nine months.”
1.6 The follow-up questions examiners actually ask
“What is the difference between immediate restoration and immediate loading?” — Occlusal contact.
Restoration is out of occlusion; loading is in occlusion. Both are within one week.
“You said 35 Ncm. What if you get 25?” — I would not restore immediately. I would place a healing
abutment or submerge, and load conventionally, confirming stability with resonance frequency analysis
before restoring, and looking for a rising rather than falling ISQ trend.
“Why can’t you load an implant in D4 bone immediately?” — Because primary stability depends on
mechanical interlock with the bone, and D4 has a thin cortex over sparse trabeculae, giving the lowest
insertion torque and the least resistance to micromotion. It is the bone type with the highest failure rate,
and immediate loading would exceed the micromotion threshold.
“What is progressive loading?” — A Misch concept: in soft bone, occlusal load is increased gradually,
through a provisional in acrylic kept out of or in light occlusion and then in progressively firmer contact
over weeks, to allow the bone to mature and remodel before full function. I would say I know the concept
and that the evidence supporting it is modest.

“When would you use a two-stage rather than a one-stage protocol?” — Where a membrane or graft
must be protected from exposure; where primary stability is compromised; where the soft tissue is thin or
needs to be manipulated at second stage; and where the patient must wear a mucosa-borne denture over
the site.
“How long after a sinus floor elevation would you load?” — Following the ITI decision tree: with simul-
taneous placement, prosthetic loading at 3 to 6 months. Where placement is staged, implant placement 4
to 8 months after grafting with particulate autogenous bone, or 9 to 12 months with bone substitute alone,
and then loading 3 months after placement.
“The patient wants teeth on the day. What do you say?” — Explain the criteria, assess whether they are
met, grade the protocol on the evidence, and offer a well-made interim prosthesis that does not load the
site. Patient autonomy allows refusal of treatment; it does not compel me to provide a protocol that is not
in their interest.

2.1 Start with the three mechanisms
“Every graft works by one or more of three mechanisms. Osteogenesis — the graft contains living cells that
form bone, and only autogenous bone does this. Osteoinduction — the graft induces host mesenchymal
cells to differentiate into osteoblasts, mediated by bone morphogenetic proteins; autogenous bone and,
variably, demineralised allograft. Osteoconduction — the graft acts as a scaffold along which bone grows
from the host; all graft materials do this. Some authors add osteopromotion, meaning the enhancement
of regeneration without the material itself being osteoinductive — which is how a barrier membrane and,
arguably, platelet concentrates act.”

“Which material has the best evidence?” — Deproteinised bovine bone mineral is the most extensively
documented material in implant dentistry, particularly for ridge preservation, jumping gaps and contour
augmentation.

would say which of the four is most at risk in this particular case.

can reach the graft. It is the “A” of PASS.

position, denture pressure or smoking — and record it.

Set-piece 3 — Incision and flap design
3.1 Start with the principles
“I design every flap against six principles: adequate access for the whole procedure, including the graft and
the membrane, not just the implant; a base wider than the apex so the blood supply is preserved; incisions
over sound bone, not over the defect and not over the graft or membrane edge; preservation of the papillae
where aesthetics matter; a design that permits tension-free closure; and atraumatic handling throughout,
because the flap’s blood supply and the periosteum determine how the graft beneath it heals.”
The blood supply point is the one to explain if asked. A mucoperiosteal flap is perfused from its base
by supraperiosteal vessels running in an apico-coronal direction. A flap that is narrower at its base than
at its apex, or that is criss-crossed by badly placed releasing incisions, has its supply interrupted — the
consequences are marginal necrosis, dehiscence and, over a graft, loss of the graft.

PART 7 • SOE
3.3 Design by clinical situation — the answer to “what flap would you raise?”
Routine posterior placement, adequate keratinised tissue, no graft: Mid-crestal incision with short in-
trasulcular extensions; full thickness; usually no releasing incision. One-stage with a healing abutment.
Aesthetic zone, single implant with simultaneous contour GBR: Palatally displaced crestal incision,
papilla-sparing intrasulcular extensions to the adjacent teeth, one vertical relieving incision at the mesial
line angle of the tooth one further along — away from the graft. Full thickness, atraumatic. Periosteal
releasing incision for tension-free closure. Two-stage submerged.
Second stage where keratinised tissue is abundant: Tissue punch or a small crestal incision.
Second stage where keratinised tissue is scarce: Palatally displaced crestal incision with an apically
positioned split-thickness flap, to reposition the keratinised band buccally rather than excise it. Consider
a simultaneous connective tissue graft if the phenotype is thin.
Ridge preservation after extraction: Flapless. Raising a flap to close a socket sacrifices vestibular depth
and keratinised tissue and further compromises the buccal plate’s blood supply. Use a socket seal or
membrane and a figure-of-eight suture.
Peri-implantitis — resective, non-aesthetic site: Intrasulcular incisions with relieving incisions for access;
full thickness; granulation tissue removed; apically positioned flap so the decontaminated and smoothed
surface is accessible for cleaning.
Peri-implantitis — reconstructive, intrabony defect: Access flap preserving as much keratinised tissue
as possible; primary closure over the graft is the goal, so a periosteal release may be needed.
Severely atrophic mandible / near the mental foramen: Crestal incision placed slightly buccal or lingual
to the crest as the anatomy dictates, careful blunt identification and protection of the mental neurovascu-
lar bundle, and no deep periosteal releasing incision in the premolar region.
3.4 Atraumatic elevation — the exact words to use
“I incise firmly to bone in a single stroke, because repeated shallow passes shred the tissue. I elevate with a sharp
periosteal elevator working against bone, not against tissue, starting at a corner or at the vertical incision so the
periosteum lifts cleanly and completely. I retract with a broad retractor resting on bone, never crushing the flap margin,
and I handle the flap only at its base with tissue forceps. I keep the flap moist with saline-soaked gauze throughout and
I minimise the duration of retraction. When I close, I approximate without strangulating — tension causes ischaemia,
necrosis and dehiscence, which is the commonest cause of membrane exposure.”
3.5 The periosteal releasing incision — describe it safely
“I hold the blade almost parallel to the inner surface of the flap and score the periosteum horizontally at the base
of the buccal flap, through the periosteum only, then complete the release by blunt dissection. I test the release by lifting
the flap passively with tissue forceps and confirming it reaches 3 to 4 mm beyond the closure line without tension. The
risks are bleeding, perforation of the flap, and — in the mandibular premolar region — injury to the mental nerve,
so I identify the foramen first and keep the incision shallow there.”
3.6 Matching the closure to the flap
• Over a graft or membrane: horizontal or vertical mattress sutures to evert and carry the tension, with
interrupted sutures between them to adapt the margins; monofilament or ePTFE, never braided silk,
which wicks bacteria; 5/0 in the aesthetic zone, 4/0 elsewhere; removed at 10 to 14 days.
• Simple placement: interrupted 4/0 monofilament, removed at 7 to 10 days.
• Apically positioned flap: periosteal sutures to hold the flap at its new level, plus sling sutures around
teeth or healing abutments.
• Over an extraction socket with a graft: figure-of-eight or crossed mattress suture.
• Rule: pass from mobile to fixed and from thin to thick; enter perpendicular about 3 mm from the
margin; equal bites both sides; knot off the incision line.

PART 7 • SOE
3.7 Complications attributable to flap design
Wound dehiscence and membrane exposure; marginal flap necrosis from an inadequate base or a com-
promised blood supply; papilla loss from an incision through a papilla; gingival recession on adjacent
teeth from sulcular incisions in thin phenotypes; loss of vestibular depth and keratinised tissue after
coronal advancement; visible scarring from vertical incisions placed in the aesthetic zone; nerve injury
from vertical or periosteal releasing incisions near the mental foramen and from lingual incisions in the
molar region; haemorrhage; and delayed healing where the flap was crushed or allowed to dry.
3.8 Delivering it in the SOE
Model sentence. “I would use a palatally displaced crestal incision across the edentulous site with papilla-sparing
intrasulcular extensions to the adjacent teeth, and a single vertical relieving incision at the mesial line angle of the
tooth one further along, placed over sound bone and away from where the membrane will sit. Full thickness, raised
atraumatically with a sharp elevator working against bone, retracted on bone and kept moist. Because I am grafting, I
would add a periosteal releasing incision at the base of the buccal flap and test that the flap reaches passively beyond the
closure line before I place the membrane. I would close with horizontal mattress and interrupted 5/0 monofilament,
with the suture line lying over sound bone rather than over the membrane edge, and remove them at 10 to 14 days.”
3.9 The follow-up questions examiners actually ask
“Why palatally displaced?” — To carry the keratinised band buccally, where it is needed both for the
aesthetic result and to give a robust, well-vascularised closure over the graft.
“Why not simply raise a big flap for better access?” — Because every millimetre of elevation costs blood
supply, increases morbidity and swelling, and in the aesthetic zone risks papilla and marginal recession.
I raise the smallest flap that gives adequate access for the whole procedure.
“Where exactly would you place the vertical incision, and why?” — At a line angle, never through a
papilla and never at the mid-facial aspect of a tooth; extended beyond the mucogingival junction so the
flap can be advanced; diverging slightly apically so the base is wider than the apex; and positioned so that
the finished suture line lies over sound bone, away from the graft and membrane.
“When would you avoid a vertical releasing incision altogether?” — In the aesthetic zone where scarring
is a concern and access can be obtained by an envelope design; in thin phenotypes; and where the incision
would approach the mental foramen.
“What is the difference between a full- and a split-thickness flap, and when do you use each?” — Full
thickness includes the periosteum and is used whenever bone must be exposed or grafted. Split thickness
leaves the periosteum on the bone as a vascular bed, and is used when soft tissue is being repositioned or
when a graft needs a periosteal bed — a free gingival graft, a connective tissue graft recipient site, or an
apically positioned flap.
“You are grafting and cannot close without tension. What do you do?” — Perform a periosteal releasing
incision and re-test passively. If it still will not close, reduce the graft volume, reconsider whether the
augmentation is achievable, and be prepared to abandon and stage rather than close under tension —
because closure under tension will lose the graft anyway.
“How does the flap design change if you are placing flapless?” — There is no flap, so I lose visuali-
sation of the bone entirely. That means the anatomy must be certain from CBCT, the ridge width and
keratinised tissue must be ample, no grafting must be anticipated, and I must be prepared to raise a flap
intra-operatively if I find a dehiscence.

PART 7 • SOE
How to drill the three set-pieces
Work one case at a time from Part 7C. In each case, force yourself through all three:
1. “State the placement type and the loading protocol for this patient, with the criteria and the evidence grading.”
2. “State the graft material, the reason for that material, the consent points and the most likely complication.”
3. “Describe the incision, the flap, the release and the closure.”
If you can do that in three minutes for any case in this notebook, you have covered the majority of the
domain 3 marks in the structured oral examination before the examiners have asked anything case-specific.
